identification: Look for a branched plant roughly 2 to 5 feet tall with fine hairs covering the stems and both sides of the leaves. Lower leaves are deeply divided into narrow, rounded lobes; leaves higher on the stems become smaller. The yellow flower heads are tiny, about one-eighth of an inch across, rather than large, daisy-like blooms.

Common mugwort usually has greener upper leaf surfaces and broader, more pointed leaf divisions. Native Louisiana wormwood generally has narrower, lance-shaped leaves, sometimes with a few teeth near the tip, rather than absinthium's deeply divided leaves. Photograph the whole plant, a lower leaf and its underside, and any flower heads. Color alone is not enough to distinguish these plants.
actions: If you think you have found absinthium, confirm the leaf features before deciding what to remove. Keep seed-bearing plants out of places where soil, hay or garden waste will be moved. For an established patch, preventing seed production is only part of the job: repeated mowing can reduce seed production but does not reliably kill the roots. Burning is not a dependable control method and can encourage its spread.

After control work, help desirable vegetation cover the disturbed soil and check the site again in following years. Washington's weed board reports that seeds can remain viable for three to four years. In a pasture, discuss control with an agricultural adviser; this plant can be toxic to livestock. Do not use its history in drinks or herbal products as evidence that it is safe to eat.

sources.label: Missouri State University: Absinth wormwood identification
Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board: Absinth wormwood

identification: Start with the leaves near the base. They can be spoon-shaped, toothed or deeply cut into backward-pointing lobes. Higher leaves are smaller and narrower, sometimes with small arrow-shaped lobes where they meet the stem. Look at several leaves rather than expecting every leaf to have the same shape. The branching flower stems carry small, pale yellow heads, with a narrow green covering around each head. Kew's Flora of Oman treatment describes that covering as about 9 to 13 millimeters long.

Photograph the whole plant, its lowest leaves, a leaf attached to the stem, and a flower head from both the side and front. These details are more useful than a distant picture of yellow flowers. A confident comparison with similar local daisies still needs a regional botanical reference or specialist review.
actions: For a suspected sighting, record the location, date and habitat, along with close photographs of the leaves and flower heads. Include whether the plant is growing alone, in a patch or in cultivated ground. Those observations help a reviewer assess both identity and the setting in which it occurs. Avoid moving the plant or its seed heads to another site while identification is uncertain.

A photograph match alone is not a reason to clear surrounding vegetation or apply a herbicide. First confirm the plant with a regional botanist or Extension office, then discuss an approach suited to that population and its location.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online: Launaea intybacea and Flora of Oman treatment
Flora of North America treatment via University of Florida BioGator: Launaea intybacea

identification: Under magnification, look for an elongated oval animal usually around 2 to 4 millimeters long, although larger individuals have been reported. The sides curl toward the underside, producing a folded body rather than a broad, flat outline. Its color can be dark green or yellow-brown. Size, color and a curled outline together are useful clues, but they do not replace specialist identification of a tiny marine animal.

If you can document it without disturbing the habitat, include a close image with a size reference and a wider view of the seaweed or surface on which it was found. Note the location, date and water depth if known. A phone photograph may show the setting well while still leaving the species uncertain; keep that distinction in the report.
actions: Avoid moving attached seaweed or small marine organisms between shorelines, harbors or aquariums. Clean visible organisms and debris from equipment before leaving a site, drain retained water where appropriate, and let equipment dry before using it elsewhere. These are general aquatic biosecurity steps, not a tested treatment for Convoluta convoluta.

Report a suspected new occurrence with photographs and location details for review instead of attempting to treat the surrounding habitat. Do not scrape away seaweed beds or use chemicals on the basis of an uncertain identification. Research in the southern Gulf of Maine found that these animals could eat very young mussels, but estimated a limited overall effect under the conditions studied. That finding does not establish the same impact everywhere the species occurs.

sources.label: Smithsonian Environmental Research Center: Convoluta convoluta
Byrnes and Witman (2003): Impact assessment of Convoluta convoluta
US Fish and Wildlife Service: Clean, Drain, Dry

identification: Look closely along pine needles for narrow, spindle-shaped aphids about 2 to 2.5 millimeters long. They have thin legs, antennae and small dark spots on the body; some individuals develop wings. The pale coating is wax on the insect, rather than loose dust on the needle. A magnified photograph can help show the body shape and spots that are difficult to see with the naked eye.

Check both affected and apparently healthy needles, and photograph the whole branch as well as the insects. Record the type of pine if you know it. Yellowing, sticky honeydew or sooty mold can help you locate an infestation, but none identifies this aphid on its own. Identification from a general photograph of a damaged tree should remain tentative.
actions: First check whether living aphids are still present and whether fresh damage is continuing. Notice natural enemies as well: lady beetles, lacewing larvae, hoverfly larvae and tiny parasitic wasps help keep these aphids in check. NC State notes that populations can be conspicuous in winter, when their natural enemies are less active. Continued observation may be more useful than treating old needle damage after aphid numbers have fallen.

If a valuable pine continues to decline, share close photographs and the pine's identity with an extension service or qualified plant-care professional. Horticultural oils are an option in NC State's guidance when natural control is insufficient, but they can remove the bluish surface wax from some pines and change their appearance. Any product must be appropriate for that tree and used according to its label.

sources.label: NC State Extension: Powdery pine needle aphid

identification: Examine leaves for low, flattened, oval-to-triangular insects with a narrower front and a rounded rear. USDA describes adult females as pale green or yellow-green, without an obvious wax covering or a visible egg sac. Photograph the leaf surface, the insect close up and the plant as a whole. Include a size reference without moving the insect to another plant.

Kilifia americana and Kilifia deltoides are important lookalikes. Reliable separation uses tiny structures on a prepared specimen, including features of the legs and plates near the rear of the body. Those details are not usually visible in a phone photograph. Treat a visual match as a possible identification and arrange specialist confirmation when the exact species matters, especially for a nursery shipment or a new local report.
actions: If a houseplant has suspected scales, separate it from other plants while you check the leaves and nearby plants. Photograph the insects before removing affected material so that useful identification details are not lost. UC IPM advises acting early on houseplant infestations; removing a limited number of affected leaves may help when the problem is small. Avoid passing infested plants or cuttings to someone else.

For a nursery, orchard or outdoor tree, request an identification before choosing a treatment. General houseplant advice is not a verified control program for acuminate scale on every host. Keep the plant name, purchase or arrival history, location and photographs together in the report. These details distinguish a contained infestation from wider establishment.

sources.label: USDA Identification Technology Program: Kilifia acuminata
University of California IPM: Houseplant problems

identification: Look along pine twigs and stems for small patches of white wax. Under magnification, the covering may reveal eggs, young insects and rounded, reddish-brown adult females about a millimeter long. An infestation can resemble a fungal growth from a distance; seeing insects beneath the wax is an important first distinction. Photograph a complete affected branch and a close view of the colony, and record the pine species if known.

Separating Pineus boerneri from other pine adelgids requires more than these field clues. Published investigations have used carefully examined specimens to establish the identification. A photograph can support a suspected adelgid report without establishing the exact species. Do not assume a white patch on a spruce, hemlock or other conifer is this pine-associated insect.
actions: Keep a record of the affected branches and check whether fresh damage is appearing, rather than judging the tree from old needle loss alone. Avoid carrying infested pine material or moving nursery plants to a new site while identification is unresolved. Published research describes spread through wind and the movement of infested material, making careful handling relevant even when an infestation looks small.

For a declining garden tree or a nursery or plantation outbreak, send close photographs and the host identity to an extension service or forest-health specialist. Ask how to submit a sample before mailing live insects or branches. Colombian researchers investigated a locally occurring lacewing predator; that is not a recommendation to purchase or release that insect elsewhere. A treatment choice should follow a confirmed identification and an assessment of current damage.

sources.label: Oliveira and colleagues (2008): Pineus boerneri in Brazilian pine plantations
Rodas and colleagues (2015): Biology, incidence and host susceptibility in Colombian pine plantations

identification: Look for an upright or bushy plant with narrow, pointed leaves and groups of fragrant flowers near the stem tips. Typical garden forms are about 10 to 50 centimeters tall, although cultivar and growing conditions affect size. The flowers are roughly three-quarters of an inch wide, usually with four petals arranged around the center. After flowering, long seed pods develop and eventually split open.

Take photographs of a flower face, a whole flowering stem, the lower woody portion and any mature pods. Other wallflowers can share the same colors and general shape, so a yellow four-petaled flower is not enough for a reliable species determination. If a plant came from a garden, keep any cultivar or purchase information with the observation. Hybrid garden plants can be especially difficult to name from a photograph alone.
actions: For a plant growing beyond a garden, note whether it is an isolated escape or part of a patch producing seedlings. Photograph the flowers and pods before deciding whether management is needed. Where you want to prevent further self-seeding, remove developing seed pods before they open and collect the material rather than scattering it. Keep garden debris out of nearby natural areas.

A wallflower growing in masonry needs a different approach from one in a flower bed: do not pull apart old walls or disturb a protected structure to remove it. Ask the owner or site manager first. The references reviewed are botanical and horticultural accounts, not evidence that every escaped wallflower requires eradication or that this plant has the same impact in every region.

identification: Start with the low, spreading habit and narrow leaves, then examine the flowering tips. The flower clusters occur at the ends of stems and may also appear where leaves meet a stem. The mature fruit is particularly useful: it is only about 1.6 to 2 millimeters long, has a strongly wrinkled surface and does not open to release the seed in the way some other amaranths do. A hand lens or sharp macro photograph is often needed to see that texture.

Photograph a full branch, several leaves, the tip of a flowering stem and mature fruits beside a scale. General pictures of green foliage are less useful for distinguishing this plant from other amaranths. Published accounts differ in leaf dimensions and growth form; do not rule the species in or out using a single leaf measurement. A regional flora or herbarium can help resolve a doubtful specimen.
actions: Photograph the patch before disturbing it, especially if mature fruits are available for identification. Keep fruiting material contained, and avoid moving soil or garden waste from the patch to a clean site. For a few confirmed, unwanted plants, remove the root crown as well as the visible shoots where this can be done without damaging surrounding vegetation. A plant with a surviving rootstock may grow again.

Revisit the location for new seedlings or returning shoots. In a crop, have the identification checked and choose a plan suited to that crop and setting. Preventing new seed and checking for regrowth are practical starting points; they do not guarantee that one removal will clear an established patch. Leave an uncertain plant in place long enough to obtain useful photographs rather than clearing nearby plants that may be different species.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Amaranthus muricatus
Spain Ministry for the Ecological Transition: Amaranthus muricatus atlas account
Bayón: Identifying the weedy amaranths of South America
Flora of North America: Amaranthus muricatus
Flora of South Australia: Amaranthus muricatus

identification: Look for shiny, pointed oval growths arranged alternately along wiry climbing stems. These leaf-like structures have several fine, roughly parallel veins and are broader than those of many other ornamental asparagus plants. Small greenish-white flowers have six parts that curve backward; later berries change from green through pink to red. Photograph the entire climbing plant, the leaf-like structures against a scale, and flowers or fruit when present.

If roots are already exposed during permitted work, photograph how the swollen storage roots attach to the underground stems. Do not dig up surrounding vegetation simply to obtain that picture. Different forms of this species can vary in the shape and arrangement of their underground growth. A familiar ornamental appearance should not substitute for checking the whole plant.
actions: Start with small plants or the edge of a patch where removal will not damage surrounding vegetation. NSW guidance recommends digging out all connected underground stems for physical removal to work. Collect berries, including green ones, because fruit can continue to ripen after stems are cut. Keep that material and contaminated soil from being dumped elsewhere.

Cutting the climbing shoots can make a site easier to work in, but it will not reliably kill the plant beneath the ground. Return to look for new shoots and seedlings. For a large patch or plants intertwined with valued shrubs, seek a site-specific plan that protects those plants. Australian biological-control releases and seasonal treatment schedules are specific to that setting; they are not instructions to release insects or fungi in the United States.

sources.label: South African National Biodiversity Institute: Asparagus asparagoides

identification: Look for flat, narrow leaves on stems rising above a network of runners close to the soil surface. Botanical treatments describe leaves roughly 5 to 16 centimeters long and 2 to 6 millimeters wide, with considerable variation among forms. Several slender flowering branches spread from the top of each flowering stem. At a leaf's junction with its sheath, magnification can reveal a short fringe of hairs.

Photograph the flowering head, a leaf and its attachment, and a runner with rooted joints. Common bermudagrass can look very similar above ground but also produces underground rhizomes. Other stargrasses and cultivated hybrids complicate identification, so absence of an obvious underground stem in one photograph is not proof. Keep cultivar or planting records with a report if the grass was originally sown or planted for forage.
actions: Check the edges of a planting for runners entering places where the grass is unwanted. Avoid moving live stem pieces or soil containing them to another site; stargrass is deliberately propagated from such pieces. Where removal is appropriate, collect connected runners rather than chopping and spreading them through the ground. Inspect disturbed edges again for regrowth.

Do not rely on repeated cultivation alone to eliminate a patch. Tropical Forages notes that resilient runners can survive ploughing and that cultivation can improve a stand. A larger escape needs a plan suited to the site, nearby plants and land use. In a working pasture, distinguish management of a useful forage from control of an unwanted escape. Appearance, forage use and presence in this catalog do not establish an identical ecological impact everywhere.

sources.label: Naturalis: Gramineae of Northern and West Tropical Africa, Cynodon nlemfuensis

identification: Look for a small mouth, a body flattened from side to side, and irregular dark markings on the chin, throat or lower head. The back may appear olive or metallic green, while the sides are silvery with bronze tones. Large males can have a gold patch on the gill cover. Young fish may show a dark spot near the beginning of the soft-rayed part of the dorsal fin.

Take a clear side photograph that includes the complete dorsal fin, tail and gill cover, plus a view of the lower head if possible without unnecessary handling. Black coloring alone is not a secure identification: other tilapias change color with age and breeding condition. A specialist may need fin-ray and scale details that a distant photograph cannot show.
actions: Do not move a suspected blackchin tilapia to another pond, canal or aquarium, or use it to stock a waterbody. Its ability to live across a wide range of salinities makes transfers between freshwater and coastal sites a concern. Record the exact location and date, and keep photographs with the observation rather than relying on a common name alone.

If you encounter an unfamiliar population or a fish die-off, contact the state fisheries or aquatic invasive-species program. Hawaii's aquatic-resources agency monitors both spread and disease events. Ask for instructions before retaining or transporting a live fish; rules differ among states. Removal projects described by agencies are supervised work, not a reason to net a whole pond or apply chemicals yourself.

sources.label: Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute: Sarotherodon melanotheron
Hawaii Division of Aquatic Resources: Blackchin tilapia
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service: Blackchin tilapia risk screening, 2026 web version
Kishida and Specker: Paternal mouthbrooding in blackchin tilapia

identification: Check the leaf shape from more than one angle. The leaves are thick and nearly cylindrical, rather than simply narrow blades, with lengthwise ribs and faint darker bands across their gray-green surface. In larger forms they can exceed a meter in length, but dwarf cultivars are much smaller. Size by itself is therefore a poor test.

Photograph the base, the fan-like arrangement and a close view of the ribs and pointed tips. If flowers are present, look for a tall stalk bearing fragrant, pale tubular flowers with the narrow tips curling backward. Retail plants can consist of separate rooted leaf cuttings, so a tidy row or braid may conceal the plant's usual arrangement. Include that cultivation history when asking someone to identify it.
actions: Keep unwanted leaves and underground stems out of outdoor dumping sites. This species can be propagated from leaf cuttings and divisions, so discarded living pieces are worth containing rather than scattering. When removing an unwanted clump with the owner's permission, check for connected underground stems and revisit the area for new shoots. Those precautions follow its documented growth habits; the references do not establish a tested eradication program for every setting.

Handle the stiff pointed leaves carefully, particularly where children or pets might brush against them. Do not use the plant as food. If you find it growing away from cultivation, record the size of the patch and any smaller plants nearby. That helps reviewers distinguish planted material from possible spread without assuming every household specimen is an ecological threat.

identification: Look for a woody shrub with stiff thorn-tipped branches and smaller spines along the sides. Mature plants can reach several meters tall. The leaves are smooth-edged, thick and usually gathered in small groups on short shoots; they are roughly spoon-shaped to oblong, often with rounded tips. Small cream, pale mauve or white flowers occur singly or in small groups, followed by round red berries commonly around a centimeter across.

Photograph the whole shrub, a leafy thorn-bearing branch and flowers or fruit. Include a scale without placing your hand among the thorns. Other Lycium species can also have spiny branches and red fruit, so neither feature alone establishes this name. A regional botanical key or herbarium review is especially useful where native relatives occur.
actions: Avoid working barehanded in a mature thicket: the long, rigid thorns make handling and removal difficult. If removal is appropriate, plan how the cut material will be contained and moved before starting. Keep berries with the collected debris rather than spreading them along a track. Look for seedlings beneath nearby bird perches as well as immediately beside the original shrub.

Cutting the canopy does not necessarily kill the plant. The Victorian account records regrowth from cut stumps and broken roots, so follow-up checks are important after physical work. Large shrubs or plants beside waterways may need a coordinated site plan. Australian treatment calendars and legal classifications should not be applied automatically in the United States; use guidance appropriate to the location and confirm any product's permitted use before treatment.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Lycium ferocissimum

identification: Look for a tufted perennial grass with upright stems, sometimes connected by underground stems. Leaves are narrow and pointed, while the flower head is a tightly packed, upright cylinder surrounded by persistent bristles. The smaller flowering units fall away as they mature, but the bristles remain attached. Many forms have blue-green foliage and yellowish bristles.

Photograph the clump base, a complete flowering stem and the place where a leaf blade meets its sheath. A close view there can show the small fringed structure called the ligule. Flower heads may range from a few centimeters to several tens of centimeters long. Because closely related bristlegrasses share the bottlebrush appearance, an identification should use the whole plant and mature flowering material rather than head color alone.
actions: First check whether the patch is a planted forage stand or unwanted growth beyond it. Where spread is unwanted, keep mature seed heads and rooted stem pieces out of soil, hay and garden waste moved to other sites. A variety that makes little seed can still spread through rooted stems, so simply removing flower heads may not be enough.

Return after cutting: established plants can persist under repeated cutting or grazing. Avoid treating livestock as a simple removal tool, because the grass's oxalate content can create animal-health problems under some feeding conditions. Ask an agricultural adviser about management appropriate to the variety and site. The sources describe forage biology and spread, not a single removal schedule that is proven to work everywhere.

identification: Look closely at the feet. The front toes are unwebbed, while the large hind feet are fully webbed and carry black claws on the three inner toes. The head is small and wedge-shaped, with eyes on top, and the smooth back is often mottled olive or brown. Adults can exceed five inches in body length. Tadpoles look very different: they are partly transparent and have conspicuous whisker-like projections near the mouth.

African dwarf frogs sold as pets are an important lookalike. They remain much smaller, have webbing on the front feet, and have eyes positioned farther toward the sides of the head. Photograph the front feet and head position when possible. Do not rely on color alone, particularly for a captive animal with unusual pigmentation.
actions: Never release a pet or laboratory frog into a pond, drain or stream, or relocate a wild frog to another waterbody. If one is found outdoors, record the location and photograph it without carrying it elsewhere. A clear image of the feet can be more useful for review than a distant picture of the whole pond.

Report a suspected new population to the relevant state wildlife or invasive-species program; California specifically requests reports through its invasive-species program. Ask that agency how to proceed before attempting collection. These frogs can carry pathogens affecting other amphibians, so keep aquarium water and equipment away from natural waters. Do not add chemicals to a pond or attempt a large removal on your own. A confirmed population needs a plan that also protects the other animals living there.

sources.label: California Department of Fish and Wildlife: African clawed frog
Jim Rorabaugh, Tucson Herpetological Society: African clawed frog

identification: Look for a substantial clump of upright leaves and a flowering stem roughly 0.5–1.5 metres tall, often with a small number of branches. The flowers are uneven in shape: the upper lobe extends much farther than the others. Later, rounded capsules contain several orange seeds. Photograph the whole plant, a side view of an open flower, and the arrangement of flowers along the stem.

Crocosmia can look similar, but its flower lobes are more nearly equal. Names can also be misleading: Chasmanthe aethiopica has often been used incorrectly for this species. In the HortFlora treatment, true C. aethiopica has a one-sided flower arrangement and fewer flowers. Leaf fans alone are not enough to settle the identification.
actions: If plants are appearing beyond a planting, mark the edge of the patch and photograph flowers before removing them. Keep seed capsules, corms and surrounding soil contained rather than dumping them in a vacant lot, ditch or natural area. A clump that disappears above ground may still have living corms below it.

For a small, confirmed patch on your property, ask your local extension service about removing the underground corms with as little soil disturbance as possible. Check the same spot during the next growing season. These steps address its known spread pathways; they are not a guarantee that one digging or cutting will clear an established patch.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria, HortFlora: Chasmanthe floribunda

identification: Look for dense tussocks with rough leaf blades about 4–12 mm wide. The young leaves may be rolled, and older tips can curl. The cylindrical flower heads are commonly 8–30 cm long, with many slender bristles around the small flowering units. At the junction between blade and sheath, there is a dense fringe of hairs rather than a long, smooth membrane.

Photograph the entire clump, the flower head, and that leaf junction. Several ornamental fountain grasses have bristly heads, so a distant photograph is not enough. A grass specialist may need a flowering specimen to examine the spikelets and their bristles. Note whether shoots appear away from the main crown, but do not dig up or transport an uncertain plant just to check its rhizomes.
actions: Avoid moving soil or machinery through a confirmed patch, especially when seed heads are present. Clean plant fragments and soil from equipment before leaving the site. Cutting off the visible stems alone leaves the underground rhizomes available to regrow.

Small plants may be removed by digging out their crowns and rhizomes where that can be done without damaging surrounding vegetation. Contain the material and ask about local disposal; do not put it in soil or garden waste that will be moved elsewhere. Larger patches need a follow-up plan with a weed specialist. Revisit treated ground for returning shoots and seedlings rather than assuming a single treatment has finished the work.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online: Cenchrus macrourus

identification: Adults are roughly 2 mm long, with a yellowish-brown body, red eyes and clear wings. The contrasting lengthwise stripes on the head and the body section just behind it are the most useful first clue. Photograph the fly from above under good light, with a size reference if possible.

The markings help distinguish it from the more uniformly colored fruit flies commonly seen indoors, but a striped fly is not automatically this species. A specimen or a sharp close-up may be needed to distinguish related Zaprionus species. Larvae inside fruit are much less distinctive; keep a note of the fruit type, whether it was intact or damaged, and where it was growing.
actions: Harvest ripe fruit promptly and remove fallen, damaged and overripe fruit from the growing area. Refrigerate harvested fruit when appropriate for the crop. This reduces opportunities for flies to breed and helps protect fruit quality; it does not establish which fly species is present.

If losses continue, send photographs and crop details to your extension office. Fine insect netting can help exclude flies when the mesh and edges are suitable, but it must fit the crop and its pollination needs. Monitoring traps can show that flies are active; they should not be treated as a stand-alone cure. Before using a pesticide, have the pest identified and check advice for that specific crop and product.

sources.label: University of Kentucky: African fig fly, ENTFACT-232

identification: Look for a body flattened somewhat from side to side, bright blue spotting, and a conspicuous dark blotch on the gill cover. The tail is rounded. Breeding fish can be strongly red, but a subdued brown or tan individual should not be ruled out because it lacks that color.

Take a clear side photograph showing the head, full dorsal fin and tail, and record the waterbody and exact location. Closely related jewel cichlids can look very similar, particularly in aquarium strains. Color alone cannot resolve them. A museum or fisheries specialist may need fin counts, a specimen, or other diagnostic evidence to confirm a record outside its known range.
actions: Never release an aquarium jewel cichlid into a pond, canal or other waterbody. If you can no longer keep one, arrange a return or rehoming through an aquarium retailer or an appropriate animal-care contact. Moving wild fish to a new site can also spread a population.

For an unfamiliar wild population, photograph it and report the location to the state fisheries or invasive-species program. Include the name you were given, but let the reviewer know if the identification is uncertain. Ask for instructions before collecting or transporting fish. Do not drain a pond or apply a fish toxicant yourself; those actions can harm the rest of the aquatic community and require professional planning.

sources.label: Belfiore and Schofield: Genetic characterization of African jewelfish in Florida
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service: African jewelfish risk screening, March 2026

identification: Look for long stems that trail or lean before their tips turn upward. Lower stem joints can produce roots where they contact the ground. The leaves are narrow, commonly about 2–6 mm wide, and the plant is generally smooth rather than densely hairy. Some stems or sheaths have reddish coloring.

The flowering structures are slender, inconspicuous spikes, sometimes occurring in small groups near the upper leaf axils, where leaves meet the stem. They do not form the broad, feathery head seen in many ornamental grasses. Photograph rooted joints, leaf bases and any flowering spikes. Several creeping pasture grasses look alike when mown, so a short lawn photograph is unlikely to establish the species.
actions: Where limpograss is deliberately grown, check the boundary between the planting and adjacent ditches, wetlands or unmanaged ground. Photograph shoots that are extending beyond it and note whether they are connected by trailing stems. Do not move cut stems or soil from a suspected escaped patch to another moist site.

For a confirmed unwanted patch, discuss removal with an extension or land-management specialist, particularly beside water. Stem pieces capable of rooting need to be contained, and follow-up checks matter. Published advice on controlling other weeds inside a limpograss pasture is intended to protect the forage; it should not be mistaken for instructions to remove limpograss itself.

sources.label: University of Florida IFAS: Limpograss overview and management

identification: African mustard has branching stems often 15–50 centimeters long, with broader, lightly toothed lower leaves and smaller leaves above. Its four pink or violet petals measure about 6–9 millimeters. Mature pods are narrow, usually 4–6 centimeters long, with scarcely any beak at the tip. A hand lens shows branched, star-shaped hairs without glandular tips. Blue mustard (Chorispora tenella) also has purple flowers, but bears stalked glands and often upward-curving pods with a conspicuous, elongated beak. Photograph the whole plant, lower leaves, an open flower, and mature pods beside a ruler. Close views of hairs and pod tips are particularly useful. Young plants without flowers or fruit need closer examination.
actions: Photograph a suspected African mustard patch while flowers and pods are present, and ask a regional herbarium or Extension office to confirm an unfamiliar occurrence. For a small, confirmed unwanted patch, remove plants before pods mature to reduce opportunities for seed release. If pods are already ripe, contain them during handling rather than shaking plants over the site. Clean adhering soil and plant material from tools before moving elsewhere, and revisit the patch after favorable growing weather. These are cautious prevention steps based on its annual, seed-producing life cycle. Extensive clearing is unnecessary for an uncertain identification and could remove similar native mustards.

sources.label: UAE National Red List — regional Strigosella africana assessment
University of British Columbia E-Flora BC — Chorispora tenella, Illustrated Flora of British Columbia
Homrani Bakali, Léger and Mombrial (2024) — Chorispora tenella: comparison with similar-looking species

identification: African oil palm has one upright trunk, often marked by woody, roughly triangular old leaf bases, and can reach about 15 meters tall. Long feather-shaped leaves carry narrow leaflets in irregular groups pointing in several directions. Strong spines line the leaf stalks. Fruit bunches develop among the leaf bases; individual oval fruits may be red or black and reach about 5 centimeters long. American oil palm (Elaeis oleifera) is a close lookalike, but is shorter, has a more creeping trunk, and has regularly spaced leaflets arranged in one plane. Photograph the whole crown, trunk base, leaflet arrangement, and fruit from the ground. Seedlings without adult leaves or a visible trunk may need specialist examination.
actions: Check beyond a cultivated palm for young plants, noting whether they are in maintained ground or nearby natural vegetation. Before removing seedlings, confirm their identity and the land manager's wishes; a palm-shaped leaf alone is not enough. Keep collected fruit and planting material out of unmanaged areas. Do not climb a mature palm or stand beneath a fruit bunch while someone cuts it: the fruit clusters are heavy and leaf stalks are spiny. Arrange professional work on large trees. An unwanted planting needs a site-specific plan; being a major crop does not establish its ecological effect at your site.

sources.label: Kew — Elaeis guineensis, Flora of Tropical East Africa
Oklahoma State University Extension — Properties of palm oil
USDA IDtools — Elaeis guineensis, Identifying Commonly Cultivated Palms

identification: The African olive described in Australian weed guides commonly reaches 5-10 meters, with opposite leaves often ending in a small hook. Their undersides are green to yellow-brown. European olive (Olea europaea subsp. europaea), including escaped cultivated trees, usually has whitish or silvery leaf undersides and lacks the hooked tip. Small cream flowers are followed by purple-black fruit. These features help compare familiar olives, but they do not reliably distinguish the African and Asian brown-olive groups separated by recent genetic research. Photograph both leaf surfaces, leaf tips, their attachment to the stem, bark and ripe fruit. Keep the location and any nursery or planting records with the images so a botanist can assess the intended subspecies.
actions: For a confirmed unwanted African olive escape, remove small seedlings with their roots before they become fruiting trees, where digging will not damage nearby vegetation. Check again for seedlings and new shoots: cutting an established plant alone can leave a living base that resprouts. Keep fruit-bearing waste out of natural vegetation and arrange professional help for large trees or dense stands. If the subspecies is uncertain, keep photographs and the original name together when requesting botanical advice. Australian guidance supports these observations and prevention steps, but a local adviser should assess the plant and site before recommending a treatment program.

sources.label: NSW WeedWise — African olive under the broader cuspidata usage
Besnard et al.: Brown olive subspecies revision, author deposit
Besnard et al. brown-olive subspecies revision, publisher abstract

identification: Plants are often several tens of centimeters tall. The flattened pods are about 2–3 millimeters long, with a shallow notch at the end. Their short stalks curve outward and carry a row of fine hairs. White petals may be minute or absent. The related Lepidium pseudotasmanicum can have more deeply divided lower leaves; fruit shape overlaps and should not be used alone. Stems may be hairless or finely hairy; check the lower leaves and the row of hairs on each fruit stalk together. Photograph lower and upper leaves, stems, and several mature pods with a scale. A regional key is especially important if the plant does not match the usual hairless form.
actions: Keep a clear photographic record before removing an unfamiliar pepperwort. Similar species may be native, and their tiny differences are hard to judge without mature fruit. Once a small unwanted patch is confirmed, contain seed-bearing stems and lift plants where that can be done without disturbing neighboring vegetation. Check again for seedlings and surviving bases rather than assuming every plant dies after one season. Clean soil and seedpods from tools before leaving the site. For a larger patch, ask a local botanist or weed adviser to confirm the identification and plan removal around nearby plants.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria — Lepidium africanum
Manaaki Whenua — Flora of New Zealand, Lepidium africanum

identification: Adults found in Florida average about 10 feet long. Young snakes are much smaller, so size alone cannot identify one. Look from a safe distance for irregular, partly connected dark markings and a dark spear-shaped area on the head bordered by pale stripes. Burmese pythons generally have more clearly separated back blotches. African rock pythons also have dark mottling across the pale belly, but never lift or roll a snake to check this. Photograph the body pattern and head only if visible without approaching. A specialist can compare those images; a distant glimpse may not settle the identification.
actions: Give the snake space and keep children and pets away. Do not corner, grab, or try to move it. From a safe position, record the location, time, and a clear photograph. In Florida, report a suspected northern African python promptly through FWC's IveGot1 reporting service or its invasive-species hotline; include the location even if the snake moves out of sight. Elsewhere, contact the responsible wildlife agency. Let trained responders decide how to handle the animal. Never release an unwanted captive python outdoors; ask the wildlife agency about an appropriate surrender route.

sources.label: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission — Northern African python
FWC — Report sightings of nonnative species

identification: Look for long leaves divided into many opposite pairs of oval leaflets, each ending in a small point. Flowers open progressively from the bottom of an upright cluster, with dark bracts still covering the buds above. Flat brown pods follow, their outlines indented between the seeds. The foliage has an unusual smell often compared with popcorn, although people describe it differently. Use the leaf arrangement, buds and pods together; scent alone is a poor way to separate this plant from other sennas.
actions: In Florida, choose an alternative rather than adding this shrub to the landscape. Around an existing plant, check for young seedlings beyond the bed, especially near disturbed ground. Collect pods before they scatter and keep seed-bearing trimmings out of natural areas. Photograph any apparently self-sown plants with the parent shrub and location noted. A plant growing in a pot is a different kind of record from seedlings establishing on their own. Where escapes are already spreading, ask the local invasive-plant program to help plan removal and follow-up.

sources.label: University of Wisconsin Extension: Popcorn cassia

identification: The leaves are tiny, alternating scales pressed against the twigs, rather than the broad leaves of many streamside shrubs. White to pale pink flowers grow in cylindrical clusters, commonly on thicker wood from the previous year. Each flower has five petals. Record that position on the branch as well as close views of flowers and leaves. Specialists may need floral details that a whole-tree photograph cannot show. A general resemblance to saltcedar is enough to request help, but not enough to settle the species.
actions: If you find a possible escape, photograph the flowering branches and note whether it stands beside a planting or among naturally established vegetation. Avoid moving cut branches, seed-bearing material or wet soil to another waterway. Ask a herbarium or local invasive-plant specialist to check the name before arranging large-scale work. Streambanks may need protection and replacement vegetation during removal, so simply clearing a stand can create another problem. Keep the original identification and any later correction together when reporting the observation.

sources.label: University of Evora Biodiversity Museum: Tamarix africana
Malta Wild Plants: Tamarix africana flora account

identification: Look for large leaves divided into paired leaflets with one leaflet at the tip. The flower clusters sit above the foliage; swollen, curved buds open into broad cups with orange-red petals and often a yellow edge. Long woody seed capsules stand upright and split into boat-shaped halves, releasing thin seeds with papery wings. Photograph both the whole leaf and an open capsule if available. Yellow-flowered trees also occur, so flower color alone is not a reliable guide to whether a plant can spread.
actions: In affected tropical areas, avoid planting additional trees and check nearby forest edges for seedlings. Remove small, confirmed plants before they become difficult to handle, with the landowner's permission. Plan follow-up because cutting an established tree can produce vigorous regrowth. Large trees and brittle branches call for a qualified arborist, especially near buildings or paths. Keep cut material and seeds out of waterways and unmanaged land. For a spreading stand, use the local invasive-species program's current treatment guidance rather than assuming one cutting will finish the job.

sources.label: Universidad Francisco Marroquin Arboretum: Spathodea campanulata
Big Island Invasive Species Committee: African tulip

identification: Look for a broad, flattened head with fleshy facial bumps, long upward-curving upper tusks and shorter sharp lower tusks. The body is sparsely haired, with a coarse mane along the back, relatively slender legs and a tasseled tail. Warthogs often lower themselves onto their front wrist joints to graze. Native collared peccaries are smaller and lack the same conspicuous facial bumps and curved tusks. Photograph from a safe distance, ideally showing the head and body profile rather than approaching for a closer look.
actions: Give the animal room to leave and keep people and pets away from it. Do not feed, corner or attempt to catch it; a frightened warthog can injure someone with its tusks. Record the date, location, number of animals and any young, then contact the state wildlife agency or local land manager about an unexpected free-ranging sighting. Note whether fences or a nearby exotic-animal facility are present without assuming the source. Any capture or removal should be arranged through qualified people following local requirements.

sources.label: Journal of Mammalogy: occupancy and activity of peccary, wild pig and common warthog in southern Texas

identification: The broad, heart-shaped leaves grow alternately and have several strong veins radiating from their bases. Stems are rounded rather than prominently winged, and bulbils develop along the vine. Winged yam often has opposite leaves and angular, winged stems. Native yams can also have heart-shaped leaves, so leaf shape alone is not enough. Photograph a section showing several leaf attachments, the stem and a bulbil together. Do not taste a tuber or bulbil to try to identify the plant.
actions: Collect loose bulbils and prevent them from being carried in soil, yard waste or equipment. Bag reproductive material for disposal following local guidance; do not leave it in a brush pile where it can sprout. Cutting a vine helps stop its immediate climb but leaves underground reserves to regrow, so revisit the site and deal with new shoots. Avoid pulling heavy vines out of tree canopies. In Florida, ask Extension about the established air-potato beetle program and an integrated control plan for larger infestations.

sources.label: University of Florida IFAS Plant Directory: Dioscorea bulbifera
Florida Museum: Five facts about air potatoes in Florida
US Forest Service: Dioscorea species review
UF/IFAS: Invasive Plants in Natural Areas, Air Potato

identification: Turn an affected leaf over and look for powdery orange patches, then compare the upper surface for yellowing or browning. Note whether damage is scattered or affects much of the crown, and whether leaves are falling earlier than nearby healthy alders. These symptoms suggest a rust infection but do not identify this species. Specialists examine spore shape, surface ornamentation and the structures that release spores; DNA testing can help separate it from similar Melampsoridium fungi. Photographs of the host tree and both leaf surfaces support that work.
actions: If a nursery plant or unusual outbreak is involved, contact a plant diagnostic service before moving affected stock. Ask how to package a sample so that useful leaves reach the lab without spreading material around the site. Record when symptoms began and revisit the same trees to track recovery or repeated defoliation. Avoid removing nearby larches or applying fungicides solely from a photograph: the diagnosis and local growing conditions should guide any treatment. Keep confirmed laboratory results with the observation rather than replacing them with a visual guess.

sources.label: California Department of Food and Agriculture: Melampsoridium hiratsukanum
First Documentation of Life Cycle Completion of Melampsoridium hiratsukanum in the Eastern Alps

identification: Look for fine, light-green needles carried mostly in bundles of two; occasional bundles of three also occur. The needles are generally about 6-10 centimeters long. Small woody cones have short stalks and may remain on branches for several years, so cones of different ages can be present together. Older trunks can become bowed or twisted. Related pines, including Eldar pine, may look similar from a distance. A useful identification photograph shows a needle bundle at its base and a cone still attached to its twig.
actions: Around a planted tree, check whether small pines are appearing beyond maintained ground, and distinguish seedlings from recently planted replacements. Record their distance from the parent and the habitat they are entering. Have an uncertain identification checked before removing young pines, especially where native species also occur. If a confirmed escape conflicts with restoration goals, discuss early removal and follow-up with the land manager. Mature trees near roads, buildings or power lines need professional assessment; their presence in this catalog is not a reason to cut them without a site-specific decision.

sources.label: Oregon State University Landscape Plants: Pinus halepensis

identification: Look for one pale, ringed trunk topped by a smooth green crownshaft, the sheath just below the fronds. The arching leaves are feather-shaped, and the individual leaflets have blunt, uneven tips that look as if they have been torn off. Branched flower clusters emerge below the crownshaft, followed by small red fruits. Several palms planted close together may look like a clump, so check whether each stem arises separately. Close views of leaflet tips, trunk rings and fruit are more informative than a distant silhouette.
actions: In areas where escapes are a concern, inspect beneath fruiting palms and along the nearest unmanaged edge for seedlings. Remove unwanted, correctly identified seedlings while they are small and keep fruits and plant waste out of natural areas. A nearby mature palm helps explain a possible seed source but does not replace identification. Record whether seedlings persist when maintenance stops. Leave work high in the crown to a qualified palm-care professional, and use local assessment guidance when deciding whether to retain an existing planting or replace it with a suitable native species.

sources.label: CSIRO Australian Tropical Rainforest Plants: Ptychosperma elegans

identification: The thick oval leaves grow in opposite pairs, with many closely spaced, nearly parallel side veins visible on both surfaces. Leaf tips are often rounded or slightly notched. Small clusters of white flowers have conspicuous yellow stamens, followed by smooth, round green fruits that turn brownish with maturity or drying. A mature tree often has a short trunk and spreading lower branches. Photograph the paired leaves, their veins and a fruit together; common names containing laurel are shared by unrelated trees and are not reliable identification on their own.
actions: If you notice seedlings beyond a coastal planting, record their location and whether they are rooted and growing rather than simply washed-up fruits. Keep unwanted fruits and nursery waste from being dumped into shore vegetation or waterways. Ask the land manager to confirm the species and local priorities before undertaking removal, particularly on an erosion-prone shoreline. Do not assume that reports about a different Calophyllum apply to this one. In a maintained garden, monitor reproduction and choose future plantings with local native habitat in mind.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online: Calophyllum inophyllum regional flora accounts

identification: Look for leaves divided into three leaflets, with the terminal leaflet on a short stalk and small teeth concentrated toward the leaflet tips. Clusters of usually purple, pea-shaped flowers develop into curled or coiled pods. The stems arise from a persistent crown rather than from a creeping mat of runners. Similar clovers can share the three-leaflet appearance, so include flowers or mature pods in photographs. Flower color varies in the wider alfalfa group, and an image of one bloom alone may not resolve a subspecies or hybrid.
actions: When documenting alfalfa, say whether it is deliberately sown, left over from a former field or growing outside cultivation. For an unwanted small patch, preventing seed production is useful, but a single mowing should not be mistaken for removal of the perennial crown. Revisit the site for regrowth and plan any further work around the vegetation you want to retain. In a working pasture or hay field, consult the grower or Extension before treating it as a weed; removing a crop plant can undermine the purpose of the field.

sources.label: Canadian Food Inspection Agency: Biology of Medicago sativa
Kansas State University-hosted Missouri prairie plant identification guide: Alfalfa
Penn State Extension: Are My Forages Dead or Dormant?

identification: Typical plants have three leaflets, the end leaflet on a short stalk, with teeth near the outer ends. Blue-purple flowers grow in compact clusters, followed by pods curled into tight spirals. The British Columbia flora contrasts these with the usually yellow flowers and curved, rather than spirally coiled, pods of subsp. falcata. Hybrids can blur that contrast. Photograph several flowering stems and mature pods from the same plant; if those features disagree, retain the broader species identification until a botanist can examine it.
actions: For a sighting, note whether the plant is a crop, a volunteer at a field edge or an established roadside escape. Include the fruit photographs rather than relying on a familiar purple flower. If removal is appropriate in a restoration bed, address the crown and monitor for regrowth; routine forage cutting demonstrates how readily a healthy plant can recover. Avoid spreading seed-bearing cuttings into nearby habitat. On agricultural land, coordinate with the owner before any intervention, because alfalfa may be an intended and useful part of the field.

sources.label: Canadian Food Inspection Agency: Biology of Medicago sativa
UBC E-Flora BC: Medicago sativa subsp. sativa

identification: Look for reddish-brown, cylindrical branches forming loose, tangled clumps rather than broad flat blades. Plants may attach to shells or other firm objects, become caught among animals' tubes, or accumulate as drifting mats. Color and branching change with conditions, and several native and introduced red algae look similar. A photograph can document the growth but may not establish this species. Include a close view of the branches and a wider view showing whether the material is attached, loose or mixed with seagrass.
actions: Record the date, shoreline location and approximate area covered, then share the observation with a local marine monitoring program. Do not move live seaweed, shells or fouled equipment to another waterbody. Remove hitchhiking material from gear where it can be contained and disposed of ashore. Avoid dragging a rake through a mixed seaweed and seagrass bed: that can disturb the habitat you are trying to protect. Where mats are changing access or vegetation, ask the responsible coastal manager to assess the site before removal.

sources.label: Smithsonian Environmental Research Center NEMESIS: Gracilaria vermiculophylla
NOAA repository: Genetic identification of source and likely vector of a widespread marine invader
NOAA repository: Gracilaria habitat and juvenile blue crab study

identification: A broad red blade is a starting clue, not a reliable identification. Several Grateloupia species produce flattened, branching seaweeds whose appearance changes with age and growing conditions. The confusion in the Rhode Island records shows why a confident-looking photograph can still receive the wrong name. Photograph the entire attached plant, its base and the branching pattern without pulling it off the shore. Include a scale and the tidal setting. A seaweed specialist may need reproductive structures or genetic evidence to separate the possibilities.
actions: If you encounter a suspected plant outside its documented range, send the photographs and exact location to a herbarium or marine monitoring program. Keep the original name attached to any older record and note who subsequently checked it. Avoid transporting living material on boats, gear or shells. Do not clear a patch on the assumption that it is the introduced species described in an old report. Wait for an identification and advice appropriate to that shoreline, especially where native seaweeds are growing together.

sources.label: Smithsonian NEMESIS: Grateloupia turuturu, identification history
Gavio and Fredericq 2002: G. turuturu reassessment
Rodriguez et al. 2018: seaweeds of La Libertad, Peru

identification: Look for a low rosette of spoon-shaped leaves and a much-branched flowering stem rising above it, sometimes around half a meter tall. The small pale pink flowers occur in short, repeated clusters along the branches. Leaves are broader near the tip and narrow toward the base. Other sea lavenders, including native plants, can look similar. Photograph the rosette, branching stem and close flower clusters together. Some California plants have been assigned to a subspecies, but that name should not be assumed from a general photograph.
actions: Report a suspected patch to the refuge, park or local coastal restoration program, with its size and position relative to the marsh edge. Stay on established access routes rather than trampling sensitive vegetation for photographs. Prevent seed-bearing material from being moved in maintenance debris. Small confirmed populations are worth addressing before they expand, but removal in a marsh should follow the land manager's plan. Revisit treated areas for seedlings and recovery of native cover; one cleared patch does not establish that the surrounding seed supply is gone.

sources.label: Archbald and Boyer: invasion of Pacific estuarine transition zones

identification: Leaves grow in opposite pairs along the stem and have smooth edges. Small white flower heads resemble papery clover flowers and rise on stalks above the leaves. Floating stems are commonly hollow, but stems growing on land can be firmer and less obviously hollow. Note the leaf arrangement and stalked white heads together; other aquatic plants may share one feature without sharing the others. Photograph a flowering stem in place and include the shoreline or ditch setting rather than breaking off pieces to carry home.
actions: Keep fragments out of drains and waterways when cleaning equipment or maintaining a bank. Do not mow or rake an infestation into the water, and do not put live pieces in a garden pond or an ordinary loose brush pile. Contact the waterbody manager or local invasive-plant program before attempting removal from a substantial mat. Physical removal can leave rooted pieces behind, so plan containment and follow-up. Biological control is used in some regions, but effectiveness and availability vary; obtain local advice rather than moving insects or plants yourself.

sources.label: UF/IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants: Alligatorweed
Texas A&M AquaPlant: alligator weed management

identification: Start by looking for a line of small white punctures near a leaf tip, followed by winding mines or damaged inner leaves. Cream-colored, legless larvae can reach about 8 millimeters; brown pupae may be tucked into leaf bases. Adult flies are about 3 millimeters long, dark overall with yellow areas on the head and legs. These clues together are more useful than a photograph of a tiny fly alone. Other insects and diseases damage alliums too, so ask Extension to check a suspicious first finding.
actions: Inspect susceptible beds during local fly activity and photograph both the puncture rows and any larvae or pupae. Avoid sharing infested transplants or planting garlic from a suspect crop. Fine insect netting or row cover can keep adults out when installed before they arrive and sealed around the edges. Plant the next crop in a clean bed before fitting covers: covering soil where pupae remain can trap emerging flies inside with the plants. Ask local Extension about disposal of infested crop material and a monitoring schedule suited to your area.

sources.label: University of Maryland Extension: Allium leafminer

identification: Look for opposite pairs of glossy, leathery leaves with smooth margins and visible oil glands. Small white flowers develop in branching clusters, followed by rounded berries that change from green to dark purple or nearly black. Leaves commonly measure several inches long, and the plant develops a woody trunk rather than remaining a low herb. Related aromatic trees may look similar. Photograph the leaf arrangement, flowers or fruit and overall tree shape together. Do not taste an unfamiliar berry to decide whether you have found the culinary species.
actions: Around an existing planting, check for seedlings beyond the maintained bed and record whether young plants are establishing in nearby vegetation. Avoid dumping ripe fruit or seed-bearing pruning waste in natural areas. If you find an apparent escape, send photographs and the location to a local herbarium or Extension office for confirmation and regional advice. There is no need to infer harm from the scent or common name. Any decision to remove an established tree should consider its identity, local status and the surrounding habitat.

sources.label: Indian Council of Agricultural Research, Indian Institute of Spices Research: Allspice

identification: Adults have gray forewings with relatively faint markings and a wingspan of roughly 16 to 30 millimeters. Look inside suspect packages for silk-bound food, feeding debris and larvae rather than relying only on a moth resting on a wall. Small holes in packaging and webbing around storage equipment are useful clues. Other pantry moths cause similar damage, and accurate separation may require an entomologist. Photograph the adult and the affected product, and keep the package details if the problem involves a recently purchased item.
actions: Inspect nearby dry foods, including pet food and birdseed, so that an overlooked package does not keep the infestation going. Seal and discard confirmed infested food, then vacuum shelf joints, cracks and spilled material; empty the vacuum afterward. Put unaffected foods into tightly closing containers. Do not spray insecticide into food or cupboards as a substitute for removing the source. If moths continue appearing, inspect again and ask Extension or a qualified pest professional for identification. In a commercial store, isolate the affected lot and follow the facility's food-safety procedures.

sources.label: University of Minnesota Extension: pantry pests

identification: Check the bases of leaves and rolled or damaged leaf ends. Beneath a light, fuzzy wax coating, the small oval insects can appear orange-brown or dull green. The wax may leave two bare-looking strips along the back. These features help you locate a colony, but mealybugs and other small insects can still be confused with it. A specialist uses microscopic features, including its unusual lack of the paired tubes found on many aphids. Photograph the insects closely and include the whole host plant.
actions: Keep a suspect plant apart from other aloes and haworthias while you seek an identification. Inspect offsets and new purchases before sharing or moving them into a collection, paying attention to hidden leaf bases rather than only the outer foliage. Record where the plant came from and whether neighboring plants are affected. Ask Extension or a plant-health clinic for advice suited to that host and setting. Avoid treating every white patch as an aphid colony or using an unverified home mixture that may injure succulent leaves.

sources.label: Korean Journal of Applied Entomology: Aloephagus myersi on imported Aloe vera

identification: Look for three smooth leaflets with finely toothed edges, generally without the pale V-shaped marking often seen on red or white clover. Small rounded heads of pinkish-white flowers sit on stalks arising from upright or ascending stems. White clover usually has creeping stems, while red clover has larger flower heads and hairier growth. These comparisons are more useful together than flower color alone. Photograph the stem, leaflets and flower head, and ask someone experienced with pasture plants to confirm a suspect stand.
actions: Do not use an unidentified clover-rich patch or hay lot as horse feed while you are checking it. If a horse develops unusual sunburn-like lesions, appetite changes or other signs of illness after grazing, remove access to the suspect feed and contact a veterinarian promptly. Keep a sample or clear photographs of the pasture plants for that assessment. Review seed mixtures before renovating a horse pasture, and work with Extension on maintaining suitable forage. Treatment decisions for an animal belong with a veterinarian rather than a plant identification guide.

sources.label: Ontario: alsike clover poisoning in horses
Penn State Extension: plants toxic to horses

identification: Look for narrow alternate leaves, branched stems and small flowers whose yellow petals have notched tips. The flowering stalk lengthens as the rounded pods develop. The most useful distinction is tiny: A. strigosum has star-shaped hairs mixed with much coarser, forked hairs on its fruit. In A. simplex, the fruit hairs are star-shaped, although some rays can be unusually coarse. A general picture of a yellow roadside flower will not resolve that difference. Detailed photographs of mature pods, preferably with magnification, are important.
actions: Ask a regional herbarium or botanist to review a suspected finding, particularly if it would represent a new locality. Include the whole plant, flowers, mature fruit and exact location, and follow the herbarium's instructions before collecting material. Do not relabel older records without keeping their original determination and the reason for any correction. Avoid moving seed-bearing soil or plants while identification is unresolved. Large-scale removal or a claim of ecological damage would require stronger evidence than the uncertain historical records currently available for this exact species.

sources.label: Flora of North America, Al-Shehbaz: Alyssum simplex discussion of A. strigosum
Sirin et al. 2022: morphology, anatomy and pollen of Alyssum strigosum

identification: Winged individuals can have a dark head and thorax with an olive-green to reddish-brown abdomen. Color is variable and is not enough to distinguish this species from the other aphids using amaranths. Specialists examine features such as the sensory structures on the antennae and the small tail-like tip of the abdomen. For an initial report, show the host plant, where the colony sits and a close view of several insects. Note whether they were on leaves, at the soil line or on exposed roots.
actions: If a colony appears on a crop or nursery plant, keep that plant and its root ball from being moved to another growing area until the insects are checked. Record any visible damage and whether neighboring plants are affected instead of judging the problem by aphid numbers alone. Send photographs to Extension and ask how to submit a specimen if needed. Avoid a broad spray based only on color or the presence of ants. Identification and the condition of the host should guide whether further management is warranted.

sources.label: Florida Department of Agriculture TRI-OLOGY: Aphis amaranthi on Amaranthus spinosus
Aphids of Costa Rica: Aphis amaranthi diagnostic treatment

identification: Look for a broad, flattened head, a downward-facing sucker mouth, rows of hard body plates and a large, sail-like dorsal fin. Belly markings have traditionally helped separate related sailfin catfishes, but researchers caution that color patterns and even a single DNA marker may be misleading in hybrid populations. An aquarium label saying pleco is not a species identification. Useful photographs show the side, spread dorsal fin and underside when those can be obtained safely without unnecessary handling. Leave a fish in the water rather than catching it just for a photograph.
actions: Never release an aquarium fish into a pond, stream or storm drain. If you can no longer keep one, seek a responsible aquarium rehoming option and keep it contained until that is arranged. For a wild sighting, note the waterbody, date, approximate size and number of fish, then report it to the state fish and wildlife agency. Do not move a captured fish to another waterbody. Follow local instructions about handling and disposition; a suspected nonnative identity does not remove fishing or wildlife requirements.

sources.label: US Fish and Wildlife Service: Amazon sailfin catfish ecological summary
Guimaraes and colleagues: karyotypic and molecular analysis of Pterygoplichthys pardalis

identification: Look for a relatively open, branching crown and very large leaves whose lobes spread outward like the fingers of a hand. The leaf stalk joins the blade inward from its edge, with prominent veins radiating from that point. Male and female flowers occur on separate trees, and flower or fruit clusters provide useful additional details. Related Cecropia species can look very similar, including plants with intermediate features. Photograph leaf surfaces, stalk attachments and reproductive structures rather than relying on the familiar umbrella-like silhouette alone.
actions: For a possible escape, record whether the tree was planted, whether seedlings are appearing nearby and what habitat they occupy. Send those details to a regional herbarium or invasive-plant program for a checked identification. Avoid distributing seed or dumping fruiting material along drainage channels. Do not treat every similar tree as this species or assume that a name used in an older source is still correct. Where a population is confirmed as spreading, plan removal and follow-up with the land manager, taking care to protect the riverbank or surrounding vegetation.

sources.label: Conn and colleagues (2012): Status of Cecropia in Malesia
Fernandes and colleagues (2026): Sexual segregation and herbivory in Cecropia pachystachya

identification: Females are only about 2.2 to 2.5 millimeters long. Separating them from other small ambrosia beetles requires close examination of body structures, including features on the wing covers and a small hair tuft associated with the fungus-carrying organs. A round entry hole or boring dust is therefore a clue to a wood-boring insect, not a species-level diagnosis. Photograph the affected wood and tree condition, and retain a beetle only if a diagnostic service gives instructions for submitting it.
actions: Avoid transporting suspect logs, firewood or nursery trees while an identification is being checked. Note the host tree, recent stress or injury and whether the material was cut or still alive. Ask Extension or a forestry diagnostic service to assess the insect and the tree together. Routine spraying based on holes alone may miss the cause and will not identify what is already inside the wood. If removal is recommended, arrange disposal locally and follow the advice on timing so that emerging beetles are not carried to another site.

sources.label: USDA Agricultural Research Service: Rabaglia, Vandenberg and Acciavatti (2009), first North American records
USDA Agricultural Research Service: Milbrath and Biazzo (2024), Anisandrus maiche biology study

identification: Compared with other North American Euwallacea, the adult is unusually slender and light brown. Specialists examine the nearly square outline of the shield behind the head and the sloping rear surface of the wing covers. On that surface, rows of punctures diverge and a prominent pair of small bumps helps distinguish the species. Other Euwallacea and Xyleborus can look much alike in ordinary photographs. A hole in bark, sawdust, or a declining branch cannot identify the beetle or prove which organism caused the decline.
actions: If beetles appear in nursery plants or recently delivered wood, record the material, its origin, and the date before it is moved again. Photograph the insect beside a scale and ask an extension entomologist or plant-health service how to submit a specimen. Keep suspect wood and plants at the site while identification and any movement requirements are clarified. Have an arborist assess tree stress and structural problems separately. Avoid treating every nearby tree or transporting infested firewood on the assumption that all ambrosia beetles need the same response.

sources.label: University of Florida and US Forest Service: North American Xyleborini identification tool
Netherlands NVWA: Quick scan for Euwallacea similis

identification: Young leaves are simple and arrow-shaped, sometimes marked with white, silver, or pink. Mature climbing growth develops much larger leaves divided into several spreading sections. Look along the same vine for this transition rather than expecting every leaf to match a houseplant photograph. Long leaf stalks and fleshy stems are helpful clues. Golden pothos can occupy similar places, but its leaves do not undergo the same division into separate spreading leaflets. Mature arrowhead vine can produce flowers enclosed by a pale, hoodlike bract.
actions: In places where it escapes outdoors, prevent cuttings and discarded pots from reaching drains, woodland, or wet soil. For a small accessible patch, wear gloves and long sleeves, lift vines carefully, and collect broken pieces; the sap irritates skin and eyes. Do not use a string trimmer, which scatters material and exposes the sap. Arrange contained disposal through the local waste service and revisit the site for rooted fragments. Large vines in trees need a coordinated removal plan that protects people, branches, and the plants beneath them.

identification: A pointed spine projecting forward from the top of the head is an important clue. Mature males have prominent grasping limbs, while females develop a brood pouch beneath the body. Females and young animals can be much harder to separate from other Caprella. Body size and some features vary among populations, and older records include a complex of forms. A close side photograph showing the head and grasping limbs is more useful than a distant view of a fouled rope. Confirmation may require an amphipod specialist and a properly preserved specimen.
actions: For boat owners, the practical priority is limiting movement of attached marine growth. Inspect hulls, ropes, fenders, and other immersed equipment before moving to another harbor. Use a marina-approved cleaning service that captures removed material rather than scraping living fouling directly into the water. Do not transfer dock growth or live organisms to another site for identification. Photograph the fouling community and record the harbor, depth, and surface involved, then ask the local marine invasive-species program whether a sample is wanted. Let the local marine program guide any broader response so other marine life is protected.

sources.label: Smithsonian Environmental Research Center NEMESIS: Caprella scaura
Cabiddu and colleagues: Occurence of the alien species Caprella scaura in three Tyrrhenian lagoons

identification: Leaves grow opposite one another and divide into several smooth-edged leaflets. Mature bark is gray-brown and deeply furrowed; exposed inner bark is conspicuously yellow, although a healthy tree need not be cut for identification. Rounded fruits darken to black and hang in clusters, sometimes into winter. Ashes also have opposite compound leaves, but their fruits are winged rather than berry-like. Tree-of-heaven has alternate leaves. Record the arrangement of whole leaves on the twig, not just the apparent pairing of leaflets along one leaf.
actions: Start by surveying beneath fruiting trees, along bird perches, and into adjacent woods. Small seedlings can be pulled when soil is moist, taking care around native seedlings. Cutting a larger corktree once often leads to vigorous resprouting, so arrange a complete follow-up plan with a qualified land manager or arborist before felling it. Contain fruit-bearing branches during disposal and return in later seasons to find seedlings and sprouts. When replacing a landscape tree, choose a locally appropriate species and check current local restrictions on planting or sale.

sources.label: University of Illinois Extension: Invasive Amur corktree

identification: Modern descriptions emphasize a red stripe between the eye and snout, a dusky crescent at the base of the pectoral fin, and rows of darker marks along the body. Specialists also examine scales and fin characters, with genetic evidence helping resolve close relatives. The fused pelvic fins form a disc in these gobies, but that feature alone cannot identify R. brunneus. A photograph of a small brown bottom-dwelling fish is especially easy to overinterpret. Keep the original name and determination date attached to older records.
actions: Do not release aquarium fish or move live bait between waters. If an unfamiliar goby is found, record the exact location and photograph both sides and the fins without unnecessarily handling the animal. Contact the state fisheries or aquatic invasive-species program for identification and collection instructions; do not move it to another waterbody or mail a live fish. Managers revisiting historical records should seek the original specimens or voucher information. Species-specific impact claims and removal priorities should wait for that taxonomic check rather than borrowing biology from another Rhinogobius.

sources.label: USFWS: Amur Goby Ecological Risk Screening Summary
Jeon et al. 2025: First Record of Rhinogobius brunneus from Korea

identification: Look for opposite leaves with long, tapering tips and pale undersides. Paired flowers open white and age to yellow; rounded red berries follow close to the twigs. Older bark peels in narrow strips, and mature branches have hollow pith. Other introduced bush honeysuckles can share several of these features, so pointed leaves, flower color, and branch details should be considered together. Native honeysuckles also occur in many regions. Use a regional key before treating a shrub solely because it has opposite leaves or red berries.
actions: Work first on small outlying plants and seed-producing shrubs near intact woodland. Young plants can be pulled from moist soil where this will not damage nearby roots or destabilize a slope.
