Larger shrubs need a planned treatment and repeat inspections; simply opening the canopy does not finish the job. Contain ripe fruit during removal and check the newly lit ground for more honeysuckle seedlings. Restore suitable native groundcover and shrubs as space becomes available. For extensive thickets, ask a local conservation or extension service to help sequence removal and follow-up.

sources.label: University of Illinois Extension: Invasive Amur bush honeysuckle

identification: An adult female may resemble a short thread attached to the skin or fin, sometimes with two egg sacs at the exposed end. The embedded anchor is not normally visible without examination. Plant fibers, fungal growth, and other parasites can give a misleading first impression. A fish-health professional can examine the affected tissue microscopically and distinguish the parasite from these lookalikes. Young stages are much less conspicuous than the adult, so a fish that appears clear on one inspection is not necessarily free of infection.
actions: Keep new fish in an appropriate separate quarantine system and inspect them repeatedly before introduction. If a suspicious strand appears, photograph it and contact an aquatic veterinarian or fish-health laboratory. Avoid pulling at an embedded parasite yourself; incomplete removal can leave tissue damage while other stages remain in the system. Maintain good water quality and keep nets and other wet equipment separate between affected and unaffected tanks. Treatment must account for the fish species, all parasite stages, and whether fish are intended for food. Do not release unwanted or infected fish into local waters.

sources.label: University of Tokyo Fish Parasite Database: Lernaea cyprinacea

identification: The underwater leaves are narrow and fan-like; leaves held above water are broader and supported on slender stalks. Those stalks are not swollen into the buoyant bladders often associated with floating waterhyacinth, Eichhornia crassipes. Check the connection to the bottom rather than assuming every blue-flowered mat is freely floating. The flowers are blue to purple, with fringed inner petal margins. Individual flowers are short-lived, and the flower stalk bends toward the water as fruits develop. Current references may use the name Pontederia azurea for the same species.
actions: Do not plant or exchange a suspect specimen before checking local aquatic-plant rules. If it appears in a pond or waterway, photograph the leaves, flowers, and rooted stems and report it to the local aquatic invasive-plant program. Avoid dragging a mat through the water, which can leave viable pieces behind. Remove attached vegetation from boats, trailers, and equipment before departure and contain it away from the water. A small patch may be manageable by trained removal, but larger work should include fragment collection and follow-up rather than an improvised one-day clearing.

identification: The flowers hang singly and are fragrant, with a long narrow base widening into a flared white trumpet. Botanical descriptions give flowers roughly thirty centimeters long. The green calyx around the base forms a tube with five lobes. Leaves are broad, oval to oblong, softly hairy, and generally smooth-edged, with an often uneven base. Other angel's trumpets and garden hybrids can look very similar. Flower size or a nursery common name alone is not enough to establish this species; include the calyx and leaf surfaces in identification photographs.
actions: Keep plants and pruning waste away from children, pets, and livestock, and do not use flowers or leaves in food, tea, or home remedies. Use gloves for pruning and wash afterward. If ingestion is suspected, seek prompt medical or veterinary advice rather than trying a home treatment. Where a shrub has escaped, document whether it is persisting from an old planting or establishing additional plants nearby. Arrange removal and contained disposal with the landowner when needed, and check for regrowth. In a garden, retain a reliable plant label so its poisonous identity remains clear.

sources.label: Cambridge University Botanic Garden: Brugmansia suaveolens
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew: Brugmansia suaveolens

identification: Pads are oval to rounded, green, and dotted with closely spaced cushions of white or yellow bristles. These bristles, called glochids, are not soft hairs despite their fuzzy appearance. Creamy-yellow flowers may be followed by reddish-purple fruit. Blind cactus, Opuntia rufida, is a close lookalike with reddish-brown bristles and is sometimes sold under the same common name. Cultivated forms can also alter pad shape and bristle color. Photograph the whole plant and a close view of the bristle cushions without touching them.
actions: Keep loose pads and fruit off soil and out of garden-waste dumps. Before handling a plant, plan how every fragment will be collected; use suitable tools and protective clothing rather than gripping the pads directly. Ask the local waste or weeds service for a contained disposal option, especially where the cactus is regulated. Do not mow or shred a patch, which creates more loose material and exposes bristles. Inspect the original site and equipment afterward for overlooked pieces. For a large or inaccessible stand, use an experienced contractor instead of attempting bare-handed removal.

sources.label: NSW Department of Primary Industries WeedWise: Bunny ears cactus

identification: Several narrow flowering branches spread from near the top of the stem. Look closely for a dense band of short hairs on the stalk immediately below the lowest flowering branch, a useful feature in this species. The small flower units are paired, and long awns extend from them. Related bluestems can have very similar fingerlike heads, so the hairs and individual spikelets matter more than the broad silhouette. Photograph a mature head and the stem below it, and have a grass specialist compare it with other local Dichanthium and Bothriochloa.
actions: For a pasture planting, verify the seed identity and discuss local suitability with a forage adviser before sowing. Keep seed-bearing material out of nearby native grasslands and inspect disturbed margins for new clumps. If a small unwanted population is confirmed, prevent additional seed production and plan removal of the persistent crown and any rooted stems. Return to inspect the patch rather than assuming clipped leaves mean the plant has died. On a grazed conservation site, assess grazing pressure and desired vegetation together; removing one grass while leaving bare disturbed soil may not solve the underlying problem.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Kew: Dichanthium aristatum

identification: Adults are small tan to grayish-brown moths with narrow, fringed wings. The hindwings have a distinctive pointed extension that is best examined under magnification. Kernels may look fairly intact until emergence, although feeding has hollowed them internally. Round holes can also be made by grain weevils, so the hole alone does not distinguish the cause. Unlike several other storage moths, this species does not tie the grain together with conspicuous external silk. Save an adult and a representative grain sample for identification rather than relying only on visible damage.
actions: Separate a suspect lot from clean grain and ask an extension stored-products specialist or grain inspector how to sample it. Clean spilled grain, old residues, and handling equipment before new grain enters storage. Keep records of the lot, storage conditions, and where moths are found. Appropriate drying, aeration, and sound storage structures reduce favorable conditions, but they are not a substitute for checking concealed infestations. Do not spray household insecticide into food or feed. Any commercial fumigation must be handled by qualified professionals under the applicable rules; it is not a do-it-yourself response.

sources.label: Canadian Grain Commission: Angoumois grain moth
FAO: Sitotroga cerealella in stored-product pest identification
University of Kentucky: Insect Pests of Stored Grain - Angoumois Grain Moth

identification: Uneven yellowing, mosaic patterns, distorted leaves, or stem injury may raise suspicion, but none is a reliable visual diagnosis of this virus. Nutrient stress, other viruses, and mixed infections can look similar. Whiteflies on a crop establish that a possible vector is present, not that the plants carry cowpea mild mottle virus. A plant diagnostic laboratory can use molecular testing to identify the infection. Useful records include the crop and cultivar, planting date, seed lot, symptom distribution, and any photographs showing changes over time.
actions: Contact a crop adviser or diagnostic laboratory before sending samples, and follow its packaging instructions. Mark affected areas and avoid moving suspect plants or saved seed into clean production while the diagnosis is being resolved. Monitor whiteflies and discuss prevention with the adviser as part of the whole crop system, including neighboring host plants and planting material. Insect control cannot reverse an infection already inside a plant. Do not destroy a field solely on leaf appearance or adopt a treatment threshold from another region without confirming that it applies to the crop and virus involved.

sources.label: Wei et al. 2021: Identification of a new genetic clade of cowpea mild mottle virus and interaction with soybean mosaic virus
Silva - UNESP thesis, chapter 1: Effects of cowpea mild mottle virus on soybean cultivars in Brazil
EPPO: Carlavirus vignae identity and common names

identification: The long awn bends sharply and twists near its base. Mature flower units usually shed together in a pair, although threshing or other processing may separate them. A prominent hairy base and papery tips are useful under magnification. Wild oat, Avena fatua, has similar elongated, hairy, awned units, but they generally shed separately and are often smaller. A green oat-like seedling cannot reliably settle the distinction. Photograph the mature panicle and intact seed units, and retain a sample for a seed-testing or weed-identification laboratory.
actions: Use reliably cleaned planting seed and investigate an unfamiliar oat in a cereal seed lot before sowing it. In a field, mark patches early and discuss a crop-specific plan with an agronomist before seed sheds. Clean harvesting and transport equipment after working through an infested patch, and keep contaminated grain or straw separate from clean planting material. Follow-up needs to include later seedlings, not just the standing plants seen on one visit. Seed and weed rules vary by jurisdiction and crop, so check applicable requirements with the supplier or local agricultural authority.

sources.label: Canadian Food Inspection Agency: Weed Seed - Avena sterilis

identification: Look for feathery leaves with soft hairs and sometimes pale silvery markings. Hollow flowering stalks support umbrella-shaped clusters of small flowers. The mature fruits are relatively long, curved, and brown, providing useful characters after flowering. Scent can support an identification but should never replace the leaves, fruit, and a regional botanical key. Several carrot-family plants resemble one another, including dangerously poisonous species. Do not taste a leaf or root to decide which one is present, and do not assume an old garden label is a reliable identification.
actions: For a garden plant that is spreading too freely, remove developing seed heads before they shed and watch nearby damp, lightly shaded ground for seedlings. If removing an established plant, account for its substantial root system and avoid scattering root pieces into compost or soil moved elsewhere. Revisit the spot for regrowth. In a natural area, first confirm that the plant is Myrrhis rather than a native Osmorhiza, then record the patch and consult the land manager about intervention. Keep suspected plants separate from harvested herbs until their identity has been settled.

sources.label: University of Oxford Plants 400: Myrrhis odorata
Native Plant Trust Go Botany: Myrrhis odorata

identification: Lower leaves are deeply lobed, usually with a large end lobe, while upper leaves become smaller and less divided. Stems and leaves can have stiff, simple hairs. The strongest clue is the mature fruit: a narrow lower section supports a rounded, ribbed upper section ending in a slender beak. Many yellow-flowered mustards instead have elongated pods, so photographs should include developed fruits as well as blossoms. Leaf shape varies along the stem. A picture of only the youngest rosette can therefore be misleading even when the plant is correctly named.
actions: Check disturbed field edges and newly opened ground before fruits mature. In a small garden patch, remove the confirmed plant with its taproot while the soil allows it to lift cleanly, and collect fruiting stems without shaking them over bare ground. Avoid carrying seed-bearing debris on mowing or earthmoving equipment to another site. In a roadside or conservation area, identify nearby native plants and work with the land manager on timing rather than clearing every yellow flower. Record the patch and inspect for new seedlings after removal; stopping seed return is a practical objective, not a promise of immediate eradication.

sources.label: University of Texas: Vascular Plants of Williamson County, Rapistrum rugosum
University of Sydney: Rapistrum, Vascular Plants of the Sydney Region

identification: Leaves have a boat-shaped tip and are folded in the bud. A small, pale membrane stands at the junction of leaf blade and sheath. Flowerheads are open, branched clusters that can appear at very low mowing heights. Kentucky bluegrass and rough bluegrass also have boat-shaped tips, so that feature is not exclusive to Poa annua. They generally look darker; Kentucky bluegrass spreads through underground stems and rough bluegrass through surface runners. Examine several plants, including the leaf junctions and growth at the base, before deciding which grass is invading the turf.
actions: Remove isolated plants before they seed and return regularly, because later seedlings can replace the first ones. Clean mowers and other maintenance equipment after working in an infested area. Repair bare spots with suitable turf or planting cover, and adjust irrigation so the surface is not kept constantly wet when the desired plants do not need it. Mowing lower is unlikely to solve the problem. For a heavily infested lawn or golf surface, ask a turf specialist to assess the desired grass and persistent bluegrass forms before choosing a program; one treatment rarely fits every site.

sources.label: University of California IPM: Annual bluegrass
Iowa State University Extension: Annual bluegrass

identification: Look for flat blades and a dense oval to short cylindrical head. The overlapping outer flower bracts are pale cream to green, marked with darker green veins and broad wings toward their upper ends. At the leaf junction, a pale membranous ligule has an irregular edge. Other canarygrasses may also make compact heads, so a mature spikelet examined with a hand lens is more useful than head shape alone. Photograph the bracts, leaf junction, and whole tuft. A persistent spreading stand should prompt a particularly careful check that the species name is right.
actions: Around bird-feeding areas, clean up accumulated seed and check adjoining beds for seedlings before they form new heads. Small unwanted plants can be lifted with their fibrous roots; collect mature heads separately so seed is not shaken onto fresh soil. Keep birdseed out of restoration seed mixes and do not scatter it as a way to establish wildlife grass cover. If plants recur away from an obvious spill, record the site and consult a local botanist about establishment. In a crop or seed-production setting, use identification and seed-purity advice tailored to that system rather than a reed-canarygrass control plan.

sources.label: University of British Columbia E-Flora BC: Phalaris canariensis
Flora of New Zealand: Phalaris canariensis

identification: Flowers are white or pale violet, and the upright stems carry narrow leaves with teeth or shallow divisions. The stems may have short hairs. Once flowering finishes, look for small flattened fruits with broad wings and a notch at the top; the flower cluster has by then stretched into a longer fruiting stalk. Other candytufts are grown in gardens, including perennial kinds, so check the plant base and mature fruit rather than relying on flower color. A persistent woody base would not fit the ordinary annual habit described for this species.
actions: If seedlings are appearing where they are not wanted, remove or deadhead plants before the winged fruits mature. Collect ripe fruiting stems carefully and avoid spreading their contents with garden soil or discarded bedding plants. In a maintained border, decide whether limited self-seeding is acceptable and watch the boundary with neighboring habitat. An isolated escape can usually be documented and assessed without treating the whole surrounding area. For repeated establishment in a conservation site, ask the land manager to confirm the identification and choose a response that protects nearby native annuals. Follow-up seedlings matter more than the appearance of the first removed plant.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Iberis amara

identification: The plant forms small tufts with very narrow, often inrolled blades. Its slender, sometimes nodding flowerhead is commonly partly enclosed by the uppermost leaf sheath. Under magnification, the two outer bracts of each spikelet are strikingly unequal, with the lower one much shorter. Squirreltail fescue, Vulpia bromoides, is a close comparison, usually with a more exposed flowerhead and a relatively longer lower bract. These are small characters: keep a mature head with its upper leaf sheath attached when seeking confirmation, rather than sending only a few loose bristles.
actions: Scout cereal fields and margins early enough to prevent another seed crop. Mark patches and work with an agronomist on rotation and the timing of operations between crops; measures need to fit the soil-conservation system as well as the weed. Keep contaminated seed-bearing residue and equipment from carrying the grass into clean fields. Small noncrop patches can be removed before seed shed, followed by checks during later cool-season emergence. Ask for current local recommendations, and do not assume that one season without visible plants means the seed reserve is gone.

sources.label: Ball et al. 2008: Biological Attributes of Rattail Fescue
Flora of New Zealand: Vulpia myuros
Flora of New Zealand: Vulpia bromoides comparison

identification: The leaves are simple, opposite, and toothed. Flowers are whitish to pale yellow, with a hooded upper lip and a more open lower lip. Several small flowers occur together around the upper part of the stem. Other Stachys and pale-flowered mint relatives can resemble it, especially before flowering. Look at the complete plant, leaf attachment, flower shape, and whether the base shows an annual or persistent growth habit. Avoid identifying it from a leaf pair alone. Photographs that include both lower and upper leaves help a regional botanist make the comparison.
actions: For an unfamiliar patch in a field margin, record its location and obtain confirmation before broad weed control. Where the plant is unwanted in a cultivated bed, removing young plants before seed matures is a proportionate first step. Collect mature flowering stems rather than carrying loose seed through the garden. Watch the disturbed spot for replacement seedlings and maintain suitable crop or garden cover. In a meadow or conservation area, coordinate with the land manager so similar native mint-family plants are spared. For a large agricultural infestation, obtain crop-specific local advice rather than borrowing a control program for a perennial mint.

sources.label: Native Plant Trust Go Botany: Stachys annua
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew: Stachys annua

identification: Leaves are opposite, oval to narrower and pointed, with toothed edges. The upright stems branch freely and are mostly hairless. Male flowers form conspicuous slender spikes above the leaf joints; female flowers occur much closer to the stem, singly or in small groups. The fruit is a small, distinctly lobed capsule. Nettles and other plain green weeds may look similar at a glance, but flower arrangement is much more useful than leaf color. If both flower sexes occur on one plant, have a botanist check the taxonomic interpretation rather than forcing an identification.
actions: Keep a flowering specimen or detailed photographs with any report, including the leaf shape and position of both flower types. For a few unwanted plants in cultivated ground, remove them before capsules mature and avoid shaking seed-bearing material over clean soil. Check later seedlings and keep a record if the patch expands. Nursery or agricultural findings deserve a local diagnostic review before a risk label or treatment program is chosen. Do not assume that California spread reports or restrictions written for M. ambigua apply to every annual-mercury record. Use the confirmed scientific name when requesting management advice.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Mercurialis annua
USDA APHIS: Weed Risk Assessment for Mercurialis annua, 2016

identification: The plant forms a tuft, with stems sometimes bent at their lower joints. Blades are narrow and flat, and the leaf junction has a thin, pale membrane with a ragged tip; there are no clasping ear-like lobes. The dense head can be cylindrical or somewhat lobed. A close view reveals many fine awns on the outer flower bracts, creating the fluffy appearance. Other Polypogon species, including ditch polypogon, can occur in similar places. Keep the leaf junction and mature head in identification photographs rather than relying on fuzziness alone.
actions: In an irrigated bed or orchard, check whether a leaking line or unnecessary surface watering is maintaining the patch. Remove small confirmed plants before seed ripens and collect mature heads without scattering them. Reinspect during the next favorable growing period, since the timing may differ between climates. Clean mud and seed from equipment before leaving a wet infested area. At a pond, stream, or wetland, do not drain the habitat or strip the bank simply to remove this grass. Ask the site manager to weigh the extent of the patch, nearby native vegetation, and an appropriate low-disturbance response.

sources.label: University of California IPM: Rabbitfoot polypogon
Flora of New Zealand: Polypogon monspeliensis

identification: Leaves are narrow and glossy, particularly underneath, and new leaves are rolled in the bud. At the leaf junction, conspicuous little claw-like lobes clasp the stem. The flowering spike carries alternating spikelets, commonly with long awns. Lower sheaths may be reddish. Perennial ryegrass, Lolium perenne, is very similar, so examine the leaf-bud arrangement and mature flowering structures rather than judging from lush green foliage alone. Closely related ryegrasses and cultivated material can complicate identification; a specialist may need a complete flowering plant.
actions: Before sowing a cover crop or temporary lawn mixture, check the seed label and plan how the stand will be ended before it produces unwanted seed. In a grain field, map patches early and seek crop-specific advice while control options are still practical. Avoid mixing seed from a weedy patch into clean planting stock, and clean equipment when moving between fields. For a few plants in a garden bed, remove the crown and fibrous roots before flowering. Persistent or recurring populations need follow-up and a reviewed management plan, rather than repeated reliance on the same unverified treatment.

sources.label: University of Missouri Weed ID: Italian ryegrass

identification: Lower leaves have toothed or lobed margins, sometimes with broad triangular lobes. The flowering stems usually carry relatively few leaves and lack a woody base. Flowers have four small yellow petals, followed by long narrow pods on short stalks. Perennial wallrocket, Diplotaxis tenuifolia, tends to have leafier stems and larger flowers, but fruit attachment and other key characters are needed for a dependable separation. Include the basal leaves, whole stem, flowers, and mature pods in photographs. A cropped image of one yellow blossom leaves out most of the useful evidence.
actions: In a maintained path or vegetable bed, remove unwanted rosettes or young flowering plants before pods ripen. Collect mature pods carefully so the seeds do not spill into adjacent soil, and inspect disturbed spots for replacement plants. Avoid spreading contaminated soil or mowing debris along another verge. On walls or fragile historic masonry, do not wrench out roots without the owner's advice, since removal can damage the structure. In a natural area, confirm the species and document its extent before choosing broader control. An isolated verge plant does not by itself show that neighboring habitat is being damaged.

sources.label: Natural History Museum Vienna: Diplotaxis muralis
Royal Botanic Gardens Kew: Diplotaxis muralis
Flora of New Zealand: Diplotaxis muralis
Flora of New Zealand: Diplotaxis tenuifolia comparison

identification: Inspect a flowering stem and a mature pod together. The flowers are only a few millimeters long, while the small pods have a netted surface and contain very few seeds. Yellow flowers alone do not separate it from yellow sweetclover, and a three-leaflet leaf can also suggest several other legumes. Include the whole plant, leaflet margins and a close view of the fruit when requesting identification. A plant lacking flowers or pods may need another visit.
actions: In a cultivated bed, remove confirmed unwanted plants before their pods mature, keeping disturbed soil to a minimum. Check the surrounding ground after rain or irrigation for another flush of seedlings. In an orchard or vineyard, discuss the vegetation-management objective with the grower before clearing all legumes from the floor. Note whether it is interfering with the crop or simply occupying bare ground, and choose a response that fits that use. Keep seed-bearing material out of planting mixes and avoid using a different sweetclover's impacts as the reason for removal.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Melilotus indicus

identification: A tiny ant emerging from a hollow twig is a useful observation, not a species diagnosis. Document the nest material and its height above the ground as well as magnified views of workers. Other small arboreal ants can occupy the same sort of cavity. Longino's Costa Rican account uses a broad species concept and explicitly raises the possibility of hidden species, so those colonies should not automatically be equated with every Florida record. Preserve the locality information with any specimen.
actions: Where ants are living in outdoor vegetation without causing a practical problem, leave the nesting material undisturbed. A native Florida ant should not be targeted simply because it appears in this catalog. If workers enter a building, trace their route and seek identification before deciding what needs attention; an indoor sighting does not establish that the outdoor colony is an introduced pest. Avoid moving occupied twigs with nursery plants to a different area. Record an unusual occurrence through a local entomology or natural-history program rather than trying to establish a colony elsewhere.

sources.label: Moreau, Deyrup and Davis 2014: Ants of the Florida Keys
John T. Longino: Tapinoma litorale natural history

identification: The spring founder on dogwood and later root-feeding generations should not be compared as though they were the same form. Closely related Anoecia, especially A. corni, require a specialist key and microscopic characters. Record the exact host, the feeding site and whether the insects have wings. The original founder description was based on collected insects associated with a verified colony, not on color alone. Avoid attaching a precise body-size estimate to an uncertain field photograph.
actions: On a dogwood, photograph the occupied shoot before disturbing it; for insects already exposed on grass roots, retain the root and host information together. Ask an extension diagnostic service how to submit a small sample. Do not excavate a lawn or remove a dogwood merely to search for a suspected seasonal connection. A winged aphid caught in a trap needs identification before it can support a local occurrence record. If plants are declining, investigate moisture, roots and other pests as well; this species' contribution to local damage remains unresolved.

sources.label: Depa and Mroz 2014: Description of fundatrix of Anoecia vagans
Wieczorek et al. 2012: male genitalia of Aphididae

identification: Compare suspected colonies with spirea aphid, Aphis spiraecola, rather than deciding from their shared greenish appearance. Reliable separation uses tiny features that are difficult to capture in a casual garden photograph. Keep several images of adults, the occupied shoot and the host's leaves. Loquat is especially relevant to Florida observations, while the older Asian host emphasis differs. A plant label and collection location therefore belong with the identification request, but neither replaces examination of the aphids themselves.
actions: For a loquat or other valued shrub, mark affected shoots and check whether new growth is becoming distorted or losing vigor. Keep an infested nursery plant apart from clean stock while identification is arranged, and inspect plants that arrived with it. Ask local extension staff to distinguish a consequential colony from a small transient presence before selecting control. Preserve predatory insects found with the colony. The available species accounts do not justify assuming virus transmission or applying a treatment schedule intended for spirea aphid; the response should match the confirmed insect and actual plant injury.

sources.label: Skelley et al. 2025: Adventive arthropods in Florida, 1990-2023

identification: Examine the grass base and exposed roots, where the waxy colony can resemble pale debris or other small sap-feeding insects. Record whether wax coats separate insects and whether they are actually attached to the plant. Bermudagrass is a documented host, but that association cannot by itself identify the aphid. A root-feeding specimen should be checked with a microscopic key, since aboveground aphid photographs are poor comparisons. Do not infer the species from a bare or yellow lawn patch alone.
actions: If a colony is discovered during routine turf work, photograph it in place and keep the grass identification with the observation. Compare the affected patch with nearby healthy turf and note irrigation, compaction or recent disturbance. Consult a turf or insect specialist before treating the soil; a yellow patch can have several causes, and the hidden aphids may not explain all of the decline. Avoid transporting occupied sod or rooted nursery material to another site while the diagnosis is pending. Extensive digging solely to find hidden insects can damage the turf and obscure other causes of decline.

sources.label: Silva - Occurrence of Asiphonella dactylonii on bermudagrass in Bahia; Brazilian Entomology Congress abstract

identification: The flattened body and waxy border can suggest an armored or soft scale at first glance. Look for individual insects rather than treating a white-edged patch as a single growth on the leaf. Distinguishing C. lataniae from C. brasiliensis requires finer anatomy than the outline usually reveals. An Amazonian study corrected earlier palm records from lataniae to brasiliensis, illustrating why an old name on a photograph or host list may need rechecking. Save the palm identification and collection history.
actions: Inspect newly acquired palms before placing them beside established plants, particularly the parts carrying visible colonies. If an identification is uncertain, keep the plant separate and ask a diagnostic service what material it needs. Do not assume that wax means the insects are dead, or scrape living palm tissue to expose them. Record plant condition as well as insect numbers. Treatment or claims of damage attributed to C. brasiliensis should not be applied automatically to this name; a confirmed species and a local assessment are needed before choosing a response.

sources.label: Lunz et al. 2011 - Cerataphis brasiliensis: correct identification of aphids on Amazonian palms

identification: Reddish curled leaves on hawthorn and wax-dusted aphids around carrot crowns describe different parts of a complicated species group. Record which host is involved and where insects are feeding. Look beneath loose surface soil only where roots are already being inspected; a curled leaf or poor carrot growth is not enough to identify the aphid. Ordinary morphology cannot reliably separate this species from D. apiifolia and D. foeniculus; a specialist may need additional evidence. American carrot populations should not be assumed to alternate with hawthorn simply because some European populations do.
actions: In a vegetable bed, compare affected carrots with nearby plants and check whether aphids are actually present at the crown or roots. Ask a crop adviser to evaluate the colony before treating, since a crop symptom alone does not identify the aphid responsible. Keep root samples and their plant labels together for diagnosis. Do not remove nearby hawthorns as an automatic control measure: the seasonal connection may not apply to the local population. A harvest problem should be assessed for soil conditions and other root pests as well as aphids.

identification: Turn over several linden leaves and look for the insects themselves, their shed skins and fresh droplets beneath the canopy. Sticky paving and blackened surfaces can reveal a colony before leaves show much change, but neither sign is unique to linden aphid. Wing markings and the dark lateral pattern help support an identification. Inspect more than one branch and compare young trees with established specimens; the practical significance of feeding depends on the condition and size of the host.
actions: Decide whether the main concern is a sticky surface or deteriorating tree growth. Wash affected outdoor objects as needed and monitor the tree rather than treating nuisance honeydew as proof that a mature linden is dying. Young or stressed trees deserve closer assessment. Look for predators before choosing an intervention, and seek local tree-care advice if growth is reduced. Avoid a calendar spray based only on last year's honeydew. A professional should account for the tree, site and beneficial insects before considering any pesticide treatment.

identification: Check whether the conspicuous feature is an ant-built mound rather than a lesion made directly by aphid feeding. A pale insect among roots cannot be identified as Geoica from color alone. Photograph the turf surface, the mound and any already exposed root colony separately. Record the ant association without assuming that the ant and aphid share the same origin or pest status. Microscopic examination may be needed to distinguish the aphid from other root inhabitants.
actions: For a lawn or sports surface, map the mounds and note whether they interfere with use or cover living grass. Ask a turf specialist to investigate the ant-aphid association before selecting a response aimed only at one partner. Avoid repeatedly opening large areas of healthy turf to locate insects. If a sample is requested, keep the roots, aphids and associated ants clearly labeled by location. Keep photographs from later visits so the adviser can see whether the mounds are increasing, remaining stable or disappearing between maintenance operations.

sources.label: USDA ARS: Geoica setulosa occurrence and turfgrass ant association

identification: Root-feeding wingless individuals and winged migrants can differ in wax and dark markings, so compare like forms when using a key. Keep the morning-glory identification and the root attachment with the specimen record. Other waxy insects also inhabit roots; loose white material alone is not diagnostic. The possible connection to Pistacia in some literature remains uncertain and should not be used as a shortcut to identify a colony or reconstruct its seasonal movements.
actions: When insects appear during repotting or root inspection, set that plant aside and seek advice about submitting a labeled sample. Avoid carrying its soil or rooted pieces to another garden until the colony is identified. Document whether the host is actually wilting or losing growth; the aphid's presence does not establish the cause of every root problem. Do not remove a nearby Pistacia tree in an attempt to interrupt an unproven life cycle. Keep the first photographs and compare the same plant on later visits so new feeding and changes in growth can be assessed together.

sources.label: Casarrubias Trujillo 2004 - Aphid fauna of Chihuahua, species 59

identification: The unusually long, hairy tubes at the back of a Greenidea aphid are a strong clue to the genus. To separate G. ficicola from G. psidii, a specialist examines their surface pattern and other fine structures. Photograph the insect from above and from the side if possible, along with the fig's youngest leaves. An aphid found on Ficus is not necessarily this species, and a single flying insect should not be described as an established feeding colony.
actions: Inspect tender fig growth when bringing ornamental plants into a collection. If colonies are present, keep the affected plant apart while seeking an identification, and check nearby plants that shared its nursery source. Record changes in leaf growth rather than judging severity only by the unusual appearance of the aphids. Avoid moving infested cuttings between homes or gardens. A local horticultural adviser can help decide whether a small colony warrants action. Keep photographs of the same shoots over time, including new leaves that remain healthy, so the adviser can assess the plant rather than just a close-up of the insects.

sources.label: Halbert 2004 - The genus Greenidea in the United States

identification: A coating of pale wax on a slender green aphid is not enough to distinguish the almond-associated member of this group. Hyalopterus pruni and other closely related forms can overlap in general appearance and host use. Photograph the colony and identify the Prunus host carefully, then obtain a specialist determination when the record matters. The molecular and morphological revision shows why a name based solely on almond, peach or reed can be misleading. Preserve the season and location as supporting evidence.
actions: In an orchard, record colony distribution and plant symptoms and ask an adviser to confirm which Hyalopterus is involved. Keep a few occupied shoots available for diagnosis rather than treating every waxy aphid as the same pest. Do not clear nearby reeds solely on the assumption that they are the source of the orchard population. Ask that the identification report state any remaining uncertainty within the species group, especially when comparing records from another region. Management should follow the confirmed insect, crop and observed injury, with attention to beneficial insects already present.

sources.label: Lozier et al. 2008 - Molecular and morphological evaluation of Hyalopterus; USDA technical abstract
2013 European Hyalopterus morphology and COI study

identification: Inspect currant shoots in spring and the stems or flower-bearing growth of nearby sowthistles when documenting a seasonal change. Similar green aphids can occur on both plants, so host sequence is evidence to record rather than proof of identity. Include winged and wingless individuals if available. Yellowing or curled leaves can reflect feeding, disease or other stress. A suspected lettuce virus needs plant-diagnostic testing; seeing an aphid cannot confirm either infection or the direction in which a virus moved.
actions: In a currant planting or vegetable garden, inspect incoming plants and note whether colonies persist or increase. If lettuce develops unusual symptoms, contact an extension plant clinic and provide the crop history and aphid observations together. Avoid moving symptomatic plants or infested sowthistles between growing areas. Manage unwanted sowthistles before seed dispersal as part of the garden's weed plan, without claiming that their removal alone prevents disease. Seek locally appropriate advice before treating: the original seasonal study was conducted in New Zealand, and its calendar should not be copied unchanged to another climate.

sources.label: Leong 1977 - Biological and ecological studies of the currant-sowthistle aphid; Lincoln University abstract

identification: Look just below the flower heads of an identified oxtongue or hawksbeard, and record the exact host rather than calling every yellow-flowered plant a thistle. The aphid's glossy yellow-green appearance can resemble other species. Fine antennal and rear-tube characters require magnification and a suitable key. A swollen, brownish aphid may instead be a parasitized individual; retain photographs of those forms with the living colony. Their presence provides ecological context but is not a species diagnosis by itself.
actions: For a small outdoor colony without evident plant injury, observation is more informative than an immediate general insect treatment. Mark the host and compare the colony on later visits, noting predators or parasitoid mummies. If the host is an unwanted weed, manage the plant according to the site's vegetation plan rather than trying to eradicate an aphid independently of it. Ask for specialist identification before reporting a new locality. The French parasitoid study demonstrates a natural-enemy association there; it does not establish the same wasps, impact or control outcome in a U.S. garden.

sources.label: Generalist Aphid Parasitoids Behave as Specialists at the Agroecosystem Scale, 2020

identification: Search the upper parts of an identified tansy plant, including developing flower heads, for loose aphid colonies. Other aphids also use tansy, and the host alone cannot separate them. Photograph a complete insect and its feeding position rather than only a crowded patch. A laboratory or garden experiment on this species can explain responses to plant conditions, but it does not show that every colony has the same effect on a wild tansy stand.
actions: If tansy is being removed as an unwanted plant, contain its reproductive material and follow the local plant-management plan; there is no need to move the aphid colony onto another host. On a retained ornamental, compare new growth and colony size over time before deciding that intervention is necessary. Preserve predators observed with the aphids. Do not add fertilizer simply to change aphid numbers: experimental responses depended on plant nutrition and competition. For persistent injury, bring photographs of occupied and healthy shoots to a local adviser, together with the recent watering and fertilizer history.

sources.label: Mahdavi Arab et al. 2014 - Aphid-tansy experimental study

identification: The purple marking is a useful clue, but its shape varies and it should be considered with the long black appendages and pale body. Check that the host is a true lily, Lilium, rather than another ornamental called a lily. Photograph a single aphid as well as the colony and developing buds. Related Macrosiphum can have similarly long legs and rear tubes. Winged forms may occur alongside wingless ones; that difference alone does not indicate two pest species.
actions: Inspect tender growth on newly purchased lilies before placing them among established plants. Where a small colony is accessible, a gentle stream of water can dislodge aphids without treating the whole bed; avoid damaging delicate buds. Recheck the plants and look for predators or parasitized aphids before escalating control. Honeydew is a reason to inspect, not proof of serious plant injury. If growth remains distorted or colonies repeatedly rebuild, ask a local horticultural adviser for a diagnosis. Do not use a guessed seasonal migration schedule to decide when treatment is needed.

sources.label: NC State Extension: Purplespotted lily aphid
University of Maryland Extension: Aphids in home gardens

identification: Start with a reliable identification of the grass. Miscanthus is a much stronger clue for this aphid than a general resemblance to a cereal or sugarcane aphid. Color can range across tan and purplish individuals and is not a dependable separator. Photograph the insects on the blade or sheath and ask a specialist to examine adults if an exact record is needed. Reports from ornamental trade material should be kept distinct from evidence of establishment in surrounding natural vegetation.
actions: Inspect Miscanthus plants arriving from another nursery and note whether a colony persists after planting. Keep occupied divisions separate from clean stock while identification is pending, and avoid distributing them to other gardens. Monitor the plant's condition instead of treating the presence of a Melanaphis as an automatic crop emergency. If new leaves remain healthy, record the colony and recheck it rather than assuming a crop emergency. For continuing decline, bring both the aphid and grass identification to a local adviser.

sources.label: Skelley et al. 2025 - Adventive arthropods in Florida, Melanaphis sorini account

identification: A pale grass aphid with dark markings on its winged form needs closer examination before assigning it to this species or one of its subspecies. Record the grass host and retain the original level of determination in the observation. The cereal-associated form has been distinguished by anatomical characters, not merely by finding an insect in wheat. A winged adult landing in a field may have arrived from another host; document feeding colonies separately from isolated flying insects.
actions: On wild grasses, begin with photographs and a specialist identification rather than clearing the vegetation. If the insects occur in a crop, ask the diagnostic service explicitly whether it can resolve cerealium or only the broader species. Keep that answer with the monitoring record. Do not apply greenhouse crop-loss findings for cerealium to every M. festucae observation. Revisit occupied plants to establish whether a colony is reproducing and whether injury develops. A treatment decision should use the confirmed taxon, crop condition and current regional advice, not a catalog name alone.

sources.label: Michaud 2018 - Metopolophium festucae cerealium, a new aphid in Kansas wheat

identification: Inspect several wheat leaves and shoots for both winged and wingless insects. The pale body and dark dorsal markings of winged adults help recognition, but an adviser should distinguish this form from other cereal aphids. Record crop stage and whether nymphs are present. Kansas's initial detection involved winged specimens, so a new adult sighting should not automatically be described as a reproducing outbreak. Keep photographs and collection details with any submitted sample.
actions: Use regular field scouting to follow the colony and its natural enemies rather than responding to a single trapped aphid. Pay attention to later-maturing wheat and to neighboring spring cereals as the season advances, as Kansas guidance recommends vigilance in those situations. Consult local crop advisers when numbers or injury increase. The Pacific Northwest researchers distinguished greenhouse effects from field injury that still required evaluation; do not turn a laboratory result into an invented economic threshold. Preserve existing biological control and avoid a routine spray simply because the aphid is newly recorded.

sources.label: Michaud 2018 - Metopolophium festucae cerealium, a new aphid in Kansas wheat
REACCH investigators - Insects: expanding distribution of a newly introduced aphid

identification: Inspect young leaves along the midrib and note whether the colony is on rose or shrubby cinquefoil. A small green aphid on a rose is not necessarily the familiar large rose aphid, and several Myzaphis species require detailed examination. The modern revision compared museum specimens and fine surface characters to clarify those names. Photograph the host and the insects from more than one angle. Preserve winged and wingless forms separately in the observation so their differences do not create a false second species.
actions: In a garden, mark a few occupied shoots and check their growth on later visits. If the colony is small and the plant is developing normally, observation can provide better evidence than an immediate broad treatment. Keep newly acquired plants apart from existing roses while an uncertain infestation is identified. Avoid spreading occupied cuttings or divisions. For persistent distortion or loss of vigor, request a local diagnosis rather than using another rose aphid's threshold. Include close views of the leaf midrib and a whole-shoot photograph, so the adviser can compare the insects with the pattern of plant injury.

sources.label: Kanturski et al. 2018 - A comparative morphological revision of Myzaphis

identification: A tightly rolled, reddish peach leaf is a reason to inspect inside the roll, not a diagnosis by itself. Record whether pale wingless aphids or darker winged forms are present and compare unaffected leaves on the same tree. Other peach aphids and non-insect problems can distort foliage. A specialist may need actual insects to separate the species. Keep photographs of the leaf damage and aphids together; disease symptoms and vector identity are two questions that require different evidence.
actions: Avoid moving infested peach shoots or cuttings to another planting while identification is pending. If an orchard has unusual symptoms suggesting a virus, contact a plant-diagnostic service and follow its sampling instructions. Do not conclude that nearby clematis is infected merely because experimental transmission has been demonstrated. Monitor young peach growth and natural enemies, and obtain regional advice before intervention. Keep notes on the first affected shoots and subsequent new growth. Do not remove nearby clematis in the hope of controlling a disease that has not been diagnosed.

sources.label: Manachini et al. 2004 - Transmissibility of PPV by Myzus varians to Clematis vitalba

identification: Look beneath an identified chrysanthemum leaf and photograph individual aphids as well as yellowed tissue. The pale color is shared by other aphids and cannot resolve this name. Specialists compare the shape and stems of tiny body hairs with P. glandulosus and related forms. A greenhouse label or an older record using chrysanthemi is useful history, but it does not settle the taxonomic boundary. Keep a sample's plant source and date attached to the identification request.
actions: Set an occupied chrysanthemum apart from clean stock while the insects are examined, especially before distributing cuttings. Compare new leaves with older affected foliage and record whether discoloration continues after the colony changes. Yellowing can also reflect growing conditions, so avoid attributing every symptom to aphids without inspection. Ask the diagnostic service to state whether the identification is definite or part of a species complex. Keep that qualification with the plant record and use the confirmed pest identity and plant condition to guide local advice.

sources.label: Amin et al. 2023: new alien aphid data from Pakistan

identification: On honeysuckle, look for occupied leaf rolls and record the color of adults and young. On grasses, photograph the feeding location and identify the grass rather than assuming that any wetland colony is the summer form. Ask a specialist to compare the seasonal forms; a pair of similar-looking colonies on honeysuckle and grass does not prove that one moved between the plants. Other honeysuckle and grass aphids require a suitable key. Preserve the season, locality and host for both kinds of observation.
actions: If honeysuckle growth is affected, inspect a few rolled leaves and monitor subsequent shoots before treating the whole shrub. Do not remove vegetation along a waterway simply to interrupt a presumed aphid migration. A grass may itself need management for a separate reason, but that decision should use the site's plant and habitat plan. Avoid transporting occupied cuttings between gardens. Request specialist confirmation for a new locality or substantial injury; include the exact host and season so observations from honeysuckle are not confused with those from grasses.

sources.label: Andrew Jensen, AphidTrek: Rhopalomyzus field observations

identification: This root aphid is commonly listed under the spelling Rhopalosiphum rufiabdominale. Look at insects actually attached to exposed roots rather than diagnosing from yellow foliage alone. A rusty rear patch may help recognition, but other root aphids can overlap in color. Document the crop, potting medium and feeding position. A specialist examination is particularly useful when winged individuals appear away from the roots and could be mistaken for a different aphid.
actions: Inspect roots during normal repotting or when a diagnostic sample is needed, and separate an occupied container from clean stock. Keep reused pots and tools free of old roots and loose growing medium. Do not exchange infested plants or root divisions while the cause is unresolved. The recent host-choice experiment found differences in preference and reproduction, but it did not prove a practical trap-crop control system. Seek crop-specific advice for persistent injury and consider irrigation, root disease and other pests alongside the aphid rather than assuming one explanation for poor growth.

sources.label: Ong et al. 2025 - Rice Root Aphids Preferentially Choose and Multiply Faster on Monocotyledonous Plants

identification: Check damp-site grasses carefully with magnification; the insects are small enough to disappear against a leaf blade. A pale dorsal stripe differs from a reddish body tint, and neither alone proves identity. The identification handbook uses body hairs and microscopic surface features to separate this species from other Sipha. Record sedge or rush hosts accurately if those are involved. Do not assume that a green grass aphid is the black cereal-associated S. maydis simply because both belong to this genus.
actions: For a colony in wet vegetation, photograph the host and feeding site before disturbing it. Keep observations from a natural margin separate from those in a crop or managed lawn. Do not drain or clear damp habitat solely to remove an uncertain aphid population. If plants show substantial injury, submit a labeled sample and ask for a species-level diagnosis before choosing management. A record of the same patch over several visits can help distinguish a brief colony from persistent feeding associated with declining growth.

sources.label: Halbert, Miller & Ames 2013 - The genus Sipha in North America; USDA abstract
Stroyan 1977 - Royal Entomological Society identification handbook, Sipha glyceriae, pages 39-41

identification: Inspect the bases of grass leaves and look for compact dark aphids with conspicuous stiff hairs. That appearance helps separate them from many green cereal aphids, but confirm the insect rather than relying on leaf injury. Record the crop, growth stage and whether young are present with adults. A dark colony on a non-grass host needs particular scrutiny. If disease is suspected, have the plant tested; a possible vector's presence does not identify a virus or demonstrate transmission at the site.
actions: In a cereal field, map occupied areas and compare their plant condition with unoccupied portions of the crop. Contact local agricultural extension when a new or increasing colony is found, providing clear photographs and collection details. Preserve predators and avoid moving occupied grass material to a clean planting. Keep a dated record of the patches and any changes in leaf condition so an adviser can assess how the situation is developing. Management should use a confirmed identification and regional crop guidance rather than assuming that every black aphid warrants the same intervention.

sources.label: The genus Sipha in North America (Halbert, Miller and Ames, 2013)

identification: Verify that the tree is Chinese elm, then inspect the underside and veins of leaves for aphids. Pale blue-green bodies with white wax markings are useful clues, especially in winged forms, but other elm aphids can be similar. Include the whole leaf, its attachment and close insect views in a record. Seasonal observations from Australia should not be used to predict identical overwintering behavior in Florida or a northern U.S. planting. A specialist may need fine anatomical characters.
actions: Check new elm nursery stock before planting it beside established trees, and retain supplier information when a colony is found. On a landscape tree, follow leaf growth and colony density rather than treating an isolated winged aphid as a damaging infestation. Ask a diagnostic service to confirm an unfamiliar elm aphid before reporting a new locality. Avoid transporting infested shoots between sites. Photograph the same branches over time, including new leaves that remain healthy; any substantial injury should be assessed with the tree's overall condition and other stresses.

sources.label: Hales 2020: Overwintering biology of three Calaphidine aphids

identification: Inspect a fresh cherry leaf curl for the insects and photograph both its outer discoloration and sheltered interior. Dark adults and brighter young can occur together, so their different colors need not indicate separate species. Other Tuberocephalus and unrelated causes of leaf distortion complicate recognition. Record the cherry species and the collection date. An Artemisia association in the literature is not enough to identify aphids found on any nearby herb, especially where older Japanese names have been confused.
actions: On an ornamental cherry, mark affected shoots and watch whether new leaves develop normally. Avoid removing large healthy branches solely because some leaves are curled. If damage persists or young trees lose vigor, ask a local tree or insect specialist to examine occupied leaves. Do not excavate Artemisia roots or remove a surrounding herb layer in an attempt to interrupt an unverified local migration. Keep infested nursery plants from being shared until identified. Record when fresh curls first appear, since the timing of local growth and insect activity is more useful than a calendar copied from another climate.

identification: Check that the host is a Picris oxtongue, since superficially similar yellow-flowered composites can carry different aphids. The contrasting pale tail-like tip and darker rear tubes are more useful than a general reddish color. Photograph a complete adult beside the feeding position below a flower head. Related Uroleucon can require microscopic examination, and older records on other host genera may involve different species. A dried collection label is historical evidence, not proof of a living population at that site today.
actions: Leave a small colony on unmanaged vegetation in place while obtaining an identification if no plant-management problem is apparent. If the oxtongue is being removed as a weed, contain its seed heads and do not transfer occupied stems to another planting. Record predators or parasitoid mummies before disturbing the colony. For a proposed new locality, ask a specialist to verify both host and aphid. Include a flowering stem in the photographs so the host can be checked, and keep the original observation label if a later identification changes the name.

sources.label: Noordam 2004: Aphids of Java Part VI
Tizado and Nieto Nafria: A new species of Uroleucon on Andryala

identification: Look for a dry, swollen aphid shell and, after emergence, a neat round exit hole. These mummies show parasitoid activity, but other wasps also produce them, so they do not identify Aphidius ervi on their own. Adults are tiny and need close examination to separate from A. colemani and other parasitoids. The identity of the living aphids matters as well, because a wasp used for one pest is not automatically appropriate for every aphid in a greenhouse.
actions: When mummies appear among a crop's aphids, count them alongside living aphids and observe whether the pest population is changing. Avoid a broad insecticide application that could disrupt an already useful natural-enemy population without discussing alternatives with an adviser. If biological control is being considered, ask a qualified supplier or extension specialist to match the parasitoid to the confirmed aphid and growing conditions. Do not collect and release unidentified wasps outdoors or move mummies between unrelated sites. Finding this beneficial insect is not, by itself, a reason to attempt its removal.

sources.label: Kansas State University: Aphidius colemani and Aphidius ervi
Alabama Cooperative Extension: Practical tips for using biological control agents

identification: Inspect the tips and undersides of young apple leaves, including vigorous upright shoots. Green apple aphid and spirea aphid can be very difficult to distinguish in the field, so a specialist may be needed for an exact species record. Honeydew, shed skins and nearby predators help locate an active colony but do not settle its identity. Record whether the tree is young or established, because loss of tender growth can matter more to a developing tree.
actions: Monitor occupied shoots and their natural enemies before choosing treatment. A small colony on an established tree can be a different problem from persistent feeding on a young nursery tree. Ask local orchard advisers to interpret numbers, growth stage and injury rather than importing a threshold from another region. Avoid unnecessary stimulation of tender growth through excessive fertilization. If intervention is warranted, use current crop guidance and protect beneficial insects. Do not diagnose a plant virus from aphids or sooty mold alone; the sticky coating is evidence of feeding, not a disease test.

sources.label: University of California IPM: Green Apple Aphid
NC State Extension: Green Apple Aphid / Spirea Aphid

identification: Photograph a full leaf to show its paired leaflets, a flowering branch and any cylindrical pods. Several forms within the Cassia javanica group differ in leaflet shape, hairiness and the position of flower clusters. Pink blossoms are attractive but insufficient for separating those forms or all similarly named ornamental cassias. Keep a nursery name with the record without treating it as a botanical determination. An apple-like common name does not indicate an edible fruit or a relationship to apple trees.
actions: For an established ornamental, first decide whether the issue is ordinary tree care or actual escape beyond cultivation. Look for seedlings around the planting and record their distance from the parent tree. Remove unwanted young plants before they become difficult to manage, after confirming they are the same species. A large tree near structures should be assessed by an arborist rather than pruned heavily on the basis of its catalog listing. If seedlings persist outside the planting, share a dated location record with a local herbarium or land manager to help assess whether the tree is naturalizing there.

sources.label: South China Botanical Garden: Flowering Cassia javanica

identification: A reliable determination needs more than a flowering canopy photograph. Record how flower clusters attach to young leafy shoots, then include leaflet surfaces, stipules and hairs on the shoot. Those structures are used in comparisons within the group. Keep the original var. indochinensis label when seeking a determination as subsp. agnes, so the proposed synonym can be traced. Take close views of those structures rather than relying on a distant canopy image, and include the same shoot in an overall photograph.
actions: Keep the original nursery name with the planting record and ask a botanist to check it against the current subspecies name. If seedlings appear beyond a garden, document them and establish their identity before describing a variety-specific escape. Manage an unwanted young tree according to the site's needs, while leaving the exact infraspecific name provisional if the evidence is incomplete. Avoid moving pods or seedlings to new sites as a way of preserving a questionable label. An established tree can be cared for according to its condition and position while the finer points of its name are checked.

sources.label: USDA GRIN: Cassia javanica var. indochinensis
Flora Malesiana: Cassia javanica subsp. agnes
Kabila, Sidhu & Ahluwalia (2023): Identification of Cassia javanica subspecies using morphological features - original study abstract

identification: Inspect bark crevices and protected parts of shoots for wax-covered insects and egg sacs. Other mealybugs can look similar, and the Phenacoccus aceris group contains difficult boundaries. Photograph the insect as well as its wax and feeding site; a fuzzy patch alone is inadequate. In a cherry orchard, aphid-like leaf symptoms or small fruit do not identify either the insect or a virus. A specialist determination and plant testing answer different questions and may both be needed.
actions: Keep newly acquired fruit trees apart from established stock when a suspicious colony is found, and ask an extension diagnostic service how to submit insects and plant material. In a region managing little cherry disease, follow current local orchard guidance rather than a generic houseplant-mealybug treatment. Do not transport occupied cuttings or nursery stock to another orchard while the diagnosis is pending. Monitor nearby trees and record symptoms, but do not assume every infested tree carries little cherry virus 2. Control decisions should be coordinated with the orchard's disease-management plan.

sources.label: Wang and Wu 2017: Species recognition in the Phenacoccus aceris group

identification: Look for opposite, rounded leaves with a soft hairy surface and a strongly wrinkled texture. Flowering spikes and the arrangement of leaves help confirm that the plant is a mint, but hybridization and cultivated selections can blur species boundaries. Do not identify a volunteer solely by crushing or tasting a leaf. Photograph the whole shoot, both leaf surfaces and the flower head, and note whether stems extend underground beyond the original clump. Smooth-leaved mints may require a different determination.
actions: In a garden where applemint is wanted, keep its spreading underground stems within a monitored area and inspect the bed edge regularly. Remove escaped pieces with their connected roots where practical, rather than only clipping the visible tops. Avoid discarding rooted fragments into wet ditches or natural vegetation, where they may remain viable. Revisit cleared ground for new shoots. If a larger escape occurs beside a stream, ask the land manager for a plan that protects the bank and surrounding plants. A culinary garden use does not justify releasing it beyond cultivation.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew: Mentha suaveolens

identification: Examine the blue flower and the angular, inflated covering around the fruit together. Groundcherries also have papery fruit coverings, so the husk alone is a poor guide and should never be used to decide that an unknown fruit is edible. Include a whole leaf, stem and open flower in photographs. A young plant without flowers can be confused with other nightshades. Keep uncertain plants away from children or animals likely to investigate the fruit while identification is arranged.
actions: Remove a confirmed unwanted annual before its fruits mature, taking care not to spill seeds around the garden. Wear gloves for handling and keep fruiting plants out of a casual compost pile unless the disposal process reliably prevents seed spread. Check the area in later growing seasons for seedlings rather than assuming one removal finishes the problem. Do not promote it as a homemade insecticide or sample the fruit because of its common name. For a substantial field occurrence, use local weed advice that accounts for the crop and the actual species.

sources.label: NC State Extension Plant Toolbox: Nicandra physalodes

identification: Check the glossy simple leaves and the structure of several flowers, including whether a cultivated form has multiple petal layers. Scent is suggestive but is shared by many plants called jasmine. Other Jasminum and unrelated fragrant ornamentals need comparison with a botanical key. Photograph a leafy shoot and the flower from the side as well as above. A common name referring to Arabia is not evidence of native origin, and a pot label may identify a cultivar rather than the botanical species.
actions: For a retained garden plant, inspect the planting boundary and any stems that have spread into neighboring vegetation. Prune to suit the site and handle rooted pieces so they are not dumped into natural areas. If a volunteer appears away from cultivation, document it and ask local extension or herbarium staff to confirm the species before calling it an invasion. Keep a record of the parent planting and check whether the volunteer persists or produces additional growth beyond the cultivated area. Do not assume that fragrant white flowers identify material suitable for food, tea or homemade remedies.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria: Jasminum sambac
Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew: Jasminum sambac

identification: Collect clear photographs of mature flower parts as well as the low, fine-leaved clump. Schismus barbatus is a close lookalike, and separating the two often requires magnification of the lemma and its hairs. A carpet of short dry grass cannot be assigned to arabicus from color or height alone. Record whether other annual grasses are mixed through the patch. Their combined fuel contribution matters to a site assessment, but does not justify attaching every observed fire effect to one species.
actions: On a small managed site, address confirmed plants before seed maturation and avoid spreading dry seed-bearing material along trails or equipment routes. Coordinate larger desert work with the land manager so removal does not damage native annuals or disturb soil unnecessarily. Watch the site after wet seasons, when annual-grass growth can change quickly. Do not burn a patch as a casual weed-control measure: the relevant concern is its contribution to connected fine fuels. Use a regional restoration and fire-management plan rather than assuming a single removal produces lasting control.

sources.label: California Invasive Plant Council: Schismus arabicus
US Forest Service: Nonnative annual grass fuels and fire in California Mojave Desert

identification: Look for a very flattened true bug in association with decaying wood or fungal growth, but do not identify it from that habitat alone. Other flat bugs occupy similar sheltered spaces, and a specialist may need fine body and antennal characters. Photograph the insect and the fungus or substrate separately. The microscopy study also documents unusual antennal development, so a single abnormal specimen should not define the normal species appearance. A bug on a trunk is not proof that it attacks living tree tissue.
actions: Leave a harmless-looking observation in natural deadwood undisturbed while seeking identification; removing every fungus-bearing log would erase useful habitat without an established benefit. If the insect is found in cultivated bracket fungi, separate the affected growing material and ask an agricultural or entomological adviser to assess the actual feeding. Avoid transporting occupied wood or fungal cultures to another site. Record damage directly rather than assuming it from presence. A useful report shows the affected fungus and the insect together, with photographs of any feeding injury and the condition of nearby growing material.

sources.label: USDA ARS: Henry et al. 2013 Brachyrhynchus membranaceus
Taszakowski and Kaszyca-Taszakowska 2020: Teratological cases of antennae in Aradidae

identification: Inspect fresh Araucaria shoots and the bases of young needles, where small insects can be concealed by the foliage. The broad oval outline and yellow-orange coloration help recognition, but other aphids on conifers need microscopic comparison. Keep the host tree's identity with the record rather than labeling every ornamental conifer an Araucaria. Photograph adults and younger individuals separately if possible. A broad tropical distribution does not, on its own, establish where the species originated or whether a particular locality represents an introduction.
actions: Check newly acquired Araucaria plants before moving them into a collection, especially where young shoots are crowded or discolored. If a colony is present, keep the plant separate and obtain an identification rather than treating it as a different conifer aphid. Record whether growth is actually affected and inspect for other causes of shoot decline. Avoid sharing occupied cuttings or nursery stock while the diagnosis is pending. Photograph the same growing tip over time so an adviser can see whether a brief colony coincides with continuing injury or the plant resumes healthy growth.

sources.label: Noordam 2004: Aphids of Java Part VI

identification: Inspect the dark cover closely without assuming that a black spot on Araucaria is this particular scale. Other armored scales and non-insect marks can look similar. The female beneath the cover provides the microscopic characters used in identification, while the host and feeding position provide context. Photograph both sides of an affected leaf or twig. The Croatian survey documented several hosts, so a palm or olive occurrence is plausible but still needs the insect checked.
actions: Keep an occupied nursery plant separate from clean stock and avoid exchanging cuttings until the scale is identified. Mark a few affected branches and monitor fresh foliage for new settlement or declining growth. A local extension service can help determine whether the apparent covers contain active insects and whether intervention is warranted. Do not extrapolate a Croatian infestation level to every ornamental planting. Where treatment is considered, use the confirmed species, host and current local guidance; old cover appearance alone is a poor measure of whether a response has succeeded.

sources.label: Bjelis et al. 2024: status of Lindingaspis rossi in Croatia

identification: Look for upright, trunk-forming growth and broad gray-green pads carrying fine pale hairs as well as conspicuous white spines. Other prickly pears can become large, so photograph a mature pad, its spine clusters and any flowers or fruit. Small barbed glochids are easily overlooked and make bare-hand examination unwise. A detached pad may still be capable of establishing a plant; finding one beside a garden does not necessarily indicate a seedling or a new species.
actions: Where it has escaped cultivation, do not mow, slash or scatter the pads. Keep people and animals away from sharp material and arrange collection with tools and protective equipment suited to cactus work. Contain every loose segment and use local disposal advice so fragments are not dumped into suitable habitat. Large stands need a coordinated land-management plan and follow-up for surviving plants. The Australian weed guidance describes a regional problem; confirm the local status before applying that label to a Mexican native population or a planting elsewhere.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Opuntia leucotricha
NSW Department of Primary Industries: Aaron's beard prickly pear

identification: Workers in a trail are small and fairly uniform in size, with a brown body and a single waist node. Other small brown ants need comparison, so photograph a worker from the side as well as the whole trail. Follow the route to see whether ants are entering through a crack, using a plant bridge or tending sap-feeding insects outdoors. A large trail can connect several nests; removing the few visible workers is not the same as addressing the colony network.
actions: Start indoors by sealing food, removing sugary spills and correcting accessible water sources. Seal entry gaps where practical and trim vegetation that bridges to the building. Once identification is confirmed, extension guidance favors a suitable bait strategy over repeatedly spraying visible trails; use only a product labeled for the site and keep it inaccessible to children and pets. Outdoors, assess the connected nests and honeydew-producing insects rather than treating every ant on the property. Do not move occupied pots or mulch to a new location.
Do not use insecticide sprays while using ant baits.

sources.label: University of California IPM: Argentine Ant

identification: Look for a large, robust lizard with black-and-white patterning and a heavy banded tail. Juvenile green heads can make young animals look different from adults. Other tegus and large lizards also occur in the pet trade, so a photograph showing the head, back and tail is more useful than a brief color description. Keep a safe distance and record the exact location and direction of travel. A single sighting outside an established range does not prove a breeding population.
actions: In Florida, report a suspected free-ranging tegu through the state's invasive-wildlife reporting system and include clear photographs when safely possible. Keep pets away and do not attempt to corner or handle a large unfamiliar lizard. Follow the wildlife agency's current instructions about removal; rules and authorized methods differ by place. Never release an unwanted pet. Owners needing an alternative should contact an appropriate reptile surrender or amnesty program. Where nests of native wildlife are vulnerable, qualified managers should assess the site rather than relying on improvised traps or poisons.

sources.label: University of Florida IFAS: Florida Invader, Tegu Lizard
Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission: Argentine black and white tegu

identification: A mature plant may have lost the deeply divided leaves that were obvious earlier, so examine the lower stem and any younger plants nearby. Close views of the flattened, rounded fruit and its shallow tip notch are particularly useful. Other pepperweeds can have similar tiny pale flowers, sometimes with petals too small to notice. Include stem hairs and fruit stalks in photographs. Do not identify a plant as edible pepperweed merely because its pods resemble a familiar mustard.
actions: In a cultivated bed, remove confirmed unwanted plants before mature pods scatter seed and watch the disturbed area for new seedlings. Keep fruiting material out of clean soil or seed mixes.
