For a plant in natural grassland, obtain a regional identification before disturbing neighboring mustards or assuming an invasive impact. The New Zealand and Australian floras describe the plant well but do not establish a U.S. ecological effect or a special control method. Record the location, population size and habitat if an escape appears unusual, so later observations can be compared.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Lepidium bonariense
Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney: Lepidium bonariense

identification: Look beneath leaves of a correctly identified yew, plum-yew or Podocarpus for pale covers through which the reddish insect may show. Other armored scales can produce yellow feeding marks, so leaf color and host alone are not enough. Photograph the cover in place and ask a specialist whether a sample is needed for microscopic examination. Tiny emergence holes can indicate natural-enemy activity, but neither a hole nor a nearby wasp identifies the scale or proves that control is adequate.
actions: Inspect incoming conifer ornamentals before adding them to an established collection. Keep an affected plant apart while diagnosis is arranged, and record whether yellowing or twig decline is spreading. Avoid a general spray solely because scale covers remain visible; have active infestation assessed first. The Japanese study found several parasitoids, but that does not justify collecting and releasing wasps or assuming the same community exists locally. Use current local nursery or landscape advice if injury warrants intervention, and evaluate the plant's overall health alongside the insect observations.

sources.label: Uematsu1972: Studies on Marietta carnesi, I. Host Relation

identification: Compare several covers on affected conifer foliage, noting how their color changes with age. Other scales can inhabit arborvitae, so the tree's common name does not settle the insect's identity. Photograph discolored foliage and healthy-looking shoots as well as the insects. A diagnostic sample should retain the host and collection location. Empty covers may house other tiny animals; their presence should not be mistaken for proof that every visible object is a living scale insect.
actions: Mark affected twigs and monitor new growth before deciding how extensive an infestation is. For nursery plants, prevent movement into clean stock while the identification is unresolved. Have an extension service or qualified plant-health professional distinguish active scales from old covers and investigate other causes of dieback. The Pennsylvania parasitoid and mite observations are interesting evidence of natural enemies, but they do not establish a tested treatment. Do not transfer Connecticut crawler dates to another climate without local monitoring, and avoid releasing organisms collected from the covers.

sources.label: Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station, Bulletin 1059: armored scales
Schneider et al. 2019: arborvitae scale natural enemies (USDA ARS abstract)

identification: Inspect bromeliad leaves closely, especially where dark specks persist after loose dust has been removed gently. The covering can be small enough to escape notice during a quick nursery check. Other scale insects and leaf spots can look similar, so retain photographs of the whole plant and the occupied leaf surface. A specialist may need the female and its retained skin to identify the insect. Do not assume that every dark mark on a bromeliad is alive or is this species.
actions: Separate a suspect plant from other bromeliads and inspect plants that shared its source or growing space. Avoid distributing pups or divisions while an active colony remains unresolved. Ask a plant clinic to confirm the insect and assess whether fresh settlement is occurring before choosing treatment. Gentle observation is preferable to scraping or injuring the leaf to remove every speck. The California greenhouse detection is a historical event, not a current statement about all outdoor populations or legal status. Follow regional advice for an actual infestation rather than extrapolating from that record.

sources.label: California Department of Food and Agriculture: Fly speck scale assessment

identification: Look for partly concealed pale covers on woody material, but do not cut into living bark simply to investigate a suspected scale. Other insects and normal bark features can create similar bumps. Photograph exposed covers and the surrounding tissue, and retain host identification with any sample collected on professional advice. Scale covers can become hidden beneath host tissue, but that observation does not show how the insect reached its concealed position. The name mining scale is not proof of an excavated tunnel.
actions: For an orchard or nursery, document which branches carry scales and whether growth or fruit is actually affected. Keep infested planting material from being moved into clean stock. A diagnostic service can distinguish Howardia from other armored scales found in the same orchard and advise on checking active stages. Avoid using a generic scale-generation calendar as though it had been measured for this species. Include unaffected branches in the comparison, so an adviser can judge whether the occupied areas are developing differently from the rest of the tree. Address any substantial decline through an integrated plant-health assessment.

sources.label: University of Hawaii CTAHR: Howardia biclavis
Lazaro-Castellanos et al. 2023: armored scales associated with Mexican avocados

identification: Examine the brown, elongated covers on an orchid leaf or stem and photograph the discolored tissue around them. Related Lepidosaphes can have nearly the same mussel-like outline, so microscopic features beneath the cover are needed for an exact determination. The avocado record broadens the known host context but does not make every scale on avocado this species. Keep the host name and feeding position with the sample. An orchid collection can contain several scale species at the same time.
actions: Set an affected orchid apart from clean plants and check newly acquired plants and divisions before sharing them. Monitor whether fresh feeding spots or small new covers appear, rather than judging success only by the disappearance of old covers. Ask a diagnostic service for identification and a plant-appropriate response if colonies persist. Do not scrub tender orchid tissue aggressively or apply a treatment intended for another host without checking suitability. The Mexican orchard observation does not establish the same impact or a treatment schedule in a household orchid collection.

sources.label: Lazaro-Castellanos et al. 2023: armored scales associated with Mexican avocados

identification: Inspect the spaces alongside corky wings on burning-bush twigs, where brown covers can be hidden. White male covers and dark female covers of Unaspis euonymi should not be treated as the same insect merely because the host is Euonymus. A close side view of the twig and an individual cover will help a specialist. The sources differ about occurrence on leaves, so absence or presence there should not be used as an absolute rule for excluding this species.
actions: On a planted shrub, mark infested twigs and check whether new shoots remain healthy or die back. Have active scales confirmed before responding to old covers. Consult local extension guidance about monitoring crawler emergence; Massachusetts or Illinois dates should not become a fixed calendar for every climate. Avoid moving infested shrubs or cuttings into another planting. Photograph the same sections of bark during follow-up visits, alongside current leaf and shoot growth. This helps distinguish persistent old covers from a colony associated with worsening plant condition.

sources.label: University of Illinois Extension: Winged Euonymous Scale

identification: Search bark cracks for narrow tan covers with darker material at one end. Their flat shape can blend with bark and resemble other small armored scales. A pink or reddish insect beneath a cover is a useful clue, but examining the female's microscopic structures is still necessary. Photograph the bark surface before collecting anything, since position and host help interpret the sample. The historical comparison of specimens across regions confirms identity in those collections, not current abundance on a particular property.
actions: If found on purchased woody plants, keep the lot separate and ask a diagnostic service to identify a representative sample. Retain supplier, date and host information, and avoid distributing cuttings while an active infestation is unresolved. In a landscape, compare affected branches with unaffected growth and investigate whether visible decline has another explanation. Do not treat a historical low-damage report as a guarantee of safety, or a catalog listing as evidence of severe harm. Keep close photographs of the occupied bark alongside whole-branch images so a local adviser can compare the insects with the pattern of plant injury.

sources.label: Takagi 1970: Diaspididae of Taiwan, Part II

identification: Check both leaf surfaces, especially near veins, for pale covers with a darker retained-skin patch. Camellias host several kinds of scale, and discoloration alone cannot separate them. Photograph a leaf showing the distribution of insects and a close view of individual covers. Ask for microscopic examination when species identification matters. The Galicia survey's affected plants are direct observations, but a small documented sample cannot establish the severity of every infestation or explain all yellowing in a collection.
actions: Separate newly acquired camellias carrying suspicious scales and inspect adjacent plants before exchanging cuttings. Mark a few occupied leaves and observe whether fresh colonies or new discoloration develop. Preserve useful diagnostic material until a specialist has identified the insect. Avoid stripping many leaves or treating an entire collection simply because one plant has old covers. If active feeding and decline continue, seek local advice that accounts for plant condition and other pests. Check the plants that shared the same nursery source, and keep each sample labeled so a diagnosis from one camellia is not accidentally applied to all of them.

sources.label: International Camellia Society: Research on scale insects in Galicia

identification: The scale can be partly obscured by host tissue, so a reddish or dark bump on lychee bark needs more examination than a color match. Photograph the surrounding branch and any exposed pale covering. Other armored scales occur on tropical fruit trees, and microscopic female characters may be needed. Keep a record of the host and where the plant originated. The name in an island checklist establishes a regional record; it does not prove the insect caused a nearby tree's decline.
actions: Inspect tropical nursery plants before sharing them and keep suspect stock apart while identification is arranged. Do not move occupied branches or propagation material to another growing site. In a lychee planting, document the affected parts and changes in vigor, then seek a specialist assessment rather than treating every concealed scale as the same pest. A record from another island or orchard does not explain the condition of your tree; compare occupied areas with nearby healthy growth. Any response should be based on an active infestation and local crop guidance, with the plant's other stresses considered.

identification: On Euphorbia, look for separate white disks with an off-center yellow-brown patch rather than treating a pale crust as one continuous growth. Several scales can have this appearance, so a specialist may need insects beneath the coverings. Photograph the stem and plant label without breaking tissue unnecessarily; many Euphorbia plants have irritating sap. The British report concerns one imported glasshouse plant, and does not show that this scale was established outdoors in the surrounding region.
actions: Keep an occupied succulent apart from the rest of a collection and inspect plants received from the same source. Avoid exchanging cuttings while the infestation is unresolved. Ask a plant clinic how to obtain a sample without damaging the host or exposing skin to sap. Record whether new covers or injury appear after any advised intervention. Keep the plant label and purchase date with the diagnosis, particularly if several imported succulents arrived together. Different scale species may occur in the same collection, so check each affected plant.

sources.label: Malumphy et al.2010: First incursion of Contigaspis zillae, contextual S.albus record

identification: Inspect the upper leaf surface for thin disks with a pale margin and an off-center darker patch. The actual insect, rather than the yellowing around it, is needed for identification. Other round armored scales can occur on citrus or rubber trees. Include a healthy-looking leaf for comparison and record whether scales also occur on fruit or other tissue. The Brazilian study's seasonal peaks and clone differences are useful research findings, but they are not a universal identification or risk calendar.
actions: Monitor a consistent set of leaves or branches so changes in an orchard can be compared over time. Keep affected nursery plants from being moved into clean stock and obtain a diagnostic determination before selecting control. If leaf injury increases, ask a crop adviser to interpret it alongside plant vigor and natural enemies. Do not choose a rubber clone as resistant solely because it had fewer scales in one study, and do not import that site's seasonal schedule to another climate. Follow-up should assess active insects and new injury rather than old cover counts alone.

sources.label: Silva etal2020: Population Fluctuation of Selenaspidus articulatus in Rubber Tree

identification: Inspect the trunk and woody branches as well as leaves. The conspicuous white material is largely the covering of immature males, while the females are darker and less obvious. This mixture helps distinguish snow scale from a fungal coating, but other citrus scales still require comparison. Photograph bark cracks, branch condition and both cover types. A white-coated trunk alone cannot show whether every cover contains a living insect or whether all nearby decline has the same cause.
actions: Keep citrus trees in good growing condition and correct water or nutrient problems with local advice, without overfertilizing. Have a suspected snow-scale colony identified and ask about monitoring active stages before choosing treatment. Inspect incoming citrus plants and avoid distributing occupied branches or cuttings. Trees with substantial bark splitting or dieback need a broader health assessment, not merely removal of the visible white material. Use current regional citrus guidance for any intervention and recheck active infestation afterward; do not transfer a fixed spray calendar or confuse old covers with treatment failure.

sources.label: University of Florida IFAS: Citrus Snow Scale
Clemson Extension: Citrus insects and related pests

identification: Search under both Andaspis punicae and Lepidosaphes punicae when reviewing an identification, but keep the original label attached to its record. Long brown covers on lychee can resemble other armored scales. Photograph a branch with its occupied areas, and obtain a microscopic determination before attributing dieback to this species. The association with corky bark reported in Florida is not proof that the insect alone causes that condition. Plant symptoms and insect identity need to be evaluated separately.
actions: Inspect lychee propagation material before moving it between groves, and keep affected nursery stock apart while diagnosis is arranged. Record branch dieback and scale density over time rather than relying on a single view of old covers. Consult a local fruit-crop adviser if active colonies are associated with declining vigor. Historical experiments tested several interventions, but their products and results are not a current recommendation for every location. Do not attempt to import parasitoids independently or treat an unconfirmed corky-bark problem as a settled scale diagnosis.

sources.label: USDA ARS: Andaspis punicae in lychee

identification: A brown ridged cover may suggest Fiorinia but does not identify the species. The female's projecting head feature is microscopic, not a large snout visible on the leaf. Similar adventive Fiorinia can be separated through detailed examination of females and other stages. Photograph the plant, leaf surface and distribution of colonies, and retain material only as the diagnostic service directs. Small differences between Taiwanese and Florida specimens make an overly rigid field description particularly unhelpful.
actions: Keep an occupied citrus or ornamental plant from being moved into clean stock while a specialist checks it. Inspect neighboring plants that arrived in the same shipment and retain their source information. Record fresh settlement and leaf condition rather than assuming all visible brown covers are active. Keep the insects and host labels linked, since several similar Fiorinia species may arrive through the same nursery pathway. For an unusual finding, contact the appropriate plant-health or extension service before discarding diagnostic material or sharing plants with others.

sources.label: Takagi1970: Diaspididae of Taiwan, Part II, Fiorinia proboscidaria
Ahmed etal2021: Taxonomic and identification review of adventive Fiorinia of the United States

identification: The hanging flower head combines a pale pink or mauve sterile portion with a yellow fertile portion. Look also for spines, finely divided leaves and clusters of twisted pods. Many thorny legumes have divided leaves, so the complete combination is more useful than the local name aroma. Inspect the base and nearby shoots carefully: a young stem may be connected to an older plant through a root rather than being an independent seedling. Photograph without reaching through the thorns.
actions: Before removing a thicket, establish whether the shrub is native, introduced or being managed for woody encroachment at that location. Use a local land-management plan that accounts for grazing, habitat and follow-up. Cutting visible stems alone may leave connected roots, so monitor the boundary and new shoots after work. Wear protective equipment around thorny branches and keep cut material away from paths. Do not assume that burning or grazing will solve the problem; the South African study found root suckers under multiple disturbance regimes rather than identifying one universally effective treatment.

sources.label: Kew: Dichrostachys cinerea, Flora of Somalia and FTEA descriptions
Wakeling and Bond2007: Disturbance and root suckering in Dichrostachys cinerea

identification: Wait for a flowering head before trying to name an unfamiliar clump. Photograph the many branches from above and the paired spikelets close up, and include a blade, its hairy base and the lower stems. Other Paspalum species have far fewer flowering branches, but branch count alone is not a complete key. A young leafy clump without mature spikelets may need to be revisited. Record whether the plant is growing in a maintained lawn, pasture edge or less disturbed vegetation.
actions: If a confirmed clump is unwanted in a garden, contain the mature seed head before disturbing it and avoid carrying occupied soil to another bed. Check the spot for surviving growth and nearby seedlings during later visits. A pasture or natural-area population deserves a local botanical assessment before broad removal, since grasses in the same genus can have different regional roles. Share photographs and the location with an extension or herbarium service if the occurrence is unusual. Do not assume that an introduced record by itself means that the plant is damaging the site.

sources.label: New South Wales Flora Online: Paspalum paniculatum
Pohl and Davidse: Flora Mesoamericana, reproduced in WFO Paspalum paniculatum

identification: Follow a leafy shoot down to its cane and look for new shoots beyond the original clump. Broad leaves alone do not separate arrow bamboo from Sasa or Pleioblastus, which can also run through gardens. A photograph should include leaves, cane nodes and the planting's outer edge. Check for creeping underground stems only where digging is safe and permitted. The Maryland expert response identifies a running-bamboo problem, rather than providing a definitive species determination from every submitted image.
actions: Map the outermost shoots before starting work so you can see whether the patch expands. Coordinate with a neighbor if underground stems cross a boundary. A small patch may allow removal of canes and accessible rhizomes, followed by repeated checks for returning shoots; established stands require a longer plan. Avoid moving rhizome-bearing soil to another part of the property. Seek local advice on containment or removal near trees, utilities and buildings. Ordinary selective broadleaf lawn products will not solve a bamboo problem, and a single cutting should not be mistaken for eradication.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Pseudosasa japonica
Maryland Extension: Running bamboo identification and management response

identification: Look at the point where the leaf stalk meets the blade: it joins at the basal notch, a useful contrast with many Colocasia leaves whose stalk enters farther inside the blade. Photograph the whole leaf, that attachment and the base of the clump. Other large aroids and garden cultivars can still be confusing, especially without flowers. Underground growth may connect several leafy shoots, so a new stem beside the parent need not have come from seed.
actions: Before planting or sharing divisions in Florida, check the current UF/IFAS assessment for the relevant zone; its conclusions differ within the state. Keep garden material away from drainage channels and do not dump tubers or divided clumps beside streams. If an escape is confirmed, obtain a site-appropriate removal plan that accounts for underground parts and repeated visits. Along a bank, avoid tearing out a large patch in a way that leaves bare eroding soil. Wear gloves for routine handling and do not treat an ornamental elephant-ear label as an edible-plant identification.

sources.label: University of South Florida: Arrowleaf elephant's ear

identification: Leaves usually attract attention long before the small flower structure appears. Photograph both the leaf pattern and its shape, but remember that cultivated caladiums include many selections and hybrids. A brightly colored leaf is not enough to settle the ancestry of a named cultivar. Check the label and growing history as well as visible features. Tubers can remain when seasonal foliage dies back, so loss of the leaves does not necessarily mean the planting has disappeared.
actions: Place caladiums where children and pets will not chew the leaves or tubers, and use gloves when dividing plants if sap contact is a concern. Keep divisions labeled and contained rather than discarding live tubers in a natural area. If a patch is unwanted, locate the remaining underground material and watch for renewed growth when conditions are favorable. For an unidentified escape, obtain a botanical determination before assigning an invasive status. This ornamental's tropical origin and irritating tissues do not by themselves show that it is a harmful invader at every planting site.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online: Caladium bicolor
NC State Extension Plant Toolbox: Caladium bicolor

identification: Look for a very thin, soft colony in which the tiny individual animals are embedded in one shared sheet. Other colonial tunicates, sponges and films can resemble it, and colony color varies with background and condition. Photograph the colony underwater with a scale reference if that can be done safely. A marine specialist may need closer examination to separate similar species. A new colony on a hull is evidence of fouling, not a reliable clue to the species' original home. Genetic research has found deeply separated lineages within this name, so visual records should retain the broad species-complex qualification.
actions: Before taking a fouled boat or other marine equipment to another harbor, ask the marina or relevant authority about inspection and approved cleaning facilities. Arrange cleaning so removed growth and wash water are captured rather than scraped directly into the harbor. Do not transfer occupied ropes, floats or shellfish equipment between sites without appropriate advice. Record the location and substrate of an unusual colony and submit photographs to a marine monitoring program. Avoid experimental chemical or freshwater treatments in open water; a contained, professionally advised response is the appropriate way to address uncertain tunicate identification.

sources.label: Rhode Island Coastal Resources Management Council: Diplosoma listerianum identification card
Perez-Portela et al. 2013: Cryptic speciation or global spread?

identification: Unlike a thin sheet of tunic, this colony has individual upright bodies joined by connecting strands. Look for the two openings on each body and the network at its base. Other colonial sea squirts need comparison, so underwater photographs should show both individual shape and colony arrangement. Researchers also describe dormant rounded structures that can persist when conspicuous animals are scarce. A seasonal reduction in visible zooids therefore does not necessarily mean that an occupied rope or dock is free of the species.
actions: Inspect fouled ropes and equipment before moving them between marinas. Ask the harbor manager about identification and cleaning arrangements that capture removed material and wash water. Do not scrape an uncertain colony into surrounding water or try to alter harbor salinity. Laboratory differences in budding at different salt concentrations are not a do-it-yourself treatment recipe. Keep a dated photographic record if the colony appears to shrink and return, and share it with a marine monitoring program. The species' first description from Peru should not be used alone to decide whether a local population is native.

sources.label: Salinity-mediated limitation of asexual reproduction in Polyandrocarpa zorritensis (2024)

identification: Turn over affected leaves to examine the immature stages, rather than relying only on clouds of flying adults. Pale wax and droplets on the immatures are helpful clues, while honeydew and dark sooty mold show why the leaves may look dirty. Other whiteflies also make honeydew, so a specialist may need a leaf sample. Compare young and old foliage and note whether the tree is losing leaves or merely carrying a light infestation.
actions: In places where natural enemies already suppress ash whitefly, avoid an automatic broad-spectrum spray that could disrupt that control. Monitor the undersides of several leaves and look for changes in infestation and tree condition before deciding whether action is needed. Obtain local advice if damage persists, particularly on a young or stressed plant. Check nursery plants before moving them to another site. The successful California biological-control program does not mean homeowners should purchase or release unidentified wasps or beetles; conservation of established natural enemies is the more useful first step.

sources.label: University of Florida IFAS: Ash Whitefly

identification: Examine the pale undersides of several mature leaves and count their leaflets. Photograph the leaf tips, teeth, stem hairs and the small green structures beneath a flower. Potentilla intermedia can be similar; narrower leaflets and coarser hairs around the flowers help distinguish P. inclinata, but flower color alone is unreliable. A plant without flowers may be worth revisiting later in the season. Include habitat and location with the images so a regional botanist can compare the appropriate local species.
actions: For a confirmed unwanted garden plant, remove it before mature seed is scattered and check the same spot for renewed growth. Keep seed-bearing material out of clean planting soil. In grassland or along a road, confirm the identity and local status before removing a patch that may contain other cinquefoils. Ask the land manager how an unusual occurrence should be recorded. The gray foliage is a useful recognition clue, but it is not evidence that the plant is causing ecological damage or that a particular removal method will work at that site.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Potentilla inclinata
German Federal Agency for Nature Conservation FloraWeb: Potentilla inclinata

identification: A juvenile's bold bands and reddish tail can be much easier to notice than the adult's softer, speckled pattern. Photograph the whole animal without chasing it, ideally including the head and tail. Florida's native reef gecko and other small introduced geckos can complicate identification. Color changes with age mean that two differently patterned animals nearby may still belong to the same species. Daylight hunting observed in Cuba is a site-specific natural-history record, not a rule that every animal must be active at that hour.
actions: Leave an uncertain gecko undisturbed while seeking identification from clear photographs. Do not clear all leaf litter or spray sheltered areas merely because a tiny lizard is present. If found in a shipment of plants or landscape materials, notify the supplier or appropriate local wildlife contact before moving the material elsewhere. Never relocate an unfamiliar gecko to another outdoor site or release a captive one. An unusual sighting is useful when accompanied by date and location; it does not, by itself, demonstrate ecological harm or a breeding population.

sources.label: Heagy and Frank2008: The Reef Geckos of Florida
deArmas2022: Natural history of four lizards in an urban locality of western Cuba
Somma and Krysko2008: Sphaerodactylus elegans, Broward County record

identification: Look for the narrow basal leaves and upright stalks ending in compact rounded heads. Photograph several heads and the plant's base without trampling surrounding wetland vegetation. Other pipeworts are similar, and their minute flowers often need magnification for a reliable determination. A grass-like seedling cannot confidently be named from a distant photograph. Record whether the plant is in a rice field, a pond margin or another wet setting, since that context helps a botanist interpret the specimen.
actions: In an agricultural field, have the pipewort identified before deciding whether it is part of a crop-management problem. Clean visible plant material from equipment before moving between fields, and avoid moving seed-bearing mud into a new planting. In natural wetlands, do not drain or excavate a patch simply because the species has an introduced record elsewhere. Report an unusual occurrence to the relevant herbarium or land manager, with photographs and a precise location. Native pipeworts may occur nearby, and protecting them depends on getting the identification right first.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Eriocaulon cinereum

identification: Examine the flower head closely enough to see its small bristled spikelets. Include the leaf sheath, base of the stems and any rooting joints in photographs. Similar Polypogon and related grass hybrids can be difficult to distinguish without mature material, so a common name containing bluegrass is not a reliable guide. A loose clump in wet ground may look quite different from a pressed specimen. Ask a regional botanist to compare a complete flowering shoot when the identification matters.
actions: Where the grass is unwanted in a managed bed, collect mature seed heads before disturbing the clump and keep rooted stem pieces with the removed material. Check damp edges and recently moved soil for additional plants. At a field margin, record its extent and discuss any crop interference with local extension before selecting a response. Avoid broad treatment of a wet ditch while the identity is uncertain; other grasses and wetland vegetation may share the site. Its ability to root at lower joints makes careless movement of cut plants a poor containment practice.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand VolumeV: Polypogon fugax

identification: The pale leg bands and golden lines on the thorax help narrow the possibilities, but several mosquitoes have banded legs. Local mosquito-control staff can identify an adult or larvae more reliably than a photograph of a bite. Check artificial containers in shaded places, including discarded tires and neglected water-holding items. A container with larvae should be addressed even before the species is known. Do not use the presence of this mosquito to diagnose an illness or to assume that a particular pathogen is circulating nearby.
actions: Empty and scrub water-holding containers regularly, store unused items so they stay dry and keep gutters draining. Cover rain-storage containers appropriately and maintain window and door screens. For personal protection, use an EPA-registered repellent according to its label and wear clothing that reduces exposed skin when mosquitoes are active. Contact the local mosquito-control program about persistent breeding sites or unusual collections. Do not drain natural rock pools or wetlands as a household response; concentrate on avoidable artificial breeding sites and follow current local public-health advice about disease risk.

sources.label: University of Florida IFAS: Asian Bush Mosquito
University of Illinois Division of Research Safety: Mosquitos

identification: Confirm that the host is a true chestnut, Castanea, and inspect buds, new shoots and leaves for rounded green or pink swellings. Old brown galls may remain long after the insects have emerged, so note their age and whether fresh galls appear on current growth. Other injuries can distort a shoot, and a tiny wasp nearby is not enough to name the cause. Photograph the gall's position on the tree and include the host's leaves for identification.
actions: Check nursery chestnuts and propagation material before purchase or movement, and ask about origin if gall wasp is a local concern. Apparently healthy dormant material can still be difficult to assess, so follow current plant-health advice rather than relying only on visible galls. Report a suspected new regional occurrence through the appropriate forestry or plant-health service. Avoid indiscriminate pruning of old galls, which may no longer contain the pest and can shelter natural enemies. For a small tree with fresh injury, obtain local advice about timing and management before cutting or treating it.

sources.label: University of Florida IFAS: Asian Chestnut Gall Wasp
UK Forest Research: Oriental chestnut gall wasp

identification: Look on tender citrus flush for adults feeding with their rear ends raised and for flattened yellow-orange nymphs with white waxy tubes. Aphids, scales and leafminers can also affect young leaves, so include close photographs rather than relying on distortion alone. Citrus greening requires a separate official assessment: an unevenly yellow leaf does not prove infection, and finding a psyllid does not mean every tree nearby carries the bacterium. Record both the insect and the tree's location.
actions: Contact your state citrus or plant-health program promptly about a suspected new infestation and follow its sampling instructions. Keep citrus plants, cuttings and other potentially occupied material on site until you know the applicable movement guidance; do not mail a sample unsolicited. Inspect new flush during routine tree care and use clean, appropriately sourced planting stock. If disease is suspected, seek official testing instead of trying to treat leaf color alone. Coordinate any pest response with current regional advice, since neighboring trees and plant movement affect the usefulness of an individual household's efforts.

sources.label: University of California IPM: Asian Citrus Psyllid and Huanglongbing Disease
USDA APHIS: Citrus greening and Asian citrus psyllid

identification: A tan cockroach with dark stripes behind the head can strongly resemble the German cockroach. Ready flight toward lights and an outdoor mulch source favor Asian cockroach, but behavior alone is not a perfect identification. Save a clear photograph or a safely contained specimen for an extension service or pest professional. Note whether sightings occur around an open lit doorway at dusk or repeatedly within kitchens and other indoor hiding places; that pattern helps guide the inspection.
actions: Repair screens and door gaps, and reduce the attraction of bright lights immediately beside entrances where practical. Inspect nearby leaf litter or mulch as part of understanding the outdoor source, without treating every sheltered garden area. Persistent indoor sightings deserve species confirmation before selecting a control plan, because a German-cockroach infestation requires a different response. Do not assume that one flying adult calls for whole-house treatment. If an outdoor population becomes a nuisance, ask for a site-specific approach and use any control product only according to its label.

sources.label: UF/IFAS EDIS: Asian Cockroach, Blattella asahinai Mizukubo
University of Georgia Extension: Insect and Arthropod Pests of Southeastern Neighborhoods: A Guide to Identification and Management

identification: Look for the leafy bracts around the inconspicuous female flowers and fruits. In Asian copperleaf they are broad and heart-shaped, with shallow teeth rather than the deep fingerlike divisions of several native copperleaf species. Rhomboid and Virginia copperleaf can be very difficult to separate before flowering. Waterhemp is another possible confusion, but its leaf margins lack the teeth seen here. Photograph a whole plant and a close view of several mature bracts, not just a reddish young leaf.
actions: Inspect suspicious plants beneath the crop canopy and along field edges before harvest. Mark the location and ask an extension agronomist to confirm the bracts before making treatment decisions. If isolated plants can be removed without spreading ripe seed, contain the seed-bearing parts and check the patch again later. Clean soil and plant debris from equipment before leaving an affected field. Reports of herbicide resistance from overseas do not establish resistance in your field; any crop treatment should follow local identification and resistance advice.

sources.label: Iowa State University Extension: Asian copperleaf
University of Illinois Extension: Asian Copperleaf

identification: Examine the shell's raised ridges and projecting shoulders, but do not identify an oyster drill from a bored shell alone. Native predatory snails and other introduced drills also leave holes in shellfish. Photograph the intact snail from the side and from the opening, with a ruler nearby. Attached clusters of yellow egg capsules can strengthen a report. Young snails develop in capsules rather than through a freely drifting larval stage, making movement of infested oysters and equipment especially important.
actions: Before transferring oyster stock, shells or growing gear, follow the receiving area's shellfish-health and pest-inspection procedures. Do not relocate a suspect snail to another beach. For a new observation, record the location and photograph the snail and attached capsules for the local marine-pest or shellfish program. Growers can discuss targeted collection of adults and capsules with that program; University of Washington work found capsule removal particularly useful for reducing population growth. Avoid broad scraping of natural habitat simply because a shell has a drill hole.

sources.label: University of Washington Ruesink Lab: Oyster drills

identification: The flowering head deserves a closer look than the grasslike foliage. Several branches hold small spikelets, and a few long green bracts extend well beyond them. A hand lens reveals the pointed green midribs of the yellow-brown scales. Other flatsedges, including Cyperus iria, can look similar, so neither wet ground nor a triangular stem is enough for identification. Save clear views of the entire flower arrangement and individual spikelets while they are mature and still attached.
actions: In a cultivated bed, a confirmed unwanted annual can be removed before ripe seed is scattered. Keep seed-bearing material out of soil moved to another site and return to inspect the same damp patches. A plant on a natural riverbank needs a regional identification and impact assessment before removal is justified. At a U.S. site, check whether it is interfering with the intended vegetation before choosing a response. Similar-looking sedges can have different local roles and management needs. Treat a new regional record as something to document carefully rather than an automatic call for broad treatment.

sources.label: InfoFlora: Cyperus microiria, Flora Helvetica description

identification: The midrib runs through the broad blade, while a mature plant develops folded, frilly reproductive tissue around the lower stalk. Other brown seaweeds may have torn or wavy blades, so photograph the base as well as the largest sheet of tissue. Young wakame may lack the obvious reproductive frill. Its visible frond is only part of the life cycle: microscopic stages can remain on hard surfaces, which helps explain why removing a few large plants does not necessarily clear a site.
actions: Report a suspected new patch with the observation date, precise location and photographs before moving it. Check mooring lines, hulls and other immersed equipment through the local marina's approved cleaning arrangements. Avoid cleaning a fouled boat in a way that releases material into another harbor. A coordinated removal program may reduce biomass, but repeated inspection is needed for microscopic stages and new arrivals. Do not assume harbor-grown wakame is suitable to eat because the same species is commercially cultivated; water quality and local collection rules still matter.

sources.label: Monterey Bay National Marine Sanctuary: Undaria invasion FAQ

identification: Check both the insect and its host tree. The adult's white blotches and antennae longer than its body are useful, but several native longhorned beetles can cause confusion. Photographs should show the upper body and antennae clearly. On a living hardwood, look for round emergence holes, oval egg-laying wounds and frass collecting beneath a branch. These signs are a reason for expert inspection, not proof by themselves, because other borers and mechanical damage can leave superficially similar marks.
actions: Photograph a suspect beetle or damaged tree and report it promptly to your state plant-health agency or USDA's Asian longhorned beetle program. Note the tree's location and any recent movement of firewood or wood packaging. Keep potentially infested wood on site until officials advise otherwise, and observe applicable firewood movement restrictions. Do not cut branches to search for larvae or apply a preventive pesticide on your own: an official inspection can guide the response while preserving evidence. Stay clear of weakened limbs when taking photographs.

sources.label: University of Minnesota Extension: Asian longhorned beetle

identification: At this size, a dark speck on marsh litter may be easy to miss or mistake for another small snail. Use close photographs with a scale to show the shell's blunt cone, opening and brown surface. Record whether it was on vegetation, mud or debris and how high it sat relative to the tide. Those habitat details help a specialist compare it with native marsh snails, but they cannot replace examination of the animal's diagnostic characters.
actions: Leave marsh vegetation and sediment in place while documenting a suspected occurrence. Avoid carrying wet marsh debris on boots, traps or sampling gear to another estuary, and follow the site's cleaning procedures. Send photographs and location details to a regional marine-invertebrate specialist if the snail seems new to the area. A few tiny snails are not a reason to disturb an entire marsh. Have the species checked before deciding whether any intervention is needed. Do not spread bait, salt or chemicals through a marsh to target tiny snails; such treatment could damage the surrounding community.

sources.label: Wada, Kuroda and Kamada (2023): Distribution pattern of macrobenthos in salt marsh of Yoshino River, Tokushima

identification: Follow a stem through the waterline if that can be done without breaking it. The change from feathery underwater foliage to firmer emerged leaves is particularly helpful. Flowers arise close to the upper leaf axils on very short stalks. Limnophila indica and a hybrid reported from Louisiana can complicate identification, so a submerged aquarium cutting alone may not be enough. Photograph the emerged flowers and leaf arrangement as well as a whole submerged shoot for a knowledgeable aquatic botanist.
actions: Never empty aquarium plants or water containing plant fragments into a storm drain, ditch or pond. Contain unwanted plants for locally approved disposal and clean equipment before using it in another water body. Report a suspected outdoor population to the local aquatic-plant or agriculture program. Avoid casual mowing or raking through a patch, since some sufficiently developed fragments can regrow. Treatment in a natural waterway needs a site-specific plan and appropriate permissions; a photograph of feathery leaves should be checked before native aquatic plants are disturbed.

sources.label: University of Florida IFAS: Limnophila sessiliflora
California Department of Food and Agriculture (2024): Limnophila sessiliflora Pest Rating Proposal

identification: Start with the basal leaves: they are rough and often deeply lobed, while the taller flowering branches carry relatively few leaves. The pale yellow flowers are small, and long narrow pods soon become more conspicuous than the blossoms. Other annual mustards can occur nearby, including species with purple flowers or different leaf shapes. Take photographs of the rosette, flowers and mature pods together. The fast-growing plant may already be forming seed while a desert wildflower display is still developing.
actions: Check disturbed entrances, washes and road edges after suitable rain, and return as later seedlings appear. Small confirmed patches can be pulled before seed maturity where the land manager permits it, taking care not to trample surrounding wildflowers or fragile soil surfaces. Contain plants with developing pods, and clean footwear, tools and vehicle debris before leaving. Seed in the soil can produce new cohorts, so a single visit is rarely enough. Larger desert populations need coordinated, repeated work timed to prevent another crop of seed.

sources.label: University of California IPM: Sahara mustard
National Park Service: Death Valley non-native plants

identification: Look for alternate, glossy leaves with toothed edges and several strong veins arising near the base. Small flowers sit in clusters where leaves meet the branch, and the round capsules eventually split to release seeds. A scrambling branch may root where it contacts soil, adding to the tangle. Other coastal shrubs can have shiny leaves, so document fruit, leaf arrangement and the plant's climbing habit. Common names such as nakedwood are not sufficient to distinguish related native shrubs.
actions: In affected Florida coastal habitat, address a small confirmed plant before it grows through neighboring vegetation. Avoid dragging seed-bearing branches through an uninvaded area, and check for rooted branches beyond the main stem. Ask the land manager about removal and follow-up suited to the shoreline, particularly around mangroves or other sensitive plants. Do not use aggressive clearing that strips the whole site. In its native Asian coastal range the same species is part of the local flora, so an invasive label from Florida is not a reason for removal there.

sources.label: University of Florida IFAS: Colubrina asiatica
Singapore National Parks Board: Colubrina asiatica

identification: The small workers are dark brown to black with lighter legs and mouthparts. Appearance overlaps several other ants, and a painful sting does not identify the species. Colonies may occupy several damp pieces of wood or sheltered places rather than one conspicuous mound. Photograph ants where they are active without putting a hand into the nest. A pest specialist can examine a safely obtained sample; deliberately testing whether an ant will sting or climb a container is unnecessary.
actions: Use thick gloves and tools when moving mulch, stored wood or debris in an affected area, and keep children and pets away from an active nest. If ants are entering a building or nesting beside a frequently used path, request identification and a targeted management plan. Treating every ant in a woodland would also remove native species, including seed dispersers. NC State notes that management is more realistic than simple eradication. Avoid improvised pesticides or disturbing several nests while searching for a queen; professional guidance is useful where sting exposure is likely.

sources.label: North Carolina State Extension: Asian needle ant
Virginia Cooperative Extension: Asian Needle Ant

identification: Look for a slender, trailing or climbing stem carrying leaves divided into oval leaflets. The large pea-shaped flowers usually have a blue outer face and a pale throat, although white and double-flowered cultivated forms exist. Flat pods follow the flowers. A photograph of the blossom alone can miss those variations, so include leaves, stems, and fruit. The plant can behave as a perennial in warm climates but is often grown as an annual where winters are cold.
actions: Keep garden plants supported and check around the planting for unwanted seedlings, particularly where a long warm season allows pods to mature. Collect unwanted pods before they scatter seed and keep garden waste out of natural areas. A cultivated butterfly pea does not automatically warrant removal: assess whether it is spreading beyond the intended bed and consult local planting guidance. Choose a locally appropriate replacement if repeated escapes occur. Ornamental identification is not a substitute for verifying the suitability of a plant intended for food.

sources.label: North Carolina State Extension Plant Toolbox: Clitoria ternatea
Singapore National Parks Board: Clitoria ternatea

identification: Follow a creeping stem to see whether it roots at its joints and forms a low mat. The rounded to kidney-shaped leaves have a notch at the base, a relatively smooth upper surface, and hairs beneath. Flowers are tiny and pale greenish white, so a hand lens is useful. Related Dichondra can look very similar, and names used for lawn plants have changed or been misapplied. Include leaf undersides, stem joints, and flowers when asking a botanist to check the name.
actions: For a lawn planting, first decide whether the mat is wanted in that location. Trim or lift small unwanted patches with their rooted stems and watch the edge for renewed growth; do not move living runners into another garden or natural area. In a conservation site, obtain a local identification before clearing a patch that might belong to a different Dichondra. A lawn name used overseas may not identify a U.S. population reliably. Get that name checked before choosing a treatment or deciding that the patch is harming its surroundings.

sources.label: New Zealand Plant Conservation Network: Dichondra micrantha

identification: Check the shell outline as well as its color. Asian shore crabs have a roughly square shell with three teeth along each front side edge, banded walking legs, and often reddish spots on the claws. Adult males have a fleshy swelling near the base of the movable claw finger. Color varies, so a mottled brown crab is not enough for identification. Photograph the shell from above and the claws without placing fingers within reach of a pinch.
actions: Record the shore location, date, approximate abundance, and whether the crabs were under rocks or on artificial structures. Send a suspected new-range observation to the local marine invasive-species program. Do not transport live crabs as bait or pets, and inspect wet gear before moving between shores. When looking under a rock, replace it carefully in its original position to protect the animals beneath. If removal is proposed on a popular beach, follow a coordinated local plan. Collecting crabs casually may disturb the shore without restoring its native community.

sources.label: Hobbs, Cobb and Thornber (2017): Injury, reproductive status, and distribution of Hemigrapsus sanguineus in Rhode Island

identification: Inspect leaves low in the canopy and turn them over. Rust begins as small tan or reddish-brown spots, with tiny raised spore-producing structures on the underside; advanced disease can bring yellowing and early leaf fall. These symptoms overlap with other soybean leaf diseases, so a field photograph alone may not settle the diagnosis. Record the crop stage and how symptoms are distributed across the field, and submit affected leaves through an extension diagnostic service when rust is suspected.
actions: Follow regional rust surveillance during the growing season, particularly when weather and nearby detections favor infection. Scout before making a treatment decision: windborne spores can arrive from outside the farm, while the fungus needs living hosts to persist. Ask an extension crop specialist whether a confirmed detection, crop stage, and local risk justify a currently labeled fungicide. Avoid treating every leaf spot as rust or relying on an old calendar recommendation. Keep scouting after any intervention, since protecting the remaining leaf canopy is the practical objective.

sources.label: North Carolina State Extension: Asian soybean rust
University of Minnesota Extension: Soybean rust

identification: The sticky glandular hairs are a useful clue, but combine them with the flowers and leaves. Most leaves have three to five leaflets radiating from one point; the flowers are yellow and the narrow cylindrical fruits stand on stalks near the upper leaves. A mature plant can be about waist high under favorable conditions. Other spiderflowers share the divided leaves, so include the flower color, hairy stem, and a developed fruit in photographs rather than identifying from leaf shape alone.
actions: In a cultivated bed, remove a small unwanted annual before its long fruits mature and collect any ripe pods without shaking them over bare soil. Revisit the disturbed patch for seedlings and clean soil from tools before working elsewhere. For a population outside cultivation, record the habitat and ask a regional botanist whether it is introduced locally and whether intervention is warranted. Keep the response proportionate to the site: a volunteer in a vegetable bed and an unfamiliar plant in a wetland need different decisions, with local expertise guiding the latter.

sources.label: PlantNET NSW Flora Online: Arivela viscosa

identification: A swamp eel has a long, smooth body, small eyes, and fins that are greatly reduced compared with a typical fish. Those features can suggest the group, but they cannot securely distinguish the lineages once combined under Monopterus albus. Recent Florida accounts identify Sunda swamp eel, Monopterus javanensis, and cuchia, Ophichthys cuchia. Preserve the exact collection location and photographs of the head and whole body; a specialist may need a properly documented specimen or genetic evidence to resolve the name.
actions: Never release a live food-market fish or aquarium animal into a ditch, pond, or canal. Report an unfamiliar eel-like fish to the state fisheries agency and follow its instructions about documentation and handling; do not carry it alive to another waterbody. Avoid assigning Florida impact reports automatically to this exact catalog name. Prevention is useful despite the taxonomic uncertainty, but a control plan requires the local population's identity, extent, and agency guidance rather than an assumption that draining or casual trapping will eliminate it.

sources.label: US Fish and Wildlife Service (2025): Asian Swamp Eel ecological risk screening summary
Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission: Swamp Eels
Pintar et al. 2024: Asian swamp eels in Florida,1997-2023

identification: Examine a mature leaf stalk with a hand lens: Asian sword fern has dense dark brown scales pressed against it, with paler scale margins. Short stiff hairs occur on the central veins of its leaflets. Florida's native sword ferns can look similar from a distance, and the common name Boston fern does not resolve the species. Tubers point instead toward tuberous sword fern, Nephrolepis cordifolia. Photograph the stalk scales and leaflet undersides before removing an unfamiliar fern from a natural area.
actions: In Florida, replace confirmed Asian sword fern near natural habitats with an appropriate native fern. For a small patch, wear heavy gloves and lift the plants carefully; broken underground parts can remain and produce new growth. Recheck the patch instead of considering a single clearing complete. Contain removed plants and dispose of them through an accepted local waste route, never along a woodland edge. Large or mixed fern colonies deserve experienced help so native plants are retained and any treatment follows current site-specific guidance.

sources.label: University of South Florida: Florida Invasive Plants, Nephrolepis brownii
University of Florida: Distinguishing native and non-native sword ferns
UF/IFAS sword fern identification guide PDF

identification: This parasite lives inside a fish, so a thin body or poor growth is a reason to investigate, not an identification. The tapeworm requires examination of its structures, and molecular methods can support a diagnosis. It has also appeared in older literature as Bothriocephalus acheilognathi. An independent Colombian study documented it in Parodon magdalenensis, illustrating that its host range extends beyond carp. Keep the host species, collection waterbody, date, and any fish movements with a diagnostic submission.
actions: Do not release aquarium fish or unused live bait, and do not transfer fish from a suspect pond to another waterbody. Fish growers should consult a fish-health professional before stocking or moving a lot with unexplained poor performance. Ask the receiving laboratory how it wants samples collected and transported; an unplanned shipment can compromise identification. A research assay is not automatically an available field test. Any treatment or stocking decision should follow professional diagnosis and current fish-health requirements, with special care around waters supporting vulnerable native fishes.

sources.label: USGS: Asian fish tapeworm detection study
Rave et al. (2025): Asian fish tapeworm in Parodon magdalenensis

identification: Look for a single pale stripe running down the top of the dark thorax, together with conspicuously banded legs. Photograph the back as well as the legs because several mosquitoes have pale leg markings. The aquatic larvae develop in small water-holding containers, including pots, tires, and plant cavities. Eggs can remain on container walls through a dry period and hatch when water rises. An adult's appearance can help identify the mosquito, but cannot show whether that individual is carrying a pathogen.
actions: Once a week, empty and scrub items that collect water, turn unused containers over, and cover stored water securely. Refresh animal water responsibly rather than leaving animals without it. Check gutters and small items hidden in vegetation as well as obvious buckets. Use EPA-registered repellent according to its label, wear protective clothing, and maintain window screens. Persistent mosquito problems can be reported to the local mosquito-control program. Bite avoidance is worthwhile without assuming that a sighting proves a local disease outbreak.

sources.label: University of Florida IFAS: Asian tiger mosquito
CDC: Life Cycle of Aedes Mosquitoes
EPA tips to prevent mosquito bites

identification: The broad dark and pale bands across the abdomen are conspicuous, but body color varies with the surroundings and size. Adults can become much larger than many familiar local shrimp; juveniles are less obvious and may need specialist examination of the rostrum and other structures. Take a clear side photograph with a scale, showing the head and abdomen. Note whether the animal came from an estuary or offshore catch, since young and mature tiger shrimp use different coastal habitats.
actions: Report an unusual tiger shrimp catch to the state marine fisheries or aquatic invasive-species program with the capture location, date, approximate depth, and size. Follow its instructions if a specimen is needed. Never release live farmed or aquarium shrimp, or move a catch alive to another waterbody. Aquaculture operations should use approved stock and prevent escapes through their established biosecurity procedures. Your report helps agencies track whether populations persist and spread. Include an honest count of the catch rather than assuming that one animal represents an established population.

sources.label: FAO: Cultured aquatic species fact sheet, Penaeus monodon

identification: Look very close to the mud surface for small branching stems with opposite leaves and roots emerging at the joints. Flower and fruit stalks are important: this species can have conspicuous little stalks beneath its fruits, unlike some close waterwort lookalikes. A useful record includes a magnified view of a flowering or fruiting stem, a scale, and the water depth. Elatine triandra is a frequent source of confusion, including in the aquarium trade, so an overall photograph of a green mat may be insufficient.
actions: Keep aquarium plants, sediment, and rinse water out of streams, ponds, and irrigation channels. At a rice field or wetland, document the patch before disturbing it and ask a botanist to confirm the species. Clean clinging mud and vegetation from field equipment before moving to another site. A patch in an irrigated crop and one in a natural wetland may call for different responses. Its presence alone does not show how much it affects the surrounding plants. A removal or water-management plan should await local advice rather than relying on a treatment developed for another aquatic weed.

sources.label: INRAN / RECA Niger: Note sur Elatine ambigua
Flora of North America: Elatine ambigua

identification: Look for a thick, rounded triangular shell with closely spaced, raised concentric ridges. Shell color ranges from yellowish to brown, and the inside may differ among populations. Native fingernail clams and young mussels can be confused with small specimens, so photograph both valves with a ruler and ask for confirmation. The name Corbicula fluminea has been used provisionally for several introduced genetic lineages; shell appearance alone cannot resolve that history. Empty shells document occurrence, but not necessarily a living population at that moment.
actions: Remove sediment from anchors and other equipment before leaving an infested waterbody, then follow local cleaning, draining, and drying instructions. Lake George researchers found that anchor mud could carry clams, making this an especially useful place to check. Report suspected new populations with location and shell photographs; do not move live clams as bait or aquarium animals. Avoid laying improvised bottom barriers over a patch. Lake George trials reduced clams temporarily but also harmed other bottom-dwelling organisms, and populations later returned.

sources.label: Farrell, Nierzwicki-Bauer and Rose (2024): ASSEMBLE, Asian clams section, pp. 30-32

identification: Visit in the morning to see the flower before it fades: two broad blue petals sit above a much smaller pale petal. The pointed leaves clasp the stem in a sheath, and sprawling stems may root where they meet moist soil. Other dayflowers can share the blue color, so record the unequal petals, the folded flower bract, and a leaf base. A plant without open flowers is still identifiable, but photographs of the whole patch alone are less useful than these close details.
actions: In a small garden patch, lift unwanted plants while they are young and collect the trailing stems as well as the original root system. Pieces left against damp ground may remain a problem, so do not pile them at the edge of the bed. Recheck shaded, moist corners where plants were previously established and prevent new seed production. In a crop, confirm the identification with an extension adviser before selecting a weed program. Tolerance to particular herbicides should not be generalized to every product or every population.

sources.label: Iowa State University Extension: Asiatic dayflower
North Carolina State Extension: Asiatic dayflower

identification: A large basal rosette and tall dock-like flowering stalks are starting clues, not a final identification. Several Rumex species produce broad leaves and dense fruiting stems. Photograph the lowest leaves, the junctions of leaves and stems, and mature fruits, keeping a scale in view. A local flora or botanist may need fruit characters to separate this species from familiar docks. The size of a patch can reflect both seedling recruitment and underground spread, rather than a single unusually large plant.
actions: Mark the edge of a suspected patch and avoid moving its soil or mature seed heads to another site. Where identification is confirmed, seek a regional weed specialist's advice before disturbing a riverside stand or prescribing a crop treatment. Germination experiments show that exposed, shallowly buried seeds benefit from light, so unnecessary soil disturbance can create recruitment opportunities; restore suitable cover after any agreed removal. For a U.S. site, confirm both the plant and the reason for intervention locally; a spreading European population is useful context, but cannot determine the outcome in another landscape.

sources.label: USDA APHIS: Weed risk assessment for Rumex confertus
Kolodziejek and Patykowski (2015): Effect of Environmental Factors on Germination and Emergence of Invasive Rumex confertus in Central Europe

identification: Look for a small, rounded cinnamon-brown adult at night or sheltering near plants during the day. It is much smaller than many familiar June beetles. A pale C-shaped grub with a brown head is only a scarab-family clue: several root-feeding beetles look that way. Correct larval identification requires examination of mouthparts and the pattern of hairs near the rear end. If seedlings are declining in patches, compare roots and soil from affected and healthy areas rather than assuming every grub is this species.
actions: Check vulnerable garden plants after dusk to connect fresh feeding with the actual beetle. In a field with a history of grub damage, arrange preplant scouting with an extension crop adviser and preserve records of affected patches. Michigan observations show that severe root injury can precede obvious stand loss, and a later spray is not a dependable rescue. Do not treat a whole lawn merely because an adult came to a light. Base any management on the identified life stage, crop or planting, and current local recommendations.

sources.label: University of Maine Extension: Asiatic garden beetle
MSU: Asiatic Garden Beetle in Michigan field crops
MSU: Asiatic garden beetles and corn field yield losses

identification: The above-ground plant is relatively small, with stiff, hairy stems, narrow leaves, and small flowers that can vary in color. Its most important feature is hidden: a specialized connection joins its roots to a grass host. A stressed corn plant beside a small flowering weed is worth documenting, but stress alone is not diagnostic. Photograph the suspect plant in place, including leaves and flowers, and note the associated crop. Do not dig through a suspected infestation simply to expose the attachment.
actions: Report a suspected U.S. occurrence promptly to state plant-health officials or USDA APHIS and leave soil and plants in place while awaiting instructions. Avoid carrying soil, crop residue, or seed from the suspect area on equipment or footwear. The very small seeds and their persistence make an isolated-looking patch a poor candidate for casual pulling followed by normal field traffic. Follow the current official survey and containment plan, including instructions for equipment and field access. Old accounts of the Carolinas program cannot tell you which restrictions apply to a particular property today.

sources.label: USDA APHIS: Witchweed biology and eradication program assessment
Southern Illinois University: Striga asiatica in the U.S.A.

identification: Check emerging spears and, later, the ferny growth on a warm afternoon. Common asparagus beetles are dark bluish to brown with cream markings; the spotted asparagus beetle is orange with black dots. Rows of dark upright eggs on spears and grayish, wrinkled larvae with dark heads support the identification. Spotted-beetle larvae mainly use the berries, so finding that species does not imply the same foliage damage. Keep adults, eggs, and larvae separate in your observations to understand which stage is active.
actions: In a small asparagus bed, handpick adults and larvae into soapy water and remove eggs from spears. Keep checking because new adults can fly into the bed. Allow useful predators and tiny parasitoid wasps to remain, and avoid unnecessary broad treatments that kill them. Remove old fern growth only after it has turned completely brown, taking that debris out of the growing area. If injury remains substantial, consult current asparagus-specific guidance; any labeled pesticide must respect harvest intervals and the plants' flowering period.

sources.label: University of Wisconsin Vegetable Entomology: Asparagus beetle
University of Minnesota Extension: Asparagus beetles

identification: First establish which asparagus fern the plant actually is. A recent Bishop Museum specimen review separates upright, densely arranged Asparagus densiflorus from the weakly sprawling Asparagus aethiopicus previously recorded under its name in Hawaii. Nursery labels and familiar cultivar names may not follow that distinction. Photograph the whole plant's posture, stem branching, clusters of green leaf-like structures, flowers, and berries. A botanist may need more than a photograph to resolve a garden plant, especially when published horticultural accounts combine the names.
actions: Keep an uncertain plant contained while its identity is checked, and collect unwanted berries before they are spread beyond the garden. Do not dump root masses or potting soil into natural areas. In a region where asparagus ferns escape, ask a local invasive-plant specialist which species is present and which removal approach fits the site. Do not transfer impact reports for sprawling A. aethiopicus to true A. densiflorus automatically. A correctly named plant makes local advice much more useful, especially when deciding whether a contained garden specimen or an escaping patch needs action.

sources.label: University of Wisconsin Extension: Asparagus fern, Asparagus densiflorus
PlantNET NSW Flora Online: Asparagus aethiopicus
Bishop Museum 2024: Misapplied names in the Hawaiian introduced flora
Wong et al. 2022: three Asparagus chloroplast genomes

identification: Inspect both sides of an affected aspen leaf. A blotch between the leaf surfaces, sometimes drawn into a raised fold by silk, points toward a leafminer, while open holes or chewing along the edge suggest another kind of injury. This moth is tiny and easily overlooked. Larvae and pupae inside a mine can help an entomologist distinguish it from other miners. Record the host tree, season, and whether the mines are scattered or widespread; a single mine does not establish the scale of injury.
actions: On a small tree, remove a few confirmed infested leaves when practical, as the Pacific Northwest handbook recommends, while leaving enough healthy foliage for the tree. For an established tree, monitor the extent and recurrence of mining rather than stripping the crown. Seek a local tree-health assessment if repeated heavy injury accompanies declining growth. The Turkish study describes a particular regional life cycle; its timing should not be copied as a spray calendar elsewhere. Planting a locally suitable, less susceptible tree may be preferable where serious infestations recur.

sources.label: Pacific Northwest Insect Management Handbook: Poplar-Aspen leafblotch miner
Tozlu, Hayat and Ozbek (2002): Phyllonorycter apparella, a new record and a new pest of trembling aspen in Turkey

identification: Young hairy fleabane and horseweed can be difficult to tell apart. Look for gray-green, often crinkled leaves and a mixture of short stiff hairs and longer soft hairs. Mature hairy fleabane tends to branch lower on the stem, while horseweed usually branches mainly above. The small flower heads have no showy daisy-like rays and later become pale fluffy seed heads. Photograph the stem base, leaves, hairs, and mature heads; height alone is unreliable because growing conditions change the size of the plant.
actions: Remove small unwanted plants before the fluffy seed heads form, preferably while the root system is still easy to lift. In orchards and other repeatedly disturbed sites, check the margins and gaps as well as the main planting rows, since windborne seeds can arrive from outside. Keep useful ground cover where it suits the crop and site. A mature seed-bearing patch requires care to avoid scattering seed during work. For persistent agricultural problems, seek a locally appropriate integrated weed program instead of assuming all populations respond alike to a herbicide.

sources.label: University of California IPM: Hairy fleabane
Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Conyza bonariensis

identification: Look for a tall, branching flower cluster that retains a strong central axis, with numerous small heads and narrow leaves along the stems. The bracts immediately surrounding the heads are mostly hairless, an important contrast with some other weedy fleabanes. A hand lens and mature flowering material are much more useful than a distant photograph. Erigeron sumatrensis has repeatedly been confused with this plant in older records, so record the name used by the identification source as well as the plant's location.
actions: If it is an unwanted plant in a cultivated bed, remove it before the heads release their fine-bristled seeds, collecting mature heads carefully. Check nearby disturbed ground for additional plants and avoid spreading seed with moved soil or garden waste. For a natural-area or agricultural infestation, have a specimen checked before importing management advice attached to another Conyza name. For a U.S. site, confirm the current name and the local reason for intervention. Similar appearance and overlapping older names can otherwise lead to a treatment aimed at the wrong fleabane.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Erigeron floribundus
Liendo et al. (2021): Annual weedy species of Erigeron in the northern Iberian Peninsula: a review

identification: The foliage can resemble a she-oak or a conifer from a distance, but the tiny leaves closely sheath slender, jointed twigs. Small pinkish-white flowers occur in narrow clusters, and older trunks develop rough, furrowed bark. Casuarina produces woody cone-like fruits, while athel tamarisk has small seed capsules. Photograph a flowering twig and the trunk as well as the overall tree. Do not assume that the impact or reproductive behavior of another saltcedar species applies unchanged to this large tree.
actions: Check planted trees near drainage lines for young plants and report spread into waterways to the local land manager. Where removal is appropriate, small seedlings are easier to address than established trees with extensive roots. Mature riverbank trees need a planned approach that considers access, bank stability, regrowth, and replacement vegetation. Avoid dumping cut branches where floods can carry them away. Queensland's documented river impacts support careful prevention in susceptible places, but Australian restrictions and treatment instructions should not be treated as U.S. rules.

sources.label: Oregon State University Landscape Plants: Tamarix aphylla

identification: Separate the juvenile and adult growth before comparing leaves. Ground-running shoots usually have lobed leaves and root along their stems; flowering shoots higher on a support carry less-lobed leaves and later dark fruits. English ivy and Atlantic ivy are difficult to separate confidently from one leaf, and cultivar names add another complication. Use a regional key or specialist when the exact name affects a report. In the Pacific Northwest, the management concern is especially clear where ivy is covering native ground vegetation or climbing trees.
actions: Wear gloves and protective clothing, then pull small ground patches carefully when soil is moist, collecting rooted stems. On a tree, cut accessible vines without cutting the bark and clear the lower stems; leave high attached vines to die rather than pulling down material from the canopy. Keep removed stems from touching moist soil and rooting again. Revisit for seedlings and resprouts over subsequent seasons, and restore appropriate ground cover. Large trees, steep slopes, or extensive mats may require an experienced crew.

sources.label: Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board: English and Irish ivy

identification: Turn over leaves and examine the tiny dark oval cases with magnification. Mature immature stages are well under a millimeter long and can look like small scales or specks rather than obvious whiteflies. Color and host plant are insufficient because other whiteflies also have dark cases. Reliable identification commonly relies on slide-mounted specimens examined by an insect diagnostic laboratory. Photograph the colony and record the host plant, but ask the laboratory how to collect material before clipping and shipping leaves.
actions: Inspect new nursery plants, especially leaf undersides, before placing them among established plants. Keep a suspect plant separate while identification is arranged and avoid giving away cuttings carrying the insects. Record actual yellowing or growth changes separately from the number of whiteflies, since a detection does not itself demonstrate damage. CDFA's 2022 assessment reported no significant known California impacts at that time. A pesticide decision should therefore follow identification and a current local assessment, not a treatment schedule borrowed from a more damaging whitefly.

sources.label: California Department of Food and Agriculture: Aleuroclava aucubae assessment
Seljak (2012): Six new alien phytophagous insects recorded in Slovenia
Seljak: Aucuba whitefly diagnostic figure and context
