actions: Provide the diagnostician with the plant name, root photographs and whether nearby Pistacia galls were observed. Keep those observations separate until an expert connects them. Inspect replacement plants for concealed root problems and avoid sharing suspect rooted material. Management of a crop root infestation needs local advice; removing unrelated Pistacia trees is not warranted by an uncertain aphid observation.

sources.label: Smynthurodes betae — Aphids on the World’s Plants
Gall defense and facilitation in Smynthurodes betae

identification: Small mottled beetles without a long snout; round holes in stored beans and pale larvae within seeds. Inspect the bean surface for both tiny entry marks and larger round emergence holes. An adult's short wing covers leave the end of the abdomen exposed, another useful seed-beetle clue. Other stored-product beetles can occur in the same cupboard, so keep a specimen associated with the actual damaged lot.
actions: Label and isolate affected packages, check neighboring beans and clean spilled material from storage crevices. Use sound, clean containers for uninfested supplies. For seed intended for planting, ask a seed or storage specialist before using heat or cold treatments that could affect germination. Do not mix suspect beans into a clean lot merely because adults are no longer visible.

identification: Large glossy, deeply lobed basal leaves and tall spikes of white flowers with purple, spiny bracts. Examine the leaf divisions and the spiny bracts surrounding the flowers together. Large leaves without a flowering stem can resemble other garden perennials, while different Acanthus species differ in how deeply and sharply they are cut. Photograph the base of the clump to show the growth arrangement rather than only the ornamental spike.
actions: Choose a bed where the clump's edge can be inspected without disturbing neighboring plants. When moving or removing an unwanted planting, collect underground pieces and watch for shoots returning from missed fragments. Wear gloves around the flower spikes. A well-contained ornamental does not need removal simply because the species can spread under favorable conditions.

identification: Look for creeping, rooting stems and compact, lobed green flower heads without long projecting bristles; a grass key is needed for similar species. Check whether a low stem is rooting at a joint, and photograph the leaf collar and mature panicle at close range. Its comparatively unbristly heads contrast with long-awned rabbit's-foot grasses. A wet ditch is useful habitat context but does not establish identity; individual spikelets provide stronger evidence than the overall green plume.
actions: Keep a botanical record of the patch before undertaking work near water. If it is confirmed unwanted, ask the land manager about a method that limits soil disturbance and protects other bank plants. Clean mud and plant pieces from tools before another site visit. Avoid turning a tentative grass identification into broad ditch or streamside clearance.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Polypogon viridis

identification: With a flashlight, inspect mattress seams, nearby furniture joints and other narrow hiding places for flat, oval brown adults, pale young bugs, shed skins and dark spotting. Keep a suspected insect for identification and photograph it beside a size reference. Carpet beetles and bat-associated bugs can be confused with bed bugs. Skin reactions alone cannot establish the cause, so record exactly where the insect or signs were found rather than relying on the appearance of bites.
actions: Avoid scattering belongings through the home while investigating. Coordinate with building management when appropriate and use a pest professional's integrated plan for inspection, containment and follow-up. Do not improvise room heating or apply outdoor products indoors. Keep monitoring after treatment according to the plan, because a single inspection without visible insects does not establish that all hiding places are clear.

sources.label: Bed Bugs Appearance and Life Cycle

identification: Check leaf undersides for pale aphids wrapped in white wax, sticky deposits and downward-curled leaf edges. Wool on bark alone points to other possible insects. Turn over fresh leaves to locate the insects beneath the wax. A white covering on the trunk or a large colony on twigs may involve a different beech-associated insect. Include leaf curling and the host's overall condition in photographs. The conspicuous wax can make a modest colony appear more alarming than the actual injury.
actions: For a vigorous established beech, observe new foliage and natural enemies before considering treatment. Avoid unnecessary spraying of a hedge that is otherwise growing well. If young plants remain stressed or growth declines, ask a local adviser to confirm both the aphid and any contributing watering or root problem. Do not diagnose beech bark disease from these leaf colonies.

sources.label: Study on intensity of infestation, biology and harmfulness of woolly beech aphid

identification: Bark lesions or dieback warrant examination, but symptoms are not species-specific. Reliable identification requires laboratory work, including microscopic or DNA comparisons. Show the whole affected trunk or branch and close views of lesion margins, including any fruiting structures. Red fungal dots, when present, are not a reliable species test. European and North American beech bark disease literature uses closely related names, so the host and location must accompany a modern laboratory determination.
actions: Arrange a tree-health assessment that considers drought, wounds and other possible pathogens alongside this fungus. Keep people clear of branches a professional considers unsafe. If sampling is requested, follow the laboratory's directions rather than cutting indiscriminately into the trunk. Finding a fungus in a sample should be interpreted with the symptoms and test method before major tree work is planned.

sources.label: Phylogenetic relationships of Neonectria/Cylindrocarpon on Fagus in North America
Fungi Associated With Woody Tissues of European Beech and Their Impact on Tree Health

identification: Look for beech scale's white wax followed by patches of damaged, cankered bark. A plant laboratory must distinguish N. faginata from other canker fungi. Separate white scale wax from later bark lesions in the photographs. Cankers can merge and obscure the sequence, so earlier pictures are useful. Other Neonectria species can participate in beech bark disease, and the visible canker does not tell them apart. Record whether the host is American beech or another planted beech.
actions: Have structural concerns assessed promptly where a diseased tree could affect a path, building or gathering area. A specialist can advise whether laboratory sampling would change management and how to handle affected wood. Monitor nearby beeches without peeling healthy bark. Do not transfer the name of a European beech pathogen to this tree solely because an older guide uses it.

sources.label: Phylogenetic relationships of Neonectria/Cylindrocarpon on Fagus in North America

identification: Hold a leaf toward the light to check for dark interveinal bands, and compare nearby leaves for thickening and distortion. Confirmation needs specialist assessment. Record whether affected and apparently healthy leaves occur together on a branch; overall yellowing alone is less informative. Photograph the tree crown from a repeatable position so changes can be assessed over time. Banding is a useful warning sign, but other injuries can coexist, and a photograph cannot show the microscopic nematode itself.
actions: Record the first date of symptoms and the beech's planting history if known. Ask the local diagnostic service whether it needs leaves, buds or photographs at the current season. Avoid sharing cuttings or moving suspect nursery trees while the problem is assessed. Care decisions should follow current local tree-health advice rather than a homemade nematode treatment or indiscriminate pruning.

sources.label: Beech leaf disease symptoms caused by newly recognized nematode subspecies Litylenchus crenatae mccannii
Borden et al.2025: developing fluopyram for beech leaf disease
Burke et al.2026: quantitative nematode inoculation and beech resistance

identification: The nematode itself is too small for ordinary field identification. Dark bands between leaf veins are a useful warning sign, but laboratory examination confirms the organism. Photograph affected buds as well as leaves if poor bud opening is noticeable. Retain both a close view of the interveinal pattern and a whole-branch view showing healthy-looking foliage nearby. Laboratory staff use nematode body characters and genetic comparisons; the small organism cannot be confirmed from the visible bands alone.
actions: Keep reports tied to the original tree, with its host identity and symptom dates. Contact a tree-health service before taking material elsewhere, and request its sampling instructions. Continue observing crown condition while advice is obtained. If the tree is in a collection, avoid distributing young plants from the affected group until the movement risk has been professionally assessed.

sources.label: Beech leaf disease symptoms caused by newly recognized nematode subspecies Litylenchus crenatae mccannii
Borden et al.2025: developing fluopyram for beech leaf disease
Burke et al.2026: quantitative nematode inoculation and beech resistance

identification: Check for opposite, broad toothed leaves, square stems and small flowers in narrow spikes. Leaf color varies among forms and is not enough for identification. Inspect the leaf arrangement and stem shape together, since purple foliage also occurs in many unrelated ornamentals. Small flower spikes and developing seed structures help distinguish a mature plant from other aromatic mint-family herbs. Do not taste a leaf to identify it, particularly when the plant is growing in a pasture or mixed forage.
actions: Mark suspect patches so they are not inadvertently cut into hay or offered as forage. Consult an agricultural adviser about confirmed plants and a veterinarian if animals may have eaten them. For unwanted garden volunteers, prevent seed production and check nearby disturbed soil later. Culinary cultivation of selected forms does not establish that an unidentified pasture plant is safe for livestock.

sources.label: Perilla frutescens — Plants of the World Online

identification: Look for smooth, striped caterpillars with a dark spot above the second true leg, scale-covered egg clusters and grouped young larvae. Similar armyworms require closer comparison. Look for groups of small larvae near a covered egg mass, then examine older caterpillars separately. Body color varies, so combine the smooth surface, striping and side spot with host and feeding observations. Include damaged fruit or foliage in the record; an adult moth at a light does not prove larvae are injuring the crop.
actions: Check new feeding damage during crop inspections and record the size of larvae, since timing affects management choices. Consult local extension guidance for the crop rather than transferring a recommendation from another vegetable. Conserve predators and parasitoids where possible, and avoid unnecessary treatments when injury is minor. Reassess fresh growth after any authorized response.

identification: Look for paired flowers and berries, opposite smooth-edged leaves and older stems with hollow centers. Hybrid identification needs comparison with both parent species. Compare hairiness on young twigs and leaf undersides as well as paired flowers. The hybrid can be intermediate between its parents, and a red berry or hollow old stem alone does not resolve that relationship. Photograph flowers at different ages if available. Native bush honeysuckles deserve careful separation before any clearing begins.
actions: Map confirmed shrubs and check for nearby seedlings in areas where local guidance calls for control. Plan work before berries are widely dispersed and contain fruiting branches. Cut established shrubs may require follow-up for regrowth, so obtain a method suited to their size and site. Retain surrounding native cover where possible to reduce unnecessary disturbance.

sources.label: Flora Novae Angliae: Lonicera morrowii × L. tatarica hybrid paragraph

identification: Check the upright branching habit, narrow leaves, papery joint sheaths and tiny flowers near branch tips. Mature fruit and a regional key are needed for similar knotweeds. Include lower and upper leaves in the same photographic record, since their difference in size is useful. Examine the papery sheath around a stem joint and the small flowers nestled near it. Other knotweeds occupy similar disturbed ground; a fruiting specimen and regional key are more dependable than general upright habit.
actions: Ask a botanist to check the mature material before assigning a new occurrence record. Note whether it grows in a cultivated bed, recently exposed soil or a seasonally wet margin. Where it is confirmed unwanted, plan work before ripe fruits are scattered. Avoid moving contaminated soil from the patch, but do not remove neighboring knotweeds without establishing their identity.

sources.label: Virtual Guide to the Flora of Mongolia: Polygonum patulum

identification: Look for lobed leaves with sticky hairs on their stalks and edges, small reddish flowers and seed capsules. Green-leaved plants occur as well as purple forms. The sticky gland-tipped hairs distinguish it from physic nut, Jatropha curcas, whose leaf stalks and margins lack those hairs and whose flowers are yellow-green. Castor bean usually has more leaf lobes and different flowering structures. Photograph a young shoot carefully without using taste or skin contact as an identification test.
actions: Mark the patch before mowing or earthmoving so workers do not scatter capsules and fragments. Obtain disposal advice before uprooting established shrubs, particularly along waterways. Keep animals away from suspect forage and seek veterinary advice after possible ingestion. Subsequent checks should look for seedlings and surviving root pieces, with management adapted to the location and local requirements.

sources.label: Jatropha gossypiifolia — Flora of the Cayman Islands and Kew

identification: Under magnification, compare the pale scale patches near the front and rear of the wing covers and the even covering of hairs on the shield behind the head. The similar Ptinus fur has more distinctly tufted hairs there. Males are relatively parallel-sided and females rounder, so differing outlines do not necessarily indicate two species. Retain adults from the actual package or crevice where they were found, keeping that location with the specimen for a pest diagnostician.
actions: Check old flour and other dry goods for the likely breeding source, keeping samples separately labeled. Clean spills and inaccessible food residues as part of a confirmed stored-product response. Do not discard unrelated possessions or apply a room-wide treatment based on one unidentified beetle. A pest diagnostician can help distinguish an active food infestation from an incidental adult.

sources.label: Beetles associated with stored products in Canada: an identification guide
Annotated list of insects and mites associated with stored grain and cereal products

identification: Look for trumpet-shaped blue or violet flowers, opposite toothed or lobed leaves and paired leafy bracts beneath each flower. Compare with related cultivated Thunbergia vines. Photograph the paired bracts beneath a fresh bloom and the leaf stalks attached to a square young stem. Flower color varies with lighting, and other cultivated Thunbergia can be similar. A cut flower without foliage misses useful characters; note whether a vine is planted on a support or climbing freely through other vegetation.
actions: Inspect the base before planning removal, because cutting the canopy does not address the underground root system. Avoid pulling heavy vines out of tree crowns without professional advice. Keep capsules and root fragments contained and arrange an appropriate disposal route. Return to the site to check for renewed shoots, especially where the original root system could not be fully reached.

identification: Unusually elongated flower parts and seed-replacing galls are useful warning signs. Microscopic and, where needed, DNA examination are necessary for species identification. Compare an affected grass head with a normal one from the same host and photograph the elongated galls. Preserve the host identity as carefully as the gall sample. Other seed-gall nematodes and grass disorders can produce superficially similar heads; modern species attribution should not simply repeat an old broad host list.
actions: Label suspect seed lots separately and consult the testing laboratory before cleaning, mixing or transporting them. Give the laboratory information about the field, host grass and collection date. A confirmed finding may affect seed handling, but it does not establish the same risk in every grass species. Follow crop-specific advice for contaminated seed and subsequent monitoring.

sources.label: First report of Anguina agrostis from Poa palustris in Wyoming
First Report of Bentgrass Seed Gall Nematode in Virginia and Minnesota

identification: Look for fine gray-green leaves, underground spreading stems and an open flower head with a mixture of awned and awnless flower clusters. A grass key is needed. Inspect a flowering stem and its basal growth together, including the leaf collar. An open panicle alone resembles several other bentgrasses, and the presence of an occasional awn does not settle the identity. Close examination of several spikelets helps account for variation within one plant and separates it from similar turf grasses.
actions: Keep a flowering sample associated with photographs of the original patch so a botanist can assess both structure and habit. In a lawn or pasture, identify the grass before changing management of the entire stand. If a small unwanted patch is confirmed, contain mature heads and soil during work and monitor for returning growth from underground stems.

sources.label: Agrostis castellana — Flora of New Zealand
Agrostis castellana — Plants of the World Online

identification: Look for an open, often drooping flower head, narrow leaves and tiny bent awns. Mature heads may break away; a botanical key is needed for close relatives. Include a close view of the tiny flower clusters and the point where the uppermost sheath surrounds the flower stalk. Related wind grasses overlap in size and habit, and their fine floral hairs and awns matter in a key. An airy panicle or a detached head by itself cannot establish this species.
actions: In a lawn, wet margin or restoration site, note whether the plant was intentionally sown and retain the seed-mixture label if available. Ask a local botanist to examine mature material before treating a population as an introduced weed. If management is justified, avoid scattering ripe heads while working and clean soil from footwear before visiting another habitat.

identification: Look for three heart-shaped leaflets, clustered yellow flowers on leafless stalks and small underground bulbs. Distinguish it from low, creeping wood sorrels. Trace the flower stalk back to the leaf cluster and compare the broad, heart-shaped leaflets with smaller creeping wood sorrels nearby. Purple leaf dots may be present but are not required. A bare patch in summer can still contain living bulbs, so season and previous photographs help interpret what is visible.
actions: Mark the patch while leaves are visible so its extent is not forgotten during dormancy. Where removal is appropriate, work carefully to collect the small bulbs without distributing soil into clean beds. Repeated checks are more useful than assuming one digging has succeeded. Do not identify or consume a plant merely from its sour-sorrel reputation or buttercup name.

sources.label: Oxalis pes-caprae — Flora of Iraq and Kew

identification: Check for rooting runners, underground stems, a fringe of white hairs where leaf meets sheath and three to seven fingerlike flower-head branches. Follow a surface runner to its rooted joints and inspect a flowering stalk for the radiating branches. Other lawn grasses can resemble it when mown short, so include the leaf collar and underground stems if already exposed during garden work. Seasonal brown foliage may be dormancy rather than death.
actions: Decide whether the patch is desired turf or an unwanted extension into another bed before intervening. Inspect edges regularly during warm growth and collect cut runners rather than leaving them on moist soil. Persistent incursions need a sustained boundary and follow-up plan. Seek lawn or landscape advice before changing watering or treatment across a mixed grass area.

identification: Check an intact bundle attached to a twig: this pine has five long needles that droop, especially on older shoots. Photograph their length beside a ruler and include a mature, resinous cone with its stalk visible. Other five-needle pines can resemble it, so needle number alone is insufficient. The combination of pendulous foliage, elongated hanging cones and the change from smooth young bark to fissured older bark provides a stronger identification than a distant silhouette.
actions: For a cultivated specimen, allow for its eventual tree size and keep its original nursery label. Monitor naturally appearing seedlings without assuming that every nearby pine belongs to the planted tree. An arborist can assess major pruning or structural concerns on a large specimen. Botanical identification and local naturalization guidance should precede any decision to remove an otherwise healthy tree.

sources.label: Pinus wallichiana — Plants of the World Online

identification: Use magnification to check the dark head and abdomen, pale middle and two-part waist. Confirm a collected specimen because other small household ants can look similar. Photograph several workers along the trail through a hand lens, showing the light middle of the body between the darker ends. A close side view may reveal the two waist segments. Other minute ants have similar color patterns, so a picture of a trail without individual detail rarely settles identification.
actions: Trace the trail to its source without carrying pots or branches to another property. Indoors, store sweet foods securely and clean spills, then ask a pest specialist to identify a retained worker sample. In plant collections, check cavities and honeydew-producing insects as part of inspection. Avoid broad outdoor treatments based solely on the presence of a small ant trail.

sources.label: Monomorium floricola — Ants of Costa Rica
Two New Exotic Pest Ants Collected in Mississippi

identification: Look for opposite, untoothed leaves and small white flowers; compare petal length with the sepals before identifying it. A low mat can be confused with common chickweed until the hairs and flower parts are examined. Take a side view of the calyx as well as a face-on flower photograph, showing whether the notched petals extend beyond the sepals. Subspecies attribution requires more care than a general mouse-ear chickweed label.
actions: Observe the patch through flowering if its identity is uncertain and there is no immediate need for intervention. In a maintained bed, remove only confirmed unwanted plants and contain seed-bearing material. For a botanical record, include the complete stem, leaf pairs and flowers. Ask a local flora specialist to confirm the subspecies rather than automatically applying it to every Cerastium fontanum observation.

sources.label: Info Flora: Cerastium fontanum subsp. vulgare

identification: Look for relatively large, drooping oval flower clusters on threadlike stalks, with broad overlapping scales. Photograph several dangling spikelets beside a ruler and show the fine stalks supporting them. Smaller quaking grasses have different combinations of spikelet size and number, so a broad view of the whole panicle is useful too. The papery overlapping parts become more conspicuous as the annual plant ripens and dries.
actions: If grown ornamentally, keep mature seedheads from being scattered beyond the bed and check nearby open ground for volunteers. Where local guidance identifies it as unwanted, act before the ripe heads are disturbed by mowing or collection. Preserve other grasses in a mixed patch until identified. Keep seed-bearing dried arrangements out of natural areas and contain any loose seeds when disposing of them.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Briza maxima

identification: A complete leaf has five leaflets: the lower pair lies close to the stem and can resemble separate stipules. Include this attachment and a naturally exposed hollow stem in photographs, together with several yellow flower clusters on their long stalks. Birdsfoot trefoil can look similar from a single blossom. Close views of the small calyx teeth beneath the petals give a botanist useful additional characters without relying only on the plant's wet growing site.
actions: At a damp meadow or drainage margin, first establish whether the trefoil is planted forage or an unwanted population. Avoid disturbing a whole wet area based on a tentative leaf identification. If local management is needed, work before pods ripen and keep plant debris contained. Follow up on surviving creeping growth, using advice suited to the soil and neighboring vegetation.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Lotus pedunculatus

identification: The eyes sit low on a very large head. Dark body blotches and a belly ridge extending only from the vent to the pelvic fins help distinguish it from silver carp. Photograph a suspected catch from the side, showing the large head, low eye and blotched scales. The shorter belly keel helps distinguish bighead from silver carp, but hybrids can complicate identification. Do not assume that a large fish lacking common carp's mouth barbels is necessarily this species.
actions: Record the waterbody, access point and catch date before contacting fisheries staff. Follow their instructions on retention, reporting or disposal, since rules differ by jurisdiction. Never use an uncertain juvenile as live bait or stock it in another pond. Keep a record of photographs and any agency identification so an unusual catch can be assessed accurately.

sources.label: Missouri Department of Conservation: Bighead carp
California Department of Fish and Wildlife: Bighead carp

identification: Look for yellow globe-shaped flower heads, brown overlapping bracts and rough lance-shaped leaves on upright stems. Photograph the brown cup beneath an open flower head and compare upper and lower leaves. Other yellow-flowered composites may look alike at a distance, but the large rounded head and papery bracts are useful together. A garden label can help distinguish an intentional planting from a self-sown patch beyond it.
actions: Before cutting mature heads, arrange a way to contain seeds and obtain disposal guidance for your area. Mark the rooted plants so follow-up is possible after flowering stems are gone. Where digging is advised, minimize disturbance to surrounding grasses and inspect for returning shoots. Established garden plants need the same attention to seed escape as roadside volunteers in an affected region.

identification: Look for two distinct worker sizes, with conspicuously large heads on the larger workers. Have an expert confirm the species. Collect or photograph both large-headed and small workers from the same trail, because the smaller form alone may be difficult to recognize. Loose soil beneath paving is not species-specific evidence. Other Pheidole ants also have large-headed workers; a specialist should examine the relevant waist and body characters before a treatment is chosen.
actions: Keep pots and soil from a confirmed infested area from becoming an unnoticed route to a new site. Indoors, remove food residues and trace entry points while identification is pending. For a persistent outdoor colony, coordinate advice across property boundaries where practical. Use a targeted plan and follow-up checks rather than repeatedly treating whichever workers happen to be visible.

sources.label: Western Australia DPIRD: Coastal brown ants

identification: Look for broad, pleated leaf blades and long, branched flower clusters with bristles beneath individual spikelets. Include the pleated leaf surface, leaf base and entire flowering head in photographs. The bristles are associated with individual spikelets and may need magnification to see clearly. Setaria lindenburgiana is a similar broad-leaved grass with smaller foliage and flower clusters; mature material helps a botanist compare the two.
actions: Before sharing a division, confirm the plant's identity and whether it is suitable for the receiving landscape. A moist woodland edge is a different setting from a maintained ornamental bed. For an unwanted clump, consult local guidance on handling the persistent rootstock and mature seedheads. Keep dug material contained and check the original site for surviving growth. Include a flowering stem with any identification request.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Setaria megaphylla

identification: Check for opposite leaves with tiny hairs along their margins and five-lobed blue-violet flowers; small periwinkle has smaller, usually hairless-edged leaves. Examine the fine hairs along a leaf margin with a hand lens and show where a trailing stem roots. Flower color alone does not separate bigleaf and small periwinkle. Variegated cultivars can obscure the usual green-leaf impression, so the leaf base, margins and stem arrangement remain useful clues.
actions: Start at the edge of a small confirmed patch and track rooted nodes so they are not left behind. Collect broken stems promptly, especially near drainage channels. Larger creekside infestations need land-manager advice to avoid bank damage and loss of neighboring plants. Keep inspecting after removal and arrange a suitable replacement cover where exposed soil would otherwise remain.

sources.label: California Invasive Plant Council: Vinca major

identification: Look for blotch-like mines with pale larvae inside fresh birch leaves. Several other birch leafminers cause similar damage, so species confirmation may need expert help. Hold a recently affected leaf to the light to see whether the mine still contains a larva. An old brown blotch may be empty and no longer vulnerable to an insect treatment. Record the birch species and season, since different leafminers can produce overlapping damage patterns on the same tree.
actions: Assess how much fresh foliage is affected and whether the tree otherwise grows well. A few conspicuous leaves on a vigorous tree may need only observation. For repeated heavy damage, discuss the active life stage and tree stress with an arborist or extension adviser. Avoid treating every browned leaf as evidence of an ongoing infestation by this particular sawfly.

sources.label: University of Minnesota Extension: Birch leafminers
Kirichenko et al.: Global invasive leafminers

identification: Look for compound leaves ending in branched tendrils and one-sided clusters of blue-purple pea flowers. Follow a leaf to its terminal tendril and photograph the rows of leaflets. Several vetches have purple pea flowers, but the long one-sided flower clusters and perennial growth provide additional context. Mature pods and stem hairiness can help a regional key resolve plants that are difficult to identify from flowers alone.
actions: Mark where climbing stems originate before disentangling them from desirable plants. In a confirmed unwanted patch, contain ripe pods and avoid transferring soil that may carry underground parts. Large stands at woodland edges need a follow-up plan rather than a single cutting. Protect supporting shrubs and remaining native herbs during any locally recommended management. Record the patch boundary before flowering stems obscure neighboring plants.

sources.label: University of Alaska Anchorage: Bird vetch risk assessment

identification: Each complete leaf has five leaflets, including a lower pair close to the stem. The yellow flowers develop into several slender, straight pods radiating from a common point, giving the plant its birdlike name. Other trefoils share yellow flowers, so examine several stems and fruits rather than one blossom. Photograph the leaf attachment and a developing pod cluster together; the radiating arrangement becomes much clearer after flowering.
actions: Establish whether the stand is managed forage or an unwanted escape before removing plants. In prairie restoration, arrange repeated checks for new seedlings after the first work, because visible clearance does not empty the seed bank. Keep ripe pods from being scattered into clean ground. Seek a site-specific plan for large areas and protect desirable legumes growing among the trefoil.

sources.label: University of Minnesota Extension: Birdsfoot trefoil
Flora of New Zealand: Lotus corniculatus

identification: From standing height this tiny plant can resemble moss. A close lens view reveals paired narrow leaves and minute flowers or capsules on slender stalks, usually with four sepals. White petals may be shorter than the sepals or absent, so an apparently petal-less flower does not rule it out. Include the basal growth and any stem rooting at a joint in photographs; related pearlworts need comparison with a regional key rather than a general mosslike impression.
actions: In paving or a garden bed, decide whether the plant is actually causing a problem before disturbing it. In a natural wet site, check the local flora and avoid clearing native pearlwort on appearance alone. Keep photographs of flowers and basal growth with the location. Clean mud from tools and footwear if moving between sensitive habitats.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Sagina procumbens

identification: Look for four-lobed blue flowers on slender stalks and hairy, toothed leaves; the lower leaves are paired while upper leaves alternate. Photograph the face of an open flower and the stalk emerging from a leaf axil. Other speedwells also have blue flowers, but leaf arrangement, hairiness and mature fruit shape help separate them. A plant viewed only after petals fall can be harder to identify, so retain a flowering photograph when possible.
actions: For a small confirmed garden patch, work before mature seed is shed and avoid dragging ripe plants across clean soil. Recheck places where the ground was disturbed. In lawns or crops, assess the extent and growth stage with a local adviser before treating a broader area. Similar blue-flowered plants should be identified individually rather than removed by flower color.

identification: Look for leaves divided into groups of toothed leaflets and flat clusters of small white flowers. White-edged garden forms can produce plain green growth. Photograph a whole divided leaf with its stalk, not just one leaflet. The white flower clusters resemble those of other carrot-family plants, including hazardous lookalikes, so do not taste material to identify it. Plain green shoots can arise among variegated garden growth and may be easy to overlook at the edge of a bed.
actions: Map the spreading margin before digging and collect rhizome pieces rather than chopping them into surrounding soil. Persistent patches need repeated monitoring and an appropriate local management plan. Keep waste out of woodland edges and informal compost heaps where living pieces could survive. When clearing a mixed groundcover, distinguish rooted goutweed from neighboring native plants before disturbing them.

identification: The flower heads begin green and ripen red on short stalks near the soil, separate from the taller leafy shoots. Include that arrangement in photographs when comparing this plant with other ornamental gingers. The red cone is made of overlapping bracts; the small flowers emerge between them. Other gingers bear colorful bracts too, so a cone alone is less useful than photographs showing both flowering and leafy stems in the same clump.
actions: Record whether a patch is a maintained cultural or ornamental planting or is spreading into surrounding vegetation. Where unwanted, contain excavated rhizomes and inspect for new shoots when seasonal growth resumes. Do not assume a dormant clump has died. Ask a local specialist about the appropriate response in culturally important plantings or sensitive wet habitats.

sources.label: National Tropical Botanical Garden: Zingiber zerumbet

identification: Look for the paired dark side blotches, but have a specialist check fin spines and scale markings to distinguish it from chanchita. Take a full side photograph with fins visible and record any clear scale markings. The two blotches are useful clues but are shared with similar cichlids. Anal-fin spine counts and other details distinguish chanchita, which has been confused with black acara in Florida. A photograph may need follow-up examination by a fish specialist.
actions: Keep aquarium purchase information separate from evidence for a wild occurrence. For a catch in natural or connected waters, report the exact location and date and follow fisheries instructions about handling. Arrange responsible rehoming for unwanted aquarium stock. Do not move an unidentified acara to a different ditch or pond while trying to determine its name.

sources.label: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission: Black acara
Robins et al.: Identification of acara established in Florida

identification: Look for mature dark canes alongside younger green ones, narrow leaves and the grooved stems typical of Phyllostachys. Some named forms remain green or mottled. Compare canes of different ages, since new green shoots do not contradict a black bamboo identification. Photograph the groove along an internode, branching and mature dark stems. Some named forms differ in coloration, and other bamboos can darken, so the complete plant should be checked rather than relying on one black cane.
actions: Walk the boundary during the shooting season and mark any new culms beyond the intended planting. Discuss a suitable containment or removal plan before excavating large rhizomes near utilities or neighboring gardens. Collect rooted pieces during work and revisit the area for emerging shoots. A tidy above-ground clump does not prove its underground spread has stopped.

sources.label: Trees and Shrubs Online: Phyllostachys nigra

identification: Look for a roughly five-millimeter black bug with yellow head markings and a pale, wavy line across the front of the shield behind its head. Photograph the insect from above with the head and front of the shield in focus. It can resemble a small beetle because the shield covers much of the back. Other plataspid bugs require comparison of markings and structure, so a shiny black body or a bean host alone is insufficient.
actions: Record whether adults, eggs or young bugs are present and whether actual feeding injury is visible. These observations help plant-health staff distinguish an incidental visitor from a breeding population. Keep suspect plant shipments separate while advice is sought. Avoid claiming a new host or applying broad crop treatments from adults resting on one plant without further evidence.

sources.label: Florida Department of Agriculture: Black bean bug pest alert
Añino et al.: Black bean bug in Ecuador and host plants

identification: At a leaf joint, look for the thin sheath characteristic of a knotweed. Tiny greenish flower clusters and dark, three-sided mature fruits add useful evidence, while the leaves are pointed and arrow-shaped. True field bindweed has much larger funnel-shaped flowers and different underground persistence. When several vines are tangled together, follow one stem from leaf to flower or fruit so the record does not accidentally combine structures from neighboring plants.
actions: Trace the annual vine to its rooted base before pulling it from a crop or garden support. Work while seed is immature where practical, taking care not to damage the plant it climbs. Check harvested or moved material for mature fruits. Persistent agricultural infestations need crop-specific advice, since simply cutting the visible tangle may leave seed to replenish the patch.

identification: Body color alone is unreliable. Black carp and grass carp, especially young fish, may need expert examination to tell apart. Obtain a clear side image showing the head, scales and fins, with a size reference if safely possible. Do not try to inspect deep throat teeth on a live fish yourself. Juveniles can be particularly difficult to separate from grass carp, so retain photographs and follow the fisheries service's identification procedure.
actions: Keep the fish at the capture site while obtaining instructions rather than carrying it live to another waterbody. Include the date and precise location in a report, even if the identification is uncertain. Aquaculture operators should use verified stock and secure containment appropriate to local rules. A dark carp-like fish should not be stocked or used as bait on a guess.

sources.label: Missouri Department of Conservation: Black carp
USGS: Black carp biology, assessment and control

identification: Look for a dark oval adult about 3-5 mm long, or a tapered brown larva with a long tail tuft. Other carpet beetles require comparison. Inspect a larva or its shed skin through a lens, showing the tapered body and terminal hair tuft. An adult near a window may have entered from flowers and is not by itself proof of textile damage. Photograph the affected material and insects together so the likely feeding source can be assessed.
actions: Check quiet storage areas, seams and accumulations of animal hair rather than treating only the room where an adult appeared. Follow fabric-care guidance for washable items and seek specialist advice for museum specimens or valuable textiles. Keep cleaned material protected from reinfestation. A confirmed source and repeated inspection are more useful than applying products to unrelated furnishings.

identification: Shiny brown-black to black aphids clustered inside curled cherry leaves; adults may be winged or wingless. Unfold a few curled leaves gently to see whether live aphids remain inside. Old curled growth can persist after a colony has departed, so damage alone does not establish current activity. Photograph the dark adults and host twigs, including eggs if noticed during dormant-season inspection. Other causes can also distort cherry shoots.
actions: Compare fresh shoot growth and predator activity before deciding whether a tolerable colony needs attention. Young trees and a fruiting orchard may require different responses. Keep the cherry variety and symptom dates with any request for advice. Avoid spraying empty curls simply to improve their appearance; ask the adviser about the active stage and protection of beneficial insects.

sources.label: UC IPM — Cherry Pest Management Guidelines

identification: Dull black adults on tender growth suggest this species, but antenna and wing details distinguish it from similar dark citrus aphids. Examine several adults on a fresh shoot rather than assuming every black citrus aphid belongs to the same species. Details of the antennae and wing veins help separate similar aphids, including other citrus-associated species. Honeydew and leaf curl are feeding clues, not a complete identification or evidence for a particular plant virus.
actions: Record the host, affected flush and whether predators or parasitized aphids are present. Recheck the newest growth to judge whether colonies are increasing or declining. If symptoms suggest more than feeding injury, seek a plant diagnosis separately. Select any response with a local crop adviser, since the importance of this broadly feeding aphid differs among crops and places.

identification: Look for coarse hairy foliage, a sticky feel and foul odor; use photographs rather than handling or tasting a suspected plant. Flowering plants bear pale yellowish flowers with conspicuous purple veins and a dark center. Later, enlarged papery cups surround the seed capsules. Those structures are more useful than odor alone, and there is no need to touch or crush a leaf to check them. A nonflowering rosette may need expert comparison.
actions: Mark a suspected patch so it is not included in hay, grazed or handled casually during weeding. Use local guidance for protective equipment and disposal of confirmed plants, especially if capsules have formed. Seek medical or veterinary advice after possible ingestion. Historic medicinal use does not establish a safe dose, and home preparation is not an appropriate management or identification method.

sources.label: University of Nevada, Reno — Managing Black Henbane
Montana State — Black Henbane Identification, Biology and Integrated Management

identification: Variable-sized dark workers, two waist segments and ten-segmented antennae ending in a two-part club. Hybrid fire ants can look intermediate. Observe the mound from a safe distance and use photographs already obtainable without provoking the colony. Worker size varies within one nest. Dark coloration can overlap with hybrids and other ants, so definitive identification may require laboratory methods as well as a close morphological comparison by a specialist.
actions: Keep children and pets away from suspected active mounds. For work in infested ground, obtain advice on avoiding contact and managing the specific site. Do not move nursery soil or equipment carrying colonies to another property. A coordinated targeted approach should follow identification; repeatedly disturbing mounds can expose people without establishing control. Seek urgent medical help for a severe sting reaction.

sources.label: University of Georgia — Managing Imported Fire Ants in Urban Areas

identification: Three leaflets with fine teeth near their tips, a stalked middle leaflet, yellow flower clusters and black mature pods. Photograph the leaflet tips, the stalk of the middle leaflet and ripe pods. Yellow-flowered clovers may resemble it at first, but the dark curved pods are useful once mature. A low mat alone is not diagnostic, especially in frequently mown turf where flowers are removed before they can be inspected.
actions: In a garden, remove confirmed unwanted plants while the root can still be lifted cleanly and collect pods if already present. In turf, look at compaction, bare areas and growing conditions with a lawn adviser. Retaining a small harmless patch may be reasonable where it is not competing with desired plants. Avoid treating every clover-like leaf as this species.

identification: Prickly woody stems, many paired leaflets, pink rounded flower heads and densely bristly pods distinguish it from low-growing sensitive plants. Use a side view to show the woody, prickly stem and a close view of a leaf with its many small leaflets. Mature bristly pods provide additional evidence against smaller sensitive plants. Do not repeatedly touch foliage or shake fruiting branches to test an identification; photographs can show the important features without scattering material.
actions: Flag the site and record its extent before entering dense growth. Wetland infestations may involve water movement, soft ground and mixed native vegetation, so coordinate management with the responsible land manager. Keep machinery and footwear free of attached pods and mud when leaving. Any large removal should include a plan for seedlings and regrowth, rather than a single clearing.

sources.label: USDA NRCS — Common Weeds in Puerto Rico and U.S. Virgin Islands

identification: Check the short four-angled pods held close to the stem, bright yellow petals and contrast between lobed lower and narrow upper leaves. Photograph the fruiting stem from the side to show how closely the pods are held against it. Yellow four-petaled flowers occur in many mustards and cannot establish black mustard on their own. Retain pictures of lower leaves before they wither, since upper leaves are narrower and can give a misleading impression.
actions: In a small confirmed unwanted patch, prevent ripe pods from opening over clean soil during removal. Ask an agricultural adviser about larger crop or pasture infestations before changing field management. Keep the scientific identification with any record, including the alternative genus name used by the reviewing flora. Culinary familiarity with mustard does not justify tasting an unidentified wild plant.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand — Brassica nigra

identification: Small white flowers with yellow anthers, clustered dark berries and unarmed green or purple-tinged stems; expert comparison is needed within the black-nightshade group. Include open flowers, mature berries and the small calyx beneath a berry in photographs. Fruit color alone does not separate the closely related black nightshades. A botanist may need a specimen with several developmental stages to distinguish genuine S. nigrum from other species recorded under that name historically.
actions: Keep children and animals from eating unidentified berries while the plant is being assessed. If a garden volunteer is unwanted, contain ripe fruit during removal rather than scattering seeds. Obtain professional medical or veterinary advice after a suspected ingestion. Do not transfer recipes or edibility claims from another member of the nightshade group to a plant identified only by appearance.

sources.label: Native Plant Trust — European Black Nightshade

identification: Finely divided leaves, clusters of tubular blue-purple flowers and flattened woody seed capsules are useful combined clues. Photograph the twice-divided leaf structure and a persistent woody capsule as well as the blossoms. Purple flowers alone can suggest unrelated flowering trees, and leafless flowering branches may obscure the foliage clues. Retain the planting context and any nursery label when distinguishing a cultivated specimen from a naturally established seedling.
actions: Choose a site with room for the mature crown and consider access beneath it before planting. For an established tree, consult an arborist about pruning rather than removing major branches casually. Note whether seedlings persist outside maintained ground and check regional guidance before distributing seed. A specimen's ornamental value and its local escape behavior should both inform the decision.

identification: A pointed muzzle, relatively large ears and a tail longer than head and body distinguish adults from stockier Norway rats. Look for a slender body and long tail in a clear side image if one can be obtained without approaching the animal. Droppings and gnaw marks reveal rodent activity but rarely identify the species alone. Juveniles and poor night images can be misleading, so a pest professional may need additional evidence.
actions: Reduce access to fruit, pet food, rubbish and dense shelter near the building. Have entry gaps assessed and repaired as part of a coordinated exclusion plan. Ask a professional how to handle contaminated spaces safely rather than sweeping droppings into the air. Choose any trapping or control method with pets, children and nontarget wildlife in mind, and monitor afterward.

identification: Dark oval to elongated scales up to about 5 mm long; body shape changes with the feeding surface. Confirm against other soft scales. Photograph scales on both leaves and twigs because their shape can change with the surface they occupy. The common name black scale is also applied to Saissetia oleae, so a dark bump alone is ambiguous. A diagnostician can examine adult female structure and determine whether the visible covers contain living insects.
actions: Record fresh honeydew, sooty mold and the condition of new growth rather than counting old attached scales alone. Inspect replacement plants before mixing them with a collection. If an infestation is damaging, discuss a targeted response that preserves parasitoids and predators where possible. Also check for ants tending the honeydew, and report them to the adviser without assuming they identify the scale.

identification: Brown-black adult females about 5 mm across with an H-shaped back ridge; tiny yellow-orange crawlers require a hand lens. Use a lens to look for the raised H pattern on mature females and compare younger stages nearby. Other soft scales also look brown or black, while empty old bodies may remain attached after the insect has died. Photograph both the scale-bearing twig and fresh sticky foliage to document the current situation.
actions: Ask a crop or landscape adviser to check whether a substantial living population is present and which life stage is active. Avoid unnecessary broad sprays that disrupt parasitoids. Pruning should suit the tree and its growing conditions, rather than opening the canopy excessively. Continue monitoring new growth and honeydew after any response, since old sooty deposits can persist.

sources.label: UC IPM — Black Scale in Olive

identification: Look for the heavily spined tail and dark crossbands, rather than assuming that a black spiny-tailed iguana is entirely black. Photograph from a safe distance, including the tail scales, body bands and head profile. Young green animals can be mistaken for other iguanas, while an adult need not be black overall. The stiff rings around the tail are useful clues, but closely related spiny-tailed species can still require expert comparison.
actions: Keep pets away and avoid cornering or feeding the animal. If an unwanted captive iguana needs a new home, contact a responsible reptile service rather than releasing it. In a region with established introduced populations, follow local wildlife instructions for reporting and management. Trapping or removal near buildings should be handled by appropriately qualified people using humane methods.

sources.label: UF/IFAS — Black Spiny-tailed Iguanas on Gasparilla Island

identification: Dark branching colonies with projecting tubular polyp cups suggest it; photographs and specialist skeletal comparison are needed to separate similar sun corals. Take an in-place photograph showing the colony's branching pattern and close views of the projecting cups when conditions allow safe observation. Dark living tissue is not the same as a dark skeleton. Black corals belong to a different group, and color alone cannot separate this species from all similar colonial animals.
actions: Give marine specialists the depth, structure type, date and coordinates of an unexpected observation. Divers should follow site access and safety rules rather than approaching restricted offshore structures for a closer look. Keep colonies attached and avoid moving fouled equipment between sites without an appropriate cleaning plan. Removal from a reef or platform requires specialist assessment, not casual collection.

sources.label: Schuhmacher — Reef-building properties of Tubastraea micranthus
Sammarco et al. — A new coral species introduced into the Atlantic

identification: Opposite pointed leaves, twining stems, tiny dark-purple star-shaped flowers and narrow seedpods; pale swallow-wort has different-colored, longer petals. Photograph the small flower face closely enough to show the short triangular lobes, along with paired leaves and developing pods. Pale swallow-wort can be confused with it before flowering. Upright native milkweeds differ in habit, so trace the twining stem through surrounding plants rather than assigning every nearby pod to the vine.
actions: Mark the rooted crowns before disentangling a confirmed patch. Contain mature pods before they open and carry silky seeds away. Revisit treated ground for surviving plants and seedlings according to local guidance. In mixed vegetation, protect supporting shrubs and desirable milkweeds. Large established stands benefit from a coordinated management plan rather than repeated cutting with no follow-up.

identification: Very slender dark covers about 2-3.5 mm long and roughly eight to ten times as long as wide, with a pale cast skin at one end. Use a close photograph to show the elongated cover and its pale terminal cast skin. A dark line on a palm may instead be damage or debris, and several armored scales can occur together. The living female beneath the cover requires magnified examination; cover shape is a strong clue but not definitive confirmation.
actions: Keep suspect incoming palms separate while an adviser checks whether scales are alive and damaging. Inspect several leaves and stems, recording the occupied surfaces. Do not infer success from covers remaining attached or failure from their persistence after treatment. A targeted plan should be based on the confirmed species, active stages and plant condition rather than blanket spraying of a collection.

sources.label: Naturalis — Diaspididae of the World: Ischnaspis longirostris

identification: Tiny entrance holes underneath wilting twigs, with a brood chamber inside; adult females are dark beetles roughly 1.5-2 mm long. Look along the underside of a recently wilted twig for a tiny round entrance. Follow the affected twig back toward healthy tissue and photograph that transition. Wilting can also result from disease, drought or other borers, and a pinhole without an insect specimen cannot confirm the species.
actions: Ask a diagnostician which fresh twigs to sample and keep their host labels attached. For confirmed attacks, obtain advice on the extent and timing of pruning and on containment of cut material. Inspect neighboring susceptible plants afterward. Good plant care remains useful, but do not dismiss the possibility of this borer merely because a host looked healthy before twig death.

identification: Dull black, broad-snouted adults with pale yellowish flecks; white C-shaped, brown-headed, legless grubs among roots. Inspect leaf margins after dark for adults and note whether a potted plant's roots are also affected. Notches can remain after a beetle has moved away. The curved, legless grubs differ from many other soil larvae, but a specimen should be checked before assuming all root loss is due to vine weevil.
actions: Keep suspect nursery plants apart and examine root balls before sharing or planting them. For valuable container plants, seek an adviser's help with the concealed larval stage rather than focusing only on adults above ground. Avoid moving infested potting material to clean pots. Reassess plant recovery and inspect new foliage after any authorized response. Include the potting history when requesting a diagnosis.

sources.label: University of Minnesota — Black Vine Weevil

identification: Photograph a complete twice-divided leaf, including the hairy central axis and its glands between or near the leaflet-bearing branches. Many tiny paired leaflets create the feathery appearance, but other wattles share that general form. Pale cream-yellow flower balls, hairy young twigs and narrow pods pinched between seeds strengthen the comparison. A branch showing several of these structures gives a botanist more useful evidence than bark color or a distant view of the canopy alone.
actions: In its native range, recognize its place in the local vegetation before proposing removal. Elsewhere, distinguish a planted specimen from self-sown seedlings and consult regional guidance on escape risk. Avoid spreading ripe pods or soil from an unwanted population. Large trees and dense stands need a site-specific plan that considers neighboring vegetation and safe access.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney — Acacia mearnsii

identification: The flattened fans of sword-shaped leaves point to an iris relative even when the spotted orange flowers suggest a lily. Each flower has six spreading parts. Later, an opened capsule displays shiny black seeds in a cluster, giving the plant its blackberry name. Photograph both an intact capsule and one that has opened naturally. Those exposed seeds are not a fleshy berry, and the resemblance to fruit should not be used as an edibility test.
actions: Keep decorative seed stems away from children who might mistake them for fruit. In a garden, monitor volunteers and contain mature seedheads where unwanted spread is a concern. Confirm local status before removing a planted clump or recording an escape. If dividing an established specimen, keep rooted pieces within cultivation and retain its correct botanical label.

identification: Follow a twining stem to a pair of triangular or heart-shaped leaves, then photograph a bloom from the side to show its long tube and broad opening. This vine differs from the upright, daisy-headed Rudbeckia also called black-eyed Susan. The leaf stalk can have narrow wings, a useful detail in close views. Garden selections vary in flower color, so familiar orange petals and a dark eye alone do not establish the species.
actions: Provide a support appropriate to the planting and watch for stems extending into neighboring vegetation in climates where it persists. Retain nursery labels and use the botanical name when sharing seed or recording a plant. Where escape is a concern, contain garden waste and mature seed. An annual display in a cold region should not be treated as proof of naturalization.

identification: Look for long, narrow leaflike phyllodes with three to five prominent veins, pale round flower heads, twisted pods and dark fissured bark. Show the strong veins in a mature phyllode and the colored seed stalk looping around a dark seed in an opened pod. Juvenile foliage may differ from the adult leaflike structures, so young plants can be confusing. Other Acacia species require comparison of veins, flowers and pods rather than bark color alone.
actions: Check whether there is enough room for a forest-sized tree and consult regional guidance before planting near natural vegetation. Record self-sown seedlings separately from the original ornamental. If removal is locally justified, obtain advice on handling a large tree and subsequent regrowth. Avoid carrying pods or rooted material to another site while its suitability is being assessed.

sources.label: Plants of the World Online: Acacia melanoxylon

identification: Look for hairy opposite leaves, five split white petals and a veined swollen flower cup. Separate male and female plants and the hairy foliage help distinguish it from Silene vulgaris, which also bears the common name bladder campion. Photograph the inflated cup from the side, showing the veins and surrounding hairs. Silene vulgaris is generally much less hairy and has a different calyx appearance. White petals alone are not enough, and pink-tinged plants may reflect hybridization with red campion rather than an entirely different growth form.
actions: Keep the scientific name with all photographs so a shared common name does not lead to a mistaken record. In a garden or field where confirmed white campion is unwanted, contain mature capsules and seek local advice for persistent plants. Do not clear other campions on the strength of a common-name match. Revisit the site as flowers and fruits develop.

sources.label: ITIS: Silene latifolia accepted name and common names
University of Maine Extension: white campion

identification: Before flowering, the glossy leaf rosette is conspicuous for its white marbling and sharp marginal spines. On a flowering stem, look beneath the pink-purple head for the broad bracts with stiff projecting spines. Numerous other thistles have purple flowers, so use the leaf and bract pattern together. Photograph from a safe distance or use tools to avoid contact, and retain a view of the whole plant as well as the individual head.
actions: Where local guidance calls for control, plan work while plants are still manageable and before ripe seed spreads. Keep heads contained during transport and avoid equipment that scatters them across pasture. For large stands, ask a weed adviser about follow-up and restoration of desirable cover. Historic herbal use should not substitute for professional advice about an unfamiliar plant or livestock exposure.

identification: Check the elongated, club-shaped capsule and the flattened hairs near the top of the flower stalk; flower color alone is unreliable. An intact fruiting stalk is more informative than fallen petals. Compare several capsules and the direction of hairs immediately below them, using a close side view and a size reference. Other red-flowered poppies can vary in their dark petal markings, so a flower with no black spot does not settle the species.
actions: Keep a photographic record through flowering and fruiting if the initial identity is uncertain. In a confirmed unwanted patch, contain ripe capsules before they shed seed and avoid moving contaminated soil. Ask a botanist to distinguish similar field poppies before reporting a new occurrence. A decorative seedhead or an attractive garden volunteer should not be distributed under an unconfirmed botanical name.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Papaver dubium

identification: Look for red powder-puff flower heads and twice-divided leaves with one pair of main leaflet-bearing branches. Check pods and leaves as well as flowers. Show the division of a complete leaf rather than only individual leaflets. Several powder-puff shrubs have red stamens, so their number of main leaf branches and mature pod form provide useful additional clues. Photograph a flower cluster from the side to reveal its many projecting stamens instead of treating the red threads as petals.
actions: Allow room for the spreading crown when choosing a garden position, and check regional advice on escape before sharing pods or seedlings. Monitor plants appearing beyond the maintained bed and keep their location distinct from the parent shrub. If pruning is needed, collect pod-bearing material rather than discarding it into neighboring vegetation, and retain the nursery identity with the planting.

sources.label: Plants of the World Online: Calliandra haematocephala

identification: Look for opposite narrow leaves, milky sap and red-orange flowers with raised yellow crowns; pods contain seeds attached to silky hairs. Photograph the contrasting flower parts and narrow leaf pairs without breaking a stem to expose sap. Other milkweeds can host monarchs, so a caterpillar does not identify the plant. Garden color selections may differ from the familiar red-and-yellow form, and a mature pod with silky seeds is shared with other milkweed species.
actions: Ask a local monarch or extension program which native milkweeds fit the site and how to manage existing tropical milkweed in your climate. Winter persistence matters particularly in warm regions. Avoid insecticides on caterpillar food plants without expert advice, and use gloves when handling cut stems. Do not infer from butterfly use that leaves, pods or sap are safe for people or pets.

identification: Look for low clumps, deeply cut palm-shaped leaves and five-petaled pink-magenta flowers with darker veins. Cultivars can differ in flower color. Compare the deeply divided leaves at the base of the plant with the five broad petals above them. Other hardy geraniums can also bear pink blooms, while bedding pelargoniums commonly sold as geraniums have a different form. A whole-clump photograph helps show the low spreading habit that a close flower portrait misses.
actions: Keep the edge of a cultivated clump within its intended bed and note seedlings or growth appearing beyond it. Where an unwanted escape is confirmed, collect rooted divisions rather than dumping them at a woodland margin. Do not equate an ornamental planting with a wild population. For uncertain records, provide flower, leaf and fruiting-stage images to a local botanical recorder.

identification: Use magnification to check the flat-ended tail and two corner spines; the native Great Lakes Mysis diluviana has a forked tail. Collect a close photograph of the tail end if this can be done without transporting living organisms. Red color varies and can fade, so it is not a dependable test. Native Mysis and other small crustaceans require comparison of the tail structure; swarming behavior or black eyes alone will not resolve the identification.
actions: Note the waterbody, exact access point, date and the structure around which a swarm was seen. Report the photographs to the regional aquatic-invasive-species program for confirmation. Remove attached organisms and follow local clean, drain and dry procedures before moving a boat or equipment. Empty water only where permitted, and never transfer an uncertain shrimp with bait into another lake or river.

identification: Older larvae have fleshy, spiny projections that create the hairy appearance behind the common name; newly hatched maggots are less distinctive. Similar Chrysomya species still require specialist comparison. For adults, metallic green or blue-green color overlaps with numerous other blow flies, so photographs should show several angles if obtainable safely. Keep the observation context clear: larvae in carrion and larvae in a wound on a living animal call for different kinds of assessment.
actions: For a live animal with maggots in a wound, arrange veterinary care promptly rather than attempting species identification first. Do not apply household insecticides to the wound. For an incidental fly observation, retain photographs and location information without disturbing animal remains. Forensic interpretation of larval age or arrival belongs with trained specialists and cannot be inferred from a photograph alone.

sources.label: Hairy maggot blow fly: Chrysomya rufifacies

identification: Use magnification to follow an antenna from its base to the tip. Gradual darkening toward the end supports blue alfalfa aphid, whereas distinct dark bands at the joints suggest pea aphid. Their body colors overlap and both can occupy the same field, so compare several adults on a shoot. Record the alfalfa growth stage and condition of the shoot tips alongside the close photographs, linking the insects to any fresh injury rather than color alone.
actions: Use local crop-monitoring guidance and record natural enemies alongside the aphids. Ask an adviser about resistant varieties suited to the area and crop purpose before reseeding. A field with cool-weather shoot injury needs a different assessment from a few aphids on vigorous growth. Avoid broad treatments from color alone, and recheck fresh shoots after any justified response.

identification: Look for square, rough stems, rings of narrow leaves and tiny mauve-pink flowers with four lobes. It is easily overlooked among small bedstraws. Look closely at the flower tube and the ring of leaflike parts beneath a flowering tip. Bedstraws share whorled foliage, so a tiny mauve bloom is an important addition to the stem and leaf evidence. Photograph the whole low mat as well as the small flowers, using a lens if needed.
actions: Identify a patch while flowering before deciding whether it is unwanted in the lawn, bed or field. Where local guidance calls for removal, act before mature fruits are scattered and inspect disturbed soil afterward. Preserve neighboring small herbs until identified. A rough-textured mat without visible flowers may need a botanical comparison rather than an immediate species label.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Sherardia arvensis

identification: Look for abnormal swellings and distorted shoots on blue gum eucalyptus. Confirm the insect through an entomologist; gall shape alone is insufficient. Show where each swelling sits on the shoot and include foliage that can establish the eucalyptus host. Several gall-forming insects occur on eucalypts, and a gall's size or color may change as it ages. Adult wasps emerging from a properly handled sample can provide stronger evidence than a photograph of the swelling alone.
actions: Contact an entomology or plant diagnostic service before cutting or transporting samples and ask how to contain any emerging insects. Keep nursery purchase information with the record. Avoid moving affected blue gum stock to another site while identification is pending. Decisions about pruning or management should reflect the confirmed insect and tree condition, rather than assuming every distorted eucalyptus shoot needs removal.

sources.label: A new species of invasive gall wasp on blue gum in California

identification: Look for large stem joints, broad leaves with a strong midrib, short rhizomes and open seed heads that droop with maturity. Photograph the conspicuous joints, leaf midrib and a fully expanded panicle with a size reference. Other large forage grasses can resemble it before flowering. Include basal growth if it is already exposed, since the short underground stems help distinguish its perennial habit from a temporary flush of annual grasses.
actions: Before using an unfamiliar stand as feed, ask a local livestock or range adviser to confirm identity and assess the growth conditions and stage. A forage planting does not imply that every escaped patch is suitable for grazing. If management is needed, contain mature heads and avoid transferring rooted pieces in soil. Monitor the original clump for persistence after any authorized work.

identification: Look for broad simple leaves, four-angled stems, bluish pea flowers and hairy, inflated pods. Check mature pods to distinguish similar Crotalaria. Use a side view of a flower to show the darker keel and photograph a mature hairy pod still attached to the plant. Broad simple leaves separate it from many divided-leaved Crotalaria, but flower color can vary. A rattlepod nickname or a loose seed is not sufficient for a reliable botanical determination.
actions: Keep a record of the plant's setting, including whether it is a planted specimen or a volunteer on disturbed ground. Where locally unwanted, collect pods before moving cut material and check nearby soil for seedlings. Avoid using an unidentified Crotalaria as food or forage. Ask an agricultural adviser about plants in livestock areas rather than assuming all legumes are suitable feed.

sources.label: Plants of the World Online: Crotalaria verrucosa
Digital Flora of Eastern Ghats: Crotalaria verrucosa

identification: Wood discoloration alone cannot identify this species. A fungal laboratory must compare microscopic features and current taxonomic references. Tell the laboratory whether the sample comes from standing timber, stored logs or mushroom-production material, and name the tree if known. A blue or dark stain can have several fungal causes. Microscopy, culture and current DNA references are needed to connect a sample to the modern Jamesreidia name rather than an older broad staining category.
actions: Keep suspect production logs labeled separately and record when discoloration or poor mushroom growth began. Consult a mycologist or plant-pathology service before discarding a whole batch or selecting treatment. Prevent unnecessary movement of affected wood while advice is obtained. Follow the facility's sanitation guidance; a stain alone neither establishes this fungus nor provides a reliable measure of timber strength.

sources.label: Generic boundaries in the Ophiostomatales reconsidered and revised
Commodity risk assessment of maple veneer sheets from Canada, Appendix A.1.1.8

identification: Check the deep compressed body, small mouth, irregular tail bands and pink-red tail edge. Similar tilapias and hybrids may require expert confirmation. Photograph the full side, tail markings and dorsal fin when the fish can be viewed safely. Color varies with age and condition, and hybrids can obscure the usual pattern. A red-edged tail is useful context but not a stand-alone species test among tilapias, particularly for an unusual wild record.
actions: Arrange responsible rehoming of unwanted aquarium fish and maintain secure aquaculture facilities under local guidance. For a suspected catch in natural waters, record the location and date and ask fisheries staff what photographs or specimen information they need. Do not move live fish to another pond for identification. Keep cultivated-stock records distinct from evidence of a self-sustaining wild population.

sources.label: Blue Tilapia Ecological Risk Screening Summary

identification: Look for narrow leaves, nodding blue flowers and cylindrical purple fruits. Seek expert confirmation where Billardiera fusiformis or horticultural hybrids are possible. Include a close view of the flower center, leaf attachment and mature fruit for a modern key. Billardiera fusiformis overlaps in general color and habit, and older Sollya labels may not resolve the difference. A nursery tag saying bluebell creeper should be treated as a starting point rather than a confirmed species determination.
actions: Before sharing a cutting or planting near bushland, have uncertain stock checked and consult regional horticultural guidance. Monitor seedlings and stems extending beyond the intended support. Keep fruiting waste contained so it is not dumped into natural vegetation. If a population has escaped, ask a botanist to establish its identity before applying impact claims or control advice written for a different Billardiera.

identification: Look for deeply lobed leaves, coiling tendrils and white flowers with a blue-and-white filament ring. Orange oval fruits provide another useful clue. A side view reveals the elevated flower center above the ring of colored filaments. Compare the deeply lobed leaves and coiling tendrils on the same stem, since cultivated passionflower hybrids can resemble the species. An orange fruit by itself is less informative than a record combining foliage, flowers and attached fruit.
actions: Choose a support that allows the vine's boundary to be inspected and check for growth extending into neighboring shrubs. Where regional advice identifies escape concerns, contain fruit and rooted material during pruning. Avoid pulling a heavy vine from a tree canopy without suitable help. Do not rely on the passionfruit name to decide that any part of this ornamental vine is edible.

sources.label: New South Wales Flora: Passiflora caerulea

identification: Tiny pale scales give the broad leaves their gray-silver appearance. Examine several branches because blades can range from oval to nearly circular on the same shrub. Where fruit is present, photograph the enlarged paired bracts enclosing it; these structures are more useful than one unusually round leaf. Male and female flowers usually occur on separate plants. A record of the whole shrub and its reproductive structures helps distinguish it from other gray saltbushes in the area.
actions: In native dryland vegetation, establish the local identity and ecological setting before proposing management. For a new planting, obtain advice on soil, space and regional suitability rather than assuming tolerance of salt or drought makes it appropriate everywhere. Keep seed and planting records if grown for land rehabilitation. Any intended forage use should follow agricultural advice matched to the site and animals.
