identification: Look for clustered fluffy flower heads and broad hairy leaves with rounded teeth. Garden cultivars vary in height and flower color. Photograph the leaf surfaces and the bracts beneath a flower head, not only the fluffy tops. Other Ageratum species can look similar, and compact bedding cultivars may differ substantially from taller plants. Keep a nursery label when available, but use botanical features to confirm a volunteer found away from a bed.
actions: Record whether the plant is watered and maintained, persists from an earlier planting or is producing independent volunteers. These distinctions make an occurrence report more useful than a flower photograph alone. Where seed spread is unwanted, remove mature heads and contain garden waste. Check nearby disturbed ground later, and ask a local botanist about uncertain Ageratum records before assigning the species.

sources.label: Vascular Plants of North Carolina: Floss-flower

identification: Adult beetles are roughly 4.5-7 mm long and metallic blue to green. A specialist looks for a deep lengthwise groove on the forehead and the absence of small keels near the rear corners of the shield behind the head. Keep an adult associated with its emergence branch where possible. D-shaped exit holes suggest a jewel beetle but are not unique to this species, and an adult merely resting on honeysuckle does not establish a breeding host.
actions: Label fresh symptomatic branches and photographs with the shrub identity and collection date. Ask an entomologist how to package a sample without releasing emerging beetles elsewhere. Once an infestation is confirmed, obtain local advice on pruning and disposal of affected stems. Avoid removing an entire healthy honeysuckle planting merely because one blue-green beetle was seen nearby.

sources.label: Westcott, Williams & Grotta (2019): Agrilus cyanescens discovered in Oregon
Telfer and Phillips: Genome sequence of Agrilus cyanescens

identification: Look inside the folded, boat-shaped purple bracts for small white flowers with three petals. These are a stronger clue than purple leaf undersides alone, a color shared with several other tropical foliage plants. The long pointed leaves form tight rosettes on short, thick stems, rather than the tall canes of some similar houseplants. Photograph the whole clump and a flowering bract together. Striped garden forms may differ from the familiar green-above, purple-below leaves.
actions: Wear gloves when dividing or pruning and avoid getting sap on skin or in the eyes. Keep rooted rosettes and fragments within the intended planting and use local disposal guidance for unwanted material. Before placing a houseplant outdoors permanently, check whether it can escape in the region. Revisit removed patches for surviving pieces rather than assuming detached foliage cannot persist.

sources.label: Tradescantia spathacea: Oyster Plant, Moses in the Cradle

identification: A close view of several leaves should show heart-shaped bases and unusually long, narrow tips. Include the small paired figs near the leaf bases, if present, and note their color as they ripen. Smooth gray bark and white latex are shared with other Ficus, so neither feature is decisive alone. There is no need to wound the tree to check its sap; leaf, fruit and whole-tree photographs can provide the useful features without causing injury.
actions: Allow space for a large mature tree and consider nearby structures before planting. Respect the cultural role of established specimens and obtain professional arboricultural advice for pruning or removal. Photograph young trees growing outside intended sites before deciding on management. Check local guidance rather than transferring the species' behavior in Singapore or another tropical location directly to a different landscape.

sources.label: Plants of the World Online: Ficus religiosa

identification: Check the three-angled stems with slightly hollowed sides, bladeless basal sheaths and clustered brown spikelets. Mature fruits help separate similar sedges. Use close photographs of the flowering cluster, the bract beside it and basal sheaths. A triangular stem is shared by many sedges, so it is only one part of the comparison. Mature small fruits often supply the characters needed by a regional key; an immature green clump may remain uncertain.
actions: Observe from firm ground where possible and avoid trampling wetland vegetation to obtain a specimen. Ask the land manager or botanist what material is needed before collecting. Clean mud and plant pieces from equipment before another site visit. If a confirmed unwanted population requires management, use a wetland-specific plan that protects water quality and similar native sedges rather than clearing the entire margin.

sources.label: Plants of the World Online: Schoenoplectiella mucronata

identification: Look for arching branches, long dangling tubular flowers, hairy reddish leaf stalks and elongated dark berries. White-tubed garden forms also occur. Photograph a hanging flower cluster from the side and include a leaf stalk with its hairs visible. Garden forms with pale tubes can otherwise look unlike the familiar scarlet plant. Other fuchsias also have pendant flowers and dark fruits, so their arrangement, tube length and foliage should be compared together.
actions: Keep a cultivated shrub within its intended space and note any seedlings appearing beyond maintained ground. Before sharing cuttings or fruit-bearing material, check regional planting advice for mild, moist climates. For uncertain escapes, provide both flowers and mature leaves to a botanical recorder. Prune with attention to the plant's size and location, containing seed-bearing waste rather than depositing it along a natural edge.

sources.label: Plants of the World Online: Fuchsia boliviana

identification: Viewed from above, the gray-brown bands on an adult's wings form an X. Photograph adults together with the circular wax nests and the skirtlike wax around young stages on the same leaf, before handling disturbs them. Other nesting whiteflies make conspicuous wax too, while sooty mold only shows that honeydew has accumulated. A diagnostic service examines the appropriate life stage microscopically to separate close relatives; the wax pattern alone is insufficient.
actions: Keep newly received plants separate if wax nests or whiteflies are present, and retain the nursery label. Ask a diagnostic service how to sample occupied leaves while preventing adults from escaping during transport. Assess new foliage and plant vigor alongside insect abundance. Select any response with local extension advice and conserve natural enemies where possible, rather than treating old wax alone.

sources.label: Pest Identification Guide: Bondar's Nesting Whitefly
Distribution and Molecular Diversity of Whitefly Species Colonizing Cassava in Kenya

identification: For boneseed, look for upright branches, toothed leaves, yellow flower heads and pale round seeds. Bitou bush has rounder leaves, more spreading growth and differently shaped seeds. Photograph the leaf margins, growth habit and fruit together, and ask the identifier to state the subspecies. Rounded black fruits and yellow heads occur in both forms. The pale seed is useful for boneseed, but an isolated seed without the parent plant can still leave the botanical context uncertain.
actions: Use regional weed guidance that applies to the confirmed form and site. Before working on fruiting shrubs, plan how to contain the fruits and avoid spreading them with equipment or footwear. Arrange follow-up for seedlings after removal. Before extending work to another nearby shrub, check whether it is boneseed, bitou bush or a different native plant; similar yellow flowers alone are not enough.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Chrysanthemoides monilifera

identification: Look for a low, basally branching shrub with narrow toothed leaves, terminal flower clusters and three-lobed capsules. Close flower and fruit photographs are useful. Include the leaf base and toothed margin, a flowering tip and a mature three-lobed capsule in photographs. Other Croton species can share modest flowers and lobed fruits, so a low woody habit alone is insufficient. A botanist may need closer views of hairs and floral structures to resolve an unfamiliar plant.
actions: Record whether the plants are volunteers in disturbed ground or part of an intentional planting. Where local guidance calls for removal, contain ripe capsules before moving the stems and avoid transporting soil that may carry seed. Photograph the full patch and nearby seedlings so local staff can assess whether plants are spreading at this site. Preserve nearby unidentified plants until their identity has been checked.

sources.label: Plants of the World Online: Croton bonplandianus
Digital Flora of Eastern Ghats: Croton bonplandianus

identification: Look for opposite, smooth-edged oval leaves, narrow white flower clusters and small black fruits. An uncut shrub can become wider than it is tall. Follow one branch to see how the paired leaves are attached; a trimmed hedge hides both the natural branching pattern and many flowers. Photograph a flowering tip and a fruiting tip when available.
actions: Check local invasive-plant guidance before planting. Confirm escaped shrubs and contain fruiting material during any locally recommended removal. Distinguish a maintained hedge from young shrubs appearing beyond the planting. Record where those seedlings or escapes occur and whether fruit is present. If replacing a hedge, choose a locally suitable alternative and arrange disposal of fruiting branches before cutting, so berries are not scattered along the route.

sources.label: Cornell Turfgrass and Landscape Weed ID: Border privet

identification: Look for tendrils with adhesive discs, mostly three-lobed glossy leaves and blue-black berries on reddish stalks. Juvenile leaves can have three leaflets. Virginia creeper usually has five separate leaflets, whereas mature Boston ivy commonly has a single lobed blade. Inspect several leaves because young shoots can look different. The small flowers are much less conspicuous than the autumn foliage and may be hidden beneath it.
actions: Check local planting guidance and document escapes separately from planted vines. Check where established stems attach before pruning a wall-grown vine. Pulling firmly attached live growth can damage the surface; seek advice for delicate masonry or painted surfaces. Keep a clear space around gutters and inspect nearby trees periodically, particularly where new shoots bridge from a wall or fence into branches.

identification: Check opposite leaves with three to five strong veins, smooth stems and pink-white flowers backed by a long tubular calyx. Double garden forms may obscure the normal petal count. A side view of a flower shows the long calyx more clearly than a photograph taken straight down onto the petals. Summer flowering makes roadside patches easier to recognize.
actions: Keep unwanted garden spread contained and confirm plants before removal. Do not treat historical soap use as evidence that the plant is edible. Treat a surviving old garden patch differently from a new escape into neighboring habitat. Mark the edge of an unwanted patch before working so that later growth is easy to compare. Keep rooted pieces with the removed material, and avoid sharing divisions from a spreading patch until its identity and local suitability are clear.

identification: Inspect boxwood for striped green caterpillars with black heads, silk and chewed leaves. Adult white-and-brown wings are suggestive, but similar moths require confirmation. Look inside the shrub as well as across its outer surface: early feeding and silk can be tucked among the branches. Caterpillars can remain sheltered between leaves over winter. A single brown branch is not enough to distinguish this insect from disease, weather injury or other boxwood problems.
actions: Photograph suspected insects and damage and report them through your state plant-health service. Avoid moving suspect boxwood plants or clippings until you receive guidance. Include the location and date in the report. Keep nursery labels or purchase details if available. Inspect adjacent boxwoods while awaiting advice, and ask the plant-health service about current movement restrictions before transporting any associated plants, containers or green waste.

sources.label: CFIA: Box tree moth fact sheet

identification: Look for blistered or discolored boxwood leaves containing pale larvae; empty pupal skins may project from leaf undersides after adult emergence. Compare the upper and lower surfaces of affected leaves. The mine is within the leaf rather than a patch of silk on its surface. Larvae remain in leaves through winter, and adults emerge in spring; old exit skins can remain visible after the short adult flight period.
actions: Have the damage confirmed before treatment. Monitor affected shrubs and consider locally recommended resistant boxwood selections when replacing plants. Note whether damage is confined to old leaves or appears on the new flush. Take an intact affected leaf to an extension adviser if requested, keeping it enclosed during transport. Pruning or treatment timing should follow the confirmed life stage, since an empty old mine does not demonstrate that a live larva remains inside.

identification: Look for a small branching annual with opposite leaves and pink stalked flowers. Compare flower stalks and the flower tube with similar centauries. Include the base of the plant and the short stalk below an open flower in your photographs. The flower tube narrows above the ovary, and the foliage lacks the ground-level rosette typical of several similar plants.
actions: Use close photographs of the whole plant and flowers to confirm it. Check regional status before removing a small pink-flowered plant from natural habitat. Return in bright conditions if the flowers are closed; their shape is easier to record when open. Avoid pulling a plant simply to inspect its roots. In a lawn or path, establish whether the patch causes a practical problem before removing it, and leave surrounding small wildflowers undisturbed while seeking identification.

identification: Look for a hard, layered crust with pale growing margins and darker older growth. Colony shape and color are insufficient for a firm identification; microscopic skeletal features need specialist examination. The colony is an animal community, even when its rigid surface looks like stone or a crusty plant. A close view may show regular rows of tiny chambers. Similar Schizoporella species overlap in outward appearance, so photographs should document the surface and growing margin without promising a species-level answer.
actions: Photograph the colony and its location before seeking identification. Have attached growth assessed before moving marine equipment between waters. Record whether it is attached to a hull, dock, shell or natural rock. Ask a marina or marine biosecurity service how to handle fouling before cleaning equipment. Keep removed material and cleaning waste out of the water, and leave natural colonies in place unless collection or removal is specifically advised.

sources.label: Tompsett, Porter & Taylor (2009), Taxonomy of Schizoporella unicornis and S. errata

identification: Look for succulent stems, softly hairy green leaves, very pale hairy stipules and small white flowers. Look closely at the uneven leaf bases and the hairy stipules beside the leaf stalks. The fruit is a small winged capsule, rather than a berry. Tiny flowering plants may already be reproductive, so size alone cannot tell you whether a seedling is too young to spread.
actions: Confirm identification before removing a small begonia. Keep unwanted seedlings and seed-bearing potting material contained rather than discarding them into nearby vegetation. Inspect the surface of neighboring pots and damp crevices when an unwanted plant begins producing capsules. Remove seedlings before shifting potting mix between containers. Keep a specimen in place long enough to photograph flowers and fruit if its identity is uncertain; other small begonias can share the same soft, hairy appearance.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online: Begonia hirtella
Australian Tropical Rainforest Plants: Begonia hirtella

identification: Check for opposite leaves with three stalked leaflets, the middle leaflet usually larger, and clusters of white tubular flowers. Leaf hairiness varies and should not be used alone. Follow a leaf stalk back to the stem to confirm that the three leaflets belong to one leaf. A cluster of separate simple leaves can be misleading. Mature fruit is dark and often two-lobed, while young stems may be much hairier than older woody growth.
actions: In areas where it escapes, avoid planting it near natural vegetation. Photograph flowers and leaves for confirmation, and seek local advice before tackling large vines in tree canopies. Inspect the ground beneath nearby perches for seedlings where the vine is locally unwanted. Do not pull a heavy canopy vine down from below, because branches may fall with it. Plan removal with the land manager, including how to reach rooted stems and check for new growth after the visible canopy has been reduced.

sources.label: UF/IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants: Jasminum fluminense
Kew: Jasminum fluminense, including Flora of Somalia account

identification: Look for paired leaves, young reddish or purplish hairy stems and small white flower heads on stalks. Leaf color varies with growing conditions and cultivated forms. Compare stems in sun and shade before ruling it out because a leaf is green. The stalked white flower heads and opposite leaves are more consistent clues than purple color. A low branch touching damp soil may have roots even while still attached to the parent plant.
actions: Lift the edge of the planting carefully to see whether branches have rooted beyond the intended bed. Keep those rooted sections and any fruiting flower heads together with the trimmings. Avoid putting fresh cuttings on damp ground while cleaning up, and inspect the same margin later to see whether overlooked stems have established new plants.

sources.label: UF/IFAS: Alternanthera brasiliana weed risk assessment

identification: Look for a prickless climber with deeply lobed leaves, clusters of mauve-blue flowers and red berries about a centimeter wide. Photograph flowers and fruit together for confirmation. A flowering shoot is particularly helpful because the star-shaped corolla, deeply divided leaves and lack of prickles can be checked together. Photograph the entire leaf, including its stalk, rather than one narrow lobe. Red fruit is conspicuous but is not a safe identification or edibility test.
actions: Prevent garden vines from spreading into nearby vegetation. Seek local identification and control advice if a plant appears outside cultivation. Keep fruiting growth within the cultivated area while arranging any locally appropriate control. Check fences and shrubs next to the planting for shoots that have become difficult to see among other foliage. Document separate plants beyond the garden edge, and obtain help with tangled woody growth before cutting stems whose origin you cannot trace.

identification: Look for alternate compound leaves, usually five to nine leaflets, small pale flowers and dense clusters of red, peppercorn-sized fruits. Do not crush leaves to test their scent; sap can irritate skin. Count leaflets on a complete leaf rather than counting neighboring leaves. The small pale flowers and later red fruit clusters help distinguish this tree from unrelated shrubs with red berries. Leaflet edges can be nearly smooth or finely toothed, so that character alone is unreliable.
actions: In affected regions, seek local guidance for removal and follow-up because cut or damaged plants can sprout again. Photograph the trunk base and surrounding seedlings when planning work. Large thickets may shelter other vegetation that can be retained during staged removal. Where local control is warranted, arrange follow-up visits for stump shoots and seedlings rather than assuming the job ends when the canopy is cut. Keep sap-covered tools and trimmings away from bare skin.

sources.label: US Forest Service FEIS: Brazilian pepper

identification: The older variety name cannot be confirmed from general field features. For the broader Brazilian peppertree species, inspect a complete alternate leaf with its several leaflets, then look for small pale flower clusters or red fruits. Photograph those details together with the whole plant and retain any previous determination. A nursery label preserves useful history, but it cannot establish a separately recognizable botanical variety. Ask a specialist to explain how the older name relates to the current treatment rather than trying to distinguish it by one leaflet or fruit.
actions: Confirm the taxonomic meaning of any record using this variety name before assigning an identification or management recommendation. Keep the original spelling, location and date with any older observation so that a specialist can trace how the name was used. If a living tree needs attention, have it identified at species level and follow the local guidance for that identification. Do not collect or remove a separate plant merely to fit an obsolete variety label.

sources.label: Kew taxonomy mirror: Schinus terebinthifolia var. raddiana

identification: Check angular, bristly stems, opposite toothed leaves and narrow flower spikes. Floral bracts are about as long as the calyx, unlike the generally shorter bracts of V. bonariensis. Look at the leaf base where it meets the stem: the leaves sit directly on the stem without strongly clasping it. The small bracts among the flowers are best seen in a sharp close-up. Overall height and purple flower color also occur in other verbenas.
actions: Have flowering material identified before removing tall verbenas, which include similar species. Where control is warranted, prevent mature seed from being moved with cut vegetation. If the plant is in a mixed meadow, mark the suspected stems before work and compare flowering plants individually. Avoid treating every tall purple-flowered plant as the same species. Follow the site manager's priorities for a confirmed escape, and revisit the patch while young growth is still easy to separate from neighboring vegetation.

identification: Look for upright emergent growth, basal leaves with heart-shaped bases, unswollen leaf stalks and a many-flowered branching cluster. Seek a specialist determination when no flowers are present. The shape of the leaf stalk matters as much as the broad leaf blade. Include a side view showing how the leaves emerge above the water and how the flower cluster branches. A photograph of a detached leaf cannot reliably separate this plant from other aquatic members of the family.
actions: Photograph leaves, stalks and flower clusters in place. Confirm identity and local status before removing or moving an aquatic plant. Leave unknown aquatic plants in place while arranging identification, especially where native emergent vegetation is mixed together. Record water depth and whether the plant appears anchored in sediment. Never release a garden or aquarium specimen to test whether it will grow locally, and avoid moving sediment or plant pieces between ponds during inspection.

identification: Look for leaves usually in rings of four or five, closely spaced near shoot tips, and conspicuous white three-petaled flowers. Related waterweeds require careful comparison of leaf size and arrangement. Leaf rings can vary along one stem, so count several below the crowded tip. Fine marginal teeth are much less obvious than the sharp teeth of some lookalikes. A view of the entire shoot and a close-up of successive leaf rings is more useful than a photograph of the surface mat alone.
actions: Do not release aquarium plants into waterways. Keep plant fragments off equipment being moved between waters, and report suspected new growth through local aquatic-weed channels. Check anchors, propellers, trailers and fishing gear before leaving an affected waterbody. Small broken shoots can be easy to miss among other weeds. Keep removed aquarium or pond material contained for appropriate disposal, and ask the local waterbody manager before cutting a patch because disturbance can spread fragments beyond the work area.

sources.label: Washington Invasive Species Council: Brazilian elodea

identification: Look for alternate heart-shaped leaves with silvery hairy undersides and branched clusters of small white flowers. Turn a leaf gently to see the contrast between its upper surface and the silvery underside. The tiny flowers form a large branched spray, so both a whole spray and a close view are useful. White flower clusters alone can be confused with several unrelated ornamental vines.
actions: Keep cultivated vines from spreading onto nearby vegetation. Seek local advice for large plants in trees, and avoid moving unidentified vine material to new sites. Trace low stems before pruning so that neighboring plants are not cut accidentally. Where the vine is kept in cultivation, inspect the fence line and nearby shrubs for growth reaching beyond its support. For a large escape, record its extent and contact the land manager before entering tangled vegetation or pulling heavy growth from trees.

sources.label: Bishop Museum Plants of Hawai‘i: Poranopsis paniculata
Flora of North America: Poranopsis paniculata

identification: Look for coarse hairs, narrow lower leaves and dense clusters of pale blue-lilac bells at the stem tip and upper leaf axils. Compare the leaves near the ground with those higher on a flowering stem, and show the bristly hairs in a side-lit photograph. The upper clusters contain many bells close together, unlike bellflowers whose blossoms hang singly along an open stem. Young rosettes are much harder to distinguish.
actions: Record a suspected occurrence with photographs and a precise location. Leave a suspected wild population intact until its regional status is known. Photograph several plants without trampling the surrounding rosettes, and record whether the habitat is open woodland, an edge or managed grassland. If mowing is planned, share the location with the land manager so that identification can be resolved before the flowering stems disappear.

sources.label: Bavarian Environment Agency: Campanula cervicaria conservation
Conservatoire botanique de Lorraine: Campanula cervicaria

identification: Look for a compact, bristly, oval head with paired fertile and fanlike sterile spikelets. Look at the head from the side as well as from above. Its short, crowded shape differs from the long open flower branches of many meadow grasses. A close photograph should show the bristles and the small comb-like sterile units alongside the fertile spikelets.
actions: Identify surrounding grasses before removal. Where local control is needed, pull small plants before seed set while minimizing disturbance to thin soils. In sensitive grassland, work from a confirmed patch boundary and avoid scraping the soil bare. Bag heads that have already matured rather than shaking them over nearby vegetation. Recheck the patch in a later growing season, since removing visible annual plants does not remove seed already present in the ground or introduced along paths.

sources.label: Garry Oak Ecosystems Recovery Team: Cynosurus echinatus
Flora of New Zealand: Cynosurus echinatus

identification: Examine the basal leaves and their branching hairs, then compare mature seed heads. The well-developed feathery fruit bristles across the head help separate it from L. saxatilis. Do not identify a yellow head on color alone. Photograph the leaf hairs with a hand lens if possible, then include the leafless flowering stalk and mature fruits. Smooth-looking individuals can occur, so the absence of obvious coarse hairs does not automatically exclude this hawkbit.
actions: Check local status before deciding whether a patch needs removal. For a small uncertain patch, observe flowers and fruit before making a management decision. Note whether the plants persist as rosettes in the same spot and whether mowing is concealing the flowering stalks. Avoid collecting every head for identification; a few detailed photographs may allow a botanist to direct any further examination without disturbing the patch.

sources.label: FAO: Site-specific grasses and herbs, Leontodon hispidus

identification: Check the long fringe on each papery stem sheath, alternate lance-shaped leaves and narrow pink flower spikes. A leaf blotch alone does not distinguish it from other smartweeds. The sheath is a thin sleeve around the stem just above a leaf attachment. Photograph its upper edge against a plain background so the long bristles can be seen. Several smartweeds share pink flower spikes or marked leaves, making those broader features useful only in combination.
actions: Where an unwanted patch is confirmed, avoid carrying seed-bearing material to new locations. Check more than one stem in a patch because related smartweeds can grow together. If the plants are unwanted in a managed bed, work before ripe seed is shed and keep disturbed soil close to the original site. In wet or natural habitat, confirm the species first and avoid clearing neighboring smartweeds on the strength of a leaf blotch.

sources.label: Fontenelle Forest Nature Search: Bristly lady's thumb

identification: Look for hooked bristles on raised leaf bumps and three to five broad outer bracts beneath each yellow head. These bracts help separate it from other yellow-flowered roadside herbs. View a flower head from below to compare the broad outer bracts with the narrower inner ring. On the leaves, the raised bases beneath the bristles are more informative than roughness alone. Dandelions and many other yellow-flowered herbs lack this combination of conspicuous outer bracts and bumped, bristly leaves.
actions: Use gloves if handling the coarse foliage. Take identification photographs before cutting flowering stems, while the supporting bracts remain attached. If the plant is confirmed unwanted, prevent mature heads from scattering seed during handling. Keep the work limited to identified individuals in mixed roadside vegetation, and cover exposed ground appropriately afterward so that repeated disturbance does not leave another open seedbed.

sources.label: Kew: Helminthotheca echioides, Flora of Iraq

identification: Look for recurved narrow leaves with obvious marginal teeth and no spines along the stem. The curved leaf blades often give shoots a compact, prickly outline underwater. Tiny flowers may be missed entirely; mature seeds and the shape of the leaf bases are more useful for an expert comparison. Native naiads can look similar in a handful of tangled aquatic vegetation.
actions: Remove aquatic fragments from boats and equipment, drain retained water, and follow local drying guidance. Report suspected new occurrences before attempting large-scale removal. Photograph a shoot spread in a shallow tray of water if local collection guidance allows it. Keep every fragment with the sample and do not return it at a different access point. If a new patch is suspected, note the shoreline position and approximate extent so the waterbody manager can check it without unnecessary disturbance.

identification: Check square bristly stems, opposite stalked leaves and two-lipped flowers in tight leaf-axil clusters. The middle lower-lip lobe is unnotched, helping distinguish it from G. bifida. A close side view of the open flower shows the hooded upper lip and patterned lower lip. The swollen-looking stem nodes and stiff hairs are useful supporting details, but leaves alone can resemble several unrelated plants.
actions: Use photographs of open flowers and stem nodes for confirmation. Avoid carrying mature seed-bearing plants between sites when removing a confirmed unwanted patch. Check whether a mixed patch contains more than one mint-family species before cutting. For unwanted plants in cultivated ground, remove or contain stems before mature seed is dispersed. Keep seed-bearing waste off paths and machinery, and revisit the disturbed spot rather than repeatedly clearing a larger surrounding area where the identification is less certain.

identification: Look for broad lower leaves with heart-shaped bases and slightly wavy edges. Check the toothed, three-winged coverings around mature fruits; their mature shape helps identify the dock. Look low on the plant for the broadest leaves; upper leaves are smaller and can give a misleading impression. The fruit coverings enlarge as they mature, making their toothed edges easier to inspect later in the season. Curly dock commonly has narrower leaves with more strongly rippled margins.
actions: Confirm the mature fruit characters before removing docks. For an unwanted established plant, use local weed guidance that accounts for its persistent taproot. Mark established crowns before removing an unwanted patch so that regrowth can be checked in the same places. Cutting only the tall seed stalk leaves the perennial root system behind. Keep mature fruiting stems contained, and consider why bare or disturbed soil remains available around the patch when choosing how to restore the managed area.

sources.label: University of Missouri WeedID: Broadleaf dock

identification: Look for alternate parallel-veined leaves and small orchid flowers with a constricted, pointed lower lip. Confirm flowering plants with an orchid specialist before disturbing them. Photograph an open flower from the front and side, including the lower lip, rather than relying on a tall leafy stem. Leaf bases and the arrangement of flowers along the stalk are useful supporting details. Flower color varies, so a greenish blossom does not exclude this orchid.
actions: Check local identity and status before removal because native orchids can occur nearby. Keep a small marker beside a garden plant if it may be mown before identification. Do not dig it merely to see the underground parts. If local advice supports removing a confirmed unwanted helleborine, keep surrounding native orchids and other woodland vegetation intact and revisit the exact location for later shoots.

sources.label: University of Maryland Extension: Orchid in my garden

identification: Check flat basal leaves and an open, branched cluster of rounded flower heads. Similar woodrushes usually have conspicuous hairs along their leaf margins; this rush lacks that fringe. Photograph the open branching structure of a mature head, with some brown capsules visible. A close view of a leaf margin helps show whether a conspicuous fringe of hairs is present.
actions: Photograph flowers or capsules as well as the leaf bases before identifying a grasslike wetland plant. Check regional status before disturbing a patch. Avoid trampling a wet margin to obtain a sample. A clear photograph from the track may be enough to begin identification. Note whether the clump is in natural wetland, a drain or recently disturbed clay, and keep muddy boots or tools from carrying seeds into another wet area.

sources.label: New Zealand Plant Conservation Network: Juncus planifolius

identification: Look for many upright stems, smooth foliage, broad basal leaves and dense white flower clusters. The broad lower leaves and smaller upper leaves should be recorded together. Mature stands often contain many similar upright stems, but a new plant may still be only a rosette. Hoary cress and other white-flowered mustards require comparison of the leaf bases, flowers and small fruits.
actions: Prevent movement of contaminated soil and root pieces. Small seedlings may be pulled, but established patches need a sustained local management plan and follow-up for regrowth. Map the edges of an established patch before soil work, especially beside a ditch or wetland. Digging can leave viable root pieces behind or carry them on equipment. Seek a plan that fits the water setting and protect neighboring vegetation during follow-up. Check beyond the original stems for shoots appearing from the connected root system.

sources.label: UCSB Riparian InVasion Research Laboratory: Perennial pepperweed

identification: Look for an exposed narrow flower cluster and compare the two unequal glumes at each spikelet base. A close-up of mature spikelets is more useful than a distant grass photograph. Photograph a mature spikelet from the side so that both glumes and the awned flowers can be compared. Similar annual fescues can share thin rolled leaves, so a photograph of the clump alone is usually insufficient.
actions: Avoid moving ripe seed heads with soil or equipment from an unwanted patch. In a mixed grassland, identify flowering plants before mowing or hand removal. If a patch is unwanted, contain ripe heads and clean seed from tools before using them elsewhere. Leave the surrounding vegetation in place where possible, and check whether repeated soil disturbance is creating new open ground for annual grasses.

identification: Look for flattened, light-brown adults, orange nymphs with dark markings, and clustered black eggs on eucalyptus leaves. Confirm suspected specimens with a specialist. Use a close photograph with a scale reference to show the insect's very small size. Examine both leaf surfaces for adults, nymphs and eggs together. Bronzing without insects can have other causes, and several eucalyptus-feeding insects may occur on one tree at the same time.
actions: Photograph insects and damage, seek local forestry or plant-health advice before treatment. Note the eucalyptus species if known and whether the damage affects scattered branches or much of the crown. Keep newly purchased plants apart while suspect insects are identified. A forestry adviser can judge whether continued monitoring or a management response is warranted; avoid moving infested cut branches between properties while arranging that advice.

sources.label: FAO: Bronze bug forest pest profile
Novoselsky and Freidberg: First record in the Middle East

identification: Look for hairy, branched stems, narrow toothed leaves and small pink, two-lipped flowers. Inspect several open flowers and the narrow leaves along the branched stem. This leafy plant differs in appearance from the pale, leafless spikes often called broomrapes. Its connection with grass roots is not something that should be tested by uprooting a plant in a natural meadow.
actions: Photograph flowering plants and their habitat, and confirm local status before removal. Keep seed-bearing material contained if local guidance calls for control. Record the associated grassland and whether the plant is scattered or forms a dense patch. Keep the scientific name with photographs because common names can refer to quite different parasitic plants. In a conservation area, leave the plants undisturbed and ask the land manager to resolve identification and local priorities before mowing or collecting them.

identification: Look for a relatively short snout, bold back markings and, in displaying males, an orange-red throat fan with a pale border. Watch from a little distance for a side-on view of the head and any throat-fan display. Females and young animals may not show the conspicuous male display, so back pattern and body proportions also matter. A native green anole in its brown phase can be mistaken for this species.
actions: Inspect potted plants, boats and stored equipment before moving them. retain varied vegetation and trees that provide habitat for native wildlife. Let the lizard move away rather than chasing it into a container. Check the sheltered spaces beneath pots and around transported outdoor items without transferring animals to another yard. For a suspected new occurrence, record the location and photographs through the appropriate wildlife reporting service; avoid releasing a captured pet or hitchhiking lizard outdoors.

identification: Look for upright brown-to-purple branching tufts, with tiny beadlike brood chambers along branches. Microscopy supports identification of the complex; genetic work may be needed to distinguish its constituent species. Close photographs can show the repeated units and pale rounded brood chambers. Neither the brown color nor a harbor location identifies a particular genetic lineage within this closely similar group.
actions: Photograph colonies in place and seek marine-specialist confirmation. Inspect and clean fouled vessels and equipment using local biosecurity procedures before moving between waters. Note the surface carrying the colony and whether the vessel or equipment has recently arrived from elsewhere. Arrange cleaning where fouling debris can be collected appropriately. Do not move an attached colony to another harbor for identification, and ask a marine specialist whether a sample is needed before detaching growth from natural rocks or shells.

sources.label: Fehlauer-Ale et al.: Cryptic species in the Bugula neritina complex

identification: Look for small tufts, smooth stems, narrow leaves and branching clusters of short, flattened dark spikelets. Mature fruit and flower scales help distinguish similar sedges. Look along the flattened spikelets to see how the small scales overlap. A mature head and fruit are more useful than leaf width alone. The same plant can appear greener when young and darker as its flowering structures develop, so color should not be used as the deciding character.
actions: Check local conservation and nonnative status, and avoid moving mud or seed-bearing material between wetlands. Record the exposed mud or sand habitat while water levels are low. Avoid creating a larger bare patch while examining a small annual sedge. Where a population is locally protected or its status is uncertain, leave it in place and send photographs to a botanist instead of collecting plants or treating the margin as a weed bed.

identification: Look for a globular, finely wrinkled shell with irregular brown spiral bands and pale flecks; mature shells have a turned-back opening lip. Confirm against local snails. Young snails may lack the developed lip of adults. Slime trails and chewed leaves indicate mollusk activity but cannot identify which snail or slug was responsible without seeing the animal.
actions: In affected gardens, reduce unnecessary damp shelter, irrigate early and hand-pick confirmed pest snails with gloves; check local disposal advice. Inspect under pot rims and on container bases before bringing plants home. In a confirmed problem area, monitor during damp conditions when snails are active, and remove unnecessary hiding places close to vulnerable plants. Avoid collecting every snail indiscriminately: native species may share the garden, and management should target the animals actually causing the damage.

sources.label: Dekle and Fasulo: Brown Garden Snail

identification: Look for a dark brown-to-black catfish with paired rows of body armor and two pairs of long chin barbels. Breeding males have enlarged pectoral spines. Photograph both the side and the head. Other armored catfish can look similar in a net. A floating mass of bubbles and vegetation is suggestive nesting habitat, but the nest alone cannot confirm the fish.
actions: Report suspected new occurrences to local fisheries staff, recording the exact waterbody rather than only the nearest town. If a fish is caught, keep hands clear of the stout fin spines and photograph it promptly without unnecessary handling. Ask fisheries staff how to handle the catch where its status is uncertain. Never use an unfamiliar live fish to stock a pond or as transferred bait, and do not move it between water bodies.

sources.label: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission: Brown Hoplo
Nico and Muench: Nests and nest habitats of Hoplosternum littorale

identification: Check for alternating pale and dark antennal bands and banding along the exposed abdomen edges. Several native stink bugs are brown, so shape and color alone are insufficient. Photograph the antennae and exposed side edges of the abdomen, keeping the whole insect in view. The pale bands are more useful than a general impression of mottled brown. Adults on a wall in autumn may be seeking shelter rather than feeding on the building or its contents.
actions: Check screens, door seals and gaps around utility openings before seasonal gatherings begin. For orchard or vegetable damage, record the crop, fruit injury and insects together so monitoring can distinguish this pest from native stink bugs. Avoid treating the entire garden because a few adults have appeared on the house; match any response to a confirmed problem.

sources.label: Penn State: Brown Marmorated Stink Bug
University of Maryland Extension: Brown Marmorated Stink Bug

identification: Look for alternate leaves, yellow flowers with four petals and long pods containing round seeds. Cultivar leaf shape varies; flowers and mature pods help distinguish other mustards. Inspect the upper leaves as well as the lower rosette, since their shapes differ on a flowering plant. A purple-leaved garden form can look unlike a green escape while belonging to the same crop. The long pods and four-petaled flowers help narrow the identification but still require comparison with other brassicas.
actions: Check local weed guidance rather than assuming every mustard planting is invasive. In a vegetable bed, decide whether seed is wanted before the pods mature and split. Keep named seed crops separate from uncertain roadside plants, and do not use an identification based only on leaf taste. If volunteer plants are unwanted, manage them before seed shed and check the next crop for additional seedlings.

identification: Look for slender brown adults with a visible head and clubbed antennae, fine powder and small round holes in hardwood. Retain a specimen for species confirmation. Photograph fresh powder beside an exit hole with a ruler, and keep any emerged adult for identification. Old holes alone may remain long after activity has stopped. The type of wood and whether damage is limited to sapwood help a specialist distinguish this beetle from other wood-boring insects.
actions: Separate a small suspect object from unaffected stored items while obtaining advice. Record when new powder appears after gentle cleaning, without sanding away the evidence. Valuable furniture or museum objects need a conservator's assessment; structural concerns need an appropriate building professional. Do not assume that every old exit hole means an active infestation requiring treatment.

sources.label: Natural History Museum: Lyctus brunneus identification

identification: Look for brown needle spots or bands, sometimes with yellow margins, dying tips and early shedding. A plant diagnostic laboratory should distinguish it from Dothistroma and other needle pathogens. Include both affected needles and a photograph of the whole crown, noting whether older needles or the newest growth are involved. Laboratory examination can look for the fungus itself instead of relying only on the pattern of browning.
actions: Ask a diagnostic service how to submit suspect needles before moving material. For confirmed disease, discuss airflow, tree spacing and suitable care with a local arborist or forestry adviser. Record when yellowing and needle fall began and whether nearby pines show the same pattern. Keep nursery origin information for recently planted trees. Do not send loose needles through the mail without the diagnostic service's packaging instructions. Once confirmed, choose care that reduces avoidable stress and fits the pine species and site rather than applying a universal treatment.

sources.label: UMass Extension: Brown Spot Needle Blight
Scion: Brown spot needle blight factsheet

identification: Look for irregular brown spots and yellowing that begin on lower soybean leaves. Several diseases look similar, so symptoms alone may not confirm the fungus. Compare lower, middle and upper leaves rather than photographing a single spot. The upward progression of yellowing and spots can help explain severity, while bacterial blight and other problems may produce a similar appearance. A diagnosis should take the crop stage and recent weather into account.
actions: Ask a crop diagnostic service to confirm the cause before treatment. Record how much of the canopy is affected and whether symptoms are spreading before making a treatment decision. Keep a few clear field photographs for comparison at the next visit. A crop adviser can weigh confirmed disease severity, field history and crop stage; the presence of a few lower-leaf spots alone does not establish an economic reason to intervene.

sources.label: NC State Extension: Brown spot of soybean

identification: Compare the body spots, relatively square tail and head with a regional trout guide; lake fish may show less obvious spotting. Photograph the side of the fish, including the tail and fins, while keeping handling brief. Red or orange spots and pale halos around dark spots are useful clues in many stream fish. Color can change with habitat and condition, so use several traits rather than expecting every brown trout to look golden.
actions: Never move live fish between waters. Check current rules before fishing because neighboring waters can have different conservation priorities. Avoid disturbing shallow gravel areas used by spawning trout during autumn movements. Clean fishing equipment before changing waters, and report an unfamiliar fish where it may affect a native-fish recovery program. Stocking and relocation decisions belong with the responsible fisheries authority.

sources.label: National Park Service: Yellowstone fish ecology

identification: Photograph the spider and any spiky egg sacs from a safe distance. Color and an hourglass mark alone do not reliably separate it from other widows. Look under the rims of furniture and sheltered ledges visually before putting a hand into the space. Egg sacs can remain when the spider is out of sight. An orange hourglass on a brown spider is suggestive, but immature black widows make a close comparison necessary.
actions: Reduce clutter around occupied areas and seek identification advice if unsure. Use tools rather than bare fingers when moving clutter from a suspected web site, and keep children from investigating the egg sacs. Obtain identification before arranging targeted removal around frequently used seating or play areas. If spiders recur, inspect the same sheltered corners and reduce hiding places instead of assuming that every outdoor web belongs to a widow.

sources.label: UC Riverside: How to identify brown widow spiders

identification: Look for small, mottled brown forewings with dark spots and a hairy head. Similar Niditinea species may require specialist confirmation. A clear dorsal photograph should show the dark markings on the pale brown wings, as well as the hairy head. Traps sold for another clothes moth can also catch this species. A trap catch is therefore a reason to investigate, not proof that wool garments are being eaten.
actions: Inspect feathers, taxidermy and other stored animal material if catches continue, especially in attic storage. Isolate a suspect object while a specialist checks larvae and damage. Avoid disturbing occupied bird nests; outdoor nesting material can be a source without indicating an indoor collection infestation. Use monitoring records to locate the source before choosing any treatment.

identification: Photograph the paired, oval leaves and dense spikes of overlapping leafy bracts, including any small pale flowers. Look at a flower spike from both the side and above to show the stacked leafy bracts that make it look squared. The small flower may be partly hidden. Trace low stems carefully: an upright flowering shoot may belong to a trailing section already rooted elsewhere.
actions: Check local invasive-plant guidance before moving it. For a confirmed unwanted plant, gather rooted nodes along the ground rather than removing only the visible flowering top. Keep moist fragments off bare soil during cleanup. Check beneath neighboring plants for overlooked stem sections, and avoid moving potting mix containing roots or seed to another garden bed. In mixed vegetation, identify each patch before disturbance.

sources.label: University of South Florida FLIP: Ruellia blechum
Flora of China: Ruellia blechum, page 435

identification: Photograph the side and underside of a flower head to show its broad, irregularly torn brown bract tips; hybrids can be difficult to name. Check several heads because bract shape can vary within a patch, particularly where hybrids occur. The plant lacks the sharp spines of a true thistle, although its flower heads can give a similar first impression.
actions: Seek local identification help before management, and check your state's knapweed guidance before moving plants or seed. Record the size of the patch and whether it borders hay, pasture or natural grassland. Where local control is appropriate, limit seed movement on mowers and cut material. Ask an adviser how to handle a mixed or hybrid population, and keep surrounding desirable plants intact rather than clearing every purple-flowered stem in the same area.

identification: Look from a distance for dark, hairy caterpillars with white side markings and two red spots near the rear, or compact winter webs at branch tips. Winter nests are compact bundles of silk and retained dead leaves near branch tips. Web size or a white adult moth alone can be misleading when similar species are present.
actions: Avoid touching caterpillars or nests. Consult local forestry guidance for safe management and reporting; avoid disturbing infested material in ways that send hairs into the air. Observe nests from the ground and record their position on the tree for a qualified adviser. Avoid mowing, blowing or shaking material beneath an active infestation if that would spread the hairs. Follow current local guidance for the season and setting, and use professional help for nests that cannot be reached safely without disturbing them.
Shed hairs can remain irritating for several years. Seek emergency medical care for difficulty breathing or swallowing, or swelling of the mouth, tongue or throat.

sources.label: Browntail moth in Acadia: National Park Service

identification: A red edge and darker center can show where a colony is growing, but several encrusting marine animals share that pattern. Photograph the margin, surface and attachment site. The minute openings in the skeleton, rather than broad colony color, are what specialists compare among similar Watersipora species.
actions: Photograph suspected colonies and their location. Follow marina and local biofouling guidance; avoid moving fouled equipment or scraping organisms into another waterbody. Include vessel or equipment movement history when reporting an unfamiliar colony to a marina or biosecurity service. Plan maintenance before moving to a new harbor, using a facility that can contain the removed fouling. Leave growth on natural rock undisturbed while identification is pending, and do not assume that an apparently clean painted surface cannot carry this bryozoan.

sources.label: Reverter-Gil and Souto: Watersiporidae in Iberian waters

identification: Look for a basal rosette of narrow leaves with prominent lengthwise ribs and leafless stalks carrying compact flower heads. During flowering, pale stamens project around the short head, while the stalk itself carries no leaves. Broadleaf plantain has a wider blade, so include a whole leaf and the flowering head in identification photographs.
actions: Where removal is needed, remove the crown as well as the leaves before seed develops; mowing alone often leaves the plant alive. A few plants in a lawn may not need action unless they interfere with the intended use. Where a patch is unwanted, inspect the growing point after removal and revisit for remaining crowns or seedlings. Improve thin turf or other bare cover as appropriate for the site, since repeated mowing of the flower stalks does not remove the low rosette.

identification: Adults are roughly 1-2 mm long, pale yellow to green, with short antennae and short rear tubes. Winged forms have a darker head and thorax. Look beneath lower potato leaves and photograph a colony before disturbing it. Include winged and wingless individuals if both are present. Pale color and small size are shared by several aphids, and the short rear tubes need a close view rather than a distant photograph of curled foliage.
actions: Have crop colonies identified by an extension adviser before interpreting their virus risk. Record which plants carry colonies and how rapidly numbers change between visits. Virus concerns need a crop-specific assessment, since removing visible aphids does not reverse an infection already transmitted. Keep natural enemies in mind when considering treatment, and ask a crop adviser about the actual local risk before removing nearby shrubs or applying broad insect control.

sources.label: Government of New Brunswick: Buckthorn aphid

identification: Alternate arrowhead-shaped leaves, hollow stems that may redden, and clusters of five-parted white flowers. Follow the leaves up a stem to see their alternate arrangement and pointed, arrowlike bases. The small clustered flowers differ from the inconspicuous flowering spikes of true cereal grasses. A plant can begin flowering while still quite small, so height alone is not a reliable guide to maturity.
actions: For a deliberately planted buckwheat cover crop, decide when to end the planting before seed ripens if volunteers would interfere with the next crop. Monitor field edges and equipment for seed movement, particularly where buckwheat could contaminate another grain harvest. Retain the flowering crop for its intended use when suitable, while treating stray plants in neighboring beds according to that setting.

identification: Usually 4-6 cm long; pale tail keel, spotted gray-brown body and a dark central stripe on the sole. The keel is the raised ridge along the tail behind the mantle, not a stripe painted on the skin. Photograph an extended animal to show that ridge and the dark spotting. The sole pattern is useful, but similar slugs and variable individuals can still need expert examination.
actions: Photograph the back and underside for identification, and inspect bulbs and root crops where feeding damage occurs. Keep a suspect slug contained briefly for a photograph rather than transferring it to another garden. If the crop damage is significant, ask local extension staff to distinguish this species from other slugs and choose monitoring or control appropriate to the affected planting.

sources.label: John Innes Centre: Budapest keeled slug

identification: Oval females about 1.5-2.5 mm long, with yellow-orange wax and pyramid-shaped tufts; males form small white cocoons. Use a magnified photograph of a mature female to show the pointed wax tufts, especially those around the body margin. White cottony material alone is not enough: several mealybugs and other insects leave similar wax. Sticky leaves or black mold show a problem worth inspecting but do not identify the insect.
actions: Check protected leaf bases and the undersides of foliage before a nursery plant joins an established collection. Keep affected plants separate while the insect is identified and inspect neighboring pots for colonies. Note ant activity and the host plant in a report so an adviser can assess both the mealybug and conditions helping it persist.

identification: Coarse bunchgrass with rough bluish-green leaves and dense cylindrical, bristly seed heads that turn tan. Look for a dense clump with older dry leaves beneath newer growth, and photograph a seed head before removing it. Fountain grass and native bunchgrasses can also have bristly heads, so the entire clump and leaves matter. Dry tan plants may still be important fuel even when they are no longer growing.
actions: Report new desert patches and join trained local removal efforts; follow up for regrowth. In the Sonoran Desert, give new small patches attention before they join into continuous cover between native plants. Work with a trained local group to protect cacti and other nearby vegetation. Clean tools and clothing after work, contain seed heads, and return after subsequent growth periods to check for plants missed beneath the original clump.

sources.label: Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum: Save our saguaros

identification: Twining woody vine with alternate heart-shaped leaves and loose masses of small white to pinkish flowers. Follow a stem around its support to see the twining habit. The many tiny flowers can make a large vine look white from a distance, but a close view should also show the heart-shaped leaves and developing winged fruits. Other vines called fleeceflower may have different growth habits.
actions: Keep cultivated vines within their support with regular pruning, and remove unwanted growth before it spreads over neighboring plants. Choose a support and location that leave room for regular access to the whole plant. Check for shoots crossing into shrubs, gutters or adjoining property while they are still easy to reach. Where an established vine has become too large, plan staged work and support assessment rather than pulling down heavy tangled growth in one piece.

sources.label: University of Arkansas Extension: Silver lace vine

identification: Look for aphid colonies on roots, bulbs and tubers; species confirmation requires an aphid specialist rather than host plant alone. Look in the folds of bulbs and around sprouting tubers, where aphids can be hidden from an overhead inspection. Photograph a colony with the affected plant material and a scale reference. The host is a clue to where to look, but many aphids use roots or stored planting material.
actions: Separate suspicious bulbs or tubers from clean stock and check the surrounding storage area. Keep purchase labels and storage dates with a sample if an adviser requests one. Do not share apparently infested planting material while waiting for a diagnosis. In a crop, combine the insect identification with plant-virus advice instead of assuming every pale or distorted shoot has the same cause.

sources.label: Petrovic-Obradovic and colleagues: First record in Serbia

identification: Swordlike basal leaves and tall tubular-flowered spikes; inspect stems for brown bulbils in the bulbil-producing form. Include the base of the leaf fan and the whole flower spike in photographs. Look for small hard cormlets attached along the stalk after flowering; they are not ordinary seed capsules. Not every garden Watsonia plant produces those bulbils, so the presence of swordlike leaves alone does not establish the troublesome form.
actions: Keep corms and bulbils out of dumped garden waste. For small unwanted clumps, carefully collect underground corms and stem bulbils and monitor regrowth. Before dividing or moving a garden clump, check whether cormlets are scattered nearby. Keep excavated soil close to the work area and collect loose corms rather than shaking them into adjacent vegetation. Revisit an unwanted patch when new leaves appear, since an overlooked underground corm can remain after the flowering stalks have been cleared.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Watsonia meriana

identification: Small bunchgrass with boat-tipped leaves, swollen basal shoots and often sprouting bulblets in the flower head. A close view of the flowering head may show tiny green shoots emerging where ordinary grass flowers would be expected. Check the swollen bases separately, because they are easy to miss beneath old leaf sheaths. The combination is more useful than the plant's early spring growth alone.
actions: Photograph both the plant base and flowering head. Avoid carrying bulblets in soil or equipment when working through a patch. Record the clump while it is green and its head is developed; later dry growth is harder to recognize. Keep detached bulblets with any removed material, and brush them from tools before moving to another site. Assess the patch in the context of local pasture or habitat management instead of assuming that every occurrence of an introduced grass needs removal.

sources.label: University of Illinois Extension: Bulbous bluegrass

identification: Coarse clumps with broad grass blades, swollen shoot bases, a membranous ligule and dense spike-like flower heads. Examine the leaf collar to see the thin membranous ligule, and include the base of a shoot if it can be viewed without disturbing nearby vegetation. A dense cylindrical head can resemble several other grasses. Mature spikelets, shoot bases and broad leaves together give a botanist a more dependable comparison.
actions: Remove small unwanted patches with follow-up checks; avoid cultivating established clumps into fragments, which can regrow. Map an unwanted clump before it blends into taller seasonal growth. Where digging is appropriate, keep removed underground pieces contained and check the same footprint later for shoots. On streambanks or wet ground, discuss the work with the land manager so soil disturbance does not create erosion or spread fragments into adjoining areas.

sources.label: Cal-IPC: Phalaris aquatica, Harrington and Lanini
Flora of New Zealand: Phalaris aquatica

identification: Spiny-winged stems, coarse prickly leaves with woolly undersides, and large purple heads surrounded by sharp bracts. Compare the upright stem with native thistles rather than identifying the plant from a purple flower alone. The continuous spiny wings down the stem and the coarse upper leaf surface are especially useful. A first-year rosette lacks the conspicuous tall flowering shape, so photograph both leaf surfaces carefully.
actions: Confirm the identification against native thistles. Remove small rosettes below the soil surface before flowering and revisit for seedlings. Use gloves and suitable tools when working around sharp rosettes. If a confirmed plant has already formed seed, contain the head before moving the stem. Coordinate pasture work with grazing and ground-cover management so bare ground does not invite another flush of seedlings. Preserve identified native thistles, which can occur near introduced ones and support local wildlife.

sources.label: University of Nevada Extension: Bull thistle
University of Florida: Thistle control in pastures

identification: Finely divided leaves, small white flower umbels beside upper leaves, and short oval fruits covered in hooked hairs. A close view of a mature fruit should show the hooked surface and the short, smooth beak at its tip. The small flower clusters sit beside upper leaves rather than forming one large showy umbrella. Fernlike foliage by itself is unreliable among the many members of the carrot family.
actions: Photograph ripe fruits for a reliable identification. Pull small confirmed patches before seed ripens and brush burrs from clothing and equipment. Do not taste an unfamiliar carrot-family plant as an identification test. Keep ripe burrs from catching on bags and cuffs while inspecting a patch. For locally unwanted growth, work before fruits become easily detached and check nearby shaded ground for additional plants. In riparian habitat, avoid pulling large mixed mats that would expose soil or damage the roots of neighboring shrubs.

sources.label: University of California: Bur and wild chervil
University of British Columbia E-Flora: Bur chervil

identification: Three rounded leaflets with toothed margins, small yellow pea-shaped flowers and coiled, prickly pods. Look for the tightly coiled pod after the yellow flowers fade; the fruit is much more distinctive than a three-leaflet leaf. The teeth along the leaflet margins also help when compared with true clovers. Some pods are less conspicuously hooked, so use several fruits and flowers for confirmation.
actions: Remove unwanted plants before the pods harden and detach; check clothing and animal coats for burrs after crossing a patch. In a lawn or play area, act before the hard burrs become a nuisance underfoot. In a deliberately planted cover crop or forage area, follow the growing plan instead of treating the plant as an automatic weed. Clean burrs from mower parts and footwear after working a seeding patch, and check wool or fur without scattering the pods along a path.

identification: Broad lance-shaped leaves, low spreading stems and short flower branches with long reddish awns. Show the whole flowering axis in a photograph, not just a single bristle. Several short side branches carry the spikelets, whose awns extend well beyond them. The rippled leaf surface is a useful clue, but broad leaves also occur in other basketgrasses with different regional status.
actions: Photograph leaves, stems and mature flower heads for botanical confirmation before removing an unfamiliar basketgrass. Before moving soil or planted material from a patch, check for ripe flower heads caught among the leaves. Keep samples enclosed if a botanist requests them. Where basketgrass is unfamiliar, record whether it forms a small path-edge clump or an extensive carpet, and wait for a species-level assessment before deciding whether surrounding grass needs to be removed.

sources.label: University of Richmond Kaxil Kiuic flora: Oplismenus burmannii

identification: Clustered smooth trunks and large, twice-divided leaves with broad, ragged-edged fishtail leaflets. The leaf is divided twice, with the distinctive ragged leaflets attached along smaller branches of the main leaf. Count the stems at ground level to distinguish a clustering palm from a single-trunked relative. Flowering on one trunk does not mean every stem in the clump will die together.
actions: Avoid handling crushed fruit; wear gloves when cleaning beneath plants and keep fruit away from children and pets. Plan the removal of a spent trunk with someone experienced in palm work, especially where it leans over a path or building. Leave healthy neighboring stems alone unless the whole planting needs removal, and check local planting guidance before establishing another clump.

identification: Large tan snake with dark puzzle-piece blotches and a dark arrow-shaped marking on the head; do not approach for a closer look. A distant photograph of the back pattern and head, taken without approaching, can help wildlife staff compare it with native large snakes. Water or dense vegetation may hide much of the body. Do not try to reveal the head or stretch out a snake to improve an identification photograph.
actions: Keep a safe distance, take a distant photograph and report suspected Florida sightings through the state wildlife reporting system. Keep people and pets back and note a precise location, direction of movement and time. Use the current wildlife reporting route for the area, particularly for a suspected new locality beyond known populations. Leave capture to trained, authorized responders. Owners of captive snakes should arrange an appropriate rehoming option rather than releasing an animal that has become difficult to keep.

sources.label: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission: Burmese python
USGS: Diet of invasive Burmese pythons, 1995-2020

identification: Climbing tendrils, alternate leaves divided into five shiny, serrated leaflets, and small orange-salmon flowers. Trace a complete leaf to its stem attachment to see how the five leaflets are arranged. Virginia creeper can also have five leaflets, so flower details and leaflet arrangement matter. A broad view of the vine shows its tendrils and the plants it is covering, while a close-up documents the small flowers.
actions: Seek a site-specific removal plan and revisit cut patches for new shoots. Identify where the vine enters the soil before cutting, and avoid disturbing roots unnecessarily during nearby digging. Root pieces can travel with moved soil even after the visible foliage is gone. For a canopy infestation, arrange safe access and a follow-up plan rather than pulling heavy vines from branches. Check the surrounding ground for shoots beyond the original crown.

identification: Bushy evergreen eucalypt with smooth, variably pink-gray bark and cream to green-yellow flowers; compare buds and fruit with a regional key. A general eucalypt silhouette is not enough for a confident name. Photograph unopened buds, open flowers and mature woody fruit on the same tree if possible, and include the bark at both the base and higher branches. Closely related yates can look much alike without those reproductive structures.
actions: Record flowers, buds and woody fruit for identification before managing a self-sown eucalypt; common names can cover similar species. Distinguish an intentionally planted tree from separate seedlings before deciding on management. Where a seedling appears outside cultivation, record its location and consult a regional eucalypt key or botanist. Large-tree pruning or removal needs an assessment of branch weight, access and nearby structures; a common-name match alone is not a reason to remove a mature ornamental tree.

sources.label: Botanic Gardens of South Australia: Bushy yate

identification: Narrow alternate leaves and two-toned yellow snapdragon flowers with long backward-pointing spurs. View an open flower from the side to show its long spur. The narrow leaves and orange-yellow raised center distinguish the familiar flowering form more clearly than a distant patch of yellow. A small cluster of stems may be connected underground, so visible stem count does not equal the number of separate plants.
actions: Remove small unwanted patches with their roots and monitor for regrowth; repeated management is usually needed. Avoid tilling an established patch casually because broken roots can produce more shoots. For a small confirmed infestation, plan repeat checks after removal and keep root pieces from being moved with soil. In mixed wildflower plantings, read the seed mixture before sowing and distinguish this species from desirable yellow-flowered plants before undertaking control.

sources.label: University of Minnesota: Butter and eggs

identification: Two-lobed, butterfly-shaped leaves; large pink-purple flowers and long, flat brown pods. Look for a single leaf blade with a deep notch dividing it into two rounded lobes, rather than two separate leaflets. Close photographs of the flower and its stamens help distinguish similar orchid-trees and hybrids. A flowering tree and a pod-bearing tree can look very different from a distance.
actions: In regions where it is invasive, choose an alternative tree and remove unwanted seedlings before they mature and produce pods. Check beneath the canopy and nearby fence lines for seedlings where this tree escapes locally. Collect unwanted mature pods before they are carried away with garden waste, and keep identification labels when replacing a planted tree. If a large tree requires removal, arrange qualified help and consider the effect on neighboring plants rather than clearing the entire shaded area.

identification: On butternut, look for expanding branch dieback, dark sunken cankers, cracked bark and black-brown stained wood; laboratory confirmation may be needed. First confirm that the host is a butternut rather than a black walnut or a similar planted tree. Photograph the whole crown and individual bark lesions, noting whether dieback has increased between seasons. Several cankers may join into a larger damaged area, while smaller branch lesions can be easy to overlook.
actions: Ask a tree-health specialist to assess suspected cankers. Disinfect pruning tools between cuts and retain apparently healthy butternuts for conservation review. Avoid cutting into healthy bark merely to look for staining. Ask the specialist which samples, if any, are needed and how tools should be cleaned during work. Apparently healthy survivors can be important to conservation efforts, so discuss them before removal. Evaluate hazardous dead branches separately from the decision about retaining a living tree.

sources.label: University of Minnesota: Butternut branch dieback

identification: Low rosette with deeply divided leaves and clustered, woolly fruiting heads near the base; fruits have a stiff terminal spine. Examine the center of the rosette, where the heads may be hidden among leaf stalks. The mature fruit shape helps distinguish this species from other Soliva plants, so a photograph of fernlike leaves alone may not settle the identification. A low patch can remain below normal mowing height.
actions: Photograph mature heads for confirmation, then remove unwanted plants before burrs scatter; keep detached burrs contained. Check bare spots in lawns and other used ground before fruiting clusters become hard and prickly. For a confirmed unwanted patch, contain the mature heads rather than scattering them during raking. Wear suitable footwear around burr-bearing plants and gloves when handling them. Reestablish appropriate ground cover after removal so the same open patch does not repeatedly fill with annual seedlings.

sources.label: New South Wales Flora Online: Soliva anthemifolia
Flora of New Zealand: Soliva anthemifolia

identification: Fleshy branching stems, toothed oval leaves and flat five-petaled flowers, sometimes doubled in cultivated varieties. Look at a flower from the side as well as the front to include its curved rear spur. Cultivars vary in color and petal number, so a double blossom need not resemble the familiar flat single form. Compare the fleshy stems and toothed leaves with other commonly sold impatiens.
actions: Keep garden waste out of natural areas. If plants develop downy mildew, remove infected material and do not place it in a home compost pile. Check the undersides of yellowing leaves for the pale fuzzy growth associated with downy mildew, then seek confirmation if the cause is unclear. For a previously affected bed, choose a resistant cultivar or suitable shade alternative. Keep good records of where diseased plants grew rather than assuming all impatiens types have identical susceptibility or that every yellow leaf indicates infection.

identification: Thick, waxy leaves, yellow cross-shaped flowers and elongated seedpods; cultivated forms vary widely in shape. Identify the cultivated form as well as the species when possible: a leafy kale and a swollen kohlrabi stem should not be expected to look alike. If a plant has bolted, photograph its waxy leaves, flower cluster and pods. A cabbage-like seedling alone may be difficult to separate from other brassicas.
actions: Identify volunteers before removal. Rotate vegetable beds and remove unwanted plants before pods split if reseeding is a concern. Manage planted vegetables for harvest and crop health, keeping volunteers only where they fit the bed plan. Inspect transplanted plants for caterpillars and disease before introducing them to clean beds. If saving seed, obtain advice on the crop's flowering and crossing behavior; seed from mixed flowering forms may not reproduce the parent plant's familiar appearance.

sources.label: University of Wisconsin: Growing cole crops
