identification: Striped larvae and silk webbing around brassica growing points; moth appearance alone does not reliably separate related Hellula species. Inspect the tender center of a young plant, where feeding can be concealed before obvious damage appears. Silk mixed with droppings is a useful warning sign, but diamondback moth and related webworms can also be involved. A clear larval photograph is more informative than a brown moth seen nearby.
actions: Check transplants before planting and revisit young crops frequently enough to find concealed feeding early. Keep affected plants and larvae available for a diagnostic photograph rather than discarding all evidence immediately. In a commercial crop, ask an adviser to match the response to the confirmed pest and crop stage, especially where multiple brassica caterpillars are present together.

sources.label: University of Hawaii Crop Knowledge Master: Hellula undalis
University of Georgia IPM: Cabbage webworm

identification: White adults have dark forewing markings. Caterpillars are soft-looking green with faint yellow lengthwise lines, reaching about an inch. Watch how the larva moves: cabbage loopers arch their bodies conspicuously, whereas imported cabbageworms usually move more slowly without that looping gait. The velvety surface and faint yellow lines are helpful close-up features. Large ragged holes alone cannot distinguish the several caterpillars that feed on brassica leaves.
actions: Inspect both leaf surfaces, handpick larvae, and fit row covers before butterflies lay eggs; remove spent crop debris. Check beneath covers after installation so that larvae already on the plants are not enclosed with the crop. Continue inspecting the growing center as heads develop, where older larvae and droppings can be hidden. Keep beneficial predators in mind before choosing an insecticide; small, targeted garden actions can preserve the natural enemies that help limit repeated infestations.

identification: Small beetle about 3-4.5 mm long, usually metallic blue with orange-red legs; pale larvae mine brassica stems and leaf stalks. Adults can jump when disturbed, so obtain a photograph before handling the leaf. Record the leg color and body shape as well as the metallic sheen. Leaf holes and internal tunneling represent different stages of attack; neither pattern alone separates this insect from all other brassica pests.
actions: Monitor emerging brassica crops for feeding and inspect stems if growth weakens; use local pest thresholds and advice rather than spraying on appearance alone. Note crop growth and recent weather, since slow-growing seedlings may be less able to replace eaten tissue. Ask a crop adviser how to assess larvae in leaf stalks and stems, and use guidance for the local crop rather than transferring a calendar from another country.

sources.label: AHDB: Cabbage stem flea beetle in oilseed rape

identification: Orange-red, dark-banded larvae inside cactus pads; spine-like egg sticks and leaking, hollowed pads. Look for egg sticks on the cactus surface without touching the spines. A damaged pad may contain a group of larvae, but opening intact pads unnecessarily can injure the plant. Native cactus-feeding insects can produce similar damage, so report photographs of both the outside symptoms and any larvae already visible.
actions: Do not move suspect cacti. Photograph the damage and report it to a state plant-health authority for identification and disposal guidance. Keep nursery labels and purchase locations with a report if the cactus was recently acquired. Do not share pads for propagation or discard suspect pads where another cactus grows. Follow the plant-health service's instructions for sampling and disposal, and let trained responders decide whether nearby native prickly pears need a survey.

sources.label: USDA APHIS: South American cactus moth

identification: Adults are shiny brown to black with a distinct constriction behind the thorax. Larvae are whitish with a black head and dark rear projections. Include the narrow junction behind the adult's front body section in a close photograph. A larva's dark head and paired rear projections are useful clues, but other stored-product beetles can occur in the same bin. Holes in food or nearby wood do not identify a species by themselves.
actions: Keep affected food or grain apart from clean stock while obtaining identification. Inspect cracks, old sacks and residues beneath equipment as well as the visible grain surface. Cleaning only the main container can leave insects hidden in storage materials. For a commercial store, seek an assessment of the grain and structure before filling the space again.

identification: Look for alternate rough leaves, often shallowly lobed, pink flowers with darker centers, and burr-like fruits that split into five parts. Compare both surfaces of a leaf: the rough upper face and paler underside are useful when the plant is not flowering. The small pink blossoms sit at leaf axils, and later fruits separate into hooked segments. Several mallows have pink flowers, so mature fruit is particularly helpful.
actions: Check cuffs, bags and footwear before leaving an infested site so burrs are not dropped along the next path. If a confirmed patch is locally unwanted, work before the fruits become numerous and easy to detach. Keep seed-bearing waste contained during transport, and revisit the patch after removal rather than assuming that cutting the shrub removes seed already on the ground.

identification: Photograph the leaf veins and the fingerlike flower spike. The introduced form generally has one strong midvein; native American sweet flag has additional prominent veins. Inspect several mature leaves for the vein pattern and include the base of the flowering stalk in photographs. An iris-like leaf is not enough to distinguish sweet flags from other wetland plants. The flower spike is a dense cylinder of tiny flowers, not a large iris blossom.
actions: Avoid dividing or transplanting a stand until its identity is settled. Moving rhizomes can both spread an introduced form and damage a native population if the names are confused. Record whether the stand appears planted or occurs in natural wetland, and ask a botanist which features or samples are needed without clearing the surrounding wetland vegetation.

identification: Mature females are roughly pea-sized, dark brown or black with conspicuous pale blotches; younger scales are flatter. Photograph affected twigs and leaf undersides, including any honeydew deposits. Black sooty mold grows on the sugary coating and does not by itself identify the scale species or show how many insects are alive.
actions: Inspect twigs and leaves, assess honeydew and tree vigor, and use local crawler monitoring to time any treatment. Record which trees are affected and whether growth, leaf retention or branch health is changing. An adviser can check for live scales and natural enemies before recommending action. If monitoring is appropriate, revisit the same branches so changes are comparable. Do not transfer a crawler-treatment date from a distant region without checking local seasonal development.

identification: Check the broad, glossy oval leaves, nearly hairless young shoots, pyramidal clusters of white flowers, and small dark fruits. Examine young, untrimmed shoots because hedge clipping can remove flowers and disguise natural growth. The broad leaf blade and nearly hairless twig help compare it with other privets. A close side view of an open flower shows the relatively long tube, a useful feature that a distant hedge photograph misses.
actions: Check the area beyond the planted row, especially where birds perch and seedlings may become established. Distinguish those escapes from shoots belonging to the maintained hedge. If replacing an unwanted planting, plan fruit containment and later seedling checks, and choose a hedge suited to local conditions and guidance rather than relying on the common name alone.

identification: Female covers are round and reddish-brown, about 2 mm across; male covers are smaller and more elongated. A hand lens helps distinguish the round female covers from narrower male covers and other armored scales. Look at fruit, woody growth and leaves rather than only one surface. A dry, empty cover can remain attached after the insect is gone, so cover counts alone can exaggerate current activity.
actions: Keep observations of live scales separate from old blemishes when assessing a tree. Protect parasitoids and other beneficial insects by avoiding unnecessary broad treatments. For nursery stock, inspect plants before bringing them into a clean growing area. A crop adviser can help match any response to the host, active life stage and local seasonal pattern.

identification: Look for broad arrow- to heart-shaped leaves, a white funnel-shaped spathe and a yellow central spike; leaves arise from a fleshy rhizome. Photograph that arrangement together with a whole leaf and its long stalk. Other cultivated callas have different colors or leaf markings, so a cut flower alone may not establish this species.
actions: Keep divisions and discarded rhizomes contained, and use gloves when handling this irritating plant. When lifting a clump, keep fleshy underground pieces together rather than leaving them in damp waste piles. Do not dump unwanted divisions beside a drain or wetland. In a maintained garden, decide whether the clump simply needs room or division before treating it as an escape. Ask for identification and local guidance if similar plants appear beyond cultivation.

identification: White spring flower clusters, glossy broad leaves and small round fruits are useful clues; escaped trees often have sharp thorns. Photograph the leaves and small fruits after spring flowers have finished; flowering cherries and crabapples can create a similar white display. Thorns are especially useful on escaped seedlings, but their absence on a named garden cultivar does not rule out Callery pear. Growth form varies with planting and competition.
actions: Choose an alternative for new plantings, remove young escapes, and plan follow-up for stump or root sprouts when larger trees are removed. Survey neighboring fence lines and field edges when planning to replace a seed-producing tree. Handle thorny seedlings with suitable protection and contain fruiting branches. Get professional help for large trees near buildings, overhead lines or public paths. Replanting the space with an appropriate tree or vegetation helps support the intended landscape while reducing another seed source.

sources.label: Callery pear: history, identification and control

identification: Check leaf undersides for narrow brown covers. Male covers are brown, unlike the conspicuous white male covers of tea scale; definitive identification may require microscopy. The scale covers lie close to the leaf and may be easier to see when the leaf is turned over. Check both young and old foliage, and include the host plant in photographs. Oystershell-shaped covers occur in several species, so an expert may need more than a surface image.
actions: Separate newly acquired plants with suspicious scales from established camellias while arranging identification. Look for small emergence holes that can indicate parasitoid activity and record whether leaves are falling prematurely. A few persistent covers do not prove a severe active infestation. Ask an adviser whether live scales and plant damage justify action before selecting a treatment.

sources.label: Lepidosaphes tapleyi: comparison with L. camelliae

identification: Look for spine-tipped branches, alternate smooth-edged leaves, small pea flowers and strongly constricted seedpods. The narrow constrictions between seeds make mature pods look segmented, but the segments remain part of one pod. Photograph a flowering branch from the side to show its sharp tips and small leaves. A low shoot may be only the visible part of a larger underground colony.
actions: Mark patch boundaries before earthmoving or ditch maintenance, and tell anyone moving soil where the roots occur. Repeated cutting without a follow-up plan can leave the underground system intact. Where local control is required, coordinate the work across the whole affected area and revisit beyond the original shoots. Protect access routes from loose thorny branches during cleanup.

identification: Look for convex brown round or oval covers with an off-center orange-yellow shed skin; authoritative species identification requires a slide-mounted adult female. The colored spot on the cover is shed skin, not the insect's head. Its off-center position and the rounded, raised cover help narrow the comparison, but several armored scales look similar. Photograph different stages on the same plant and record the host instead of assuming camphor is the only possible host.
actions: Check sheltered leaf and stem surfaces on newly purchased ornamentals before placing them with other plants. If damage is suspected, ask the diagnostic service how to submit intact scales and host material. Preserve evidence of live insects and natural enemies, and avoid treating every old cover as a living scale needing another application.

identification: Adults are black and about 3.4-3.9 mm long, with a short, compressed abdomen. A clear magnified side view is more useful than a distant picture of a bore hole. Many ambrosia beetles make small entries into wood. Identification should connect an actual beetle with the damage rather than naming the pest from sawdust alone.
actions: Photograph damage and collect a beetle if practical; ask Extension to identify it and assess tree stress before treatment. Inspect affected trees for drainage problems, injury or other stress while arranging a diagnosis. Keep suspect nursery trees from being moved to new properties until advised. Check damaged fuel containers for safe handling and replacement rather than trying to use a leaking container as an insect trap. Record fresh holes and the timing of decline to help separate current activity from older injury.

identification: Look for alternate glossy leaves with three prominent basal veins, round purple-black fruits. Examine how the main veins spread from near the leaf base and photograph both a twig and mature fruit. Scent can support an identification, but it is unnecessary to crush foliage when clear structural photographs are available. Several evergreen trees have glossy leaves, so combine leaf arrangement, venation and fruit.
actions: Where locally invasive, avoid planting it, remove young seedlings, and obtain advice for mature trees because cutting can prompt resprouting. Distinguish seedlings beyond the planting from low shoots attached to an established tree. If a mature tree is locally unwanted, arrange a removal method and follow-up appropriate to its size and surroundings. Keep fruiting material contained, and inspect bird-perch areas nearby for new seedlings rather than focusing only on the original trunk.

identification: Rotate a stem gently between your fingers to check its distinctly flattened shape, then photograph the leaf collar and flowering head. A short grass cut repeatedly in a lawn may not show its mature panicle. Kentucky bluegrass and other Poa species need comparison of several characters rather than leaf color alone.
actions: Confirm the grass from flowering material, then match management to the site; avoid carrying seed or rooted soil into restoration areas. In a restoration site, record the patch edge and compare flowering material before soil work. Avoid bringing rooted turf from a confirmed unwanted patch into a clean area. In a managed lawn or pasture, assess its role and performance against the intended vegetation before choosing a response; a common name or introduced origin alone does not decide the management goal.

identification: Look for upright shoots in spreading patches, sharply spiny leaves and clusters of relatively small purple flower heads. Compare the relatively small heads and patch-forming growth with the larger heads and spiny-winged stems of bull thistle. Several shoots can arise from connected roots, even when the ground between them looks clear. Native thistles also have purple heads and prickly leaves, making a complete plant photograph useful.
actions: Map the whole patch, including shoots beyond the densest center, before work begins. Keep soil containing roots on site unless disposal is arranged appropriately. Revisit the same boundary over several growing seasons and maintain suitable competing cover. Choose timing and methods with a local adviser so repeated effort weakens the plant without unnecessarily damaging the desired surrounding vegetation.

identification: A single thick trunk, diamond-patterned leaf scars, long pinnate leaves and stout spines near the leaf bases distinguish mature trees. Photograph the crown and trunk from a safe position, then include fallen fruit if present. Young palms may not yet show the stout scarred trunk of a mature tree. Other date palms can look similar, so crown shape, trunk form and leaf-base details should be considered together.
actions: Keep cut fronds out of walkways because the basal spines remain hazardous after pruning. Ask an arborist to assess access and tree health before crown work, and avoid climbing into the heavy leaf bases. Where unwanted seedlings appear, identify them while small and check the fruit-producing parent planting before choosing a locally suitable response.

identification: A tall shrub with narrow, unstalked leaves, flattened or two-lined stems, yellow flowers and no black glands in the foliage. Look at a young stem from several angles to see the paired longitudinal lines or flattened shape. Photograph a leaf against light and include open flowers. A tall yellow-flowered shrub should be compared with other Hypericum species rather than identified solely from the familiar St. John's wort name.
actions: Prevent further planting where invasive; confirm identification and arrange repeated follow-up after removing an established patch. Record the edges of an escaped stand before removal so later shoots and seedlings can be compared with the original extent. Keep seed-bearing cuttings contained and avoid spreading rooted material with soil. In coastal scrub or grassland, coordinate work with the land manager to retain desirable vegetation and reduce the bare disturbed ground left behind.

identification: Look for deeply lobed leaves and tall, stiff flower spikes; check a flower from more than one angle. Look at a flower from the side to show its projecting spur, and include a mature leaf with its deep divisions. Garden selections can have fuller flower spikes or unusual colors. A nursery hybrid label may describe cultivated ancestry more accurately than a confident identification as a wild species.
actions: Support tall stems, deadhead unwanted seed production, and prevent children, pets and livestock from eating plant material. Place supports early enough to guide the stems as they grow, and check ties after wind or rain. Keep pruned material away from grazing animals and dispose of unwanted seed heads securely. If a similar plant appears outside cultivation, confirm its identity before removal; native larkspurs and garden escapes can require quite different local decisions.

identification: Look for broad alternate leaves, often lobed when young, pale terminal flower clusters and rounded fruits containing one or two hard dark seeds. Compare young and older leaves on the same tree before assuming that differently lobed foliage belongs to separate species. The pale canopy, broad leaves and rounded fruits together provide stronger clues than a single fallen seed. Photograph the fruit with its outer covering as well as the hard seed if already exposed.
actions: Keep seedlings only where a tree has room to develop its broad crown. When managing an unwanted patch, consult the landowner about cultural use and local ecological priorities before cutting established trees. Collect unwanted fruit from maintained paths without distributing it to new sites, and check the same planting edge for later seedlings after cleanup.

identification: Look for a large, heavily built brownish toad with conspicuous glands extending behind the eyes; compare carefully with local native species. In Florida, native southern toads have raised ridges on the head that cane toads lack. Photograph the head and shoulder glands from a safe distance, rather than handling the animal to compare them. Young cane toads can overlap native species in size, so a small animal is not automatically harmless or correctly identified.
actions: Bring pets away from the area while identification is pending and remove attractants such as accessible food. Do not relocate a suspect toad to a pond or another property. Follow local wildlife advice for humane management only after confirmation, and obtain prompt veterinary help if contact with a pet has occurred.

For any authorized handling, use gloves and protect your eyes and skin. If a pet bites or mouths a cane toad, contact an emergency veterinarian immediately. FWC advises washing toxin forward out of the mouth for ten minutes without directing water down the throat, and wiping the gums and tongue.

identification: Look for fibrous plugs over tunnels and pale legless grubs inside affected tissue; larvae alone need specialist confirmation. Record the affected host and photograph the tunnel opening, fiber plug and any exposed insect. A pale grub inside a palm is not a reliable species identification because several borers have similar larvae. Declining foliage or trunk weakness also needs assessment for other causes and for immediate structural risk.
actions: Keep people away from an unstable palm and arrange qualified inspection rather than cutting into the trunk yourself. Retain nursery or transport records for a recently acquired plant. Do not move infested stems, cane cuttings or palms while seeking plant-health guidance. Any cleanup should include the concealed material where larvae remain, using the disposal instructions provided for the confirmed pest.

sources.label: Cane Weevil Borer: Queensland original study abstract

identification: Glossy alternate leaves, small cream flowers and yellow to orange fruits, often pointed, with large brown seeds are useful clues. Photograph the leaf arrangement and flowers as well as ripe fruit; several unrelated tropical fruits can be yellow and pointed. Canistel fruit shapes vary even among cultivated selections. The firm mature fruit usually needs time to soften, so yellow color alone does not describe the texture of a ready-to-eat fruit.
actions: Use well-drained planting sites, harvest mature fruit, and remove unwanted volunteer seedlings rather than moving them into natural areas. For an established garden tree, maintain access for harvesting without climbing weak outer branches. Keep fallen fruit from accumulating where unwanted seedlings are a concern. Obtain cultivar and harvest advice from local fruit-growing specialists, and confirm unfamiliar volunteer trees before keeping or sharing them. A cultivated fruit tree does not require removal simply because it originated elsewhere.

sources.label: Canistel growing in the Florida home landscape

identification: Trailing or climbing vines bear tendrils, broad rough leaves, yellow flowers and highly variable fleshy fruits; cultivar identity is needed for finer distinctions. A flower with a small swelling behind it can be distinguished from a pollen-bearing flower without an obvious young fruit. Follow a vine back to its planting position when several cucurbits are tangled together. Leaf shape alone may not separate all cultivated melons or establish a named variety.
actions: Allow flower-visiting insects access when plants begin setting fruit, and use crop-specific advice if covers are being used for early protection. Keep leaves and fruit off persistently waterlogged ground where possible. Save the seed packet or plant label so harvest cues can be matched to the cultivar rather than assuming every melon develops netting or slips from its stem.

sources.label: Flower and fruit set in cucurbits

identification: Look for a basal rosette of toothed leaves and an upright stem bearing large bell-shaped flowers; cultivated forms may be double. Compare the large open bells with the smaller flowers of other bellflowers, and photograph the leaf rosette as well as the stem. The upper leaves are smaller and sit close to the flowering stem. A double-flowered garden selection can obscure the normal flower shape, making its label useful.
actions: Keep track of first-year rosettes when weeding a planted bed so they are not discarded before their flowering season. If volunteers are welcome, leave room for a few replacement plants; otherwise collect fading flower stems before the capsules open. Check the neighboring bed after flowering and remove only the seedlings you have identified as unwanted Canterbury bells.

identification: Photograph the floating leaf margins as well as the raised flower. The colored extensions at the tips of the anthers are more useful than simply calling the flower blue. Photograph the flower center closely and note whether flowers stand above the surface. Pond hybrids may share these traits, so color and a floating leaf alone do not settle the name.
actions: Contain pond plantings and dispose of unwanted rhizomes away from waterways; obtain specialist identification before managing a wild stand. Keep the purchase label with photographs when asking a waterlily specialist for help. Do not dig into an unfamiliar wetland to examine the rhizome without permission and a clear sampling plan. During pond maintenance, collect underground pieces and keep the waste from drains, streams and ponds where it was not planted. Recheck contained plantings after divisions or major cleaning.

identification: Look for opposite compound leaves with toothed leaflets, tubular orange-red flowers and long narrow seed capsules. Count leaflets on several mature leaves rather than a single young shoot. The flower tube has spreading, unequal lobes at its opening, while the long dry capsules provide another character after the display ends.
actions: Manage the plant's spread by pruning and checking for rooted stems or seedlings; contain discarded cuttings. Inspect stems where they rest on soil before trimming a spreading plant. Any rooted sections need to be managed with the original planting if its boundary is being reduced. Keep an access gap beside paths so pruning remains practical. In a garden where it is appropriate to grow, regular size management is more useful than assuming that every vigorous shrub is an ecological invader.

identification: Look closely at where each leaf joins the stem to see the small basal appendages. The flower has a slender tube ending in five spreading lobes, with several flowers grouped together. Its loose arching habit can look vine-like when tied to a support, although the plant is a shrub.
actions: Prune to maintain the intended boundary, use well-drained sites, and keep discarded plant material out of natural areas. Check low stems and the edge of the clump when reducing its size, including any suckering growth. Wear gloves if handling foliage because contact can irritate skin. In a container, make sure excess water can drain away rather than collecting beneath the roots. Retain healthy garden plants where suitable, while promptly checking any volunteers or spread beyond the intended bed.

identification: A close photograph of the leaf surface can show the tiny pale or reddish dots without detaching the leaf. Look above the mat for loose flower clusters and the miniature plants that may replace flowers. These plantlets are different from the leaf-edge plantlets of some other commonly grown succulents.
actions: Contain cuttings and plantlets, remove rooted stems carefully, and monitor for regrowth rather than leaving fragments on bare soil. Work over a container or sheet when lifting plants from a small maintained bed so loose plantlets are easier to recover. Inspect the soil surface and nearby paving cracks after the main mat has been lifted. Do not leave rooted pieces in damp garden waste beside natural vegetation, and revisit after rain when missed fragments may become easier to see.

identification: Look for an annual tuft of narrow leaves with dense panicles and very long, twice-bent, twisted awns. The long bristles bend and twist beyond a compact head; photograph the whole head and a close view of an attached seed. Do not use a grass's dry brown color or its presence in a desert alone as identification.
actions: Clean seeds from clothing and equipment; document new patches and remove small plants before seed maturity where authorized. Avoid walking or driving through ripe seed heads when another route is available. Inspect footwear, animal bedding and field equipment before moving between sites. For a small confirmed patch, arrange work before the sharp seeds become easy to detach. Record both the patch location and its approximate extent so the land manager can plan follow-up with the surrounding native seasonal vegetation in mind.

sources.label: Stipellula capensis: GrassBase and Flora of Oman
Flora of North America: Stipellula capensis, Barkworth

identification: Glossy fleshy leaves have five to seven pointed lobes; small clustered yellow flower heads lack the showy ray petals of some similar vines. Include the leaf base and the way the stem climbs in photographs. Ivy-like leaves by themselves can lead to confusion with unrelated ornamental climbers.
actions: Contain all fragments, protect nearby native plants during removal, and arrange repeated follow-up, especially near streams. Plan where cut vines will go before beginning work, especially on a bank where fragments can fall into moving water. Lift loose pieces without tearing out the native vegetation beneath them. Large tangles above head height need an assessment of the supporting branches. Return to the treated edge and cleared ground for small shoots rather than waiting for another blanket of growth.

identification: Photograph a fully open head from above so the dark center is clear, and turn over a leaf to show its woolly underside. Young rosettes can resemble other daisies before flowering. A creeping capeweed planting nearby does not prove that every similar seedling belongs to the same species.
actions: Prevent seed production, clean soil and seeds from equipment, and distinguish it from creeping A. prostrata before planning control. In a small confirmed unwanted patch, inspect for developing heads before soil disturbance or mowing scatters material. Remove soil and attached seeds from tools before using them elsewhere. Keep desirable ground cover where possible and check exposed patches for new rosettes after rain. If the plant is part of a mixed lawn or pasture, ask for advice suited to that use before undertaking broad control.

identification: Check for long creeping stems and flower heads with yellow centers; fertile A. calendula usually has dark centers. Trace one runner gently along the soil to see whether it roots at several points. Those connected rosettes show how a patch expands. A yellow flower center supports the comparison with fertile capeweed, but a fading or closed flower may be misleading; use fresh, fully open heads.
actions: Avoid planting where it escapes locally; remove rooted runners, contain fragments and recheck the patch for regrowth. Start at the patch edge when lifting runners so attached rooted sections are less easily missed. Keep lifted material together rather than dragging it across clean ground. Revisit gaps between paving and the adjoining bed, where small retained pieces can be overlooked. Where a maintained planting is being replaced, choose locally suitable ground cover and continue watching its former boundary as the replacement establishes.

identification: A large brown rodent with a barrel-shaped body, blunt head, no visible tail and partly webbed feet; do not confuse young animals with nutria. A view of the rear body helps distinguish the tailless outline from a nutria with its long visible tail. Use an object already nearby for scale rather than approaching the animal. A swimming animal may show little more than its eyes and ears, so wait for a clearer view without cornering it.
actions: Do not feed, approach closely or release captive animals; document unexpected sightings and contact local wildlife authorities. Report the time, location and number of animals, noting any young or signs of an enclosure nearby. Keep dogs on a lead and give the animals an unobstructed route away from people. Feeding can encourage repeated visits and closer contact. If an animal appears injured or trapped, describe the situation to wildlife responders instead of attempting to catch it.

identification: Look for large alternate leaves with toothed, wavy edges, conspicuous veins beneath and dense hairs, plus lavender, five-lobed flowers. California plants can carry the name var. caracasana, so include any original plant label when seeking an identification. Photograph the undersides of leaves only where this can be done without contact; the coarse veins and dense hairs help show the foliage structure. Include a side view of an open flower and the curling cluster. A garden label or record of planting may help connect an escaped stand with the appropriate named form.
actions: Photograph leaves and flowers without touching the hairs. Wear protective clothing if handling is necessary, avoid relocating plants from escaped colonies, and seek local advice on established patches. Keep a safe working gap beside paths where the hairy leaves project into pedestrian space. If managing a confirmed escaped stand, plan how to carry cut material without brushing it against exposed skin or passersby. Ask a local botanist or land manager to check the identification and extent before treating an entire colony.

sources.label: Wigandia urens var. caracasana — Prigge and Gibson flora
Wigandia urens — University of Lisbon ISA

identification: Look for finely divided leaves, small compound umbels and narrow ridged aromatic fruits; a full botanical identification is needed for a wild plant. Include lower leaves, upper leaves and mature fruit in photographs because the leaf segments change along the stem. Several carrot-family plants have white umbrella-like clusters. The small ribbed fruits are a useful botanical feature, but smelling or tasting an unidentified plant is not a safe identification method.
actions: Harvest or remove seed heads to limit self-sowing, and keep uncertain wild Apiaceae out of food preparations. Keep cultivated caraway labeled, particularly where volunteers mix with other herbs or wild seedlings. Choose whether to retain a few identified plants for the next flowering season or remove ripening heads to limit spread. Avoid disturbing the roots of plants you intend to keep. Ask for a full botanical identification of an unfamiliar roadside or field-margin plant before considering any food use.

identification: Very large, deeply lobed, spiny leaves with pale woolly undersides and purple thistle-like heads. Cultivated artichokes are close relatives and can complicate identification. Photograph the rosette, stem and outer bracts around a mature flower head. Some cultivated forms are less spiny, and flower shape alone does not establish whether a plant is an escaped wild form or a vegetable selection. Nearby garden plantings can help explain its appearance without proving its identity.
actions: Use protective gloves and plan follow-up where a confirmed escaped patch needs removal. For an unwanted established patch, assess access to the deep roots before beginning excavation. Cutting flower stems can prevent this season's seed only if done before it matures; it does not necessarily kill the perennial plant. Revisit treated plants and check beyond the original rosettes for seedlings. Keep intentional vegetable plantings separate from decisions about escapes in surrounding habitat.

identification: Mature females are roughly 3-5 mm long, dark brown to black and hemispherical, with an H-shaped ridge. A close side view shows the female's raised dome, while a top view can reveal the H-shaped ridge. Other soft scales can share that outline, and young stages are harder to recognize. Record the host plant and include a twig with several stages when requesting expert identification.
actions: Inspect incoming plants and infested twigs. Preserve natural enemies; a neat round exit hole may indicate a beneficial wasp. Seek crop-specific advice before treating. Check whether the bumps contain live insects and whether honeydew is fresh before deciding that the problem is increasing. Look for ants tending the honeydew and for evidence of parasitic wasps. In a fruit planting, record affected branches and fruit rather than relying only on sooty mold elsewhere. Use local crop guidance to protect natural enemies while addressing a confirmed damaging population.

sources.label: A Guide to Scale Insect Identification: Caribbean Black Scale

identification: Brown S-shaped markings cross otherwise clear wings; a dark spot occurs near the rear of the thorax. White, legless larvae inside fruit are not enough for species identification. A clear top view of the adult's wings is particularly useful, but related Anastrepha flies may still require a specialist examination. Keep the host fruit name and collection location with the photograph.
actions: Photograph the fly and affected fruit, keep suspect fruit contained, and contact the local plant-health or agricultural office for identification and disposal guidance before transporting it. Keep the affected fruit away from fresh produce intended for transport or sharing. If the plant-health office requests a sample, follow its packing and delivery directions so larvae cannot escape along the way. Record whether the fruit came from a garden, market or shipment; that history helps responders decide where to investigate. Do not release a live captured fly after suspecting a reportable pest.

sources.label: Caribbean Fruit Fly Pest Profile — CDFA

identification: Photograph the five to seven leaflets joining at one central point, together with their grey-green upper and silvery lower surfaces. Include the corky trunk and a flowering branch. A distant yellow crown is not enough to distinguish related ornamental trumpet trees. Older labels may use Tabebuia argentea for silver trumpet tree, so keep the label with the photographs when seeking confirmation.
actions: Check local planting guidance and monitor seedlings around ornamental trees before assuming they need removal. Keep nursery labels and planting records where several yellow trumpet trees are grown together. Collect fallen leaves for comparison only where permission allows, instead of breaking branches from a mature tree. If seedlings appear outside the maintained planting, document their position and obtain local identification and planting advice before deciding whether the tree is spreading undesirably.

sources.label: Silver Trumpet Tree — Hong Kong Greening
James Cook University: Tabebuia aurea, synonym T. argentea

identification: Twice- or three-times-divided leaves, small white umbels with few rays, and fruits about 6-12 mm long bearing rows of hooked spines. Mature fruit is important for separating similar carrot-family plants. Count the few main rays beneath a mature umbel and photograph the hooked rows on the fruit without carrying them to another site. A finely divided leaf and white flower alone can fit many carrot-family plants. Fruit size and spine arrangement are therefore better evidence than a distant flowering view.
actions: Leave a population in place while checking local conservation guidance, particularly in traditional arable habitat. Record whether it occurs among crops, beside a field or on recently disturbed soil. Clean attached fruits from clothing before leaving the site, containing them there rather than spreading them along a road. Share the record with a local botanist if the plant is unfamiliar or potentially significant.

sources.label: Caucalis platycarpos — Kew, Flora of Iraq account

identification: Leaves are compound, usually with four to twelve leathery leaflets. Woody, yellow-orange capsules split into three sections to expose shiny black seeds with yellow-red coverings; inner bark can be orange. Look for the swollen base of the compound leaf stalk and several leathery, smooth-edged leaflets. Orange inner bark is a supporting clue, not a reason to damage an intact trunk for identification.
actions: In invaded areas, pull small seedlings with their roots and contain seed pods. Arrange suitable professional treatment for larger trees and continue checking for bird-dispersed seedlings. Check below bird perches and along the planting boundary, since seedlings may occur well away from the parent. Work on small plants before their roots become difficult to lift, where removal is appropriate and authorized. For a mature tree beside buildings or other vegetation, obtain a professional plan and keep the follow-up area under observation after the main work is finished.

sources.label: Carrotwood — UF/IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants

identification: Look for a caterpillar inside a portable silk-and-fiber case and a buff adult with three dark forewing spots. Webbing clothes moth larvae feed in attached silk tubes instead of carrying a case. The fibers incorporated into a moving case can match the damaged textile and help locate the feeding site. Carpet beetle larvae can also damage wool, but they do not make these silken cases. A moth near a window is not by itself evidence that stored clothing is infested.
actions: Clean items using suitable laundering or dry-cleaning methods, vacuum rug edges and storage areas, and store clean woolens in sealed containers. Inspect folds, rug undersides and items that have been stored undisturbed, including nearby animal-fiber materials. Isolate affected pieces before moving them through the house. Choose cleaning methods that suit the textile care label; delicate or valuable objects may need a textile conservator. Recheck cleaned storage and newly stored items for fresh cases or damage so an overlooked source can be found.

sources.label: University of California IPM: clothes moths
Clothes Moths — University of Maryland Extension

identification: Compound leaves bear several pairs of leaflets; terminal clusters hold yellow flowers with unequal petals. Long, hanging, cylindrical or slightly flattened pods turn dark. Photograph a whole compound leaf, the flower cluster and a mature pod. Several commonly planted sennas have yellow flowers, so the number and shape of leaflets and the long pod are useful comparisons. A tree's ornamental setting does not exclude seedlings spreading into adjacent forest gaps.
actions: Where it is invasive, identify and remove small seedlings before seed set, contain pods, and monitor regrowth. Survey the area beyond the parent tree before beginning work in an invaded site, and record both small seedlings and established stems. Collect seed-bearing pods without scattering their contents. Where an established stand is being removed, plan repeated checks and recovery of suitable forest vegetation with the local land manager. Management needs to reflect the documented regional invasion and the condition of the particular habitat.

sources.label: Reproductive biology of Senna spectabilis — Journal of Threatened Taxa

identification: A woody shrub with alternate, long-stalked leaves divided into narrow lobes, milky sap and thickened storage roots. Do not taste plant material to confirm identification. Look at the point where the long leaf stalk meets the deeply divided blade and include the alternating leaf arrangement. The storage roots belong below ground and do not need to be exposed simply to take an identification photograph. Other ornamental spurges can share milky sap, so sap alone proves little.
actions: Keep discarded stem cuttings out of natural areas and waterways. Use established food-safety guidance for processing cultivated cassava; do not eat raw roots or leaves. For an unexpected stand, record whether it is an active crop, an abandoned planting or growth beside discarded stems. Clear discarded stem sections from places where they could take root unintentionally. Keep children and animals away from raw harvested material awaiting processing. For unfamiliar volunteer plants, confirm the species before cultivation or harvest; the shape of a swollen root does not establish that it is a safe food crop.

identification: Large, glossy leaves have pointed lobes and toothed edges. Flower spikes bear petal-less flowers; rounded, spiny capsules contain smooth mottled seeds. Leaf and stem colors range from green to reddish purple. Photograph the attachment of the leaf stalk and the cluster of developing capsules from a safe distance. The mottled seeds should be recognized from reliable photographs rather than collected or handled to complete the identification.
actions: Avoid touching or collecting seeds. Wear gloves for necessary handling, prevent capsules from maturing, and obtain local disposal advice for unwanted plants. Keep children, pets and livestock away. Before working on a plant with mature capsules, arrange containment and disposal so seeds are not scattered onto accessible ground. Check the surrounding area for new seedlings after the main plant is removed. Where a tall specimen stands near a path, use an approach suited to its size and protect people from falling material. Do not leave cut capsules where children or animals can investigate them.

identification: Look for opposite leaves with two leaflets and a three-pronged, claw-like tendril, large yellow trumpet flowers and long flat capsules. Native crossvine has reddish-orange flowers; jessamines lack these claw tendrils. Examine a shoot tip to see the small hooked tendril between the paired leaflets. This is more informative than the yellow flower color alone. Young creeping stems can be inconspicuous beneath a larger climbing vine, and a visible canopy tangle may connect to several rooting points below.
actions: Remove small seedlings with their underground tubers where feasible, contain fragments and seed capsules, and revisit for regrowth. Trace ground-level growth before cutting so the extent of the infestation is clear. Keep tubers and stem fragments together during cleanup and prevent them from washing downstream. Avoid wrenching tangled vines from a tree where branches could fall. After planned treatment, check both the original rooting points and nearby bare ground for new growth, while retaining the native plants needed for recovery.

identification: Smooth fleshy leaves have scalloped margins; upper leaves commonly divide into several oval leaflets. Look for small marginal plantlets and hanging bell-shaped flowers. Bryophyllum pinnatum is a widely used synonym. A fallen leaf with miniature plants at its notches is a useful clue, but other kalanchoes also make plantlets. Photograph the broad leaflet shape and the hanging flowers to strengthen the identification.
actions: Collect dropped leaves and plantlets when containing or removing it, and keep garden waste out of natural areas. Keep plants and trimmings away from grazing animals; do not use them as food or home remedies. Use a tray or other containment when moving a potted plant so fallen leaves are not left along the route. Inspect the ground beneath the pot and nearby cracks for small rooted plants. When an outdoor patch is locally unwanted, remove loose leaves as well as the standing stems and revisit the site. Keep collected material secure until appropriate disposal rather than passing it on as unidentified cuttings.

sources.label: Mother of millions: resurrection plant comparison — NSW WeedWise

identification: Opposite, softly hairy, triangular to oval leaves have coarse teeth and heart-shaped bases. Square stems carry crowded clusters of small two-lipped, whitish flowers with pink or purple markings. The softly hairy leaf surface and broad, toothed blades help compare it with ornamental catmints that have different flower colors or finer foliage. Scent is a supporting feature, not a substitute for those characters.
actions: To contain garden plants, remove spent flower stems before seeds mature or grow them in containers. Identify volunteer seedlings before removing them and avoid confusing catnip with other ornamental catmints. Check around the base of a garden plant for volunteers before they blend into neighboring herbs. If keeping the planting, allow room for its mature growth and use well-drained soil. Remove unwanted seedlings while their identity is clear, and leave other flowering plants undisturbed. A contained, managed planting can still provide flowers for visiting insects without allowing seed to spread throughout the bed.

identification: Look for dense perennial clumps, mostly hairless leaf blades with a few long hairs at their bases, and a branched panicle whose central axis exceeds its branches. Mature spikelets may be needed for expert confirmation. Examine an intact flowering stem rather than a mown tuft. The plant is densely tufted rather than a lawn of creeping runners, and its numerous fine branches give the flowering head a more open outline than the compact spikes of some familiar pasture grasses.
actions: Photograph mature seed heads, leaf bases and the whole clump. Work from clean ground toward the affected patch so that clothing and machinery do not carry mature seed into uninfested prairie. Mark the clumps and revisit them while flowering heads are present; a specialist can then compare the spikelets with other Bothriochloa and native bluestems. Base any larger control project on that confirmed identification.

sources.label: Rangeland and Pasture Grasses of Kansas — K-State Research and Extension

identification: Look for a low, spreading mat with fleshy, toothed leaves arranged in paired rows and small star-shaped flowers. Cultivars vary considerably in leaf and flower color; rooting stems are a useful shared feature. Needle-leaved stonecrops can make similar low mats but have very different foliage. Flowering shoots stand a little above the leafy carpet. Red or bronze winter foliage can belong to a named cultivar, so color alone is unreliable.
actions: Keep creeping stems within the intended planting area and collect cuttings rather than dumping them outdoors. Check local guidance before planting beside natural rock outcrops or other sensitive habitat. Inspect the edge of a planting for stems rooting beyond the bed, especially where it meets open rocky ground. Lift unwanted rooted pieces with their attached stems and collect loose fragments. Retain labels when plants were purchased as Sedum spurium; that older name can help resolve a nursery identification without implying a different species.

identification: Opposite, toothed oval leaves have prominent veins and a wrinkled surface. Slender curved spikes bear small blue-purple, occasionally white flowers in succession; mature fruits sit in pits along the spike. Young stems can be four-sided and green or purple before becoming woody. Photograph both leaf surfaces, a whole spike, and the plant's height. Upright shrub growth and strongly textured leaves help with comparison, but flower color alone will not separate this plant from native porterweeds or cultivated selections.
actions: Confirm the species before removal, especially where native porterweeds occur. In unwanted patches, remove plants with their larger roots, contain seed-bearing spikes, clean equipment and check for seedlings. Check disturbed soil around a confirmed unwanted plant after removal, because small seedlings are easier to address than woody shrubs. Keep removed flower spikes contained and avoid moving soil from a seeding patch into clean ground. Where it is intentionally grown, watch the surrounding area for self-sown plants and choose locally appropriate replacements if it is escaping.

identification: Look for irregular light-and-dark leaf mosaics, yellow flecks, vein banding, wrinkling or reduced growth on susceptible plants. These signs are not diagnostic, and symptomless Brugmansia can carry the virus. Check new and older leaves on the same plant, noting whether mottling is accompanied by puckering or smaller growth. Record which Brugmansia varieties are affected and whether cuttings came from a shared parent. Those observations help a laboratory choose samples; they cannot distinguish this virus from another virus or a mixed infection.
actions: Stop sharing or propagating suspect plants and contact a plant diagnostic laboratory. Use tested healthy stock for propagation, prevent sap transfer between plants, and follow diagnostic advice for removing confirmed infected stock. Keep the suspect plant's label and propagation history with your photographs. Separate it from plants being prepared for sale or exchange, and ask the laboratory how to package material before sending anything. Clean propagation tools between plants using its recommended procedure. A plant that looks better later should not automatically be treated as virus-free propagation stock.

sources.label: Colombian datura virus pest rating proposal — CDFA
First Report of Colombian datura virus in Brugmansia in Canada — Rott et al.

identification: Twice-divided leaves have several pairs of branches carrying lance-shaped leaflets commonly 2-5 cm long. Look for pale spherical flower heads, flat pods, and dark, deeply fissured bark at the base of mature trees. The leaflets are much larger than those of many finely feathery wattles: each is a small lance-shaped blade, rather than a tiny dot along the leaf branch. Include a complete divided leaf and a ruler in photographs. Pale flower balls and mature flat pods provide useful additional checks.
actions: Record leaflets, pods and the planting context. Outside its native range, monitor nearby bushland for seedlings and seek local management advice; arrange professional assessment before removing large trees. Distinguish seedlings beyond a planting from the planted parent, and map their distance from the garden edge. If local advice calls for removal, deal with manageable seedlings before they become trees and continue checking beneath nearby vegetation. Do not cut a mature tree simply because it is an acacia; native status, ownership, safety and exact identity all matter.

sources.label: SAPIA News 8: alien Acacia identification key

identification: Look for clusters of four-petaled yellow flowers, lobed leaves, and long, slender seed capsules. Do not deliberately expose skin to the sap. The four broad petals and narrow upright capsules are especially useful together. Lesser celandine has glossy, less divided leaves and more numerous petals, so the similar common names are misleading. A flowering stem and an attached seed capsule make better photographs than a single yellow flower.
actions: Wear gloves when removing small unwanted plants, and work before they set seed. Recheck the area for seedlings. Keep sap off skin and eyes and collect removed flowering or fruiting stems rather than leaving them on disturbed ground. In a mixed woodland edge, identify neighboring plants before digging. Follow the original patch through the next growing period and remove only confirmed unwanted seedlings; one clearance does not show that the soil is free of seed.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online: Chelidonium majus

identification: Long, thin legs and an inverted position in an irregular web suggest a cellar spider. The familiar Pholcus phalangioides and other pholcids can occupy the same sorts of sheltered spaces. Photograph the body from more than one angle without pulling the legs, and include a scale if possible. Adult anatomical details are needed for a reliable species determination.
actions: Photograph the spider and its web if documenting a sighting. Seek identification before treating a familiar house spider as this species. Leave an undisturbed spider in place when it is not causing a practical problem. If a web must be cleared, ordinary household cleaning is a more proportionate response than treating every room with insecticide. For a distribution record, retain the location, date and building context and ask a local arachnologist whether photographs or a specimen are needed.

sources.label: USDA Forest Service: Spiders of Milbridge, Maine

identification: Look for light-green blades alternating along creeping runners and a slender, single seed spike. St. Augustinegrass has opposite leaves. Examine an unmown runner with several attached leaves. The blades have blunt or rounded tips, and fine hairs occur near the collar where blade and sheath meet. A single upright seed spike is useful when present, but frequent mowing can remove it before it is noticed.
actions: Keep planted turf within its intended area. For unwanted patches, confirm the grass before selecting a removal method with local extension advice. Trace runners at the lawn boundary rather than assuming every pale patch is the same grass. Where containment is needed, remove encroaching runners from the adjoining bed and check for rooted pieces. Ask for a turf identification before changing fertilizer or irrigation, since centipedegrass has different needs from other lawn grasses and extra fertilizer is not a remedy for every pale lawn.

sources.label: UF/IFAS: Identification of Common Florida Lawn Grasses

identification: Compare young and mature leaves and look for clasping aerial roots. Deeply divided mature leaves differ from the simpler juvenile foliage. Follow one stem from its smaller leaves to the higher, mature foliage if this can be done safely. The divided adult leaf can look unlike the juvenile plant below it. Golden pothos and other climbing aroids also change with age, so neither a houseplant label nor one detached leaf is sufficient.
actions: Keep cultivated vines contained and do not discard living cuttings in natural areas. Photograph several growth stages for identification. In warm outdoor settings, check where stems contact soil or climb into neighboring vegetation. Keep trimmings together and use a disposal route that prevents living nodes from rooting elsewhere. Do not climb trees to collect mature leaves: a photograph from the ground can document the growth stages while a local botanist advises on identity and appropriate containment.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online: Epipremnum pinnatum

identification: Identification requires microscopy of the circular valve, pore arrangement, and specialized structures. Specialists compare coarse polygonal pores, the arrangement of pore rows, and details around the valve margin; small size alone does not securely identify the named form. Ordinary photographs of a pond cannot show these features. The freshwater form has been discussed under the spelling subsalsa, so retain the name originally attached to a sample as well as any later determination.
actions: Have a qualified diatom specialist examine samples. Record sampling details; do not attempt species-specific treatment based on water appearance. For a useful record, note the sampling date, water depth and whether the material came from living plankton or sediment. Preserve and label samples only as directed by the receiving laboratory. Do not add algicides or disturb sediment to address an unconfirmed identification; water-quality concerns need their own assessment, separate from the presence of this diatom.

sources.label: Diatoms of North America: Actinocyclus normanii
USGS Great Lakes: Actinocyclus normanii form account

identification: Specialists look for very small cylindrical cells joined in chains by marginal structures. Reliable identification may require detailed microscopy. The small cells may appear singly or in short chains, with delicate connecting structures near their edges. Those structures and the shape of the silica walls matter more than the general appearance of a chain. Other small centric diatoms can be mistaken for it, especially in routine low-resolution counts.
actions: Document the waterbody and sampling conditions and seek specialist confirmation. Avoid transporting untreated water or wet equipment between waterbodies. Keep any microscope images linked to the sample location and collection method. A specialist may request higher-resolution imaging or an additional sample rather than accepting an identification from one indistinct cell. Drain and clean field gear before moving between sites, following local aquatic biosecurity guidance; a record of this species alone is not a reason to treat a waterbody.

sources.label: USGS Great Lakes account: Skeletonema potamos
Duleba and colleagues: Skeletonema potamos in the River Danube

identification: Stunting and poor patches are warning signs, not a diagnosis. Root and soil samples need laboratory examination to distinguish related cyst nematodes. Compare weak patches with healthier plants of the same crop and growth stage. Small pale females or brown cysts on roots may support suspicion, but related cereal cyst nematodes can look similar. A laboratory needs the roots and surrounding soil, not just a photograph of yellow leaves.
actions: Use confirmed species identity to guide crop rotation and resistant-variety choices. Ask about sample timing before digging, and keep samples from affected and comparison areas clearly labeled. Avoid carrying adhering soil on machinery from a confirmed infested field into clean fields. Discuss rotations and suitable resistant cultivars with an agronomist after identification, because host response and effective resistance can differ between nematode species and local populations.

sources.label: PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Wheat cereal cyst nematodes, March 2026

identification: Look for blue-winged, orange-thoraxed adults and waste-coated larvae feeding along leaves. Similar Oulema beetles may need expert separation. Larvae feed in narrow tracks that leave pale strips in the leaf, and their dark coating can make them resemble small slugs. Turn leaves gently to look for eggs and feeding stages. Adult color is suggestive, but closely related Oulema species can require examination of reproductive structures.
actions: Preserve beneficial insects rather than spraying automatically after a single sighting. Record how many stems or leaves were checked and the crop's growth stage rather than reporting only the worst damaged leaf. Revisit the field to see whether larvae are still feeding and whether natural enemies are present. Use current local crop thresholds to decide whether any intervention is justified; isolated adults do not establish an economically damaging infestation.

sources.label: Utah State University Extension: Cereal Leaf Beetle

identification: Confirm the whole plant rather than relying on the name rye. Examine a mature head as well as the leaf blade. Rye carries its spikelets directly along a central axis, producing a dense grain head with long bristles, rather than a loose branching spray. Young plants without heads can be difficult to separate from other cereal crops and volunteer grasses.
actions: Where rye is unwanted, document whether it is planted or growing independently. Ask local extension about preventing further seed production. Check the sowing history before calling a patch an escape, particularly in cover-cropped fields and gardens. If volunteers are unwanted, address them before grain matures and inspect field margins afterward. For intentional cover crops, plan termination with the next crop and soil protection in mind; removing all green cover immediately may defeat the reason rye was planted.

identification: Look for leaves arranged in two ranks, pale flowers with prominent yellow-orange anthers, and shiny blue berries. The flowers and fruit sit on a branching stalk, unlike a grass seed head, and the blue fruits are berries rather than dry grains. Several other Dianella are cultivated and can look similar when sterile. Photograph the base, leaf arrangement and a flowering or fruiting stalk together.
actions: In Florida, follow UF/IFAS advice against its use. Elsewhere, check local guidance before planting and prevent unwanted fruit or rhizome spread. Do not use the blue berries as a taste test, and keep removed fruit out of areas where it can be spread. When local guidance calls for removal, account for the underground rhizomes and revisit for shoots rather than simply trimming the foliage. Confirm the species before replacing a planting sold under the broad nursery name flaxlily.

identification: Mosaic-patterned leaves and abnormal fruit can suggest a virus, but laboratory testing is needed to distinguish CGMMV from other problems. Compare symptoms across the same crop and note when they first appeared, particularly after transplanting, pruning or harvest work. A normal-looking plant may still carry infection. Fruit symptoms can differ from leaf symptoms, and a mosaic pattern does not reveal which virus is present.
actions: Pause movement of suspect plants and contact a plant diagnostic laboratory or extension service. Follow their sampling and disinfection instructions. Keep seed lot labels and transplant records so a confirmed problem can be traced. Avoid sharing seedlings, tools or harvested plant material from a suspect area until you receive advice. Ask the laboratory what tissue it needs and how to package it. Use tested planting material and a crop-specific hygiene plan rather than relying on insect control alone.

sources.label: USDA APHIS: Cucumber Green Mottle Mosaic Virus
Agriculture Victoria: Cucumber green mottle mosaic virus

identification: Turn a leafy side branch over to find the small round capsules beneath it. The neatly paired-looking blades are simple leaves on a branch, not leaflets of one compound leaf. The close-fitting fruits help distinguish it from long-stalked chamberbitter, whose fruits hang on more obvious little stalks.
actions: Check nursery containers before bringing them into beds, and pull young unwanted plants while their roots are still manageable. Return often during warm weather, since small plants can already be producing seeds. Maintain suitable mulch in planted beds and correct unnecessary irrigation where practical. Mowing a lawn alone may leave this low-growing annual able to flower and reseed. When pulling, hold the stem near the soil so the young plant comes away with its root; avoid shaking ripe capsules into the bed.

identification: Look for heart-shaped leaves and a short flower spike surrounded by four white bracts. Leaf coloration varies among garden forms. Look beneath nearby vegetation for plain green shoots as well as the brightly variegated garden form. Heart-shaped leaves alone are shared by many plants; the short central flower spike and surrounding white bracts are better clues. Avoid assuming a patch has disappeared just because its leaves die back seasonally.
actions: Avoid planting it beside natural wetlands. Where removing a patch, collect creeping stems carefully and monitor for regrowth rather than only clipping leaves. Trace shoots beyond the obvious patch before starting work, and avoid scattering rhizome pieces through soil cultivation. A container can help keep an intentional planting manageable, but check any drainage openings and surrounding ground. If removing it from a mixed bed, work carefully around neighboring roots and plan repeated checks for fresh shoots rather than expecting one digging to finish the job.

identification: Look for slender, grooved leaves with a few teeth and plantlets near their tips. Related mother-of-millions hybrids have broader leaves. Inspect the end of a leaf for small developing plantlets and the narrow, almost cylindrical leaf shape. Broader, boat-shaped leaves suggest a related species or hybrid. Hanging flowers may be absent on young plants, while fallen plantlets can already be taking root around the parent.
actions: Keep animals away from the plant and collect fallen plantlets when removing it. Follow local disposal guidance; do not dump living material outdoors. Before lifting an unwanted plant, gather the small offspring scattered beneath it and keep them with the parent material. Do not mow through a patch and spread succulent fragments. In grazing areas, arrange removal and disposal so livestock cannot reach the cut plants. Revisit nearby cracks, bare ground and pot edges for new plants after the larger stems have gone.

identification: Look for different flower colors on one cluster, small five-lobed corollas, and hooked hairs on the calyx. A hand lens helps. Compare newly opened and older flowers on the same stem, rather than flowers from separate plants. The tiny corollas are only a few millimeters across, and the curved cluster lengthens as fruits develop. Hooked calyx hairs are useful under magnification when distinguishing it from other small annual forget-me-nots.
actions: Include a close photograph of the calyx and a wider view of the leaves and branching stem. If it is an unwanted garden annual, remove confirmed plants before their nutlets are dispersed and check the same open soil for seedlings. In natural vegetation, seek local identification first; being an introduced forget-me-not does not by itself establish serious ecological damage.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Myosotis discolor

identification: Photograph the shell, grooves, and egg mass without moving them. Expert examination may be needed to separate it from other introduced apple snails. Record whether eggs are attached above the water on stems or hard surfaces, and photograph the shell opening as well as its outer coils if already visible. Similar apple snails can vary in shell color, size and grooves. Do not rely on the label golden apple snail, which has been used for more than one species.
actions: Do not release aquarium snails or move snails, eggs, or contaminated plants between sites. Ask local aquatic or agricultural authorities about suspected populations. Leave animals and eggs at the site while obtaining advice rather than transporting them for a casual identification. Check aquatic plants and equipment before moving them, and never empty aquarium water or unwanted pets into a ditch or pond. Where a crop is affected, use the local agricultural response plan and protect native snails from indiscriminate collection.
If an authorized response requires handling snails, wear gloves and wash your hands afterward.

sources.label: EPPO Global Database: Pomacea canaliculata datasheet
Levin and colleagues: Apple snails in Hawaii

identification: Look for four yellow petals, rough or hairy foliage, and elongated pods. Other yellow-flowered mustards can be very similar. Examine lower and upper leaves together: their shape can change along the stem. Developing pods and their terminal beaks are more useful for distinguishing mustard species than the yellow flowers alone. Photograph a flower cluster with attached pods, and include the stem hairs and leaf attachment in close views.
actions: In crop fields, use local weed-management advice and monitor for later seedlings. Pull small confirmed plants when the ground allows roots to come free, before the pods become dry and shatter. Keep seed-bearing material contained if maturity has already been reached. In a field, combine timely control with crop competition and attention to seed return. Recheck disturbed patches after later germination rather than assuming all plants emerged at once.

identification: Look for a relatively smooth, thin shell with a purple interior. Native and other introduced mussels require expert comparison. Include the whole attached group and the substrate in a sighting photograph. Color alone is unreliable because shells vary with age and condition, and crowded growth can obscure their outlines. A specialist may need an empty shell or an authorized specimen to examine interior features without confusing it with native mussels.
actions: Photograph suspect mussels in place and report unfamiliar fouling to local marine-resource staff. Avoid moving live mussels or fouled equipment between waters. Keep boats, ropes and aquaculture gear from transferring attached mussels to another estuary. Follow the harbor or farm's approved cleaning procedure, capturing removed fouling where required rather than washing living material into new water. Note approximate patch size and whether it is on natural habitat or equipment; repeated observations can show change without presuming an ecological effect.

sources.label: Wells and colleagues: Charru mussel in the upper Gulf of Thailand

identification: Look for tendrils holding the vine to its support, rough cucumber-like foliage and the characteristic single-seeded fruit. Fruits may be smooth or prickly, so prickles alone do not distinguish another species. Photograph the vine's flowers and attachment points when immature plants have no fruit to compare. The fruit is fleshy and broadly pear-shaped rather than a long cucumber, though size and surface ridges vary among cultivated forms.
actions: Keep cultivated vines on suitable supports and within the growing area. Document escaped growth separately from deliberately planted crops. Inspect beyond the trellis for shoots entering neighboring vegetation and guide or prune garden growth back into the allotted space. Collect unwanted fruits and living trimmings rather than dumping them beside waterways. When documenting a possible escape, record any nearby garden source and whether the plant persists independently; a planted food crop is not automatically an invasive population.

sources.label: Indian Institute of Science: Sechium edule

identification: Look for soft hairs on the leaves and sheaths, a prominent membranous ligule, and nodding seed heads with long awns. Follow the seasonal change from soft green growth to reddish or straw-colored seed heads. The loose, drooping branches and long awns help separate it from grasses with compact upright heads. Other annual bromes can resemble it, so include the leaf sheath, ligule and mature spikelets in identification photographs.
actions: Clean seeds from boots and equipment. For established patches, plan control before seed maturity and pair it with recovery of suitable perennial cover. Remove clinging awns before leaving an infested site, especially from footwear, pet fur and field gear. Small unwanted plants are easier to handle before their seeds harden and detach. In larger areas, avoid leaving bare soil as the only outcome of treatment: coordinate follow-up and appropriate revegetation with local rangeland or restoration staff.

sources.label: Montana State Extension: Cheatgrass identification, biology and integrated management

identification: Rounded scalloped leaves; tiny white to pale mauve flowers; wrinkled, wheel-shaped fruits distinguish it from common mallow. Check flowers and mature fruit rather than identifying every round-leaved seedling as cheeseweed. The very short pale petals and rough, segmented fruit are useful distinctions from other mallows. Leaves have radiating veins and long stalks, while stems may spread along the ground or grow upright.
actions: Pull or hoe seedlings while small, removing the taproot before seeds develop. Mowing alone often leaves live buds. Work after soil has softened enough to release the root, and collect plants with developing fruits before the seeds scatter. Inspect newly disturbed soil and the edges of irrigated beds for fresh seedlings. If a plant has become woody, avoid repeatedly cutting only the top and leaving the crown to regrow; choose a method suited to the site and nearby desirable plants.

identification: Glossy three-part leaves, hooked prickles, large single white flowers and bristly hips. Count the leaflets on several leaves and look for the glossy surface rather than relying on a single rose flower. The large solitary blooms and bristly, pear-shaped hips help separate it from many roses with clustered small flowers. Native climbing roses should be compared carefully before any removal.
actions: Wear sturdy gloves around the canes. Avoid new planting in regions where it spreads aggressively. Inspect the outer canes where they reach surrounding shrubs, and keep an intentional planting from growing into adjacent natural vegetation. Wear eye protection and protective clothing when handling thorny stems. For a large unwanted thicket, get local advice on staged removal and regrowth checks, especially where pulling canes could damage trees or disturb nesting wildlife.

identification: Brownish forewings patterned with orange and metallic markings; pale larvae beneath loose or cracked bark. Look for damage at bark cracks and wounds, including the lower trunk, rather than assuming a leaf-chewing caterpillar is responsible. Fine orange and metallic markings on the adult's brown forewings can be hard to interpret in a blurred photograph. Other bark borers and diseases can produce gum or dieback.
actions: Photograph the trunk damage and contact an extension diagnostician. Avoid moving infested nursery trees or bark to new sites. Keep the host tree's identity, planting date and source with photographs of the whole trunk and close views of damaged bark. Avoid peeling away extensive bark to search for larvae, which adds injury. A diagnostic service can advise whether an adult, larva or bark sample is needed and whether neighboring host trees should also be inspected.

identification: Thick evergreen leaves with glands underneath near the midrib; upright white flower clusters and purple-black fruits. Turn an attached leaf over to photograph the small glands near its base. Its broad leathery leaves can resemble some hollies and other cherry laurels, so compare the leaf glands, edges and fruit as well as flowers. Hedge pruning may remove flowers and fruit, so document an untrimmed shoot if one is available.
actions: Dig small plants when soil is moist and watch for seedlings. Plan follow-up for cut stumps; keep foliage and fruit away from people or animals that might eat them. Inspect beneath bird perches and along woodland edges for young plants outside the hedge. If removal leaves exposed soil, stabilize and replant it with locally suitable vegetation rather than allowing another weed patch to form. Large rooted plants on slopes need a careful plan; repeated monitoring for stump shoots and seedlings is part of management, not evidence that initial identification was wrong.

identification: Finely toothed oval leaves, five-petaled spring flowers and small rounded plums; leaf color varies by cultivar. Flowers commonly occur singly or in small groups, and the finely serrated leaves may be green even near a purple-leaved garden parent. Include a short leafy twig and any fruit in photographs. Other ornamental plums and hybrids can be difficult to separate without these details.
actions: Photograph flowers, leaves and fruit together for identification. Check nearby uncultivated ground for volunteer seedlings before allowing a planting to spread.
