Check whether small shoots are seedlings or attached to a planted tree before digging near its roots. Where volunteers are unwanted, remove them while manageable and revisit after fruiting seasons. Have large trees assessed by a qualified arborist if removal is being considered; a garden specimen's color or ornamental origin alone does not establish a need to fell it.

identification: Chestnut bark cankers, orange fungal structures, persistent wilted leaves above damage and new shoots below it; laboratory diagnosis separates look-alike diseases. Check the relationship between the canker and the dead leaves above it, and photograph any shoots below the damaged section. Orange structures can be minute and may not always be visible. Root diseases and other chestnut cankers can also cause crown decline, so the tree's full condition matters.
actions: Ask an extension or tree-health service to assess suspected cankers. Do not move suspect chestnut bark, wood or nursery plants. Keep a record of the tree's species and whether it is a planted hybrid or a naturally occurring chestnut. Do not strip bark to expose a suspected infection without diagnostic instructions. If branches or trees must be removed, ask how to handle the wood locally and arrange work safely; apparent recovery or sprouting does not establish that the fungus has gone.

identification: Brown or pale chalky decay inside chestnut kernels; shoot cankers may occur, but testing is needed to identify the fungus. Photograph the outside and a cut surface of affected nuts, keeping track of which tree or stored lot they came from. Similar decay can have different causes, and a healthy-looking shell does not guarantee a healthy kernel. Twig cankers also overlap in appearance with chestnut blight and other diseases.
actions: Set aside representative affected nuts and ask a plant diagnostic laboratory for sampling instructions before moving nursery or grafting material. Keep suspect lots separate while asking for diagnosis, and record harvest and storage conditions for the laboratory. Do not select grafting wood from a tree solely because its foliage looks normal. A confirmed result can guide nursery hygiene and orchard decisions; applying a home remedy to the shell will not demonstrate that an internal infection has been eliminated.

identification: Soft or spongy stems, simple narrow leaves and dense cylindrical spikes of very small white flowers. Examine the smooth fleshy stem and the tightly packed terminal spike together. The light-green leaves are arranged singly around the stem, and the lowest stem may show spongy tissue associated with wet ground. A dense white flower spike alone can resemble unrelated wetland herbs, so include leaves and stem in photographs.
actions: Photograph the whole plant and flower spike without carrying wet soil or seed-bearing material between fields. In cultivated ground, identify young plants before they set capsules and coordinate weed work with the crop's water management. Keep muddy boots and tools from carrying material into a clean field. In natural wetlands, seek local guidance before pulling plants or altering water levels; its rice-weed reputation does not justify disturbing an entire wetland community.

identification: Many paired leaflets, pale pea flowers and inflated pods that turn black at maturity. Each divided leaf has many small leaflets, and the swollen mature pods provide a useful check beyond the pale flower color. Other milkvetches and locoweeds should not be judged interchangeable from a common name. Photograph flowers, leaves and pods on the same plant when possible.
actions: Confirm identification before treating a forage stand. Monitor the edges of plantings for seedling or underground-shoot spread. Keep the seed label and cultivar information for an intentional forage planting, and discuss any unexpected spread with the land manager. Inspect adjoining ground for new plants and avoid moving mature pods with equipment. Do not transfer the documented forage use of cicer milkvetch to an unidentified Astragalus; accurate species identification matters before making grazing or removal decisions.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online

identification: Blue, strap-flowered heads along wiry stems; dandelion-like basal leaves and smaller leaves clasping the upper stems. Inspect a flower head closely: the blue strap-shaped florets have toothed ends and there is no yellow central disk. Visit in the morning if flowers were closed on an afternoon walk. A basal rosette by itself is easy to confuse with dandelions and other members of the daisy family.
actions: Confirm the plant before removing garden volunteers. Where unwanted, prevent seed production and remove the root rather than only clipping the flower stalk. If you want to keep a garden plant, manage its seed heads before they spread into unwanted places. When removing it, collect root fragments as well as the crown because pieces can regrow. Distinguish cultivated leaf or root crops from roadside volunteers, and do not use plants from a roadside or uncertain identification for food.

identification: Narrow leaves, hairy stems, yellow flowers aging reddish and elongated capsules; confirm against other evening primroses. Photograph both an open flower and one beginning to fade, since the changing color is informative. Narrow rosette leaves may already be gone when the stem flowers, so a later visit can reveal a different-looking plant. The long tube below the flower and upright capsules help separate it from other evening primroses.
actions: If an unwanted garden escape is confirmed, remove it before capsules mature and keep seed-bearing waste contained. If a rosette cannot be identified confidently, mark it and return during flowering instead of clearing all similar plants. In a confirmed unwanted patch, work before dry capsules shed seeds and check disturbed soil for the next generation. Keep local flowering season in mind rather than applying Southern Hemisphere dates directly to a North American observation.

identification: Huge toothed leaves, prickly stalks, large rhizome buds and conical flower spikes; compare garden hybrids before naming a plant. Look at the entire clump and flower spikes as well as a leaf. Giant garden gunneras have often been sold under names that do not match current identifications, particularly the hybrid Gunnera x cryptica. Winter buds and old leaf stalks can reveal a dormant clump even when the large leaves are absent.
actions: Prevent garden plants from spreading and use an approved local disposal route for unwanted crowns or rhizomes. Seek advice before disturbing waterside colonies. Do not divide and share an unwanted clump as a way of disposing of it. Keep rhizome fragments and seed-bearing flower stalks together, and avoid moving contaminated soil to another wet site. Large colonies beside water need a plan that protects the bank and neighboring plants, including follow-up for regrowth rather than only removal of the visible foliage.

sources.label: Northern Ireland Environment Agency species account

identification: Narrow entire leaves, tubular yellow-green flowers, black berries and brittle green young stems. Include both flowers and fruit when possible: other Cestrum species have similar leaves but different flower colors or fruit characters. The tubular yellow-green flowers and dark berries together are better clues than a narrow shiny leaf alone. There is no need to crush or taste foliage to test its identity.
actions: Keep livestock away from plants and cut foliage. Wear gloves, contain removed material and obtain local weed-control advice for established shrubs. Arrange a barrier around a suspect patch where animals could browse it, including any piles of cut branches. Handle removal so that berries and roots are not scattered onto clean ground or into waterways. Revisit confirmed sites for seedlings or shoots and use professional help for large shrubs; discarded foliage should not be left accessible simply because it is no longer growing.

identification: A brown recluse-like spider; color and a violin marking alone cannot establish this species. Expert examination may be necessary. A useful photograph shows the body and leg arrangement from above without approaching closely enough to touch it. Several unrelated brown house spiders are routinely mistaken for recluses. A specialist may need adult reproductive structures to separate this species from other Loxosceles, so a violin-like patch is only one clue.
actions: Avoid handling it bare-handed. Photograph it safely and seek identification from an entomologist or qualified pest professional. Keep hands out of unseen storage spaces and use gloves when sorting undisturbed boxes or debris. Reduce clutter where spiders have been confirmed and ask a qualified professional about targeted inspection. Do not infer this spider's presence from a skin mark or remove every brown spider in the building; identification of an actual specimen is the starting point.

identification: Large twice-divided leaves with toothed leaflets, lavender flowers and persistent yellow fruits. Look at the whole divided leaf, not just one toothed leaflet, and compare the hanging fruit clusters after leaf fall. The small lilac flowers have a darker central tube. Other trees can have similarly divided foliage, so photographs of the leaf structure and fruit are especially useful together.
actions: Avoid planting where invasive. Keep children and livestock away from fallen fruits and seek a local management plan for unwanted trees. Check below the canopy and along nearby disturbed edges for young plants before they grow into larger trees. Keep fruit-bearing branches contained during work and avoid leaving fallen fruit where animals can reach it. Where removal is appropriate, arrange safe tree work and planned regrowth checks; the need for management depends on local ecology and the tree's setting.

sources.label: Kew POWO: Melia azedarach accepted taxon and range

identification: Smooth gray bark, entire leathery leaves, small figs beside the leaves and dangling roots on larger trees. Inspect small figs near the leaf bases and photograph the leaf tip and veins, since several ornamental figs have smooth bark and aerial roots. The swollen exposed roots of a bonsai sold as Ginseng are a horticultural feature, not the shape every wild or landscape tree will show.
actions: Inspect nearby walls, trees and planting beds for seedlings. Keep unwanted rooted material out of natural areas and seek local advice before removing a large tree. Pay particular attention to small seedlings in masonry cracks or in the fork of another tree, where later removal can become difficult. Have an arborist assess roots near structures and large established trees. An indoor bonsai and an outdoor seed-producing tree present different containment questions, so record the growing conditions instead of treating all cultivated plants alike.

identification: Large heart-based, often three-lobed leaves; yellow flowers with purple markings; long slender capsules. Photograph flower color in natural light and include the branching flower cluster, because white-flowered native catalpas can have similarly large leaves and long capsules. Leaf lobes can vary, and garden hybrids further complicate a foliage-only identification. Old hanging capsules can remain useful clues after the leaves fall.
actions: Use flowers and capsules to distinguish it from native catalpas. Look for seedlings in open ground around an ornamental parent and confirm their identity before removing them. Avoid using a perceived leaf smell as the deciding test; that feature can be variable. If the tree is deliberately planted and contained, assess its actual behavior locally rather than assuming that every nonnative catalpa is displacing native vegetation.

identification: Stiff, sharp, lance-shaped leaves; small clustered cones; flaking brown-gray bark and drooping branch tips. Examine a twig from the side and underneath: the leaves are flattened but sharply pointed, with pale bands beneath, and the cones are relatively small. These details distinguish it from true firs and other conifers with softer or shorter foliage. Photograph naturally fallen material when reaching live branches would be unsafe.
actions: Handle pointed foliage carefully. Confirm seedlings or suspected escapes before deciding whether removal is appropriate locally. Keep pointed branches away from paths where people may brush against them. For a possible escape, document seedlings separately from the planted tree and include cones or a twig in the identification record. If browning is a concern, compare old interior foliage with new growth and ask an arborist to evaluate the tree rather than diagnosing disease from color alone.

identification: Look for stout spines, spoon-shaped leaves, white flower clusters and scarlet fruits, and confirm which taxonomic treatment is being used. Firethorns and their cultivars can share bright fruit colors, so a red berry cluster does not settle the name. Include close views of leaf tips, margins and the young shoots, plus a whole branch showing the thorns. A regional flora may use a narrower concept than a global checklist. A population study found the sampled leaf traits did not reliably separate the traditional species.
actions: Wear gloves around spines and photograph leaves, flowers and fruits. Resolve the name before applying a species-specific management claim. Keep the original nursery label and the exact identification supplied by a botanist alongside photographs. Where an unwanted thorny shrub is already spreading, contain its fruit and protect hands and eyes during handling while seeking local management advice. Do not transfer a regulatory or ecological claim from another firethorn merely because the two names appear together in a synonym list.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online: Pyracantha fortuneana
Feng et al.2021: multivariate Chinese Pyracantha taxonomy

identification: Large twice-compound leaves, yellow flower clusters and inflated three-sided papery capsules. Examine an entire leaf to see the second level of branching, rather than mistaking a leaflet for a leaf. The papery capsules look inflated and change color as they ripen. Other golden-rain trees can bear similar capsules, so leaves, flowers and fruit should be compared together.
actions: Confirm the subspecies when possible, and prevent unwanted seedlings around plantings. Prefer locally suitable alternatives where garden escapes are a concern. Check open soil around an ornamental tree and beneath places where capsules collect, and remove confirmed unwanted seedlings while small. Keep planting records or cultivar names when asking for identification of the Taiwanese form. Do not extrapolate Queensland weed behavior to every growing region; local climate, subspecies and actual escape records should guide decisions about an established tree.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online

identification: Alternate glossy leaves with toothed upper margins, smooth gray bark and small round orange-to-red fruits. Examine leaf margins near both the tip and base, since the teeth are concentrated toward the outer part of the blade. Native hackberries can look similar, particularly as seedlings. Include the leaf attachment, bark and small fruit in photographs rather than naming a tree from its crown shape alone.
actions: Check creek banks and disturbed ground near plantings for young trees. Confirm identification and use local control guidance before tackling a large stand. In a garden, separate deliberately planted trees from volunteers under bird perches or along drainage lines. Young confirmed unwanted plants can be addressed before their roots become substantial. Larger creekside stands need a coordinated plan that protects bank stability and restores suitable vegetation; Australian impacts do not establish the same degree of harm at every North American site.

identification: Curved red tubular flowers emerging through broad, round orange-red calyces; toothed oval leaves and scrambling woody stems. View a flower from the side to see the narrow curved tube passing through the wider saucer. The colored saucer is the calyx, which can remain noticeable after the corolla has faded. Flower shape and the plant's woody scrambling habit are more useful than a common name shared by unrelated ornamental plants.
actions: Keep garden growth within its intended space and dispose of unwanted rooted material responsibly. Confirm an apparent escape before reporting it. Keep the stems on their intended support and inspect where they extend into neighboring vegetation. Record any separate plants beyond the garden, including whether there is evidence of a former planting. Collect unwanted rooted cuttings rather than discarding them beside a hedge or watercourse. Local observations of spread are more informative than assuming every vigorous ornamental is invasive.

identification: Hairy gray-green leaves and branching sprays of small blue, pink or white forget-me-not-like flowers. The hairy leaves and bushy branching distinguish it from the delicate appearance of many Myosotis forget-me-nots, but flowers alone can mislead. Include the base of the plant and any developing fruits in photographs. White or pink flowers may be garden selections rather than a different species.
actions: Remove unwanted volunteers and seed-bearing stems before they spread. Do not confuse it with other hound's-tongue species when assessing local risk. Keep nursery labels and inspect the surrounding bed after plants have flowered, since self-sown seedlings may appear outside the original row. Collect unwanted seed-bearing stems instead of scattering them while tidying the garden. Before treating a large patch, confirm that it is this cultivated species rather than another Cynoglossum with a different local status or risk.

identification: Open branched seed heads and flattened, many-flowered spikelets that may mature purplish red. A grass specialist should compare the spikelets and leaf joints. Hold a mature head against a plain background to show the loose branches and flattened spikelets. Include a scale and a clear view of several intact spikelets, because a purple tinge occurs in other grasses too. A hand lens can help, but a regional key may require finer floral details.
actions: Photograph mature seed heads and leaf joints for a grass specialist. Avoid moving seed-bearing soil or cuttings while identification is unresolved. Keep a flowering specimen only if collection is permitted and a receiving specialist requests it, with seeds contained during transport. Note whether the grass is in a lawn, roadside, damp hollow or natural grassland. If it is a confirmed unwanted annual in a bed, prevent seed return while protecting adjacent grasses whose identity has not been established.

sources.label: Kew GrassBase and Flora of Oman

identification: Large mantis with a fairly square, vertically striped facial shield; rounded tan egg cases. Compare smaller native Carolina mantises carefully. Look at the face from a safe, close photographic angle and compare the body length with a visible reference. Young nymphs lack adult wings, so wing markings are unavailable at that stage. The round tan egg case is useful in winter, but an empty case does not show how many mantises remain nearby.
actions: Observe rather than release purchased egg cases outdoors. Confirm the species before removing an egg case, since native mantises occur alongside it. Preserve photographs and the twig location if an egg case needs identification. A mantis taking a pest insect is also capable of taking a pollinator, so purchased releases are not a selective pest-control method. In a mixed garden, avoid broad spraying prompted by one mantis sighting and seek local advice before disturbing egg cases that could belong to native species.

identification: Hairy claws with pale tips, a notch between the eyes and four spines along each side of the shell; very small juveniles have less hair. Include the top of the shell, the claws and the front edge between the eyes in photographs. Adult hairy claws are striking, but small juveniles can be overlooked because the hair is sparse. Other crabs may have hairy limbs, so the shell spines and notch must be considered together.
actions: Photograph the crab and exact location, keep it from returning to the water if safely contained, and contact the local aquatic invasive-species authority. Never move it alive to another waterbody. If a crab is already caught, prevent escape without handling its claws, and request local instructions for identification and disposal. Do not carry it to another stream or keep it as a live curiosity. Record whether it was found in fresh, brackish or tidal water; that context helps investigators interpret a sighting along its migratory route.

sources.label: California Department of Fish and Wildlife

identification: Rounded unbanded shell with strongly rounded whorls; hard operculum closes the opening. Shell alone may not resolve closely related mysterysnails. Photograph the opening with the shell point upward, showing the right-sided aperture and the closing plate if visible. Banded mysterysnails and native freshwater snails can be confused with it, and small individuals are especially difficult. Shell color may change with age, algae or weathering and should not decide identity.
actions: Never release aquarium snails or water outdoors. Remove attached organisms from equipment and report suspected new populations with photographs. Check plant baskets, boat recesses and other places where a snail could remain attached before moving equipment. Keep any aquarium disposal separate from storm drains and natural waters. For a new outdoor sighting, provide the waterbody, date and several photographs without transporting live animals. A washed-up empty shell and an established living population are different observations.

identification: An armored scale requiring slide-mounted examination; diagnostic body indentations and posterior structures separate close relatives. Photograph the host plant and the affected section of twig, but do not expect the external cover alone to distinguish the insect. Scale covers can remain after the occupant has died. A specialist examines the female's prepared body, including the posterior edge and pores, against closely related armored scales.
actions: Ask an extension diagnostician to examine infested twigs before treatment. Keep a suspect nursery plant separate from clean stock and retain its purchase or import information. Ask which twigs or leaves to submit and avoid scraping all the scales away before a sample is taken. Wait for confirmation of living pests and species identity before choosing treatment; a historical report on crabapple does not establish that every crust on an apple branch is this scale.

sources.label: Korean Journal of Applied Entomology import-interception study

identification: Smooth green bark, large heart-based leaves with three to five lobes, and open pod-like fruits carrying round seeds. Lobed leaves alone can resemble other large-leaved trees, but this combination is more distinctive. Young vigorous plants may have particularly large leaves, while winter observations can rely on the trunk and remaining fruit stalks.
actions: Check beneath and beyond mature trees for volunteers. Where invasive, choose a locally native shade tree and remove small seedlings before they establish. Inspect beyond the shaded area under the parent, including disturbed soil where seedlings have room to grow. Remove confirmed unwanted young trees before they develop larger roots, and recheck after seed fall. For a mature tree, discuss safe work and local ecological concerns with an arborist rather than treating the presence of green bark as a removal instruction.

identification: Evergreen narrow leaves, white flower clusters, red round fruits and initially hairy young shoots. Compare leaf margins and young shoots, because many evergreen shrubs have white flowers followed by red fruit. Its narrow leaves and initially hairy growth are useful alongside the flower clusters. Garden hybrids and other photinias can resemble it, so keep the nursery name when asking for an identification.
actions: Photograph flowers, fruit and leaf margins together to separate it from other photinias. Monitor unwanted seedlings near garden plantings. Watch the area beyond the planting for separate seedlings and record whether red-fruited shrubs were deliberately installed there. If unwanted volunteers are confirmed, remove them while small and check again after later fruiting seasons. Maintain an existing garden shrub according to its actual spread and local guidance; the alternative name Photinia davidiana is not evidence of a second invading species.

identification: Opposite small oval leaves, often with hairs beneath the midrib; white flower clusters and dark purple-black fruits. Examine an untrimmed twig for opposite leaf pairs and hairs on the underside of the midrib. Several other privets have white flowers and dark fruits, while some native shrubs resemble it when sterile. Leaf size, twig hair and fruit clusters should be considered together rather than relying on an old hedge label.
actions: Choose a locally native hedge instead. Plan repeated follow-up for established thickets and check surrounding ground for seedlings and suckers. Start by locating small satellite plants beyond the main thicket, including those under bird perches. Protect native seedlings during work and avoid leaving all cleared ground bare. Large shrubs and root systems need a site-specific plan, particularly beside streams. Revisit for shoots from surviving roots and for new seedlings instead of assuming a cut hedge has stopped supplying new growth.

identification: In the NSW account, plants have four-ribbed stems, opposite lower leaves and tiny eight-ribbed fruits. Subspecies determination requires mature fruit. The leaf pairs near the base can give way to alternate leaves higher on a stem. Mature fruit details are much more informative than the tiny flowers alone. In the Australian treatment, the location of hairs and surface bumps on the fruit helps separate the two subspecies.
actions: Photograph the whole plant, stem, leaves and mature fruits. Ask a herbarium to check the subspecies before recommending removal. For a useful observation, include a scale beside the tiny fruits and note whether the plant is in standing water, damp open soil or a disturbed margin. Do not generalize the appearance of the New South Wales subspecies to every Asian or Pacific plant. Leave native wetland vegetation intact while a specialist checks the specimen and its regional context.

identification: Plants about 20-45 cm tall; narrow toothed leaves and tiny ribbed, bumpy fruits with short curved hairs. Under magnification, the fruit is globular with glistening bumps between the ribs as well as on them. That pattern is more useful than simply noting that the fruit is rough. The other subspecies has hairs mainly along the ribs and can show a different fruit outline.
actions: Record mature fruit details and habitat without disturbing the wetland. Confirm local status and identity before control. Use close photographs or a specimen requested by a herbarium to document those small structures; a distant image of a damp patch will not settle the subspecies. Record whether the plant is within its native eastern Australian range or elsewhere. Do not clear a wetland patch based only on the catalog listing, and avoid carrying mud or fruiting stems between sites.

sources.label: Flora of Australia volume 18: Gonocarpus key

identification: Brown oval scarab about 10-12 mm long with pale hairs and three outer teeth on the front tibia; expert examination separates A. compressus. Examine the adult beetle itself rather than treating a lacy leaf as diagnostic. The pale hairs may be rubbed away on older adults, and similar scarabs can occur nearby. A specialist may need detailed leg and reproductive characters to separate Adoretus sinicus from its very similar relative.
actions: Visit affected foliage with a light after sunset, photograph the beetles, and record which plants are actually being fed upon. Avoid digging out every grub nearby on the assumption that it caused the leaf injury. Keep any requested sample contained and labeled with host and time of collection, then use current local advice to decide whether the level of damage warrants action.

identification: Arching grass clumps, often several feet tall, with feathery flower plumes; leaf stripes and mature size vary among cultivars. Compare the whole clump with seedlings nearby, which may not retain a parent cultivar's leaf pattern. The large feathery heads and arching blades are useful, but other ornamental grasses can have similar silhouettes. A flowering stem with its leaf base is a better identification sample than a loose plume.
actions: Avoid new planting where invasive. Remove escaped seedlings early and obtain local advice for established root masses. Keep seed-bearing plumes contained during disposal and avoid distributing divisions from a plant that is escaping. If a large clump must be removed, allow for its substantial root mass and repeat checks for shoots. Select a replacement grass suited to local moisture and light conditions, so the cleared space becomes a stable planting rather than an open site for reinvasion.

identification: Alternate simple leaves with rounded bases and long tips; milky sap; three-part capsules opening to white seeds. Photograph the leaf attachment and slender pointed tip, and inspect the three-lobed fruit before or after it opens. The exposed white objects are seeds rather than fleshy berries. In autumn, leaf color can be conspicuous, but many unrelated trees also turn red and yellow.
actions: Pull small seedlings before seed production. Use qualified help for mature trees and plan for stump sprouts and later seedlings. Inspect drainage routes and ground beneath bird perches around a seeding tree, where new plants can appear beyond the parent. Keep fruits and seeds contained during work, and avoid moving contaminated soil into restoration plantings. Larger projects should include suitable replacement vegetation and monitoring; cutting a trunk is a first operation, not evidence that roots or the seed supply have been exhausted.
Wear gloves and protective clothing, and avoid skin contact with the sap.

sources.label: NSW Department of Primary Industries: Chinese tallow tree

identification: Opposite egg-shaped leaves and trumpet flowers. Small white flowers with two purple blotches suggest subsp. micrantha; confirm with fruit and flower details. Photograph flower size with a scale and show the markings on the lower lobe, as well as leaves and mature capsules. The subspecies distinction matters because an Australian account of small white flowers does not describe every ornamental form. Square stems and paired leaves alone are shared with other plants.
actions: Keep cut stems out of garden dumping areas and waterways. Where removal is appropriate, collect roots and stem fragments and check for regrowth. Trace sprawling stems to their rooted nodes before lifting a small unwanted patch. Collect loose fragments rather than scattering them with mowing or cultivation, and inspect the edge again for new rooted growth. In a mixed planting or natural area, identify the form first and obtain local guidance before clearing vegetation solely because its flowers resemble a picture of Chinese violet.

identification: Woody counterclockwise-twining vine; spring blue-violet flower clusters and velvety pods. Native American wisteria has smooth pods and generally blooms later. Look at the pods and the timing of flowers relative to leaf emergence. Chinese wisteria commonly flowers before its leaves fully open; the vine's twining direction is another clue, but observation angle can confuse it. Japanese wisteria and hybrids make a single-character identification unreliable.
actions: Avoid planting near natural areas. Cut accessible stems carefully and arrange repeated follow-up; obtain local guidance for established infestations. Avoid pulling heavy entangled vines down from a tree, where they may bring branches with them. Arrange safe work on large stems and keep ground-level rooted sections in the follow-up plan. Check the surrounding woodland for separate vines and seedlings. When choosing a replacement, confirm that the nursery plant is a suitable native species rather than another invasive wisteria.

identification: The name Dioscorea oppositifolia and the common label Chinese yam do not reliably identify the same plant; compare botanical characters carefully. True Dioscorea oppositifolia is a leafy climbing plant with an underground tuber. Indian flora accounts describe broad leaves in opposite pairs, with conspicuous veins running from near the base toward the tip. A climbing habit and a yam-like tuber alone cannot separate it from other Dioscorea.
actions: Have the original taxon record checked before applying Chinese yam control advice or changing a species identification. Keep the source of a nursery label or earlier identification with photographs of the vine, paired leaves and any flowers or capsules. Ask a herbarium to distinguish the true species from Chinese yam before transferring occurrence records or deciding on removal. Avoid moving tubers or living cuttings while identity is uncertain, and do not dig up a large patch simply to test a name.

sources.label: Kew POWO: Dioscorea oppositifolia accepted concept
Ummalyma et al. 2018: Dioscorea oppositifolia in Manipur

identification: Hairless herb with lobed lower leaves, clasping upper leaves and cylindrical pods about 6-8 mm long in the Shanghai flora. Examine leaves low on the stem and near the flowers, since they can look quite different on one plant. The upper leaves have small ear-like bases clasping the stem. Other yellowcresses may share yellow flowers, so the short cylindrical pods and their attachment deserve close photographs.
actions: Document basal leaves and mature fruit for expert identification. Check regional status before deciding whether removal is warranted. Include a ruler beside mature pods and record the habitat, particularly whether plants are on cultivated or disturbed ground. If identification remains uncertain, preserve photographs from more than one growth stage rather than naming every yellow-flowered mustard alike. Where it is a confirmed unwanted garden plant, prevent further seed production without clearing neighboring vegetation that may include native mustards.

identification: Long needles in bundles of three, non-resinous winter buds and elongated ovoid cones; compare cones and needle bundles with other pines. The foliage hangs in long, slender bunches, but several cultivated pines share three-needle bundles. Include the woody cone scales in photographs: their projecting tips help distinguish chir pine from Canary Island pine. Older bark develops large plates, while young shoots and buds provide useful supporting characters when cones are absent.
actions: Record cones, needle bundles and any independently growing seedlings. Consult regional forestry guidance before removing or planting trees. Keep an observation of a planted specimen separate from a report of regeneration. If seedlings occur, record their distance from mature trees and whether they persist beyond maintained ground. Leave mature-tree work to qualified arborists; a regional tree specialist can assess identification and the need for action together.

identification: Small pale warehouse moth, roughly 15-20 mm wingspan; similar Ephestia species can require examination of genitalia. A pale adult near food storage is a useful clue, not a species-level diagnosis. Related Ephestia moths overlap in size and markings, and a clear photograph may still be insufficient. Record whether the insect was found indoors, at light, or emerging from a particular stored commodity; this context helps the identifier.
actions: Inspect stored products and keep suspect stock separate while identification and appropriate storage-pest management are arranged. Check adjoining packages as well as the first affected product, and keep a dated record of where insects appear. Store sound supplies in well-sealed containers and remove spilled material from shelves and crevices. Commercial tobacco or food stores should arrange a professional inspection before moving suspect stock between premises.

identification: Palmately arranged groups of five leaflets; twining woody stems, reddish-purple spring flowers and elongated purple fruits. Each leaf divides into separate oval leaflets on short stalks, rather than a single blade with five lobes. Flowering and fruiting shoots are especially useful for comparison with other ornamental vines. A bare winter stem is harder to name, since foliage retention varies with climate and exposure.
actions: Avoid new planting where invasive. Check nearby vegetation for escaped stems and seedlings and seek a removal plan for established vines. Trace escaped shoots back to their base before cutting through neighboring plants. Record where the vine reaches shrubs or trees and look beyond the original planting for separate seedlings. Check managed areas again after work, because a single pruning can leave established stems able to resume climbing.

identification: Toothed oval to narrow leaves, clustered small flowers and rounded hairy capsules; flower color varies among regional accounts. Look for alternate simple leaves and crowded flower heads rather than assuming that any toothed wet-ground herb is chocolateweed. A hand lens can reveal the fine hairs and the rounded, divided capsules. Photograph both an open flower and a mature fruit, since foliage alone overlaps with other small mallows.
actions: Photograph leaves, flower clusters and fruit. Confirm local native status and land-management needs before removing a population. Keep a record of whether plants occupy cultivation, disturbed margins or intact native vegetation. Where a crop adviser confirms a weed problem, deal with plants before their capsules mature and avoid transferring seed-bearing soil. In natural habitat, seek local botanical advice before treating a common-name label as a removal instruction.

sources.label: Kew hosted Flora of Tropical East Africa

identification: Tall herb with opposite toothed leaves and globular clusters of orange, hairy flowers surrounded by pointed floral structures. The flower heads form distinct balls at intervals up the stem, with orange tubular flowers projecting from persistent pointed cups. Include a side view showing this arrangement and a close view of a leaf edge. Other Leonotis share orange flowers, so one isolated bloom is less useful than the whole flowering shoot.
actions: Where control is needed, remove young plants before seed production and clean soil from equipment. Revisit the patch for seedlings. Work carefully around the pointed dried heads and contain mature seed-bearing tops before carrying them away. Mark the patch and check disturbed soil after later rain. Near waterways, seek local advice on disposal and bank protection so that removing a colony does not leave loose soil or seed to wash downstream.

sources.label: Kew hosted Flora of Tropical East Africa

identification: Tufted grass with mostly basal leaves; enclosed spikelet clusters and long, bent, twisted awns, often 5-9 cm long. This is an annual grass, although a large clump can look substantial. Compare the papery enclosure and the arrangement of sterile and fertile spikelets, not just the long bristle. Related perennial Themeda can retain old leaf bases, while intact mature flowering material allows a specialist to check the small diagnostic structures.
actions: Photograph mature seed heads and the whole clump. Seek a grass specialist's confirmation before control or moving seed-bearing material. Record the habitat and whether the plant is part of a native grassland before deciding it needs control. Avoid stripping seed heads merely for a casual photograph. If collection is permitted and requested by an identifier, keep the flowering sample contained and label the locality, date and growth form.

sources.label: Northern Territory Pastoral Land Board 2019-2020: Themeda field key

identification: Dark aphids with short black cornicles; wingless adults about 1.5 mm, nymphs brick red; colonies concentrate on chrysanthemum growth. Look at several stages together: wingless adults are compact and dark, while small nymphs have long legs and antennae against a brick-red body. Winged adults can appear as crowded colonies disperse. Cast skins and sticky deposits help locate feeding sites, but neither identifies the aphid without examining the insects themselves.
actions: Inspect chrysanthemums weekly and separate incoming plants for inspection. Remove heavily infested plants and seek crop-specific advice while conserving natural enemies. Pay particular attention to new terminal growth, stems and leaf undersides when stock arrives. Keep suspect pots apart from clean plants while obtaining advice. In a greenhouse, continue scouting while chrysanthemums remain present, since warmth and a continuing host can support feeding through winter rather than a single outdoor season.

sources.label: NC State AG-136 via University of Minnesota

identification: About 3 mm long, rounded and reddish brown; serrated antennae and smooth-looking wing covers distinguish it from drugstore beetle. Use a hand lens to examine the antennae and wing covers; reddish color and small size alone fit other pantry beetles. The pale larvae are curved grubs with legs, often concealed within the product. A beetle at a window may have flown away from its food, so record emergence sites if possible.
actions: Inspect dry goods and stored plant material, isolate suspect packages and ask an Extension or pest professional to identify the source. Check seldom-used spices, dried plant decorations and animal foods as well as everyday pantry staples. Keep confirmed infested material sealed for disposal or professional assessment, then clean remaining food debris from the storage area. Recheck unopened packages and replacement stock; removing adults alone leaves concealed larvae and their food source behind.

identification: Glossy, leathery leaves, reddish new growth and three to five strong basal veins; small pale flowers and dark oval fruits. Photograph a shoot showing paired or nearly paired leaves and the strong veins that run lengthwise from near the base. Include mature green leaves as well as reddish new growth, since color changes with age. Other aromatic laurels can look similar, so a nursery name or familiar smell should be checked against flowers and fruit.
actions: Use leaves and fruit for identification rather than tasting bark. Check local guidance before planting and watch for seedlings beyond cultivation. Keep any nursery label and planting history with the record. Where trees are cultivated for spice or ornament, distinguish deliberately planted young trees from volunteer seedlings. If growth appears outside the planted area, document it for local assessment rather than assuming either harmlessness or ecological damage from the tree name alone.

sources.label: Kew hosted Flora of Tropical East Africa

identification: Female covers circular, dark brown and strongly convex, about 1-1.3 mm wide; usually on needle undersides. Confirm against other armored scales. Examine several needles from different branches, including the lower crown where infestation may first be noticed. Rounded scale covers differ from the loose white wool of hemlock woolly adelgid, but other armored scales still require comparison. Yellowing alone has many causes, so photographs should show the attached insects as well as the tree.
actions: Inspect lower needle surfaces with magnification. Have a diagnostic service confirm the scale and time any management to locally observed crawlers. Save a small affected twig only as directed by the diagnostic service, and keep nursery material from being transferred while an infestation is assessed. Record whether scales are alive and whether new needle loss is developing. Local crawler monitoring is more useful than applying a calendar date taken from another state.

identification: Look beneath leaves for flat young scales and along twigs for convex gray females, up to about 6 mm long. Brown soft scale is generally smaller and browner; identification should include life stage. Check the same tree at more than one growth stage: a leaf colony of nearly flat juveniles can later appear as larger females on woody growth. Brown soft scale often has mixed sizes together, whereas citricola populations are more synchronized in California. A close photograph with a size reference helps separate these overlapping appearances.
actions: Photograph both leaf and twig colonies and ask an extension specialist to confirm the scale. Preserve predators and parasitoids; management timing varies with local climate and the insect's stage. Note the scale stage, affected branches and presence of ants when seeking advice. Check whether fresh honeydew or new growth loss is increasing rather than judging only by old blackened leaves. Avoid choosing a treatment from color alone, since protecting natural enemies and timing work depend on the confirmed insect.

sources.label: Citricola scale in citrus plantations in Croatia

identification: Look for linear leaves only a few millimeters wide, an underground bulb, and yellow flowers about 3-4 cm long on stalks roughly 15-25 cm tall. Confirm with flowers rather than foliage alone. The leaf blades are much narrower than a typical lily leaf, and a flowering stalk rises separately above them. Include a side view of the yellow flower and its basal sheath in the record. Other rain lilies can be yellow too, so a flower color match does not settle the name.
actions: Record whether plants were planted or are appearing independently nearby. Photograph flowers, leaves and the surrounding habitat; avoid discarding bulbs or seed-bearing material in natural areas. Keep bulbs from garden divisions and spent flowering material within managed disposal routes. If a patch appears away from a bed, revisit it when flowering and note whether additional plants arise over time. There is no need to excavate a healthy garden clump simply to document the bulbous growth form.

sources.label: Kew: Zephyranthes citrina, descriptions and distribution

identification: Hard-spot symptoms include small, circular, sunken lesions with gray or tan centers and dark margins. Other forms look quite different; have suspicious fruit and leaf symptoms assessed by a plant diagnostic service. Record fruit maturity as well as the lesion pattern: hard spots often become conspicuous as the rind changes color, while earlier blemishes can be smaller and less distinctive. Photograph several fruits and both leaf surfaces if affected. Raised corky canker lesions and other fungal spots can be confused with black spot in casual images.
actions: Photograph suspect fruit and contact local extension or the state plant health office. Avoid moving potentially infected citrus plants, fruit or fallen material until you receive local guidance. Keep the location, citrus variety if known, and date of first symptoms with the report. Ask the receiving service how material should be sampled before sending anything. Do not distribute fallen leaves, nursery stock or suspect fruit to another garden while the cause and any local movement requirements are being checked.

sources.label: UF IFAS: A guide to citrus disease identification

identification: Check leaf undersides for eggs laid in spirals and dark, spiny immature stages. The final immature stage has a pale waxy fringe; adults have slate-blue to blackish wings. Turn over leaves from several shoots: eggs, newly settled young and older spiny covers may occur together. A soot-like film on the upper surface can originate from insects feeding above it. Related Aleurocanthus species also have dark immatures, so the wax fringe and spines need expert comparison for an unexpected record.
actions: Inspect incoming plants and photograph the underside of affected leaves. Seek identification and local advice before treatment, especially where parasitoids already suppress this pest; avoid moving infested nursery plants. Keep recently purchased host plants separate if suspicious colonies are present, and note the seller and purchase date for tracing. Check nearby woody hosts as directed by a local adviser. Broad treatment based only on sooty mold can disrupt parasitoids while missing the actual feeding insect or the source plant.

identification: The species name alone cannot identify the historical citrus-infecting pathovar. Trace the original record, diagnostic result or cited name before assigning citrus canker symptoms to this entry. Bacteria cannot be identified by ordinary garden photographs. Host plant, lesion appearance and a complete laboratory name belong together, including any pathovar given after the species. A record using only a shortened historical name cannot establish that the organism is the citrus-infecting bacterium rather than another member of the genus.
actions: Ask a plant diagnostic service to interpret an incomplete or historical bacterial name before drawing conclusions about citrus canker. Keep the original identification with the plant history. If the practical concern is a symptomatic citrus tree, send photographs and its location to a plant health service without mailing leaves or cuttings first. Retain the full wording and date of any previous laboratory report. The reviewer can then connect the affected host to an appropriate diagnostic test and reporting route.

sources.label: EPPO: Xanthomonas citri pv. citri datasheet

identification: Look for raised, rough or crater-like brown lesions, often with a water-soaked edge or yellow halo. Similar-looking damage needs laboratory or plant-health confirmation. Inspect leaves, young twigs and fruit together; a single brown mark is less informative than a repeated pattern across these tissues. Note whether lesions project above the surface, rather than simply being dark or depressed. Citrus black spot, scab and mechanical injury may resemble parts of the pattern and should remain in the comparison.
actions: Document symptoms without transporting the plant or affected material. Contact extension or the local plant health authority for sampling instructions and applicable movement requirements. Provide the tree location, planting history and recent movement of nursery material when reporting a suspicion. Do not share budwood or cuttings from the tree. Ask for local instructions before pruning, collecting samples or disposing of fallen material, since handling and movement decisions depend on diagnostic results and the regional disease situation.

sources.label: UF IFAS: A guide to citrus disease identification

identification: Asymmetric yellow blotching across a leaf's midrib is a useful warning sign. Small lopsided fruit and shoot dieback add concern, but nutrient disorders and other problems can look similar; laboratory testing is needed. Compare both sides of several leaves rather than relying on one yellow shoot. Uneven patches that cross the midrib differently are more concerning than a consistently symmetrical nutrient pattern, but neither pattern is conclusive alone. Record which part of the crown first changed and whether fruit size or shape also differs.
actions: Photograph suspicious foliage and fruit and contact the local plant health office. Avoid moving citrus plants, cuttings or suspect green waste until you have appropriate guidance. Keep nursery labels and propagation history available for the diagnostic service. Do not share budwood from a tree under investigation, even if another branch looks healthy. Follow the authority's sampling instructions; testing and any subsequent tree-management decisions need to account for the local disease program and the possibility of symptomless infection.

sources.label: USDA APHIS: Citrus greening and Asian citrus psyllid

identification: Look for winding mines with a central dark line on tender leaves and a curled leaf edge where pupation occurs. Adults are tiny silvery moths with dark marks near the wing tips. Examine the newest expanding leaves, where the pale tunnel runs within the leaf rather than sitting on top like a loose thread. Older mines can remain after the insect has left. Rolled leaves without a visible mine may instead reflect aphids, psyllids or other injury, so check for the actual feeding trace.
actions: Keep damaged leaves that are still functioning, and avoid unnecessary pruning or excessive fertilization that prompts repeated flushes of tender growth. Preserve parasitoids and seek local advice if young trees are badly affected. Judge the effect on the whole tree and its age before acting on a few damaged tips. Keep a record of new flush and whether fresh mines continue to appear. Where citrus canker is a concern, ask a local citrus adviser to assess the combined disease risk rather than treating every mine as an emergency.

sources.label: UC IPM home landscape citrus leafminer

identification: Females have white wax, a faint grayish stripe along the back and short marginal filaments, with the rear pair slightly longer. Look for cottony egg sacs and hidden colonies; related mealybugs can require expert examination. A magnified view should show a segmented insect beneath the white wax, rather than only a cottony patch. Compare the length of the tail filaments with the body; long-tailed mealybugs can be mistaken for this species. Check leaf axils, overlapping fruit and other sheltered joints that are hidden in a whole-plant photograph.
actions: Inspect and isolate newly acquired houseplants when insects are found. Remove small accessible colonies, then recheck crevices over several weeks; obtain pest-specific advice for persistent or extensive infestations. Keep infested pots from touching neighboring plants and inspect the supporting surfaces as well as the foliage. Where a few insects are removed by hand, return to the same hidden sites repeatedly to look for young stages. Avoid moving a plant back among clean stock merely because its obvious white colonies have disappeared.

identification: A strong hand lens is needed: adults are less than about 0.25 mm long, pale yellow to brownish and wedge-shaped, with four legs near the front. Confirm the mite rather than relying on rind color alone. Look for living mites on affected fruit and foliage with magnification; old russeting can remain after the population changes. Pink citrus rust mite overlaps in size, and reliable separation uses fine body characters rather than rind color. Record the citrus type and whether new damage is appearing on developing fruit.
actions: Inspect affected fruit with magnification and assess the amount of injury before considering treatment. Garden fruit with superficial blemishes may not need intervention; growers should use local monitoring thresholds. Monitor more than one part of the canopy and keep dated photographs of the affected rind. A commercial fresh-fruit grower may have different quality thresholds from a home gardener keeping fruit for household use. Seek local advice before intervention, with attention to natural enemies and the number of active mites rather than discoloration alone.

sources.label: UC IPM: Rust mite or silver mite

identification: A tapered, many-segmented worm with bristled side appendages and four eyes is consistent with this group, but not enough for species identification. Specialists use fine anatomical features and sometimes molecular evidence to separate similar Hediste. Include the head and side appendages in photographs, but do not try to name the worm from its segment count or color alone. Species separation depends on tiny jaw-area teeth and bristle structures. Native Hediste may share the same mudflat, so a worm found at an introduced-species locality is not automatically this species.
actions: Record the location and habitat without transferring worms or sediment between sites. Ask a marine invertebrate specialist to assess a suspected record; photographs alone may not resolve the species. Leave burrows and sediment in place during casual observation. Bait worms, attached mud and other collected material should never be released into a different estuary. For a suspected new locality, provide the original site, salinity setting and date to a marine specialist, who can decide whether a properly documented specimen is needed.

sources.label: Filter-feeding behavior of three Asian Hediste species

identification: Look for prostrate or partly ascending stems, small oval leaves with wavy or toothed margins, glandular hairs and dense, tiny whitish flower clusters where leaves meet stems. Confirm against other small goosefoots. A close side view can show the tiny flowers packed at the leaf bases rather than forming a conspicuous terminal spike. The leaves are small, with margins ranging from wavy to almost smooth. Examine the glandular hairs with magnification; the spreading habit and aromatic foliage together help narrow the choice among goosefoots.
actions: Photograph the leaf margins, flower clusters and growth habit. Ask a local herbarium or extension service to confirm uncertain plants before deciding whether removal is warranted. Record whether the patch is in a garden, track edge or natural vegetation and retain the date for a local comparison. If confirmed as an unwanted garden plant, contain flowering material instead of spreading it with soil. Native populations should be assessed in their own regional context before any control is proposed.

sources.label: Kew: Dysphania pumilio, Flora of Tropical East Africa account

identification: Check for hairy, mostly stalkless leaves that partly clasp the stem and coiled flower clusters with blooms arranged along one side in two rows. It is often called blue heliotrope. The curved flower clusters gradually unfurl, with small blooms appearing along the upper side. Include the crowded flower head, hairy leaf surface and the way the leaf joins the stem in photographs. Related heliotropes can differ in flower color and growth form, while damaged plants may be difficult to distinguish without flowering shoots.
actions: Keep livestock away from suspected patches until a local agricultural adviser confirms the plant and assesses the situation. Record patch size and flowering details; obtain locally appropriate management advice. Avoid shifting soil or root fragments from a confirmed patch to clean ground. Mark its boundary and monitor regrowth after any locally approved control, since loss of the visible shoots does not necessarily remove the deep-rooted plant. Keep contaminated plant material out of animal feed and follow agricultural advice on grazing access.

identification: Look for deeply dissected lower leaves, strongly clasping rounded upper leaves, four small yellow petals and flattened, roughly oval fruits about 4 mm long. Other clasping mustards need comparison. The upper leaves can make the stem seem to pass through a rounded green shield. Check lower foliage before it withers, because its finely divided form provides a useful contrast. Mature pods are short and broad, unlike the long narrow pods of many mustards; a photograph showing flowers and fruit together is especially helpful.
actions: Include upper and lower leaves, flowers and mature pods in photographs. Consult a local flora or extension service if the plant cannot be distinguished from similar mustards. Note whether the plant occurs as scattered individuals or a dense patch within a crop or pasture. Where removal is warranted, act before mature pods shed and avoid moving seed-bearing material with soil. A regional assessment should separate ordinary disturbed-ground occurrence from an established agricultural problem or a locally regulated weed.

identification: Look for a low upright plant, oval to oblong clasping stem leaves, small white flowers and broadly winged, notched pods. Fruit shape helps distinguish it from other small spring mustards. The narrow wings around the flat pod widen toward its notched tip, giving a mature fruit more diagnostic value than the tiny flowers. Compare both sides of several pods and the stem-clasping leaf bases. Other pennycresses differ in pod proportions, so an immature round fruit may be misleading.
actions: Photograph mature pods beside a scale along with the upper leaf bases. Ask a local herbarium or extension specialist to resolve uncertain identification before treating it as a weed of concern. Keep a dated record while waiting for fruit to mature if identification is uncertain. In a planted bed, distinguish a few annual volunteers from a persistent crop-management problem. If local advice supports removal, contain fruiting stems and check the same disturbed soil in a later growing season rather than assuming one pass is definitive.

identification: Curled leaves and thickened veins are warning signs, not a species-level diagnosis. Other viruses, pests and growing conditions can cause similar-looking damage. Include whole-plant views and close photographs of both leaf surfaces, showing whether veins as well as the blade are altered. Record whether the affected plant is cotton, okra or an ornamental mallow. A familiar leaf-curl appearance on one host does not show that an isolate behaves the same way on another.
actions: Document the host plant and visible symptoms and consult an extension plant pathologist or official plant-health service. Let qualified professionals determine whether further diagnostic assessment is appropriate. Keep the plant's source and the dates of new symptoms with the report. Avoid sharing cuttings or relocating suspect nursery plants until the diagnostic service advises on handling. For crop observations, describe whether the pattern is isolated or widespread; do not infer a particular virus solely from nearby whiteflies or a photograph.

sources.label: NVWA: Quick scan for cotton leaf curl Gezira virus, EPPO summary
Introduction of Cotton leaf curl Gezira virus into the United Arab Emirates

identification: Examine alternate, unlobed leaves and mature fruiting flower parts. In this species the latter are commonly about 4.2-6.5 mm long and narrow abruptly near the base; compare carefully with Fallopia scandens. Look for the thin sheath at a stem joint, a useful clue to the knotweed family rather than a morning glory. Measure several mature winged fruiting structures if this can be done without damaging surrounding vegetation. The transition from the broad winged portion to the narrow base matters when separating the native climbing relatives.
actions: Photograph ripe fruiting structures and leaf bases, not just the climbing habit. Seek a botanist's confirmation before removing a vine that could be a native lookalike. Trace the vine through its supporting vegetation gently so photographs do not damage the host plant. Record whether it is flowering or fruiting and revisit if only immature material is available. Where a non-native identification is confirmed and control is warranted, contain mature fruits rather than pulling them through neighboring stems and scattering them.

identification: Look for clusters of purple, backward-curving petals surrounding a yellow cone, red ripe berries and alternate leaves that may have two small basal lobes. It is also called bittersweet nightshade. Leaves on one plant can vary from unlobed to distinctly lobed at the base, so this difference alone does not indicate two species. Photograph the yellow anther cone and the reflexed purple petals when flowers are available. Berries change color while ripening, making a green-fruited shoot less immediately recognizable than a mature one.
actions: Keep children and pets from eating berries and wear gloves when handling the plant. Ask local extension for identification or management advice, particularly around waterways or mixed native vegetation. If a confirmed unwanted vine is removed, keep the berries and underground stem pieces contained rather than dumping them beside a stream or hedge. Check the original site for regrowth. In a mixed planting, trace stems to their base carefully so that native climbers and the shrubs supporting them are preserved.

identification: Young climbing shoots have small heart-shaped leaves and attaching roots; mature projecting branches carry larger oval leaves and sometimes green-to-purple, pear-shaped figs. Compare the close-clinging juvenile mat with any stiff shoots projecting away from the support. Their larger leaves are a normal age-related change, not necessarily a different fig. The adhesive roots distinguish its climbing method from a vine that winds around a support or holds on with tendrils.
actions: Keep established garden vines within their intended space and assess the surface before allowing them to climb a building. Photograph both juvenile and mature shoots when requesting identification. Inspect a managed vine regularly around joints, fixtures and the edge of its support, where vigorous growth can make later maintenance difficult. Plan pruning while access is manageable and seek building or arboricultural advice before pulling old attached stems from a surface. Check discarded trimmings and nearby unmanaged ground for continued growth.

identification: Look for a transparent bell a few centimeters across, a colored cross and numerous fine tentacles associated with submerged plants. Small size and similar jellyfish make expert confirmation valuable. The cross and attachment pads identify a clinging-jellyfish type rather than resolving every member of the Gonionemus complex. Genetic studies separate northeastern Pacific G. vertens from some Atlantic and northwestern Pacific lineages historically given that name. A photograph cannot determine lineage or predict the severity of a sting.
actions: Avoid touching or collecting suspected animals. Follow local beach or marine-agency advice and report a sighting with its location and a photograph if one can be taken safely. Note whether the animal was attached to eelgrass, seaweed or another submerged surface and include the date and water body in the report. Observe from a safe position without pulling up vegetation to find more animals. Use current local advisories when planning water activities, since records and sting risk differ among populations.

sources.label: Rhode Island DEM: Clinging jellyfish found in Point Judith Pond
Swedish Agency for Marine and Water Management: Jellyfish, clinging jellyfish section
Govindarajan et al. 2019: toxic and cryptogenic Gonionemus on the Swedish west coast

identification: Look for slender twining stems, leaves reduced to minute scales and tightly packed clusters of tiny five-parted flowers. Flower details are needed to separate it from other dodders. A hand lens reveals tightly packed pale flowers along the fine threads. Specialists compare the flower tube, lobes and tiny structures inside it; stem color by itself is variable and not decisive. Include an undamaged host shoot in the photographs, because the host association helps interpret the plant without replacing floral identification.
actions: Photograph the flowers, threads and host plant. Seek local botanical or agricultural advice before removal, particularly in native heathland or conservation areas. Avoid carrying tangled host cuttings or contaminated seed between planting areas while identification is pending. In forage production, consult an adviser about affected crop material and seed sources. In native heathland, leave the association intact until a botanist assesses it, since a parasitic growth habit does not by itself make a plant non-native.

identification: Adults are about 4 mm long, mottled brown with pale markings and fine raised hairs. Larvae are white grubs with pale brown heads. Leaf notches and root scars are clues, not proof of the species. Several root-feeding weevils can notch forage leaves, so pair an adult specimen or detailed image with the root symptoms. The pale larvae are hidden in soil and are much less distinctive in a casual photograph. Record plant age and whether declining plants occur in patches, including areas with different drainage or crop history.
actions: Have an agricultural adviser assess declining forage and identify any insects found. Record whether damage involves leaf margins, roots or both rather than assuming every weakened patch has the same cause. Use the adviser's sampling instructions rather than digging up many plants at random. Keep field notes on previous forage stands and the timing of visible decline to help separate insect feeding from other root problems. Management should reflect the confirmed species and local crop situation, not the presence of a few adult leaf notches alone.

sources.label: Utah State University: Clover root curculio

identification: Possible signs include cupped or crinkled young leaves, reddish veins and unusual shoot growth. These signs overlap with other cotton disorders and require professional diagnostic assessment. Compare affected and apparently normal plants of the same variety, including the youngest leaves and the upper canopy. Stunting early in development and elongated, poorly fruiting terminal growth later can look quite different. Record the growth stage and any recent field operations so that herbicide injury and other causes remain part of the assessment.
actions: Document symptoms and their pattern across the field and contact an extension cotton specialist or plant pathologist. Treat visual suspicion as a reason to investigate, not a confirmed virus record. Keep dated photographs and a simple map of affected rows for the diagnostic adviser. Do not assume that every curled leaf has the virus or that symptom severity predicts yield loss. Before changing crop management, obtain a diagnosis and region-specific advice based on the cotton variety, field history and current observations.

sources.label: Mississippi State Extension: Five things to know about cotton leafroll dwarf virus
Alabama Cooperative Extension: Cotton leafroll dwarf virus

identification: Look for succulent stems, broadly heart-shaped leaves with scalloped or toothed margins, white-to-pink flowers and three-winged capsules. Do not assume every bedding plant sold as wax begonia is this species. Look closely at the uneven leaf base and the fine teeth along the wavy margin, then include a mature winged capsule if present. Fleshy stems and familiar pink flowers alone also fit cultivated begonias. A nursery label may name a hybrid series rather than this botanical species, so retain it as context.
actions: Record whether plants are cultivated or growing independently beyond a garden. Photograph flowers and capsules, and ask a local botanist or extension service to distinguish species from cultivated hybrids. Where escaped seedlings are confirmed, contain them before the tiny seeds disperse and keep uprooted pieces from settling into damp ground again. Check the disturbed margins around a planting as well as the bed itself. Follow local planting advice, especially in warm regions where this species has established beyond cultivation.

sources.label: UF IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants: Begonia cucullata

identification: Look for rounded, shallowly five- to seven-lobed leaves and nearly stalkless flower clusters in the leaf axils. The small wheel-like fruit separates into segments whose surface details help distinguish similar mallows. Inspect where several flowers gather at a leaf base and compare their short stalks with those of nearby mallow species. Once petals fall, the ring of fruit segments remains useful. A hand lens can reveal the segment surfaces; photograph several mature fruits rather than relying on a single damaged or unripe one.
actions: Photograph open flowers and mature fruit as well as the whole plant. Request a botanical identification if the fruit characters are unclear; a broad leaf photograph alone is often insufficient. Keep garden provenance with observations near cultivation, since a cultivated mallow and a spontaneous population require different interpretation. If a confirmed unwanted patch is managed, collect fruiting material before moving it through the garden. Revisit uncertain plants for mature fruit instead of removing all similar mallows based on leaf size alone.

sources.label: Kew: Malva verticillata, Flora of Tropical East Africa account

identification: Look for hairless, prostrate or ascending stems, three small finely toothed leaflets and compact globular flower heads in the leaf axils. Heads are essentially stalkless, unlike those of many other clovers. Trace the flower head to its attachment point: the tight ball sits at a leaf joint rather than at the top of a long stalk. Examine several heads because young clusters can be partly hidden by the leaves. The plant is generally hairless, and the small leaflets broaden toward their tips.
actions: Photograph the attachment of a flower head to the stem and the leaflet edges. Consult a local flora or extension service when several small clovers occur together. Record whether flowering plants occur within a lawn, pasture or unmanaged vegetation and avoid identifying every pink clover by color. If a confirmed patch is unwanted in a bed, prevent mature heads from being scattered with soil. Where clovers form part of existing vegetation, check the local management objective before removing them.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Trifolium glomeratum

identification: Check for spaced flower or fruit clusters, leafy bracts beneath many whorls and three small, smooth-edged fruit valves, each with a prominent swollen grain. Mature fruit is needed to separate similar docks. Use a hand lens to inspect several ripe fruits, since the swollen grains on the three inner coverings can be hard to see in young flowers. The lower leaves are stalked and relatively broad compared with the narrow upper foliage. Hybrid docks and immature plants may not fit a simple photograph-based comparison.
actions: Include the lower leaves and close-up mature fruit in a record. Ask a botanist or extension service to check difficult plants, especially where several dock species or hybrids occur. Record the moisture conditions and whether the plant is growing in pasture, cultivation or a wetland margin. If control is locally justified, keep mature fruiting stems contained and avoid disturbing banks unnecessarily. Recheck the perennial base after management, and do not treat every leafy flowering dock as this species without examining fruit.

sources.label: Kew: Rumex conglomeratus, Flora of Iraq account

identification: Look for narrow stem leaves with toothed bases that clasp the stem, small cylindrical heads and no showy ray flowers. Closely related Senecio species can require examination of head bracts and mature fruits. Photograph the toothed lobes where an upper leaf clasps the stem and the green bracts surrounding each flower head. These small structures are more useful than height alone. Plants intermediate with related Senecio occur, so unusual bract numbers or a poor fit to the leaf characters deserve a specialist check.
actions: Photograph leaf bases, flower heads and the whole plant. Confirm the identification and local native status with a herbarium before considering management. Include the surrounding habitat and any recent disturbance in the record. In its native range, an upright colonizing herb in wet forest is not automatically a weed needing removal. For an unexpected population elsewhere, obtain a confirmed identification and regional status assessment before moving flowering or seed-bearing material between sites.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Senecio minimus

identification: Look for narrow phyllodes with three or four main veins, spherical yellow flower heads and thick pods that twist after opening. The conspicuous red-orange structure around each dark seed is especially useful. The leaf-like phyllodes are flattened stalks, with several strong lengthwise veins visible in good light. Open pods give the clearest view of the bright loop around the seed; yellow flower balls alone fit many wattles. Compare pods and foliage together, especially near plantings containing several Australian Acacia species.
actions: Record pods, seeds and foliage when seeking confirmation. Check local native status and land-management guidance before planting or removing coastal wattles, particularly in dune or conservation areas. Where coastal managers confirm an invasive population, ask for a plan that includes seedlings and follow-up after mature shrubs are removed. Keep pod-bearing branches from being scattered along access tracks. In native Australian coastal habitat, retain the same identification care and avoid treating a conservation threat reported overseas as a universal removal instruction.

identification: Look for rough-hairy, toothed leaves, long solitary flower stalks and a small yellow-centered head with only a few short, often three-toothed pale rays. Mature fruits carry feathery bristles. Check the rough hairs and opposite leaves on the lower stems, then look at the few short rays around the central disc. The pale ray tips are often divided into three teeth, unlike the long broad petals of many ornamental daisies. A mature head carries feathery bristles around the small dark fruits.
actions: Photograph the flower head from above and the leafy stems below it. Confirm uncertain plants with a local flora or extension service and note whether the patch is in disturbed ground or natural vegetation. Document whether low stems have rooted where they touch the soil. Where a confirmed patch is unwanted, remove young plants before mature heads disperse and keep rooted pieces out of fresh soil. Around native vegetation, first check local status and the management objective; widespread occurrence does not by itself establish ecological damage.

sources.label: Kew: Tridax procumbens, tropical flora descriptions
Indian Institute of Science Herbarium JCB: Tridax procumbens

identification: Look for elongated, flattened green pads and red flowers with conspicuously projecting stamens. Other prickly pears can look similar; photograph flowers and the whole plant. The flattened pads are stems, with small areoles spaced over their surface. Tiny leaves may appear briefly on new growth, while mature plants can look almost spineless. The narrow red flowers and their projecting reproductive parts are more informative than a detached green pad when comparing other cultivated prickly pears.
actions: Avoid bare-handed handling. If a plant is spreading outside cultivation, photograph it and ask a local plant specialist to confirm its identity before removal. Keep broken pads and pruning waste contained, since a discarded pad can root where it lands. Do not move fragments into dunes, dry scrub or other unmanaged ground. For a large escaped plant, seek a handling and disposal plan that accounts for irritating bristles and follow-up checks for pieces left behind.
