Its alternate leaves are divided more than once into small rounded or oblong segments, giving the blue-green foliage a finely cut appearance. Leaves are hairless and dotted with glands; avoid crushing them against bare skin to test their scent. Small yellow flowers occur in upright terminal clusters, with four or five petals surrounding a prominent green center. Brown capsules split to release dark seeds. The woody lower stems distinguish an established plant from a purely herbaceous seedling. For identification, include the complete leaf structure and a close view of flowers or capsules. Finely divided blue-green foliage alone is not sufficient to separate rue from unrelated ornamental herbs.
actions: If Common rue is intentionally planted, watch for seedlings outside the bed and remove unwanted volunteers while they are small. To reduce reseeding, clip developing seed clusters before the capsules open. Wear gloves and long sleeves when pruning or lifting plants, keeping cut foliage away from exposed skin. Check the leaves for swallowtail caterpillars before removing an occupied plant, and avoid unnecessary broad insecticide treatments around this host plant. If the shrub is unwanted, dig out the crown and roots and inspect the area for later seedlings. Keep it clearly separate from edible herbs; traditional use does not establish that home ingestion is safe. No broad eradication treatment is warranted solely because it is introduced.

sources.label: Eickhorst, DeLeo and Csaposs 2007 — Rue-associated phytophototoxicity

identification: Adult Common rustic moth has forewings about half an inch long. Their color ranges from olive-brown to reddish or nearly black, and the pattern can be mottled or almost plain. A pale cream or white kidney-shaped mark is often the strongest visible feature. The hindwings are dark brownish gray. Adults are most often recorded in July and August in the Pacific Northwest. Native Mesapamea fractilinea can look nearly identical; definitive separation relies on specialist examination of reproductive structures. In Europe, Lesser Common Rustic (Mesapamea didyma) is another close lookalike. Take sharp upper-wing photographs with a size reference and preserve the date and locality. A brown moth at a porch light should remain a tentative identification unless the necessary distinguishing evidence is available.
actions: Photograph a suspected Common rustic moth and send the record to a regional moth recorder, university insect collection, or extension entomologist, especially if it occurs beyond known local records. Ask before collecting a specimen because expert examination may be needed to distinguish the species. Do not infer that nearby crop injury was caused by this moth solely because an adult visited a light. If grasses or cereals show damage, document the affected plants and any larvae together and seek a crop-specific diagnosis. Avoid broad spraying of lawn or garden vegetation in response to a single adult. The available North American account supports observation and identification, rather than a routine homeowner eradication program.

sources.label: Common Rustic — Butterflies and Moths of Northern Ireland

identification: Common Sheep Sorrel commonly reaches about 6–18 inches tall. Leaves vary with age and position: many middle leaves have two outward-pointing lobes near the base, while young or upper leaves may lack those lobes. Slender flowering stems branch toward the top. A thin papery collar surrounds each stem joint and becomes brown and torn with age, a useful clue to the buckwheat family. The flowers are tiny, followed by very small three-sided brown fruits. Male and female flowers usually occur on separate plants. Do not identify it by tasting. Show several leaves from the same plant, the stem collars, and mature fruit; an unlobed seedling can look quite different from the familiar arrow-shaped adult foliage.
actions: For a small unwanted patch, lift the crowns and trace the shallow horizontal roots as thoroughly as practical. Common Sheep Sorrel can produce new shoots from short root fragments, so simply snapping off stems or chopping the soil once is unlikely to finish the job. Remove flowering shoots before seed matures and check repeatedly for regrowth. In lawns or pasture, use a soil test to guide any lime or fertilizer, and improve the competitiveness of the vegetation you want to keep. Do not apply lime solely because sorrel is present. Avoid moving soil containing roots into clean beds. Where the patch occupies a natural area, assess the surrounding plant community before making broad soil amendments.

sources.label: Red sorrel — Ohio perennial and biennial weed guide
Rumex acetosella — Fire Effects Information System
Forb seedling identification guide — Rumex acetosella

identification: Mature Common Sowthistle usually stands about 1–5 feet tall. Its smooth, hollow stem bears alternate leaves, with the upper leaves clasping the stem through pointed, angular lobes. Leaves are dull green to blue-green, often deeply cut, and commonly have a broad triangular terminal lobe. Their teeth may be prickly but are softer than those of Spiny Sowthistle (Sonchus asper), whose shinier leaves have rounded, curled stem-clasping lobes and sharper marginal spines. Yellow flower heads occur in small terminal clusters and become loose white seed heads. Seedlings are harder to separate. Photograph the upper leaf base where it wraps around the stem, a lower leaf, and an open head; these are more informative than a photograph of the yellow flowers alone.
actions: Pull or hoe Common Sowthistle while plants are small and before the white seed tufts develop. A hand fork helps lift the short taproot without scattering much soil. If heads are already ripening, contain them before moving the plant and avoid carrying uncovered seed heads across the garden. Check bed edges, fences, and nearby uncultivated strips for plants that could replenish the site. Maintain mulch or desired vegetation over open ground and revisit after rain or irrigation brings another seedling flush. In vegetable gardens, remove unwanted plants near crops as part of routine weed sanitation. Distinguish this annual from perennial sowthistles before assuming that the same removal strategy will control an extensive root-spreading patch.

identification: Common Speedwell has hairy stems with the hairs distributed around them, opposite toothed leaves, and flowering stems that trail near the base. Plants are often roughly 4-20 inches in extent or height depending on their posture. The small flowers are about 4-8 millimeters across and occur in stalked clusters arising from leaf axils, where a leaf meets the stem. They usually have four unequal lobes and two projecting stamens. Germander Speedwell (Veronica chamaedrys) has more upright flowering stems and larger flowers, about 8-13 millimeters across. Inspect the whole growth habit as well as a close flower. Include a stem segment showing leaf arrangement and hairs; a lone blue flower is not enough to distinguish the many speedwells.
actions: Decide first whether Common Speedwell is causing an actual problem in the planting or habitat. Where a small patch is unwanted, gently lift the trailing stems and roots with a hand fork, keeping nearby desired plants intact. Recheck the patch for surviving shoots and seedlings rather than treating one removal as complete. Avoid moving rooted pieces in soil or garden waste. In a lawn or managed bed, repair sparse vegetation and reduce repeated disturbance that leaves open establishment sites. If it is growing in a natural area, seek local botanical advice before broad removal because similar speedwells complicate blanket recommendations. A small garden cleanup is not evidence that the species needs eradication from every habitat.

sources.label: Common speedwell — wild blueberry weed images
Flora of the Pacific Northwest: revised Veronica key

identification: Common St. John's Wort usually grows about 1–3 feet tall, with several smooth stems that become woody near the base and branch above. Leaves are small, opposite, and stalkless. Examine a leaf against light for translucent dots, then check the five yellow petals for dark dots around their edges. The numerous stamens form a conspicuous tuft in each flower. Stems have two subtle longitudinal ridges rather than a broad, leafy wing. Common Tansy and Tansy Ragwort also carry yellow clusters, but their heads consist of many tiny flowers rather than individual five-petaled flowers. Native Hypericum species can resemble it more closely; a local flora may be needed. Include leaf glands, stem ridges, and an open flower in the record.
actions: Prioritize new patches and scattered plants beyond an established Common St. John's Wort stand. Dig or pull small plants with their crowns and lateral roots before seed develops, then revisit because remaining underground parts can regrow. Remove the material from the site rather than leaving it where shoots or seeds could survive. Repeated cutting may limit seed production but is not a dependable one-time cure. Restore suitable vegetation after removal and avoid overgrazing that leaves open soil. Keep livestock away from heavily infested forage while a local adviser assesses the situation. For large pasture or conservation-land patches, use a coordinated management plan; biological-control insects should be handled through an established local program.

sources.label: Hypericum perforatum — Fire Effects Information System

identification: Common St. Paul's wort often reaches roughly 1–3 feet tall, with hairy stems and opposite leaves on short stalks. Leaves range from narrow and spear-shaped to broader triangular shapes, usually with toothed edges. The yellow flower heads are only about a quarter to half an inch across. Five elongated outer bracts spread beyond each head and carry conspicuous dark, stalked glands; these are more distinctive than the yellow color alone. Small yellow outer rays surround the central florets, followed by dark, slightly angled fruits about 2–3 millimeters long. Closely related Sigesbeckia species can require a botanical key. Photograph the bracts from the side, leaf bases, and a complete flowering branch rather than relying on the outline of a single leaf.
actions: Remove a small unwanted patch of Common St. Paul's wort before its heads develop mature dark fruits. Lift young plants with their roots, minimizing disturbance to nearby vegetation. If fruit is already present, contain the heads before transporting the plants and check clothing or equipment for adhering material. Avoid dumping garden waste where surviving seed could establish. Record the location and obtain a botanical confirmation for an unfamiliar occurrence in a natural area, especially where another Sigesbeckia species may be present. Revisit the cleared patch after favorable growing weather and cover bare garden soil with suitable planting or mulch. These are practical seed-prevention measures; widespread removal needs a local assessment of actual impacts.

sources.label: Sigesbeckia orientalis — Flora of New South Wales
Sigesbeckia orientalis — Plants of the World Online

identification: Common Tansy commonly grows 3–4 feet tall, sometimes taller. Its alternate leaves are divided into many narrow, toothed segments, giving them a fernlike outline. Brownish to reddish stems support numerous rounded yellow heads, each roughly a quarter to half an inch across. Unlike a daisy, each head lacks the surrounding strap-shaped ray flowers that look like petals. This separates it from Tansy Ragwort, whose yellow heads usually have a clear ring of rays. Common St. John's Wort has individual flowers with five broad petals and small opposite leaves, not finely divided alternate leaves. Flowering is typically in summer into early autumn. Include both the flower cluster and a complete leaf; persistent brown seed heads can help locate old patches.
actions: Dig or pull small Common Tansy patches when soil is moist, removing the underground stems as thoroughly as possible. Wear gloves and return regularly to remove shoots arising from missed pieces. Cutting before flowering can prevent seed production, but mowing alone will not kill the established underground system and must be repeated. Contain mature flower or seed heads before carrying plants through unaffected areas. Clean seeds and soil from equipment before moving to another site. Replant disturbed ground with suitable vegetation and monitor over multiple growing seasons. On pasture or extensive natural-area infestations, arrange local weed-management advice rather than relying on livestock to graze it down. A sustained plan is more realistic than a single clearing.

identification: Adult Common thrip is about 1.3–1.5 millimeters long, appearing dark brown to nearly black; newly emerged individuals may be more reddish. Young stages begin pale and become yellow-orange to red. Under strong magnification, adults have a broad middle body section and unusual blister-like swellings along the forewings. These structures, together with antenna details, are important to specialist identification and cannot usually be resolved in a phone photograph. Greenhouse Thrips (Heliothrips haemorrhoidalis) and other small leaf-feeding thrips can produce confusing observations. Inspect older leaves, including their undersides, and photograph both the insects and the affected foliage. Record the host plant and whether immature stages are present. A diagnostic laboratory may need preserved specimens or infested leaves to confirm the species.
actions: Keep a newly acquired plant with suspected Common thrip separate from other susceptible plants until the insects are identified. Inspect older foliage on neighboring roses, grapevines, or tropical ornamentals rather than checking only fresh shoots and flowers. Do not distribute cuttings or move visibly infested plants to another property. Ask extension or a plant diagnostic laboratory how to submit a contained sample, including the plant's identity and the location of the feeding injury. If treatment is warranted, choose it with an adviser for that host and growing setting; an outdoor tree, greenhouse crop, and household potted plant need different approaches. Reinspect after action because surviving immature stages may be missed in an initial check.

sources.label: Thrips new to Florida — Entomology Circular 365
Retithrips syriacus — Thrips of California key

identification: Common Velvetgrass often reaches 3–4 feet tall when flowering. Short white hairs cover the leaf blades, the sheaths wrapped around the stems, and the stem joints. Gently separate a blade from its sheath to see the thin membranous ligule at the junction. The flower head is a branched panicle with numerous closely packed, pointed spikelets; it can appear narrow before opening into a broader triangular shape. Pinkish color is variable and should not be used alone. Creeping Velvetgrass (Holcus mollis) is a close relative, and hybrids have been reported, so unusual plants may need a specialist. Photograph the leaf surface, stem joints, ligule, and mature flower head together. A mown patch without flowering material can be difficult to confirm.
actions: Target small outlying Common Velvetgrass clumps before tackling a large stand. Lift or hoe unwanted clumps with their crowns and roots, taking care to avoid tearing up neighboring desirable grasses. Prevent seed production where possible and contain mature heads before moving cut material. Hand removal is laborious and may reduce abundance without exhausting the soil seed bank, so inspect the area repeatedly after rain and disturbance. Clean soil and grass seed from mowers and other equipment before entering uninfested sites. Reestablish appropriate vegetation over cleared patches. In wet meadows or conservation grassland, coordinate mowing or other treatment with the land manager so that timing protects desired plants and wildlife as well as limiting this grass.

sources.label: Holcus lanatus — Fire Effects Information System

identification: Common viper's bugloss typically reaches 1–3 feet tall above a deep taproot. Lower leaves are long and narrow, often up to about 6 inches, while stem leaves become smaller upward. Stems and leaves feel harsh because of stiff hairs. Flowers are funnel-shaped with five unequal lobes, pink in bud and usually bright blue when open. Four long stamens project prominently, with a fifth shorter one. Patterson's Curse (Echium plantagineum) has larger purple-blue flowers with only two conspicuously projecting stamens and less harsh leaves. Young rosettes are harder to identify than flowering plants. Include the stamens, side of a flower, lower leaves, and stem hairs in close photographs, while avoiding bare-skin contact with the plant.
actions: Check wildflower seed lists before sowing and avoid adding Common viper's bugloss where it could escape into pasture or natural areas. Remove small unwanted rosettes while the soil is moist, digging deeply enough to lift the crown and taproot. Wear gloves and protective sleeves because the stiff hairs can irritate skin. Revisit plants that were incompletely removed, since they can regrow. Prevent flowering plants from releasing mature nutlets, and contain seed-bearing material before transport. Clean tools and footwear after working in a seeding patch. Keep removed plants out of livestock feed. A local weed adviser can help plan larger infestations and choose an accepted disposal route for the material.

sources.label: Echium vulgare — New Zealand Plant Conservation Network

identification: Adults are roughly 5½–8 inches long, including the tail. Look for a slender, somewhat flattened body, long toes, and a long tail, with a brown or gray back and darker spots or bands along the sides. Some individuals have a netlike pattern across the back; underside colors vary and should not be treated as a single defining mark. Introduced Italian wall lizards can be confused with this species, so a distant photograph of a brown lizard is insufficient. Photograph the back, side of the head, and entire body without catching or restraining it. Include location and approximate length, and note whether several animals or young lizards were present.
actions: Record the location, date, number seen, and photographs, then share an unexpected population with the relevant state wildlife agency or local herpetology program. Indiana specifically requests photographed sightings through its wildlife survey contact. Do not move lizards to another garden or release captive animals outdoors. Before relocating landscape materials from an occupied site, inspect crevices where animals may shelter. Avoid glue traps or broad pesticide applications: neither provides a sound identification or population-management plan. If animals repeatedly enter a building, address gaps around doors and foundations and ask a wildlife professional about humane exclusion appropriate to the site.

sources.label: Center for North American Herpetology — Podarcis muralis

identification: Common wheat is an annual grass, often approaching 3 feet tall, with broad, flat leaves and a dense, unbranched grain head. At the junction of blade and sheath, look for small projections that clasp the stem; these often carry hairs. Heads may have conspicuous bristles or lack them, depending on the cultivar, so bristles alone cannot identify wheat. Barley has a different arrangement of its flower units: each barley spikelet contains one flower, whereas wheat spikelets contain several. Durum wheat and wheat–rye hybrids can require closer examination. Photograph the whole plant, the leaf collar, and a mature head from both sides; seedlings or a bag of detached grain may not resolve the species.
actions: If Common wheat is unwanted in a garden, pull or hoe young plants before the heads develop mature grain. Remove ripe heads carefully so seeds are not scattered during cleanup. Look for the source of repeated volunteers, such as spilled feed, seed mixes, or grain handling, and correct that source before treating the same patch repeatedly. In a crop field, ask local Extension about volunteer-wheat management suited to the crop rotation rather than applying a garden recommendation at farm scale. Keep useful records of when plants emerge and whether they set seed; ordinary planted wheat does not need removal merely because it is introduced.

identification: Compact brome commonly reaches about 20 inches tall and has several stems from a fibrous root system. Lower leaves can be noticeably hairy while upper portions are less hairy. The seedhead branches and flower clusters spread enough that the supporting axes remain visible. Red brome, Bromus rubens, has a more tightly packed head, although both plants can develop reddish colors. The UCLA regional treatment also reports later flowering in Compact brome, but that local timing is not a reliable nationwide test. Photograph mature heads against a plain background, the lower leaf sheaths, and the whole plant. A botanist may need measurements of individual flower parts to separate these bromes confidently.
actions: Check a suspected patch while the heads are developing, before ripe bristly seeds can be carried on clothing or equipment. For a small confirmed patch, pull plants with their roots when the soil is workable and contain any developed seedheads. Clean footwear and tools before moving to an uninfested area. Revisit the patch after subsequent rains because removing visible annual plants does not remove seeds already in the soil. Retain or restore appropriate ground cover where repeated disturbance favors germination. For larger infestations, ask a local weed specialist to distinguish Compact brome from red brome before selecting a treatment or interpreting fire-risk advice.

sources.label: US Forest Service FEIS — Compact brome and red brome
Prigge and Gibson — Bromus madritensis subsp. madritensis

identification: Adult females are small, oval insects covered in white wax, with short wax threads around the sides and longer threads at the rear. UC IPM describes the rear pair as about one-quarter of the body length and the wax covering as thicker than in citrus mealybug. Longtailed mealybug instead has tail threads longer than its body. Newly hatched young, called crawlers, have little wax and can be yellowish, orange, or pink. Inspect sheltered places around fruit stems, leaf joints, and bark crevices. Photograph an individual sharply enough to show its rear threads and record the host plant. Worn wax, immature insects, and crowded colonies can obscure identification, so a diagnostic laboratory may need specimens.
actions: Inspect new plants and keep suspect stock separate while identification is arranged. On established plants, follow ant trails and examine tender shoots and fruit stems for living insects rather than judging infestation from old mold alone. Remove heavily infested small plant parts when practical and collect orchard litter that can shelter overwintering stages. Preserve lady beetles and other natural enemies; indiscriminate insecticide use can work against them. For a persistent infestation, send close photographs and host information to Extension and ask about treatment timed to crawlers. Monitor the plant afterward, because hidden mealybugs and eggs can remain even when exposed colonies have been removed.

sources.label: Agriculture and Agri-Food Canada — Pear crop profile

identification: A supported vine can reach about 20 feet, although clipped or ground-cover plants are much shorter. Leaves occur in opposite pairs and are simple, glossy, leathery, and smooth-edged. New foliage may be bronze or purplish. The small white flowers have five slightly twisted, overlapping lobes that give a pinwheel appearance, usually appearing most abundantly in late spring. Broken stems release milky sap; do not deliberately expose skin to it as an identification test. True jasmines can also have scented white flowers, so combine flower shape with leaf arrangement and stem characters. Photograph a flowering shoot, a pair of leaves, and the climbing habit; the similar Asian jasmine (Trachelospermum asiaticum) needs closer examination. HortFlora distinguishes it by a hairless flower throat, unlike the finely hairy throat of Confederate jasmine.
actions: Keep planted Confederate jasmine within its intended area by checking trailing stems and pruning after the main flowering period. Remove stems that have rooted beyond the bed, including the rooted portions rather than only cutting the connecting vine. Collect cuttings instead of leaving them on moist soil or dumping them along a woodland edge. Wear gloves and clean sticky sap from tools after pruning. If an escaped patch is covering valued plants, trace its stems to the base before removal so neighboring vegetation is not torn out with it. Recheck the area for rooted pieces and new shoots, and use a locally suitable replacement where repeated escape makes maintenance impractical.

sources.label: JC Raulston Arboretum — Trachelospermum jasminoides collections
Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria HortFlora — Trachelospermum jasminoides

identification: Female covers are approximately 1.8–2.1 millimeters long, slightly oval and raised, with gray margins and a central light-brown or yellowish remnant of the insect's earlier skin. Male covers are smaller, more elongated, and paler. Look along needles and twigs with a hand lens and photograph the cover beside a millimeter scale. Include the conifer's name and pictures of affected branches. Elongate hemlock scale and other conifer-feeding armored scales can be mistaken for this species; host and needle damage alone will not separate them. Reliable confirmation may require an adult female removed from its cover and examined on a microscope slide, as nursery inspectors use specialist identification.
actions: Keep suspect nursery stock or holiday greenery separate from living conifers until the insect is identified. Do not carry infested branches to another property or leave them beneath outdoor host trees. Contact Extension or the state plant-health office with clear photographs and the source of the material, especially for recently purchased stock. Ask that office how to contain and dispose of confirmed infested greenery locally; an enforcement action in another state is not automatically the right instruction for your site. For a living landscape tree, have the infestation and tree condition assessed before pruning extensively or choosing a treatment timed to vulnerable young scales.

sources.label: Minnesota Department of Agriculture — 2023 Nursery Certification Report

identification: Mature Cooper's cyathea can reach about 40 feet, with triangular fronds reported up to 20 feet long under favorable conditions. The trunk shows oval scars where old leaf stalks have fallen away, and the stalks bear pale or whitish hairs and scales. Hawaii's native hapuu tree ferns have reddish hairs and a thick fibrous covering around the trunk, providing useful local comparisons. Height alone is unreliable because young tree ferns have not developed their mature trunks. Photograph the entire plant, the trunk surface, a close view of the stalk covering, and the undersides of mature fronds. Identification outside Hawaii should use the locally present tree-fern species rather than assuming the hapuu comparison covers every lookalike.
actions: Check around an established planting for small ferns emerging beyond the garden, particularly in damp shaded ground. Have volunteers identified before removal so native ferns are not mistaken for this species. Avoid planting additional Cooper's cyathea beside vulnerable moist forest where local invasive-plant guidance advises against it. Small confirmed volunteers may be removed carefully with their growing base; a tall trunk needs an appropriate professional removal plan. Contain fronds and soil during cleanup and do not dump them in natural areas. Where a local program requests reports, send location and diagnostic photographs first; Hawaii specifically asks for reports of this fern on Molokai.

sources.label: Hawaii Invasive Species Council — Australian Tree Fern
Botanic Gardens of South Australia — Cyathea cooperi

identification: Plants can reach about 33 feet tall and have smooth bark, finely divided gray to bluish leaves, and round golden flower heads borne in clusters. Young pods may have a bluish color. Some garden forms have purple foliage, so leaf color is not fixed. The lowest pair of main leaf divisions is shorter and can turn back around the stem, a useful detail to photograph. Silver wattle, Acacia dealbata, and other feathery-leaved wattles can look similar, and this species can hybridize with related wattles. Include close photographs of a whole leaf, its attachment to the twig, flower clusters, and pods. A broad canopy photograph alone generally cannot establish the species or exclude a hybrid.
actions: Remove small unwanted seedlings while roots can still be lifted without major soil disturbance, preferably before they produce flowers and pods. Collect seed-bearing branches and pods instead of moving them to another garden or dumping them along a roadside. Recheck around the parent tree and disturbed soil for new seedlings, including after hot conditions or fire. Large plants require a site-specific removal plan, especially near structures or native vegetation. Do not use fire as a casual control method: heat can stimulate seeds already in the soil. Replace escaping plantings with a locally suitable species and keep follow-up records, because the persistent seed supply can outlast the first cleanup.

sources.label: Australian National Botanic Gardens — Acacia baileyana
California Invasive Plant Council — Acacia baileyana
Plants of South Eastern NSW — Acacia baileyana

identification: An unaided view of a tiny swimming copepod cannot establish Cyclops strenuus. Specialists examine adult body proportions and detailed structures of the antennae, swimming legs, and tail branches under a microscope. USGS describes the genus Cyclops as having 17-segmented first antennae and a particular two-segmented fifth leg, but those genus characters do not settle this species. Cyclops sibiricus, Cyclops divergens, and Cyclops canadensis are especially important names in the history of North American identifications. Preserve the collection date, waterbody, sampling method, and original identification with any specimen. A modern taxonomic key and review of archived material are needed; no single size range or photograph-based species distinction is asserted here.
actions: Treat a suspected record as a request for expert identification, not a reason to treat a pond or lake. Contact a freshwater invertebrate specialist, state aquatic-invasive-species program, or university laboratory and ask what specimen preservation and collection documentation they require. Do not move live samples or aquarium water into another waterbody. Clean and dry sampling equipment between sites as a general precaution against moving aquatic organisms. If the record came from an older dataset, retain its original name and evidence while flagging it for taxonomic reassessment. A change to the accepted identification should be documented explicitly rather than silently replacing the species name.

sources.label: USGS Great Lakes Copepods — What's New
Einsle 1988 — Cyclops canadensis and C. scutifer
USGS Great Lakes Copepods — Cyclops sibiricus identification
Connolly et al.2022: Cyclops in the Great Lakes
Holynska and Dahms2004 comparative Cyclops microcharacters, digitized abstract

identification: The body is slightly flattened and boat-shaped, narrowing toward a rear section that may bend beneath it. Adult females have short first antennae with seven segments, and the tail branches are roughly as broad as they are long. These are microscopic characters, not features a phone photograph of pond water will normally capture. Smithsonian lists the marine and estuarine Harpacticus pacificus and Harpacticus uniremis as possible confusions. Young stages need particular care because adult diagnostic features are not fully developed. Provide a calibrated microscope image, the complete specimen, sampling location, and whether it came from sediment or open water. Adult females are about 0.8 millimeters long and males about 0.7 millimeters.
actions: Do not attempt to remove this copepod by draining, chemically treating, or disturbing a waterbody on the basis of an unconfirmed observation. A useful contribution is a well-documented sample reviewed by an aquatic invertebrate specialist. Ask the receiving laboratory for its collection and preservation instructions before collecting or shipping material. Keep water and sediment from the sampling site out of other waterways, and clean and dry nets, boots, and containers between sites. Reports should distinguish a newly confirmed occurrence from a claim of ecological damage. There is no species-specific homeowner eradication method supported by the sources reviewed here.

sources.label: Ishida 1987 — Freshwater Harpacticoid Copepods of Hokkaido, Northern Japan

identification: Adults are around half a millimeter long; females measured in the original California introduction report were 0.44–0.54 millimeters. The body has a broad front section and a narrower, segmented rear, with small appendages that must be examined under magnification. Limnoithona sinensis is a close lookalike. A taxonomic diagnosis uses the fifth pair of legs, including four spines or bristles on the free outer segment, rather than body color or swimming behavior. Early developmental stages are harder to assign. A useful record includes a calibrated microscope image, an adult specimen, collection date, location, and salinity if available. Ordinary photographs of water cannot confirm this species or distinguish it from other minute copepods.
actions: An apparent new occurrence should go to an estuarine plankton specialist or the state aquatic-invasive-species program for confirmation. Ask for instructions before collecting and preserving a sample; the net mesh and life stage affect what can be identified. Do not release live samples into a different creek, bay, pond, or aquarium outlet. Clean and dry sampling gear between sites and dispose of retained water away from connected waterways according to local guidance. For vessel operators, ballast-water management is the relevant prevention pathway. Removing these animals individually or adding chemicals to a waterbody is not a realistic landowner response to an established plankton population.

sources.label: Orsi and Ohtsuka 1999 — Asian copepod introductions

identification: Adult females in the material summarized by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service measured about 1.21–1.52 millimeters; males were about 0.74–0.88 millimeters. These are adult measurements, not sizes for every immature stage. Mesocyclops edax and Mesocyclops americanus can look similar. Unlike M. edax, M. pehpeiensis lacks hairs along the inner tail branches and lacks an inward-pointing spine on the base of the first swimming leg. The plate joining the fourth pair of legs has long spine-shaped projections; M. americanus has much smaller pointed projections there. These features require a microscope and sometimes dissection. Supply intact adult specimens, calibrated images, collection date and waterbody, and details of any association with purchased aquatic plants.
actions: Keep water from purchased aquatic plants and aquarium cultures out of natural waterways. Do not transfer this copepod between ponds as a home mosquito-control experiment; choose locally recommended mosquito prevention instead. If a suspect population is associated with newly received aquatic stock, keep the stock contained and contact Extension or an aquatic-invertebrate laboratory before distributing plants. Clean and dry nets, buckets, and other equipment between waterbodies. For a reported new wild occurrence, preserve location and sampling details and obtain an expert identification. Avoid treating a whole pond for an unconfirmed identification; other small freshwater animals could be affected too.

sources.label: Connolly et al. 2019 — Asian cyclopoid copepod Mesocyclops pehpeiensis in western Lake Erie
Hwang, Kumar and Ku 2009 — Impacts of Mesocyclops pehpeiensis predation on four cladoceran species

identification: Females measure about 0.5–0.75 millimeters and males about 0.5–0.6 millimeters. Under a microscope, specialists look for a narrow forward projection on the head and tail branches approximately twice as long as wide. Other useful characters include a small rear plate edged with about ten teeth and the arrangement of spines on the swimming legs. Those characters cannot reliably be judged from a blurry image of a moving speck. Nitokra incerta is a documented lookalike; specialists compare the fifth legs and other microscopic structures. Size and habitat alone are insufficient. Submit an intact adult specimen or calibrated microscope images with the date, waterbody, and sampled substrate; juveniles may remain unidentified at species level.
actions: Focus on preventing transport with water, aquatic plants, and wet equipment rather than trying to remove individual animals from a lake. Clean and dry sampling nets, waders, buckets, and similar gear before taking them to another site. Keep collected sediment and water at the source or follow the receiving laboratory's disposal instructions; never empty a live sample into a different waterbody. If identification would extend the known range, ask a state aquatic-invasive-species program or specialist to review the specimen and its collection record. Do not apply pond chemicals on the strength of a suspected identification. The reviewed management synthesis offers no established physical removal method for this species.

sources.label: USGS and NOAA GLANSIS — Nitokra hibernica
NOAA — Management of established Great Lakes nonindigenous species
Briski, Wiley and Bailey 2012 — Role of domestic shipping in introduction or secondary spread
Bolduc et al. 2026 — Taxonomy and Functional Traits Modulate the Environmental Niche Dimensions of Crustacean Zooplankton Communities in Submerged Aquatic Vegetation Beds

identification: Adult females are about 0.54–0.62 millimeters long, with males approximately 0.47–0.53 millimeters. Under magnification, females have a downward-pointing projection at the front of the head and may carry two egg masses. The slender rear body and tail bristles are useful structures to photograph, but are not unique by themselves. Specialists examine antenna segments, tail proportions, and small leg structures to distinguish Oithona davisae from Oithona brevicornis, Oithona nana, and other relatives. Males differ in head shape and antenna structure, so a female-only key cannot simply be applied to them. Provide adult specimens, calibrated microscope images, location, date, and salinity if measured; young stages require additional caution.
actions: Report a suspected new population through the relevant marine-invasive-species or plankton-monitoring program and obtain a specialist identification. Keep live samples contained, and do not discard them into a different bay, pond, or drain connected to surface water. Clean and dry sampling gear between sites. For commercial vessels, preventing transport in ballast water is the practical intervention; follow the applicable vessel-management process rather than improvising treatment. A shoreline landowner cannot selectively eradicate established microscopic plankton by hand. Avoid adding chemicals to estuarine water or treating all small crustaceans as this species, because native copepods occupy the same habitats and are important parts of aquatic food webs.

sources.label: Washington Invasive Species Council — Invasive Zooplankton

identification: Adults are roughly 1.5–2.3 millimeters long in the populations summarized by Smithsonian, with measured ranges differing among locations and studies. The feeding limbs are conspicuously clawlike under a microscope. Both sexes have an unevenly shaped rear body, and the right tail branch is slightly longer than the left. Females have distinctive right-side projections on rear body segments; males have modified antennae and an uneven fifth pair of legs. Tortanus discaudatus is a related comparison, but immature stages cannot be confidently assigned using an adult description alone. Photograph the whole adult and rear body at known magnification, preserve the specimen as directed by a specialist, and record the sampling site and salinity.
actions: A suspected occurrence outside an already documented estuary should be reviewed by a marine plankton specialist or state invasive-species program. Preserve the sampling record and ask for suitable specimen-handling instructions before shipping material. Prevent movement of live samples, retained water, and wet gear between estuaries; clean and dry equipment after sampling. Vessel operators should address the ballast-water pathway through their established compliance and treatment procedures. Do not attempt a chemical treatment of a bay or pond from an uncertain microscope identification. Monitoring abundance and distribution is a useful response, while claims about effects on fish should be tied to research rather than inferred solely from the copepod's presence.

sources.label: Orsi and Ohtsuka 1999 — Asian copepod introductions

identification: Plants generally form mats under about 14 inches tall, with stems that become woody as they age. The smooth, pale blue-green leaves occur in opposite pairs and are fingerlike, with a rounded triangular cross section and blunt tips. Flowers are commonly about 1–2 inches across, with many narrow petals; their upper surfaces may be orange, red, or yellow while the undersides are pinkish purple. Hottentot fig, Carpobrotus edulis, has more sharply triangular leaves and usually larger flowers, about 6–10 centimeters across. Flower color alone is insufficient. Photograph a flowering stem from above and below, a leaf pair, and a ripe capsule if available. A regional flora may be needed to distinguish related cultivated ice plants, especially nonflowering material.
actions: For a small escaped patch, lift the mat carefully and collect rooted stem joints as well as loose pieces. Avoid dragging fragments through adjacent vegetation or leaving them on moist bare soil. Contain seed-bearing material and dispose of it through an appropriate local green-waste route instead of dumping it on dunes, bluffs, or streambanks. Check the cleared area after rain for rooted pieces and seedlings. On slopes or among native plants, work in sections and arrange suitable replacement cover so removal does not expose an entire bank at once. Repeated garden escape is a reason to replace the planting rather than keep trimming the same advancing edge.

sources.label: Prigge and Gibson: Aizoaceae identification key

identification: Coral vine can climb 25 feet or more, although seasonal growth and cold damage affect its size. Leaves are alternate, simple, and usually heart-shaped to triangular, with long-pointed tips. Curling tendrils and clusters of many small pink flowers are useful visible features; white-flowered forms also occur. The flowers can continue over a long warm season, and dry flower parts remain around the small fruits. A heart-shaped leaf alone could belong to many unrelated vines, so photograph the tendrils, a flowering cluster, leaf attachments, and the base of the plant. Related ornamentals sold under names such as queen's wreath can create common-name confusion; confirmation should retain the scientific name Antigonon leptopus.
actions: Remove small plants before they produce mature seeds, collecting any developing fruits during the work. Trace cut stems back to the root crown and remove the enlarged underground roots when feasible; these are reserves from which new shoots can grow. Where digging would damage surrounding plants or soil, repeated cutting can weaken the vine but requires several visits. Keep cut material and seeds out of waterways and do not move them to new planting sites. Recheck after frost or an apparently successful cleanup. For a large infestation covering trees, seek a local invasive-plant specialist's plan and work carefully around the plants being rescued rather than pulling the whole canopy down.

sources.label: UF IFAS — Antigonon leptopus plant directory

identification: Coralbush is usually a shrub around 6–10 feet tall, though floras report larger plants under favorable conditions. Leaves are carried on long stalks and divided almost to the base into roughly 9–11 narrow, pointed lobes; individual lobes may themselves be cut or toothed. Small red flowers form relatively flat clusters at the ends of long stalks. Yellowish, three-angled fruit contains seeds. Other Jatropha species also have red flowers or lobed leaves, so the depth and pattern of leaf division are more informative than flower color alone. Photograph a complete leaf, its stalk attachment, the flower cluster, and fruit without opening it by hand. Do not taste any plant part to help identify it.
actions: Inspect beneath and beyond a planted Coralbush for unwanted seedlings and remove small confirmed volunteers before they develop fruit. Wear gloves when pruning or uprooting, avoid contact with sap, and keep collected fruit and seeds away from children and animals. Do not place cuttings or seed-bearing waste along roadsides or natural-area edges. If the plant repeatedly escapes, replace it with a suitable local alternative and revisit the old site for volunteers. Ask Extension to confirm uncertain plants before extensive removal, especially when only seedlings are present. Management should respond to documented spread at the site; an ornamental shrub's introduced origin alone is not evidence that all established specimens need removal.

sources.label: Queensland Poisons Information Centre — Coral plant

identification: This hybrid forms perennial marsh-grass stands with upright stems and narrow leaves. Plant height and leaf color change with growing conditions, so they cannot reliably separate it from related cordgrasses. A taxonomic treatment distinguishes this group from smooth cordgrass partly through longer flower units and broader flower-cluster axes, but Spartina x townsendii and Spartina anglica overlap strongly in outward appearance. The decisive distinction is fertility: the hybrid's pollen is sterile, whereas Spartina anglica is fertile. Pollen testing or other specialist work may be required. Photograph the whole patch, mature flowering heads, leaf collars, and site context, but do not claim a definitive hybrid identification from those images alone.
actions: Send a suspected nonnative cordgrass patch to the local estuary manager or invasive-plant program before digging or cutting. Record its location and extent from accessible ground, avoiding disturbance of marsh vegetation and wildlife. Specialist confirmation should distinguish this sterile hybrid from native cordgrasses and fertile Spartina anglica before a treatment plan is chosen. Do not transplant plants or move sediment and underground stem fragments to another shoreline. Where removal is approved by the responsible site manager, follow that program's timing, access, and disposal directions. A private effort based on a photograph can remove native marsh grass or move viable fragments without resolving the underlying identification problem.

sources.label: USGS — San Francisco Bay nonindigenous species report

identification: These are perennial tidal-marsh grasses with upright stems, narrow blades, and flowering heads made of several slender branches. Size and leaf form vary considerably across the hybrid population and with marsh conditions; there is no single dependable height or color test. Some hybrids have reddish or purplish leaf bases, but others do not. Native California cordgrass can look very similar, particularly before flowering. The Invasive Spartina Project combines mature-plant measurements with genetic evidence to improve identification. Photograph the full patch, flowering heads, leaf bases, and position relative to the tide line without trampling into it. Treat an identification from appearance alone as provisional when native cordgrass is present.
actions: Report an unfamiliar or expanding cordgrass patch to the local marsh manager or an established cordgrass-control program. Provide location, photographs, and an estimate of patch size; specialist review is needed before removal to protect native California cordgrass. Do not transplant marsh plants or transport mud and underground stem pieces between sites. Avoid cutting or digging an unidentified patch independently, especially in wildlife habitat. Coordinated treatment needs to account for seed production, tides, access, and bird breeding, and the Invasive Spartina Project explicitly adjusts work around these factors. After professional treatment, support follow-up monitoring rather than assuming one visit has eliminated all hybrid seedlings or surviving plants.

sources.label: Invasive Spartina Project — Monitoring and Treatment
UC Davis — Spartina alterniflora × foliosa hybrids scorecard
San Francisco Estuary Institute — Smooth cordgrass

identification: Coriander generally grows about 1–2 feet tall. Lower leaves have broad lobes resembling parsley, while upper leaves are much more finely divided. Small white or pinkish flowers occur in umbrella-shaped clusters, followed by round yellow-brown fruits. The changing leaf shape can make a flowering plant look unlike the cilantro sold as fresh bunches. Parsley is a useful comparison for the lower leaves, but leaf resemblance or smell alone does not establish identity among the carrot family. Photograph the lower and upper leaves, their attachments, flower clusters, and developing fruits. Do not taste an unidentified roadside plant; a known garden source and the combination of mature characters provide much stronger evidence.
actions: Where Coriander volunteers are unwanted, pull or hoe seedlings while they are small and remove flowering plants before mature fruits drop. If you want a contained herb crop, harvest or collect ripe fruits deliberately rather than allowing all of them to fall around the bed. Check nearby paths and recently disturbed soil for the next flush of seedlings. Keep seed-bearing garden waste out of natural areas and inspect seed mixes or spilled kitchen seed if plants repeatedly appear in the same place. There is no need for a broad eradication campaign against an ordinary managed herb planting; address actual escape and interference at the site.

identification: Mature Cork oak can approach 65 feet tall, though many planted specimens are shorter and branch low. Leaves are alternate, roughly 1½–3 inches long, dark green above and pale gray beneath, usually with several short teeth along each edge. Acorns sit in cups with elongated scales that can look loose or shaggy. The exceptionally thick corky bark is most useful on older trees; seedlings lack that conspicuous character. Holm oak and native evergreen oaks can resemble its foliage, so a leaf alone may not settle identification. Photograph both leaf surfaces, a twig showing leaf arrangement, bark, and acorns with their cups. Avoid stripping bark to expose an identification feature.
actions: Check beneath a planted Cork oak and beyond the maintained area for self-sown seedlings. Remove unwanted small seedlings while the roots can be lifted with limited disturbance, after confirming they are not locally native oaks. Collect fallen acorns where concentrated recruitment creates a recurring problem, and avoid moving acorn-bearing soil into restoration areas. A mature tree should be assessed in the context of documented spread, shade, habitat, and site use before removal is considered. Use a qualified arborist for work on large trees. Do not strip or damage the bark as an improvised control method; commercial cork harvesting is a specialized practice, not a homeowner removal technique.

identification: The modern revision describes closely related crust-forming fungi with tiny pores, differing in color, spores, and crystal-coated microscopic structures. Those features are not a dependable field diagnosis of Rigidoporus vinctus, because the name has covered multiple species. Rotten corms, discolored roots, or a photograph of a crust do not establish Rigidoporus vinctus. A useful diagnostic submission includes the host's scientific name, affected tissue, photographs of symptoms and any fruiting body, and collection location. The final identification must connect the specimen to a current taxonomic description; color, season, and host symptoms alone cannot resolve this name's complicated history.
actions: Keep affected planting material separate from healthy stock while a plant-diagnostic laboratory evaluates it. Record where it came from, which plants are affected, and whether decay appeared in storage or after planting. Ask the laboratory what tissue to submit before discarding every symptomatic piece; material from the active margin of a lesion may be more useful than completely decomposed tissue. Do not distribute suspect corms, roots, or soil to another garden while the cause is unresolved. Avoid choosing a fungicide, destroying nearby trees, or assigning a quarantine status from this name alone. The first necessary action is confirming the organism and its relationship to the observed disease.

sources.label: Miettinen and collaborators — Revised Cerrenaceae classification
NCBI Taxonomy: Lividopora vincta and the Rigidoporus vinctus name

identification: Plants commonly stand about 8–24 inches tall, with hairy leaf sheaths and narrow blades. The mature flowerhead is open and often one-sided, carrying a relatively small number of large, nodding spikelets. Their bristles twist and spread outward as they dry. Japanese brome, Bromus japonicus, is particularly similar; Corn brome usually has fewer, larger flower clusters, and the small enclosing flower scales have more sharply angled sides. These distinctions need ripe material and often a hand lens. Photograph the whole head, a close side view of several spikelets, the leaf sheaths, and a ruler. Seedlings and freshly emerging heads generally do not provide enough evidence for a confident separation.
actions: Confirm the grass before treating a mixed brome patch, especially where native grasses occur. Pull isolated plants before ripe seed is shed and collect any mature heads separately so their bristles do not catch on clothing or equipment. Inspect spilled grain, feed areas, and recently imported seed if the same site repeatedly produces plants. Clean mowing or collection equipment before leaving a seeded patch. For a larger stand, work with local Extension on timing and desirable replacement cover rather than leaving extensive bare soil. Recheck the site in the next growing season, since removing annual plants does not remove the seeds already present.

identification: Plants usually grow about 6–24 inches tall with upright, branching stems. Basal leaves have stalks and broad, toothed outlines; upper leaves divide into three narrow segments and may have little or no stalk. The small yellow flowers have five petals. After flowering, several flattened, spine-covered fruits form a compact head. Bulbous buttercup is a named lookalike, but it has a swollen base and does not share Corn buttercup's narrow upper leaf divisions. Photograph the whole plant, lower and upper leaves, and a mature fruit head with a ruler. A yellow flower alone is insufficient, and very young plants may need to be revisited when their upper leaves or fruits develop.
actions: Remove small confirmed patches before the spiny fruits mature, lifting plants and roots when soil conditions permit. If fruits have already formed, collect them carefully rather than shaking or mowing them across the site. Wear gloves during handling and keep removed plants out of livestock feed and harvested material. Inspect field margins and disturbed patches for new seedlings during the next growing period. In pasture or crops, ask Extension for management matched to the forage or crop and the infestation's stage. Maintain suitable cover after removal, and verify nearby buttercups individually rather than assuming every yellow-flowered plant belongs to the same species.

sources.label: University of Missouri WeedID — Corn Buttercup

identification: Plants can reach about 2 feet tall, with branching stems and finely divided alternate leaves. Individual flowerheads are usually around an inch across, with white rays and many small yellow flowers in the center. As the head matures, the center becomes more raised. Stinking chamomile, Anthemis cotula, is a close lookalike. Corn chamomile has broader papery scales throughout the central flowerhead and relatively smooth-ribbed, squared fruits; stinking chamomile has narrower scales concentrated higher in the head and bumpier fruits. These differences may need a lens and mature material. Photograph leaves, a side view of the head, and dry fruits. Published descriptions disagree about scent, so smell is not used here as the decisive test.
actions: Pull small confirmed patches before flowerheads develop ripe fruits, taking the taproot where practical. Collect mature heads before moving plants so seed is not shaken across a path, lawn, or field. Inspect seed mixes and newly disturbed ground if plants appear repeatedly, and establish suitable ground cover after removal. In a crop, pasture, or large turf area, ask Extension to identify the chamomile and advise on timing appropriate to the setting. Do not assume a tea or ornamental chamomile is the same species. Keep a few clear photographs of the mature diagnostic parts so later seedlings can be linked to a verified identification rather than a general daisy appearance.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand — Anthemis arvensis

identification: Plants range from about 4–28 inches tall, with simple or lightly branched stems covered in short hairs that lie close to the surface. Leaves occur alternately along the stem, have smooth edges, and become narrow and stalkless toward the top. Tiny white to bluish-white flowers sit among the upper leaves; each is a short funnel with five lobes. Four hard nutlets can develop from a flower. Other small borage-family plants may look similar before fruiting, so photograph a complete stem, close views of the hairs and leaf attachment, flowers, and mature nutlets. A young leafy plant or a distant image of white flowers does not provide the same confidence as those combined features.
actions: Look for Corn gromwell in thin ground cover and winter-crop margins while it is flowering, before the nutlets mature. Pull or hoe a small confirmed patch and collect fruiting stems so hard seeds are not scattered during cleanup. Avoid bringing seed-bearing soil or contaminated planting material into a clean bed. Revisit the patch after the next germination period and maintain suitable vegetation where repeated bare-ground disturbance favors annual weeds. For substantial populations in crops or pasture, use local Extension advice matched to the production system. Do not feed removed plants to animals or treat the plant's commercial oilseed use as a basis for consuming wild material.

sources.label: USDA NRCS — Forb Seedling Identification Guide

identification: Wingless adults are roughly 2 millimeters long and usually bluish green to olive, with dark legs, short antennae, and two short black tubes near the rear. Dark or purplish patches surround the bases of those tubes. Young aphids resemble smaller adults, while winged forms occur when populations disperse. Russian wheat aphid can be confused with it because both are small and have short antennae; Corn leaf aphid has prominent dark rear tubes and lacks the extra rear projection described for Russian wheat aphid. Photograph several individuals with a scale, including side and top views, and record the grass or crop. Honeydew and yellow leaves alone do not identify the species.
actions: Inspect developing leaves, tassels, and nearby host grasses, recording whether colonies are increasing and whether the crop shows injury. Look for lady beetles, hoverfly larvae, and parasitized aphids before deciding intervention is needed; these natural enemies can suppress populations. In a small garden, monitor individual plants closely rather than spraying the entire planting automatically. In field crops, consult current Extension thresholds for the crop and growth stage, especially when virus risk or pollination is a concern. Avoid moving infested seedlings to new plantings. UC's small-grain guidance says this aphid seldom requires treatment, so the presence of a few insects is not a treatment threshold.

sources.label: Oklahoma State Extension — Corn leaf aphid
UC IPM — Corn Leaf Aphid in Small Grains

identification: Typical Corn poppy plants have branching, bristly stems around 1–2 feet tall, though size varies with conditions. Leaves are alternate and deeply lobed or divided. Flowers stand singly on long hairy stalks and usually have four broad scarlet petals, often with dark blotches near the base. Numerous dark stamens surround a disk-topped central capsule that becomes conspicuous after petals fall. Oriental poppy is a commonly grown perennial lookalike, whereas Corn poppy is annual; color alone cannot distinguish them. Photograph the leaves, hair direction on the flower stalk, and mature capsule as well as the open flower. Garden cultivars may obscure typical flower characters, so fertile fruit is particularly useful.
actions: If Corn poppy is unwanted outside its intended bed, remove seedlings early or collect developing capsules before seeds are released. Bag ripe capsules before handling whole plants so their small seeds do not scatter. Check the contents of wildflower seed mixes and choose locally appropriate alternatives when planting beside natural habitat. Revisit disturbed soil in later seasons, where seed left from earlier plants may germinate. A cultivated patch can be managed by deliberate seed collection and removal of volunteers rather than treating every flower as a serious invasion. For a persistent crop infestation, seek crop-specific advice rather than applying a garden cleanup method at field scale.

sources.label: Colorado State Extension — Poppy identification response

identification: Look for low, spreading or rising stems with small hairy leaves. Lower leaves occur in opposite pairs and are relatively rounded; upper leaves on flowering shoots are narrower and alternate. Tiny pale-blue to violet flowers occur on short stalks, and the developing capsules are heart-shaped and hairy. Creeping speedwell and purslane speedwell are useful named comparisons, but the combination of growth habit, hairs, leaf arrangement, and fruit is more reliable than flower color alone. Photograph the entire low plant, both lower and upper leaves, and a capsule beside a ruler. A close image of one blue flower can establish a speedwell-like plant without resolving which species it is.
actions: Hand-pull small patches while soil is moist and before the heart-shaped capsules release seed. In turf, inspect the reason grass is thin—such as unsuitable mowing, persistent shade, or repeated wear—and correct the condition where feasible before reseeding. Keep garden soil covered with suitable plants or mulch rather than repeatedly leaving open germination sites. Record where winter seedlings recur so the next check happens before flowering. Extensive lawn treatment is not automatically necessary for a few plants. If the weed is persistent or mixed with other speedwells, ask Extension to verify it and recommend management compatible with the turf species and the site's intended use.

identification: Look for branching plants about 5–70 cm tall, with slender, somewhat fleshy leaves that appear in rings or crowded clusters at the stem joints. Individual leaves are about 15–50 mm long but less than 1 mm wide. The stems and leaves may carry gland-tipped hairs. Flowers have five separate white petals, each roughly 2.5–4 mm long, followed by small capsules that open to release seeds. Young seedlings already have needlelike first leaves. Several other spurries occur, including Spergula morisonii and S. pentandra; a distant photograph of white flowers is insufficient to separate them. Photograph the whole plant, leaf clusters, flowers, and mature capsules, and retain close views of seeds for a botanical identification.
actions: In a garden or small cultivated patch, remove Corn Spurry while plants are young and before capsules mature. Collect seed-bearing material rather than shaking it over clean ground. Check again after rain and soil disturbance, because a surviving seedbank can produce another flush. Clean soil and plant debris from equipment before moving between fields, and avoid transferring infested topsoil into beds. In cropped ground, use soil testing and crop-specific advice to address conditions that favor the weed; changing soil acidity without a test is not a useful blanket remedy. Record whether the patch is spreading or competing with the crop so management addresses an actual problem.

sources.label: AHDB: Distribution and biology of corn spurrey

identification: Corndaisy usually stands about 20–80 cm tall, with smooth, fleshy stems and leaves. Flowerheads are commonly 3–6 cm across and have yellow rays around a yellow center. Lower leaves may be lobed or coarsely toothed; the upper leaves attach directly to the stem and partly clasp it. This combination matters more than a yellow flowerhead alone. Crown daisy, Glebionis coronaria, generally has much more deeply divided leaves and may have white rays with yellow bases. Photograph a lower leaf and an upper clasping leaf, as well as the entire flowering plant. Mature fruits can help a botanist: outer fruits have narrow wings, and the fruits lack a tuft of bristles. Seedlings are less distinctive than flowering plants.
actions: If Corndaisy is unwanted in a bed or field margin, pull or hoe young plants before flowerheads produce mature fruit. Gather mature heads carefully so the seeds do not spill into nearby soil. Revisit disturbed patches through the growing season and record whether seedlings return the following year. Where the plant is intentionally grown, deadheading provides a simple way to limit self-sowing. Check purchased seed mixtures before sowing near natural areas or production fields. A scattered ornamental escape does not by itself justify treating a whole site; focus on established patches that are spreading or interfering with the intended vegetation, and keep soil movement from carrying their seeds elsewhere.

identification: Plants are often 60–120 cm tall and can approach 2 m. Leaves are roughly 1–2.5 cm wide, with conspicuous midribs and margins, and rise in a loose fan. The usually unbranched flower spike carries flowers mainly to one side. Flowers are unscented, with a curved tube about 3.5–5 cm long; the upper hood is larger than the lower lobes. Color varies, so red petals alone are not diagnostic. Garden gladiolus hybrids can overlap in appearance and require careful floral measurements. Photograph the whole spike, a side view showing the flower tube, leaf width, and the flower face with a scale. A dormant corm without leaves or flowers will rarely support a confident species identification.
actions: Keep Cornflag plantings within a managed bed if they are producing volunteers nearby. Remove spent flower stalks before capsules release seed, and inspect the bed edge for new shoots. When removing an unwanted clump, lift the corm and the small corms around its base; cutting leaves alone leaves the underground stem in place. Recheck the site during subsequent growing seasons for overlooked corms and seedlings. Do not discard corms, excavated soil, or garden waste along roadsides or in natural areas. For an apparent escape, photograph flowering plants before removal so a local herbarium or extension office can distinguish the species from cultivated hybrids.

identification: Adults are slender, brown to dark brown beetles about 2.5–5 mm long. The wing covers have orderly rows of punctures, and the head is visible from above. Larvae are pale, curved grubs with darker heads, usually concealed in the wood. Lyctus cavicollis is a close lookalike; specialist keys distinguish the single rows of wing-cover punctures and prominent frontal lobes of Cosmopolitan powderpost beetle from its features. Lyctus brunneus is another similar household species. Photograph any adult from above beside a ruler, and retain it in a closed container for an entomologist. Also photograph the wood, exit holes, and fresh debris. Dust or holes alone cannot identify the beetle or reliably establish that an infestation remains active.
actions: Isolate a suspect movable wooden item from other unfinished hardwood while arranging identification. Note and photograph existing holes, clear away loose dust, and check later for newly formed holes or fresh accumulations; vibrations can also dislodge old debris. Inspect incoming lumber and secondhand furniture before bringing them into storage or use. Finishing exposed wood helps prevent new egg laying, but it does not remove larvae already inside. A small affected component may be replaceable; valuable furniture, widespread damage, or structural concerns deserve a wood-pest professional's assessment. Do not choose treatment solely from an old hole or attempt improvised heating of furniture.

identification: Adults measure about 3.5–5 mm long and are brown to black with translucent whitish wings. Nymphs are smaller, wingless, and red through the abdomen. Inspect mature seed pods and open cotton bolls, where groups can look like small fleas moving between seeds and fibers. Cotton seed bug does not normally pierce intact closed cotton bolls, although damage by another insect may give it access. Several Oxycarenus species look similar. Expert screening uses wing and body coloration, leg spines, and male structures; some specimens require dissection. Photograph adults from above and from the side, their size, the host plant, and the seed pod. A red nymph or a blurry cluster is not enough for confirmation.
actions: Report a suspected Cotton seed bug to your county extension office or state plant regulatory office and provide the location, host plant, and clear photographs. Ask how to preserve or submit a specimen before shipping any live insects or plant material. Inspect seed pods repeatedly as they mature, especially on cotton, okra, and ornamental mallows near a detection. Hold suspect nursery plants, used sacks, and plant debris at the site while seeking advice rather than passing them to another property. Check nearby non-host plants and sheltered packing areas too, since resting adults can hide there. Use the confirmed identification and local response advice to decide further action.

sources.label: USDA APHIS: Cotton Seed Bug Pest Alert
UC Davis Calinvasives: Oxycarenus hyalinipennis scorecard

identification: Mature females are oval, yellowish tan with a brown border, and reach about 3 mm long. The white egg sac extending behind the body is approximately 6 mm long. Look beneath leaves, particularly on camellia, holly, and yew; immature scales may overwinter on evergreen foliage or on the bark of deciduous hosts. Newly hatched crawlers are pale yellow and need a hand lens to see well. Cottony maple leaf scale, Pulvinaria acericola, and other cottony scales can occupy overlapping hosts, so host identity and white wax alone are not decisive. Photograph the female body, its attached sac, and the leaf underside with a size reference. Preserve a representative adult for an extension specialist if the exact species matters.
actions: Inspect several branches and leaf undersides to determine whether Cottony camellia scale is scattered or widespread. On a small plant, manually remove accessible scales and egg sacs; prune a badly infested branch only where this will not seriously damage the plant. Keep removed material away from healthy nursery stock. Look for lady beetles and other natural enemies before considering a spray. Recheck for pale yellow crawlers, since egg sacs can remain empty and hatching may continue over an extended period. If foliage continues to yellow or new growth weakens, ask extension staff to confirm the scale and suggest timing appropriate to the local climate and host.

sources.label: University of Maryland: Cottony Camellia Scale
Rutgers Nursery IPM: Cottony Camellia Scale

identification: A mature Cottony cushion scale with its egg sac can approach 13 mm in total length. The actual body is much shorter and orange, yellowish, or brown beneath varying amounts of wax. The sac has conspicuous lengthwise ridges and can be two or more times the body length. Newly hatched crawlers are red with dark legs and antennae; young stages often line leaf veins, while larger insects occur on twigs and branches. Unlike many familiar scales, this insect retains legs and can move throughout life. Other wax-producing scales and mealybugs can look similar at a glance. Photograph the ridged sac from the side, the body at its front, young insects, and the host plant rather than relying on a white patch alone.
actions: Check whether Cottony cushion scale numbers are increasing and whether the host shows leaf loss, weak growth, or twig dieback. Look closely for red-and-black vedalia beetles, their larvae feeding among the sacs, or small emergence holes left by parasitic flies. Preserve these natural enemies and address ants tending the scales, using locally appropriate ant management. Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum spraying, which can remove the insects already suppressing the scale. Inspect new citrus and ornamental plants before placing them beside established plants. For a severe infestation without effective natural enemies, obtain extension advice based on the host and the presence of newly hatched crawlers before selecting any treatment.

sources.label: UF IFAS: Cottony Cushion Scale, Icerya purchasi

identification: Overwintering scales on canes are flattened, oval, and brownish to dark, commonly only a few millimeters long. Mature females can reach roughly 6 mm, with a white egg sac extending well beyond the body and tilting it upward. Crawlers later settle beneath leaves; mature egg sacs may persist after the female dies. European fruit lecanium, Parthenolecanium corni, also lives on grapes but has a more rounded brown body and lacks the conspicuous projecting cottony sac. Cottony maple scale is another lookalike, and some illustrated guides mix their images. Photograph the female, egg mass, cane, and leaf undersides with a size reference. Have an adult checked before assigning an unfamiliar infestation to Cottony grape scale.
actions: Inspect canes during normal dormant pruning and note whether scales also occupy the permanent trunk or main arms. Removing infested canes as part of appropriate pruning may reduce a small population without further treatment. Check leaf undersides for crawlers and watch for honeydew or ants during the growing season. Keep planting material from affected vines separate and seek advice before distributing cuttings. If leafroll virus is known or suspected in the vineyard, ask a grape extension specialist about identification, virus testing, and scale management together. Treating the insect alone does not cure an infected vine, and visible leaf symptoms alone do not establish the virus responsible.

sources.label: Pacific Northwest Handbook: Grape—Cottony grape scale
British Columbia Best Practices Guide: Soft Scale

identification: Adult females in the original description were about 3.5–6 mm long, very narrow or elliptical, with both ends tapering. Fresh individuals ranged from pale crimson to pink, usually with two brighter red lengthwise lines. The short white egg sac projects only slightly beyond the body margin; dried specimens can become buff or brown and lose their useful live colors. The species can resemble Aclerda scales in overall shape. Historical New World records under Pulvinaria iceryi also include misidentifications, so that name should not be substituted automatically. Photograph fresh adults on their host, the underside if safely accessible, and a ruler. A scale specialist must examine fine hairs, pores, and ducts to confirm the identification.
actions: On a suspected Cottony grass scale host, record the grass species, where scales sit on the plant, and whether leaves are yellowing or growth is declining. Photograph any ants tending the colony without assuming their identity. Keep infested potted grasses or sugarcane planting pieces separate from clean stock and avoid sharing them until the scale is identified. For a small ornamental planting, removing a few heavily occupied leaves may reduce insects while preserving a sample for diagnosis. Recheck the remaining growth. In a production field, use an extension or crop adviser to assess the scale and ant association before treatment.

sources.label: Tanaka and Kondo 2015: key to Colombian Pulvinaria

identification: Adult females are approximately 2–5 mm long, oval to nearly circular and moderately domed. Their color changes from green or yellow-green to reddish brown. A white egg sac forms beneath and behind the body, often with a groove along its middle; it may be as long as the body or longer. Check succulent leaves and new shoot tips. Pulvinaria delottoi is a very similar iceplant scale that often uses older growth, but feeding position is not a secure identification feature. Microscope examination distinguishes the thinner, mostly curved hairs along the body edge of Cottony pigface scale from the thicker, straighter hairs of that lookalike. Photograph adults, sacs, plant tips, and the host, and retain an adult for specialist confirmation.
actions: Inspect new iceplant and succulent cuttings before adding them to a collection, and keep visibly infested material separate. Avoid distributing cuttings from a colony until identification and management are settled. In a small planting, remove heavily occupied shoots into a contained waste stream and inspect adjacent new growth repeatedly. Preserve beneficial insects rather than spraying an entire groundcover at the first sight of white sacs; historical control depended strongly on natural enemies. If the host itself is an unwanted spreading iceplant, coordinate its removal rather than encouraging it to recover. Do not transport or release the scale as an improvised biological control agent.

sources.label: UCR: Biological Control of Ice Plant Scales
IUBS: Insects and Spiders, scale insect account

identification: An outdoor Council tree can reach about 25 m tall and develop buttressed or multiple trunks with aerial roots. Leaves alternate along the stem, are leathery and hairless, and may reach 20 cm long. Mature figs are oval, smooth, and up to about 2 cm across, becoming yellow to orange. The native Florida strangler fig, Ficus aurea, is an important lookalike. Council tree generally has broader, more egg-shaped leaves; the lowest pair of side veins leaves the midrib at a narrow angle and extends a third or more of the way up the blade.
