2024 checklist of fish helminths of Georgia

identification: Look for a perennial grass with narrow leaves and several fingerlike flowering branches. Plants commonly stand about 35–140 centimeters tall, with considerable variation among forms. Leaves may be smooth or hairy, and spreading forms can have long, hairy runners. The tiny spikelets are generally a few millimeters long; their hairs and arrangement are important in a grass key. A bunch-forming plant and a strongly creeping pangola plant may both belong within the broad modern concept of Digitgrass. Annual crabgrasses also have fingerlike seed heads, so that feature alone is insufficient. Examine the base for persistent crowns or runners, retain a mature flower head, and record the cultivar if the grass came from a known planting. A lawn-level photograph rarely resolves the species.
actions: Identify the form before planning containment. For a spreading cultivar, keep rooted runners and pieces of turf out of dumped soil or garden waste, and inspect the edge of the planted area for runners crossing into nearby habitat. For seed-producing forms, prevent unwanted seed production and avoid moving contaminated hay or seed. Small escapes can be lifted with their crowns and connected runners, followed by checks for pieces left behind. Maintain replacement cover where removal would expose soil. In a working pasture, discuss changes with a forage or restoration adviser rather than removing useful cover solely because the species is introduced. Document spread beyond the planting separately from the managed stand.

identification: Look for smooth, upright, hollow stems, finely divided threadlike leaf segments and yellow flowers arranged in umbrella-shaped clusters. Leaves are alternate and strongly aromatic, though smell should be used only as a supporting clue. Mature fruits, commonly called seeds, are flattened, oval and brown, with pale narrow wings along their edges. Fennel, Foeniculum vulgare, has similar fine foliage and yellow flower clusters, but its fruits are less flattened and lack Dill's narrow marginal wings. Cultivars differ in height and flowering time, so size alone is unreliable. If a volunteer is unfamiliar, show the whole plant, a leaf attachment and mature fruits to an experienced identifier. Do not use a resemblance to Dill as a reason to taste an unknown member of the carrot family.
actions: Keep Dill where you want it by collecting seed heads as the fruits turn brown or removing unwanted heads before they shed. Pull surplus seedlings while they are small; leaving a few chosen plants can provide herbs, flowers and caterpillar food without filling every bed. Before removing a plant, check for black swallowtail caterpillars and leave an occupied plant where practical. Sow new seed directly in its intended spot because established Dill transplants poorly. Avoid carrying mature seed heads into unmanaged areas or adding them to a cool compost pile where seed may survive. If volunteers recur, monitor the former bed through the growing season rather than assuming one weeding has removed the seed supply.

identification: Adults are commonly about 35–45 millimeters long. Both sexes have wings, while young nymphs lack the full adult wing covering. When documenting an adult, include the shield behind the head, the full wing outline and the underside; these views help a specialist compare structural characters. Death's head cockroach, Blaberus craniifer, and other Blaberus can look similar, and a shield marking alone is not a secure species test. University guidance explicitly warns that many members of this genus resemble one another. Keep the supplier or colony name with any sample, but do not treat it as proof if cultures have been mixed. Clear views from above and below, body length and the location found give an entomologist more useful evidence than a common-name label.
actions: Keep feeder or research colonies in secure, ventilated containers and check lids, vents and transfer areas before moving them. Although Discoid cockroach does not readily climb clean glass, do not rely on that alone to prevent escape; furnishings or accumulated material can provide a route out. Inspect incoming tropical plants and packing if an unexpected individual appears indoors. Capture it for identification and look nearby for additional adults or young. Do not release surplus colony animals outdoors. For repeated sightings in a building, remove food residues and ask an identification or pest-management service to confirm the species and source before choosing treatment. Finding one escaped feeder insect does not establish an outdoor breeding population.

sources.label: AZA Amphibian Taxon Advisory Group: Amphibian Husbandry Resource Guide, edition2.0(2012)
Imaging morphology and quantifying kinematic geometry of arthropod limbs
The medical and veterinary importance of cockroaches

identification: Plants form small tufts, often about 10–40 centimeters tall, with smooth, slender, grooved stems and very narrow leaves mostly around the base. The terminal spikelet is usually yellowish to pale brown, plump and oval, commonly about 5–8 millimeters long in the North American treatment. There may be two or three spikelets instead of one. Ditch fimbry resembles Eleocharis spikerushes, but its evident narrow leaf blades and detailed flower and fruit characters need checking in a sedge key. Mature fruits are pale, roughly 1.5–2 millimeters long, with fine surface patterns visible only under substantial magnification. Collect a whole tuft with basal leaves and mature spikelets when an authorized identification sample is needed. A clipped stem tip alone can hide important distinctions.
actions: Confirm the sedge before removing a wet-ground patch, especially where native spikerushes or other small sedges grow with it. In a maintained garden or drainage edge where Ditch fimbry is unwanted, lift small tufts before mature fruits are dispersed and collect the seed-bearing heads. Keep wet soil and plant material off tools before using them at another site. Recheck the patch for seedlings or surviving crowns. Avoid draining, filling or broadly disturbing a wetland merely to remove this plant; habitat damage could outweigh the benefit. If it is expanding through a restoration area, document its extent and ask the site's wetland botanist to assess selective management.

identification: Look for an unarmed plant with simple, egg-shaped leaves, their margins smooth or shallowly toothed. White, occasionally purplish flowers are about 1–1.5 centimeters across, often with a green or purple central star and yellow anthers. Berries are small, commonly about 5–8 millimeters across, and may appear dull green, purple or nearly black according to maturity and treatment. Solanum americanum generally has shorter anthers and a different combination of fruit sheen and calyx posture. Solanum douglasii has longer anthers; fruiting plants alone can be very difficult to separate. Specialists may also examine seed size and the small hard granules inside the berries. Show open flowers with a scale, mature fruit clusters and leaf attachments. Fruit color alone is not a safe identification rule.
actions: Check local native status and confirm the plant before managing a patch in natural vegetation. In a garden, remove an unwanted seedling while it is small and collect ripe berries before carrying a mature plant through other beds. Keep discarded fruit out of places where it could establish new plants, and inspect the site for later seedlings. Where children or animals might sample unfamiliar berries, limit access until the plant is identified. Do not taste fruit to distinguish it from another nightshade. If a population is spreading in a restoration area, ask a regional botanist to identify flowering material first; removing a similar-looking native species would not solve a misidentified weed problem.

sources.label: Flora de los bosques montanos de Medellín

identification: Look for a woody, often multistemmed shrub around 3–4 meters tall, with broad leaves usually 10–15 centimeters long. The leaves have several triangular lobes, toothed edges and long stalks; young stems and leaf undersides are hairy. Flowers may have five petals or many overlapping petals in double cultivars. Their change from pale to deep pink is useful when observed over time, though cultivar differences matter. Rose of Sharon (Hibiscus syriacus) generally has smaller, mostly three-lobed leaves, about 5–10 centimeters long. Photograph a whole branch, both leaf surfaces, a flower from the side and any hairy seed capsules. A single close photograph of a double flower can obscure the features needed for identification.
actions: Check around an established Dixie rosemallow for separate young plants, and note whether they occur beyond maintained garden beds. Where a confirmed volunteer is unwanted, remove it while small and revisit the spot for further growth. Keep seed-bearing capsules and fresh prunings out of streambanks and unmanaged ground: this plant produces seed, and cuttings root readily. Cutting a mature shrub to ground level can stimulate renewed growth, so treat pruning as maintenance rather than proof of removal. Ask a local horticultural or invasive-plant adviser about a larger escape near sensitive habitat. A planted specimen's presence alone does not justify clearing surrounding vegetation.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria HortFlora — Hibiscus mutabilis
Environmental Weeds of Australia — Hibiscus mutabilis

identification: The leafy part of a mature frond is commonly 15–45 centimeters long, divided into side branches that are divided again into smaller segments. The stalk may be another 10–50 centimeters long and is dark and glossy. Turn a frond gently to photograph its pale underside and the distribution of its tiny spore cases. Ordinary white-backed plants differ from golden-backed forms treated in the Australian flora as Pityrogramma calomelanos var. austroamericana: those have yellow wax and a different relative length of the lowest side branches. Color alone cannot settle every fern identification or varietal name. Include the entire frond, its stalk, the growing crown and close views of mature segments, without stripping the coating.
actions: Inspect nearby pots, paving cracks and disturbed soil for additional Dixie silverback fern plants before moving nursery material elsewhere. Photograph both sides of a frond first so a fern specialist can verify an unfamiliar escape. For a small, confirmed unwanted plant, carefully lift the growing crown and attached roots where this will not damage masonry or neighboring plants. Contain the removed material and avoid scattering fertile fronds during transport. Do not dump potting mix or garden waste into natural areas. Recheck the site for new growth; the advice reduces opportunities for spread but does not establish that one removal eliminates all spores.

sources.label: Australian Tropical Ferns and Lycophytes — Pityrogramma calomelanos
Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh — Ferns of Thailand, Laos and Cambodia: Pityrogramma calomelanos

identification: Dog rose often reaches about 3 meters tall. Its leaves consist of toothed leaflets, and sturdy prickles curve backward from the stems. White-to-pink flowers appear in early summer, followed by red hips. Examine ordinary leafy shoots as well as flowering ones. Sweetbriar (Rosa rubiginosa) usually has small stalked glands on its leaflets and flower stalks, and more distinctly double-toothed leaflet edges; dog rose generally lacks those glands. Multiflora rose (Rosa multiflora) has conspicuously fringed leaf-base appendages, called stipules, which dog rose lacks. Photograph those appendages, both leaflet surfaces, prickles, flowers and hips. Close relatives and garden hybrids can overlap in appearance, so a whole-plant photograph alone may not establish the name.
actions: Wear sturdy gloves and eye protection when working around dog rose's curved prickles. Confirm the species before removing a wild rose, especially where native roses grow nearby. For a few small unwanted plants, careful digging and follow-up inspection are reasonable first steps; keep hips contained rather than dropping them while carrying branches away. Record the extent of a larger patch and ask a local weed adviser for a plan that protects adjoining vegetation. Do not assume deer browsing will control it: Washington field assessment found browsing insufficient. Revisit treated ground for surviving growth and new plants rather than judging success from cut stems alone.

sources.label: Native Plant Trust Go Botany — Rosa canina
King County — Multiflora rose identification and lookalikes
Washington DNR — Rosa canina invasive ranking assessment

identification: Look for hairy lower leaves roughly 3–15 centimeters long, broad toward the tip and narrowing toward the base. Flowering plants in a published Thai treatment stood 10–40 centimeters tall; size alone is not diagnostic. The small white flower heads are grouped along spike-like branches and supported by narrow bracts. Elephant's-foot species such as Elephantopus mollis and E. scaber instead have broader bracts around their clustered heads. Under magnification, dog's-tongue has two longer bristles above each dry fruit with bent, N-shaped tips, another useful distinction. Photograph the basal leaves, entire flowering stem, side view of the heads and mature fruit with a scale. A leaf rosette without flowers is difficult to identify confidently.
actions: Before pulling a suspected dog's-tongue plant, take close photographs of the flower clusters and leaves and seek confirmation from a herbarium or Extension office if the plant is unfamiliar locally. Similar elephant's-foot plants should not be cleared solely because they have broad basal leaves. In a small, confirmed unwanted patch, lift the plant and its roots before dry fruits are shed, where soil disturbance will not harm neighboring plants. Contain flowering and fruiting stems, and clean plant fragments from tools. Check the patch again for surviving plants. These measures are cautious prevention; the sources do not establish a species-specific US eradication method.

sources.label: Flora of North America — Pseudelephantopus spicatus
Bunwong and Chantaranothai (2010) — A new record of Pseudelephantopus spicatus from Thailand

identification: Look for tan or brown leaf blotches with reddish-purple margins, dead young shoots and progressive dieback, particularly on lower branches. Cankers are damaged areas of bark that can interrupt the movement of water through a twig or branch. Affected trees may produce many new shoots along the trunk or near diseased branches. Spot anthracnose, caused by Elsinoe corni, and Septoria leaf spots can resemble the early leaf symptoms but usually cause much less serious damage. Photograph the whole crown, the transition between healthy and dead foliage, spotted leaves and affected twigs. Record the dogwood species if known. Confirmation may require a plant diagnostic laboratory; photographs cannot show all the fungal features needed.
actions: Ask an Extension plant clinic or qualified arborist to assess a dogwood with recurring leaf blight and branch dieback. Follow the clinic's instructions for collecting a fresh sample rather than mailing only dried leaves. Remove and discard blighted shoots, and collect fallen infected leaves where practical. Reduce avoidable stress by protecting the trunk from mower damage, maintaining mulch over the root zone without piling it against the bark, and watering the root zone during prolonged dry weather. Seek professional advice before removing major branches or selecting a treatment for a valuable tree. For replacement planting, choose an appropriate disease-resistant dogwood rather than assuming every dogwood is equally susceptible.

sources.label: University of Illinois Extension — Dogwood Anthracnose

identification: An average domestic cat has a body roughly 46 centimeters long, with a tail around 30 centimeters, although breed and age cause substantial variation. Look for pointed ears, prominent whiskers and a compact, flexible body; coat color can be solid, patched, striped or spotted. Most have long tails, but some breeds have naturally short tails or none. Bobcats (Lynx rufus) usually have a short tail, cheek ruffs, ear tufts and a larger body, yet a young bobcat can be mistaken for a house cat. Tail length or a spotted coat alone is insufficient. Photograph the whole animal from a safe distance, especially the face, tail and any collar or distinctive markings. A cat's friendliness, wariness or lack of a collar does not establish ownership.
actions: Give an pet cat an enriched indoor home with places to climb, hide, scratch and play; an enclosed outdoor run can provide fresh air without access to wildlife. Discuss individual needs with a veterinarian, and keep identification and microchip registration current. For an unfamiliar cat, record its location and appearance and contact a local shelter or animal service about checking ownership and arranging humane help. Let experienced personnel handle a frightened or injured animal. Do not relocate a cat to another neighborhood or natural area. Where cats repeatedly visit a bird nesting area, share observations with the land manager and animal service so they can coordinate an appropriate response.

sources.label: USDA APHIS — Free-ranging and Feral Cats
Feline Veterinary Medical Association — 2024 Indoor/Outdoor Lifestyle Position Statement

identification: There is no single size or coat pattern that identifies every domestic dog. Breeds range from tiny dogs weighing only a few kilograms to animals weighing several tens of kilograms, with great variation in muzzle length, ear shape, leg length and tail carriage. Wolf-like breeds can resemble gray wolves (Canis lupus), while some lean, pointed-eared dogs resemble coyotes (Canis latrans). Tracks overlap in size and shape: splayed toes and a wandering trail may suggest a dog, but neither proves it. Record a side view of the whole animal, its face and tail, approximate size, location and any collar, harness or markings. Puppies differ from adults, and a distant photograph cannot reliably establish breed or hybrid ancestry. Ask a wildlife professional about an uncertain wild-looking canid.
actions: Keep an pet dog within secure fencing or on a leash appropriate to the setting, and supervise it around wildlife. Do not allow chasing, even when the dog seems playful; wildlife may defend themselves. Check gates and fence gaps after an escape, and keep pet food from attracting animals around the yard. If an unfamiliar dog is running loose, photograph it only from a safe position and contact local animal control with its location and direction of travel. Do not chase, corner or approach it, even if it looks friendly. Keep children and pets away, and leave capture to the owner or trained responders.

sources.label: University of Michigan Animal Diversity Web — Canis lupus familiaris
Colorado Parks and Wildlife — Protecting Pets from Wildlife
New Hampshire Fish and Game — Lynx and Wolf Trapper Identification Handout

identification: Domestic goats vary greatly by breed, with adult shoulder heights ranging from roughly 30 centimeters in very small breeds to around a meter in large ones. Coats may be short or long, solid or patterned, and ears may stand upright or hang down. The short tail commonly curves upward. A beard can help distinguish a goat from a domestic sheep (Ovis aries), but coat texture, horns or beard alone should not be used as a universal test. Goat breeds also differ in coat texture, so an animal's overall shape and several features are more useful together. Split-hoof tracks and pellet droppings can resemble those of sheep or deer. Photograph the full animal, tail, head, ears and any ear tags without approaching. Include whether kids or other goats accompany it.
actions: Inspect goat fencing and gates regularly, including places where animals can climb, squeeze through or crawl underneath. Maintain shelter, water and adequate forage within the enclosure; tethering is not a substitute for suitable routine housing. If using goats for vegetation management, keep the work supervised and contained rather than releasing animals into unmanaged land. For loose goats, note the location, number, tags and nearby roads, and contact the likely owner, local livestock or animal service, or the responsible land manager. Keep dogs away and avoid chasing goats into traffic or steep ground. Established groups on conservation land need a coordinated assessment of browsing and humane management options.

sources.label: University of Michigan Animal Diversity Web — Capra hircus
NSW Department of Education — Goats: Environment
New Zealand Department of Conservation — Wild goats
San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance — Goat and Sheep

identification: Look for long ears, a short upright mane, relatively narrow hooves and a tail with a tuft toward its end. Domestic donkey breeds span approximately 80–150 centimeters at the shoulder, so size alone is a poor identification guide. Some burros have a dark stripe down the back and another across the shoulders; leg stripes can also occur, but markings vary. Mules and hinnies are horse–donkey hybrids and can share the conspicuous ears and other features. A mule has a donkey father and horse mother; a hinny has the reverse parentage. Do not assign hybrid status from ear length alone. Photograph the animal's complete side profile, mane, tail and markings from a distance. Ownership information or an experienced equine assessor may be needed for an uncertain animal.
actions: Do not feed or approach a free-ranging donkey, including a foal that appears alone. Feeding can draw burros toward roads, and unfamiliar animals can bite or kick. Record the location and visible condition without blocking traffic or attempting to herd the animal. Report an apparent livestock escape to its owner or local animal service; for wild burros on Bureau of Land Management land, contact the responsible BLM office about injury, distress or conflict. Let trained personnel handle capture and movement. Owners should maintain secure enclosures and arrange knowledgeable equine care. Never release an unwanted donkey into open country or assume a young burro needs to be taken home.

sources.label: San Diego Zoo Wildlife Alliance Library — African Wild Ass and Domestic Donkey: Physical Characteristics
Bureau of Land Management — Wild Burros in Arizona
EU Platform on Animal Welfare initiative — Guide to Good Animal Welfare Practice for Donkeys and Donkey Hybrids

identification: Plants are often about 50–160 centimeters tall, with large lower leaves whose edges are gently wavy. Examine several mature fruits with a hand lens: the three inner flower parts enlarge into rounded or kidney-shaped wings, called valves, typically around 5–6 millimeters long. Their edges are smooth, and they generally lack the obvious central bumps found in some other docks. Patience dock (Rumex patientia) normally has a distinct bump on at least one valve; curly dock (R. crispus) usually has developed bumps on all three. Western dock (R. occidentalis) has a less distinct, unswollen joint on the small fruit stalk, unlike the conspicuous swollen joint of dooryard dock. Photograph the lower leaves, entire plant, fruit stalk joints and several fruits against a scale. Immature plants and suspected hybrids need expert examination.
actions: Confirm dooryard dock from mature fruit before removing plants among other docks. Where a small, confirmed plant is unwanted on your property, carefully loosen the soil and lift the root rather than only cutting off the leaves, then inspect the spot for renewed growth. Collect fruiting stems before moving material through the site, and keep them out of dumped garden waste or soil destined for another location. Clean adhering soil and plant material from tools. These are limited prevention steps, not a demonstrated eradication program. For an extensive patch, a shoreline location or an uncertain identification, send detailed photographs to a local botanical or land-management adviser before disturbing the ground.

sources.label: Native Plant Trust Go Botany — Rumex longifolius
USGS GLANSIS — Rumex longifolius Fact Sheet

identification: Look for dead twigs, yellowing leaves, early leaf fall, and sunken or discolored bark, especially near branch junctions. Older cankers may develop cracked bark and raised wound tissue around their edges. Small, dark, pimplelike fruiting bodies can form in affected bark, sometimes releasing pale spore tendrils in wet weather. Shoots growing below a girdled area are another sign of disrupted growth. Cytospora canker can also kill poplar branches and produce spore masses, so bark appearance alone does not establish Dothichiza canker. Record the host poplar, the position and extent of lesions, and recent drought or transplant injury. A plant diagnostic laboratory can examine the active canker margin and fungal structures.
actions: Reduce avoidable stress on valuable poplars: water newly planted trees appropriately during dry periods, protect trunks from equipment damage, and choose planting sites suited to the tree. Inspect nursery plants and cuttings before planting, and avoid taking propagation material from cankered trees. If a branch or stem is dying, seek a diagnosis before treating it as this particular disease. Ask an arborist or extension service whether affected branches can be removed safely or whether a severely cankered tree should be removed. Dead or weakened limbs near people require prompt assessment. Correcting site and watering problems also helps protect replacement trees.

sources.label: USDA Forest Service — Cryptodiaporthe (Dothichiza) Canker of Populus
Institute of Forestry Serbia — Selection of species for afforestation and amelioration

identification: Brown, dead needles remaining on a killed terminal or side shoot are conspicuous early clues. Examine the boundary between dead and living tissue for a canker and dark brown discoloration beneath the bark. Tiny black fruiting bodies, generally less than a millimeter across, may occur on dead bark or needles. Frost injury itself can resemble Douglas fir canker. In the Scion account, fungal involvement extends into older growth and darkens underlying tissues, whereas initial frost injury is usually concentrated in current growth. These are useful clues rather than a conclusive field test. Identification of the fungus relies on microscopic spore and fruiting-body features, and laboratories may use DNA markers.
actions: Give young Douglas firs a suitable planting site and reduce exposure to avoidable frost injury, drying, and stem damage. Inspect affected shoots after a damaging cold event and follow whether dieback stops or continues into older branches. Avoid unnecessary pruning injuries, especially when trees are already stressed. If several seedlings decline, a main stem becomes girdled, or symptoms continue without an obvious frost event, submit material through a plant diagnostic service. Include the transition between healthy and affected tissue and the planting and weather history. Management should address the underlying injury and the confirmed diagnosis; a routine preventive spray is not supported by the forestry account.

sources.label: Scion / New Zealand Farm Forestry Association — Fungi on conifers: Allantophomopsis pseudotsugae

identification: Plants usually stand about 4–12 inches tall, with branching stems and nearly round leaves divided into broad lobes less than halfway toward the center. Long and short hairs give the foliage a soft feel. The pink flowers are small, roughly 5–9 millimeters across, with five deeply notched petals. Mature fruit segments are hairless and have transverse wrinkles, a useful close-up feature. Small-flowered cranesbill, Geranium pusillum, is a close lookalike; its flowers are generally smaller and its flower stalks lack the conspicuous long hairs of Dovefoot Geranium. Examine several flowers, stalk hairs and mature fruits together, since flower size overlaps and a leaf photograph alone may not separate these geraniums.
actions: Where Dovefoot Geranium is unwanted, remove young plants before their beaked fruits mature and release seed. A hand fork can help lift plants from compacted soil without leaving the base behind. Collect fruiting material rather than shaking it across a bed. In lawns, address bare patches and maintain turf suited to the site; in garden beds, reduce open soil where repeated seedlings appear. Keep checking through both autumn and spring because germination is not confined to one season. Seed can persist for several years, so removing one crop of plants may not finish the job. Crop infestations warrant advice matched to the crop and local growing conditions.

sources.label: AHDB — Distribution and biology of dove's-foot crane's-bill

identification: Check young shoots first: Downy birch generally has soft hairs and lacks the conspicuous resinous warts typical of silver birch, Betula pendula. Leaves tend to have a rounded base and relatively simple teeth, while silver birch more often has triangular leaves with stronger double teeth. Hairiness is also useful on young leaves. Bark ranges from whitish to gray or brownish and is less reliably diagnostic than a combination of twig and leaf features. The crown is often rounded or irregular rather than strongly weeping, but branch posture varies. Intermediate-looking birches can be difficult to name confidently. Include close views of current shoots, mature leaves and the whole tree when seeking a botanical identification.
actions: Before removing a birch from a natural area, confirm both its identity and its local status; native birches and variable forms can look similar. If unwanted seedlings are appearing around a planted tree, remove small plants while roots can be lifted with little disturbance and revisit the area for new recruits. Keep work on wet ground light enough to avoid rutting or damaging neighboring vegetation. For a large tree, seek an arborist's assessment of removal or retention, especially near buildings and paths. A regional botanist or land manager can help decide whether a population is a planting escape, an established local component, or a taxonomic question needing closer study.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online — Betula pubescens

identification: Plants are commonly about 8–20 inches tall. Lower leaves usually have five leaflets with uneven teeth or deeper cuts; the central leaflet is often roughly 2–4.5 centimeters long. Examine the underside: it has soft hairs but lacks the dense white, feltlike covering of silver cinquefoil, Potentilla argentea. Small yellow petals are about 3–5 millimeters long. Norwegian cinquefoil, P. norvegica, commonly has three leaflets, although leaflet counts should be checked across several leaves. Ashy cinquefoil, P. inclinata, is another difficult comparison; its leaf undersides are more densely gray-hairy and its anthers are larger. A flowering specimen with lower leaves and mature fruit is much more informative than a distant photograph.
actions: Confirm Downy cinquefoil before removing plants from mixed grassland or a roadside containing native cinquefoils. For a small unwanted patch, lift individual plants with their root crowns and collect stems bearing mature fruit. Work before the numerous flowers produce a fresh seed crop where possible, and avoid scattering collected material along access routes. Revisit disturbed soil for seedlings and regrowth rather than assuming one pass has removed the population. Where plants are sparse and not causing a documented problem, identification and monitoring may be the most proportionate response. A local flora specialist can help resolve plants that combine features of several cinquefoils.

sources.label: Flora of North America — Potentilla intermedia
Kew Plants of the World Online — Potentilla × intermedia

identification: Look for green canes that age toward gray, often with gently zigzagging lower sections. Flora of China describes typical canes about 2–4 centimeters thick and leaves about 8–12 centimeters long. New shoots retain protective sheaths that are especially useful for identification: these are green-brown with purple veins and small brown spots, and their narrow upper blades bend back. The little ear-shaped projections found on some bamboo sheaths are absent. At the genus level, Phyllostachys usually has two unequal branches at a mid-cane node and a flattened or grooved side above it. These features separate the group from many clumping bamboos but do not prove the species. Preserve photographs of fresh shoot sheaths for specialist comparison.
actions: Mark the full extent of emerging shoots before planning containment. Remove unwanted new shoots while they are soft, and inspect beyond the visible canes for rhizomes; cutting shoots alone leaves the underground system alive. A properly installed, continuously monitored rhizome barrier can help contain a retained planting, but gaps and shoots crossing the top need attention. Remove rhizomes already outside the barrier or repeatedly cut their regrowth. For complete removal, expect excavation and follow-up rather than a single mowing. Keep rhizome fragments out of dumped soil and yard waste that could establish elsewhere. Large colonies near utilities, walls or neighboring gardens may need an experienced contractor.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online — Phyllostachys flexuosa
University of Connecticut — Identification of Phyllostachys
University of Maryland Extension — Containing and removing bamboo

identification: Plants are often about 4–16 inches tall, with smooth, slender stems and alternate leaves divided repeatedly into small lobes. The flowers are narrow and tubular, roughly 7–10 millimeters long, with a short spur at the back and darker tips. Their shape is more useful than the fernlike foliage when separating fumitories from unrelated seedlings. The fruit is a small, rounded, one-seeded body about 2–2.5 millimeters across, flattened or slightly indented at its top. Other Fumaria species can be very similar. A reliable comparison needs fresh flowers, the small sepals beneath them, fruit shape and flower-stalk details; leaf color or a distant view of a pink-flowered patch is insufficient.
actions: Remove unwanted Drug fumitory while plants are young and before their small rounded fruits mature. Hand weeding or shallow hoeing is practical in accessible beds, provided nearby crop roots are protected. Collect fruiting stems so they do not scatter seed during cleanup. Recheck recently disturbed soil, especially during the spring emergence period, and reduce unnecessary bare ground with planting or suitable mulch. In crops, record patch size and whether plants are interfering with establishment or harvest, then seek advice specific to that crop. Small plants outside production areas need not automatically trigger broad treatment, particularly where keeping other vegetation intact is the more useful goal.

sources.label: AHDB — Distribution and biology of common fumitory
National Institute of Plant Health Management — Illustrative guide for detection of weeds
Aarhus University and SEGES — Fumaria officinalis weed biology

identification: Adults are roughly 2–3.5 millimeters long, cylindrical and reddish brown, with the head tucked downward beneath a hoodlike thorax. Under magnification, their wing covers have lengthwise rows of pits and fine hairs. The antennae end in a distinct club of three enlarged segments. Cigarette beetles, Lasioderma serricorne, are a common lookalike, but have saw-toothed antennae and smoother wing covers. Larvae are small pale grubs, often curled, and are usually found inside the food source. Look for round exit holes in packages, insect waste and live larvae as well as adults. A sharp close-up of the antennae and wing covers, or a retained beetle specimen, is more useful than packaging damage alone.
actions: Inspect all dry goods in the affected area, including spices, pet food, birdseed, dried decorations and old grain-based rodent bait. Seal and discard infested products, then clean spilled food and residue from shelves, corners and crevices. Store unaffected supplies in sturdy containers with tight lids and use older stock first. Check new purchases for damaged packaging or insects. Avoid spraying food or treating pantry shelves as a substitute for finding the source. Beetle numbers should decline after cleanup; continued activity means another breeding material may remain. If the source cannot be located, an extension insect specialist or pest professional can help trace it.

sources.label: University of Wisconsin Extension — Drugstore beetles
Defense Centers for Public Health — Drugstore beetle

identification: Look for small piles of hard, dry fecal pellets beneath tiny openings in wood, or shed wings near windows. Unlike subterranean termites, this species does not depend on mud tubes connecting the colony to soil. Soldiers have a distinctive dark, rough, pluglike head; winged reproductive adults have two pairs of iridescent wings with prominent veins near the leading edge. Other drywood termites can produce similar pellets. Incisitermes soldiers have more projecting jaws, while close Cryptotermes relatives require finer examination; C. brevis lacks a small pad between the foot claws. Save intact soldiers or winged adults for an identification service. Workers, damage patterns and pellet photographs alone usually cannot establish the exact species.
actions: Arrange an inspection by a qualified timber-pest professional if pellets, swarmers or damaged wood suggest an active infestation. Keep a sample and record exactly where it appeared before cleaning, then use newly appearing pellets or wings to help monitor activity. Do not give away, sell or relocate suspect furniture until the infestation has been assessed; moving wood can move the colony. Ask about the extent of infestation and whether a localized or whole-structure treatment is appropriate. Treatment and disposal need a plan that reaches termites concealed inside the wood. Follow local disposal guidance, and avoid breaking up or distributing infested timber during repairs.

sources.label: University of Florida — West Indian drywood termite
New South Wales Department of Primary Industries — West Indian drywood termites
University of Florida — Western drywood termite

identification: Look below the surface for a rooted plant with broad, thin leaves on long stalks. Mature blades may be roughly 4–8 inches long, with lengthwise veins connected by cross-veins that give a quilted appearance. The leaf edges and stalks can be toothed. Flower stalks carry cylindrical green coverings, called spathes, with three or more ruffled wings; petals may be white or pale pink to lavender. Water plantains, Alisma species, arrowheads, Sagittaria species, and burheads, Echinodorus species, can resemble it. The combination of submerged cross-veined leaves and winged flower coverings is more useful than leaf shape alone. Photograph those structures in place and record water depth; young narrow-leaved plants are harder to recognize.
actions: Report a suspected new Ducklettuce population to the state aquatic-plant or invasive-species program, with the location and photographs, before attempting a large removal. Avoid moving plants, muddy equipment or water from the site into another waterbody. Clean boats, trailers and tools carefully, and never release aquarium plants or their water outdoors. For a small confirmed patch, ask the responsible manager whether hand removal is appropriate and how to contain fruiting plants and dispose of them. Seed persistence means follow-up matters even after visible plants disappear. Do not improvise a herbicide treatment in water; a site-specific plan must account for other aquatic life and water uses.

sources.label: USFWS 2025: Duck Lettuce (Ottelia alismoides) Ecological Risk Screening Summary

identification: Typical cultivated plants reach about 3–8 feet, though pot size and cultivar strongly affect stature. Leaves are broad and pointed, often 7–15 inches long, with a strong midrib and asymmetric bases. Their markings vary considerably, and some plants are mostly green. The stout green stem bears rings of old leaf scars and usually branches little. Flowers, when present, consist of a central spike surrounded by a green sheath; indoor plants seldom flower. Similar variegated aroids cannot reliably be separated by cream blotches alone. Examine leaf bases, the sheathing leaf stalk, stem form and any flower structures. Older nursery names such as Dieffenbachia maculata and D. picta may refer to this species rather than separate plants.
actions: Wear gloves when cutting or dividing Dumbcane, keep sap away from eyes and mouth, and wash hands and tools afterward. Place retained plants where children and pets cannot chew them. If disposing of one, contain cut stems and roots rather than dumping them into a warm, moist garden or natural area, since stem pieces can produce new plants. Check a cleared outdoor planting for rooted fragments or regrowth. If someone chews the plant or gets sap in an eye, contact a poison center for case-specific advice; difficulty breathing or swallowing needs urgent medical attention. For a suspected pet exposure, contact a veterinarian.

identification: Older larvae are narrow, cylindrical and yellow to yellow-brown, with a tough outer covering; large larvae are around three-quarters of an inch long. Adult Dusky wireworm beetles are commonly about 7–10 millimeters long and brown to dark brown. Agriotes lineatus and A. sputator are particularly similar. A modern identification study uses fine features such as the breathing openings along the abdomen and markings on the last segment; some distinctions require more than 50-fold magnification. Worn larvae may remain impossible to separate confidently from A. lineatus by appearance. Collect intact specimens from beside damaged roots and record the crop, soil conditions and location. Specialist microscopy or molecular identification may be needed for a species-level record.
actions: Inspect soil around damaged plants to verify that wireworms, rather than another root problem, are responsible. For a planned vegetable bed or crop, investigate risk before planting, especially after long-standing grass. Bait traps can reveal wireworm presence, but catches do not reliably predict population size or crop loss. Remove grass weeds within production beds and discuss crop choice, rotation and cultivation with an extension crop adviser if damage has recurred. Avoid placing especially vulnerable potatoes in a known infested area, and consider timely harvest where damage risk is high. Keep yearly records: the larvae's long development means a problem can persist across several crops.

sources.label: AHDB — Identification and management of wireworms in field crops
Furlan and colleagues — Species identification of Agriotes wireworms
Polish Plant Breeding and Acclimatization Institute — Wireworms

identification: Watch for a branch or section of the crown turning yellow, wilting and browning during the growing season while other branches remain green. This localized symptom is often called flagging. Brown or purple streaks may be visible in the outer wood beneath the bark of affected living twigs. Drought and other causes of branch death can look similar from a distance. Ophiostoma novo-ulmi and O. ulmi cannot be separated by these canopy symptoms; a laboratory must examine or test the fungus. Ask a diagnostic service which recently wilting branches to submit, rather than sending only fully dry wood. Record when symptoms began and whether neighboring elms are also declining.
actions: Seek an arborist or plant diagnostic service promptly when an elm begins flagging. Early assessment can determine whether limited therapeutic pruning is still realistic or whether the tree needs removal. Where nearby elms may share roots, have the professional assess root connections before felling an infected tree. Keep infected elm wood from becoming a beetle breeding source and do not transport it as firewood; arrange disposal or processing consistent with local guidance. Preventive fungicide injections may be considered for selected valuable trees, but require professional advice and repeated treatment. When replacing trees, use suitable disease-resistant selections and a diverse planting rather than relying on one susceptible elm type.

sources.label: University of Minnesota Extension — Dutch elm disease
Tennessee Department of Agriculture — Dutch elm disease
Plant Health Australia: National Diagnostic Protocol37, Dutch elm disease caused by Ophiostoma spp., V1

identification: Leaves on one or more branches may yellow, wilt and turn brown before the rest of the canopy. Peeling bark from a suitable symptomatic twig can reveal streaks in the outer wood, but collecting material is best guided by the diagnostic laboratory. These are Dutch elm disease clues, not visible characters unique to Ophiostoma ulmi. The fungus is microscopic, and the distinction from O. novo-ulmi requires laboratory methods, including species-specific DNA tests. A slowly declining tree is not necessarily infected with the less aggressive species: host resistance, season and infection route also affect symptoms. Include the elm's identity, symptom dates and a map or description of other affected trees with a sample.
actions: Have a newly wilting elm assessed quickly, particularly where healthy elms stand nearby. A professional can judge whether a small, early infection can be pruned out and whether root grafts need to be disrupted before removing a diseased tree. Arrange prompt handling of dead or infected elm material so bark beetles cannot continue breeding in it. Do not assume that cutting a tree into firewood makes it harmless; ask the local forestry or extension service about debarking, processing and disposal. For retained high-value elms, discuss preventive treatment and monitoring with an arborist. Replacements should include locally suitable, disease-resistant trees and a mix of species.

sources.label: Forest Research — Dutch elm disease: origins and background
University of Illinois Extension — Dutch elm disease
University of New Hampshire Extension — Dutch elm disease fact sheet

identification: Plants are commonly about 3–7 feet tall, with opposite leaves roughly 1–3 inches long, often broadest above the middle. Mature upper leaf surfaces become relatively smooth while the undersides remain hairy. The cream to yellow-white flowers occur in pairs on stalks longer than 5 millimeters; red berries follow. Amur honeysuckle, Lonicera maackii, has much shorter flower stalks and leaves drawn into long, sharp tips. Morrow's honeysuckle, L. morrowii, is harder to separate: Dwarf honeysuckle has shallower cuts in the upper flower lip and glandular hairs on the small structures beneath the flower. Hollow older stems are supporting evidence for introduced bush honeysuckles, but should not replace a regional key and flower examination.
actions: Confirm the shrub before removal, particularly where native honeysuckles occur. Pull seedlings and small plants when soil is moist enough to release the roots, and minimize disturbance around desirable plants. Larger shrubs can be dug or extracted where access and soil conditions permit. Cutting alone can produce regrowth, so plan repeated follow-up rather than treating a freshly cut stump as a finished job. Collect berry-bearing branches carefully and avoid moving fruit into uninfested areas. Check beneath bird perches and along the edge of the original patch for seedlings. Replanting suitable native shrubs can help occupy the opening while providing replacement cover and food for wildlife.

identification: Plants are commonly about 5–24 inches tall, with upright, branching stems and opposite, oval to somewhat rounded leaves. The leaf margins have conspicuous teeth, and long stinging hairs stand among shorter ordinary hairs. Tiny green flowers occur in short clusters close to the stem, with male and female flowers mixed in the same cluster. The perennial stinging nettle complex, Urtica dioica, generally grows taller, develops spreading underground stems and has longer flower clusters. Size alone is unreliable when comparing young plants. Examine flower-cluster arrangement and the base of an already removed plant, using gloves. A sting confirms neither this species nor whether the nettle is locally native.
actions: Wear gloves and cover exposed skin when working around Dwarf nettle. Pull small plants or hoe them out before seed matures, taking care around crop roots and desirable seedlings. Its annual habit makes preventing seed production more useful than treating it like a deep-rooted perennial nettle colony. Collect mature seed-bearing plants rather than shaking them through the garden, and avoid moving contaminated soil to clean beds. Keep checking cultivated ground because the seedbank can persist for years. Mulch or maintain suitable ground cover where repeated bare-soil disturbance encourages germination. In crop fields, base further action on actual interference with the crop and locally appropriate advice.

Flora of New Zealand — Urtica urens

identification: Plants usually stand about 2–12 inches tall, with slender branched stems. Lower leaves are opposite, while upper leaves alternate along the stem; the blades are narrow, entire and roughly 1–3 centimeters long. Each small flower sits alone on a relatively long stalk arising where a leaf joins the stem. The two-lipped lavender flower is about 6–8 millimeters long, with an open mouth and short blunt spur. Blue toadflaxes in Nuttallanthus can look similar, but Dwarf snapdragon has conspicuous glandular hairs and much smaller flowers in the cited comparison. Examine a flowering stem, the lower leaf arrangement and mature capsules together. A tiny purple flower alone is not enough to identify it.
actions: In a garden bed or other place where Dwarf snapdragon is unwanted, remove plants before their capsules release seed. Hand pulling or shallow hoeing suits small patches in loose gravel or cultivated soil. Collect stems already carrying ripe capsules and avoid scattering the fine seed during cleanup. Revisit the site for new seedlings after disturbance, and reduce unnecessary bare ground where vegetation is acceptable. Do not enter railway rights-of-way to remove plants; report maintenance concerns to the responsible operator. For sparse plants in low-impact disturbed habitat, monitoring may be proportionate. Confirm unfamiliar small toadflaxes before broad treatment so nearby native plants are retained.

identification: Look for four wedge-shaped to fan-shaped leaflets at the top of a slender stalk, with individual fronds spaced along a creeping stem. Aquatic forms may have stalks around 10-30 centimeters long; plants on exposed mud can be much shorter. The most useful identification structures are sporocarps, the small, firm cases containing spores near the leaf-stalk bases. Accounts of the typical form describe cases roughly 3-4 millimeters long, often in small groups, with two prominent teeth. Other Marsilea species, including M. quadrifolia and M. crenata, can closely resemble it. Leaf shape changes with habitat, and sterile plants may need specialist or DNA examination. Record sporocarp shape, attachment and number rather than relying on aquarium labels.
actions: Keep aquarium waterclovers and their discarded material out of ponds, streams and drainage systems. If a suspected population appears outside cultivation, photograph the patch and its leaf bases and ask an aquatic botanist or state invasive-plant program to confirm it before broad removal. Native waterclovers may occur in the same region. Where a small introduced patch is confirmed and hand removal is appropriate, lift the shallow creeping stems carefully and collect fragments instead of raking them into open water. Clean muddy tools and footwear before moving elsewhere, and revisit for regrowth. Larger wetland work needs a plan that protects the substrate and neighboring aquatic vegetation.

identification: Garden plants often reach about 2–3 feet, although botanical accounts record shrubs up to 2 meters. Leaves are simple, rather than divided into leaflets, and are narrow oval to lance-shaped, generally 1–4 centimeters long. Yellow flowers about 1–1.5 centimeters long appear near the ends of branches, followed by flattened pods roughly 1.5–3 centimeters long. Scotch broom, Cytisus scoparius, is usually taller and commonly has lower leaves divided into three leaflets, though its upper leaves can be simple. Compare several leaves, the branching habit, flowers and pods rather than a single shoot. Hairiness varies in Dyer's greenweed, so smooth versus hairy stems alone is not a dependable identification.
actions: If Dyer's greenweed is spreading beyond a planting, remove small volunteers before their pods ripen and release seed. Lift the root crown where this can be done without excessive soil disturbance, and collect pod-bearing branches separately from material likely to be scattered. For a retained specimen, watch the surrounding ground for recruits and avoid sharing seed where escapes are a concern. Larger established shrubs may need repeated follow-up after cutting or excavation; inspect the base for renewed shoots. Ask a local weed program for advice when a patch enters meadow or conservation land. Restore disturbed ground with suitable vegetation and keep records of whether the patch is expanding.

identification: Plants commonly grow about 1.5–3 feet high but can lean and scramble through other vegetation. The stems have four angles and small recurved hooks, which are also present along the leaves. Narrow, pointed leaves appear in whorls, usually four to seven around a node, and are often about 2–4 inches long. Tiny star-shaped flowers are yellow to yellow-green, commonly with five lobes; fruits become dark purple to nearly black. Bedstraws in Galium can have similar whorled leaves and catching hairs, but their fruits are dry rather than the fleshy fruits of Rubia. Include mature fruit, leaf arrangement and a close view of the stem angles when requesting confirmation; vegetative tangles are harder to name reliably.
actions: Keep a retained Dyer's madder planting within a defined bed and inspect its edges for shoots connected to creeping underground stems. Where it is unwanted, wear gloves for the hooked stems and carefully lift the crown and accessible underground stems, working outward from the visible shoots. Avoid moving root-filled soil to another garden or natural area. Collect fruiting material before it is scattered, and revisit the cleared area for seedlings or renewed growth. Large intertwined patches may be easier to manage in stages that protect neighboring plants. Confirm the identity before removing similar native bedstraws, and use local botanical advice if the plant is found away from cultivation.

identification: Flowering Dyer's woad commonly stands 2–4 feet tall. Look for blue-green leaves with a conspicuous pale midvein; leaves higher on the stem clasp it at their bases. Small flowers have four yellow petals arranged in a cross. The strongest clue comes afterward: flattened, hanging pods turn dark brown to purplish black, with one seed inside each. Rosettes can resemble hoary cress, which develops white flowers rather than yellow ones. Many other yellow-flowered mustards produce slender pods instead of these broad, dangling fruits. Photograph a lower leaf, the way an upper leaf joins the stem, and mature pods. A rosette alone deserves a second look before removal.
actions: Pull or dig small patches before pods develop, working carefully to remove the root. Taller second-year plants can be easier to locate than low rosettes, but do not postpone work once flowering begins. Bag flowering and seed-bearing material for an accepted disposal route; keep it out of ordinary yard waste. Mowing near early flowering can reduce seed production in accessible open areas, but revisit the patch for regrowth and missed plants. Check nearby bare ground in later seasons for new rosettes. Where Dyer's woad is uncommon, send the location to the local weed program so it can help contain a new patch.

identification: Earleaf acacia can reach 50 feet or more, with a single trunk or several stems and no thorns. Its narrow, sickle-shaped leaf stalks are commonly 5–8 inches long, with several strong lengthwise veins and a small gland near the base. Yellow to orange-yellow flower spikes develop toward branch tips. The broad, flattened pods curl and twist as they mature; open pods reveal dark seeds attached by conspicuous orange strands. Bark becomes more fissured with age. Other acacias also have flattened leaf stalks, so curved foliage by itself is not decisive. A useful identification set includes the veins and base of the foliage, flower spikes, and opened ripe pods.
actions: Inspect the ground beneath Earleaf acacia and the edges of nearby natural vegetation for seedlings. Pull small seedlings with their roots while they are manageable, and check again after further germination. Collect fallen pods where practical and contain them during disposal so seeds are not scattered with debris. For a mature tree, arrange removal with a qualified tree professional and ask how stump regrowth and later seedlings will be handled. Choose a locally appropriate replacement that will fit the available space. In areas where Earleaf acacia is spreading outside cultivation, avoid distributing its seeds or planting additional trees near wild vegetation.

Acacia auriculiformis — NParks Flora & Fauna Web
Earleaf Acacia: An Invasive Threat to Florida — UF/IFAS

identification: Look for a woody plant with broad, pointed leaves, often 9–30 centimeters long, that are gray-green above and paler underneath. Dense branched hairs cover the leaves and young stems, but the plant has no prickles. One or two small, stalkless leaves often sit beside the base of a larger leaf stalk. Flowers are about 1.5–2.5 centimeters across, with five violet lobes and a yellow center; the rounded berries are about 1–1.5 centimeters wide. Solanum marginatum has conspicuous spines, while Brugmansia has large hanging trumpet flowers instead of these small star-shaped clusters. Photograph the leaf-stalk junction and flowers without rubbing or crushing the foliage. Reported mature height varies substantially with growing conditions.
actions: Wear gloves and clothing that keeps the hairs off your skin when handling Earleaf nightshade, and avoid creating airborne debris. Pull small plants when the soil is moist, removing their roots. Larger plants may need digging or a coordinated removal plan; simply cutting the stem can leave a plant that grows back. Collect fruiting branches carefully before disturbing them, and use local disposal guidance for material that could carry seeds or take root. Revisit cleared ground every few months for seedlings and shoots. Keep children and animals from eating the berries, and seek professional poisoning advice promptly if ingestion is suspected.

sources.label: Solanum mauritianum — New South Wales Flora Online

identification: Early water grass forms upright clumps commonly about 40–120 centimeters tall, with flat leaves and a loose seed head that leans sideways or droops. Individual flower units are roughly 4–7 millimeters long and often carry long bristles, called awns. At the junction of leaf blade and sheath, it lacks the thin flap, or ligule, found on rice. This separates it from rice but not from other Echinochloa grasses. Barnyardgrass and late watergrass require closer comparison of mature flower units, their enclosing scales, and flowering time; awn length alone is unreliable across all populations. Save clear views of the leaf collar and mature head, and use a regional grass specialist for uncertain specimens.
actions: In rice fields, plan control early with a crop adviser rather than waiting for obvious seed heads. Use clean seed, watch for plants that survive treatment, and prevent those survivors from adding seed where feasible. Early water grass can emerge through shallow flooding, so the water regime must be considered with the crop and the whole weed community. A stale seedbed—encouraging weeds to emerge before planting, then removing them—can help reduce pressure. Severe infestations may justify crop rotation where the site allows it. Ask for resistance testing when a correctly applied treatment repeatedly fails; changing products blindly may leave the same resistant population.

identification: Published comparisons describe Helodrilus oculatus as approximately 35–80 millimeters long, with about 90–150 body segments and little body pigmentation. Small bristles are closely paired, but these details require magnification. Adults develop a thickened reproductive band, the clitellum, toward the front of the body; its exact segment positions and nearby reproductive structures help specialists identify the species. Those positions vary somewhat between published accounts, so a photograph of a pale worm is not enough. Native Sparganophilus worms can occupy similar wet places, and habitat alone cannot distinguish them. Record whether the worm was in submerged mud, a seep, or a bank, and photograph its entire body beside a scale.
actions: Do not relocate worms from a wetland, stream bank, or pond edge to another site. Avoid moving soil containing worms, and never empty unused fishing bait into natural habitats. If a find could represent Helodrilus oculatus outside a documented locality, send photographs and precise habitat information to a museum worm specialist or local biological-recording program. Ask before collecting specimens so the receiving specialist can explain what is useful and how to preserve it. Leave the surrounding wetland intact while identification is pending; draining, excavating, or applying chemicals to a bank would be a poor response to an uncertain worm identification.

identification: Look for hairy stem joints and broad leaf blades with lengthwise folds, commonly 5–30 centimeters long and about 1–3 centimeters wide. Flowering stems can reach roughly 2 meters. At the junction of blade and sheath, the ligule is a short fringe of hairs rather than a broad membrane. The open flower head has short side branches and tiny oval spikelets about 2.5–3 millimeters long, with slender persistent bristles. Setaria intermedia has narrower, flatter leaves, smooth stem joints and smaller spikelets, according to the comparative weed key. Photograph the whole head, a stem joint, the leaf base and a ruler beside several spikelets. Bristle placement varies between descriptions, so avoid identifying the plant from the number of bristles on one branch.
actions: Inspect a suspected patch while it is flowering, and have unfamiliar grasses checked before removal. For a few confirmed unwanted plants, lift the clumps and any lower stems that have rooted into the soil before seeds mature. Collect seed-bearing heads rather than scattering them during mowing or cleanup. Check tools, footwear and equipment for attached seed or soil before moving to another site, and keep removed material out of drainage channels. Revisit the patch for seedlings or missed rooted sections. Larger infestations in crops or natural vegetation warrant local advice based on the site; the management needs of this tropical grass cannot be inferred from an ordinary lawn-crabgrass program.

sources.label: Flora of North America via NEON — Setaria barbata

identification: Flowering stems may be only a few tens of centimeters high or approach a meter. Narrow leaves have fine hairs in many plants, and a small, thin membrane sits where each blade joins its sheath. Several slender flower branches arise together or along a short central axis. Their tiny spikelets occur in pairs and are about 2–3.5 millimeters long. Southern crabgrass (Digitaria ciliaris) is a documented source of confusion; reliable separation uses the small scales and hairs of the spikelets, not the fingerlike head alone. In East indian crabgrass, the lowest scale is absent or minute and the next is much shorter than the spikelet. Include close photographs of these parts, the leaf base and rooted stems. A specialist may need a flowering specimen.
actions: First establish whether the grass is unwanted at that particular site and confirm its identification. For a small patch in a managed bed, loosen the soil and lift both the central plant and trailing stems rooted at their joints. Check the ground afterward rather than assuming that removing the tallest shoots removed the entire plant. Collect mature heads before moving material, and clean soil and seed from tools and footwear. Avoid transporting rooted clumps in planting soil. Where plants occur in natural habitat, seek local botanical advice before clearing them, especially in regions where this species is native. Extensive growth in a crop requires locally appropriate weed-management advice.

identification: Adults are roughly 3–4 millimeters long. Look for long legs and antennae, a narrower section behind the head and broader wing covers, sometimes with pale scale patches. The decisive feature is on the small shield behind the head: two dense tufts of upright hairs with a smooth, shiny area between them. The whitemarked spider beetle (Ptinus fur) also has paired hair tufts, but the intervening surface is dull and finely sculptured. Ptinus bicinctus lacks those distinct upright tufts. Males and females differ in body shape, so a slender specimen and a rounder one may be the same species. Save an intact adult in a closed container for an extension identification service; magnified views of its upper surface are more useful than pictures of food damage alone.
actions: Inspect flour, cereals, seed, pet food and older packages near the sightings. Isolate suspect containers, discard confirmed infested food securely, and check neighboring items before returning them to storage. Vacuum shelf joints, corners and accumulated food debris, then empty the vacuum contents securely. Store replacement supplies in tightly closing glass, metal or sturdy plastic containers. Finding a few adults after cleanup means the search may need to extend beyond the first affected package. Do not spray food or rely on spraying shelves to solve a hidden infestation. If insects continue appearing or involve museum material or commercial stock, seek professional identification and a management plan suited to those materials.

identification: Garden plants are commonly about 10–25 centimeters tall, with slender branching or trailing stems. Lower leaves are broader and toothed, while leaves near the flowers become narrow and may have smooth edges. The flowers are roughly 1–2 centimeters long and strongly uneven: three broad lower lobes make a small fan below two narrower upper lobes. Small capsules follow the flowers and contain numerous tiny seeds. Color alone is unreliable because cultivars differ. Other lobelias share the two-lipped flower, so record the whole plant's height and habit rather than identifying a detached bloom. Photograph lower and upper leaves, a flower from the front and side, and a mature capsule. Plants without flowers may need comparison with a regional flora.
actions: If Edging lobelia appears beyond a planted bed, note whether it is a single volunteer or part of a recurring patch. Remove unwanted small plants with their roots before capsules mature, and collect spent seed-bearing material when cleaning containers. Keep potting soil and garden waste out of stream margins and other unmanaged ground. Recheck the site during the following growing season for seedlings. A healthy cultivated plant does not need removal solely because this species appears in a registry; consider local behavior and nearby habitat. Do not eat the plant or use it in home remedies. Ask a local botanist about uncertain wild plants before removing them.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand — Lobelia erinus

identification: Look for a multistemmed woody plant that may reach about 3–10 meters tall, with pale gray bark and large alternate leaves. The leaves commonly have three to five broad lobes and a rough upper surface; their size and degree of lobing vary. Figs develop where leaves join the branches and may ripen green, yellowish, brown or dark purple according to the cultivar. A small opening at the far end is a useful detail. The plant loses its leaves in cold seasons, making bare shoots less distinctive. Photograph a leafy branch, bark, fruit and any shoots emerging away from the main trunk. A photograph does not reliably establish cultivar, pollination requirements or whether a small shoot is a seedling rather than a root sucker.
actions: Watch for young Edible fig plants beyond the planting area, especially along drains or moist ground. Remove unwanted small seedlings while their roots are manageable, but check whether they are attached to a larger root system. Avoid skin contact with the milky sap; wear gloves and protective clothing when cutting. Collect fallen fruit and keep fresh branches or root pieces out of waterways and dumped garden waste. Cutting an established plant can produce vigorous new shoots, so plan follow-up rather than treating one cut as removal. For large trees or thickets beside a stream, ask a qualified local adviser about removal that protects the bank and surrounding vegetation.

sources.label: California Invasive Plant Council — Edible Fig, by John M. Randall

identification: This is a microscopic identification rather than one made from a photograph of an eel. Gyrodactylus has a rear attachment organ armed with hooks, and specialists compare the shapes and measurements of those hardened parts. Gyrodactylus anguillae and G. nipponensis have both been reported from cultured European eels, so the host's identity alone cannot separate them. Other organisms can occur on the same skin or gills. Useful information for a diagnostic laboratory includes the eel species, where and when it was acquired, water conditions, recent movements and the onset of any symptoms. Ask the laboratory how it wants samples collected and preserved; damaged or deteriorated worms can lose the features needed for a reliable species identification.
actions: Do not move suspect eels into another pond, aquarium or natural waterbody while arranging a diagnosis. Keep records of the source of each group and any recent additions so a fish-health professional can assess possible transmission. Use a separate quarantine setup for new arrivals and equipment that is not shared with established fish. For affected animals, arrange prompt professional examination rather than trying to identify the parasite from behavior alone. Report unusual illness or deaths in wild eels to the local fisheries authority with the location and date. Follow the diagnostic service's instructions for specimens and wastewater; an improvised salt bath or medication is not a substitute for determining the cause.

identification: Adults are around 1–1.5 millimeters long in the University of Tokyo comparison, although preserved specimens and life stages differ. A microscope reveals the rear attachment organ, or haptor, and the hooks that hold the worm to a gill. Pseudodactylogyrus anguillae has relatively long, slender anchors and a roughly heart-shaped haptor; P. bini has shorter, stouter anchors and a more oval haptor. These are specialist characters, not features visible on a swimming eel. The similar Australian species P. rohdei requires additional comparison of internal structures and the attachment apparatus. Provide the diagnostic service with host identity, origin, salinity and recent transfer history. General gill irritation, excess mucus or breathing difficulty cannot establish which parasite, if any, is responsible.
actions: Pause transfers of eels from an affected holding system and contact a fish-health veterinarian or diagnostic laboratory. Record whether fish came from fresh or brackish water, their supplier and any shared equipment or water connections. Quarantine new eels separately, including apparently healthy arrivals. Avoid moving used nets or untreated holding water between systems. Because this parasite has an egg-laying life cycle, removing visible worms from a fish does not demonstrate that its environment is clear. Have the professional plan follow-up checks as well as any treatment. For unusual illness in wild eels, report the site and observations to the fisheries authority without transporting live fish elsewhere.

identification: An adult is approximately 2 millimeters long in the University of Tokyo account. Under magnification, its rear attachment organ bears a pair of substantial anchors, around 50–60 micrometers long in that description. Pseudodactylogyrus bini has a broadly oval attachment organ and shorter, stouter anchors than P. anguillae, whose anchors are longer despite its often smaller body. Size alone is inadequate because age and specimen preparation affect measurements. Another close relative, P. gusevi, was separated from some older Australian records using reproductive and attachment structures. A fish photograph cannot resolve those distinctions. A laboratory needs suitable gill material and the eel's identity and origin. Let trained staff obtain samples; handling or cutting gills without appropriate expertise can harm the fish.
actions: For a suspected infection, keep the affected group separate and ask a fish-health professional to examine the gills. Tell the service about recent arrivals, water temperature, mortality and any previous treatment. Do not sell, release or transfer suspect eels to clear space in the tank. Have a professional assess the entire holding system, because eggs and developing stages may persist beyond the worms currently found on the fish. Clean and manage empty equipment or ponds under that plan rather than applying an unverified treatment to occupied water. Maintain separate nets for separate groups and document follow-up results before resuming transfers. Healthy-looking skin alone is not a clearance check.

identification: Most garden Eggplant plants grow about 60–120 centimeters tall and develop several branches. Leaves are alternate, broadly oval and sometimes shallowly lobed, with branched, star-shaped hairs best seen through a hand lens. Stems, leaves and the green cup around a fruit may carry prickles in some varieties. Flowers generally have five or more pointed violet lobes around yellow anthers. Fruit size, shape and color vary too widely to use one supermarket form as a universal guide. Other Solanum species also have star-shaped flowers and hairy or prickly foliage, so do not identify an unfamiliar wild nightshade as Eggplant from the flower alone. Photograph a complete branch, leaf hairs, the fruit's attachment and several developmental stages; a known planting history is especially helpful.
actions: Keep deliberate Eggplant cultivation within managed beds or containers, and collect unwanted ripe or damaged fruit rather than dumping it on unmanaged ground. Remove a confirmed unwanted volunteer with its roots while it is small, then check for further seedlings. If the plant's identity is uncertain, photograph it and obtain horticultural advice before eating any fruit. Leaves and other non-fruit parts should not be used as food. In an established vegetable bed, harvest by clipping the fruit stalk rather than pulling and tearing the plant. Diagnose unusual leaf damage or wilting before taking action; insect feeding, disease and growing conditions can produce different problems that need different responses.

sources.label: University of Minnesota Extension — Growing Eggplant

identification: Look for upright, sticky-hairy shoots near a possible host plant, sometimes hidden beneath its leaves. The stems may be simple or branched and carry small triangular scales. Flowers are tubular and purple to pale, with an upper lip divided into two lobes and a lower lip divided into three. Flowers about 20–35 millimeters long are typical of Egyptian broomrape; the similar branched broomrape (Phelipanche ramosa) usually has flowers no longer than about 20 millimeters. There is overlap, so flower length is a clue rather than a final determination. Photograph the plant in place, nearby hosts and flowers from several angles with a scale. Native broomrapes and borderline Phelipanche specimens require a botanist's examination; do not dig up the attachment to prove the association.
actions: Leave a suspected Egyptian broomrape in place and promptly send photographs and its precise location to your state agriculture department or local agricultural extension service. In California, the county agricultural commissioner is the reporting route given by CDFA, which specifically advises against collecting specimens. Avoid walking or driving through the patch and pause movement of soil, plants or equipment from the affected area until you receive instructions. Keep others from mowing or composting the shoots. Removal of a visible stalk does not address seeds or the underground parasite. Let the responding specialist confirm the species and coordinate containment with the grower or landowner, particularly where crops or planting materials are involved.

sources.label: California Department of Food and Agriculture — Egyptian Broomrape
UC Agriculture and Natural Resources — Broomrape Species

identification: Adults measure about 63–73 cm long. Look for a reddish-brown patch surrounding a pale orange eye, pink bill and legs, and a dark mark on the breast. A flying bird shows large white areas across the front of otherwise dark wings. Young birds retain the pink bill and legs but lack the adult eye mask, so a family photograph can help. Muscovy Duck also has conspicuous white wing patches, but typical adults are much darker and have red, wartlike skin on the face. Photograph the head, breast, legs and, if the bird opens its wings naturally, the wing pattern. Sex is less reliably judged from a distant photograph than species; males and females look similar.
actions: Observe from a distance and give pairs with young plenty of room; keep dogs from approaching or pursuing them. Do not release captive waterfowl or move free-living birds to another pond. Avoid feeding birds at a site where they are congregating, and secure spilled grain or pet feed. For a new local occurrence, record the date, location, number of adults and young, and clear photographs; a bird-recording project or state wildlife agency can assess the observation. If nesting birds create a recurring access or safety problem, contact the property manager and wildlife agency for a humane, site-specific response before handling birds, eggs or nests.

identification: Plants commonly stand about 15–60 cm high, with flat, narrow leaves and hairs along at least part of their margins. The flowering head usually has two to five short branches, each about 1–5 cm long. Look closely for a bare, pointed extension beyond the last spikelets at each branch tip. The small flap where the blade meets its sheath has a membranous base and a hairy fringe; magnification helps.
