Common sorrel usually has a less repeatedly branched cluster. Mature fruit coverings are generally smaller in narrow-leaved sorrel, but the ranges overlap. Include the whole flowering stem, lower leaves and close views of ripe fruits, and seek botanical review when the two species remain difficult to separate.
actions: Document an unfamiliar patch before disturbing it, including nearby roads, fill or former cultivation that might explain its arrival. If confirmed plants need removal, prevent seed production and account for the persistent rootstock; cutting stems once is not the same as removing the plant. Check treated ground in following seasons. For a large patch, obtain a site-specific weed plan rather than transferring control advice from a different Rumex species. Avoid moving soil containing roots or ripe seed to clean ground.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Rumex thyrsiflorus

identification: Look for a low, bushy plant with a woody base, small opposite gray-green leaves and tiny pinkish, lavender or white flowers. Leaves are roughly 6-13 mm long, with edges rolled underneath; young stems are hairy and square in cross-section. Common thyme tends to form an upright little mound, whereas some other thymes form low creeping mats. Cultivars and hybrids complicate identification. Record growth form, leaf edges and a flowering stem, and use the original nursery label as supporting information when available. Aroma alone does not identify the species.
actions: If a plant is spreading beyond an intended bed, remove unwanted rooted growth and prevent seed from reaching adjacent habitat. Do not dump live garden divisions or cuttings on open land. Keep a record of any independently established plants before removing them. For a planting that remains contained, routine pruning and monitoring are more appropriate than treating it as a major infestation. Confirm unfamiliar aromatic plants before using them in food; this profile is not a foraging identification guide.

identification: Tomato stems and leaves are noticeably hairy, often with sticky glandular hairs. Leaves are alternate and divided into several toothed or lobed leaflets. Small yellow, star-shaped flowers are followed by fleshy fruit whose size, shape and ripe color depend on the cultivar. Do not use red fruit alone as the identifying feature: other nightshades have red berries, and tomatoes need not ripen red. Photograph the divided leaves, flowers and fruit together. The strongly scented foliage supports identification but is not an invitation to taste an unfamiliar plant.
actions: Remove unwanted volunteers before ripe fruit drops, and contain discarded fruit in a managed waste or compost system. When reporting a plant outside cultivation, note whether it is near a garden, compost pile or deposited soil. Keep potentially diseased crop residues away from new tomato beds and seek a crop diagnosis if wilting or spotted leaves are the concern. Do not remove native nightshades on the assumption that all nightshade-like seedlings are tomato escapes, and do not eat berries from an uncertain identification.

identification: Leaves are opposite and divided into many toothed, narrow leaflets. Small white to pale pink flowers form clusters near the stem tips. Plants may reach about 1.5 m, and the pale fleshy underground parts have a distinctive strong odor. Native valerian species require care: Valeriana uliginosa generally has simple basal leaves or just a few basal lobes, whereas common valerian has divided basal leaves. Photograph basal and stem leaves as well as flowers; a cluster of pale flowers alone is not diagnostic.
actions: Remove small confirmed plants with their underground growth and revisit the site for shoots or seedlings. Cutting or mowing before flowering can limit seed production, but a persistent patch needs follow-up. Keep ripe heads and living root pieces from being moved elsewhere. In wetlands or near native valerian, confirm identification and coordinate removal with the land manager before disturbing soil. Do not collect wild plants for self-medication. Where the species is regulated, follow the local weed program's disposal and control requirements.

identification: Each leaf has paired leaflets and ends in a tendril. Pea-shaped flowers arise singly or in small groups close to the leaf axils. This differs from hairy vetch, which typically carries many flowers on longer stalks. Common vetch is part of a variable group that includes narrow-leaved forms; leaf width alone may not resolve a subspecies. Photograph the flower attachment, leaflets, the small stipules where leaves join the stem, and mature pods. A leafy tangle without flowers is harder to distinguish from native vetches.
actions: Where common vetch is unwanted, pull or cut young plants before pods ripen and scatter seed. Follow up along fences, bed edges and disturbed ground. When managing a cover crop, plan termination with crop-specific advice so it does not reseed into the next planting. Do not offer unfamiliar vetch seed or collected plants as animal feed; forage use requires the right species and management. In natural vegetation, confirm that the plant is an introduced vetch before removing it.

identification: Upper leaflets are narrow, commonly 1-4 mm wide. The pea-shaped flowers are about 8-18 mm long and occur close to the leaf axils, usually in small numbers. Mature pods are roughly 2.5-5 cm long, generally smooth, and darken toward black without obvious constrictions between seeds. In the NSW treatment, the pointed teeth of the flower's green calyx are shorter than its tube. Broader common-vetch forms and several native vetches can overlap in appearance. Include ripe pods, flowers and upper and lower leaves in photographs rather than relying only on narrow foliage.
actions: Remove unwanted plants before the pods dry and split. Check equipment, soil and garden waste before moving them from a patch that has set seed. In a small bed, hand removal is usually more targeted than treating the surrounding vegetation. Revisit the site for later seedlings. If plants are mixed with native vetches or are being considered for forage, obtain a firm identification first; similar-looking vetches should not be treated as interchangeable.

sources.label: NSW PlantNET: Vicia sativa subsp. nigra

identification: Leaves occur opposite one another or in small whorls, often three at a node. Five-petaled yellow flowers form branched clusters toward the tops of stems. Examine the green sepals beneath a flower: their edges are dark reddish or orange-brown. The similar ornamental Lysimachia punctata has flowers grouped more closely in leaf axils along the stem, with entirely green sepals and fine glandular hairs along the petal edges. Photograph the whole flower arrangement and the underside of a flower to show these differences.
actions: Report a suspected new shoreline patch to the land manager or weed program before digging. Small, newly established patches may be removable if all rhizomes can be recovered, but larger stands usually need a coordinated plan and repeated checks. Keep root pieces and seed-bearing material out of water and yard-waste piles. Cutting flowers can reduce seed production while a plan is arranged; it does not eliminate the rhizomes. Work in wetlands may require specialized methods and permissions, so use local guidance rather than applying ordinary garden products near water.

sources.label: Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board: Garden loosestrife

identification: Adults have a rounded brown to yellow-brown shell, usually about 25-30 mm wide, with four or five whorls and pronounced curved ribs. The opening has a pale edge rather than a broadly flared lip, and the underside lacks an open central hole. Zachrysia trinitaria looks similar but grows considerably larger; small or immature individuals still need expert examination. Photograph the top, opening and underside beside a ruler. Shell wear and age can obscure color, so include measurements and structure rather than relying on brown coloration.
actions: Inspect the bases and undersides of pots, moist hiding places and incoming nursery stock. Avoid moving infested plants or loose growing media to another property. Use gloves if handling snails and wash afterward; do not relocate them outdoors elsewhere. Photograph suspected new occurrences and ask an extension or plant-health service for identification and appropriate disposal advice. Where damage is confirmed, reducing damp debris and monitoring hiding places can support a locally recommended snail-management plan. Keep baits, if recommended, away from children and animals and follow their labels.

sources.label: UF/IFAS: Terrestrial snails affecting plants in Florida

identification: Lower leaves are deeply divided, while upper leaves become smaller and narrower. Flowers have four small pale petals and six stamens. Mature pods are flat, oval and notched at the tip, usually about 5-6 mm long, with a winged edge. Virginia pepperweed, Lepidium virginicum, usually has smaller pods and only two, occasionally four, stamens. These small features need a close photograph or magnification. Include ripe pods and flowers together, because a leafy seedling alone is hard to separate from other small mustards.
actions: If cress is reseeding where it is unwanted, remove plants before the pods mature and check nearby bare soil for seedlings. Keep discarded seed trays and seed-bearing plants within managed garden waste. For an observation away from cultivation, note nearby gardens or soil dumping and document flowers and pods. Do not remove every similar pepperweed without checking the species; native relatives may grow in the same area. No broad treatment is needed for a contained food planting solely because this species appears in the catalog.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Lepidium sativum

identification: First-year leaves are rounded or kidney-shaped, with scalloped edges. Flowering plants have more triangular, toothed leaves and small white flowers with four petals. Slender seedpods develop along the upper stems. Crushed foliage often smells of garlic, but smell alone is not a firm identification. Young violets and other woodland plants can resemble the rosettes. Photograph the lower leaves, stem leaves, flowers and pods; the transition between these features is more useful than a single leaf.
actions: Check a suspected patch in spring, before seedpods mature. In a small patch, pull carefully from moist soil and remove the root crown; broken plants can regrow. Flowering plants may still produce viable seed after pulling, so contain them and follow local disposal guidance rather than leaving them on the ground. Clean soil and seeds from boots and tools. Recheck the area for several years, protect nearby native seedlings, and avoid disturbing more soil than necessary.

identification: Stems stand upright or lean outward and may become woody near the base. Narrow, stalkless stem leaves have finely toothed edges; the leaves around the flowering branches are broader and more triangular. The upper branches repeatedly fork. What looks like one tiny flower is a cup holding several reduced flowers, with greenish-yellow glands bearing two slender hornlike tips. Mature capsules are smooth. Many spurges share milky sap and green flower clusters, so photograph leaves, forks and close-up flower cups for confirmation rather than breaking the plant to test its sap.
actions: Avoid contact with the milky sap, especially around eyes, and keep children and animals away from cut material. Record the extent of a suspected patch and contact the local weed program if it is spreading in coastal or natural vegetation. For a small confirmed patch, plan removal before capsules release seed, using protective clothing and a disposal method appropriate to the site. Revisit disturbed ground for seedlings. Larger stands need a site-specific plan; cutting visible stems alone should not be assumed to finish control.

sources.label: California Invasive Plant Council: Euphorbia terracina

identification: Adults are about half an inch long, light brown, and have two dark lengthwise stripes on the shield directly behind the head. Young cockroaches are smaller and darker, with a lighter stripe down the back and no fully developed wings. Females often carry an egg case at the end of the abdomen. Brown-banded cockroaches have crosswise pale bands, while some outdoor species can resemble German cockroaches more closely. Save a clear photograph or a contained specimen for identification before choosing a treatment.
actions: Use sticky monitors near likely hiding places, including beneath sinks and beside appliances, and note where catches are highest. Store food in sealed containers, remove crumbs and grease, repair leaks and reduce cardboard clutter. In an apartment building, tell the property manager so adjoining spaces can be considered together. Targeted baits and professional integrated pest management are generally more useful than repeatedly spraying visible insects. Follow product labels and keep bait placements inaccessible to children and pets; sanitation and follow-up remain essential.

identification: Flat, sword-shaped leaves overlap in fans. Flowers have three upright inner segments and three outer segments that spread or hang downward; the outer segments carry the characteristic fuzzy beard. A flower's color alone is not reliable because there are many cultivars. Photograph an open flower from the front and side, the leaf fan and any naturally exposed rhizomes. Iris names in gardens can cover complex hybrids, so a cultivar or exact parentage should not be assigned from a photograph alone.
actions: If an unwanted clump is confirmed, remove the rhizomes rather than cutting only the leaves, and check for regrowth from pieces left behind. Do not dump divisions into natural areas or roadside soil. Wear gloves when handling cut plants, keep the material away from pets, and do not eat any part. If reporting an escape, note whether an old garden, cemetery or discarded planting material is nearby and whether new clumps occur beyond it.

sources.label: NC State Extension: Iris x germanica

identification: Look for very narrow, pointed leaves in opposite pairs along spreading stems. The leaf bases meet in a thin, pale membrane. Tiny green flowers sit in clusters where leaves join the stem; they lack showy petals. The pointed sepals remain around a one-seeded fruit. Perennial knawel has more rounded sepals with broader white margins, and pearlwort usually has more noticeable white flowers and many-seeded capsules. A close photograph of the flower cluster and leaf bases is much more informative than a distant photograph of the mat.
actions: In a small bed or open patch, remove plants before seed matures and check again for later seedlings. Lift the central root rather than simply trimming the sprawling tips. In turf, confirm the identification before applying a product intended for grass weeds: knawel is not a grass. Reduce repeated bare-soil disturbance and maintain suitable ground cover for the site. If it is widespread in a crop or lawn, ask a local extension office about management matched to that setting.

identification: Workers are about half an inch long, with a compact body and bold yellow-and-black markings. The first abdominal segment commonly has a dark spade-shaped mark, followed by separate dark spots along the sides of later segments. These markings vary and need to be considered together. A clear photograph of the face and the top of the abdomen can help an expert separate similar species. Watch from a safe distance for repeated traffic into one small opening; do not approach or disturb the entrance to obtain a better image.
actions: Keep food and sweet drinks covered, close garbage containers, and give foraging wasps space. If a nest threatens a doorway, play area or occupied building, contact a qualified pest professional. Do not plug an active wall-nest entrance yourself: wasps may find another route into the building. Traps can reduce some foraging workers but do not reliably remove an established colony. A nest away from people may not require immediate intervention; identification and location should guide the response.

sources.label: UC IPM: Yellowjackets and other social wasps
Penn State Extension: Managing stinging insects

identification: The stems have backward-pointing prickles that help them catch on neighboring vegetation. Leaves are elongated and rough, with lower leaves more clearly stalked than upper ones. Small blue flowers appear close to the leaf bases. After flowering, the green calyx enlarges into a flattened, strongly toothed, clamshell-like enclosure around the nutlets. Photograph this fruiting structure from both sides. Forget-me-nots and other rough-leaved members of the same family can share blue flowers, but do not have this distinctive enclosing calyx.
actions: If a confirmed plant is unwanted in a small area, remove it before the fruits mature and handle the prickly stems with gloves. Keep fruiting material contained rather than dragging it through clean ground. Photograph mature features before disposal if the identification is uncertain, and check the site for later seedlings. Where it is mixed with native plants, remove individual plants selectively rather than clearing all rough-leaved vegetation.

identification: Leaves alternate along the woody stems and have toothed edges. White flowers with conspicuously long stamens form small clusters on short side shoots. In the New England key, most clusters have their own stalk and about five to twelve flowers; the leaves have short but visible stalks. Some bridalwreath and Thunberg spireas have smaller, essentially unstalked flower clusters. Several forms of germander meadowsweet differ in leaf width and cluster shape, so photograph a flowering twig, leaf undersides and the base of the shrub.
actions: Check whether shoots are appearing beyond the original planting and whether they connect to its roots. If removal is needed, plan to address the root system and revisit for suckers rather than assuming pruning will remove the shrub. Keep rooted divisions and soil containing live roots out of natural areas. Ask for help with identification before removing an unfamiliar wild spirea, since native species occur in the same genus.

sources.label: Trees and Shrubs Online: Spiraea chamaedryfolia

identification: Look for opposite, coarsely toothed leaves and two distinct lines of hairs running along the stem. Blue flowers have a white center and four unequal lobes, with the lowest lobe narrower than the others. Flowers are carried in loose, stalked clusters from upper leaf axils. The capsules are flattened, notched and roughly heart-shaped. Other speedwells may have similar flowers; photograph the hair pattern, leaf attachment and whole flowering cluster rather than relying on flower color.
actions: For a small unwanted patch, work through the rooted stems and rhizomes instead of pulling only the flowering tips. Recheck the edges for regrowth and keep live fragments out of nearby beds. In lawns, avoid treating all small blue-flowered plants as the same weed: confirm the species and choose management suited to the turf and surrounding vegetation. When reporting it outside a garden, include the patch size and whether it is spreading into other ground cover.

identification: Workers have a dark head and middle body contrasting with a very pale abdomen and legs. Under magnification, the antennae have twelve segments and no distinct club; the waist node is low and often hidden by the abdomen. The ants lack a stinger. Size or a dark head alone is not enough to separate every small household ant, so a close photograph or securely contained specimen is useful. Look along a trail without disturbing it to see where ants enter cracks or approach food and moisture.
actions: Clean up sweet spills, store food securely and repair moisture problems. Inspect potted plants and other movable items before taking them to a new room or property. For an indoor infestation, identify the ant first and use a coordinated bait-based plan rather than repeatedly spraying the visible trail. If bait is used, check whether ants are actually feeding and follow the label for placement around children and pets. Persistent or scattered trails may need professional inspection to locate several nesting sites.

identification: Look for a streamlined lizard with a long tail and well-developed legs, but do not use these general features as a final identification. Juveniles and adults can differ in pattern, and other Florida teiid lizards can look similar. Specialist keys examine scale arrangements, including the rows of large scales on the underside. Take clear photographs of the whole animal, head and sides from where you are standing, and include its approximate size. Do not catch or turn it over simply to obtain a scale count.
actions: Report an unfamiliar free-living ameiva with its location, date and photographs to the local wildlife agency or a qualified reptile specialist. Note whether you saw one animal or several and whether young animals were present. Do not release pets or move a wild-caught lizard to another location. If a captive animal needs rehoming, use an appropriate surrender or adoption route. Avoid glue traps and broad pest treatments that can injure native lizards as well.

sources.label: Smith and Krysko: Florida teiid lizards and identification key
Ugueto and Harvey2011: Ameiva revision and Florida populations

identification: The shell is rounded, with a short spire, deeply indented joins between whorls and a large teardrop-shaped opening. Color varies from yellowish to brown, often with dark bands. Fresh egg masses contain many small pink eggs and become paler as they develop. Florida's native applesnail has fewer, larger eggs, usually pale, and less deeply channeled shell joins. Pomacea canaliculata is harder to distinguish from P. maculata. Photograph the shell opening, side of the shell and an egg mass with a size reference; an expert may need more than photographs.
actions: Do not move snails, egg masses, aquarium plants or water between waterways. Inspect boats and equipment and remove attached material before leaving the site. For a suspected new occurrence, photograph it and report the location to the state aquatic-invasive-species program. Ask for local instructions before removing eggs, especially where native applesnails occur. Avoid bare-handed contact with eggs and wash after handling equipment from the site. Never release unwanted aquarium animals outdoors.

sources.label: North Carolina Wildlife: Aquatic nuisance species

identification: Adults have a broad, flattened oval body and long light-brown forewings; both sexes are winged. Large individuals can approach four inches in length. Young stages lack the adults' developed wings and can look quite different. Several Blaberus species resemble one another, and size or a dark patch behind the head is not a dependable species test. Photograph the whole insect from above and the side, include a scale, and record whether it was found indoors, outdoors or near a captive collection.
actions: If it may be an escaped captive animal, secure the enclosure and inspect nearby hiding places rather than releasing it outdoors. For an unfamiliar outdoor specimen, send photographs to an extension office or museum entomologist before using insecticides. Keep any specimen contained if a specialist requests it, and do not ship live insects without instructions. In a building, reduce access to food and damp hiding places while the identity and extent of the occurrence are checked.

sources.label: University of the West Indies: Giant cave cockroach

identification: The seedhead resembles a fuzzy bottlebrush and usually bends or nods when mature. Leaf blades have many short hairs on the upper surface, while the underside is much less hairy. At the junction of blade and sheath, the ligule is a fringe of hairs rather than a membrane. Green foxtail generally lacks the same covering of short hairs across the blade, and yellow foxtail has conspicuous longer hairs near the blade base. Photograph the seedhead, both leaf surfaces and the collar area; an immature grass without these views is harder to name.
actions: Remove small patches while plants are young and before the heads shed seed. In cultivated ground, early control is easier than waiting until strong crown roots develop, and disturbed plants may reroot in moist soil. Check field margins and recently harvested areas for plants that could replenish the seedbank. Clean seed-bearing debris from equipment before moving fields. For larger infestations, combine crop competition and locally appropriate control rather than relying on one repeated herbicide treatment.

sources.label: University of Maryland: Know your foxtails

identification: Mature flowering plants can reach roughly seven to fourteen feet tall. Look for huge, deeply cut leaves, broad umbrella-shaped clusters of white flowers, and stout green stems with purple blotches and coarse white hairs. Several plants, including cow parsnip and angelicas, can look similar. Size alone does not distinguish them, and some lookalikes also have irritating sap. Take separate photographs of the whole plant, leaf shape, flower cluster and visible stem markings without touching or entering the patch.
actions: Keep people and pets away and contact your state agriculture department or local invasive-plant program. Do not mow, string-trim or cut a suspected plant, because broken material can expose you to sap. If sap touches skin, wash promptly with soap and water, keep the affected skin covered and out of sunlight for at least 48 hours and seek medical advice; eye exposure needs urgent medical attention. Leave removal to people equipped and trained for this plant, and follow the reporting program's instructions about access and follow-up.

sources.label: New York Department of Health: Giant hogweed health advice
Cornell: Weeds and Human Health, Giant Hogweed

identification: Hollow stems have swollen joints and carry very large, alternate leaves with rounded or heart-shaped bases. Mature leaves can exceed a foot in length. Small greenish-white flower clusters appear near upper leaf joints. Japanese knotweed usually has smaller leaves with a more squared-off base, while their hybrid, Bohemian knotweed, can have intermediate features. Size alone does not reliably separate all three. Photograph several mature leaves, their undersides, stem joints and flower clusters for an informed identification.
actions: Keep soil and cut stems from the patch from being moved elsewhere. Do not mow through it and carry fragments to another site. Mark the patch's extent and ask a local weed program for a multi-year plan, especially beside water. Small clumps can sometimes be excavated carefully, but missed rhizome pieces can regrow. Repeated cutting or other treatments need sustained follow-up, and disposal must prevent live fragments from rooting. Do not interpret one season without tall stems as proof that the patch is gone.

sources.label: Penn State Extension: Japanese and giant knotweed

identification: The shell coils in a flat circle instead of rising into a tall spire. Adults commonly measure about one and a half to two inches across. Brown spiral bands often cross a yellowish shell, but some individuals are nearly unbanded. Egg masses are clear, jellylike clusters attached below the water surface, unlike the conspicuous above-water pink masses of some other applesnails. Native ramshorn snails can also have flattened shells, so photograph both shell faces, the opening and a size reference. Color alone is not enough.
actions: Keep aquarium snails, aquatic plants and tank water out of ponds, canals and streams. Inspect plants and equipment for small snails and submerged egg masses before moving them. If you find a suspected giant ramshorn in a new waterbody, photograph it and report the location to the state aquatic-invasive-species program. Do not move live specimens between waterways or release them as weed control. Any removal effort should first distinguish them from native snails and follow the receiving agency's advice.

sources.label: University of the West Indies: Giant ramshorn snail

identification: Upright, jointed canes carry broad gray-green leaves that clasp the stem. The leaves can be about two feet long and several inches wide. Large feathery flower clusters develop above the foliage, changing from a reddish-brown cast toward pale silver as they dry. Bamboo and common reed can look similar at a distance. Include photographs of the leaf bases, cane joints, entire stand and flower plume; a close view of the clasping leaf base is more useful than height alone.
actions: Do not plant it for screening or erosion control where it could spread. For an existing patch, keep rhizomes and cut material from being carried downstream or dumped in new soil. Cutting canes alone does not remove the underground system. Work with a land manager or weed specialist on treatment, follow-up and replacement vegetation, particularly along streams. Biological control is available through organized programs in some places, but it is not a reason to collect or release insects on your own.

sources.label: NC State Extension: Giant reed grass
USDA National Invasive Species Information Center: Giant reed
UC WeedCUT: Giant reed biological control

identification: Large males have exceptionally long second legs ending in claws, often blue or orange, that extend well beyond the head. The pointed rostrum projects forward and carries teeth on both its upper and lower edges. Identification keys also examine the tail tip and fine features of the claws. Females and young prawns do not have the same exaggerated male claws, and native Macrobrachium species can be confused with them. Photograph the whole animal, side of the head and claws with a scale; a specialist may need a specimen for confirmation.
actions: Never release aquarium or farm prawns, use them as live bait outside their approved setting, or move them between waterways. If found in open water, record the exact site, number seen and approximate sizes, then contact the state fisheries or aquatic-invasive-species program. Farm operators should review screens, drains and overflow routes after an escape. Follow agency instructions about retaining a specimen; do not transport live animals elsewhere simply to have them identified.

sources.label: FAO: Identifying and farming giant river prawns

identification: Pairs of green floating leaves sit above a finely divided brown structure that hangs underwater. That submerged structure is a modified leaf, not a true root. Under magnification, hairs on the upper leaves branch and rejoin at their tips, resembling tiny eggbeaters. Common salvinia has hairs whose tips remain separate. Several other members of the giant-salvinia group share joined hairs, however, so this feature narrows the identification without always proving the exact species. Photograph both the floating leaves and the submerged parts.
actions: Avoid driving or dragging equipment through a mat if you can do so safely. Inspect boats, trailers, nets and other gear, remove all plant fragments, and follow local clean, drain and dry guidance before entering another waterbody. Report a suspected new patch promptly with photographs and a location. Do not move plants to an aquarium or garden pond. Established mats need a coordinated aquatic-plant plan; unplanned removal can scatter fragments and leave enough live material for regrowth.

sources.label: Texas Parks and Wildlife: Clean, drain, dry

identification: Leaves are held upright in a rosette and have a broad arrowhead shape. In this species, the notch where the leaf stalk meets the two rear lobes is open, without a bridge of leaf tissue across it. The similar Alocasia odora has a more closed notch and often more basal offshoots. Flowers are tiny and packed onto a pale central spike partly enclosed by a hoodlike spathe. Photograph the leaf-stalk attachment, entire plant and any flower structure. Ornamental hybrids and cultivars can complicate identification.
actions: Do not discard live stems, corms or divisions beside waterways or in natural vegetation. For an unwanted plant, arrange removal of the storage stem and check the site for regrowth rather than cutting off leaves alone. Wear gloves and avoid sap contact. Do not taste it or assume it is edible because it is called taro; Alocasia tissues contain irritating compounds and can harm people and pets. If reporting an escape, show how far it lies from a planting or dumped garden material.

identification: Adults are larger than many other whiteflies and have white wings marked with irregular pale-brown patches. Eggs are placed in waxy spirals on leaf undersides. Flat, yellowish young stages remain on the leaves and later produce long, hairlike wax filaments that give a bearded appearance. Other whiteflies and mealybugs also make wax. Photograph the adults, egg spirals and settled young stages together, along with the host plant, rather than relying only on the white coating.
actions: Inspect nearby plants, especially leaf undersides, and remove a limited number of heavily infested leaves if the plant can tolerate it. Washing colonies off with water can help. Preserve lady beetles, lacewings and tiny parasitic wasps instead of applying broad insecticide sprays that kill them too. Check for renewed colonies rather than judging success only by whether old wax remains. If additional treatment is needed, choose a locally appropriate labeled product with extension advice and cover the infested leaf surfaces carefully.

identification: The original account describes wingless L. tatakaensis as a large, brownish-black aphid with rows of dark circular abdominal spots, black antennae and reddish-brown to black legs. These details are not enough for a reliable field identification. The familiar giant willow aphid, T. salignus, is often recognized by a raised, finlike structure on its back; that feature should not be transferred to this entry without resolving the name. Photograph the colony, host tree, individual aphids and the side profile, and seek specialist confirmation.
actions: Record the willow or other host, the part of the tree occupied and the date before considering treatment. Do not remove a tree or spray a colony solely because an occurrence report uses an introduced-species label. An extension entomologist can help determine which aphid is present and whether it is affecting plant health. If a specimen is requested, follow the specialist's collection instructions so the features needed for identification are preserved.

sources.label: Blackman and Eastop: Lachnus species accounts
Royal Horticultural Society: Large willow bark aphid
2017 review of giant willow aphid biology and relationships
Hassan et al.2024: Aphids of Pakistan

identification: Gibberella stalk rot can leave the internal pith shredded and distinctly pink or red, with dark streaks on lower stem sections. Small black fungal structures may appear near lower nodes in moist conditions. Other stalk rots and plant stresses can produce similar collapse or discoloration. Photograph affected plants and the pattern across the field, then follow a plant diagnostic laboratory's sampling instructions. A visual diagnosis of Fusarium is not always a confirmed identification of F. graminearum, and appearance cannot measure toxin concentration.
actions: Scout for weak stalks and discuss harvest timing with a crop adviser if lodging risk is rising. Keep suspect grain or silage lots identified and arrange appropriate mycotoxin testing before feeding or blending them. Plan future management around hybrid resistance, plant stress, residue and crop rotation; rotating corn with another susceptible cereal may not break the disease cycle. Do not assume a late fungicide spray can repair rotted stalks or remove toxins already present.

sources.label: Crop Protection Network: Gibberella crown and stalk rot
University of Minnesota: Corn disease management
Penn State Extension: Mycotoxins in grain corn and silage
Crop Protection Network: DON in corn silage

identification: This parasite cannot be reliably recognized by looking at a fish from the outside. Encysted young stages are microscopic and can occur especially around fin bases; laboratory examination and sometimes molecular methods are needed to distinguish related flukes. The broad name gill fluke should not be taken to mean that every gill problem is this species. A fish with breathing difficulty, damaged fins or no visible symptoms cannot be diagnosed from those signs alone.
actions: Do not eat raw or undercooked freshwater fish, and do not rely on a healthy appearance to judge parasite safety. Follow established food-safety guidance for preparing fish rather than assuming a home marinade removes parasites. Keep aquarium snails, fish and water out of natural waterways. If you suspect a fish-health problem, contact a fisheries biologist or aquatic veterinarian and follow their sampling instructions. If you are concerned about illness after eating fish, tell a healthcare professional what you ate and where it came from.

sources.label: Palmer and colleagues: Fishborne trematodes in California game fish
Shin and colleagues: Molecular detection of H. pumilio

identification: Adults are oval, about 2 to 4 mm long, with dark wing covers clothed in a mixture of pale, golden and darker hairs. The clubbed antennae and hair pattern help specialists distinguish them from other cabinet beetles. Larvae are densely hairy, become reddish brown as they mature and have conspicuous hair tufts toward the rear. Cast skins in stored food are useful evidence, but larvae of related Trogoderma species look similar. Keep a contained specimen for identification rather than assigning a species from a small photograph alone.
actions: For a household infestation, inspect dry foods, pet food and spilled material near storage areas. Seal and discard infested food, vacuum cracks and empty the vacuum promptly, then protect unaffected supplies in tightly closed containers. These are general stored-food pest measures, not a substitute for identifying an unusual beetle. In a grain facility, keep the affected lot identifiable and ask a grain-storage specialist about sampling and treatment appropriate to the commodity; do not move suspect material simply to clear the bin.

sources.label: Canadian Grain Commission: Glabrous cabinet beetle
Agriculture Canada: Beetles associated with stored products

identification: Look for slender stems that branch near the base and may lean before rising, with narrow, mostly smooth leaf blades. The small membrane where a leaf blade meets its sheath is very short. Flower heads are dense and spike-like, with closely packed green to purplish spikelets. Under magnification, the larger outer bract of a spikelet is strongly veined and swollen or curved near its base. Flower-head length varies between floras, so photographs of mature spikelets, the leaf junction and the whole clump are more useful than height alone.
actions: Photograph the flowering plant in place and record whether it is on a wet bank, disturbed ground or within established wetland vegetation. Ask a botanist to confirm it before removing similar-looking grasses. Avoid carrying muddy footwear, tools or seed-bearing plant material between wetlands. For a confirmed unwanted patch, agree on a small-scale approach with the land manager before seed disperses, while protecting the surrounding soil and vegetation. The sources here do not establish a species-specific herbicide program.

sources.label: PlantNET New South Wales Flora: Sacciolepis indica

identification: The four petals of each small flower are unequal, with the outward-facing pair larger. Smooth stems carry narrow, alternate leaves, and the flower clusters remain broadly umbrella-shaped as the flattened, winged seedpods develop. The pods have a notch at their tip. Bitter candytuft, Iberis amara, typically has hairier lower stems and fruit clusters that lengthen; evergreen candytuft, I. sempervirens, is a perennial with persistent leaves. Include mature fruit and lower stems in photographs, because flower color alone can be misleading.
actions: If plants are appearing beyond a bed, photograph the escape and nearby cultivated source before removal. Where reseeding is unwanted, remove the annual plants or spent flower heads before ripe pods shed seed, then check for new seedlings. Keep seed-bearing garden waste out of roadsides and natural areas. Ask the land manager before removing plants from a public site, and confirm the species if the plant is woody or remains evergreen through winter.

sources.label: Native Plant Trust: Iberis identification key

identification: Mature females are strongly rounded, roughly 3 mm across, and dark brown to nearly black, with a shiny, finely pitted surface. Look for colonies on woody growth and record the host tree. Other soft scales can become similarly brown and convex, so photograph several individuals with a size reference and ask an extension specialist to examine a sample. The tiny moving young stages, called crawlers, can help determine treatment timing, but their appearance alone is not a reliable species diagnosis.
actions: Inspect the tree's vigor and the extent of infestation before acting. Pruning a limited amount of heavily colonized wood may help where the tree can tolerate it. As general soft-scale management, protect predators and parasitic wasps, and address ants that tend the insects for honeydew. If treatment is warranted, monitor for crawlers and obtain advice for the tree, scale and local conditions. Do not copy a calendar date from another country or assume a spray aimed at mature rounded females will reach the vulnerable stage.

sources.label: Turkish Ministry of Agriculture: Apricot pests, plum scale account

identification: Adults are roughly 3 to 5 mm long, with a rounded body covered in uneven brown and golden hairs rather than a smooth, polished surface. The antennae are long and slender. Other spider beetles can look similar: the golden spider beetle is more uniformly golden, while this species has darker patches in its hair covering. Photograph the beetle from above and from the side, with a size reference, and retain a contained specimen if identification is important. A distant image of a brown dot will not reliably separate these species.
actions: Look for the source as well as the insects: inspect stored dry materials and accumulated debris around the affected area. For household food, isolate infested packages, remove the source and clean nearby cracks before protecting unaffected supplies in sealed containers. For books, textiles, dried plant specimens or other collection objects, isolate the item and ask a conservator about treatment. Do not spray an object or apply heat or freezing without checking whether its materials can tolerate the method. Keep a record of where beetles recur so hidden sources can be investigated.

sources.label: National Museums Scotland: Identifying collection pests
Agriculture Canada: Beetles associated with stored products

identification: Check several features together: alternate, oval to oblong leaves with smooth edges; curved side veins; and brown or gray twigs dotted with pale lenticels, the small pores in bark. Small greenish flowers develop into round fruits that become black. Smooth leaf margins help separate it from common buckthorn, but leaf shine alone is unreliable. Photograph a complete leafy twig, both leaf surfaces and any fruit. Native buckthorns and dogwoods deserve careful comparison before removal.
actions: Confirm the shrub before treating a woodland or wetland. Where removal is appropriate, start with small plants and prevent fruiting material from being scattered during the work. Revisit the site for new seedlings over several seasons, since seeds already in the soil can outlast the original shrubs. Ask a local invasive-plant program about established stems and wetland restrictions. A single cutting or a cleared-looking patch should not be treated as proof that the population is gone.

identification: The leaves sit opposite or nearly opposite each other and are commonly about 3-6 inches long, with a glossy upper surface and a tapering tip. Look closely at the narrow, pale-looking band along the leaf edge and the prominent pale dots on young branches. Creamy flower clusters are borne at branch tips. Japanese privet is a close lookalike; a photograph of a whole tree is less useful than clear leaf, vein, twig and fruit details. Common names such as Chinese privet can refer to more than one species.
actions: Check whether local guidance recommends removal or managed retention before deciding what to do with a planted tree. Where replacement is appropriate, include seedlings around the tree in the plan. Removing accessible fruit clusters before birds disperse them can reduce one source of spread while larger work is arranged. Use an arborist for large trees rather than trying to fell them yourself. Continue looking for new seedlings after removal and keep fruit-bearing debris out of natural areas.

identification: Each alternate leaf is divided into opposite pairs of rounded or oblong leaflets, usually with no single leaflet at the end. Many descriptions report about six to ten pairs. The upper surfaces are smoother and darker than the finely hairy undersides. Yellow flowers gather near the upper leaves, and the pods are flat rather than cylindrical, turning dark brown when mature. Several sennas share yellow flowers and similar common names. Include the leaflet count, small glands along the leaf axis, flowers and mature pods in identification photographs.
actions: Before planting or sharing seed, check regional advice for this exact scientific name. Where an unwanted plant is producing pods, contain the pods during removal so the work does not scatter seed. Monitor disturbed ground nearby for seedlings. Do not rely on cattle to remove it: Hawaii extension reports that cattle avoid it. For established shrubs in pasture, request a locally appropriate management plan rather than copying an overseas chemical treatment. Preventing new seedlings is a prudent precaution, not a claim that pod removal alone eradicates a stand.

identification: Look for elongated, narrow, brown covers about 3 mm long. Purple scale can occur alongside it and has a similar general shape, so finding a mussel-like scale on citrus is only a starting point. Examine both fruit and branches with a hand lens and photograph the insects beside a scale marker. The living female and eggs are beneath the cover; reliable separation from related armored scales may require a mounted specimen and specialist examination. Yellow leaves alone cannot identify this insect.
actions: Inspect citrus nursery stock before moving it into a collection, and keep a suspect plant apart while its identity is checked. Ask a citrus adviser whether the scales are alive and whether natural enemies are already active. UF/IFAS reports that parasitic wasps often keep Glover's scale under biological control, so an automatic broad-spectrum spray can undermine useful control. Base any treatment on a confirmed infestation and current advice for the plant and location. Do not move infested prunings to another orchard.

sources.label: UF/IFAS: A Guide to Scale Insect Identification

identification: Look for alternate, broadly oval leaves with a green upper surface and a softly hairy, grayish underside. The catkins are generally upright rather than long, dangling tassels. Photograph mature leaves on both sides as well as the current twigs and catkins. Gray willow is a particularly relevant comparison, and hybrids can blur the differences. A fuzzy spring catkin by itself does not distinguish goat willow from the other plants sold or described as pussy willow.
actions: Confirm the species and its local status before removing a willow near a stream or wetland. A planted tree may simply need enough room for its mature crown; an unwanted seedling is easier to assess before it becomes a large tree. Avoid dumping cut branches beside water or in damp ground, where living willow material may establish. For a suspected escape, record the location and whether plants are seedlings, rooted branches or part of an old planting. Get local advice before disturbing banks or removing mature trees.

identification: Check both leaf surfaces for bead-like galls, often only a few millimeters across, and for distorted new leaves. The mites are minute, pale and wormlike; they are not the larger eight-legged specks usually imagined when someone says mite. Published identification has used light and scanning electron microscopy, and several Aceria species can occur on Lycium. Photograph the host plant, whole affected leaves and close views of the swellings. A diagnostic service may need fresh leaf material rather than a photograph alone.
actions: Keep a suspect goji plant separate from other goji plants and avoid giving away cuttings until the problem is resolved. Contact a plant diagnostic service for sampling and disposal instructions, especially if symptoms appeared after a nursery purchase. Record where the plant came from and when the blisters first appeared. Do not assume that removing a few visibly galled leaves eliminates the mites. Treatment choices should come from current advice for edible goji plants; a product suitable for an ornamental shrub is not automatically suitable for a fruit crop.

sources.label: Utah State University: Goji in the Garden
Suvak: First record of Aceria kuko in Slovakia

identification: Adults have gray-brown forewings with a pale line along the leading edge and a conspicuous yellowish to reddish band crossing the wing. A research trap guide gives a wingspan of about 24-28 mm. Open suspect pods to look for chewed seeds, silk and droppings; these are clues to a pod borer, not proof of this particular moth. Photograph an adult and the contents of a damaged pod if possible. Other moth larvae can cause similar seed damage, and trap catches also require identification.
actions: Inspect developing pods in several parts of a crop rather than judging the problem from one damaged plant. Keep a record of crop stage and the proportion of pods affected, and ask an extension crop adviser to identify larvae or adults before selecting treatment. Regional guidance notes that earlier planting can sometimes allow lima beans to mature before pod borers become abundant. That is a local cropping decision, not a universal calendar rule. Avoid moving infested pods into clean seed stocks, and do not release biological-control insects without an approved program.

sources.label: CSALOMON: Lima-bean pod borer — Etiella zinckenella
PNW Pest Management Handbooks: Lima bean pod borer

identification: Look for simple leaves that clasp the stem, small flowers with four pale-yellow petals, and smooth, pear-shaped pods on slender stalks. Published descriptions commonly give mature pods as about 7-9 mm long. The plant is often nearly hairless or only sparsely hairy. Littlepod false flax, Camelina microcarpa, is a close relative with generally hairier stems and smaller pods and seeds. Photograph mature pods beside a ruler and include stem hairs and leaf bases; a seedling alone may be difficult to separate.
actions: First establish whether the plants belong to a crop or are unwanted volunteers. In an unwanted patch, preventing seed maturity is a sensible containment step, followed by checks for later seedlings. Keep loose seed out of neighboring beds and clean seed-handling equipment before moving between sites. For crop production or a persistent field problem, use local agronomic advice, since crop rotations and permitted treatments vary. Do not assume that an oilseed crop is suitable for sowing in a natural area merely because it has an agricultural use.

identification: Individual cells require microscopy. Water color, foam or dead fish can alert you to a problem but cannot distinguish golden algae from other algae, low oxygen or a chemical spill. Specialists examine the cells and may test the water for toxicity. Record the waterbody, date, color and where affected fish are concentrated. Useful photographs show the broader shoreline and affected fish without handling them. A home magnifier or phone photograph cannot establish the identity of this tiny alga.
actions: Report unusual fish deaths promptly to the relevant fisheries or water-quality authority and follow its sampling instructions. Do not eat fish found dead or dying during a suspected bloom. As a precaution, avoid moving untreated water, bait or wet equipment from the affected waterbody to another one. Pond owners should seek professional diagnosis before adding chemicals: treatments developed for managed hatchery ponds cannot simply be applied to a lake or stream. Follow any local access advisory while the cause is investigated.

sources.label: Texas Parks and Wildlife: Biology of Golden Alga

identification: The branching stems can approach a meter tall. Leaves are divided two or three times into smaller lobes, giving them a finely cut appearance. Heads are usually borne singly at stem tips and can be roughly 3.5 cm across, with yellow centers and yellow rays that sometimes fade toward cream. Other yellow daisies can look similar from a distance. Photograph the leaf divisions, the underside and side of a flower head, and mature fruits if available; specialist keys use the small bracts and fruit details.
actions: For a planted specimen, check regional guidance before allowing it to seed into neighboring habitat or sharing divisions. Where plants are unwanted, removing flower heads before seeds develop is a reasonable precaution, followed by removal of small plants and checks for regrowth. Keep seeding debris contained rather than leaving it on an open compost edge. If the plant occurs in a meadow with similar native daisies, confirm its identity first. These are containment steps, not a species-tested eradication schedule.

identification: Plants are commonly about 20-50 cm tall, with erect or ascending stems that do not root at their joints. The three oblong leaflets have fine teeth toward their outer ends and very short, nearly equal stalks. At the base of each leaf stalk are narrow, pointed stipules, the small leaf-like appendages that help in identification. The yellow flowers form dense rounded to short cylindrical heads. Compare other yellow-flowered clovers carefully, paying particular attention to leaflet stalk lengths and stipule shape rather than overall size.
actions: If golden clover is unwanted in a bed or restoration planting, identify it while flowers and leaves are present, then remove small plants before they set seed. Keep any mature heads contained during the work. Revisit open ground for new seedlings and limit repeated soil disturbance that leaves bare space for annual plants. In pasture or a species-rich meadow, first check the management objective and local flora so desirable clovers are not removed by mistake. These steps are general seed-containment precautions; the cited floras do not establish a tested eradication method.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Trifolium aureum

identification: Use a hand lens to look for circular to oval scales about 1-2 mm across, colored golden, greenish or brown, nestled into small depressions. Young twigs are a useful place to inspect. Ordinary lecanium scales stand up as more obvious brown mounds rather than sitting within pits. The appearance of the pit cannot reliably separate Asterodiaspis variolosa from its close relatives. Photograph the oak leaves for host identification and a close view of affected twigs; exact naming may need microscopic examination.
actions: Check whether the affected twigs are still growing and whether dieback is spreading before choosing treatment. Have an arborist or extension diagnostic service assess a declining oak, since roots, drought and other pests may also be involved. Avoid moving infested nursery oaks between properties. If control is warranted, timing should be based on local crawler activity, not a calendar copied from another region. Preserve natural enemies where possible and do not strip healthy bark to look for insects. A confirmed pit-scale problem can guide care while the precise species is being resolved.

sources.label: Natural Resources Canada: Insects of Eastern Forests

identification: Look for simple, glossy leaves arranged opposite one another or in whorls around the stem, together with large yellow funnel-shaped flowers with five spreading lobes. Fruits, when present, are rounded prickly capsules. Several allamandas and garden forms have similar flowers; bush allamanda is generally more compact, so flower color alone is insufficient. Photograph leaf arrangement, flower size and the plant's growth habit. Do not snap a stem just to test for latex, since the sap is an irritant.
actions: Wear gloves when pruning and keep sap away from eyes. Keep cuttings and fruit away from children and pets, and do not use this ornamental as a home remedy. Where local guidance identifies it as an escape risk, contain prunings and remove unwanted new plants rather than dumping live stems at a garden edge. Check the base for continuing growth after cutting. For a planted specimen, make sure supports and pruning allow safe access without repeated contact with sap. Seek local advice before attempting to clear a large tangle among other vegetation.

identification: Mature foliage consists of broad, curved phyllodes, flattened leaf stalks that function as leaves. They are bright green, often sickle-shaped and can hang downward. Look for a fairly central main vein, a long narrowed base and a small gland set above that base. Flower heads are round and crowded into clusters on sturdy stalks. Acacia saligna and A. obliquinervia can resemble it, so photograph the entire phyllode, its base and gland, and a complete flower cluster. Golden balls alone do not identify a wattle.
actions: Before planting or distributing seed, check advice for this exact species in your region. Where it is unwanted, address small plants before they become seed-bearing trees and keep pods from being scattered during clearance. Follow up for seedlings rather than assuming that removing the visible stems completes the job. Established trees may need a local weed specialist or arborist. In its native range, confirm that a plant is an unwanted introduction at the specific site before removing it. The sources establish identification and regional behavior, not a universal removal prescription.

sources.label: Australian National Botanic Gardens: Acacia pycnantha

identification: Look for spoon-shaped gray-green leaves and branching flowering stems on a plant commonly only a few tens of centimeters tall. Each individual flower is small; the bright display comes from many flowers grouped together. Under magnification the stems bear branched, star-shaped hairs, while the fruits are hairless in the Austrian flora description. Other yellow-flowered mustard relatives can resemble it. Photograph a close flower, mature fruit, leaf shape and the whole mound rather than relying on a mass of yellow in a garden photograph.
actions: Check regional guidance before encouraging self-seeding beyond a garden. If seed spread is unwanted, trim off flowering stems before ripe seed is shed and watch nearby gravel or open soil for seedlings. A light post-flowering tidy also helps keep a cultivated plant compact, as botanical-garden guidance notes. Remove an unwanted plant carefully without scattering mature pods. In rocky natural habitat, confirm the species before disturbing similar low plants. These steps address garden containment; the cited sources do not demonstrate that a particular cutting routine eradicates an escaped population.

sources.label: Dunedin Botanic Garden: Tiny Flowers have Big Impact
Natural History Museum Vienna: Aurinia saxatilis

identification: Adults are small dark beetles, roughly 5-6 mm long, with conspicuous yellowish or reddish hairs visible under magnification. The hairs are especially noticeable near the rear slope of the wing covers. Reddish boring dust and galleries beneath bark are useful clues but are shared with other bark beetles. Hylastes species can look similar; this beetle is generally larger and hairier than Hylastes ater. Preserve location and host information and ask a forestry diagnostic service to examine an adult before assigning a species.
actions: Do not transport suspect bark-covered logs, firewood or logging debris to a new site while identification is pending. Photograph adults and galleries without damaging living trees unnecessarily, and note whether the material was freshly cut or already dead. Ask a forestry or plant-health authority about local wood-handling requirements and approved disposal. At a plantation or timber yard, include stumps, ground-contact logs and debris in inspections. Professional timber treatments are specialized operations; neither fumigation nor a household insecticide is an appropriate do-it-yourself response.

sources.label: NZ Farm Forestry: Scion Golden-haired Bark Beetle account

identification: The leaves are usually divided once into a row of leaflets, although occasional leaves may be more divided. Leaflet edges are conspicuously toothed or lobed. Later, inflated capsules develop three papery sides and dry toward tan or brown. Related Koelreuteria species commonly have twice-divided leaves and different young capsule colors, so include a complete leaf rather than a single leaflet in photographs. Yellow flowers alone do not separate the species. Winter capsules, summer leaves and the tree's overall form make a useful combined record.
actions: Look for seedlings beyond the crown, especially in open soil and at the edges of nearby habitat. Where local guidance recommends control, remove young plants before they produce more seed and contain mature capsules during cleanup. Arrange professional work for large trees and monitor the site afterward. If retaining a garden tree, repeated seedling checks are a practical way to notice escape early. Do not distribute seedlings into natural areas merely because the parent is a common street tree; suitability depends on the region and planting site.

sources.label: University of Maryland Extension: Goldenrain Tree
Trees and Shrubs Online: Koelreuteria identification key

identification: Look for flat, mostly hairless leaf blades and a conspicuous, thin membranous ligule where the blade meets the sheath. The ligule is relatively long and may shred with age. The compact head is only several centimeters long, with clustered spikelets of different forms; the fertile florets carry slender awns. Take a close photograph of the head from both sides and of the leaf collar. Foxtail-like appearance or golden color alone is not enough, especially once the head is dry. A mature specimen makes the unusual spikelet arrangement much easier to check.
actions: If it is unwanted, act while plants are small and before mature seed clusters can break away. Contain developed heads during removal and check the same bare patches after the next germination period. Clean soil and seed fragments from footwear and tools before leaving an infested site as a precaution against accidental movement. In a garden, avoid intentionally scattering ornamental seed into adjoining open land. For a mixed grass community, confirm the identity before broad removal; the botanical sources support recognition, not a species-specific treatment schedule.

identification: Look for a long body that is more cylindrical toward the head and tapers toward the tail, with an orange-ringed eyespot near the upper base of the tail fin. In larger juveniles and adults, black scales within the dark side blotches have conspicuous pale rear margins. The formal distinction from C. marulius also uses scale and fin-ray counts, which are not easy to judge from a casual photograph. Photograph the entire side, head and tail region and include a size reference. A general snakehead identification may be more defensible than an immediate species claim.
actions: Never release an aquarium fish or move a caught snakehead into another waterbody. If one is found outside a known managed fishery, record the exact location and contact the relevant fisheries authority for identification and handling instructions. Follow current local rules rather than assuming that retention, transport or release rules are the same everywhere. Do not handle a large fish unnecessarily to count scales; clear photographs may be the safest first record. Keep the original scientific name associated with any older report when discussing its possible reidentification.

sources.label: Adamson and Britz: Channa aurolineata is a valid species

identification: The alternate leaves are broadly shaped, with three to five lobes and additional teeth or smaller lobes. Their undersides and stalks are bristly. Male flowers occur in small groups, while female flowers are single or paired on the same plant. The round fruits are about 15-25 mm across, green with pale stripes before turning yellow, and carry scattered soft, often hooked bristles. Compare both fruits and leaves with other wild melons; a fruitless seedling is less straightforward. Photograph the whole vine and a fruit beside a ruler.
actions: Prevent unwanted plants from producing mature fruit, and collect existing fruits carefully rather than scattering them while pulling vines. Keep the material out of livestock feed and do not offer the fruits as food. Monitor disturbed soil for replacement seedlings. In a crop or pasture, ask a local adviser to confirm the wild cucurbit before selecting a control plan. These are prudent containment and exposure precautions; the identification sources do not establish that one pulling pass or a particular chemical treatment will eliminate a population.

sources.label: Charles Sturt University: Identification of three cucurbitaceous weeds

identification: Look for radiating shoots with distinctly flattened, whitish or silvery bases. Leaves are folded in the bud, mostly smooth, and have a small membranous ligule at the collar. The seedhead has several finger-like branches, often with one or two set below the main cluster; the tiny flowers form orderly, zipper-like rows. Crabgrasses also have fingered heads, so check the pale compressed base and leaf collar as well. Photograph the whole clump and a close view of both features.
actions: Remove isolated plants with the central crown, the growing point at soil level, before seed develops. Simply clipping the leaves leaves that crown behind. Reduce repeated foot or vehicle traffic where practical, address compaction through appropriate lawn care, and repair thin turf with a suitable grass. Clean mowing equipment after working through flowering patches. For a persistent infestation, ask extension for options matched to the lawn species and growth stage; mature goosegrass can be difficult to control and resistant populations exist. Do not assume a crabgrass product will work equally well.

identification: Look for narrow blades and a hair fringe at the leaf collar. The panicle contains many tiny, flattened spikelets, commonly with several flowers each, clustered into a compact or interrupted cylinder. Long hairs on the edges of the inner flower bracts contribute to the soft-looking head. The stems do not normally root at their lower joints in the North American treatment. Photograph mature spikelets under magnification, the collar and the base of the plant. Other small lovegrasses require comparison of these details, especially the arrangement and hairiness of the floral parts.
actions: If a patch is unwanted, remove small plants before the heads mature and keep ripe seedheads contained during cleanup. Check nursery containers and disturbed soil nearby for additional plants. Avoid moving soil or mowing debris from a seeding patch into clean areas. Before clearing a mixed grassland, have a mature sample checked so a similar native grass is not removed. Local habitat and land use should determine whether management is needed. The available floras support identification, while these actions are cautious seed-spread prevention rather than a proven eradication program.

sources.label: SEINet: Eragrostis ciliaris, Flora of North America

identification: Look for alternate simple leaves with toothed or wavy edges, small yellowish flowers near the leaf bases and rounded fruit that darkens as it ripens. Spines may occur in leaf axils and on the trunk, but their presence and length vary. Male and female flowers are generally borne on different plants. Other Flacourtia species can resemble it; photograph the fruit tips, flowers, leaf arrangement and spines without handling them. A plum-like fruit does not make it a true plum or establish that an unidentified fruit is safe to eat.
actions: Wear sturdy gloves and protect your eyes when working around the spiny branches. Check local recommendations before planting or distributing seedlings. Where the shrub is unwanted, contain ripe fruit during removal and inspect surrounding ground for young plants. Larger, densely spiny specimens are better handled with experienced help. Do not rely on leaf shape alone before clearing similar shrubs. A local invasive-plant adviser can recommend an approach for established stems; this profile does not transfer a chemical recipe from another country or habitat.

sources.label: Kew: Flacourtia indica, regional flora descriptions
Florida Natural Areas Inventory: Flacourtia indica

identification: Adults are about 8-10 mm long, with a narrow body, very large eyes and two small waist segments between the middle body and abdomen. Color varies from dark brown or black to orange-brown or a mixture of orange and dark areas. That variability makes color alone a poor guide. Other twig ants can resemble it, so obtain clear side and head photographs without catching it in bare fingers. The large eyes and elongated waist are useful screening features; exact identification may require a specialist.
actions: Avoid breaking open occupied twigs or gripping vegetation where ants are active. Wear gloves when pruning and inspect hollow stems before carrying them indoors or sharing cuttings. If a nest is close to a frequently used doorway or work area, seek an identification and a targeted plan from extension or a pest professional. Keep unnecessary insecticide applications off otherwise healthy garden plants. For an isolated outdoor sighting, documenting the ant and leaving the nest undisturbed is often more proportionate than attempting to eliminate every ant in the area.

identification: Look for long-stalked leaves with roughly seven to thirteen lobes cut almost to the base, spreading like the fingers of an open hand. The lobes are mostly smooth-edged and hairless, with a paler lower surface. Small hanging flowers have greenish tissue marked with reddish or purplish stripes; rounded capsules contain three seeds. Compare the complete leaf, flowers and fruit with other Manihot species rather than identifying it from lobed foliage alone. The narrow lobes and their proportions are especially useful in photographs.
actions: Do not harvest leaves or roots as cassava on the strength of a common name. Before sharing seed or cuttings, check whether this ornamental is appropriate locally. Where unwanted seedlings appear, remove them early and contain mature capsules so seeds are not scattered through the garden. Recheck beneath and around the parent plant. Use gloves for pruning as a sensible precaution when handling an unfamiliar member of the spurge family. Management of a larger shrub should include follow-up for new growth; a single cut is not presented here as a proven eradication method.

sources.label: NZ Plant Conservation Network: Manihot grahamii

identification: Adult leaves are alternate, lance-shaped and darker green above than below. White flowers occur in groups, commonly seven, nine or eleven, and the small woody capsules provide an important clue: their valves curve inward when open. Eucalyptus saligna is a close lookalike whose open fruit valves are erect rather than incurved. Photograph a mature capsule from above and the side, buds, both leaf surfaces and the trunk base. Juvenile foliage can look different, so say whether a sample came from a seedling, regrowth or the mature crown.
actions: For a standing tree, begin with identification and a site assessment rather than assuming removal is needed. Its eventual size makes professional advice important near buildings, roads or utilities. Where unwanted seedlings occur beyond a plantation or garden, document them and consult local guidance before allowing a new stand to establish. Keep seed-bearing debris from being dumped in neighboring habitat as a precaution. Large-tree removal and follow-up belong in a locally appropriate plan; this account does not establish invasive status for every place where the tree is planted.

identification: A useful early clue is a fine column of compressed boring dust projecting from a pinhole in the bark, often described as a toothpick. These fragile columns can disappear after wind or rain, leaving only tiny holes. Adult females are roughly 2-3 mm long and reddish brown. Other ambrosia beetles can make similar columns, so this sign does not prove the species. Photograph the dust columns before they break, the entire affected stem and the tree's condition, and arrange specialist examination of a beetle if needed.
actions: Inspect nursery trees and recent transplants regularly, especially lower stems. Keep suspect stock from being sold or moved until it has been assessed. Ask an arborist or extension specialist whether an attacked tree can recover and how infested material should be handled. Once beetles are inside, control options are limited, so do not assume a systemic insecticide will cure the problem. Address avoidable plant stress and follow locally timed monitoring advice for nearby vulnerable trees. Any removal should contain the breeding material rather than moving it to another landscape.

sources.label: University of Georgia: Granulate Ambrosia Beetle
University of Georgia IPM: Granulate ambrosia beetle

identification: Workers are only a few millimeters long, dark brown to nearly black, with very small eyes and a finely textured, dull-looking body. The waist has one upright node, and there is a visible constriction between the first large abdominal segments. Under magnification, the node is nearly rectangular in side view and the antennal stalks are relatively long. Similar Hypoponera and Ponera ants require comparison of the underside of the waist and other minute structures. A blurred photograph of a tiny brown ant cannot resolve this species.
actions: Avoid handling ants or breaking apart a nest with bare hands. If ants appear in newly purchased pots, keep those pots separate and have a specimen identified before distributing plants or soil. Ask the diagnostic service how to collect a sample safely. For occasional outdoor findings, record the substrate and location rather than treating an entire garden. If repeated indoor encounters or stings occur, seek a targeted assessment. The sources provide limited species-specific management evidence, so generic ant baits or broad soil treatments are not presented as proven solutions.

identification: Look for a long, thick body with large dark-edged scales, an olive-brown back, silvery sides and a pale belly. The mouth faces forward and has no barbels, the whisker-like structures seen on common carp. Its dorsal fin is much shorter than that of common carp or goldfish. Bighead and silver carp have different scale and fin proportions. Photograph a whole side view and the head if this can be done without unnecessary handling. Appearance alone does not establish whether an individual is a sterile triploid.
actions: Do not stock, transfer or release Grass Carp without first checking the relevant fisheries authority's current requirements. Pond owners should identify the vegetation and assess how much cover should remain before considering fish-based control. If fish are already stocked, monitor plant coverage and outlet security with professional advice rather than adding more fish whenever growth returns. Report an unexpected catch where the species is being monitored. Follow location-specific handling rules, since a deliberately stocked fish and an unwanted escape may be managed differently.

identification: Look for opposite, stalkless, narrow leaves on smooth, distinctly angled stems. Leaf bases and the edges of the small flower bracts may have fine hairs even when the rest of the plant looks hairless. The deeply divided petals are about as long as, or a little longer than, the pointed sepals beneath them. Long-leaved starwort is a useful comparison: stem texture, sepal veins and mature seeds help separate similar plants. Photograph the stem angles, leaf bases and a flower from the side as well as above.
actions: Check a regional flora before deciding that a small white-flowered plant in grassland needs removal. Where this species is unwanted in a bed, lift small plants carefully and monitor for continuing growth rather than relying only on cutting flowers. Contain mature seed capsules during the work. In wet ground, avoid trampling or stripping surrounding vegetation simply to clear scattered stems. Ask for botanical confirmation when native starworts occur nearby. The cited treatments support recognition and perennial habit; they do not establish a single reliable eradication schedule.

identification: Part the grass carefully and examine nodes, crowns and the spaces beneath leaf sheaths with a hand lens. Mature females look like small rounded cottony lumps; the underlying body is dark brown to reddish purple. A long, thin wax filament projecting from the body is a useful clue, and a honeydew droplet may hang from its end. Mobile young crawlers differ from the settled, saclike later stages. White material alone is not enough for identification because other grass mealybugs occupy similarly concealed places.
actions: Inspect several living stems at the edge of a damaged patch before treating the entire lawn. Photograph the concealed insects and ask an extension service to distinguish them from other turf pests. Record whether patches expand and whether ants or natural enemies are present. Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum spraying, which can remove beneficial insects. If treatment is warranted, seek advice for the grass species, site and locally permitted products; the protected feeding sites make timing and coverage important. Do not move suspect sod or divisions to clean areas.

sources.label: UGA Extension: Rhodesgrass Mealybug Biology and Management
UF/IFAS: Managing Scale Insects and Mealybugs on Turfgrass

identification: Look for a loose, ascending or spreading plant with milky sap, broad oval to oblong main leaves and narrower leaflike bracts near the flowers. A Taiwan treatment describes alternate main leaves but opposite bracts, an arrangement worth photographing rather than judging from one stem tip.
