The flower cups bear small white petal-like appendages. Mature seeds have conspicuous pits arranged in rows, a specialist character useful when similar spurges are present. Do not deliberately break a stem to test the sap.
actions: If plants are unwanted in pots or beds, wear gloves and avoid getting sap on skin or in eyes. Remove small plants before their capsules mature and keep fruiting material contained during disposal. Examine neighboring pots and incoming nursery plants for similar seedlings. Photograph a whole plant, both leaf arrangements and the flower cups before asking for identification. These are practical containment precautions; the reviewed sources do not establish a particular removal schedule or herbicide treatment as reliably effective for this species.

sources.label: Taiwania: Euphorbia graminea, a newly naturalized plant in Taiwan
Kew POWO: Euphorbia graminea, general information

identification: Under the older United States concept, plants have a rosette of spoon-shaped to narrowly spoon-shaped leaves, woolly white undersides and much less hairy upper surfaces. Small flower heads crowd along the upper stems, with outer head bracts often rosy or purplish. These details describe the historical identification concept only. They do not resolve whether a particular specimen belongs to G. impatiens, G. americana or another cudweed. Close photographs of the leaf surfaces, basal rosette and individual flower-head bracts are more useful than a distant picture of gray stems.
actions: Keep the existing scientific name with the observation, but add its source and date rather than silently replacing it. Seek a herbarium or regional botanist familiar with recent Gamochaeta revisions before making a species-level report or removal decision. Preserve clear photographs and, where collection is permitted and requested, a properly documented voucher. Avoid moving seed-bearing plants or nursery soil while identification is pending. A local determination should guide management, especially where similar native cudweeds grow nearby.

sources.label: Flora of Virginia Atlas: Gamochaeta impatiens
Flora of North America treatment served by BioGator: Gamochaeta coarctata
Kew: Gamochaeta americana and included synonyms

identification: An extended adult is commonly around 3-5 cm long. The mantle, the smooth shield behind the head, is shorter than the tail section. A short ridge runs along the tail tip, and the breathing opening is in the rear half of the mantle on the right side. Dark mottling is common but not universal. Disturbed animals may produce milky mucus, but do not handle or irritate one merely to obtain that character. Unpatterned individuals can resemble other Deroceras species and may require expert examination.
actions: Check vulnerable seedlings after dusk or during damp weather, and photograph any slugs beside a size reference. Temporary refuge boards can help reveal activity if checked regularly; do not leave extra hiding places indefinitely beside tender plants. Reduce unnecessary damp debris around a small growing area while retaining habitat elsewhere for wildlife. Confirm the problem before using a bait, and follow a locally approved label with particular attention to pets and other animals. Crop-specific treatment thresholds and schedules should come from local advice, not a general identification page.

sources.label: John Innes Centre: Grey field slug identification
Oregon State Extension: Identification and Management of Pest Slugs

identification: Look for short-stalked, broadly oval leaves with several blunt teeth along each side. Lower leaves occur in pairs; the leaflike bracts farther up the flowering stem become alternate. The flowers are usually bright blue with a pale center and are only a few millimeters across. Mature capsules are small, paired-lobed structures with hairs. Common field speedwell, Veronica persica, generally has larger flowers and more widely diverging fruit lobes. Green field speedwell, V. agrestis, often has paler flowers; fruit hairs and shape deserve a close look.
actions: Photograph an open flower, the lower leaves and a mature capsule with a ruler before making a firm identification. A hand lens helps show the fruit hairs. In a cultivated bed where removal is wanted, lift young plants before seed develops and check the surrounding bare soil for later seedlings. This is a seed-containment precaution rather than a verified eradication program. Check regional status before removing plants from a wild site: abundance and conservation relevance differ between places, even for familiar garden weeds.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Veronica polita

identification: Compare several mature leaves from ordinary branches rather than relying on one oversized sucker leaf. Leaves are broadly rounded to oval, with blunt or irregular teeth, and can be slightly heart-shaped at the base. Young undersides may be very pale, becoming grayer or less hairy later. White poplar generally retains a whiter underside, while gray poplar tends toward a less strongly white appearance on older leaves. Catkin details and the combination of leaf shape, hairs and shoot type may be needed to separate hybrids confidently.
actions: Before planting or removing a tree, consider the space occupied by both the crown and its suckering roots. Photograph mature branch leaves as well as any nearby shoots when requesting identification. If unwanted suckers are appearing, map their extent and ask an arborist to assess their connection to the main tree. Avoid casually cutting major roots near buildings or established trees. A single cut does not demonstrate that the underground plant has been controlled. Check local rules and habitat value before planning removal of a mature specimen.

sources.label: Trees and Shrubs Online: Populus canescens
Flora of Zimbabwe: Populus x canescens

identification: Use a hand lens to examine the rings of tiny pointed leaf teeth at branchlet joints. A Victorian flora records commonly 12-17 teeth, sometimes more, and branchlet segments around 8-20 mm long. The branchlets droop, and mature woody cone-like fruits provide another useful feature. Counts from several normal branchlets are more informative than one unusual shoot. Other sheoaks can look very similar, and field guides use tooth counts, branchlet dimensions, fruits and suckering together; a pine-like silhouette alone cannot establish the species.
actions: Photograph a whole tree, its woody fruits and several branchlet joints before seeking confirmation. Note whether younger stems occur along roots beyond the crown. Where removal is appropriate, include those connected shoots in a professional management assessment and plan to check for further growth. Do not assume that felling the largest trunk finishes the work. Avoid moving rooted suckers or soil from a suspect stand. These are precautions based on the documented suckering habit; the sources reviewed do not establish a universal treatment method for every site.

sources.label: UF/IFAS: Field Guide to Identify the Common Casuarina Species in Florida

identification: The adult female is elongated to oval, with a gray body under white mealy wax and yellowish-brown legs. There are only a few short wax filaments along the sides, with the hind pair longest and thickest. A filamentous egg sac may cover the rear upper surface. Pink sugarcane mealybug and other Dysmicoccus species can be confused with it in the field. Definitive separation uses microscopic features of a prepared adult female, including the arrangement of wax-producing ducts and small bristle-bearing structures.
actions: Inspect leaf sheaths on several stalks, recording whether insects are scattered or concentrated in particular areas. Take close photographs before disturbing the colonies and ask a crop adviser or diagnostic laboratory how to submit material. Keep suspect propagation cane separate and avoid transferring it to uninfested plantings while identification is pending. Do not treat an entire crop solely because a few white insects are present. The reviewed sources establish recognition and host association, but do not supply a broadly applicable economic threshold or validated household treatment.

sources.label: Brazilian Journal of Biology: First record of Dysmicoccus boninsis on sugarcane in Rio Grande do Sul

identification: Look for deeply lobed leaves with slender spines at the tips and edges, green upper surfaces and densely pale, woolly undersides. Upper leaves clasp the stem. Gland-tipped hairs on the upper stems and leaf surfaces are useful close-up details. The terminal flower clusters are spherical and generally whitish to pale blue. Other cultivated Echinops species can have similar balls of flowers, so color alone is unreliable. Photograph stem hairs, both leaf surfaces and the entire flower cluster when seeking a species-level determination.
actions: Use gloves when working near the spiny foliage. If the plant is unwanted, contain maturing flower heads before they shed seed and arrange removal appropriate to an established perennial. Revisit the area for surviving growth and seedlings instead of assuming that cutting the visible stems is sufficient. Avoid dumping garden waste along roadsides or in grassland. Check local status before disturbing a natural-area population. These containment measures are prudent horticultural precautions; the cited botanical treatments do not prove a particular eradication method.

sources.label: Cambridge University Botanic Garden: Echinops sphaerocephalus
World Flora Online: Echinops sphaerocephalus, Flora of North America treatment

identification: Look for upright stems with lower leaves that are often deeply lobed and upper leaves that are less divided, sometimes nearly entire. Flowers have four yellow petals. The fruits, when present, are short oval to oblong pods rather than the long slender pods of many other mustards. Roots and rhizomes should not be excavated just to confirm a casual observation. Other Rorippa species and their hybrids can be difficult to separate; photograph leaves from different stem levels and mature fruits together.
actions: Document the patch from firm ground, including its relationship to the waterline, without trampling soft banks. Seek botanical confirmation before removing wetland vegetation. Where management is required, prevent cut stems, rooted material and muddy equipment from being moved to another waterbody. Plan follow-up because the underground rhizomes can persist after visible stems are removed. Avoid an improvised herbicide application beside water; any treatment needs locally appropriate advice and permissions. The sources support rhizomatous persistence, not a one-step removal promise.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Rorippa amphibia
Conservatoire botanique national de Brest: Rorippa amphibia

identification: Look for broad, heart-shaped basal leaves with pale woolly undersides and smaller leaves arranged alternately up the flowering stem. The stalks of the large lower leaves are normally solid and grooved on top. Purple flower heads sit on relatively long stalks in loose, roughly flat-topped clusters. The surrounding narrow bracts end in hooks. Lesser burdock usually has smaller heads and hollow lower leaf stalks; use several features together, especially if the plant is not in flower. Do not identify it as edible from leaf shape alone.
actions: Where removal is wanted, deal with rosettes before they develop mature burs and plan for the substantial taproot. Wear gloves and avoid crushing dry burs near your face, as their fine internal bristles can irritate eyes and skin. Contain burs during disposal, and remove attached burs from clothing and animal coats before leaving the patch. Recheck for seedlings rather than treating one cleared plant as the end of the problem. Seek local advice for large stands or plants close to sensitive habitat.

identification: An adult shell is oval to somewhat angular, glossy yellowish or brown, with pronounced growth ridges. The raised beak near the hinge sits off center toward the rear rather than in the middle. Size and ribbing provide useful clues, but young specimens overlap other pea clams. Specialists also examine the hinge teeth inside an empty shell. Photograph both sides and the hinge of an already empty shell with a millimeter scale; do not force a living clam open for a photograph.
actions: Leave living clams and surrounding sediment in place while obtaining identification advice from a museum, aquatic biologist or local invasive-species program. Record the waterbody, substrate and exact location, since those details make a small shell observation more useful. Clean sediment from boots, nets and boats and drain equipment before visiting another waterbody. Never transfer live clams, aquarium contents or water between sites. These are general aquatic biosecurity precautions, not a proven species-specific eradication method; indiscriminate treatment could harm native freshwater mollusks.

sources.label: Rassam et al. 2021: Pisidium amnicum treatment
Voode 2017: Taxonomic status of Pisidium amnicum and P. inflatum

identification: Check for rough-textured leaves divided into distinct lobes, rather than merely toothed along the edges. The stems are ridged, and upper leaves become smaller. Beneath each flower head, overlapping greenish bracts carry dark brown or black fringed tips. Those dark appendages do not completely hide the underlying bracts. Common knapweed, Centaurea nigra, generally has less divided leaves and lacks the conspicuous enlarged outer flowers described in the BSBI comparison. Close photographs of the bracts are important because several other knapweeds also have fringed coverings.
actions: Photograph the whole plant, a lower leaf and the side of a flower head before deciding how to manage it. Check regional guidance, especially in species-rich grassland where removal could damage a native plant community. If this is an unwanted garden escape, prevent mature heads from shedding seed and arrange removal that accounts for its perennial root system. Watch for regrowth and seedlings after the initial work. Avoid transporting flowering or fruiting garden waste into open countryside. These are containment precautions, not a species-tested universal control schedule.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Centaurea scabiosa
BSBI Ireland AnnexI Grassland Resources: Semi-natural dry grasslands on calcareous substrates(6210)

identification: Look for mostly hairless, spreading stems and deeply divided leaves with narrow lobes. Flower clusters are short and crowded, and the tiny white petals extend beyond the sepals. Mature fruits are wider than long, with a coarse, warty or ridged surface and a short pointed tip rather than a clearly notched top. A hand lens is helpful. Lesser swinecress can resemble it vegetatively, so retain photographs of mature fruits and flowers rather than relying on the flattened growth habit or a common name.
actions: Before clearing a patch outside a cultivated bed, check a regional flora: a familiar disturbed-ground plant may still be uncommon locally. Where removal is appropriate, lift young plants before fruits mature and contain any fruiting material. Avoid carrying muddy footwear or soil from the patch to a clean planting area. In a garden, reduce repeated bare-soil disturbance where practical and check for new seedlings. These are reasonable seed-spread precautions; the botanical sources reviewed do not establish a particular herbicide or one-time removal method as reliable.

sources.label: Biota of New Zealand: Coronopus squamatus treatment and name concepts

identification: Adults are gray to brown moths that hold their wings in a roof-like position at rest. The body is commonly about 13-19 mm long. Young larvae are pale; older ones become grayer, retain a brown head and can approach 25 mm long. Silk-lined feeding tunnels and tough cocoons attached to hive wood are useful signs of wax-moth activity. Pupation sites can leave shallow gouges in the wood. Photograph both the insect and damage, because larval size varies and the smaller wax-moth species may share the same comb.
actions: Keep colonies appropriately sized and well supported, and inspect stored frames rather than leaving comb unattended for long periods. If damage appears, ask a local apiculture adviser to assess both the moth infestation and the reason the colony or stored comb was vulnerable. Freezing affected stored comb is an established option, but use a beekeeper-approved duration and procedure that reaches the whole load. Protect treated comb from reinfestation. Never substitute ordinary household mothballs for products specifically authorized for beekeeping equipment, and do not put storage treatments into an occupied hive.

sources.label: Texas Apiary Inspection Service: Wax moths
NSW Department of Primary Industries: Wax moth

identification: Adult female covers are roughly round and strongly convex, commonly about 1.5-2 mm across, although crowded individuals may be irregular. They range from pale or dirty white to brownish, with a yellow-brown to darker patch of retained immature skins near the center or slightly off center. The female underneath is yellowish. Latania scale, Hemiberlesia lataniae, can look very similar. A specialist may need to examine a prepared female under a microscope; cover color and shape alone are insufficient to distinguish these close relatives.
actions: Inspect several leaves and twigs and photograph the covers with a scale reference. Ask a diagnostic service how to submit a sample that includes living insects, especially on nursery stock or valuable fruit plants. Keep suspect potted plants apart and avoid moving infested cuttings to clean areas. Before deciding on treatment, establish whether scales are alive and whether fresh settling stages are appearing. Seek locally appropriate advice on any direct control. These are detection and containment steps; the reviewed sources do not justify a universal spray program.

sources.label: University of Hawaii Crop Knowledge Master: Hemiberlesia rapax
Chile SAG: Hemiberlesia rapax identification sheet
UK CSL: Pest risk analysis for Hemiberlesia rapax

identification: Wingless adults are small, about 1.2-2.2 mm long, and yellow-green to apple green. The pair of short tube-like structures near the rear, called cornicles, is black, as is the small tail-like projection beyond them. Antennae are relatively short, around half the body length. Winged adults also have a greenish abdomen and dark rear structures. These features help narrow the identification, but Aphis pomi and other aphids can overlap in appearance. Microscopic measurements may be needed for a reliable species distinction.
actions: Examine several growing shoots and record whether colonies are expanding, leaves are becoming distorted or plant growth is suffering. Look for lady beetles, hoverfly larvae and parasitized aphids before intervening, since natural enemies can suppress colonies. Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum treatments that may disrupt that help. On fruit crops, use a local crop adviser's monitoring and treatment guidance rather than a general aphid recipe. Keep newly purchased plants under observation before placing them among healthy plants. Photographs should include the host, colony and a close view of the rear body structures.

sources.label: INRA Encyclop Aphid: Aphis spiraecola identification
Penn State Extension: Green aphids, apple and spirea aphid

identification: Look for a cylindrical seed head with fine bristles surrounding the small spikelets. Each spikelet commonly has only one to three bristles. The leaf blades are generally hairless, and the ligule at the junction of blade and sheath is a fringe of hairs. Giant foxtail usually develops a larger, drooping seed head; yellow foxtail differs in leaf hairs and seed-head proportions. Bristle direction helps distinguish green foxtail from bristly foxtail, Setaria verticillata, but that detail needs magnification and a regional key. Head color alone is unreliable.
actions: Remove small unwanted clumps before seed matures and contain any ripe heads during the work. Inspect bare patches and disturbed soil for later seedlings. In lawns, maintain a dense stand suited to the site with appropriate mowing and care; avoid creating bare ground through overly aggressive removal. In crop fields, obtain crop-specific advice because useful timing and permitted treatments differ. Photograph the seed head, leaf surface and blade-sheath junction when asking for identification. These steps target establishment and seed spread without promising that one pass will exhaust the seed bank.

sources.label: Ontario crop weed identification guide: Green foxtail

identification: Look for a hanging flap of skin beneath the throat, a row of upright spines along the neck and back, and a long tail that often has dark bands. A conspicuously enlarged round scale below the ear opening is a useful close-view feature. Mature males commonly have heavier jowls and a larger throat flap than females. Do not rely on green coloration alone or approach to inspect the head. Photograph the animal from a safe distance, including its full tail and side of the head if naturally visible.
actions: Do not feed, chase, grab or relocate an iguana. Keep pets back and record its location and behavior for a local wildlife professional, particularly if it is burrowing near a structure. Never release an unwanted pet; contact an authorized surrender or rehoming program instead. Avoid handling droppings with bare hands and wash after contact with contaminated surfaces. A cold-stunned animal may recover and become active, so do not bring it indoors to warm it. Removal and transport requirements vary and should be checked with the responsible authority.

sources.label: Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission: Green iguana
University of Michigan Animal Diversity Web: Iguana iguana
FWC: Green iguana removal announcement and cold-weather precaution

identification: Young females are green and oval, becoming darker and eventually brown after laying eggs. Mature females are slightly domed and several millimeters long. The cottony egg sac develops beneath and behind the body and can extend around its margins. These features suggest a cottony soft scale, but other Pulvinaria species can be similar. Honeydew, ants, leaf curling and sooty mold are signs of sap-feeding insects rather than diagnostic proof of this species. Exact identification may require a specialist to examine a slide-mounted adult female.
actions: Check whether live scales and small mobile young are present beneath or near the wax. Photograph leaves, young stems and an intact female with its egg sac, and keep suspect potted plants from touching healthy plants. Conserve predators and parasitic wasps by avoiding unnecessary persistent broad-spectrum insecticides. Where ants are protecting colonies, seek plant-safe local ant-management advice. If the infestation remains damaging, ask an adviser about treatment timed to active young scales and appropriate for the host. Do not judge success solely by whether old white wax has disappeared.

sources.label: EFSA: Pest categorisation of Pulvinaria psidii

identification: An adult male has a long extension of the lower tail fin, the feature behind the name swordtail. Females lack that extension and are usually fuller-bodied. Wild-looking fish are often bronze or olive with a reddish stripe along the side; captive strains can be orange, red or other colors. A small female or juvenile is much less distinctive than a mature male. Platies and their hybrids can complicate identification, and USGS documents populations first called swordtails that were later identified as hybrids. Include a side view showing the whole tail and dorsal fin.
actions: Keep unwanted fish in captivity while arranging rehoming through an aquarium shop or experienced keeper. Never empty a tank or release fish into a pond, ditch or stream. Check that outdoor ponds cannot overflow into natural water. For a suspected wild population, record the waterbody, date and number seen and send clear photographs to the local fisheries or aquatic invasive-species program. Ask that program before collecting or transporting fish.

identification: Look closely at a young twig: prominent ridges run along it like narrow wings. The leaves divide twice, with about 5-15 pairs of side branches, each bearing many narrow, well-spaced leaflets. Mature foliage and twigs are largely hairless. The flower heads are rounded, followed by flattened brown pods roughly 5-10 cm long. Other wattles have similar yellow heads, so flowers alone are not enough. Photograph the winged twig, a complete leaf and mature pods together. The combination of winged branches and widely spaced, hairless leaf divisions is especially useful.
actions: Check local guidance before planting this tree or giving away seed. Where removal is appropriate, identify small seedlings before disturbing surrounding plants and remove the entire young root system while soil is workable. Gather developing pods rather than leaving them with garden waste. Established trees require a site-specific woody-weed plan and safe tree work; cutting a large tree is not a complete follow-up strategy. Keep checking disturbed ground for seedlings after the initial work.

sources.label: Setyawati et al. (2015): A Guide Book to Invasive Alien Plant Species in Indonesia

identification: Adults are generally about 1-3 cm long, brown, reddish brown or bronze. Some have mottled dark markings; others have two pale stripes running lengthwise along the back. The hind legs are banded, the skin is slightly warty, and the slender toes have little expansion and no webbing. A pale triangle can appear between the eyes and snout. Small native frogs and young treefrogs can be confusing, so include close views of the toes, side of the head and back, plus a sound recording if possible.
actions: Inspect pot rims, drainage holes, saucers and damp packing material before moving plants between properties. If a frog arrives unexpectedly in a nursery plant, keep the plant separate and photograph the animal before asking the nursery or local wildlife service for advice. Do not release it in a new place or move it to a nearby pond. For an outdoor sighting, record the location and call; those observations are more useful for checking a possible new introduction than an unverified name alone.

sources.label: University of Florida: The Greenhouse Frog in the United States

identification: Look for an oval, dark green to dark brown body with reddish-brown legs. White wax plates form rows along the middle and edges, leaving obvious dark bare patches between them. The ribbed white egg sac projects behind the female and may be about twice her body length. Praelongorthezia praelonga has much more wax covering its back and a differently shaped, longer egg sac. Another close relative, Insignorthezia pseudinsignis, requires microscopic characters for separation. Photograph an intact insect from above and from the side before disturbing its wax.
actions: Keep a suspect plant apart from clean stock and avoid taking cuttings or sharing it while identification is pending. Inspect leaf undersides, stems and nearby plants with a hand lens, including any white sacs rather than treating them as harmless debris. Send photographs and the host-plant name to a diagnostic service; ask how to package a specimen if one is needed. Use confirmed identification and the actual crop or houseplant setting to choose management with extension staff. Broad spraying based only on white wax can miss the correct pest.

identification: Its body can be gray or nearly black, with a raised ridge along the back behind the mantle. Take a top view and a clear side view while it is extended, showing the mantle, ridge, tail and breathing opening. A single dark silhouette is not enough for a confident name. Milax nigricans and species of Tandonia are important comparisons; specialist identification may involve internal reproductive structures. Published revisions have corrected earlier records of this group, so retain the original photographs even if an initial identification seems plausible.
actions: Inspect the bottoms of pots, trays and damp packing materials before moving plants. In a garden, check after rain or at dusk and record which plants are actually being damaged. Remove unnecessary moist shelter close to vulnerable seedlings and avoid transferring infested soil or pots into clean areas. If a new introduction is suspected, ask a local extension or plant-health service how to submit a specimen. These steps reduce accidental movement and improve diagnosis; they do not establish that this slug alone caused the damage or guarantee control.

sources.label: University of California: Slugs, a guide to California fauna
Revision of the family Milacidae from Switzerland
SANBI: Introduced terrestrial molluscs of South Africa

identification: Each leaf has three hairy leaflets, with the terminal leaflet usually larger than the side pair. Leaflets are broadly oval to pointed and may carry reddish-brown or purple markings. Stems often have hooked hairs and feel sticky. Slender flowering stalks carry pink to violet pea flowers; mature pods have several strongly separated segments covered in tiny hooked hairs. Other ticktrefoils share three-part leaves and clinging fruits. Document the whole leaf, stem hairs and a ripe pod rather than identifying this species from a single leaflet.
actions: Where plants are escaping cultivation, work before the jointed pods mature and remove attached pod pieces from clothing and equipment before leaving. Trace sprawling stems to their rooted nodes; lifting only the visible tips leaves established portions behind. Keep rooted cuttings and pod-bearing waste out of drains and nearby vegetation. On agricultural land, discuss changes with the grower because this may be an intentional forage crop. Monitor the edge of the managed area, especially shaded moist ground.

identification: The canes may reach roughly 8 m, with a groove along the internodes and usually two leafy branches at a node, features characteristic of Phyllostachys. Fresh internodes are white-powdery, and young nodes can be purple. Leaves are narrow, commonly around 10-15 cm long, with a paler, bluish underside. Several running bamboos look similar once their sheaths have fallen. For species confirmation, photograph fresh shoots and intact cane sheaths, including their small ear-like projections and bristles, as well as mature leaves and nodes.
actions: Map the outermost new shoots each spring and inspect beyond the apparent clump. If the planting is spreading into an unwanted area, remove or contain escaping rhizomes with a bamboo specialist or experienced landscape contractor. Cutting canes clears the view but leaves the underground system to produce more shoots. Keep excavated rhizomes out of soil moved to another site, and do not discard divisions in nearby woodland. Check local planting guidance before adding or sharing this bamboo.

sources.label: Flora of China via World Flora Online: Phyllostachys viridiglaucescens

identification: Look for an individual soft-bodied sac covered by a translucent outer tunic, with two siphon openings. Color comes largely from the body wall beneath that covering and is not a reliable species test. Individuals can reach several centimeters long. Closely related Ascidia species may look alike in a dockside photograph; internal muscles, the digestive tract and other anatomical structures are used in specialist identification. Ascidia canaliculata has been confused with it historically. Photograph the attachment surface and both openings without removing the animal solely for a picture.
actions: Record the marina or shoreline, depth, substrate and approximate number present. Share clear photographs with the local marine biosecurity program if the animal appears unusual for the area. Before moving boats, moorings or aquaculture equipment, inspect sheltered fouling surfaces and follow local cleaning procedures. Arrange cleaning where removed organisms and wash water can be contained rather than scraped into another harbor. A specialist may request a specimen, but ask for collection and preservation instructions first.

identification: The leaves sit opposite one another on square stems. They are rounded to kidney-shaped, with broad scalloped teeth and long stalks. Blue-violet flowers arise beside the leaves, often in small groups. Crushed or mown foliage has a mint-like smell. Henbit and purple deadnettle also have square stems and purple flowers, but they do not form the same creeping, repeatedly rooted network. Speedwells and common mallow can resemble the leaves; check the square stem and rooted joints before deciding.
actions: For a small unwanted patch, loosen damp soil and lift the runners carefully, collecting rooted joints rather than snapping off the leaves. Revisit the area for pieces that were missed. In lawns, address thin turf and select grass or another groundcover suited to the light and soil so the same openings do not remain. Keep fragments out of newly planted beds. Larger infestations may need a seasonal plan with local extension guidance; one mowing or pulling session rarely removes the whole network.

identification: Look between the pot wall and outer roots for small, pale, segmented insects with a light powdery wax coating. Ground mealybugs lack the conspicuous fringe of long wax threads seen on many leaf-feeding mealybugs. Those features identify a group, not Rhizoecus falcifer specifically. Formal keys use microscopic structures, including antennal segments and pores. Keep a specimen intact for a diagnostic service and include the host name, root photographs and whether the plant recently arrived from a nursery.
actions: Isolate suspect pots and avoid sharing their trays, loose growing medium or drainage water with clean plants. Inspect neighboring root balls before moving a batch. Clean equipment that contacted affected soil and keep discarded roots in a closed container. A nursery adviser can help decide whether keeping a badly infested plant is practical, because insects hidden throughout roots are difficult to reach. These are containment steps while the exact species is confirmed, not evidence that a surface spray will clear the roots.

sources.label: Phytoparasitica: Rhizoecidae identification key in Italy

identification: Look for tiny, whitish insects crawling among the roots rather than on the leaves. Some individuals carry fine wax threads that resemble a loose net. When numerous, their wax can give nearby soil a bluish cast. In a field, the boundary between healthy and declining plants is a useful place to inspect roots. The insects and their immature stages live in the soil, so a clean-looking canopy does not rule them out. Other ground mealybugs are difficult to separate by eye; root symptoms and white wax alone cannot confirm Kondo mealybug.
actions: Keep suspect soil and rooted plants out of clean growing areas while obtaining a diagnosis. For field patches, record the boundary and inspect roots at its edge rather than sampling only dead plants at the center. In containers, inspect the root ball before sharing or repotting a declining plant. Ask a crop adviser for a plan suited to the affected host. UC guidance reports no established treatment threshold for alfalfa, and the insect can survive on several alternative plants, so crop rotation should not be assumed to eliminate it.

sources.label: Yoshida, Kubota and Suzuki: Citrus ground mealybug breeding and control study

identification: Adults are small brownish-gray seed beetles. Look for short wing covers that leave the end of the abdomen exposed, conspicuous antennae and enlarged hind legs, but seek confirmation rather than naming every beetle in peanuts as this species. Larvae are curved, cream-colored grubs with dark mouthparts. Eggs can be attached to pod surfaces, and round holes in pods or seeds show where beetles have emerged. Other stored-product insects also make holes. Photograph the beetle and the affected commodity together and retain an intact adult.
actions: Close the affected package or place the lot in a pest-proof container before inspecting nearby stored foods or seeds. Record the supplier and purchase date and keep the original label. Do not distribute suspect seed for planting or carry loose pods to another storage area. A plant-health or stored-product specialist can confirm the beetle and advise disposal or an approved treatment for the commodity. Avoid applying household insecticides to food or seed; sanitation and isolation can begin before a species-level diagnosis.

sources.label: Insecta Mundi: Caryedon serratus new to continental United States
USDA Agricultural Research Service: Handbook of the Bruchidae, volume 1

identification: The bark is smooth and flakes away in greenish to reddish-brown patches. Opposite oval leaves have prominent side veins and often a softly hairy underside. Young twigs are hairy and four-angled. White flowers have many long stamens; rounded or pear-shaped fruit turns yellow and retains a small crown of old sepals at its end. Strawberry guava has smaller, glossier leaves and generally smaller fruit, so use leaf texture, twig shape and fruit together. Photograph seedlings as well as the mature tree when documenting an escape.
actions: Where fruiting guava is permitted and retained, collect ripe and fallen fruit and check nearby beds, fences and woodland edges for seedlings. Do not dump fruit or pruned material in natural vegetation. Remove unwanted seedlings while their roots are manageable. For a mature unwanted thicket, consult a local woody-weed plan and arrange follow-up rather than assuming a single cut solves the problem. Verify the species before removing a valued fruit tree or a superficially similar native shrub.

identification: Wingless adults are pear-shaped and pale to dark brown, with long yellow-brown tubes projecting backward from the abdomen and curving outward near their tips. These tubes, called cornicles or siphunculi, bear hairs. Winged forms are narrower and have even longer, darker tubes. Greenidea ficicola is a close lookalike. Specialists distinguish the surface pattern near the base and along the cornicles, plus antennal details, so a phone photograph may establish the genus without securely identifying the species. Include the host and young growth in photographs.
actions: Inspect fresh leaf flushes rather than only older leaves, and keep suspect nursery plants apart while identification is checked. Avoid exchanging infested cuttings. Record whether colonies occupy a few shoots or are increasing across the plant, and photograph predators or parasitized aphids present nearby. For a valuable crop or an apparent new introduction, ask extension staff or plant-health officials to identify specimens and recommend management for that host. The long cornicles alone do not justify a blanket treatment of every guava plant.

sources.label: Range expansion of Greenidea psidii in the Neotropical Region

identification: Mature clumps can reach about 3 m in favorable conditions. Leaves are long and may be around 2 cm wide; the surrounding sheath can be hairy. The seed head is an open panicle, sometimes up to 50 cm long, with branches arranged in whorls. Photograph a complete panicle, the point where a blade meets its sheath and the plant base. Other large panic grasses can resemble it, so height and leaf width alone are weak evidence. The old and new scientific names refer to the same grass in these sources.
actions: Prevent unwanted plants from setting seed before mowing or moving equipment through them. Small isolated plants are easier to address than a mature clump; include the crown when removing one and check the spot for regrowth. Keep seed heads and attached soil from being moved to a clean site. Near ponds or streams, seek locally approved management and protect the bank from erosion during removal. If it is an intentional pasture planting, coordinate with the land manager before changing the stand.

identification: Look for smooth, flat blades, often 15-60 cm long, and no ligule at the junction of blade and sheath. The panicle has spreading and somewhat drooping branches, with smaller branches on at least some of the lower ones. Tiny bristly spikelets may have short awns. A pale, soft-looking, arching panicle is a useful field clue, but related Echinochloa species vary greatly. Photograph the whole head, a close view of spikelets and the leaf collar; retain mature material for a grass specialist if the name affects management.
actions: Keep seed-bearing material and muddy equipment from moving between wet sites. Where an unwanted small patch is confirmed, work before seeds mature and limit soil disturbance along the bank. Check whether bent stems have rooted beyond the main clump before deciding the patch has been removed. For crop fields or extensive wetland growth, get identification and a site-specific management plan first. The presence of a large grass at a wet edge does not by itself establish that it is nonnative or harmful there.

sources.label: Kew: Flora of Tropical East Africa treatment

identification: Leaves are opposite, often divided into three to seven toothed leaflets. Small heads have yellow centers and may lack the conspicuous white rays seen on Bidens alba, although some plants have short pale rays. Mature dark fruits project outward from the head and end in backward-catching barbs. Bidens bipinnata has more finely divided leaves. Because B. pilosa and B. alba are closely related and sometimes combined in references, document both flowers and mature fruits when an exact species name is needed.
actions: Pull unwanted young plants before the barbed fruits mature. If plants already carry seed, contain the heads before moving the rest of the plant and clean clothing, pet fur and tools on site. Inspect nursery pots and disturbed bed edges for the next flush of seedlings. Preserve nearby native Bidens where they occur rather than treating every Spanish-needles plant as the same weed. In agricultural plantings, choose management for the crop and growth stage with local extension advice.

sources.label: University of Florida: Spanish needles biology and management

identification: The first leaves make a low rosette. Later leaves have several small rounded leaflets and a larger terminal leaflet. Thin upright stems carry tiny white flowers with four petals, followed by long narrow pods that point upward. Hair is often easiest to see around leaf stalks and the rosette. Other bittercresses look similar, so include flowers, mature pods and the whole rosette in photographs. The combination of rounded leaflets, tiny four-petaled flowers and slender upright pods is more useful than the common name's promise of obvious hairiness.
actions: Remove seedlings before pods ripen, including those hiding in container edges and under benches. If mature pods are present, handle the plant gently and contain it before disturbing the stems. Keep nursery pots and purchased plants free of flowering weeds before planting them into a clean bed. Use mulch suited to the planting and check new gaps after watering or soil disturbance. Mowing may leave the low rosette intact, so inspect turf rather than assuming a short cut stopped seed production.

sources.label: University of Tennessee: W399—Hairy Bittercress(Cardamine hirsuta)

identification: Look for hairy stems and leaves divided into three main lobes or leaflets. Flowers usually have five shiny yellow petals; the hairy sepals bend sharply backward beneath them. The base lacks the obvious swollen bulb of bulbous buttercup. Mature fruits cluster into a head, and their surfaces may carry tiny raised bumps, although a regional flora notes that these can be sparse or absent. Photograph the underside of a flower, the plant base and mature fruit with a scale. A botanist may need those details to distinguish similar species.
actions: If plants are unwanted in a small managed area, confirm the identification and remove them before fruit matures. Keep fruiting material from scattering while it is carried away. In pasture, identify the buttercup species and assess the surrounding vegetation with an extension adviser before selecting a treatment or changing grazing. Record where patches persist and whether bare or disturbed soil is repeatedly recolonized. Wear gloves for routine plant handling and do not use an uncertain field identification to decide whether a wild plant is suitable as food.

identification: Look for a basal rosette of broad, elongated leaves with irregular lobes and dense hairs on both sides. Leafless flowering stalks often carry small scale-like bracts and branch to hold more than one yellow head. The heads consist of strap-shaped florets with toothed tips. Common dandelions usually have unbranched stalks carrying one head and much less hairy leaves. Other cat's ears can still be similar, so photograph a complete leaf, its hairs and the branching flower stalk together.
actions: For a few unwanted plants, loosen the soil around the crown and remove as much of the persistent root system as practical. Recheck the spot rather than counting removed flowers as removed plants. Prevent remaining heads from ripening while improving thin turf or replacing it with groundcover suited to the site. Keep a flowering specimen or clear photographs if the identification is uncertain. In pasture or a larger planting, seek local advice based on the confirmed species and the plants you want to retain.

identification: Leaves and lower sheaths have conspicuous hairs, unlike the generally smoother foliage of smooth crabgrass. The stems are flattened and often bent near their lower joints. At the blade-sheath junction is a small membranous ligule. Several slender seed-bearing branches spread like fingers from near the top of a flowering stem. Photograph the hairs, ligule and whole seed head together; a finger-shaped head alone occurs in several grasses. Native or cultivated relatives can also resemble crabgrass.
actions: Remove young unwanted plants before the finger-like heads mature, lifting rooted lower joints as well as the central crown. In turf, repair worn areas and maintain a grass cover suited to the site so exposed soil is not repeatedly recolonized. Mulch bare bed soil where appropriate and check its edges. Clean seed-bearing clippings from tools before working a clean area. Crop management should match the crop and emergence stage; a treatment chosen for another annual grass may not work equally well here.

sources.label: South Dakota State: Grass weed identification
University of California Statewide IPM: Large Crabgrass (Digitaria sanguinalis)

identification: Look for alternate, roughly triangular to heart-shaped leaves with toothed edges and prominent veins. The thin, papery leaves and young round stems are hairy. Small feathery flower clusters sit where the leaf stalk meets the stem, becoming brown as fruits develop. A mulberry tree seedling has a superficially similar leaf but lacks the same hairy young stem and compact axillary flower clusters. Photograph the stem, leaf arrangement and clusters rather than relying on the outline of one leaf.
actions: Inspect purchased pots before placing them among clean plants. Pull seedlings while small, taking the crown and roots; a broken crown can regrow. Contain flowering or fruiting plants and dispose of them through an appropriate waste route rather than beside the bed. Mulch can reduce germination, but seeds landing on its surface can still grow. Recheck irrigated corners, container rims and propagation areas regularly, because a single clean-up can miss the next generation.

identification: Run a lens over a leaf rather than judging it from a distance: short soft hairs cover the blade, and one margin often has a noticeable crinkle. The sheath is also hairy, and the ligule is a short fringe of hairs. The seed head has branches with tightly arranged rows of oval spikelets, rather than a dense foxtail brush. Prairie cupgrass is a lookalike, but Missouri's key notes differences in inflorescence hair and the fertile floret's awn. Include close photographs of the collar and seed branches.
actions: Mark a suspected patch and obtain confirmation while flowering material is available. Remove a few unwanted plants before seeds mature and clean attached seed and soil from equipment. In fields, keep an eye on early-emerging plants and field entrances where machinery may introduce seed. Work with a crop adviser on a plan that fits this species and the crop; being an annual grass does not mean it responds like every foxtail. Revisit the area in following seasons to check for new seedlings.

sources.label: South Dakota State: Grass weed identification

identification: Plants can reach about 1.5 m. The flowering head contains small spikelet clusters surrounded by bristles. A grass key examines the short stalks of the spikelets, the size of their outer scales and a distinctive three-lobed scale enclosing the sterile floret. These are lens or microscope characters, not features reliably seen in a distant photograph. Collect photographs of a whole head and its base, the leaf collar and a detached mature cluster if collection is permitted. Cenchrus polystachios and related bristly grasses deserve comparison.
actions: Do not share unidentified fountain-grass seed or divisions. If a suspect plant appears outside cultivation, mark the location and ask a herbarium or extension service to examine mature flowering material. Contain loose seed heads before moving a confirmed unwanted plant, and clean equipment that has passed through a seeding patch. Local plant-health advice is especially useful where the species is regulated. Management should be selected after identification and site assessment; cutting off one flowering head does not demonstrate that a perennial plant is gone.

sources.label: Botanical Survey of India: Flora of Papikonda National Park

identification: Plants are unarmed, without prickles, and may reach about 70 cm. Leaves are oval, with smooth to shallowly lobed edges and variable hairiness. Small white flowers occur in clusters and are followed by berries that can be slightly elongated. The orange-red ripe fruit is a strong clue among North American members of this group. Solanum retroflexum instead has dull purple berries with a pale bloom. Preserve the actual ripe-fruit color in photographs and include the flower, calyx and stem hairs; dried material can lose this useful distinction.
actions: Do not taste berries to identify the plant. Photograph flowers and fully ripe fruits before removing an unwanted garden specimen, then contain the berries so seeds are not scattered. Ask a botanical service to check an unusual report, especially where the name is not well documented. For crop or nursery infestations, seek management for the confirmed nightshade and the crop involved. A historical or catalog entry should not replace confirmation of a living plant at the site.

sources.label: Morelloid Solanum revision for North and Central America

identification: Adults have the rounded, long-legged appearance shared by spider beetles, but the useful species characters are much smaller. On the wing covers, some rows carry erect hairs markedly longer than those between them, and flattened pale scales may also be present. White-marked spider beetle, Ptinus fur, is an important lookalike. Larvae are pale grubs and are not readily named from a casual photograph. Save an intact adult, photograph it from above with a scale, and note the exact material in which it was found.
actions: Inspect flour, cereals, bran, pet food and stored grain, including spills in cracks and under shelving. Seal suspect packages while checking the rest of the store. Remove accumulated food debris and correct moisture problems rather than relying on treatment of exposed adults alone. Keep clean products in well-sealed containers. For a commercial grain lot, seek stored-product advice before movement or treatment; do not apply household insecticides directly to food, feed or packaging surfaces that contact it.

sources.label: Canadian Grain Commission: Hairy spider beetle
USDA Forest Service: Ptinus diagnostic treatment

identification: Compound leaves carry many narrow leaflets and end in branching tendrils. In the typical hairy form, stems and leaves have abundant soft hairs. Numerous purple to violet pea flowers line one side of a long flower cluster. Other vetches share tendrils and divided leaves, and some forms within Vicia villosa are less hairy. Photograph the full flower cluster, the base of an individual flower and the leaflets. A botanist or crop adviser can separate it from tufted vetch and other similar species.
actions: If it is an intentional cover crop, follow the grower's termination plan and prevent unwanted seed production. Pull small escapes before pods mature, taking care not to drag seed-bearing vines through clean vegetation. Watch fence lines and the margins of planted fields for new plants. Do not assume an unfamiliar vetch is suitable livestock feed simply because related plants are forage crops; ask a forage adviser about the identified plant and intended use. Choose control that preserves neighboring crops and native legumes.

sources.label: USDA NRCS: Forb seedling identification guide

identification: Leaves are very narrow, flat or rolled inward, and may carry scattered long hairs. Slender stems can reach roughly 75 cm to 1 m in the regional floras. The flower head is narrow and elongated, with relatively few spikelets and conspicuous outer scales. In a mature floret, the inner scale called the palea extends beyond the notch between the lemma's lobes. That detail helps distinguish this species from similar wallaby grasses. Photograph the entire head and retain mature spikelets for a grass specialist rather than identifying from a tuft alone.
actions: Before removing a wallaby grass in a meadow or restoration planting, have a mature specimen checked so desirable grasses are not lost. If an unwanted population is confirmed, map its extent and prevent seed-bearing material from being carried in hay, soil or mowing equipment. Small plants can be addressed individually with minimal disturbance to neighboring vegetation. Follow up at the same growth stage the next season. The shared common name is not evidence that advice for Rytidosperma pilosum applies without checking.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Rytidosperma penicillatum

identification: Look for hairy leaf sheaths, including hairs arising from small raised bases. The relatively compact head is often about 4-6 cm long and holds a few large spikelets. Each spikelet contains several florets, whose scales have organized hair tufts and a bent central awn with a twisted lower portion. GrassBase describes the palea as shorter than the full lemma, unlike the conspicuously projecting palea used to recognize R. penicillatum. These details need magnification. Keep the head intact and include close views of a sheath and a mature floret.
actions: Ask a herbarium or local grass specialist to verify the species before disturbing a natural grassland or sowing a collected seed lot. Do not transfer seed or divisions under the shared common name alone. For a confirmed unwanted patch, contain ripe heads and minimize movement of seed-bearing soil and clippings. Removal should preserve neighboring native grasses and be followed by checks for seedlings. Species-specific control evidence is limited here, so an ordinary mowing schedule should not be described as proven eradication.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Rytidosperma pilosum

identification: Each leaf is divided like a hand into five leaflets. Stems and leaf stalks have long yellowish to brownish hairs. The white flower is funnel-shaped, with its petals joined together; the outer sepals are especially hairy and remain around the developing fruit. The ripe capsule is rounded to egg-shaped and pale brown. Other vines can have five-part leaves, so check the flower shape and hairy sepals rather than assuming a leaflet count identifies it. Photograph one complete leaf and a flower from both front and side.
actions: Trace an unwanted vine to its rooted base before cutting or pulling it away from a shrub. Work before the capsules mature, and contain any fruiting material before carrying it off site. Remove seedlings from disturbed ground near the original plant and check supports for overlooked stems. Do not discard vines or seeds along a watercourse. If it occupies natural vegetation, get a local assessment of identity and status before planning extensive clearance; the species has a broad, complicated tropical range.

sources.label: Leon Levy Native Plant Preserve: Distimake aegyptius

identification: Adult males have a patch of fine hairs on each claw. The original species description distinguishes H. penicillatus by smaller hair patches and a different distribution of dark spots, including spots on the underside. These are comparison features, not a dependable identification from one casual photograph. Independent Korean research found individuals with mixed external characters that genetically belonged to H. penicillatus. Females, juveniles and worn or preserved specimens can be especially difficult to separate. Include sharp photographs of both claws, the upper shell and the underside if this can be done safely and legally.
actions: For an unexpected shore-crab sighting, record the precise shore location, date and habitat and send images to a marine identification service or local aquatic biosecurity program. Retain the uncertainty in the record until a specialist checks it; a photograph labelled with the older name is not enough to establish a new population. Do not move live crabs, bait or shoreline material to another waterbody. Ask the receiving program whether it needs a specimen before collecting one.

sources.label: Asakura and Watanabe: Hemigrapsus takanoi, a sibling species of H. penicillatus
KIOST: Taxonomic study of H. penicillatus and H. takanoi

identification: Plants are commonly about 20-60 cm tall. Leaves sit in opposite pairs, with their bases joined into a sheath around the stem. The leaves are narrow and grasslike, but the swollen stem joints and five pink or purple petals show that this is not a grass. Each petal has a notched tip. Look for gland-tipped hairs on the middle part of the stem and compact flower heads enclosed by overlapping brown bracts. Related Petrorhagia species are similar, and hybrids with P. nanteuilii are reported. Photograph the stem hairs, leaf sheath and flowering head together rather than relying on flower color.
actions: Where removal is appropriate, pull small annual plants before their capsules ripen, keeping the flower heads together if seed may already be present. Check disturbed soil around the original patch later in the season. Avoid carrying mature heads on mowing equipment or in garden waste. In a species-rich grassland, obtain a positive identification before clearing fine-leaved plants that may include native pinks or grasses. Restoring appropriate ground cover can reduce the open patches where new seedlings establish.

sources.label: Plants of South Eastern New South Wales: Petrorhagia dubia
Bishop Museum Plants of Hawaii: Petrorhagia dubia

identification: Look for narrow, hairy leaves and conspicuously hairy leaf sheaths around upright, three-sided stems. Lower sheaths may be reddish brown. The flower arrangement is especially useful: the upper spikes bear male flowers, while lower, often stalked spikes bear female flowers. As fruits develop, each is enclosed in a hairy, strongly veined sac with a long beak divided into two teeth. These sacs are about 5-9 mm long. Other hairy sedges can look similar before fruiting, so include a close photograph of a mature female spike and the leaf sheaths for confirmation.
actions: Mark the edge of a suspected spreading patch and obtain an identification while fruiting material is available. If the plant is unwanted and local guidance supports removal, lift a small patch carefully and trace its underground rhizomes; cutting leaves alone leaves those connections in place. Keep contaminated soil and root pieces out of clean beds. Revisit the area for new shoots. Seek site-specific advice before disturbing wet ground or removing sedges from a natural meadow, where neighboring plants may be valuable habitat.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Carex hirta
Standley (2011): Field Guide to Carex of New England

identification: Plants commonly stand about 30-90 cm tall and branch above their leafy bases. Lower leaves are lobed, while upper leaves are smaller and less divided; fine hairs can give foliage a gray-green appearance. Pink to lavender, occasionally white, flower heads sit at branch tips. The overlapping bracts below each head have smooth, papery margins rather than the conspicuous spines seen on some other knapweeds. Dark brown to black, scaly root crowns are another useful clue. Older references often use the name Acroptilon repens for this same plant.
actions: Keep suspected plants out of horse hay and obtain confirmation from a weed or forage adviser. Mark the full patch, including scattered shoots beyond its obvious edge. Avoid casually tilling it into pieces, because root fragments can produce new plants. Plan repeated treatment and follow-up with the local weed program; a single mowing is unlikely to remove the underground system. Re-establish suitable competitive vegetation after control and check equipment before moving from an affected field to a clean one.

sources.label: Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board: Russian knapweed

identification: Leaves grow opposite one another or in groups of three around the stem. They are oval to lance-shaped with finely toothed edges. The flowers hang on slender stalks, usually singly or in pairs in the upper leaf axils. Their red or pink tube opens into four long red sepals surrounding shorter purple petals, with the stamens and style extending beyond them. Older stems develop brownish, peeling bark. Fruits become dark, elongated berries. Photograph the leaf arrangement, an entire flower from the side and any fruit; double-flowered or unusually colored garden forms can be harder to place.
actions: Before planting, check whether hardy fuchsia is an escape concern in your region. Watch beneath established shrubs and along nearby boundaries for seedlings or unwanted shoots. Remove small escapes with their roots when the soil can be disturbed without harming surrounding plants. Keep cut stems and fruiting material out of woodland edges, waterways and informal garden-waste piles. For a large established thicket, identify the plant first and agree on a removal and follow-up plan with the land manager.

sources.label: Flora del Cono Sur: Fuchsia magellanica

identification: Plants are often 10-50 cm tall, sparsely branched and bluish green, with little or no obvious hair. The leaves are fleshy, oval to spoon-shaped and generally lack teeth or deep lobes. Stem leaves wrap around the stem with rounded bases. Flowers have four pale yellow, yellow-green or whitish petals. Slender upright pods may reach 4-14 cm long and are approximately cylindrical to four-sided. Turnip and related crop mustards can also have clasping leaves, but often have brighter yellow flowers and a different leaf outline. Include both lower and upper leaves and a developed pod in photographs.
actions: Pull small unwanted plants while pods are still immature and remove the root crown with them. If pods are already dry, contain the seed-bearing stems before moving the plants. Recheck open soil for later seedlings and keep seed-bearing debris off cultivation equipment. In a crop field, confirm the identification before choosing a treatment, especially where planted brassicas or their volunteers are present. A local extension office can help distinguish a new weed record from an ordinary crop escape.

identification: The whole plant has a soft, gray-green appearance. Leaves and their enclosing sheaths are densely hairy, and the upper sheath may look inflated. Flower heads are compact, oval to somewhat elongated, commonly a few centimeters long, and densely covered with silky pale hairs. They may begin greenish or slightly purplish before becoming cream-colored. Other fluffy-headed grasses, including Polypogon species, can be confused with it; those often have more elongated heads and favor wetter places. Photograph the leaf sheath, the complete head and the base of the plant, because a detached decorative head loses useful clues.
actions: Check local planting guidance before using it in a garden near dunes or other open natural vegetation. Remove small unwanted plants before the heads mature, lifting the whole annual plant. If seed heads are already dry, bag them before carrying the plants away. Do not scatter dried arrangements outdoors or dump them at a beach access point. Recheck the patch for seedlings and retain appropriate surrounding vegetation rather than opening a large area of bare sand during removal.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Lagurus ovatus
University of the Balearic Islands Virtual Herbarium: Lagurus ovatus

identification: Look for a rounded plant roughly 30-80 cm tall with bright green, hairless leaves divided into very narrow, fleshy segments. White flowers have five petals around a yellow center, backed by narrow green sepals. The fruit is a small rounded capsule divided into several chambers. Its fine leaves can suggest a young grasslike or feathery plant from a distance, but the five-petaled flowers and rounded capsules provide a better check. Photograph a whole branch with leaves, flower and fruit when available; do not identify it from dried fragments in hay alone.
actions: Keep suspect material out of feed and prevent animals from grazing the affected patch while identification and management are arranged. Avoid using cultivation or repeated chopping as an improvised fix, because surviving roots and fragments can regrow. For a small plant, careful removal may be possible, but follow-up is essential. An established patch warrants a multiyear plan with a local weed adviser. Clean soil from machinery before leaving it, use clean seed and maintain suitable vegetation around disturbed ground to reduce new establishment.

sources.label: Nevada Department of Agriculture: African rue
Canadian Food Inspection Agency: African rue
New Mexico State University: African rue control

identification: Adult females are rounded, reddish insects about 3 mm long, partly covered by white wax. Younger stages are smaller and more elongated, with reddish-brown coloring. Examine protected bark cracks and twig undersides as well as foliage. In the seasonal pattern described by extension sources, immature insects overwinter under bark and females move onto twigs in spring. Apple mealybug can look similar, but has a raised ridge or crest along its back. A close photograph should show the insect's body beneath the wax and the plant it occupies; loose white wax alone is not a species identification.
actions: Check affected twigs for live insects, honeydew and actual dieback, and record whether the population is increasing. Inspect nearby susceptible plants before moving nursery stock. Preserve predators where possible and ask an extension service or arborist to identify a persistent infestation before treating the entire tree. Bark cracks and wax can shelter insects, so a treatment aimed only at exposed adults may miss much of the population. Choose any intervention for the confirmed pest and plant rather than treating every white deposit as a mealybug.

sources.label: Colorado State Agricultural Biology: Hawthorn mealybug
University of Illinois: Hawthorn and apple mealybug

identification: Look mainly on leaf undersides for small, pale yellow to light green aphids. Myzocallis coryli has much less prominent rear tubes, called cornicles, than the darker green hazelnut aphid Corylobium avellanae. The latter also has longer legs and often gathers along shoots and leaf midribs. Under magnification, the pale winged adults of M. coryli have dark rings on their antennae and a small dark mark near the leading edge of the forewing. Photograph several individuals and the part of the hazel they occupy. Tiny nymphs are harder to identify from color alone.
actions: Inspect a consistent set of leaves over time and note both aphids and their natural enemies. Ladybirds, hoverfly larvae, lacewings, predatory bugs and spiders have all been recorded in these colonies. Avoid disrupting them for a small, stable infestation. In a nut orchard, ask the local crop adviser how to assess sustained pressure and possible effects on the crop. Before moving nursery hazels, inspect the leaves and shoots and isolate plants with a substantial infestation until the problem has been assessed.

sources.label: Pacific Northwest Pest Management Handbooks: Hazelnut aphids
Wojciechowicz-Zytko: Predators in Myzocallis coryli colonies
Aphids and their natural enemies at Dundreggan

identification: Leaves are glossy, smooth-edged and somewhat succulent, commonly with a heart-shaped base. Small fragrant white or cream flowers crowd into long hanging clusters. Look along older stems for rough, knobbly aerial tubers attached near the leaf joints; these are a much stronger clue than a heart-shaped leaf alone. The tubers may be greenish or brown and vary greatly in shape. Fleshy climbers such as Malabar spinach can resemble the foliage, so photograph the stem joints and flower clusters as well as a leaf.
actions: Do not start by pulling a large vine out of a tree: easily detached tubers can rain onto the ground and establish new plants. First map the affected area and arrange a method that contains falling tubers and plant fragments. Small plants may be lifted carefully with their underground tubers, but recheck the soil for missed pieces and new shoots. Keep all viable material away from waterways and ordinary garden-waste dumping areas. A canopy infestation needs a local weed professional's plan and repeated follow-up, not a single cutting visit.

sources.label: NSW Local Land Services: Weed identification guide, Madeira vine

identification: Flowering stems are upright and fairly stiff. The seed head is narrow, with elongated, many-flowered spikelets attached on very short stalks along its central axis. Each small flower has a short bristle-like awn. Leaves are relatively stiff, and their underside is dull and rough rather than shining. The small membrane where a leaf blade meets its sheath, called the ligule, is useful under magnification. The closely related Brachypodium rupestre is particularly difficult to separate; regional keys compare ligule length and the fine prickles on the leaf underside. A whole flowering stem and close views of these details are more useful than a distant grassy patch.
actions: Mark the patch boundary and check whether it expands between visits. Seek a grass identification before mowing or removing vegetation in a natural site. If management is justified, plan for the connected rhizomes and follow-up regrowth rather than assuming one cut will remove the plant. Do not transfer soil containing rhizomes into clean areas. Keep mature seed-bearing material contained during work, and choose restoration plants suited to the local habitat so the cleared patch does not remain open ground.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Brachypodium pinnatum
Flora of North America treatment: Brachypodium pinnatum

identification: The tiny leaves are usually only 1-3 mm long and look like overlapping scales pressed against the twig. They occur in opposite pairs, with successive pairs turned at right angles, forming four rows. Small pink, mauve or sometimes whitish flowers line the upper shoots. Garden cultivars vary in foliage and flower color. Many Erica species are also sold as heath or heather, but their leaves are typically longer and more needle-like, often arranged in whorls. Take a close side view of a leafy twig and a flowering shoot; a distant pink mound is not enough to separate these shrubs.
actions: Check local advice before planting heather near heathland, bogs or open upland habitat. If it is an unwanted escape, record seedlings beyond the planted area and remove small plants before they set seed, taking care not to damage the surrounding ground. Monitor the patch afterward for new growth. Do not use burning as a casual garden control method: heather's response to fire is complex and seedlings or shoots can reappear. In native heathland, management should follow the site's conservation plan rather than treating the species itself as a weed.

sources.label: University of Connecticut: Heath and heather
USDA Forest Service FEIS: Calluna vulgaris

identification: Stems are angular and rough with stiff, spreading hairs, especially along the ridges. Leaves are broad, roughly heart-shaped at the base, and toothed around the edge; they may be unlobed or shallowly divided into three rounded lobes. Leaf stalks are conspicuously long and hairy. Bright yellow flowers develop near the leaf joints. Mature fruits are oval, usually about 4-6 cm long, with dense soft bristles covering most of the surface. Other Cucumis species can also have prickly fruit, so photograph the fruit, leaf shape and stem hairs together. A young vine without fruit may need a botanical key.
actions: Do not assume an unfamiliar wild cucumber is edible because it resembles a cultivated vegetable. For a small unwanted patch, identify the vine and remove it before fruits ripen, collecting any developed fruit rather than leaving it on the soil. Check among nearby plants for additional stems and later seedlings. Keep fruit and seed-bearing material contained during disposal. At a nursery, field or restoration site, record where the vine appeared and inspect incoming soil or plant material before moving it onward.

sources.label: Kew Plants of the World Online: Cucumis dipsaceus, African flora descriptions

identification: Plants are often about 30-100 cm tall and have stiff hairs on stems and leaves. The lower leaves are deeply divided, with a broad terminal lobe and smaller side lobes. Upper leaves become smaller and more narrowly lobed. Flowers have four small yellow petals, only about 3-4 mm long. The seed pods are commonly around 1 cm long, narrow gradually toward their tips and sit on short, stout stalks pressed close to the flowering axis. Mustards with long spreading pods are likely to be something else. Photograph both the lower leaf shape and a fruiting branch to make identification easier.
actions: Pull or hoe young unwanted plants before pods mature. Once the pods have dried, handle the stem gently and contain it before moving it through a clean bed or field margin. Check the same disturbed soil for later seedlings. Keep crop borders and nursery containers under observation, since small plants can be overlooked until their stems elongate. If the plant is among cultivated brassicas or uncommon native mustards, seek identification before broad treatment. Preventing seed production is more useful than merely removing the yellow flowers after pods have already formed.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Sisymbrium officinale

identification: Wingless adults are pale yellow-green to greenish white and approximately 1.6-2.4 mm long. Color alone will not distinguish them from other pale aphids on daylilies. Specialists compare the two rear tubes, or cornicles, with the small tail-like projection between them: in this species the tubes are long, slender and cylindrical or tapering toward their tips. Green peach aphid has relatively shorter, more swollen tubes. These proportions and surface details require magnification. Include the host plant name, a close view of several insects and the part of the plant where the colony is feeding.
actions: Inspect the bases of new leaves and developing flower shoots before dividing or sharing daylilies. Keep substantially infested plants apart from clean nursery stock while seeking identification and appropriate management advice. Record distorted growth and honeydew, and check whether live colonies remain before repeating any intervention. Avoid moving affected divisions to another garden. If this is an unfamiliar pest in a commercial collection, send photographs or a requested sample to the plant diagnostic service. These steps reduce movement of infested plants without assuming that every pale aphid is this species.

sources.label: Blackman and Eastop: Myzus species descriptions
Blackman and Eastop: Key to aphids on Hemerocallis
Julius Kuehn-Institut: Express PRA for Myzus hemerocallis (EPPO official record and report)

identification: Adults are small, soft-bodied insects roughly 2 mm long, with long antennae and two rear-facing tubes. Color changes with season and life stage: pale cream or yellow forms may be followed by greenish, pinkish or light brown ones. Some have faint lengthwise green stripes. The close relative hop aphid looks very similar. Both can have small horn-like projections near the antenna bases, but hemp aphid has distinctive swollen-tipped hairs that need a microscope to see clearly. Other aphids also occur on hemp, so host plant and color alone do not confirm the species.
actions: Examine leaf undersides and stems regularly, keeping track of live colonies, shed skins and beneficial insects. Hold infested cuttings or plants back from sale or transfer until the infestation has been assessed. In a crop, ask an extension specialist to confirm the aphid and select management suited to the growing system and crop use. Protect natural enemies where possible. Before choosing any pesticide, verify that the product is permitted for that crop and location; recommendations for another aphid or a different crop cannot simply be transferred to hemp.

sources.label: NC State Extension: Cannabis aphid in industrial hemp
Oregon Department of Agriculture: Cannabis aphid pest alert

identification: Plants commonly reach about 1-2 m tall and branch toward their upper parts. Leaves alternate along the stem and are divided nearly to the midrib into a few pairs of long, very narrow segments. The terminal flower clusters contain many small yellow heads, each with short yellow ray florets around a central disk. Mature fruits carry white hairs that help them travel in the wind. Other ragworts and groundsels also have yellow heads; the tall leafy habit and finely cut leaves help narrow the choice, but a botanist should check the whole flowering plant.
actions: Keep suspected plants and contaminated cuttings out of livestock feed, and ask a forage adviser or plant diagnostic service to confirm the identification. If an animal may have eaten the plant, contact a veterinarian rather than waiting for visible illness. For a newly found patch, record its size and flowering stage and consult the local weed authority about removal before seed dispersal. Contain mature seed heads during handling, remove the plant thoroughly where practical and monitor for regrowth and seedlings. Do not use livestock grazing as an improvised control method.
