Toe pads have divided adhesive plates. Close relatives require comparisons of chin scales, back scales and tail structure that may not be visible in an ordinary phone image. Take clear photographs from above and the side without grabbing the tail or forcing the animal into a position.
actions: Record where the gecko was found and whether it arrived with nursery plants, freight or household belongings. Do not release a transported animal into a new place or move it elsewhere outdoors. If it is still associated with a shipment, contact the relevant local wildlife or agriculture office for instructions. Avoid injuring a gecko simply to obtain diagnostic photographs. A report with several views and the original location is more useful than an uncertain name attached to a single blurred image.

sources.label: University of Hong Kong: Garnot's gecko
O'Shea and colleagues: Timor-Leste herpetofauna update

identification: Look for a roughly hexagonal shell, six prominent teeth along each front side, and flattened ends on the last pair of legs. The upper surfaces of the claws carry dark-tipped spines; spines on the rear leg segments are also important for identification. Smithsonian descriptions note dark green coloration with purplish inner surfaces on the legs and claws, but color varies and is not a sufficient test. Include the shell edge, claws and rear legs in photographs. Native swimming crabs can look similar, so have unusual records checked.
actions: Note the exact shore or waterbody, date and circumstances of the observation, including whether the crab was in fishing gear or attached to transported material. Photograph it without placing fingers near the claws. Do not move a live crab to another waterbody or use an uncertain nonnative crab as live bait. Ask the local marine resource agency how it wants a suspected new occurrence documented. These are reporting and spread-prevention steps; the available sources do not establish a practical homeowner eradication method for an open coastal population.

sources.label: South Carolina DNR: Spiny hands crab

identification: Plants commonly stand around 2.5-4 feet tall, with narrow, flat leaves and a straight seed spike roughly 4-8 inches long. Utah State describes closely set, slightly overlapping spikelets, each containing several florets, without long awns. Small clasping projections occur where a leaf blade meets the sheath. Some plants are noticeably hairier than others, so hairiness alone is not a dependable separation from the pubescent form. Photograph a mature spike, leaf collar and the pattern of growth across the ground for a grass specialist.
actions: When documenting a patch, distinguish seeded pasture or restoration plantings from plants spreading into surrounding vegetation. Photograph the boundary and any separate young patches. If it is unwanted in a natural area, plan control around its persistent underground stems rather than assuming a single mowing removes it. Consult the site manager before disturbing a forage or erosion-control planting. For new restoration work, choose seed mixes suited to local conservation goals and check the full species list rather than relying only on a product's common name.

sources.label: USDA NRCS: Intermediate wheatgrass plant guide

identification: Mature feeding larvae are about 3/4-1 inch long, with a black head, two dark stripes along the back, and a mottled pattern of yellow, white and black. Photograph several larvae, their host pine and the affected needles. The USDA identification tool notes that late-stage larvae can be easier to separate from similar Diprion species than the adults, whose identification may require microscopic structures. Needle loss by itself is not diagnostic: other sawflies, caterpillars and tree-health problems can produce similar damage.
actions: Inspect a suspected tree while larvae are actively feeding and note whether damage is limited to a few branches or spread through the crown. Have the insect identified before selecting a treatment intended for caterpillars. On a small, accessible tree, ask extension staff whether physical removal is sufficient; larger trees and substantial defoliation need an arborist or forest-health assessment. Keep a record of the date and check again later in the season, since Minnesota observations include more than one generation. Local timing will differ with climate.

sources.label: University of Minnesota: Introduced pine sawfly

identification: The above-ground plant has soft green, compound leaves with a slightly rough texture and small flowers that range from white to purple. Underground tubers have the small buds commonly called eyes. Florida's plant-identification guide distinguishes these from sweet potatoes, whose edible roots lack those eyes and whose above-ground growth is a trailing vine. Do not use an unknown plant or an unexpected fruit as food to confirm its identity. Photograph the foliage and flowers, plus any tuber already exposed during ordinary garden work.
actions: Remove unwanted volunteer plants and remaining tubers as part of garden or crop sanitation, particularly where potatoes were diseased. Keep discarded potatoes from forming a sprouting cull pile beside a new crop. Use certified disease-free seed potatoes for planting rather than assuming saved or grocery-store tubers are clean. If foliage develops rapidly expanding dark lesions or widespread collapse, seek a plant-disease diagnosis instead of assuming the plant itself is the problem. Rotation and volunteer control help reduce disease carryover; the appropriate response depends on the disease and growing situation.

sources.label: University of Minnesota: Late blight of tomato and potato

identification: Limnoria are only a few millimeters long and resemble miniature, segmented woodlice. Under magnification, L. quadripunctata has a Y-shaped raised ridge on the fifth abdominal segment and two pairs of small bumps on the broad tail plate. The British Myriapod and Isopod Group warns that these features can be difficult to see. Similar gribbles occur in the same kind of wood, and some occur together. Photograph the animal and gallery if safely accessible, but leave microscopic confirmation to someone familiar with marine isopods.
actions: Report suspected damage to the owner or manager of a dock, piling or other marine structure. Do not cut into a load-bearing timber or enter unsafe water to collect an animal. Record whether the material is a fixed structure, driftwood or transported timber, along with the waterbody and date. Avoid moving infested wood to another coastal site. Marine engineers and resource managers can assess structural condition and suitable protection; treatments used historically are not a reason to apply preservatives directly in the water.

sources.label: British Myriapod and Isopod Group: Limnoria quadripunctata
CSIRO: The occurrence of Limnoria in Australia

identification: Look for coarse hairs, oblong to lance-shaped leaves, and blue flowers around 2 cm across on branching stems. The green calyx beneath each flower is divided almost to its base. Older flowers may shift toward blue-purple, and cultivated forms vary. Other blue-flowered members of the borage family can look similar. Photograph a whole flowering stem, a lower leaf and the calyx from the side; a close crop of a blue flower alone leaves out useful identifying details.
actions: If plants appear beyond a garden, record the distance from any planted clump and whether there are several sizes of plants. Where removal is appropriate, prevent seed maturation and follow up for regrowth rather than assuming the top growth is the entire perennial plant. Wear gloves around the coarse hairs and keep removed seed-bearing material out of garden-waste dumping sites. Ask a local botanist to confirm unfamiliar plants before clearing a patch, especially where other borage-family wildflowers occur. These are cautious garden-containment steps, not a tested eradication protocol.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria HortFlora: Anchusa azurea

identification: Adult females sit beneath a small, roughly circular, pale gray cover about 1.5 mm across, with a brown peak slightly off center. The insect underneath is pinkish, reddish or purple, a useful clue separating it from some other orchard scales. Photograph a section of affected bark and a close view with a scale reference. Several armored scales look alike from above; a laboratory may need a specimen to confirm the species. Bark cracking or poor growth by itself does not identify this insect.
actions: Inspect sheltered bark on branches and the trunk, especially during routine dormant-season checks. Record the host tree and whether there is actual dieback or only a few scale covers. UC IPM notes that damaging infestations are unusual in California and that sprays can perform poorly when insects are sheltered. Have an extension specialist assess live scales and tree condition before treatment. Avoid stripping healthy bark or removing all lichens simply because they are present; confirm the pest and the need for action first.

sources.label: UC IPM: Italian pear scale on prune

identification: Look for deeply lobed, spine-edged leaves whose bases continue down the stem as narrow, spiny wings. The leaf undersides and parts of the stems can have a pale, cobwebby coating. The University of Texas treatment describes small groups of one to five narrow heads, surrounded by pointed bracts. Photograph the lower leaves, stem wings and the entire flower-head cluster. The shape and grouping of heads help distinguish it from thistles with large solitary heads, but close relatives still need careful comparison.
actions: Deal with a confirmed small patch before seed matures, using gloves and tools that keep spines away from skin. Contain flowering or seed-bearing material rather than leaving it on disturbed ground. Follow up for new rosettes and check places where soil or equipment could have carried seeds. For a new occurrence, contact the local weed program before undertaking a large clearing effort. Portland includes Italian and slenderflower thistles in an early-detection program, illustrating why the correct local response may be reporting and coordinated removal rather than routine mowing.

identification: Mature trees develop a wide, rounded crown on a substantial trunk. The long needles occur in pairs; Oregon State gives a typical length of 10-15 cm. Mature cones are broad and heavy-looking, often 8-15 cm long, with large seeds. Photograph a needle bundle at its base, a mature cone and the whole tree. Crown shape alone is unreliable for a young specimen, and other pines also carry two needles per bundle. A cone-and-needle comparison is more useful than an umbrella silhouette by itself.
actions: Check the ground beyond planted trees for self-established seedlings and photograph them before deciding whether they need removal. Include information about nearby landscaping and any recent planting. Do not cut a mature ornamental tree merely because it appears in an introduced-species catalog. If an unwanted seedling is correctly identified, removal while small is easier to plan than work on an established tree. Larger trees require an arborist's assessment of safety and site constraints. Choose locally appropriate planting stock rather than releasing ornamental seedlings into natural habitat.

identification: The Swiss flora describes flat, bluish leaves and an otherwise hairless plant, including the flowering cluster. Flowers are golden yellow with an orange-yellow raised throat. The flower body is about 1 cm long excluding the spur, which is approximately as long again; the capsule is only about 4-5 mm. These proportions help separate it from common yellow toadflax. Photograph the flower from the side, the flowering stem and the narrow leaves. Flower color alone is insufficient, and a mature capsule can help a botanist confirm the name.
actions: Record the site, habitat and whether the plant is near an intentional planting. Avoid collecting seeds or transplanting an unidentified toadflax. If management is needed, first confirm the species with a herbarium or extension botanist and establish the patch boundary. Do not apply a control prescription for another toadflax simply because both have yellow flowers. Mark the patch on a map and revisit it during flowering so its extent and persistence can be compared over time.

identification: Look for broad grass blades with a pale midrib, bristly leaf sheaths, and sometimes supporting roots at the base. Plants can reach 10 feet or more in favorable conditions. The narrow, cylindrical flower head is segmented rather than feathery; at maturity it breaks into units containing the seeds. Photograph the seed head, the leaf sheath and the base from a safe distance. Do not run bare fingers along the bristles to test the plant. Other tall grasses require comparison of these details before a report is confirmed.
actions: Avoid moving contaminated soil, seed, hay or equipment from an infested patch. Photograph and report a suspected new occurrence to the local agriculture or weed program. If removal is advised, use protective clothing and work before the jointed heads shed seed. Inspect cleaned equipment and return to the site for later-emerging seedlings; a single visit may miss much of the season's germination. Crop and pasture infestations need a locally appropriate plan, not a general lawn-weed treatment transferred to a different growing system.

identification: The specialist Blackman and Eastop account describes wingless adults as dark brown to dull black, about 1.4-2.5 mm long. Like other aphids, they have a soft body and paired tube-like structures near the rear. Winged individuals look different, and closely related Aphis can require microscopic examination. Photograph the colony, individual insects and the host leaves. Include the growing tip or stem where they are feeding. The exact host and several clear views are more useful than the label black aphid.
actions: Check whether the colony is causing noticeable distortion or decline before deciding on treatment. Keep an affected nursery plant separate from other plants while its pest is identified, and avoid moving infested cuttings between gardens. For a persistent problem, ask extension staff to confirm the aphid and recommend a response suited to the host and setting. Do not treat black sooty mold as proof of a fungal infection within the plant; it can grow on honeydew left by sap feeders. This profile does not establish that a small colony requires chemical control.

sources.label: Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station: English ivy pests

identification: Look for alternate leaves with a heart-shaped base and three to seven shallow or deep lobes, plus simple tendrils used for climbing. The flowers are white and five-lobed. Smooth, elongated fruits mature red and are commonly around 2.5-6 cm long. Leaf shape varies considerably, so include flowers or fruit when possible. The Hawaiian flora describes separate male and female plants. A nonfruiting vine is therefore not necessarily a different species or unable to spread through plant fragments.
actions: Do not dump cut vines, roots or garden waste where they can establish. Photograph the flowers, leaves and extent of a suspected patch and contact the island or local invasive-species program. Hawai‘i specifically asks for reports on Kaua‘i or Maui. Cutting off the canopy is not a complete solution because deep roots can resprout, and fragments can contribute to spread. For vines on trees or utility infrastructure, arrange coordinated management rather than pulling them down. Record follow-up growth so a treatment plan can address the surviving rootstock.

sources.label: Hawai‘i Invasive Species Council: Ivy gourd
Smithsonian Flora of the Hawaiian Islands: Coccinia grandis
Pacific Islands Area: Ivy gourd factsheet

identification: Look for hairy leaves shaped somewhat like small ivy leaves, usually with three to five lobes and a larger middle lobe. Lower leaves are opposite, while upper leaves can be alternate. Tiny pale blue to whitish flowers arise singly on slender stalks from the leaf axils. Virginia Tech describes a small four-chambered fruit, unlike the familiar flattened, two-part fruits of some other speedwells. Photograph an entire stem, lower and upper leaves, and mature fruit if available. A mat of round leaves alone is not enough for a reliable identification.
actions: In a garden where the plant is unwanted, remove small plants before seed matures and check for later seedlings. Because this species spreads by seed, preventing new seed production is more useful than only clipping flowers after the fruits have formed. Avoid unnecessary soil disturbance that creates another open patch. For lawn problems, identify the speedwell before choosing a management approach: perennial creeping speedwell behaves differently from this annual. Keep chemical decisions tied to the actual site and current local guidance rather than treating every speedwell the same way.

sources.label: Virginia Tech Weed ID: Ivyleaf speedwell

identification: On Jacaranda mimosifolia, look for short mines that broaden toward one end, sometimes merging into an irregular brown patch. Photograph a fresh mine on both sides of the leaflet, the whole leaf and the tree. Other causes of browning cannot be identified as this fly from canopy color alone. An intact mined leaflet can help a diagnostician follow the tunnel's shape and look for the immature insect; the tiny adult fly requires specialist examination. Keeping the host identity attached to the observation is essential.
actions: If damage is new or extensive, ask an extension or plant-diagnostic service how to submit affected leaflets. Record the date and whether new leaves are also being mined. Avoid moving a nursery tree with unexplained active mines into another garden. Do not assume a surface spray will reach larvae protected inside leaves, or that every brown leaflet still contains a live larva; larvae eventually leave to pupate in soil. Keep newly received trees and their growing medium associated with the observation so a diagnostician can investigate a possible nursery pathway.

identification: Look for leaves divided into three broad leaflets and clusters of pea-like flowers, followed by long, flattened pods. PROSEA distinguishes jack bean from sword bean using a combination of flower, pod and seed characters: jack bean commonly has pale ivory or white seeds, with the seed scar shorter than half the seed. The Florida flora likewise uses large white seeds and broad pods in its key. Seed color alone is not decisive because cultivated forms and related species vary. Photograph the whole plant, leaf, flower and mature pod rather than relying on a common name on a seed packet.
actions: Document any self-established plants beyond the cultivated plot, including the number and whether they are flowering or producing pods. Where containment is needed, prevent mature seed from being scattered and keep discarded pods out of natural areas. Confirm the species before applying information about sword bean or a wild coastal Canavalia. Do not eat unfamiliar beans as an identification test. For persistent escapes or a crop management problem, consult an extension botanist; the sources here do not justify treating every planted jack bean as a harmful infestation.

identification: Adults are small, oval and soft-bodied, with a pale grayish or pinkish body beneath white wax and wax filaments around the edge. Queensland guidance gives a size of about 1-3 mm. Photograph individual insects, the colony and the host plant, including sheltered stem joints or fruit where they occur. USDA IDtools relies on microscopic pores and ducts for confirmation and explicitly notes uncertainty in published field characters. Do not use the number or apparent length of wax filaments in a casual photograph as a conclusive test.
actions: Keep an affected nursery plant apart from clean plants and avoid sharing cuttings or moving infested fruit and foliage to new growing areas. Contact an extension diagnostic service if the infestation is unfamiliar, spreading among different plants or associated with recently received stock. Include the plant's origin and the affected plant parts in the report. Treatment should follow a confirmed identification and assessment of plant damage; indiscriminate spraying can disrupt natural enemies without resolving a protected mealybug colony. Do not mail live insects or plant material before receiving submission instructions.

identification: Look for a laterally flattened body, a long grasping tail and toes grouped into opposing bundles around a branch. Many adults are green, sometimes with yellowish areas, but color can change. Adult males have three forward-pointing horns; horn development varies with sex, age and form, so a hornless chameleon is not automatically another species. Hawai'i identification guidance contrasts it with the tall, helmet-like head crest of the veiled chameleon. Photograph the side of the head, body and tail without disturbing the animal.
actions: Never release an unwanted pet or carry a wild chameleon to another outdoor site. Record the location promptly and use the local wildlife reporting system for an unusual reptile sighting. Include the island and nearest recognizable landmark, along with the date and whether the lizard was in a garden, nursery plant or natural vegetation. Do not pursue an animal into unsafe vegetation or collect it without instructions. Clear photographs and an accurate location help responders decide the next step.

sources.label: Hawai'i Invasive Species Council: Jackson's chameleon
University of Hawai'i Hilo: Vertebrate threat identification guide

identification: Typical leaves are thick, oval to spoon-shaped, and arranged in opposite pairs, attached with little or no leaf stalk. Their edges may turn red. The stems are also thick and succulent and become more woody-looking with age. Cultivars can have curled or tubular leaves, so not every jade plant has the familiar flat leaf shape. Photograph several leaf pairs, their attachment to the stem and the whole plant. Other succulents sold as jade or money plants can differ, making a trade name alone unreliable.
actions: Keep detached leaves and prunings out of dumped garden waste, because pieces can be used to start new plants. If you find plants beyond a cultivated area, photograph the patch and note nearby gardens or discarded material. Confirm the identity before removing unfamiliar succulents. Wear gloves if handling cut stems, and keep the plant and fallen pieces away from pets or children likely to chew them. UC guidance notes ingestion and sap concerns. These precautions address handling and escape prevention rather than asserting that jade plant is invasive throughout the country.

identification: Look for branching, low-lying stems, hairy leaf sheaths and several very slender seed-head branches arranged along a short central axis. The Flora of the Cayman Islands describes narrow spikelets about 2.5 mm long. Examine the spikelets and the narrow supporting axis closely rather than counting the flowering branches alone. These tiny features distinguish species that otherwise look much alike. Photograph mature flowering branches, the leaf sheath and the leaf collar; a botanist may need magnification and a specimen to finish the identification.
actions: In a small disturbed patch where removal is appropriate, act before the seed heads shed and collect rooted stem sections as well as upright shoots. Keep soil and seeding material from being carried into clean beds. Revisit the site for regrowth and new seedlings rather than relying on a single cutting. In a crop or managed lawn, confirm the crabgrass and use site-specific guidance. Make a note of stems rooted at the nodes so follow-up work can check those points as well as newly germinated seedlings.

sources.label: Colplanta, Flora of the Cayman Islands: Digitaria horizontalis
University of Florida Herbarium: Digitaria identification key, Flora of Florida

identification: Look for trailing stems and opposite, compound leaves made up of several paired leaflets. Young growth often looks silvery from silky hairs. Bright yellow flowers have five petals, and the hard fruit divides into spiny segments. Each segment commonly has two strong spines. Photograph a leaf, flower and mature fruit without handling the burs barehanded. Other puncture vines have similar fruits; flower size and stalk proportions help a botanist distinguish them, so include more than a photograph of the spines.
actions: First establish whether the plant is native, unwanted or managed at the particular site. In Hawai‘i, consult a local native-plant or land-management specialist before treating nohu as a weed. Where removal is appropriate, wear gloves, contain burs and clean shoes and equipment before leaving the patch. Florida guidance notes that mowing misses the low growth and that small plants can be pulled from moist soil. Avoid transferring burs or garden plants to new sites. Follow-up should account for seedlings appearing after the original plants are removed.

sources.label: Bishop Museum Plants of Hawai‘i: Tribulus cistoides

identification: Look for an upright or loosely branching herb with simple, oval to lance-shaped leaves and small stalked flowers arising near the leaves. The flower opens into five uneven-looking lobes at the end of a narrow tube, often with a pale center. The Brazilian flora describes plants to about 60 cm tall and upright capsules held within a persistent calyx. Photograph a flower from the front and side and the fruiting stem. A blue flower alone does not distinguish this species from other ornamental Browallia or unrelated garden plants.
actions: If plants are appearing outside a bed, note their distance from cultivation and whether they are producing capsules. Remove unwanted young plants before capsules release their many small seeds, where removal is permitted and the identity is secure. Keep seed-bearing garden waste contained and check the disturbed spot again. These are practical containment precautions, not evidence that the plant is harmful everywhere. A local botanist can help distinguish an ornamental escape from a wild species before a larger patch is disturbed.

sources.label: Jardim Botanico do Rio de Janeiro: Browallia

identification: Both plants have prickly stems, very large divided leaves, pale flowers and dark fruits. Japanese angelica tree usually has a broad flower cluster without the conspicuous long central axis typical of devil's walkingstick. The Mistaken Identity guide also describes major leaflet veins continuing to the tips of the marginal teeth. These characters overlap, especially on nonflowering plants. Photograph the entire flowering cluster and close views of leaflet veins and undersides. Do not label a plant invasive simply because it has a spiny trunk.
actions: Have uncertain plants checked by extension staff or a botanist familiar with both Aralia species. For confirmed Japanese angelica tree, prevent fruit dispersal where safely practical and plan for the connected root system. NC State warns that mowing suckers alone can stimulate further growth. A small accessible plant may be manageable, but a larger colony needs a follow-up plan rather than repeated top cutting. Wear protection around the spines, contain fruiting material, and avoid damaging nearby native plants while tracing suckers.

sources.label: Mistaken Identity: Invasive plants and native look-alikes

identification: Look for small, smooth-edged leaves clustered on short shoots, sharp spines at the nodes, and pale yellow spring flowers followed by elongated red berries. The leaves are often spoon-shaped, broader toward the tip. UConn describes arching, twiggy branches and fruits that can persist after the growing season. Native American barberry has toothed leaf edges, a useful distinction, but hybrids and cultivated forms need closer checking. Photograph leaf margins, stem nodes and flowers or fruit together rather than relying only on foliage color.
actions: Map the edges of an escaped patch and look for small plants beyond it before beginning removal. Confirm the identity, protect skin and eyes from spines, and contain fruiting branches so seeds are not carried into another area. A mature thicket needs a planned removal and follow-up strategy that accounts for surviving plants and later seedlings. For replacement landscaping, choose a suitable native shrub rather than moving an unwanted barberry elsewhere. Check current state guidance before purchasing or distributing plants, because restrictions and cultivar rules vary by jurisdiction.

identification: Look for opposite leaves with a pointed tip and fine teeth along the edge. Oregon State describes small yellow glands on the leaf undersides, a useful close-up detail. Small pinkish or whitish flowers form near the leaves during summer, followed by loose clusters of small, rounded purple berries. The leaves can turn yellowish or purplish before falling. Other beautyberries also have purple fruit, so include photographs of the leaf arrangement, undersides and the way fruit clusters attach to the branch. Fruit color alone cannot establish this species.
actions: If you find plants away from a garden, record how many there are, whether they bear fruit and whether young seedlings occur around them. Birds use the fruit, so keep the location of nearby planted shrubs in your notes rather than assuming every new shrub was planted. Before replacing a landscape specimen, confirm its identity and local status; a familiar common name may refer to a different beautyberry. Avoid discarding fruit-bearing cuttings beside natural vegetation. These are containment and documentation steps, not evidence that Japanese beautyberry requires removal everywhere.

identification: An adult is roughly one-third to one-half inch long, with a metallic green head and body and copper-colored wing covers. Look for five small white hair patches down each side of the abdomen and two more at the rear; these are more useful than metallic color alone. The grubs are pale, C-shaped and have a tan head and legs, but several other beetles have similar grubs. Photograph the adult from above and the side, along with the plant and feeding damage. Do not identify an unexamined lawn grub from nearby adult beetles alone.
actions: For a few garden plants, check regularly and knock confirmed beetles into soapy water when they are sluggish in the cool morning or evening. Penn State advises against putting baited traps in the home garden because they can attract beetles that the traps do not catch. Assess the whole plant rather than only its most damaged leaves. If damage is substantial or turf is declining, get a diagnosis before choosing treatment; adult feeding and grub problems need different decisions. Protect flowering plants and their visitors when discussing any pesticide option.

sources.label: University of Minnesota: Japanese beetle on soybean
Penn State: Japanese beetles in the home garden
Penn State: Japanese beetles in brambles

identification: Check the needles in bundles: Japanese black pine normally has two stiff, dark green needles in each bundle. Oregon State gives a typical needle length of about 6–11 centimeters. The pointed terminal buds are conspicuously silvery white, contrasting with the foliage. Mature bark becomes dark gray to nearly black and breaks into rough scales or furrows. Brown cones are roughly 4–6 centimeters long. Use the combination of paired needles, pale buds, cones and bark; a distant photograph of an irregular pine crown is not enough to distinguish it from other pines.
actions: Photograph a twig showing intact needle bundles and buds, plus any cones and nearby seedlings. For an established landscape tree, its presence in this catalog is not a reason to remove it without considering local conditions. Ask an arborist about declining branches or structural concerns rather than climbing or cutting a large tree yourself. If young pines are establishing outside cultivation, document their distance from planted trees and have their identity checked before managing them. Keep cones and nursery waste out of adjacent natural areas when containing an unwanted planting.

identification: Look for an open, branching seed head with drooping spikelets and slender bristles called awns. The leaf sheaths are hairy; blades may be hairy or nearly smooth. The Canadian Food Inspection Agency describes mature florets about 7–9 millimeters long, with awns that bend outward away from the surrounding floral scale. A close photograph of a mature spikelet is much more useful than a distant image of brown grass. Japanese brome belongs to a difficult group that includes field brome and related annual bromes, so keep a specimen only where collection is permitted and seek a grass specialist for uncertain records.
actions: Record whether the patch is actively growing, flowering or already shedding seed. Avoid carrying seed heads in machinery, clothing or loose cut vegetation to a new site. For a small confirmed patch, preventing seed production is a useful management objective, but work with the land manager on timing and protection of neighboring native grasses. A single burn should not be presented as a lasting cure: the Forest Service review describes responses that vary with rainfall and seed reserves, with plants returning after short-term reductions. Revisit treated ground in subsequent growing seasons.

sources.label: US Forest Service FEIS: Japanese brome
Canadian Food Inspection Agency: Bromus japonicus seed identification

identification: Look for a rounded, thin shell without an obvious projecting spire, carried within a grayish or brownish body marked with dark and sometimes orange spots. The head and rear of the foot extend beyond the shell; living animals can reach about 3 centimeters. Several native or introduced bubble snails look similar. European identification guidance compares the head-shield lobes and reproductive features, while some distinctions require microscopic examination. Take close photographs of a living animal from above and the side, preferably without removing it from the water. Color or shell shape alone should be treated as a tentative identification.
actions: Record the exact shoreline or marina, date, substrate and whether the animal was on oysters, algae or equipment. Do not move living snails or attached material between coastal sites to obtain an identification. Ask a marine monitoring program how it wants a suspected record documented; follow its instructions before collecting a specimen. Clean boating or aquaculture equipment using the requirements for that location, and do not release aquarium material into coastal water. These precautions address movement pathways without assuming that every similar-looking native snail should be removed.

identification: The short, pointed leaves resemble little awls and curve toward the twig, giving the foliage a soft, bottlebrush-like outline from a distance. Young trees usually have a narrow, conical crown, and the bark becomes orange-brown or reddish. Size alone is unreliable because dwarf cultivars differ greatly from tree forms. Some foliage bronzes or browns in cold winter weather and greens again in spring, according to Virginia Tech; that seasonal response should not be confused automatically with insect damage or permanent decline. Photograph the leafy twig closely, the bark and the whole plant, and include its garden setting if it has one.
actions: For a garden tree, note whether discoloration is seasonal and whether new growth returns, rather than diagnosing a pest from winter color alone. Have persistent branch dieback assessed by a qualified plant professional. If seedlings appear outside cultivation, photograph and record them before deciding they are this species, and note the distance from planted trees. Keep nursery labels or cultivar names with the observation because growth habits vary. Contain discarded planting material and choose replacements suited to local conditions; the horticultural sources do not support a blanket instruction to remove all established cryptomerias.

identification: Plants commonly stand about 3-6 feet tall. Leaves occur in opposite pairs and have smooth edges and conspicuous curved veins; young plants may resemble other familiar broad-leaved plants. The stem base can be reddish. Green flowers without showy petals occur along narrow, bottlebrush-like spikes. As fruit develops, the spikes lengthen and the fruits lie close against the stalk; stiff bracts help them cling to passing objects. Photograph the leaf arrangement, stem base and a close view of the flower or fruit spike. White vervain and lopseed have toothed leaf edges; pigweeds have alternate leaves.
actions: Avoid walking through a mature, seed-bearing patch. Check clothing, footwear, pets and equipment before leaving, and contain removed seeds rather than brushing them off at another site. Report a suspected new population to the local invasive-plant program with photographs and a precise location. Illinois Extension recommends acting before late-season seed production to reduce accidental spread; small plants may be pulled where authorized, while larger infestations need a site-specific management plan. Return to the site to look for surviving plants and seedlings. Do not transport seed-bearing stems to show someone without agreed containment instructions.

sources.label: Michigan Invasive Species: Japanese chaff flower
Kew Plants of the World Online: Achyranthes japonica

identification: Look for glossy, leathery leaves that broaden toward a rounded tip, with edges rolled slightly downward and a paler underside. They are arranged alternately, although crowded growth at the ends of branches can make them appear clustered. Creamy white flowers occur near branch tips and become yellowish as they age. The small, pear-shaped capsules turn brown and split to reveal sticky orange seeds. Photograph an individual leaf, a whole twig and any fruit. Stanford botanists caution that seedlings beneath a planted Japanese cheesewood can belong to another Pittosporum species, so proximity to the parent-looking shrub is not proof of identity.
actions: Check the leaves and mature fruit before reporting an escape or removing a young plant. Include the surrounding planting history if you know it. Where a confirmed shrub is producing unwanted seedlings, avoid scattering sticky seeds while pruning or disposing of fruiting branches, and revisit the nearby ground for new growth. Do not taste seeds or fruit as an identification method. For a large hedge or a plant near a sensitive habitat, ask the site manager about locally appropriate replacement and containment. The linked botanical records support identification and documenting escapes, not a claim that every planted specimen is causing ecological harm.

identification: Follow a thin, twining stalk to its leafy branches. The overall leaf divisions are triangular and finely divided, with narrow, elongated lobes that give them a lacy appearance. Fertile portions look especially finely cut; spore-producing structures occur along the undersides of their margins. The closely related Old World climbing fern has different, less divided leaflets, so include close photographs of both the leafy divisions and any fertile edges. A wide photograph should show whether the fern is trailing on the ground or climbing into other plants. Do not pull down a mass from a tree merely to photograph it.
actions: Report an unfamiliar climbing fern in a natural area before disturbing a large patch. Keep soil, cut material and equipment from carrying it to another location. Cutting or pulling can remove visible growth, but remaining plant fragments and spores make follow-up important; one clearing does not establish that the site is free of the fern. Work with the land manager on protecting the vegetation underneath and selecting an appropriate treatment for the habitat. Wet sites need particular care. Recheck treated areas for new growth, and avoid presenting fire alone or a single cutting as reliable eradication.

sources.label: UF/IFAS: Biology and Control of Japanese Climbing Fern
Alabama Extension: Japanese climbing fern identification and control
Texas A&M AquaPlant: Japanese climbing fern control

identification: Each leaf has three small, oblong leaflets. Look closely at the veins: they run nearly parallel to one another and meet the central vein at close to a right angle, giving the leaflet a lined appearance. Small pink to purple flowers occur where leaves join the stems. Stems become brownish-red and firm with age, with small stipules at the leaf bases. Korean clover is a close look-alike with similar three-part leaves. Photograph the whole growth habit, both leaf surfaces, flowers and stem hairs if visible; a photograph showing only three leaflets will not settle the identity.
actions: Examine young plants before they become woody and set seed, and confirm the species before choosing a control method. Do not expect cutting a lawn extremely short to eliminate it: Mississippi State reports that common lespedeza can tolerate mowing below an inch. Keep the surrounding turf healthy using guidance appropriate to its grass species rather than changing fertilizer or mowing practices on guesswork. For small unwanted patches, discuss removal before seed maturity; persistent areas may need an extension-guided plan. Keep lawn-specific recommendations separate from decisions in pastures or natural habitats, where the desired vegetation and management goals differ.

sources.label: University of Georgia: Lespedeza identification and control in turfgrass
Mississippi State: Lespedeza control in maintained turfgrass

identification: Adults have a uniformly dark shield behind the head. Males have long wings extending beyond the abdomen, while females have shorter wings covering only part of it. This difference can make the sexes look like different insects. Oriental cockroaches are a particularly important source of confusion, and young cockroaches lack the adult wing characters. Photograph the top and side, include a size reference, and record whether the specimen was indoors, under outdoor planting material, or near a delivery.
actions: Keep a suspected specimen contained and ask an extension insect identification service how to submit it. Preserve the location and date along with the photographs; those details are more useful than guessing from color alone. Inspect associated nursery containers or stored materials before moving them elsewhere. Around buildings, remove accessible food and water and close entry gaps as general cockroach precautions. Species confirmation should come before a targeted treatment plan, since the published New York finding does not prove that every outdoor cockroach requires pesticide treatment.

sources.label: WHO: Cockroaches, their biology, distribution and control
Evangelista, Buss and Ware: Using DNA barcodes to confirm a new cockroach in New York
Rutgers: Cockroach identified in New York

identification: Look at the shape of the showy bracts rather than treating them as petals: kousa bracts come to points. The flowers usually appear later than those of flowering dogwood, although the calendar changes with climate. Rounded pinkish to red fruits and older bark that flakes into patches provide useful later clues. Garden hybrids between the two dogwoods can blur these differences. Photograph bracts, leaves, fruit and bark together, and keep any nursery label if the tree is a named selection.
actions: For a tree being retained in a garden, check drainage before adding more irrigation. Kousa dogwood prefers moist, well-drained, acidic soil and does poorly when roots remain waterlogged. Some afternoon shade can help in hot settings. If you are deciding whether to plant one beside natural habitat, consult local guidance rather than assuming its ornamental popularity answers the question. Record any seedlings separately from the planted tree. Unexpected decline deserves an examination of roots, site conditions and symptoms, not an automatic diagnosis based on the word dogwood.

identification: Look for divided fronds with oblong, lobed leaflets and hairs along the main axes and veins. On fertile fronds, elongated spore clusters form a herringbone-like pattern on the underside. The frond stalk also carries scales and hairs. Several woodland ferns share a similar outline, and North American specimens have been confused with Deparia japonica. A photograph of the upper surface alone is rarely enough. Include the underside of a mature frond and close views of its stalk and leaflet bases.
actions: Leave an uncertain fern in place while seeking an identification, especially where native ferns grow alongside it. Record whether plants occur in a garden, escaped around pots, or established beside a stream. Before moving divisions or soil to another site, check the local status of this exact species. If removal is recommended, account for its creeping rhizome and revisit the patch for fresh fronds. Avoid sweeping disturbance of a damp stream bank merely to remove a fern whose identity and local significance remain unconfirmed.

sources.label: Flora of North America via PteridoPortal: Deparia petersenii

identification: Examine a complete leafy branch. The leaves are opposite, broad and heart-shaped at the base, with a pointed tip and small teeth along the edge. Fine hairs and glands occur on the foliage, especially beneath. Scarlet flowers form a spreading, roughly pyramidal terminal cluster, and their stamens project conspicuously beyond the petals. Bluish-black fruits can retain a conspicuous enlarged calyx. Other red-flowered Clerodendrum species need comparison using leaf texture, calyx and flower measurements rather than flower color alone.
actions: Keep the nursery name and photograph the flower cluster from both the side and above before deciding that a spontaneous shrub is this species. Where local advice calls for containing escaped ornamentals, avoid sharing fruiting branches, soil or rooted plants until the identity is settled. Track seedlings around an established planting and record how far they occur from it. The botanical sources establish useful identification characters, but they do not supply a universally effective removal treatment; established patches deserve locally appropriate advice before substantial digging or chemical use.

sources.label: Indian Institute of Science: Clerodendrum japonicum

identification: Leaves sit opposite each other and usually have smooth edges, although young leaves can be lobed. The paired tubular flowers grow from leaf axils, and mature berries are dark purple to black. Check the upper leaf pairs carefully: they remain separate rather than joining around the stem. Several other honeysuckle vines have fused upper leaf pairs, clustered flowers and red or orange fruit. Young stems may be reddish and hairy; older stems become woody. Use flowers, leaf arrangement and fruit together before cutting an unfamiliar vine.
actions: Where control is appropriate, start with small rooted plants and trace runners rather than treating each leafy shoot as a separate seedling. Keep fruiting material contained during removal. Established vines can regrow from surviving crowns and rooted stems, so arrange repeat checks instead of assuming one cutting finishes the work. Avoid pulling a heavy tangle out of a tree if it could damage branches. A local invasive-plant program can help plan larger work around desirable vegetation; planting a locally suitable alternative is more useful than simply leaving disturbed bare ground.

sources.label: US Forest Service: Lonicera japonica species review

identification: Look for opposite leaves divided into five to seven pointed lobes, with toothed edges. Stems carry short, downward-facing prickles that can scratch bare skin. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants: male clusters are more upright and branched, while female clusters are compact and drooping. Photograph the leaf stalk where it meets the stem, a whole leaf and any flower or fruit clusters. Leaf shape varies, so compare the complete vine rather than identifying it from one deeply lobed leaf.
actions: For a small patch requiring control, pull young plants before they develop a substantial root system and before seed matures. Wear gloves and long sleeves around the hooked stems. Recheck for regrowth and new seedlings, because a single visit rarely catches every plant. Contain flowering or seed-bearing material and avoid mowing mature seed heads into adjoining ground. Clean soil from equipment before leaving the site. Seed can persist for several years, so keep checking the area after the first apparent success, especially following disturbance or fresh deposits of soil.

sources.label: University of Minnesota: Hooked hair hops

identification: Look for alternate broad leaves with a fairly straight or squared base and a pointed tip. The upper stems often zigzag between leaves. Hollow green canes have conspicuous joints, sometimes marked red or purple, and pale flower clusters appear in late summer. Bamboo has much narrower leaves and woody canes. Giant knotweed and hybrid knotweed can look very similar; unusually large, heart-based leaves are a reason to compare those relatives rather than force a Japanese knotweed identification.
actions: Mark the patch before any excavation, mowing or soil movement. Small fragments can produce new plants, so moving contaminated soil may create a second infestation. Avoid casually shredding or dumping cut material. Obtain a plan that addresses both the visible canes and repeated regrowth from rhizomes; cutting once is not eradication. Near a watercourse, coordinate with the land manager before digging, since soil disturbance can worsen erosion. Keep dated photographs and revisit treated ground over multiple seasons so new shoots are detected while they are still manageable.

sources.label: Penn State Extension: Japanese knotweed accurate identification

identification: Plants have narrow flat blades and a short fringe of hairs where the blade meets the sheath. The open seed head carries tiny, several-flowered spikelets, with hairs at branch junctions. Under magnification, hairs along the edges of the inner flower scales and the way ripe spikelets break apart are useful characters. These details are difficult to see in a distant photograph. Include a mature head, a close view of the sheath opening and a size reference, while preserving the plant intact if a botanist requests a specimen.
actions: If it is unwanted in a small cultivated area, identification and removal before mature seed is scattered are sensible first steps. Keep a flowering sample for confirmation before clearing every plant, particularly where other small grasses occur together. Note whether it returns from fresh seedlings after disturbance. Do not apply a management recipe for another lovegrass solely because the common name matches. The available flora treatments describe the plant well, but do not establish a species-specific control program or a local invasive designation for your site.

sources.label: Indian Institute of Science: Eragrostis tenella
Singapore Botanic Gardens: Flora of Singapore Poaceae

identification: Leaves are opposite on the twigs and usually divided into five to nine pointed, toothed lobes. The paired winged fruits are another useful maple character. Slender twigs may be green or reddish, while older bark is smooth and gray. Photograph the entire leaf and its attachment rather than only a red canopy. Closely related maples and garden hybrids can need expert comparison. A cultivar label, if available, helps explain unusual foliage or growth form but should not replace examination of the tree.
actions: Give a retained garden tree protection from drying wind and pay attention to soil moisture and drainage. Brown leaf edges can follow sun, drought or wind stress, so check growing conditions before assuming an insect is responsible. Avoid keeping compacted soil constantly wet around its roots. This maple can self-seed, making nearby seedlings worth monitoring where regional guidance identifies escape concerns. Before planting or distributing seedlings near natural habitat, check local recommendations for this exact species. Choose any replacement for the conditions at the site, including the shade and space it will have as it matures.

sources.label: Wisconsin Extension: Selecting woody landscape plants for fall color

identification: Look for very small, elongated or oystershell-shaped covers on bark and branches. Female covers are dark beneath a thin white coating and are less than about three millimeters long; male covers are smaller. Those covers are protective structures rather than the exposed insect itself. Other armored scales can look similar, and species confirmation may require a prepared specimen under a microscope. Photograph both a crowded patch and an isolated cover, and identify the host plant when submitting a sample.
actions: Inspect newly acquired trees and shrubs before placing them among established plants. If suspicious scales are found, keep the plant separate while an extension service confirms the insect and whether it is alive. Management is most effective when informed by crawler activity, the mobile young stage, rather than by calendar date alone. Ask about local monitoring and treatment timing, and inspect neighboring hosts as well. Avoid assuming that all white covers represent living insects after treatment, or that a routine spray aimed at unrelated pests will reach insects protected beneath their armor.

sources.label: University of Maryland: Japanese maple scale in home landscapes

identification: Look for an upright flowering stem above simple, toothed leaves. The small flowers have two lips, often with yellow markings in the throat, and are roughly seven to ten millimeters long. Plants have short hairs and lack the long, horizontal rooting stems characteristic of creeping mazus. Flower color alone will not separate them. Photograph the base, stem arrangement and a flower close enough to show its throat; a ruler beside the flower can make a comparison much more useful.
actions: In a cultivated area where the plant is unwanted, remove confirmed annual plants before their dry seed capsules open. Check the same moist gaps again rather than assuming one flush represents the entire population. Keep a flowering example or photographs for identification if you have both garden mazus and volunteer seedlings nearby. Avoid transferring soil from the patch into another bed while seed is present. In a natural wet area, confirm the species and the management objective before disturbing the ground; the available sources do not justify treating every small mazus as an ecological emergency.

sources.label: Indian Institute of Science: Mazus pumilus

identification: Leaves alternate along the stems and are oval to lance-shaped, with sharply toothed edges. The small flowers gather in broad, fairly flat clusters at the ends of shoots or near the upper leaves. After flowering, dry brown fruits replace the pink display. New foliage may be yellow, red or purple in cultivated selections, so green leaves do not exclude the species. Compare the leaf arrangement and the shape of the whole flower cluster with other spireas before relying on a familiar garden color.
actions: Check regional recommendations before adding another plant or sharing seedlings. Where a fertile planting is being contained, remove spent flower clusters before seed matures and watch disturbed ground around it. For an established unwanted patch, plan follow-up after cutting: repeated cutting can limit spread but does not necessarily eliminate the plants. Keep seed-bearing debris out of nearby natural areas. If a nursery selection is described as sterile, retain its exact cultivar information rather than applying that claim to every Japanese spirea. A replacement plan should include the new seedlings that may appear after the old shrubs are gone.

sources.label: NC State JC Raulston Arboretum: 2023 plant sale, Spiraea japonica NCSX2

identification: White waxy insects or cottony deposits can suggest mealybugs, but that appearance does not identify this species. A modern Planococcus key separates P. japonicus using microscopic features, including short, stout hairs on the back and the form of hairs in marginal clusters. These are not reliable phone-photo characters. Photograph the colony and host plant, noting whether insects occupy leaves, stems or sheltered junctions. Keep an intact specimen if a diagnostic laboratory requests one, rather than scraping away every insect before it can be examined.
actions: Keep an affected new plant apart from other plants while its insects are identified, and do not distribute cuttings or rooted material from it. Record the supplier, arrival date and host name when the problem follows a recent purchase. Ask a plant diagnostic service for species confirmation and locally appropriate next steps. A phone photograph cannot reliably separate P. japonicus from its relatives; a prepared specimen may be needed before a treatment is chosen. Advice for citrus mealybug or Japanese mealybugs under another scientific name should not be transferred automatically.

sources.label: Australian Government: Mealybugs and viruses pest risk analysis
Zhang and Deng 2023: Planococcus from China, original paper mirror

identification: Look for stout upright stems and fairly broad, flat blades. At the junction of the blade and sheath, the ligule is absent, an important Echinochloa clue. The dense seed head has upright or spreading branches carrying clusters of plump spikelets, which can become purplish or dark brown. The lower glume is much shorter than the spikelet. These small floral parts help separate related species; photographs should show a mature head, individual spikelets and the collar area rather than just broad leaves.
actions: Keep the original seed label when Japanese millet has been deliberately planted, and record whether a suspected escape is adjacent to that planting. Clean up spilled birdseed and remove unwanted volunteers before seed ripens if you are trying to prevent another generation. Avoid assuming that an unidentified Echinochloa is a suitable forage crop. A local agronomist can help confirm mature specimens and choose management that fits the crop or habitat. Regional reports of escape justify checking nearby ground, but they do not establish that every planted stand is invasive or requires removal.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Echinochloa esculenta
University of Missouri Extension: Growing millets

identification: Each frond is divided once into broad, pointed leaflets that curve slightly like a sickle. The leaflets are leathery, with irregular teeth and a network of veins. Turn a mature frond over to look for many rounded spore clusters arranged on both sides of the leaflet midrib. Other hollyferns can look similar, so include the stalk scales, leaflet margins and underside in photographs. A close image of one leaflet usually gives more useful evidence than a picture of the entire glossy clump.
actions: For a retained garden plant, provide shelter, shade and soil that holds moisture while draining well. Check frost exposure before interpreting damaged fronds as disease; damaged foliage can be removed when new growth begins. Before sharing divisions or planting near natural habitat, consult local guidance, because the species has naturalized in some regions. Keep a record of spontaneous plants outside the original bed. If removing an unwanted clump, distinguish its actual crown from neighboring ferns first and monitor for additional small plants rather than broadly clearing the surrounding vegetation.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Cyrtomium falcatum

identification: Leaves alternate on the branches and divide into several pairs of leaflets plus an end leaflet, usually seven to seventeen leaflets altogether. Creamy, pea-shaped flowers gather in large terminal clusters. The smooth pods narrow sharply between seeds, producing a distinctive string-of-beads outline. Young stems can remain green for several years before becoming brown. Compare the pods and a whole leaf with other compound-leaved trees, and do not use the presence or absence of flowers alone: young trees may take years to flower well.
actions: Allow generous space when assessing whether an existing tree fits its surroundings. Have substantial branches and storm damage assessed by an arborist rather than attempting large cuts from the ground. Where regional guidance identifies escape concerns, check beyond the crown for seedlings and avoid distributing seed. The pods and seeds should not be treated as food. If the tree flowers poorly, consider maturity and local summer conditions before applying fertilizer or diagnosing illness. Any replacement decision should take account of the mature canopy, nearby structures and the site's local planting guidance.

sources.label: Royal Horticultural Society: Japanese pagoda tree

identification: On pear, look closely at both leaf surfaces: small upper-surface structures are followed by tube-like spore structures beneath. On Chinese juniper, brownish-orange spore masses can develop on leaves and green stems. These signs help locate material for testing but overlap with other rust fungi. Record the host species, date, recent wet weather and whether nearby junipers also show symptoms. A plant diagnostic laboratory may need microscopic examination or molecular testing to distinguish the fungus reliably.
actions: Photograph symptoms before removing affected material and ask a diagnostic service how to package samples. Keep suspect nursery junipers or bonsai separate and avoid moving them to another property while the problem is unresolved, because infection can be hidden. Do not remove every nearby juniper based on leaf spots alone. Once the disease is confirmed, discuss susceptible hosts and locally appropriate prevention with an orchard adviser or plant-health authority. Treating visible pear leaves alone does not address a perennial infection on the alternate host, and a symptom-free winter inspection does not establish that a juniper is clear.

sources.label: BMC Genomics: Comparative transcriptome analysis of infected juniper branches

identification: Examine a flowering plant with a hand lens. The leaves are narrow and linear, while small white flowers sit on slender stalks. The species commonly has five sepals and five petals, with petals slightly shorter than the sepals. The ripe capsule opens into valves, and seed-surface details can matter in a formal identification. A moss will not produce these flowers or capsules. Count parts on several intact flowers and photograph the upper stems, leaves and ripe fruit rather than relying on one damaged bloom.
actions: Keep a small flowering sample or clear close photographs before removing an unfamiliar pearlwort from a cultivated bed. Where it is unwanted, act before ripe capsules scatter seed and check the same gaps again later. Avoid transferring loose soil from a seed-bearing patch into new pots. In a natural setting, seek a regional botanical identification first, since small native and introduced pearlworts can be difficult to distinguish. The flora evidence supports recognition of the species, but does not supply a tested control schedule or justify a blanket invasive label.

sources.label: Indian Institute of Science: Sagina japonica
Digital Flora of Shanghai: Sagina japonica
Kew Plants of the World Online: Sagina japonica

identification: Look for broad, pale green, crinkled leaves gathered at the ground and relatively bare upright stems carrying several rings of flowers. The flowers in a tier open around the stem rather than forming a single ball at its tip. Other candelabra primroses share that arrangement, so flower color alone is not decisive. Photograph a complete stem, individual flowers and the leaf rosette. Retain any cultivar label, especially where several primroses or garden hybrids have been planted together.
actions: For a retained garden planting, maintain dependable moisture and protect it from intense drying heat or wind. Check the soil before repeatedly watering a wilting plant; moisture-loving does not mean that every poorly drained site is suitable. Cut back spent flower stems if you want to limit seed production, and watch for seedlings beyond the intended bed. Before moving divisions into a streamside or other natural area, check local recommendations and the site's conservation needs. If plants decline, inspect the crown and foliage and obtain a diagnosis rather than automatically treating all primrose problems as the same disease.

identification: Look for opposite, leathery leaves, commonly around two to four inches long, and branched clusters of small white flowers. Garden selections may have wavy margins or variegation. Glossy privet is a close lookalike, and heavily clipped plants may lack useful flowers or fruit. Photograph several mature leaves with a size reference, the twig arrangement and any fruit clusters. A broad evergreen leaf or the nursery name waxleaf privet is not enough to separate all the species and cultivars sold under similar names.
actions: Before adding a hedge, check the current regional assessment for Japanese privet and consider a locally suitable alternative where escape is a concern. For an existing planting, look beneath bird perches and along neighboring edges for seedlings. Remove unwanted seedlings while small and contain fruit-bearing debris. Shearing can reduce flowering, but it should not be treated as proof that a hedge cannot spread. Larger established plants require a plan for roots and follow-up growth; use local extension advice rather than transferring an unrelated privet treatment without checking the species and site.

identification: Look for alternate, broad oval to heart-shaped leaves and loose clusters of small, fragrant, greenish-yellow flowers near branch tips. The small rounded fruits sit above stalks that become conspicuously thickened as the season progresses. Gray or gray-brown bark and the overall branching form provide supporting clues. Photograph the entire fruit cluster with its stalks, rather than just a detached brown piece. Other broad-leaved trees can look similar when sterile, and a name based on food should not substitute for a botanical identification.
actions: Before planting or sharing seed, check local guidance for Hovenia dulcis, especially where it is already escaping. Around an existing tree, look for young plants beyond the maintained lawn and record whether they occur beneath likely bird perches. Contain fruiting debris if removal is planned, and use an arborist for work on a mature crown. Keep follow-up checks focused on seedlings as well as the original trunk. If retaining a tree in a cooler climate, consider cold wind and poorly matured shoots when evaluating damage instead of immediately assuming a pest problem.

identification: Look for bright green young stems and pointed oval leaves with conspicuous teeth along the edges. Flowers are carried singly on short leafy shoots. Wild-type plants usually have five yellow petals, while familiar double garden forms resemble small yellow pompons. Both can belong to the same species. Photograph a leafy shoot and the whole flower rather than relying on the name Japanese rose, which can be confused with actual roses in conversation or on an old planting label.
actions: For an established garden clump, decide how much space it can occupy and check its edges for new suckers. Remove unwanted suckers as part of routine maintenance rather than waiting for a dense patch to develop. Provide well-drained soil and avoid excessive feeding, which can encourage unwelcome growth. Some shade helps protect the flower display from fading in strong sun. If a plant has moved beyond the garden, confirm local recommendations before transferring divisions elsewhere. Cutting only the tall stems will change the appearance quickly, but it does not by itself account for the shoots spreading around the base.

identification: Look for short, stout plants with triangular stems and stiff, arching yellow-green leaves. The leaf margins have small sharp teeth, and brown scales surround the stem base. Compact flowering heads often sit below the taller leaves. These features distinguish the plant from many beach grasses, but other sedges need comparison. Photograph the stem base, an intact flower head and the leaf arrangement without trampling a larger area of dune. Avoid running bare fingers along the sharp leaf edges just to test their texture.
actions: Report a suspected new patch to the beach or dune manager, with a location and photographs. Keep vehicles, collected sand and plant debris from carrying material away from the patch. Small outlying plants may be removable under an approved site plan, but all underground material must be considered and follow-up is necessary. Do not excavate a broad dune face on your own: removal and revegetation need to protect the site from erosion. Established mats are a restoration problem that calls for repeated monitoring, not simply a one-day clearing exercise.

sources.label: Michigan invasive species program: Calligraphy sedge
Lower Hudson PRISM: Asiatic sand sedge

identification: Look for relatively broad grass blades with a pale, silvery line along the midrib and a spreading, branched habit. Examine several leaves under good light; the stripe can be less obvious in some views. Native grasses such as nimblewill, cutgrasses and rosette panicgrasses can be mistaken for it. A complete plant, its stem nodes and mature seed head are better evidence than a single striped blade. Compare texture and growth form carefully before removing an entire woodland ground layer.
actions: For a small confirmed patch, hand-pull plants before seed heads mature and keep disturbance to the surrounding soil modest. Clean shoes, tools and mowing equipment before leaving, since seed travels readily on them. In a lawn, maintaining suitable dense turf and preventing seed production can help, but woodland work needs different priorities from lawn care. Revisit the site for several seasons, including after fresh disturbance. If seed heads are already present, contain the material instead of carrying loose plants along a path. A cleared patch this year does not mean its seed bank has been exhausted.

sources.label: Penn State: Japanese stiltgrass in lawns

identification: Look for rounded to heart-shaped leaves carried on long stalks from the ground. Early flower shoots are thick and upright, bearing clusters of small pale flower heads rather than a single daisy. Male and female flowers occur on separate plants. Other butterburs can look similar, and a large summer leaf without flowers may not be enough for a confident identification. Photograph the leaf base and underside, the way its stalk meets the blade, and any early-season flower clusters.
actions: Think about the available space before planting or dividing it. Where containment is needed, monitor the perimeter for shoots arising from the rhizome system and avoid moving soil or divisions into nearby wet habitat. Cutting off the large leaves can hide the patch temporarily without removing the underground plant. Obtain local advice before attempting broad excavation beside water, where disturbance can affect the bank. For a retained ornamental, provide consistently moist, sheltered ground and remove old foliage as new growth approaches. Published food traditions are not a reason to taste an unidentified butterbur or assume every plant part is safe.

sources.label: University of Tokyo Museum: Faces and Flora catalogue

identification: Leaves are divided into many leaflets, commonly fifteen to nineteen in this species. Long drooping clusters carry fragrant, pea-shaped flowers that open progressively from the cluster base toward its tip. Fuzzy hanging pods follow the flowers. Chinese wisteria and hybrids can overlap in appearance, so leaflet number or twining direction alone should not settle the identification. Photograph a complete leaf, several flower clusters at different stages and mature pods. A garden label can help but does not rule out hybrid ancestry.
actions: Before removal, trace the vines to their bases and look for runners rooted away from the main trunk. Keep rooted pieces and seed pods contained rather than dumping them at a woodland edge. Do not pull a heavy vine from a tree canopy if branches could fall or bark could be stripped. Plan repeated checks for regrowth after cutting and obtain local advice for large established plants. When replacing an ornamental, choose a species suitable for your region and support structure. A single pruning can make the site look clear while living stems and roots remain.

sources.label: University of Maryland: Chinese and Japanese wisteria

identification: Examine the stems and both leaf surfaces for fine hairs. Leaves are paired opposite each other and carry small gland dots that may be easier to see with magnification. Yellow flowers arise singly from the leaf axils on short stalks; the green sepals remain around the developing capsule. Creeping or low-growing relatives can share the same general look. Photograph the leaf arrangement, stem hairs, a flower from the side and any fruit. These details are more useful than a distant image of a yellow-flowered patch.
actions: Record whether the plant is part of a deliberate groundcover planting or is growing independently in a moist natural area. Seek a regional flora-based identification before removing it from a stream margin, where similar plants and sensitive ground may be present. If an unwanted garden plant is confirmed, contain seed-bearing material and check for further plants before moving nearby soil. The sources reviewed support its identity and habitat but do not demonstrate a reliable species-specific eradication method. Local status and the purpose of management should guide any larger intervention.

sources.label: Indian Institute of Science: Lysimachia japonica
Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Lysimachia japonica
Digital Flora of Shanghai: Lysimachia japonica

identification: Look for stiff, narrow leaves several inches long with a conspicuous central midrib and smooth edges. Female plants can carry a seed above a swollen, colored fleshy receptacle, an arrangement quite different from a typical berry. The cultivar Maki is more compact and has smaller leaves, so size alone is not decisive. Photograph a complete shoot and any seed-bearing structures. If the only name available is Japanese yew, compare both Podocarpus and true yews before making decisions based on a common name.
actions: For a retained hedge or tree, pay close attention to drainage: this species does poorly in persistently wet soil. Consider its eventual size when deciding how close to structures it should remain. If yellow spots or leaf loss appear, inspect leaves and twigs for scale insects and obtain an identification before treating. Beaded structures on the roots are not automatically a pest; podocarps can have normal root nodules. Avoid removing healthy roots merely because they look unfamiliar. Check regional planting advice before distributing seedlings or adding plants beside natural habitat.

identification: Look closely at the flowering head rather than trying to identify a tall grass by height. The head is assembled from pairs of short flowering branches, each associated with a narrow bract. Rusty or reddish hairs on the spikelets are an important clue in the Hawaiian key. Other Hyparrhenia species can be very similar, and small hairs at the branch bases may be pale. Photograph the whole head and a close view of one paired unit, with a size reference and an intact mature specimen if requested.
actions: Report a new patch to the relevant land or weed manager where this grass is a concern. Keep mature seed heads from being carried on equipment or mixed into material moved to another property. In a dry stand, discuss fuel reduction and plant control together rather than treating burning as a simple removal method; the species can regenerate after fire. Arrange follow-up checks for regrowth and seedlings after any work. If it is part of a pasture system, seek locally appropriate forage and vegetation advice before making changes that could leave bare ground or redistribute seed.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Hyparrhenia rufa
Bishop Museum: Hawaiian biological survey records
Pacific Fire Exchange: Hyparrhenia rufa fire risk

identification: Leaves are opposite, smooth-edged, glossy and somewhat leathery, often with a conspicuous yellowish midrib. New foliage can be pinkish. Small fragrant flowers have many stamens, giving their clusters a soft, brushlike appearance. The fruit changes from green through reddish purple to shiny dark purple or black. Other Syzygium trees can have similar leaves; photograph the leaf veins, entire flower cluster and ripe fruit together. A dark fruit alone is not enough to establish Java plum.
actions: Check the regional assessment before planting or distributing seedlings, particularly in places where the tree is known to escape. Around an existing tree, inspect nearby edges and animal perches for young plants and record how far they occur from the parent. If removal is recommended, include fruit and seedlings in the plan instead of focusing only on the trunk. Have large trees assessed by an arborist, and contain seed-bearing debris so it is not dumped into natural areas. Continue monitoring after work because animals may bring seed from other nearby trees.

identification: Each long leaf stalk carries three shiny leaflets, with the middle leaflet often larger and more distinctly stalked than the side pair. Leaflets are broadly oval to elliptic and have small teeth along their edges. Tiny greenish flowers lack showy petals and occur in clusters near leaf axils. Small rounded fruits may become brown, reddish or dark. Several unrelated plants have three leaflets, so include the woody branching, leaf stalk and fruit in photographs instead of treating leaflet number as a complete identification.
actions: Check regional recommendations before planting another tree or moving seedlings from an old planting. Where removal is appropriate, map the seedlings as well as mature trees, and contain fruit-bearing debris during work. A large bishopwood needs professional assessment for safe pruning or removal, especially near buildings and roads. Keep records of any new growth after work so follow-up can be directed to actual surviving plants. In a place where the species belongs naturally, the same vigorous tree may have a different role; do not transfer a Florida impact label without checking the local context.

identification: A shrub matching this general description has opposite broad leaves and a terminal cluster of red to orange flowers with projecting stamens.
