Those characters also fit related glorybowers. The lengths of the calyx, corolla tube and lobes are important in treatments that separate C. speciosissimum from C. buchananii. Photograph a full flowering branch, both leaf surfaces and individual flowers beside a ruler. The similarly named hybrid C. x speciosum is another plant and should not be substituted merely because a search returns it.
actions: Keep the original plant label, collection location and any photographs together when seeking a botanical determination. Avoid sharing a plant as this exact species until the name is resolved. If a broad-leaved glorybower is spreading beyond a garden, document runners and new plants so local advisers can assess the actual growth pattern. Contain any material removed during that work. Have flowering material checked before choosing a species-specific treatment or interpreting regional invasive-status advice. Retain the identification source with the plant record so later comparisons use the same botanical concept.

sources.label: Florida Natural Areas Inventory: Clerodendrum speciosissimum

identification: Look for narrow oval to lance-shaped leaves with smooth, slightly wavy edges. White, star-shaped flowers occur singly or in small groups, followed by rounded orange-red berries about the size of a small marble. The plant lacks prickles. Other nightshades and ornamental peppers can be confusing when only fruit is shown. Photograph the flowers, leaf attachment and a complete branch with fruit at different stages. Do not taste a berry as an identification test; the plant is poisonous.
actions: Keep a labeled plant and any fallen berries out of reach of children and pets. If removing an unwanted plant, collect loose fruit as well as the shrub so seeds are not left scattered through the bed or dumped with garden waste. Look for subsequent seedlings in the same moist gaps. Before moving a potted specimen outdoors permanently, check local advice about escape from cultivation. For an unfamiliar fruiting shrub in a natural area, seek confirmation before clearing it. The plant's decorative use is not evidence that its fruit or leaves can be eaten safely.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Solanum pseudocapsicum
Queensland Poisons Information Centre: Jerusalem cherry

identification: Look for opposite, pointed oval leaves with strongly toothed edges and a wrinkled or corrugated upper surface. The showy white flowers usually have four petals, an unusual and helpful feature among familiar rose-family shrubs. Black fruits commonly occur in groups of four, though fewer can develop. Compare the leaf arrangement and petal count with kerria and other flowering shrubs. Photograph a leafy twig, a flower face-on and a fruit cluster; an isolated black fruit could belong to many unrelated plants.
actions: Check local invasive-plant recommendations before planting or distributing seedlings. If removal is recommended, include small plants beneath and around an old shrub, and keep the persistent fruits contained while cutting or transporting branches. Do not treat the attractive black fruits as food. For an uncertain plant, wait for flowers or obtain an expert identification before clearing nearby shrubs with similar leaves. Revisit the area after removal for new growth and seedlings. Where a planting is retained while a replacement is arranged, reducing fruit production can be one precaution, but it is not proof that spread has stopped.

identification: Mature leaves are broadly oval with a few large, irregular triangular teeth, while the earliest seedling leaves may have smooth edges. The thick branching stems are largely smooth. Upright funnel-shaped flowers emerge near leaf or branch junctions, followed by egg-shaped capsules covered in stiff prickles. Ripe capsules split into four sections. Other Datura species require comparison, especially when flowers or fruit are missing. Photograph the whole plant, leaf outline and an intact capsule; a common name such as moonflower can refer to entirely different plants.
actions: Remove confirmed unwanted plants before the prickly capsules mature, keeping hands protected and avoiding unnecessary contact with the foliage. Contain any capsules already present so seed does not spill during transport. Keep removed material out of animal feed and away from children or pets. Recheck disturbed soil for later seedlings instead of assuming the first removal ends the problem. In a crop or pasture, ask an extension adviser to assess the infestation and contamination risk before harvest. Do not rely on ornamental flowers, a historical use or a familiar common name as evidence of safety.

sources.label: Queensland Poisons Information Centre: Common thornapple

identification: Look for broad oval leaves, short hairs on the upper surface and a sheathing leaf base that often carries longer reddish hairs at its opening. Above-ground flowers sit in folded green bracts. These characters overlap with other dayflowers, including Virginia dayflower, so red hairs or blue petals alone are not decisive. Underground flowering structures are a useful additional clue when a specimen is examined. Photograph the leaf sheath, flower bract and whole growth habit, and ask a diagnostic service whether roots and lower stems are needed.
actions: Where this species is unwanted, prevent soil and plant fragments from being moved out of the patch while identification and management are arranged. Inspect the base and rooting stems rather than removing only visible flower shoots. Do not assume mowing or taking off blue flowers prevents all seed production, because the plant can also reproduce below ground. Keep removed material contained and revisit the site for new plants. In a crop field, obtain local extension guidance early: management must fit both the crop and this plant's unusual reproductive biology, rather than following a generic dayflower recommendation.

identification: Look for stout stems with broad, flat, tapering leaf blades. The conspicuous rounded or teardrop-shaped coverings can mature to pale, bluish or grayish tones and have a polished surface. A slender male flowering branch emerges above the structure that encloses the female portion. This combination is much more distinctive than the leaves alone. Photograph an intact flowering or fruiting cluster from the side, showing both the beadlike part and the projecting branch. Other broad-leaved grasses are difficult to exclude before these structures develop.
actions: Before planting or sharing seed-bearing beads, check local guidance about the species and its ability to establish outside cultivation. Around an existing planting, look along drainage routes and nearby moist ground for volunteers. If it is unwanted, collect the seed-bearing clusters before they are shed and keep them out of discarded soil or streamside garden waste. Continue checking the site after removal. A craft use does not establish that collected material is nonviable, and a grain-crop tradition should not be treated as confirmation that an unidentified wild grass is suitable for food.

identification: Look for small pansy-like flowers with five petals, a spur behind the lower petal and green sepals that are no longer than the petals. Leaves are oval to lance-shaped, and the leaflike structures at their bases are deeply divided. Flower color alone is not enough. Field pansy can be especially difficult to separate when plants are not flowering; Flora of North America notes that the usual variety cannot be distinguished from it vegetatively. Photograph the flower front and side, sepals and leaf bases together.
actions: If you welcome it in a garden, allow for seedlings to appear beyond the original clump. If you want to limit that spread, remove developing seed capsules before they dry and eject seed, then check nearby gaps for volunteers. Keep the soil moist but well drained rather than repeatedly soaking a struggling plant. In a natural area, confirm the species before treating every small violet as a garden escape. This plant's readiness to reseed does not alone establish an invasive impact, and advice for large hybrid pansies should not automatically determine its identification or management.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Viola tricolor var. tricolor

identification: Look for long, mostly hairless blades with a conspicuous pale or white midrib. At the blade base there is a membranous ligule, but no clasping auricles. Established plants have substantial rhizomes, which help separate them from similar annual sorghums. A white midrib by itself is not diagnostic. Photograph the collar where blade and sheath meet, a complete flowering head and any underground stem exposed during an authorized inspection. Young plants without flowers or rhizomes may need a weed specialist's comparison.
actions: Prevent seed production and keep contaminated soil or rhizome pieces from moving to clean ground. A casual tilling pass can redistribute living pieces, so any cultivation should be part of a deliberate local plan. Small patches require attention to underground material and repeated new shoots; mowing once only removes the visible growth. Clean machinery before it leaves an infested area. If the grass is in pasture or hay, seek livestock and forage advice before using it, especially after drought or frost. Its history as a forage crop does not guarantee safety under every condition.

identification: Look for upright hollow stems, narrow flat leaves and fine hairs along leaf edges or sheaths. The flowering spike is slender and cylindrical rather than open and branching. At maturity it breaks into firm sections that enclose the seeds; loose sections can be mistaken for bits of straw. The upper part of the spike may carry long awns. Photograph an intact head and a detached joint beside a ruler, along with the leaf collar. Seedlings need particular care because visual similarity to wheat is substantial.
actions: Use clean seed and clean harvesting equipment before entering an uninfested field. Map small patches early enough to stop seed production, and include adjoining roadsides or field margins in the plan. If jointed heads are present, contain them rather than carrying loose stems through the crop. Ask a local agronomist about rotation and treatment options that fit the actual wheat system; similar crop and weed biology makes a generic grass-control approach unreliable. Continue surveillance for several years, since seed can persist in soil and apparent success in one season may not remove the source of future plants.

sources.label: Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board: Jointed goatgrass

identification: Look for broad, pointed or rounded leaves that narrow toward their stalks, with blades ranging from roughly diamond-shaped to oval. Color alone is unreliable because green forms belong to the same species, and several unrelated ornamentals share the name Joseph's-coat. The flowers are much less noticeable than the foliage. When identifying a volunteer amaranth, photograph its flowering clusters and mature fruit as well as its leaves; a colorful leaf is not enough to separate all the cultivated and weedy relatives.
actions: Give an identified ornamental planting a sunny position and enough room for the stated cultivar dimensions. Moderate watering supports garden growth, although established plants can tolerate some dryness. Keep the cultivar label if you want to repeat a particular color scheme, and check nearby seedlings before assuming they are the same selection. Remove unwanted volunteers while small. The common names and the existence of vegetable forms do not establish the identity or suitability of an unknown plant for eating.

identification: Check the combination of glossy, finely toothed leaves, small clustered greenish-yellow flowers, and fruit containing a hard stone. Branches may carry paired spines, with one straighter and the other hooked, but some cultivars are nearly or completely thornless. The leaves fall seasonally, unlike those of many evergreen fruit trees. Record the fruit and branching pattern together; a thorny shoot alone is not enough for identification, particularly when it comes from beneath the graft of a cultivated tree.
actions: Allow access around the tree so you can notice and remove unwanted root suckers early. On grafted plants, those shoots can belong to the rootstock and should not be assumed to produce the named cultivar's fruit. Choose well-drained soil and provide regular irrigation when a good fruit crop is the aim, even though the tree tolerates drought. Protect the trunk from physical injury. If fruit performance is disappointing, check the cultivar and local growing conditions before applying extra fertilizer or assuming every jujube needs the same pollination arrangement.

sources.label: University of Arizona Extension: Chinese Jujube
UF/IFAS: Jujube as a Florida Fruit Crop
University of Arizona Campus Arboretum: Ziziphus jujuba

identification: An adult shell is only about 5 to 7 millimeters wide, with roughly four or five whorls. Look closely at the extended animal for the distinctive tail horn, and photograph both the shell and the body beside a scale. Small brown shells occur in many unrelated snails, and the shell alone can be misleading. A specialist may use detailed morphology or DNA to confirm an unfamiliar record; a published Argentine discovery used both approaches rather than relying only on its jumping behavior.
actions: If you notice a suspect snail on newly acquired plants, keep those pots separate while arranging identification through a plant-health service. Inspect pot bases, sheltered crevices, and associated plant material without transferring the material to another garden. Photograph the animal where found and retain the purchase location and date. Do not release it elsewhere. These are containment precautions, not a demonstrated eradication treatment; the laboratory reproduction findings also should not be read as a fixed outdoor development schedule.

sources.label: Barrientos 1998: Life history of Ovachlamys fulgens under laboratory conditions
Beltramino et al. 2018: Jumping snail in the Upper-Parana Atlantic Forest

identification: Mature jumping worms usually have a smooth, pale collar that wraps completely around the body and lies almost flush with the surrounding skin. They may thrash strongly or move with a snakelike motion when disturbed. Those features help distinguish the group from familiar earthworms with a raised, saddle-shaped collar, but they do not establish Amynthas agrestis specifically. Amynthas tokioensis and Metaphire hilgendorfi look similar. Juveniles are harder to assess, and granular soil by itself is only a clue.
actions: Keep soil and yard waste from an affected area on site rather than sharing plants with intact root balls or moving mulch elsewhere. Check incoming plants and clean adhering soil from tools and footwear before working in another location. Photograph mature worms and ask your extension service how to confirm and report a local finding. Removing visible adults may reduce their numbers, but it will not reliably eliminate the small cocoons already in soil. Avoid improvised chemical treatments; prevention and limiting further movement remain the most practical priorities.

sources.label: University of Maryland Extension: Invasive Jumping Worms

identification: Look first at the junction where the leaf blade meets its sheath: junglerice has neither a ligule nor auricles. The leaves often show purple bands running across the blade, but those markings can be faint or absent and are not a required character. Mature flower heads have short, compact branches. Barnyardgrass is a close lookalike, while crabgrasses and dallisgrass can also confuse a quick inspection. Photograph the collar region and a complete flower head rather than relying on banding alone.
actions: Pull or hoe young plants before they set seed, then revisit irrigated edges and other damp patches through the growing season. In crop fields, confirm the species before changing a weed program. Sri Lankan rice guidance uses early weeding and appropriate water management, but flooding is not suitable for every crop or site. Some populations resist commonly used herbicides, so repeated treatment failure deserves diagnosis rather than a stronger dose. Keep records of where surviving plants occur and seek crop-specific extension advice.

sources.label: University of California: Managing Junglerice and Other Summer Grasses in Orchards
Sri Lanka Department of Agriculture: Echinochloa colona

identification: The 2021 review describes an oval, medium- to dark-brown covering with a conspicuous lengthwise ridge. Two overlapping shed skins create an indentation near the front, and heavily occupied leaves can carry white secretions. Older descriptions mention a frosted wax layer and a whitish rear extension. These are preliminary clues rather than a reliable field test. Closely related Fiorinia can look alike, and prepared specimens are needed to compare the microscopic lobes and ducts. A normal garden photograph cannot resolve those structures.
actions: Photograph the affected plant and close views of the scales, and record which plant parts carry them. Before treating a valuable specimen, ask an insect diagnostic service to establish the scale's identity and whether living insects remain under the coverings. Keep newly purchased affected stock separate while that assessment is arranged. Do not borrow spray timing or life-cycle claims from elongate hemlock scale, ordinary juniper scale, or phantasma scale simply because the names sound similar. A local diagnosis should determine what monitoring or management the actual plant needs.

sources.label: Ahmed and colleagues 2021: Adventive Fiorinia of the United States, original mirror

identification: The leaves are usually oval to broadly oval, with toothed edges and a pointed tip. One or both of the lowest teeth may extend into a narrow, threadlike point. Inspect mature capsules for lengthwise angles or wings and the projecting, divided tips at their ends. The Florida flora distinguishes this species by capsules with three or four compartments and forked terminal awns. Other jutes can have rounded capsules or differently shaped, unwinged fruits, so leaves alone are a poor basis for a final name.
actions: If a volunteer appears in a cultivated bed, take close photographs of the leaf base, yellow flower, and mature capsule before deciding what it is. Remove unwanted plants before their capsules release seed, provided the planting is yours to manage. In a natural area, establish local status before treating a plant as a weed. A record labeled jute does not prove that it is a commercial fiber crop or suitable for food. Preserve the scientific identification with any observation you submit.

sources.label: Botanical Survey of India: Flora of Taroba National Park, Corchorus
Flora of North America: Corchorus aestuans
Florida Museum: Flora of Florida, Corchorus key

identification: Grader grass is usually an annual, sometimes lasting into a second year, and can reach roughly 2 meters or more. Its narrow leaves are spaced along relatively hairless stems. The drooping flower heads contain fanlike groups of small spikelets and bent, twisted awns. Themeda triandra is perennial and generally has larger individual spikelets; other Themeda grasses also require comparison. Photograph an intact seed head and the plant base, and have uncertain specimens checked before controlling a mixed grassland patch.
actions: Where control is appropriate, dig out a few plants before seed matures and monitor the disturbed spots for seedlings. Cutting below the flower heads at early flowering can limit seed production, but it does not kill the plants. Clean seed-bearing debris and mud from machinery, footwear, and clothing before leaving a patch. Maintain healthy pasture cover rather than creating bare ground through overgrazing. Ask the local weed authority about disposal and site requirements, because management status differs between Australian jurisdictions and cannot be inferred for other countries.

identification: Look for kernels with blackened, sooty areas, often near the base or along the groove, while part of the outer coat remains intact. Heavily affected kernels can look hollowed like a small boat. A fishy smell may accompany severe infection, but smell is not a safe or sufficient identification test. Other bunt fungi and discolored grain can be confused with it. Confirmation depends on a diagnostic laboratory examining spores and, when appropriate, using molecular tests to distinguish related fungi.
actions: If you suspect Karnal bunt, keep the grain lot identified and separate, and contact your plant-health authority or crop diagnostic service before moving or disposing of it. Preserve field, seed-source, and storage records so the finding can be traced. Use clean planting seed and follow locally applicable sanitation and movement requirements. Avoid judging an entire lot from a few visible kernels or deciding that a clean-looking field excludes infection. Treatment choices and any official restrictions should follow a confirmed diagnosis and current regional guidance.

sources.label: UC IPM: Karnal Bunt of Wheat
Plant Health Australia: Diagnostic protocol for Karnal bunt

identification: Look for oval to elliptic leaves, generally no more than about 3 centimeters long, with edges that may be wavy or nearly smooth. Glandular and other hairs cover the plant, and minute flowers cluster in the leaf axils. It closely resembles Dysphania pumilio in general appearance. The more useful distinction lies in the five flower-covering segments, which have a pronounced ridge or keel with coarse hairs. Mature seeds are very small and stand vertically within the fruit; magnification is needed for a dependable comparison.
actions: Photograph the whole plant, leaf edges, and close views of mature flower clusters before assigning a species name. A local herbarium or flora specialist can help with the tiny fruit characters. In a river corridor or conservation area, leave the plant undisturbed while checking local significance rather than assuming that a goosefoot-like herb needs removal. If it is a confirmed unwanted volunteer in your own cultivated bed, remove it before seed dispersal. Do not infer culinary or medicinal use from the name wormseed or from other Dysphania species.

identification: Look for reddish, smooth stems with alternate leaves on long stalks. Each leaf has several rounded or pointed lobes, giving it a miniature ivy-leaf outline. The flowers sit individually where leaves meet the stem. They have two lips, purple markings and two yellow swellings in the throat. Ground ivy can make similar trailing patches, but its leaf arrangement and flowers differ. A photograph showing both the leaf attachment and the front and side of a flower is much more useful than a distant view of the whole mat.
actions: On a garden wall, first decide whether the plant is wanted and whether the masonry needs attention. Remove unwanted seedlings before they mature seed, and collect trailing stems that have rooted into nearby beds. Avoid pulling vegetation forcefully from fragile mortar. Ask a building or garden professional about established growth on old masonry, and check nearby joints again for seedlings.

identification: A flowering specimen is more useful than a handful of mown blades. Look for soft green leaves, an open branched flower cluster and small spikelets that can appear green or purple. The leaf tip is blunt and curved, and the short membrane where blade meets sheath is another useful feature. In the subspecies pratensis, many blades are flat and relatively soft, sometimes mixed with narrower folded blades. Closely related forms overlap, so those features support a careful examination rather than a certain identification from a lawn photograph.
actions: Record whether the grass is planted turf, pasture or a patch beyond cultivation. Photograph an intact flowering stem, its leaf collar and the base of the plant. For a subspecies record, ask a herbarium or extension botanist to examine mature material. Where an unwanted patch borders a natural area, seek a site-specific grass-management plan before disturbing it; underground growth makes a single mowing a poor measure of whether the patch is gone.

sources.label: Soreng and Peterson: Revision of Poa in Mexico
Flora of New Zealand: Poa pratensis

identification: Leaves are oval to somewhat elongated and glossy, with a familiar citrus appearance. Look for thorns on the branches and small, rounded fruit with a relatively thin rind and numerous seeds. These features help distinguish Key lime from the larger, usually less seedy Persian or Tahiti lime, although a label or nursery history can still be useful. Photograph the fruit, leaves and a young branch together. Fruit color alone is unreliable because both maturity and growing conditions affect its appearance.
actions: Choose a sunny site with good drainage, or a movable container where winters are cold. Keep lawn equipment away from the trunk and avoid keeping the root zone constantly wet. Place mulch clear of the trunk rather than piling it against the bark. Prune lightly for shape or dead wood, and inspect unusual leaf or fruit symptoms with local citrus guidance before deciding on treatment.

sources.label: UF/IFAS: Key Lime Growing in the Florida Home Landscape

identification: Examine a stem before touching the fruit. Leaves grow in opposite pairs, often with one noticeably larger than the other. The leaves are broad and rounded to oval, while the trailing stems may be reddish and hairy. Small pale flowers cluster at the leaf joints. As the flower parts harden, those clusters become prickly. Several low weeds have opposite leaves, but this combination of uneven pairs, rooting stems and sharp clusters along the stem is particularly helpful. Include a close view of both young flowers and mature burrs.
actions: Keep people and pets away from dense burr patches while arranging removal. Brush seeds from footwear and equipment before leaving the site, and collect the debris there. Work on small plants before burrs mature, taking care to remove rooted stems as well as the central plant. Do not scatter chopped fragments with mowing or cultivation. Revisit the patch because both surviving plant parts and seed can restart growth.

identification: Look for pale to bright green blades, slightly hairy stems and leaves, and a conspicuous fringe of hairs around the leaf collar. The leaf tips are pointed. St. Augustinegrass can have a similar coarse, creeping appearance, but its blades have rounded tips and its surfaces are generally smoother. Kikuyugrass may show delicate white flower filaments above the foliage rather than a familiar exposed seedhead. Photograph a runner with several joints, a leaf tip and the collar. A close view of those parts is especially useful in a closely mown lawn.
actions: Keep runners and soil containing them out of clean beds. Clean cultivation tools and mowing equipment after working through a patch, and collect loose fragments rather than spreading them elsewhere. Maintain neighboring vegetation in good condition and inspect the advancing edge. Established infestations need repeated attention: mowing does not remove underground reserves, and chopped stem sections can root again. Ask local extension staff for a plan suited to the existing turf and site.

identification: The flowers hang in dense, slender clusters near the tops of branching stems. Broad, pointed leaves often have a heart-shaped base and soft hairs. Like other smartweeds, the plant has a sheath around each stem joint; here the sheath can end in a conspicuous leafy collar. Height and the drooping pink clusters help separate it from smaller smartweeds, but photograph the leaf base and stem sheath too. Those details are valuable when a young plant has not yet produced its characteristic flowers.
actions: Before growing it, check whether it is recommended in your area and allow enough room for its mature size. Remove unwanted seedlings while they are small, and cut fading flower clusters before seed is released if you want to limit volunteers. Keep seed-bearing material out of loose garden-waste piles near streams or open ground. Where plants have appeared beyond cultivation, record the patch and ask local extension staff whether follow-up removal is appropriate.

sources.label: Kew, Flora of Iraq: Persicaria orientalis

identification: Look for narrow blades, a ring of conspicuous hairs around the stem joints and several fingerlike flowering branches held close together near the top. The individual spikelets are small, and some carry a fine awn. University of Arizona guidance compares it with yellow bluestem, Bothriochloa ischaemum, but notes that Kleberg's bluestem lacks the translucent grooves in the flower-branch segments and stalks. That is a hand-lens character, not something a distant photograph can establish. Include the stem joints, the base of the flowering branches and a sharp close-up of the spikelets.
actions: If the grass is unexpected in a pasture or restoration, mark the patch and ask a grass specialist to confirm it before choosing control. Save photographs and the flowering date, and note whether stems root along the ground. Avoid moving seed-bearing hay or contaminated soil from a suspect patch to a new site. For a confirmed unwanted population, plan follow-up around both seed production and surviving perennial plants instead of relying on a single cut.

sources.label: University of Arizona Herbarium: Grass Identification Workshop 2024, M. Bauer
Botanical Survey of India: Flora of Yavatmal District

identification: Leaves are flat and can be either hairy or nearly hairless. The branched flower cluster carries small green spikelets that may be tinged purple. A mature fertile floret has a hard, smooth, shiny covering. VicFlora notes that Panicum schinzii can look very similar in its flowers, but is annual and has rough rather than smooth leaf margins. Other panic grasses require comparison of the lower glume and the spikelet shape. Photograph the whole plant, its base, a leaf collar and a mature seedhead against a plain background.
actions: Keep a record of whether the patch was deliberately sown and whether it is expanding beyond that area. If identity matters for pasture use or restoration, have mature material examined by extension staff or a herbarium. Do not transfer an unidentified grass in hay, seed mixtures or soil to another property. Where removal is appropriate, inspect the perennial base after cutting and plan repeat checks; a tidy surface does not establish that the living plant has been removed.

identification: Look for a long, angular head, a very long tail and expanded toe pads used for climbing. The body is usually green but can become dull brownish gray. A pale yellow or white stripe runs below the eye and over the shoulder, and males can extend a pale pink throat fan. Color alone is not enough to separate anoles, especially juveniles. Photograph the head in profile, shoulder markings and whole body from a comfortable distance, with a familiar object nearby for scale if one is already present.
actions: Observe rather than handle a wild lizard; knight anoles have strong jaws and can defend themselves. Record the location and whether more than one animal is present, then share an unusual sighting with the local wildlife agency. Keep captive reptiles securely contained and arrange responsible rehoming if needed. Do not release a pet or move a wild animal to a different neighborhood, since that can extend an introduced population.

sources.label: Meshaka: Knight Anole in Southern Florida

identification: The leaves are finely divided, and stiff hairs cover the stems and foliage. Small white to pinkish flowers form compact clusters opposite the leaves. Later, the fruits become rough or bristly. Examine how the clusters attach to the stem: the very short supporting stalks are useful, although exact measurements and fruit characters need comparison with a regional flora. Similar hedgeparsleys can be difficult to separate, and recent treatments do not always draw species boundaries identically. Take close photographs of mature fruit as well as leaves and the whole plant.
actions: Confirm the plant before collecting it, especially because many carrot-family plants share divided leaves. Brush burrs from clothing, pets and tools before leaving an affected area. If a small patch is unwanted, remove the annual plants before the fruit matures and contain any fruit already present. Recheck the same ground in the following growing season. Ask a local botanist to resolve uncertain fruit characters rather than assigning the species from its parsley-like leaves alone.

sources.label: University of the Balearic Islands: Torilis nodosa

identification: Look for a deep body, a long dorsal fin and two pairs of whiskerlike barbels around the upper jaw. Color is highly variable and should not be treated as a species test. Large goldfish can resemble koi at a glance, but the barbels are an important distinction to photograph. Separating wild carp lineages is more difficult and may require scale counts, fin-ray counts or specialist examination. A clear side view and a close photograph of the mouth are more informative than an overhead view of the color pattern alone.
actions: Keep koi in a secure pond that cannot release fish during overflow or flooding. Arrange rehoming through an experienced keeper or pond specialist if you can no longer care for them. Never release pet fish into a stream, lake or drainage pond. Report an unusual wild sighting to the local fisheries agency with the waterbody, date and photographs, and ask for advice before attempting to catch or transport it.

identification: Look closely for tiny leaves arranged in distinct rows along flattened-looking branches. The plant produces spores rather than flowers or seeds. Upright spore-bearing tips may resemble miniature cones, while long fine roots anchor the creeping stems. Mosses can make a similar green carpet, and other Selaginella species need careful comparison. Photograph a complete branch against a contrasting surface, its leaf arrangement and any spore cones. A broad photograph of a green mat usually cannot show the features needed for a confident identification.
actions: Keep container plants and discarded potting mix away from streambanks and woodland edges. Do not tip terrarium contents into the garden or a natural area. In a confirmed unwanted patch, collect loose stems and attached soil carefully, because fragments can grow again. Clean footwear and tools before moving to another damp site. Seek local advice for established carpets among native groundcover, and revisit treated areas for small surviving pieces and new growth.

identification: Leaves have three broad leaflets, often lobed, with hairs especially noticeable beneath. Young stems are hairy and older bases become woody. Purple pea-shaped flowers grow in elongated clusters, followed by flattened, hairy pods. A vine with three leaflets is not automatically kudzu: the flowers, stem hairs and pods provide important supporting evidence. Separating the varieties requires closer study of the flower parts and pods. Photograph mature leaves from above and below, the stem, flowers and fruit whenever they are available.
actions: Treat an unfamiliar, vigorous vine as an identification task before deciding how to remove it. Record the extent of the patch and whether it is climbing trees or spreading along the ground. Avoid sharing rooted pieces or moving cut vines into nearby vegetation. Ask local extension or invasive-plant staff to confirm the plant and recommend a sustained plan for a confirmed unwanted infestation. Large storage roots and extensive growth mean that cutting visible stems once does not demonstrate successful removal.

identification: Each leaf has three broad leaflets. Some leaflets are nearly unlobed while others have deep lobes, so leaf shape can vary on the same vine. Young stems and leaf margins are hairy. Mature plants may produce upright clusters of purple pea-shaped flowers and flattened pods covered with coarse hairs. Other vines also have three leaflets, so include the hairy stems, leaf undersides and any flowers or pods in an identification record. The long runners and rooted joints help explain how a patch is expanding.
actions: Map the outer edge of a suspected patch and seek confirmation before tackling a large infestation. Prevent vines from being carried into clean ground with soil or garden waste. Small, newly established plants are easier to assess than a tangled canopy, but all rooted points need attention. Ask local invasive-plant staff for a plan that includes repeated follow-up and protection of nearby trees. Report a new occurrence where local programs request early detection.

sources.label: US Forest Service FEIS: kudzu (Pueraria montana var. lobata)

identification: Adults are compact and rounded, roughly 3/16 to 1/4 inch long, with a broader rear than front. They have a mottled greenish-brown surface and reddish eyes. Their outline can suggest a small beetle, but they belong to the true bugs. Young stages and eggs are harder to recognize from a distant image. Photograph the upper surface and side of an adult, and note the plant on which it was feeding. Other small stink bugs should be compared before assigning a name.
actions: Check window screens, door sweeps and gaps before seasonal gatherings begin. Avoid crushing insects against surfaces, and use a contained collection method for individuals that enter indoors. In a soybean field, contact extension staff for local scouting guidance rather than treating insects found on a nearby wall. Record both adults and young stages on the crop. Do not move kudzu bugs to another patch as an improvised biological control.

sources.label: UGA: Management of Pest Insects In and Around the Home

identification: Mature females are almost spherical and about 3-5 mm across. Before producing eggs they can briefly show yellow or orange coloring with dark marks, then become dark brown. Young scales are flatter and may gather along veins on the undersides of leaves. Several soft scales look similar from above. An internal shelf around the attachment surface and microscopic characters help distinguish Kuno scale, so a specialist may need a specimen. Photograph the twig and leaf undersides, and include the host plant and date.
actions: Inspect sticky plants for living scales before assuming sooty mold itself is the main problem. Watch for ants tending the colony and seek advice on reducing their access while protecting beneficial insects. Keep the tree appropriately watered and avoid unnecessary broad treatments that disrupt natural enemies. If the infestation is increasing or twigs are declining, ask extension staff to confirm the scale and identify the vulnerable stage before choosing a response.

identification: Look for small round entrance holes on trunks or branches, sometimes accompanied by staining, sap or boring material. The appearance varies with the host, and similar symptoms can have other causes. Adult beetles are only a few millimeters long. Kuroshio and polyphagous shot hole borers are extremely difficult to separate visually, so a phone photograph of a beetle or hole cannot establish which is present. Photograph the whole affected branch, close details of holes and any surrounding staining, and record the tree species.
actions: Keep suspect firewood and cut branches at the site until a local tree-health or agricultural authority advises how to handle them. Moving infested wood can carry beetles and their fungi to new trees. Use locally sourced firewood and inspect valued trees for fresh attacks. Report a suspected new infestation promptly, especially beyond a known affected area. A trained arborist or diagnostic laboratory can help confirm the cause and plan safe management of damaged limbs.

sources.label: UF/IFAS EDIS: Invasive Shot Hole Borers Euwallacea fornicatus, E. kuroshio, and E. perbrevis

identification: A declining branch, stained wood or small beetle holes can suggest that the complex needs investigation, but none identifies this fungus by itself. Related Fusarium species and other causes of tree decline can produce overlapping signs. The species was distinguished through laboratory comparisons of fungal structures and several DNA regions. Later research developed molecular diagnostic tools specifically to improve identification. Photograph symptoms and the whole tree for context, but expect a diagnostic laboratory to determine whether F. kuroshium is actually present.
actions: Record the host tree, date and location, and contact local extension or a plant diagnostic service before cutting samples. Follow its instructions for collecting and packaging affected wood. Keep suspect branches and firewood on site while the cause is assessed, since wood can also carry the beetle vector. Where limbs are dying, have an arborist assess immediate tree safety. Management should address the tree and beetle-fungus complex together, rather than assuming a household fungicide will solve the problem.

sources.label: Na et al.: Two Novel Fungal Symbionts
Diagnostic system based on ascomycete pan-genome analysis

identification: There is no dependable garden-level visual test for this species. A tree may have beetle holes, stained tissues or dieback, but those signs overlap with other fungal partners and other tree problems. Researchers separated Graphium kuroshium from related fungi using cultured material, microscopic features and multiple DNA regions. Graphium euwallaceae is a close comparison, so the shared beetle association is not enough to choose between names. Photographs can document the tree's condition, while a laboratory result is needed for the fungal identity. A newer experimental assay distinguishes the fungal partners after culture; its results should not be interpreted as reliable direct testing of untreated wood.
actions: If this fungus is suspected, record the tree species, symptoms and location and ask a plant diagnostic laboratory what material it needs. Leave suspect wood on site until sampling and disposal advice is available. Do not send loose branches through ordinary garden-waste routes without checking local guidance for the beetle complex. An arborist can assess damaged limbs while the diagnosis is pending. Keep the fungal name provisional until the laboratory can support it.

sources.label: Na et al.: Two Novel Fungal Symbionts
2020 multiplex qPCR for shothole-borer fungal symbionts

identification: Look for a translucent green blade with irregular holes, wavy edges and a relatively thick, wrinkled base near its attachment point. Older blades can split into strips. Holes alone are not conclusive, because wear and grazing can also perforate seaweed. Closely related Ulva species overlap in appearance, and microscopic cell features or DNA examination may be needed. Photograph the attached whole blade, its base and its margins, with a scale. A washed-up fragment without its base often leaves the identification uncertain.
actions: Record the shore, date, tidal position and whether the seaweed was attached or drifting. Send photographs of an unusual population to a local marine recording program or herbarium rather than assuming a green accumulation belongs to this species. Clean seaweed from boats and equipment before moving between sites, following local disposal guidance. Do not transplant attached material or discard aquarium seaweed into coastal water. Large accumulations need local assessment of species and conditions before a management response is chosen.

sources.label: Hanyuda and Kawai: Genetic examination of Ulva australis type

identification: Look at the underside of a mature frond. In ladder brake, the spore-bearing structures form lines along the leaflet edges. Swamp fern, Blechnum serrulatum, can look similar, but its spore lines lie nearer the leaflet midrib. Ladder brake's leaflets are simple rather than deeply divided into smaller segments, another useful feature when comparing other Pteris species. Photograph an entire frond, a leaflet underside and the base of the plant. An unfertile young frond may not show enough detail to settle the name.
actions: If the fern is unwanted, identify it while the fronds are intact and remove small plants carefully before more spores are released. Avoid forcing roots from fragile mortar or damaging a historic wall. For established plants, plan follow-up rather than assuming removal of the fronds has removed the growing base. Ask a local botanist about uncertain ferns and local management priorities, especially where several similar species occur together.

identification: Leaves alternate along the stem and are narrow oval to lance-shaped. The stem joints are swollen and often reddish. At each leaf attachment, look for the thin sheath that wraps around the stem; its upper edge has conspicuous bristly hairs. Flower clusters are generally upright and pink to purplish. Pale smartweed, Persicaria lapathifolia, can look similar, but its sheaths lack the same bristly fringe and its clusters are often paler or nodding. Photograph the sheath closely, as well as flowers and leaves, rather than relying only on the thumb-shaped blotch.
actions: In a garden bed, remove unwanted seedlings before they flower and set seed, taking care to distinguish them from wanted plants nearby. Record whether a larger patch occupies damp disturbed soil, crop rows or a water margin. Keep seed-bearing plants out of soil or waste moved to a clean area. For extensive crop infestations, ask extension staff for a plan matched to the crop and growth stage instead of applying a treatment based only on the common name.

identification: Look for rings of six to eight narrow leaves on the lower stems, with fewer leaves around the upper flowering branches. The leaves are only a few millimeters long and may end in a small bristle. Minute yellowish flowers can have a reddish tint. Mature fruits are tiny paired structures with a finely bumpy surface, rather than the conspicuous hooked burrs of some other bedstraws. A hand lens is useful. Photograph lower leaf whorls, branching flower stalks and mature fruit; a distant view is unlikely to separate this species from related annual bedstraws.
actions: Confirm a suspected plant before clearing a patch, since other bedstraws may be part of the local vegetation. If removal is appropriate, work before the small fruits disperse and keep collected material together. Note the size of the patch and nearby disturbance, then revisit during the next growing season. For a record outside a familiar range, submit clear close-ups or ask a herbarium how to prepare a specimen.

identification: Leaves alternate along the stem and vary from broad, roughly triangular shapes to narrower leaves higher up. Their edges may be irregularly toothed or nearly smooth. The mealy coating and generally hairless, grooved stems help distinguish it from many pigweeds, although related goosefoots still require close comparison. Stems may carry reddish or green stripes. Flowers are small and lack showy petals, appearing in clusters at leaf joints and branch tips. Photograph young leaves from both sides and an older flowering branch to show the change in shape.
actions: Pull or hoe unwanted seedlings while they are small, before roots and seed clusters develop. Check regularly around crop rows and recently moved soil, where new seedlings may continue to appear. Contain mature seed-bearing plants instead of shaking them across a bed. Mulch or replant bare ground where appropriate to reduce repeated disturbance. Ask extension staff about persistent crop problems, and do not use an uncertain identification as a reason to taste or gather the plant.

identification: Each leaf is divided into three relatively narrow leaflets. The upper surfaces are nearly hairless, while the undersides may have sparse hairs. Flowers are about 8-10 mm long, yellow with darker purplish-brown veins or markings. The pods are roughly 2-3.5 cm long and become black when mature. North Carolina's flora distinguishes this species from Crotalaria ochroleuca partly by its much smaller flowers. Photograph a complete leaf, an individual flower beside a scale and mature pods rather than relying on yellow color alone.
actions: Have an unfamiliar rattlebox confirmed before using land containing it for collected forage or moving seed-bearing material elsewhere. In a small unwanted patch, remove plants before the pods mature and gather any dark pods already present. Keep contaminated soil and cut plants out of clean garden or restoration areas. Record the site and revisit after soil disturbance. For a larger agricultural patch, ask extension staff for a species-specific plan rather than treating all rattleboxes as interchangeable.

identification: Plants commonly called lantana have opposite toothed leaves, dense rounded clusters of small tubular flowers and fleshy fruits that darken as they ripen. Flower clusters may include several colors, and color changes alone do not identify a species or cultivar. Queensland guidance describes square stems with small backward-curving prickles and a heavily branched, sometimes scrambling habit. Other lantanas and garden hybrids can share much of this appearance. Photograph leaves, stems, flower clusters and fruit together, and keep any nursery label or planting history with the record.
actions: Before planting or moving a lantana, check local recommendations for the exact species or cultivar. Do not assume that a colorful nursery selection is harmless outside cultivation or that every lantana should be removed. For a shrub spreading into nearby vegetation, seek local identification and management advice. Contain fruit-bearing cuttings and avoid dumping garden waste on open ground. Large tangled shrubs may need staged work and follow-up rather than a single trim.

identification: Leaves are oval to somewhat broader toward the tip, with wavy or finely toothed margins. Their undersides are gray and hairy, and young twigs are often densely hairy as well. Catkins appear before or around leaf emergence, with male and female flowers on separate plants. Goat willow, Salix caprea, has often been confused with this species, and willows can be difficult to identify from one leaf. Photograph mature leaves on both sides, young twigs, buds and catkins, and include the plant's overall shape and habitat.
actions: Ask a willow specialist or local herbarium to confirm an unfamiliar wetland shrub before removal. Avoid planting cuttings beside natural waterways or moving pruned branches where they could establish. A confirmed unwanted stand needs a plan that accounts for regrowth, seedlings and the stability of the bank. Do not clear a large waterside area at once without suitable advice. Mark the original extent and revisit after management to look for new shoots and seedlings.

identification: Look for thick creeping stems, broad leaf blades and conspicuously inflated sheaths. At the junction of blade and sheath, the membranous ligule can be unusually long. Male and female flowers occur in separate clusters on the same plant: the male cluster is open and terminal, while female clusters are denser and arise from leaf axils. This arrangement is more useful than leaf width alone. Photograph both kinds of flower cluster if present, along with the swollen sheath and a stem joint. Other watergrasses and floating grasses can overlap in general appearance.
actions: Report an unfamiliar expanding mat to the local aquatic-plant program with the location, approximate area and photographs. Clean boats, trailers and other equipment before leaving the waterbody, collecting attached plant pieces for appropriate disposal. Avoid chopping or dragging a mat through open water because fragments can contribute to spread. Large infestations require a coordinated aquatic-management plan that protects nearby vegetation and access. Follow the site's instructions before collecting a specimen or attempting removal.

sources.label: FWS: Tropical American Watergrass risk summary

identification: Leaves grow in groups around the stem, and yellow flowers cluster in the upper leaf axils. The flowers may have small reddish marks near their centers. To distinguish it from yellow loosestrife, Lysimachia vulgaris, examine the flower arrangement and the green sepals behind the petals: L. vulgaris has a more terminal branched cluster and darker sepal margins. Other garden Lysimachia can also resemble it. Photograph a whole flowering stem, a leaf whorl and the back of a flower rather than relying only on its yellow color.
actions: Choose a contained garden position only where local guidance supports growing it, and inspect the edges of an existing clump regularly. When reducing an unwanted colony, collect underground rhizomes as well as the upright shoots. Do not dump divisions or soil containing roots along a hedge, ditch or woodland edge. Revisit the area for shoots emerging from missed pieces. If a plant outside cultivation is uncertain, ask a botanist to check its flower and sepal characters before management.

identification: Leaves can change shape as the plant develops: early floating growth may have rounded leaves, while later shoots carry narrower, pointed blades. Roots can develop at stem joints. Similar Ludwigia species share yellow flowers and overlapping leaf forms, and water conditions can alter their appearance. Specialists may need mature flowers, fruits and sometimes DNA evidence to separate them. Photograph floating and upright growth, a flower face, its underside and any fruits. Record the water depth and whether the patch is attached to the bank.
actions: Never introduce creeping water primrose to open water or discard pond plants into a drainage channel. Clean fragments from boats and equipment before moving to another site. Report a newly noticed mat to the local aquatic-weed program, especially if it is expanding. Avoid mowing or fragmenting the stand in the water. Ask the program to confirm the species and plan any removal, since a large mat can be difficult to handle without spreading pieces.

sources.label: SFWMD: 2024 South Florida Environmental Report chapter 7

identification: Look for long-stalked leaves that are broadly oval to diamond shaped, sometimes with gently wavy margins. Flower clusters occupy the stem ends and upper leaf joints. As they mature, the fruits project beyond the surrounding flower parts and enclose a much smaller, shiny seed. A spreading habit alone is not enough: several amaranths can become flattened by trampling. Photograph the stem base, a whole leafy branch, and mature clusters with a ruler. A local flora or botanist can check the fruit characters.
actions: In a garden where removal is wanted, work on a small patch before mature fruits are scattered and lift the persistent base along with the shoots. Simply clipping the visible stems may leave the plant in place. Keep fruiting material contained, then revisit the same cracks or bed edges for surviving growth and seedlings. Outside managed ground, confirm the identification and local significance before disturbing vegetation. Record whether the plant is rooted in a pavement joint, cultivated bed, or other disturbed setting; that context helps make a useful observation.

identification: Follow one frond from its shiny, dark stalk to the tip. The blade is divided once, with broad, mostly opposite leaflets and a terminal leaflet. The leaflets are roughly triangular to oval, with relatively symmetrical bases, and their surfaces and main axes are hairless. On fertile fronds, long spore-bearing lines run along the leaflet margins, interrupted near the sterile tip. Other maidenhairs can share dark stalks or pink new growth, so include both mature and young fronds and a clear underside photograph when seeking confirmation.
actions: Leave an unidentified wild fern rooted while you document it, especially in forest or streamside vegetation where similar species may belong. For a cultivated plant, retain the nursery name and photograph the whole pot as well as the leaflet details. Keep unwanted plants and potting material out of streams and natural vegetation. If an apparently escaped population is found, record its extent and setting and ask a local herbarium or land manager to confirm its identity before deciding whether any removal is appropriate.

identification: Look for shallow, usually five-lobed leaves with rounded teeth between the lobes and hairs on the leaves and stalks. The leaf stalk joins at the leaf base rather than at the center of a little umbrella. A useful distinction from Bowlesia is hair structure: this Hydrocotyle has simple hairs, whereas Bowlesia has star-shaped hairs. A hand lens or sharply focused macro photograph is helpful. Capture the creeping stem, the upper end of a leaf stalk, both leaf surfaces, and any tiny flowers or fruits.
actions: Start by mapping the patch and recording whether it is in turf, a nursery pot, or damp disturbed soil. Avoid transferring soil or plant fragments from an uncertain patch to other beds while identification is pending. In a small managed area, any desired removal should include the connected creeping stems rather than just the leaves, followed by checks for surviving growth. If the observation could be a new local record, send detailed photographs to a herbarium before clearing the whole patch, since a useful specimen may be requested.

sources.label: Thornhill and Krings: Hydrocotyle bowlesioides in Louisiana
New Zealand Plant Conservation Network: Trilepidea July 2022

identification: Adults are small, roughly 3.5 to 5 millimeters long, and dark brown to black. Their compact shape is shared with many bark beetles, making a phone photograph alone an uncertain route to identification. Look inside a naturally broken shoot for tunneling and photograph the entrance, damaged tip, and whole tree. Specialists use fine antennal and body characters to separate this species from related Tomicus beetles and other bark beetles. Keep the pine's identity, location, and date with any photographs or submitted specimen.
actions: If unusual shoot damage is appearing across several pines, contact a forestry or extension service before moving cut branches, logs, or nursery trees elsewhere. Infested pine material can carry the beetle over much greater distances than an individual normally travels. Inspect nearby stored pine wood and note when trees were cut or became stressed. Leave decisions about removing standing trees to an arborist or forester; shoot damage by itself does not establish a severe trunk infestation or justify felling an otherwise healthy tree.

sources.label: Maine Forest Service: Pine Shoot Beetle

identification: Adults are about 3 to 4.5 millimeters long, with a dark reddish-brown body and brown to reddish wing covers. The surface is relatively smooth and shiny. Identification relies on details of the face and underside that distinguish Scolytus species, so round holes in bark are not enough to assign a name. Photograph the whole affected tree, its leaves or fruit for host identification, and the damaged branch. A close, well-lit beetle photograph is useful, but a specialist may still need a specimen.
actions: Have an arborist or local plant-health service assess declining fruit trees and the stresses affecting them. Note recent drought, physical injury, or dying branches without assuming any one factor caused the attack. Avoid carrying suspect branches or firewood to another orchard or garden while the beetle is being identified. If dead material is removed, ask about appropriate local disposal and keep a record of where it came from. Do not strip healthy bark to look for galleries; that creates another wound on an already vulnerable tree.

sources.label: Smith and Cognato: A taxonomic monograph of Nearctic Scolytus

identification: Look for toothed leaves arranged alternately along ridged, hairy stems. The leaves often broaden toward their tips and can show small gland dots. Each mauve or purple head sits among a conspicuous set of leafy outer bracts, with smaller inner bracts surrounding the florets. Those green, leaflike bracts are useful when comparing it with other purple-flowered members of the daisy family. Photograph a whole stem, the upper and lower leaf surfaces, and a flower head from both above and below.
actions: If it is being grown deliberately, keep track of seedlings beyond the planted area and avoid dumping spent flowering material into adjoining land. Where an unwanted garden patch is small, remove it before mature seed is scattered and check later for new plants. The woody base may need more attention than the soft upper shoots. For a patch in pasture or natural vegetation, document its size and location and seek local identification and management advice before broad clearing. Nearby desirable plants may be easy to overlook beneath the branching growth.

sources.label: NParks Flora and Fauna Web: Centratherum punctatum

identification: Female covers are usually round, convex, and roughly 1 to 2 millimeters across, often grayish white with an off-center yellowish or brown patch from earlier growth stages. On stems they may appear browner. Several armored scales look very similar, especially greedy scale, and reliable separation can require microscope examination of the insect beneath the cover. Photograph the colony in place, the host plant, and any affected fruit or foliage. Include a size reference; a magnified white bump without context is difficult to interpret.
actions: Inspect adjacent leaves and branches before deciding how extensive the infestation is. A local extension service can help distinguish live scales from empty covers and identify the species if management depends on that distinction. Preserve natural enemies by avoiding unnecessary broad insecticide use, and address ants or dusty conditions where these interfere with biological control. For valuable plants or fruit crops, ask for advice tailored to that host and location. Do not move heavily infested cuttings to other gardens while you are working out what is present.

sources.label: UC IPM: Greedy Scale and Latania Scale

identification: Look for yellow flower centers surrounded by slender pale rays that can become pink as the heads age. Lower leaves are commonly divided into three lobes or bear a few distinct teeth, while upper leaves are narrower and often unlobed. The heads sit on slender stalks above a branching, spreading plant. Other small daisies can share the flower colors, so include the lower leaves and stem arrangement in photographs. Mature heads produce tiny fruits with a tuft of fine hairs, another useful detail for a botanical identification.
actions: Keep an eye on nearby cracks, drains, and bed edges if you grow it ornamentally. Where seedlings are unwanted, remove small plants before they mature, taking care around masonry and any neighboring vegetation. Established plants may have persistent underground growth, so a single trim should not be treated as complete removal. Contain flowering and fruiting waste rather than tipping it onto nearby land. If a colony appears away from gardens, record its extent and habitat and ask a local botanist or land manager whether it is a concern in that setting.

sources.label: Indian Institute of Science: Erigeron karvinskianus

identification: Look for hairless, shiny dark-green leaves with paler undersides and fine, closely spaced glandular teeth. Small glands also occur near the top of the leaf stalk. Catkins appear with the leaves, and male flowers usually have around five stamens, sometimes more. These details help separate it from other willows, but hybrids can combine their parents' features. Photograph both leaf surfaces, the stalk glands, a leafy twig, and catkins if available. Include the planting history when known, since cultivated willows can be especially difficult to name.
actions: Treat an uncertain tree as a willow awaiting confirmation rather than removing it on the basis of a broadleaf appearance. A herbarium or willow specialist can advise whether a specimen is needed and which seasonal features matter. On streambanks, consult the land manager before cutting or digging because the work can disturb the bank and adjacent vegetation. Keep cut branches out of waterways and avoid distributing cuttings from an uncertain planting. For a confirmed tree, management should follow its local ecological role and condition.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Salix pentandra
InfoFlora and Flora Helvetica: Salix pentandra

identification: Watch for wilting foliage that changes from green to olive or reddish brown, sometimes beginning in part of the crown. Dead leaves may remain on evergreen hosts. Small beetle entrance holes or delicate tubes of boring dust can accompany the decline, but neither proves laurel wilt. Dark staining in the sapwood is another clue that a trained diagnostician may examine. Photograph the whole crown, leaves, trunk symptoms, and host features. A plant disease clinic may need appropriately collected wood to confirm the cause.
actions: If a laurel-family tree develops unexplained rapid wilt, contact an extension office, forestry service, or plant disease clinic, particularly where the disease has not been confirmed before. Ask how to collect and package a sample before cutting into the tree. Avoid moving suspect firewood, logs, or plants to other locations, since beetles can travel in infested material. Obtain local advice on removal and disposal of confirmed trees, and check nearby susceptible hosts. Similar-looking decline has other causes, so a photograph alone should not trigger a definitive diagnosis.

sources.label: NC State Extension: Laurel Wilt Disease
Virginia Department of Forestry: Laurel Wilt

identification: Look for opposite leaves that broaden toward the tip, with a smooth surface and a series of rounded teeth along the edge. Flower clusters carry downward-facing tubes in muted reddish, pink, or purple tones. Variegated garden forms have cream margins that may be tinged pink, but that coloring is not a requirement for the species. Other kalanchoes have fleshy leaves and hanging flowers, so photograph the entire plant, a leaf pair, the leaf margin, and a flower cluster rather than relying on color alone.
actions: For a plant you want to keep, use a container with freely draining soil and avoid keeping the root zone constantly wet. Because stems are used for propagation, collect unwanted cuttings rather than leaving them on surrounding soil or tipping them into natural vegetation. Check the ground around outdoor pots for established fragments or seedlings. If plants appear well beyond cultivation, record the setting and extent and ask a local botanist to verify them before deciding on removal. Retain the cultivar label when available, since ornamental forms can complicate identification.

identification: Look for rounded to kidney-shaped leaves with shallow lobes and scalloped edges. The stalk attaches at the notch or base, not in the center of the blade as in some larger pennyworts. Tiny flowers gather in small, headlike groups, followed by minute ribbed fruits. Do not identify it from a round leaf alone: several Hydrocotyle species have similar outlines. Photograph the attachment point, leaf hairs, creeping stem, and any fruit, using a ruler to show how small the plant is.
actions: In a lawn or bed, first decide whether the patch is actually interfering with the intended planting. If removal is wanted, follow the connected stems through the vegetation and check for remaining rooted portions afterward. Avoid shifting infested soil or pot contents into another bed. A patch in a wet natural area deserves a local botanical check before disturbance, since pennywort names and native status vary by region. Note moisture conditions, shade, and the patch's extent when requesting help; these observations are useful alongside the close-up photographs.

sources.label: Smithsonian Flora of the Hawaiian Islands: Hydrocotyle sibthorpioides

identification: Look beneath the flowers for a compact rosette of spoon-shaped leaves. The flower stalks are leafless, which helps distinguish lawn daisy from taller daisies with leaves distributed along an upright stem. Garden cultivars can have pink or red flowers and extra rows of rays, so flower fullness is variable. For an uncertain plant, photograph the rosette and a complete flowering stalk together. A close-up of the flower alone can hide the growth pattern that makes this species recognizable.
actions: If the daisies suit the way you use the lawn, leaving them in place is a reasonable choice. Where a small patch is unwanted, lift the whole rosette with its rooted base and revisit the spot for surviving plants or seedlings. Mowing off flower heads alone does not remove the low-growing perennial. Keep soil disturbance modest and repair bare patches according to the needs of the surrounding turf. In a garden bed, check for seedlings outside the planted group rather than assuming ornamental varieties will stay exactly where they were placed.

sources.label: Oregon State University: Broadleaf Weeds in Lawns
NC State Extension Gardener: Bellis perennis

identification: Look for leaves only a few millimeters wide and a clear gap between the lower female spike and the longer male section above it. Flora Helvetica describes plants commonly around 60 to 120 centimeters tall, with a female spike usually about 3 to 5 centimeters long, although size varies. The leaves are well developed and may extend beyond the flowers, helping distinguish it from the smaller Typha minima. Photograph a whole flowering shoot, leaf width against a ruler, and both spike sections while the male part is still visible.
actions: In a garden pond, monitor how far the underground growth is spreading and keep removed divisions and old plant material out of nearby ditches or wetlands. Horticultural guidance warns that the roots can spread rapidly in shallow water and may damage pond liners, so placement deserves thought. An unexpected wild patch should be identified before any digging or cutting begins. Wetland work can disturb other vegetation and the water's edge; ask the land manager or local conservation staff what action is appropriate for a confirmed population.

sources.label: InfoFlora and Flora Helvetica: Typha laxmannii

identification: Leaf blight often begins as water-soaked injury near a leaf tip or margin, spreading toward the base and becoming yellow to light brown as tissue dries. Leaf streak begins as narrower, water-soaked lines between veins that can lengthen and merge. Severe blight in young plants can produce rapid wilting known as kresek. Other rice problems can resemble these symptoms. Photograph whole plants and close views of newly developing lesions, and record the rice variety, crop stage, field location, and where symptoms first appeared. A laboratory needs to establish the bacterial identity.
actions: Contact a rice extension specialist or plant-health service when an unfamiliar outbreak appears, and follow their instructions for collecting samples. Avoid transferring suspect plants or contaminated water to unaffected production areas while the cause is being investigated. Keep field and seed-lot records so a confirmed finding can be traced. For future crops, locally suitable resistant varieties are an important option, but resistance should be matched to the disease and regional bacterial populations. Do not choose a treatment simply because a leaf is yellow or streaked.

sources.label: IRRI: Diagnosis of Common Diseases of Rice
EFSA: Pest categorisation of Xanthomonas oryzae pathovars oryzae and oryzicola

identification: Look for small, black, slightly raised or rectangular marks on the leaves, often becoming noticeable later in the crop's development. Numerous lesions can darken a leaf, and affected tips may die. The location matters: leaf smut marks occur in the foliage, unlike diseases centered on the developing grain. Photograph individual lesions close enough to show their shape, then include the whole leaf and plant. Record crop stage and whether grain symptoms are present, since a second disease may be occurring at the same time.
actions: Ask a rice extension adviser to confirm an unfamiliar pattern before considering treatment. Texas A&M and Arkansas guidance do not recommend routine fungicide control for leaf smut, so spotting alone is a poor reason to spray. Review nitrogen management with the adviser if the field has received excessive fertilizer, because Arkansas observations associate leaf smut with overfertilized rice. Keep notes on the variety, affected area, and timing, and compare subsequent crops rather than assuming every dark leaf spot has the same cause.

sources.label: Arkansas Rice Production Handbook: Management of Rice Diseases

identification: For Dysaphis crithmi, the reviewed specialist account describes wingless adults as gray to greenish gray, dusted with wax, and about 1.7 to 2.2 millimeters long. The host and feeding position are useful clues, but neither confirms the species by itself. Several aphids can occur on rock samphire, and a specialist may need microscopic characters. Photograph the entire host, the colony in its original position, and individual aphids as clearly as possible. A curled plum leaf should not be assigned to this scientific name from a common-name match.
actions: If you are trying to identify aphids on a plum tree, use a local fruit-crop identification service and keep that observation separate from rock-samphire observations. For aphids on rock samphire, record the location and whether they occupy the sheathing leaf bases, then seek specialist confirmation. Avoid choosing a control method from advice for the similarly named plum aphid. Keep the original name and source attached to the observation so a specialist can trace the identification and explain any correction.

sources.label: Blackman and Eastop: Dysaphis species accounts
UC IPM: Identifying Aphids on Plum

identification: Adults are about a third of an inch long, roughly 8 millimeters, with a mottled brown-and-white appearance. Those broad features overlap with other true bugs, so the family-level common name is not enough for a confident species identification. Take a sharp photograph from above and another from the side, with a size reference if possible. Include the antennae, legs, and body outline rather than only the wings. Record whether the insect was on living Russian thistle, on another plant, or entering a building.
actions: For insects gathering at a house, begin with identification and practical exclusion, such as checking gaps around doors and window screens. Avoid crushing individuals indoors because they can release an unpleasant smell. Send clear photographs to an extension service if the species is unfamiliar in your area. Do not move bugs or occupied plant material elsewhere, even if they are feeding on an unwanted weed. The reviewed California assessment did not establish crop or environmental damage, so their presence alone should not be treated as proof that nearby garden plants are being harmed.

sources.label: University of Idaho: Centrocoris volxemi, A Newly Introduced Idaho Insect
University of Idaho: BUL-1037 publication summary

identification: Adults are around 3 millimeters long and mottled in brown, green, and white, often with a reddish cast. Newly hatched nymphs are almost transparent and later become yellowish or orange brown. Similar grape leafhoppers differ in markings and immature coloration, and specialist keys use much finer anatomical features. Examine leaf undersides for nymphs and photograph both the insects and the feeding pattern. Keep the vine's location and variety with the record, rather than identifying the species from leaf stippling alone.
actions: Check several vines and leaves at regular intervals to see whether nymph numbers and damage are increasing. Record the counts in a consistent way so an adviser can interpret the trend. Preserve predators and tiny egg-parasitic wasps by avoiding unnecessary broad insecticide applications. UC guidance notes that treatment decisions differ with grape use, region, canopy size, and leafhopper species, so a threshold from another vineyard may not fit yours. If the vines are declining or identification is uncertain, bring clear photographs and monitoring notes to a local viticulture or extension specialist.

sources.label: Dmitriev: New and little known species of Erasmoneura

identification: Begin with several mature leaves from the middle of a stem. In true E. esula, leaves tend to be widest above the middle and narrow gradually toward the base. E. virgata has much narrower leaves whose sides are more nearly parallel through the middle, with a more abrupt narrowing at the base. These are comparison clues, not a complete identification key. Photograph the entire shoot, representative leaves with a ruler, and flowering structures. A botanist may need finer leaf and floral details to settle the name.
actions: Record the plant's location and setting, but keep any management recommendation provisional until its identity is confirmed. Ask a herbarium or local weed specialist whether the observation belongs to true E. esula, E. virgata, or another similar spurge. Do not move plants or soil from an uncertain patch to a new site while that check is underway. If a regulated weed is confirmed, seek local guidance for that taxon. Keep the original identification and the botanist's determination together so later reports can distinguish the two species.

sources.label: Montana Field Guide: Leafy Spurge, Euphorbia virgata
InfoFlora and Flora Helvetica: Euphorbia esula
Meise Botanic Garden Euphorbia esula complex

identification: Look for upright stems carrying narrow, smooth-edged leaves one at a time. The upper leaves surrounding the flowers are broader and yellow-green. Damaged tissues release white latex, but deliberately breaking stems is unnecessary for identification. Cypress spurge is usually shorter with finer leaves; yellow toadflax has recognizable snapdragon-shaped flowers with long spurs. The name Euphorbia esula appears in older references, although modern treatments separate it from E. virgata. Photographs should show leaves along the stem and the flowering tip.
actions: Wear gloves and cover exposed skin when handling this plant because its sap is irritating. Mark the full patch, including scattered shoots beyond the dense center, and avoid moving contaminated soil or hay. For a small new occurrence, ask the local weed program about removal and follow-up before disturbing the roots. Large patches usually need a sustained management plan. Revisit treated ground in later growing seasons, and seek pasture-specific advice before grazing affected areas.

identification: Adults have narrow brown forewings with a pale triangular mark near the middle of each rear edge. Caterpillars are pale yellowish or greenish with a darker head and small legs. White, open-meshed cocoons attached to foliage are particularly useful clues.
