Allium leaf-mining flies cause similar damage, but their larvae lack caterpillar legs and a conspicuous brown head; their brown pupae may remain inside plant tissues. Photograph the larva and cocoon as well as the damaged leaf.
actions: Inspect the newest leaves and sheltered folds regularly, opening a damaged leaf gently to look for larvae. In gardens where the pest occurs, insect-proof mesh can prevent egg laying when installed over clean plants and secured around the edges. Rotate the planting site so emerging moths are not trapped beneath the cover with a new crop. Remove visible cocoons during inspection. Ask local extension about seasonal monitoring because the number and timing of generations differ between regions.

sources.label: AHDB: Identification and symptoms caused by the leek moth

identification: Look for relatively short, narrow leaf blades, sometimes rolled inward, and open, branching flower heads held above the foliage. Mature clusters become pale yellow or straw-colored. The plant commonly reaches around two feet, although growing conditions affect its size. Several lovegrasses have similarly delicate seed heads, and a distant photograph is rarely enough to separate them. Include the whole clump, leaf bases, and close views of several mature spikelets when asking a grass specialist to confirm the identification.
actions: Record isolated plants and the outer edge of a larger stand before deciding how to respond. Avoid carrying seed on equipment or introducing this grass in seed mixes near conservation land. Small outlying patches deserve attention while they are still manageable. Coordinate extensive work with a local land manager, including plans for replacement vegetation and repeated checks. Fire alone should not be assumed to solve the problem: Arizona guidance notes that this grass can recover quickly after disturbance and contribute substantial dry fuel.

identification: The long, straplike leaves rise from a dense base and arch outward at their tips. Leaf edges are finely rough and can cut skin. The pale, swollen bases of mature shoots resemble sturdy scallions after the outer layers are removed. Flowers are uncommon on plants grown for a single season. East Indian lemongrass and citronella grasses are close relatives, while lemon balm has broad, opposite leaves on branched stems rather than grass blades. Do not identify a cooking ingredient solely by a lemon smell.
actions: Give a known garden plant full sun, moisture and soil that drains well. In cold climates, move a manageable division indoors before frost and keep it from drying out completely. Wear gloves when dividing or cutting a large clump. Harvest selected outer shoots rather than damaging the center unnecessarily. Only use plants of confirmed culinary identity that have been grown appropriately for food; an ornamental grass with a similar smell is not automatically interchangeable.

identification: Look for smooth bark in white, cream, pinkish or gray tones, and slender adult leaves that taper to a long point. White flowers develop from small clusters of buds, commonly three together. The woody fruits are urn-shaped or barrel-shaped, with their valves enclosed rather than projecting conspicuously. Juvenile foliage can be broader than adult leaves. Photograph the trunk, mature leaves, buds and fallen fruits together; a pale trunk alone cannot separate this tree from other smooth-barked eucalypts.
actions: For an existing garden tree, begin with its size and location rather than assuming removal is necessary. Give an arborist clear photographs if its identity or condition matters to a planting or safety decision. Check local guidance before planting a species that can become a large tree, allowing room for its mature canopy and roots. If seedlings appear outside cultivation, record their location and ask the local flora or weed service whether the species needs monitoring there. Avoid spreading garden waste into nearby bushland.

identification: Leaves are flat and may carry scattered hairs. Small, curved appendages at the blade base partly clasp the stem. The cylindrical flower spike consists of repeating groups of three spikelets, with long, straight awns extending beyond them. As the head matures it breaks into these units. Closely related wall and Mediterranean barleys can be difficult to distinguish; details of the central and lateral spikelets, anthers and hairs are needed. Save clear close photographs of a mature head instead of relying on its general foxtail appearance.
actions: If the grass is unwanted, remove small patches before the seed heads mature and break apart. Collect developed heads rather than scattering them while mowing or moving soil. Keep records of where seedlings recur, since removing one year's plants does not prevent later germination. In pasture or around animals, seek local advice about management as the grass matures; useful early-season forage does not imply that dry awned material has the same value. Ask a herbarium to confirm the subspecies when exact identity affects reporting.

identification: Shiny heart-shaped or kidney-shaped leaves surround bright yellow flowers, usually with eight to twelve narrow petals. Some forms produce small bulbils where leaves join stems, and the roots carry clusters of fleshy tubers. Marsh marigold is an important lookalike, generally with a sturdier upright habit and fewer, broader yellow flower parts. Violets can resemble the foliage but have toothed leaf edges and very different flowers. Check several features together, since petal counts overlap and bulbils are not present on every form.
actions: Mark the patch while leaves are visible so it can be found again next spring. A very small colony may be dug carefully, taking the tubers as well as the foliage; leaving these structures behind allows recovery. Avoid moving soil or sharing plants from an infested bed. Work around valuable spring wildflowers and get site-specific guidance for extensive patches, especially beside water. Plan follow-up over multiple seasons rather than treating summer dieback as evidence that control succeeded.
Bag removed plants, tubers and bulbils for appropriate trash disposal; do not put them in home compost or yard-waste recycling.

sources.label: University of Maryland: Invasives in Your Woodland, Lesser Celandine

identification: Adults are only a few millimeters long, with a compact brownish body, pale hair markings, long antennae and wing covers that leave the tip of the abdomen exposed. Eggs are attached to the outside of seeds, while pale grub-like larvae develop within them. Round exit holes are a useful sign of seed-beetle activity but do not identify this species by themselves. Related Callosobruchus beetles look similar, so preserve an adult and several affected seeds for a diagnostic service.
actions: Separate a suspect packet or lot from clean supplies and inspect neighboring stored legumes. Keep the packaging, purchase date and supplier information with the sample, since these help trace the source of a problem. Use clean, sealed storage containers for uninfested material and remove spilled pulses that could shelter further generations. For commercial seed or food stocks, ask a stored-product specialist about appropriate handling and treatment. Do not apply garden insecticides to food, and do not distribute suspect planting seed while the identification is unresolved.

sources.label: Canadian Grain Commission: Southern cowpea weevil

identification: Look for upright stems with lower leaves on stalks and smaller, narrower leaves higher up. The flower head sits in a rounded cup of overlapping bracts. Their dark brown or black, comb-fringed tips can almost hide the greener bract bodies underneath. The heads generally lack the large, showy outer florets seen in some similar knapweeds. Brown knapweed and other close relatives can be confusing, so photograph the side of several heads, including their bracts, rather than only the purple tops.
actions: Before removing a patch or adding it to a seed mix, check how this species is treated locally. A plant valued in one region may be unwanted in another. Where control is appropriate, prevent mature heads from shedding seed and arrange removal of small plants with their perennial bases. Recheck the patch for regrowth and seedlings. For a meadow or restoration site, have an uncertain identification reviewed before broad mowing or spraying affects neighboring plants. Keep records of the exact scientific name used by the reviewer.

sources.label: Vascular Plants of North Carolina: Centaurea nigra

identification: Adults are slender, cylindrical, brown beetles only a few millimeters long. Fine structures on the rear slope of the wing covers help specialists distinguish them from other ambrosia beetles. Entry tunnels are roughly circular and can lead to an irregular, dark-stained brood chamber that resembles a keyhole in section. Photograph the host tree, affected wood and holes with a scale. Modern sources also use the spelling Xyleborinus saxesenii, while this entry retains the supplied catalog spelling.
actions: Assess the tree's condition and recent history, including cutting, drought or other stress, and ask a tree-health service to examine a representative sample. Keep suspect logs and firewood near their place of origin while identification is pending. In a nursery, isolate affected stock and record nearby trees showing similar holes. Decisions about pruning, removal or timber handling should reflect the host and the extent of damage. Surface treatment should not be assumed to reach beetles already protected inside the wood.

identification: The stems spread outward or turn upward from near the ground. Lower leaves are deeply divided into narrow lobes, while upper leaves become smaller and simpler. Tiny white flowers are followed by squat fruits with two rounded halves and a clear constriction between them. The leaves can have a strong unpleasant odor, but tasting is unnecessary. Before flowering, mayweed chamomile and some filarees can resemble it. Mature fruits help separate these lookalikes and related swinecresses much more reliably than the leafy rosette alone.
actions: Pull or hoe unwanted plants while small and before the fruits mature, taking care around neighboring seedlings. Because it reproduces by seed, preventing another seed crop is more useful than simply trimming the top of a mature patch. Collect fruiting material and clean soil from tools before moving to another bed. In alfalfa or dairy pasture, discuss an infestation with local extension: UC IPM reports that substantial contamination can reduce hay palatability and that grazing can affect milk flavor.

identification: Adults are small, slender, grayish to beige moths with a noticeable yellow head. The narrow pale caterpillars have brown heads and spin silk through the material they feed on. Their tough cocoons may be hidden under debris or tucked against wooden hive parts. Greater wax moth larvae look similar and usually become larger; young wax moths can also be confused with small hive beetle larvae. Photograph larvae, webbing and the affected comb together and ask an apiary adviser to check uncertain specimens.
actions: Inspect stored comb regularly and separate damaged material before the infestation spreads through a stack. Clean webbing and cocoons from reusable equipment. For occupied hives, address problems such as a failing queen or other pests with a beekeeping adviser instead of assuming the moth was the first cause of decline. Extension guidance supports freezing suitable stored comb and protecting it from reinfestation afterward; follow a complete recommended protocol for the material and freezer used. Keep household moth treatments and unapproved chemicals away from hive products.

sources.label: Mississippi State: Minor Pests of Honey Bees

identification: Adults may be green, orange or pink, so color alone is unreliable. Dark markings occur on the leg and antennal joints, and some individuals have dark patches on the abdomen. Winged forms are generally browner. Several other aphids use lettuce, including green peach aphid, which requires closer inspection of head structures to separate confidently. Unlike lettuce root aphid, this species is sought on leaves rather than in waxy colonies around the roots. Include the feeding location with any close photograph.
actions: Open the young leaves gently during routine scouting and inspect several plants across the planting, not just visibly damaged heads. Record aphids and predatory larvae together; hoverfly and lacewing larvae can help suppress populations. Avoid a broad insecticide response that removes those predators without reaching aphids inside the head. For commercial crops, seek local advice early, before heads close tightly. Check transplants before planting and keep a sample for identification if the aphid is unfamiliar or management has failed.

identification: Look around the roots of a failing plant for pale yellowish or grayish aphids covered in white, woolly wax. Wingless individuals have short antennae and lack the obvious paired rear tubes seen on many leaf aphids. Their wax can be mistaken for fungal growth until individual insects are examined. On suitable poplars, the spring gall is purse-shaped and forms on a leaf stalk. Wilt alone is not diagnostic: root diseases, drought and other root-feeding insects can produce similar symptoms.
actions: Carefully lift one affected plant with its roots and surrounding soil rather than treating from the appearance of the leaves. Photograph any waxy colonies and have them identified. Maintain appropriate irrigation while investigating because root damage is more consequential during dry conditions. Record nearby poplars and the timing of symptoms for a crop adviser, but do not remove trees solely on suspicion. For future lettuce plantings, consider host relationships and local monitoring advice when choosing the site. Leaf sprays should not be assumed to reach a root infestation.

sources.label: AHDB: Management of the lettuce root aphid

identification: Look for rounded to broadly oval leaves on distinct stalks, arranged alternately along the branches. A covering of fine pale hairs gives the foliage a felted, gray or silver appearance. The small flower heads contain yellow florets surrounded by creamy, papery bracts and occur in clusters near the ends of longer stalks. Other silver-leaved ornamentals can look similar from a distance. A useful identification photograph includes the leaf arrangement, both leaf surfaces and the flower clusters, rather than a single clipped leaf.
actions: For an established garden plant, provide a sunny position and good drainage, and keep its growth within the intended bed. Before adding it near natural vegetation, check local planting guidance; regional assessments do not treat this ornamental identically everywhere. Remove unwanted seedlings or spreading growth early and collect trimmings rather than dumping them beyond the garden. If a plant has appeared away from cultivation, record its location and flowering features for a local botanist. Do not infer medicinal safety from traditional-use descriptions.

sources.label: Universidad Francisco Marroquin Arboretum: Helichrysum petiolare

identification: Adults are small yellowish-brown to brown moths with variable darker markings; females tend to be larger and less strongly marked than males. Eggs occur in flat, overlapping groups, and mature caterpillars are green. Pupae may be found inside a leaf roll or silken shelter between leaves. These features narrow the possibilities but do not separate the species reliably from all local tortricid moths. Expert examination of adults or laboratory methods may be needed, especially for a new regional record.
actions: Inspect damaged shoots and touching fruit or leaves, noting the host plant and whether larvae are actively feeding. Keep a suspect specimen contained and contact the local plant-health authority or extension service for collection instructions. Do not move infested nursery plants or cuttings while identification is pending. For established crop problems, use local monitoring guidance to decide whether action is needed and when it will reach susceptible stages. A photograph of a plain brown moth alone is insufficient grounds for broad spraying.

sources.label: CDFA: Light Brown Apple Moth Pest Profile

identification: Look for hairy, roughly four-sided stems and opposite leaves. Lower leaves are broad, stalked and often heart-shaped at the base, sometimes with small additional basal lobes. Upper leaves become smaller. Numerous small, two-lipped violet flowers are grouped in separated whorls along the flowering branches. Other sages share square stems and paired leaves, so include the spacing of flower clusters and the shape of lower leaves in photographs. A purple flower spike by itself is not a secure species identification.
actions: In a garden, retain the plant label and compare mature flowering growth before dividing or sharing it. Check nearby ground for seedlings if keeping it within a border matters. Where it is unwanted, remove a small plant with its perennial base and revisit for regrowth rather than only clipping the flowering stalk. If it appears in a natural area, ask a local flora specialist about its status and appropriate response. Do not assume that every ornamental sage can replace common sage in cooking.

sources.label: Kew and Flora of Iraq: Salvia verticillata
University of Udine Flora: Salvia verticillata

identification: Adults are about a quarter to a third of an inch long, with glossy scarlet wing covers and a black head, legs and underside. The wing covers have tiny pits. Larvae look very different: they are soft, pale to orange-brown grubs that often carry dark droppings over their backs. Check beneath leaves for eggs and small larvae as well as looking at the upper surface. Other red beetles may resemble adults, but the combination of body shape, black parts, host plant and feeding signs is useful.
actions: Inspect lilies from the time shoots emerge and continue while leaves and buds are developing. On a small planting, remove identified adults, eggs and larvae during regular checks. Hold a container beneath adults before disturbing them so dropped beetles are easier to catch. Inspect purchased or shared lily plants and associated material before moving them into an uninfested garden. Where damage persists, ask extension about locally appropriate management and biological-control activity. Avoid treating every red insect on a flower as a lily pest.

sources.label: University of Maine: Lily Leaf Beetle

identification: Leaves are oval to diamond-shaped, with smooth edges and fine hairs. They can appear in unequal pairs along the scrambling stems. The small white or cream flowers hang singly or in pairs and form narrow bells with five short, turned-back tips. Fruits mature into pale cream or yellowish, elongated berries. True lily of the valley has much broader leaves and a different upright flower arrangement. Photograph the whole growth pattern, leaves and hanging flowers together; pale bells alone are not enough.
actions: If the plant is unwanted, map the full area of growth before cutting through tangled stems. Small infestations can be dug carefully, but removing the visible vine without its underground parts is unlikely to finish the job. Collect fruit and root pieces, and ask local waste services about disposal rather than putting material on a wildland edge. Avoid cultivation that carries fragments to clean ground. Plan repeated inspections after removal and consult a weed specialist for extensive patches interwoven with desirable vegetation.

sources.label: NSW WeedWise: Pampas lily of the valley
Flora of New Zealand: Salpichroa origanifolia

identification: Most leaves have three leaflets, with the middle leaflet noticeably larger than the pair beside it. The leaflets are leathery, and their tips may be rounded or notched. Small paired spines occur at the leaf bases. White flowers usually have three petals, and the fleshy fruits turn red as they ripen. Several thorny citrus relatives have similar foliage, so photograph a complete leaf, a stem node, flowers and fruit. An isolated leaflet can conceal the important three-part structure.
actions: Wear gloves and protect your arms when pruning or removing a plant because the spines are easy to overlook inside dense foliage. Check local planting recommendations before adding it beside natural vegetation, and inspect nearby shaded ground for seedlings. Collect unwanted fruiting branches and avoid dumping them where seeds could establish. If a shrub has appeared away from a garden, record whether there are smaller plants nearby and seek local identification advice. Do not sample unfamiliar red berries to test a proposed identification.

sources.label: New York Botanical Garden: Triphasia trifolia, Flora of St. John

identification: Look for opposite, broadly oval leaves with a heart-shaped base and toothed edges. Small blue, two-lipped flowers occur in repeated clusters along the upper flowering stems. The flower's enclosing calyx is ribbed, with three veins on its upper lip. Closely related sages can share this combination at a glance. Salvia personata is a documented lookalike with differences in flower dimensions and a looser inflorescence. Photograph lower leaves and several flowering nodes together, and retain a fruiting specimen if a specialist requests one.
actions: If it is an unwanted plant in a cultivated bed, remove it before mature seed is shed and check for later seedlings. Collect flowering or fruiting stems rather than shaking them over clean ground. A newly noticed population along a field edge or natural area is worth documenting before broad control begins. Give a local botanist its location, habitat and complete photographs, particularly if a record would extend its known local range. Avoid using the common name sage as a shortcut to culinary or medicinal use.

sources.label: Nyssen and colleagues: Lindenleaf sage in the Tigray highlands

identification: Narrow, smooth-edged leaves run along the upright stems, with lower leaves paired and upper leaves alternating. The upper plant carries glandular hairs. Flowers sit near the upper leaf axils and are commonly pink with darker lines, though pale and purplish forms occur. The uneven, egg-shaped capsules eventually open through small pores. Garden snapdragons can resemble the flowers, but their overall size and flower arrangement differ. Include a full stem, the narrow leaves and mature capsules in photographs for a confident comparison.
actions: Check a local flora or botanical recording service before removing a wild population, especially in regions where this arable plant is scarce. If it is confirmed as an unwanted garden weed, pull small plants before capsules ripen and collect seed-bearing material. Keep the disturbance limited so neighboring seedlings are not unnecessarily uprooted. For a field population, record the crop, soil disturbance and approximate extent before choosing a response. Do not transfer a weed-control recommendation from another country without checking the species' status where you are.

sources.label: InfoFlora and Flora Helvetica: Misopates orontium

identification: Adults are elongated brown beetles with lighter lengthwise stripes along the wing covers. Like other click beetles, they can spring from their backs using a clicking mechanism. Larvae are narrow, firm-bodied and yellowish to caramel-colored, with a darker head. Agriotes larvae have characteristic markings near the tip, but separating A. lineatus from close relatives requires detailed examination. Research shows that worn individuals can be especially difficult to name. Submit intact larvae with photographs of crop injury rather than labeling every hard-bodied soil larva as this species.
actions: Assess risk before planting a susceptible crop, particularly after grassland or where wireworm damage has occurred previously. Ask a crop adviser about locally suitable soil sampling or bait monitoring and keep the field history with the results. Examine damaged seedlings and tubers for actual larvae. Avoid moving potentially infested soil or nursery stock to clean ground. Management should match the confirmed pest complex, crop and local conditions; catching adult beetles or seeing a few feeding holes does not by itself justify a blanket insecticide treatment.

sources.label: Washington State: Biology and Management of Wireworms in Western Washington
AHDB: Identification and management of wireworms in field crops

identification: Look for square stems, opposite narrow leaves and rounded clusters of hairy orange flowers spaced up the flowering shoots. Each flower projects from a persistent, pointed calyx, so the clusters can remain noticeable after the petals fall. The leaves are lance-shaped and toothed. Other Leonotis species can have similar orange whorls, making foliage and the woody growth habit important supporting clues. Photograph the base and a complete flowering stem, not only a close-up of one orange tube.
actions: Choose a sunny, well-drained position for a known garden plant and allow enough space for mature growth. Pruning after flowering can help maintain a manageable shape. In colder areas, use local horticultural guidance for overwintering rather than relying on a warm-climate height or hardiness claim. Inspect around the parent for unwanted seedlings and keep cut material out of natural areas. If an unplanted specimen appears beyond cultivation, have its identity and local status checked before encouraging it to spread. Traditional names do not establish medicinal safety.

sources.label: NC State: Common Lion's Paw, Leonotis leonurus

identification: Look for alternating pale and reddish-brown bands across a large head and body, fanlike pectoral fins, and long separate dorsal spines. Fleshy projections may occur above the eyes and near the mouth. These features identify the familiar lionfish group well, but do not reliably separate Pterois volitans from the very similar P. miles in the invaded Atlantic range. USGS advises that positive species separation there requires genetic analysis. A clear underwater photograph can therefore support a lionfish report without proving this exact species.
actions: Keep your distance and do not touch or attempt to corner the fish. Record the date, location, depth and approximate number, and share observations through the relevant marine wildlife or invasive-species program. If you want to help with removal, use an established local program with training and appropriate equipment. Aquarium owners should never release unwanted fish; arrange a responsible rehoming option. Leave handling and spine removal to experienced people, and seek medical assistance after a suspected sting rather than improvising treatment from a wildlife profile.

identification: Leaves are simple, broadly oval and pointed, with a heart-shaped or nearly straight base and a long stalk. The stalk may be thickened at both ends. Flowers are pinkish or pale and carry many conspicuous stamens. Capsules split into two sections to reveal numerous seeds with bright orange-red coats. Some capsules are red, while others are greener or yellowish. Include a leaf, flower and opened mature capsule in photographs; a red bristly fruit alone could be mistaken for an unrelated tropical plant.
actions: For a garden specimen, confirm the name before using its seeds as a culinary ingredient and keep ornamental chemical treatments separate from food-growing practices. Check local horticultural guidance before planting it near natural vegetation. Where seedlings are unwanted, remove them while small and collect ripe capsules before seeds are scattered. Record spontaneous plants beyond cultivated ground for a local botanist rather than assuming every nearby shrub was deliberately planted. The species' long history of dye use does not establish that every homemade preparation is suitable for skin or medicinal use.

identification: Inspect both sides of young lychee leaves. Blistered, thickened or curled areas above may correspond to woolly patches underneath. Those patches can change from pale or whitish to amber and dark brown as they develop. The mites are too small for reliable naked-eye identification and may be difficult to find even with an ordinary hand lens. Rust-colored growth is a clue, not a complete diagnosis. A plant-health laboratory can examine affected tissue and distinguish this mite from other causes of distorted growth.
actions: Inspect new flushes regularly, especially on recently purchased or propagated plants. Do not share cuttings, air-layers or nursery trees from a suspect plant while awaiting advice. Photograph young and older symptoms and contact local extension or plant-health officials for sampling instructions. Management may combine removal of affected growth with carefully timed protection of new leaves, but product approvals and schedules differ by location. Avoid copying an overseas spray program. Continue monitoring new growth after action, since old damaged leaves alone cannot show whether mites remain active.

identification: Each leaf has three leaflets, generally widest toward the tip, with teeth near the outer end. The stems and young leaves are hairy. Small yellow pea-shaped flowers occur in small clusters and are followed by tightly coiled pods, usually with several turns and hooked spines. Black medic can look similar before fruiting, but it does not make these conspicuously spiny, multi-coiled burs. Other bur medics require closer comparison of pod coils, spines and leaf characters. Photograph mature fruit from both the side and above.
actions: If it is unwanted in a lawn or bed, remove plants before burs harden and contain mature seed. Collect fruiting plants rather than dragging them through clean areas, and check shoes or equipment after working in a patch. Because this is an annual, stopping seed production is a useful practical objective, but later seedlings may still appear. For pasture or conservation ground, identify it carefully and check local priorities before broad treatment. A few small medics in mixed vegetation do not automatically warrant removing the surrounding plants.

sources.label: InfoFlora and Flora Helvetica: Medicago minima

identification: Workers are very small, about one and a half millimeters long, and light to golden brown. They are relatively uniform in size and often move slowly. Under magnification, the antennae end in a two-segmented club, and the waist has a distinctive blocklike node when viewed from the side. These features require a close, well-lit specimen. Many tiny yellow-brown ants are harmless lookalikes, so color, size or a sting should not be treated as a definitive identification.
actions: Pause movement of suspect potted plants, soil and equipment, and ask the local ant or biosecurity program how to collect samples safely. Survey both ground-level and elevated locations using their recommended method. Do not handle colonies barehanded or scatter infested material while searching. Once confirmed, management needs to address the whole occupied area and be checked with repeat surveys. Random spraying of visible workers is unlikely to show whether hidden nests remain. Keep records of sample locations so follow-up work can compare the same places.

sources.label: Wetterer and Porter: Little fire ant review
Hawaii Invasive Species Council: Little Fire Ant

identification: Leaves alternate along the stem and vary considerably in shape and size. Lower leaves are usually broader, while those near the top are smaller and narrower; margins may be toothed or nearly smooth. The loose clusters of tiny flower heads contain tubular florets without a ring of broad daisy petals. Mature fruits carry white bristles that form a puffball-like head. Other small composites can resemble it, so include lower leaves, a flowering head and a mature fruiting head in a photograph set.
actions: For a small unwanted garden patch, pull plants before the fluffy seed heads release their fruits. Collect mature heads carefully instead of brushing them over nearby beds. Keep newly disturbed soil covered where practical and check for later seedlings. If the plant is found in a natural area, ask a local botanist about the relevant variety and local status before treating it as introduced. Botanical treatments note uncertainty around the origin of some Australian forms, illustrating why a worldwide weed label is not a reliable local management decision.

identification: Possible signs in susceptible citrus include poor growth, discolored inner bark, gum deposits and pits in the wood. These features overlap with other problems, and small leaves alone do not identify this pathogen. In experimental work, the same viroid variants produced different symptoms in mandarin, tangelo and sweet lime. Confirmation requires a plant diagnostic laboratory; photographs and a visual inspection cannot establish the variant or exclude an infection in an apparently healthy tree.
actions: If infection is suspected, pause propagation from that plant and keep its grafting material separate from other stock. Record the citrus variety, rootstock, source and symptoms before contacting a plant clinic. Ask the laboratory how to collect suitable samples and use its current instructions for submission. Contaminated grafting and pruning tools can transmit the viroid, so follow the local citrus program's sanitation procedure between plants. Obtain replacement propagation material through a recognized clean-stock program, and have confirmed nursery infections managed with the responsible plant-health adviser.

sources.label: University of Georgia: Hop Stunt Viroid Infecting Citrus Trees in Georgia
Reanwarakorn and Semancik: Correlation of hop stunt viroid variants to cachexia and xyloporosis diseases of citrus
International Seed Federation2026 HSVd identity record
Australian government Egyptian citrus risk analysis

identification: Look for a spreading, open flower head with many narrow spikelets arranged along fine branches. Each spikelet contains several closely packed florets rather than a single conspicuous flower. With a hand lens, examine the leaf edges, sheath margins and the region just below the stem nodes for small wartlike glands. A very short fringe of hairs forms the ligule where leaf and sheath meet. Other small Eragrostis species can look similar, so retain a mature head and clear photographs of those glandular areas.
actions: In a garden bed, remove unwanted plants while the seed heads are still immature, lifting the small tuft rather than simply cutting off its tallest stems. Check cracks and disturbed edges again after rain, when another group of seedlings may become noticeable. Keep mature seed heads out of soil or mulch that will be moved elsewhere. For a field record, note the substrate and whether the plant is truly annual; a local grass key or herbarium can confirm a specimen when the glands are difficult to see.

identification: Examine an individual spikelet rather than judging the whole plant from a distance. The spikelets are small, roughly triangular to egg-shaped, generally pale green and sometimes purple-tinged, and hang from very fine stalks. Their overlapping, rounded scales give them a layered appearance. New Zealand's flora describes them as about 3 to 4.5 millimeters long. Larger ornamental quakinggrasses can create the same shivering effect; measure several spikelets and photograph the open branching head, leaf sheath and membranous ligule for a more dependable comparison.
actions: Where it is unwanted, lift small annual tufts before their heads mature and scatter seed. Work carefully around neighboring grasses, which may lack obvious flowers at the time. If you are keeping an ornamental patch, watch the surrounding paths and beds for seedlings and remove those outside the intended area. For a new locality record, include a ruler in a close photograph of the spikelets and note the date and habitat. Avoid assuming that every nodding, heartlike grass head represents the same species.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Briza minor

identification: The leaves are broadly oval, with rounded teeth and a distinctly stalked base. Their size and hairiness vary, so compare several leaves from different parts of the same plant. Small pale blue, mauve or whitish flowers provide more useful evidence than foliage alone. The Victorian horticultural flora distinguishes related spurflowers using the number of leaf teeth and the density of hairs. Photograph a flowering stem, both leaf surfaces and the stem base; many cultivated plants sold simply as Plectranthus cannot be identified reliably from a nursery label.
actions: For a container plant, provide bright filtered light and monitor moisture rather than allowing the root ball to remain persistently dry. Pinching growing tips can encourage a fuller shape when the plant is actively growing. If it dies back, inspect the living base before discarding it. When moving divisions or cuttings, keep the scientific name with the material so that similar ornamental spurflowers are not mixed together. Check local suitability before placing it outdoors, and keep garden trimmings within an appropriate green-waste system.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria HortFlora: Plectranthus parviflorus
Flora of New Zealand: Plectranthus parviflorus

identification: Look for small funnel-shaped flowers, often only around 1.5 to 2 centimeters long, rather than the broad blooms of many ornamental morning-glories. Leaves may have two prominent basal lobes, producing a three-lobed outline, but some are less divided. Examine the narrow sepals beneath the flower for hairs and photograph the rounded capsules with their persistent sepals. Leaf shape alone is unreliable within this group. A useful identification set includes an open flower from the side, its sepals, several leaves and mature fruit from the same vine.
actions: Trace an unwanted vine back to its rooted base before pulling, especially when it is tangled through a valued shrub. Loosen the root and remove the vine in sections so neighboring stems are not torn. Collect developing capsules before they open, and revisit the spot for seedlings after favorable growing weather. If the identification is uncertain, retain photographs and a small flowering sample for a local botanist. Do not transfer a name from a similar-looking morning-glory without checking the flowers and fruit, particularly when regional sources use conflicting names.

sources.label: CSIRO Australian Tropical Rainforest Plants: Ipomoea triloba
Kew: Ipomoea triloba, Flora of the Cayman Islands account

identification: Look for narrow leaves that clasp the stem with pointed lobes at their bases. The plant bears both simple hairs and tiny branched hairs, best seen with a hand lens. Its pods are pear-shaped to spindle-shaped and are not flattened like the broad, disk-shaped fruits of some other mustards. Each has a short projecting style and a slender stalk. Cultivated camelina and other small yellow-flowered mustards need careful comparison, so record pod size, hair type and leaf attachment instead of relying on flower color or the common name.
actions: Remove unwanted plants before mature pods begin to release seed, taking particular care with patches beside seed crops or vegetable beds. Handle fruiting stems over a container rather than shaking them through neighboring plants. After clearing a patch, monitor the disturbed soil for another flush of seedlings. In a cropped field, map the affected area and take a representative fruiting sample to the local agronomy service before choosing a control program. Clean seed and careful handling of soil and equipment are sensible priorities when preventing movement between plots.

sources.label: University of Navarra: Flora arvense de Navarra

identification: Examine the smooth leaf sheath and the thin membranous ligule at the junction of leaf and sheath. The blades are flat, and the head is made of tightly packed, flattened spikelets. Under magnification, the spikelet's outer scales have winged keels. A fertile floret is accompanied by unequal reduced sterile structures, with the lower one vestigial. These small features help distinguish it from canarygrass, Phalaris canariensis, which is listed as a similar species by the identification key. A head photograph alone may not settle the distinction.
actions: Scout field edges and crop rows early enough to remove small isolated patches before they set seed. Keep suspect heads with their stem bases when requesting an identification, and record the crop and growth stage. Avoid carrying mature seed on harvested material, machinery or soil into a clean plot. For an established field infestation, seek a crop-specific management plan that considers the local rotation and previous control results. In a garden, lift the whole annual tuft and revisit the spot; simply clipping the visible head can leave growing shoots behind.

sources.label: National Institute of Plant Health Management: Weed identification guide

identification: Look closely for hard-looking, reddish-brown bumps with a lobed, roughly X-shaped outline. Older individuals can be obscured by sooty growth, and crowded colonies may merge visually into an uneven crust. The individual scales are only a few millimeters across, so use a hand lens and include a scale reference in photographs. Other scale insects also produce bumps and honeydew. A specialist may need an intact sample to confirm the species, particularly because older reports called this pest Paratachardina lobata before the taxonomic distinction was established.
actions: Inspect adjoining branches and nearby woody plants once a colony is suspected, and avoid moving infested nursery material to another property. Photograph both the insect and the overall plant condition before removing affected material. A local extension or plant-health service can advise whether selective branch removal is appropriate and how to contain the waste. Severely infested plants may require a broader management decision. Continue checking retained plants for fresh colonies; cleaning away black mold alone does not remove the feeding insects responsible for the problem.

sources.label: Kondo and Gullan: Taxonomic review of Paratachardina
Florida Department of Agriculture: Lobate lac scale pest alert
UF IFAS Gardening Solutions: Lobate Lac Scale

identification: The lower leaves are deeply divided, with a larger terminal lobe, while leaves higher on the stem become smaller and narrower. Small pale yellow flowers have four petals and sit near the growing tips. Behind them, long, very slender cylindrical pods develop along an elongating stalk. Photograph the whole rosette, upper leaves, flowers and mature pods together. Hedge mustard and eastern rocket can look similar; the arrangement and dimensions of the pods are more useful for separating them than the general yellow-flowered appearance.
actions: In a garden, lift young rosettes before they produce a crop of seed, taking care to remove the rooted crown. If pods are already developing, contain the stems while handling them and avoid scattering them through mulch or soil. Recheck bare ground after the next germination period. In an orchard or field, record the extent of the patch and seek advice suited to the crop before selecting further control. A clear fruiting sample is especially helpful when several mustard weeds are growing together and their seedlings look alike.

identification: Look for a narrow, spike-like flower head with clusters that may be separated by visible gaps, especially near the base. The spikelets sit on very short stalks and contain many tightly arranged florets. Leaves are smooth and may lie flat or roll inward, and the ligule is a short fringe of hairs. New South Wales and Victorian treatments describe plants reaching roughly 80 centimeters. Other lovegrasses can also have contracted heads, so photograph the branching pattern and retain a mature spikelet for checking with a regional key.
actions: Before removing a patch from grassland or a restoration planting, establish its local identity and status; this species belongs to the documented Australian flora. Mark a representative tuft and return when the seed head is mature enough to examine. If it is unwanted in a cultivated bed, remove the whole tuft before seed dispersal and keep seed-bearing material out of soil being moved. For a botanical record, note whether the base persists between seasons and describe the surrounding habitat rather than assuming that its common name indicates a weed.

identification: An adult female has an oval, wax-covered body with short filaments around the sides and two exceptionally long filaments extending from the rear. Those rear filaments may be as long as, or longer than, the body. They can break off, so their absence on one individual does not exclude the species. Check several insects under magnification, including those sheltered beneath leaves and along stems. Other mealybugs and some wax-covered beneficial insects can resemble them, making an intact adult and a close photograph especially useful.
actions: Separate an affected container plant from neighboring plants while you inspect the collection. Turn leaves over and check crowded stem junctions, then look for honeydew, sooty growth and ants that may be attending the colony. Remove small localized infestations carefully where this can be done without damaging the plant, and continue checking for young insects. Reduce excessive crowding around susceptible plants. Persistent infestations deserve an identification and management plan from a local horticultural adviser; protecting natural enemies and addressing attending ants can be part of that plan.

identification: Look for deeply cut leaves with sharp-edged lobes and stiff hairs on the stems. The small flowers occur in short groups and have pink to mauve petals, sometimes with darker veins. Mature fruit carries a conspicuously long beak, commonly several centimeters long. The individual seed-bearing segments have pits and distinct grooves near the base of their awns. Those tiny structures are important for separating similar Erodium species, including plants treated as E. brachycarpum in some floras. Photograph them with a hand lens rather than relying only on leaf shape.
actions: Remove unwanted plants while the fruits are still immature, lifting the rooted base from the soil instead of leaving it behind with clipped stems. Contain mature fruit during handling so it is not scattered across a path or garden bed. Revisit disturbed patches for new seedlings and check material being moved from an infested area. For an uncertain record, collect photographs of both flowers and intact fruit, and use the regional flora's treatment of related stork's bills. Taxonomic boundaries can differ between references, which makes a documented specimen valuable.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Erodium botrys

identification: Look for an elongated, pale grayish to yellow-brown body and legs that are dramatically longer than the body. Darker markings may be visible on the front body section or abdomen. A disturbed spider may vibrate rapidly in its web, making its outline difficult to follow. The name daddy longlegs is also used for harvestmen and crane flies, so it is not a reliable identification by itself. Other cellar spiders can resemble this species; a clear body photograph is more informative than a distant view of the legs.
actions: If a spider is in an unobtrusive corner, leaving it in place allows it to continue catching small household arthropods. Where a web is inconvenient, guide the spider into a container and move it to a suitable sheltered place nearby, then remove the web. Avoid pulling it by the legs. Persistent numbers can prompt a check for insect entry points and accumulated clutter. For a species record, photograph the spider before relocation and note whether it was indoors; a specialist may need closer structural details to distinguish similar cellar spiders.

sources.label: Natural History Museum: Daddy long legs spider

identification: Look for narrow, lance-shaped leaves with sparse teeth and a mixture of long hairs and shorter glandular hairs on the stems and foliage. Flowers arise from the upper leaf axils, with a floral tube commonly around 8 to 10 centimeters long. The fruit is an elongated, hairy capsule that opens into four valves. Other evening primroses also have yellow flowers, so photograph the tube, buds, leaves and capsule together. Regional accounts differ in plant height and whether an early rosette is present; neither feature should be used alone.
actions: In a garden, keep track of the plant through flowering and fruiting before deciding whether it belongs in the intended planting. If seedlings are appearing beyond that area, remove unwanted plants and collect developing capsules before they release seed. Avoid dumping fruiting stems along roadsides or woodland edges. For a botanical identification, measure the floral tube separately from the petals and include a side-view photograph. When working with old records, check whether the name Oenothera longiflora was used in a regional, misapplied sense rather than assuming it identifies the same plant everywhere.

sources.label: Biota of New Zealand: Oenothera affinis, Flora of New Zealand account

identification: The leaves are flat, with slightly rough edges, and may be softly hairy or nearly hairless. At the leaf junction is a short, membranous ligule that can look toothed or torn. The nodding spikelets carry prominent awns, while the small outer glumes are much shorter than the rest of the spikelet. Within each spikelet are sterile structures surrounding the fertile floret. Photograph a whole head and a single spikelet with a ruler. Checking both the annual base and the awned spikelet structure is more dependable than judging leaf width alone.
actions: Where removal is appropriate, lift the annual tuft before mature seed is dispersed and collect any heads that are already drying. Check neglected corners, soil stockpiles and disturbed bed edges for additional plants. Avoid moving seed-bearing material with soil or garden waste. If you are distinguishing it from another Ehrharta species, retain the base and a mature head for an experienced grass identifier; management can differ when a perennial grass is involved. After clearing a patch, restore suitable ground cover and monitor it through the next local growing season.

identification: The adult is slender and dark, roughly a centimeter long, with the extended antennae characteristic of longhorn beetles. Body length and general color are only starting points because many unrelated wood-boring beetles share that appearance. Photograph the upper surface, side, antennae and a size reference before seeking confirmation. Larvae concealed in a branch are even harder to name from a casual inspection. Record the tree species and whether the branch was alive, dying or already dead when the insect was found.
actions: Keep wood associated with a suspected finding at its original site while an identification is arranged, especially if it came from packing material or recently moved branches. Save an adult in a secure container for a local entomologist or plant-health service if asked to do so. An arborist can separately assess declining trees and decide whether dead branches need removal for safety or plant care. Avoid treating a healthy tree merely because an adult visited a light nearby; a confirmed insect, host association and evidence of activity are needed to judge the situation.

sources.label: California Department of Food and Agriculture: Icosium tomentosum assessment
New records for the Maltese Islands

identification: Workers are about 2 to 3 millimeters long, with unusually long legs and antennae. The first antennal segment extends far behind the head, a particularly useful feature under magnification. Their dark bodies may show a faint bluish sheen, and scattered pale hairs stand away from the surface. Several different ants are called crazy ants, so rapid movement alone is not diagnostic. Collect clear close photographs of the head, antennae and body, or have a specimen examined before applying advice intended for another species.
actions: Start by removing accessible crumbs and spills, storing food in closed containers and checking the routes workers use around doors, pipes and windows. Observe ants carrying food to help locate their nesting direction, then address suitable entry gaps. Inspect nearby plants for aphids, scales or mealybugs, which may supply honeydew. If activity persists, have the species confirmed and use a coordinated plan suited to the building and nest location. Spraying a few visible workers is unlikely to explain where the colony is living or prevent renewed foraging.

sources.label: UF IFAS: Crazy Ant, Paratrechina longicornis
University of Utah ant natural history: Paratrechina longicornis

identification: Look for elongated leaves with sharply serrated, sometimes double-serrated edges and dense terminal flower spikes. The small flowers are crowded along the spike, and the fruit is a small, slightly flattened capsule. Other upright speedwells and their garden hybrids can be very similar. Record the leaf shape, hairiness, branching and flower-spike arrangement together, and retain the cultivar label if the plant was purchased; flower color alone will not establish the species.
actions: Match a garden plant to a site with dependable growing-season moisture and observe how it performs through the local summer rather than assuming every cultivar has identical needs. Keep a record of flowering, stem strength and survival if comparing selections. If it begins appearing outside the intended bed, remove unwanted seedlings and cut seed-bearing stems before dispersal. For a wild record, document whether it is close to an old planting or truly part of a natural meadow community, then consult a regional flora before assigning a name or management status.

sources.label: Burke Herbarium: Veronica longifolia, Flora of North America description
University of Greifswald: Flora of Mongolia, Veronica longifolia

identification: Look for a relatively small slug with a short keel near the tail, watery colorless mucus and a breathing pore whose rim may be noticeably pale. Some individuals show a two-tone pattern, with the head, mantle or tail tip lighter than the sides. These are clues rather than definitive species characters. Research on its distribution shows that it can be confused with Deroceras laeve, D. sturanyi and D. panormitanum. Reliable confirmation may require specialist anatomical or molecular examination, so a photograph should remain a provisional record.
actions: Inspect vulnerable seedlings after dark or during damp weather to see which animals are actually feeding. Reduce unnecessary damp hiding places immediately beside a propagation tray, and check pot rims, containers and soil before moving plants to another site. Do not relocate collected slugs into natural areas. If a new distribution record matters, ask a mollusk specialist how to document or preserve a sample. Base garden management on observed damage and the local slug community rather than treating every small brown slug as this species.

sources.label: John Innes Centre Slugwatch: Brown field slug
A biography of an invasive terrestrial slug: spread, distribution and habitat of Deroceras invadens

identification: Examine the individual structures replacing the kernels. Their thin gray membranes rupture readily, leaving dark spore masses and eventually a conspicuous pointed or curved central column. An affected head can look more open than a healthy one. Covered kernel smut and head smut are different diseases, so an overall photograph of a blackened panicle is insufficient. Take close photographs before the spores disperse, record the sorghum variety and growth stage, and ask a plant diagnostic service to confirm the cause if the distinction affects crop decisions.
actions: Mark affected patches and avoid saving seed from visibly diseased plants. Contact the local crop adviser before harvesting or handling large numbers of smutted heads, and follow the diagnostic service's instructions when collecting a sample. For the next planting, use an appropriate healthy seed source and discuss locally recommended seed protection and resistant material. Texas A&M guidance emphasizes prevention through seed-applied protection; the useful decision is made before infection, rather than by trying to restore grain already replaced by smut. Keep notes so the following crop can be checked early.

sources.label: Moharam: First report of loose kernel smut of sorghum caused by Sporisorium cruentum in Egypt
Texas A&M AgriLife: Diagnosis and Management of Sorghum Diseases

identification: Look for stiff, leathery leaves with toothed edges, a glossy upper surface and dense gray-brown or rusty hairs beneath. Leaves tend to gather toward the ends of branches. Fragrant white flowers appear in terminal clusters, followed by rounded or oval yellow-orange fruit. Flowering and fruiting dates vary with climate, so do not exclude a tree merely because it is fruiting at a different time from a regional guide. Photograph the leaf underside, flower or fruit cluster and the entire tree. The common name Japanese plum can refer to more than one plant.
actions: Record whether the tree was planted and look for younger plants beyond the garden boundary. Where containment is appropriate, collect unwanted fallen fruit and keep fruit-bearing waste out of nearby forest or drainage areas. Have seedlings identified before removal, especially where other fruit trees grow. Established trees may need a managed removal plan rather than repeated pruning. The older Hawaiian guide describes cut-surface treatment, but its historical mixture is not a general prescription for current use. Ask the land manager about the site and follow up for seedlings after any removal.

identification: Look for drooping, rope-like flower clusters, often red or burgundy but sometimes gold or greenish in cultivated forms. Plants commonly reach about 3-5 feet, with alternate, simple leaves that can be green or reddish. The leaves have smooth edges rather than deeply cut lobes. Flower color and height vary, and seedlings lack the characteristic tassels. Other amaranths can be difficult to separate before flowering; photograph the complete flower head, a leafy stem and the leaf attachment. A red-leaved seedling alone is not a reliable species identification.
actions: If an ornamental planting is producing unwanted seedlings, remove or contain mature tassels before loose seeds are scattered into nearby soil. Check the ground again during the next growing season rather than treating one removal as the end of the problem. Record how far plants have spread from the original bed and whether they persist without care. In agricultural ground, ask for confirmation before applying advice intended for other pigweeds, which may have different growth habits or resistance concerns. Do not assume an unfamiliar volunteer is suitable to eat merely because some amaranths are cultivated as food.

sources.label: Purdue University: Quick Guide to Ornamental Annuals (archived PDF)

identification: The Flora Zambesiaca treatment describes slender upright stems, usually no more than about 20-30 centimeters tall, with very narrow leaves arising near the base. At the top are small clusters of flattened, narrow spikelets, accompanied by two to four leaf-like bracts. The tiny floral scales range from yellow to dark brown, have pale margins and a small backward-curving point. These details require a close view or magnification. Photograph the whole plant beside a scale, its basal leaves and a mature seed head. Many small sedges look alike, so a general flatsedge identification may be the most reliable initial report.
actions: Keep the exact habitat in your notes, including whether the plant grows in standing water, a seasonally wet patch or disturbed soil. Avoid moving mud or seed-bearing material between sites while seeking an identification. A botanist may need mature spikelets or fruits, so ask how to document or collect them before disturbing a wetland. For an unwanted patch on managed ground, first confirm its identity and local significance. Take photographs before any cutting, since removing the mature heads can make a small sedge much harder to identify later.

identification: Examine the small pale pink or nearly white flowers where the leaves join the stem. Their five petals are about as long as, or only slightly longer than, the green calyx beneath them. The mature fruit is a flattened disk, usually with ten or eleven segments. The backs of those segments are strongly wrinkled, with sharply angled edges rather than broad wings. These tiny features distinguish it more usefully than the general low-growing appearance. Include a ruler in photographs of flowers and mature fruit, and retain the scientific name used by the source if checking an older record.
actions: Have the identity checked before applying a management guide for common mallow or little mallow, which are different species. For a few unwanted plants in a garden, preventing seed production is a sensible containment objective; avoid carrying mature fruit in discarded soil or garden waste. Photograph the plant before removal and revisit the patch for seedlings. In a larger agricultural infestation, diagnosis should come before a treatment decision because the available general mallow advice does not establish equal effectiveness for every species. A plant found beside a road should be documented without stepping into traffic or disturbing land without permission.

sources.label: University of Washington Burke Herbarium: Malva pusilla

identification: The Flora of China account of A. humilis describes a smooth, woody shrub with leathery, unlobed leaves that are elliptic or broader toward the tip. The leaf edges are entire, and the flower clusters occur mainly at branch tips. Small pink or purplish-red flowers are followed by rounded fruit becoming dull red to purplish black. These features help document a candidate, but dark berries and glossy leaves also occur in related ardisias. Photograph where the flower or fruit cluster attaches, both leaf surfaces and the whole shrub; do not rely on the shoebutton common name alone.
actions: If you find a suspected plant outside cultivation, record its location and whether seedlings surround it, then send the photographs to a botanical or invasive-plant specialist. Explain that the name may have been confused with A. elliptica. Avoid distributing berries, seedlings or nursery stock under an uncertain identification. Do not copy removal requirements or control recipes from a shoebutton ardisia guide until the species concept has been checked. Keep any original nursery label or historical reference with the record, as that information may help explain the mismatch.

sources.label: Field Museum Laos Ardisia humilis DDS15034

identification: Look for long, narrow, glossy leaves arranged spirally along the stems. Large funnel-shaped flowers are usually yellow, although orange-flowered forms occur. The fruit is broad and somewhat triangular or diamond-shaped, becoming dark brown to black when ripe; it contains hard seeds within a stone. Smithsonian descriptions distinguish this shape from a round berry. Photograph the foliage, intact flower and fruit without breaking stems or handling seeds. Common oleander has a different leaf arrangement and fruit form, so a yellow flower or the word oleander alone is not enough.
actions: Keep children, pets and livestock away from fallen fruit and pruning waste. Do not taste the fruit or use plant preparations as a home remedy. If managing an unwanted specimen, arrange safe handling and disposal rather than leaving cut material where animals may reach it. Record seedlings beyond cultivation and keep fruiting branches out of natural areas. Florida currently identifies a high predicted invasion risk while reassessment is underway; that assessment is a regional planning tool, not proof of harm at every planted tree. Confirm local guidance before deciding on removal.

sources.label: Smithsonian Flora of Hawaii: Thevetia peruviana

identification: Look for slim gray trunks marked by rings of old leaf scars and a short, smooth green crownshaft below the leaves. The leaves are feather-shaped, with broad, flat leaflets whose ends look jagged or bitten off. Branched flower stalks emerge below the crownshaft, producing small cream-colored flowers and clusters of bright red, roughly half-inch fruit. The leaflets are darker above and paler beneath. Photograph the trunk base as well as the crown, leaflet tips and fruit. A photograph of red palm fruit alone will not separate this species from several other ornamental palms.
actions: For a suspected escape, note whether the young plants stand apart from the main clump and record their distance from planted adults. Have their identity checked before removal, particularly where native palms occur. If containment is needed, collect fallen fruit and avoid discarding fruiting stalks in unmanaged vegetation. Tall palms and heavy fronds should be assessed by someone equipped for the work rather than climbed casually. The cited references primarily describe cultivation and identification, so the presence of a garden clump does not by itself justify calling the palm an ecological threat at that site.

identification: Look for arching, prickly canes and leaves divided into several small, leathery, toothed leaflets. White, five-petaled flowers usually appear singly, sometimes in twos or threes. A useful detail is the set of large, leaflike bracts tucked beneath each flower, with deeply cut edges and hairy undersides. Photograph these from the side, along with the leaves and prickles. Plants often form tangled clumps. Other wild and cultivated roses can look similar, so a thorny cane or a rose hip alone is not enough to identify this species, especially near gardens containing hybrids.
actions: Map the edges of a suspected thicket and record whether it is expanding into pasture, woodland openings or paths. Wear protective clothing if approaching canes, and do not enter a dense patch simply to obtain a closer photograph. Small new plants are easier to assess than a large established thicket. Texas A&M provides species-specific management guidance for landowners; use a plan suited to the site rather than assuming ordinary mowing or one pruning will solve the problem. Keep follow-up visits in that plan, and protect nearby desirable vegetation when arranging treatment. Obtain the landowner's permission before any removal.

sources.label: University of Georgia invasive species: Macartney rose
Texas A&M: How to control Macartney rose

identification: The University of Florida describes an upright, rounded or oval crown with thick, leathery, olive-green leaves that can reach about six inches long. Small yellow flowers are easily missed, although fragrant. Rounded fruit develops from yellow toward dark purple at maturity. Photograph the leaves from both sides, a leafy branch and any flowers or fruit; a distant crown outline is not sufficient to distinguish this tree from other evergreen ornamentals. Include the setting in the photograph, particularly if the plant could be a remnant of an old landscaped area.
actions: When checking for escape, look beyond the planted tree for younger individuals and record their number and distance from the nearest known planting. Keep fallen fruit and fruit-bearing landscape waste out of nearby natural areas where containment is a concern. Confirm seedlings with a botanist before removing them, and ask an arborist or land manager to assess a larger tree. Do not treat old landscaping recommendations as current invasive-species guidance. Mark suspected seedlings on a site sketch and revisit them; their survival and growth help distinguish a persistent escape from a single season's fallen fruit.

sources.label: Gilman and Watson: Noronhia emarginata, original abstract via AGRIS

identification: Look for glossy green leaves and flowers with a slender tube opening into five broad, spreading lobes. Many flowers have a contrasting central eye. Cultivars range from white through pink, red and purple shades, so color alone is not diagnostic. Mature fruit consists of paired, narrow follicles rather than a fleshy berry. Plants may be upright or spreading depending on the cultivar. Photograph the whole plant, leaves, flower face and flower tube, and include any paired fruit. Do not identify it solely from a nursery label saying periwinkle, since that name is also used for creeping Vinca groundcovers.
actions: If plants appear away from a maintained bed, record whether they are seedlings or established flowering plants and how far they occur from cultivation. Prevent unwanted seed movement by containing mature fruit and garden waste rather than dumping plants beside natural vegetation. Have the identity checked before using advice for Vinca major or Vinca minor. Florida assessments distinguish southern areas needing caution from other regions, reinforcing the need for local context. Keep the plant out of food preparations; its use in medicine does not make home-grown material safe to consume. Report persistent escapes without assuming every ornamental planting needs removal.

identification: Look for opposite, leathery leaves, gray-brown stems with pale wart-like spots and trumpet-shaped pink or purple flowers with five spreading lobes. Large fruits occur in opposing pairs, opening when mature to release many seeds with silky hairs. The South African research account describes pale leaf stalks and midribs as useful comparison features. Photograph those structures and the flower side view, not just flower color. Do not break stems to test for the milky sap. A specialist may need the combination of leaves, flowers and fruit to distinguish the two rubbervines.
actions: Keep people and animals from eating any part of the plant. If it is climbing into trees, document the base and extent without pulling overhead tangles down on yourself. Report a new wild population to the local invasive-plant program; Hawaiian agencies specifically prioritize rubbervine response. Prevent mature pods from being scattered and avoid sharing cuttings or seeds. Arrange a site-specific removal and follow-up plan, especially near waterways or valuable native plants. The regional restrictions described in Australian or South African references do not automatically apply to a United States property.

identification: Look for a low, branched plant with opposite, thick leaves and rounded scallops or teeth along their edges. Dense clusters of small, tubular flowers rise above the foliage. Flower colors vary widely among cultivated forms, including red, orange, yellow and white. The fleshy leaves and compact clusters together are more useful than flower color alone. Photograph a complete leaf pair, the stem and a flower cluster, and retain a cultivar label if available. Do not apply a description of a tall, leaf-plantlet-producing kalanchoe to this species simply because the plants share a genus.
actions: For plants found outside a pot or maintained bed, record whether they appear rooted and growing independently or have only recently been discarded. Contain unwanted plants and living cuttings rather than dumping them on rocks, drainage edges or natural vegetation. Check around a former planting for new growth after cleanup. Confirm the identity before deciding whether local invasive-plant guidance applies; the cited Florida account does not currently treat this species as a general problem there. If a suspected escape persists or expands, document repeated observations so reviewers can distinguish a surviving garden plant from an established population.

sources.label: Universidad Francisco Marroquin Arboretum: Kalanchoe blossfeldiana

identification: Look for narrow, pointed leaves with conspicuous teeth, lower leaves gathered near the base and additional leaves along the stem. Each white flower opens into a star-like face from a very long, slender tube. The Smithsonian flora distinguishes the solitary flowers at leaf joints and tubes about 10-15 centimeters long from related plants with shorter or differently colored flowers. Photograph the flower from the side as well as face-on so that the tube is visible. Do not break a leaf or stem to demonstrate its white sap, which can irritate skin and eyes.
actions: Keep children and pets from handling or eating the plant, and wear gloves when authorized removal is appropriate. Avoid touching your face while working with damaged stems. Record the habitat and whether plants occur beyond an intentional planting, and seek local advice before clearing vegetation where native status is uncertain. Contain unwanted flowering or fruiting material instead of depositing it in another shady, moist spot. For a suspected new population, photographs and location details are a safer first submission than transporting a live plant. The sources support caution and identification, not a universal eradication prescription.

identification: Look for leaves widest toward the tip, narrowing toward the base, with fine teeth concentrated toward the outer end. Branched greenish-yellow flower structures occur at the stem tips, and smooth, three-lobed capsules develop afterward. Stems may have a reddish tinge. The plant contains milky latex, but do not break it to test that character. Photograph the upper branching pattern, leaf edges and mature capsules. Petty spurge is a useful comparison, while narrow-leaved perennial spurges differ in overall foliage. Regional accounts disagree about some leaf-arrangement and seasonal details, so those are not used here as decisive characters.
actions: If the plant is unwanted on managed ground, identify it while flowers or fruit are available and prevent mature seed from being moved with soil or plant waste. Handle damaged stems cautiously and keep sap away from skin and eyes. Small annual patches should be addressed before seed dispersal, with later checks for new seedlings. Do not assume a root-control strategy written for leafy spurge is appropriate. In crops, have the species confirmed before selecting treatment, since crop safety and the growth stage matter as much as the common name.

sources.label: Danish Crop Protection Online: Euphorbia helioscopia

identification: Look for relatively small, broad oval or rounded leaves with finely toothed edges and a short pointed tip. Fragrant white flowers with five petals grow in short clusters. Small cherries change from green through red to glossy black, with a large stone inside. Young stems have conspicuous pale pore-like marks, while older bark becomes fissured. Other cherries share white flowers and dark fruit, so photograph a leafy twig, the flower cluster and mature fruit with a size reference. A tree growing beside an abandoned orchard is not automatically the same species as the former crop.
actions: Document seedlings around and beyond an old planting, especially where they are entering unmanaged vegetation. Confirm the species before removing young trees that might be native cherries. Where removal is appropriate, Washington guidance notes that small plants can be pulled or dug, while established trees may resprout after cutting. Plan follow-up rather than assuming a bare stump means the tree is gone. For larger plants, arrange professional help and site-appropriate treatment instead of using an unspecified chemical recipe. Keep records of the original location and management so later observers can interpret new seedlings accurately.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Prunus mahaleb

identification: Look for narrow leaves in opposite pairs along upright or reclining stems. The five petals are sharply toothed at their outer ends and often carry a darker ring near the flower center, sometimes with pale speckles. Flowers are commonly pink to reddish purple, although white forms occur. Basal leaves are somewhat broader toward their tips than the narrow stem leaves. Other garden pinks and hybrids can resemble it, so photograph the leaf arrangement, the green tube beneath the flower and several flowers together. Flower color alone is unreliable because cultivated forms vary.
actions: If a planting is producing unwanted volunteers, record whether new plants arise close to the clump or farther away, and prevent mature seed from being scattered during cleanup. Where removal is justified, account for underground growth as well as the visible flowering stems. Revisit the patch in the following season to check for surviving shoots or seedlings. Have uncertain wild plants identified before clearing them, particularly in places with native members of the pink family. Its use as an ornamental and its appearance in a regional weed guide do not establish the same management priority at every site.

identification: The Flora of New Zealand describes reddish-brown, wiry branchlets and small leaves that may vary in shape even on one plant. They can be rounded, oval or broader toward the end, with a darker upper surface and paler underside. Small inconspicuous flowers develop into glossy, black, three-angled fruit surrounded by enlarged, fleshy white flower parts. Photograph the branching habit, several leaves and any fruit. Record whether the plant climbs into surrounding vegetation or remains a low mat; that helps a botanist compare it with other Muehlenbeckia species.
actions: If the vine is spreading from a planting, document the rooted base and the area covered before cutting it back. Avoid pulling a heavy tangle off another plant in a way that damages branches beneath it. Contain removed material and watch for surviving growth rather than assuming one pruning removes the established plant. Save photographs of fruiting stems before pruning; cutting away those features can make it harder to distinguish this vine from another wire vine. Confirm the identity and local priorities before arranging more extensive control.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Muehlenbeckia complexa
UC ANR: Enchanting plants or garden thugs
Kew: Muehlenbeckia complexa accepted identity and range

identification: Look for opposite, mostly smooth leaves and white flowers with five deeply split petals. Beneath the petals, the fused sepals form a swollen, bladder-like tube marked by a conspicuous network of veins. Stems and leaves are usually much less hairy than those of white campion, although some accounts note fine hairs, so hairlessness should not be treated as an absolute rule. Photograph the inflated tube from the side, the flower face and a leafy stem. A basal rosette in grass may be difficult to recognize before it develops flowering stems.
actions: On managed ground, record the extent of the patch and whether new shoots appear after cutting. Prevent mature seed capsules from being carried into another field with plant waste or equipment.
