For suspected spread into sensitive habitat, send photographs and a location to the land manager or a regional herbarium before arranging removal. Do not cut a large tree simply because it is nonnative; consider site goals, safety and habitat effects. Where confirmed seedlings are unwanted, remove them while small with the owner's permission and check for further recruitment. Leave seed-bearing cones and excavated soil at the site until appropriate disposal is arranged rather than distributing them to new areas.

sources.label: Nebraska Extension: Tree Identification Manual (4H332-DL; publisher purchase record) (publication record)

identification: Inspect an already loose sheath for concentrated white wax and the insects beneath it, without stripping healthy stems simply to search. Photograph the whole bamboo, the affected stem joint and a close view of the colony. Living Antonina pretiosa cannot reliably be separated from A. nakaharai by appearance. Specialists examine slide-mounted specimens: A. pretiosa has abdominal plates and lacks, or has only a few, dorsal multilocular pores near the anal opening. Record the bamboo name if known and whether the insects occur on new shoots, older stems or both.
actions: Keep an affected potted bamboo apart from other plants while obtaining identification, and pause moving divisions, cut stems or nursery stock from it. Ask an extension diagnostic service how to submit a sample containing insects, wax and the relevant sheath. Include when the bamboo arrived and where it came from if that information is available. Do not apply a treatment intended for another bamboo insect based only on the common name. A confirmed identification and assessment of the plant condition should come before a control plan.

sources.label: Lahey, Powell and Miller 2026 FDACS circular: differential diagnosis of Antonina pretiosa and A. nakaharai

identification: Broad, strongly pleated leaves rise from the base beside a separate, upright flowering stem. The flowers have a striking contrast between pale outer surfaces and reddish-brown inner surfaces, with a pinkish to purple, partly tubular lip. Photograph both the front and back of a flower, its lip, the whole flower stem and the leaf bases. Cultivated hybrids and closely related swamp orchids can complicate identification. Leaf size or flower color alone is not a reliable way to settle the name, especially on plants with a nursery history.
actions: If you find one outside cultivation, record whether it is near a garden, discarded potting material or an apparently undisturbed wetland. Photograph it in place and ask a botanist or land manager to confirm the identification before removing an unfamiliar orchid. Do not collect wild plants or transfer them to another natural area. Keep garden divisions and spent plant material out of wetland edges. For a confirmed escaped population, let the managing agency decide whether monitoring or removal is appropriate for that location.

sources.label: North American Orchid Conservation Center: nun's orchid

identification: Mature females are strongly domed and roughly 5-6 millimeters across, ranging from brown to gray-brown. Young stages are much smaller and can be pinkish or orange-yellow. Inspect several twigs and leaf undersides rather than judging the tree from one bump. Photograph colonies with a size reference, the host leaves and a wider view of the branch. Several soft scales look similar to an unaided eye; a specialist may need a specimen to distinguish nut scale from other rounded brown scales. Note whether you see living insects, mobile young or only dead females.
actions: Keep a record of the affected branches and whether the tree shows reduced growth or substantial leaf damage. Ask an extension service or qualified arborist to identify the scale and assess the severity before treating a large tree. Do not move infested nursery plants to a new site while that assessment is pending. If management is warranted, its timing should follow the locally observed vulnerable stage rather than a calendar copied from another country. Avoid stripping bark or pruning healthy major limbs simply to remove scattered scales.

sources.label: Alford (2012): Pests of Ornamental Trees, Shrubs and Flowers, second edition — publisher citation record
Gallipoli Cognato regional park: Eulecanium tiliae
NIBIO Plant Protection Encyclopedia: Eulecanium tiliae

identification: Look for a heavy brown body, a pale muzzle with conspicuous white whiskers, and a long, rounded tail with sparse hair. A beaver has a broad, flattened tail; a muskrat has a narrower tail flattened from side to side and usually dark whiskers. Nutria also have webbing on the hind feet. Size alone is unreliable because young nutria can overlap with other rodents. From a safe distance, photograph the face and tail as well as the whole animal. For tracks, include a familiar object for scale without stepping into unstable banks.
actions: Report a suspected nutria with the exact location, date, photographs and number seen to your state wildlife agency or the land manager. In California, the wildlife department specifically asks for prompt reports to its invasive species program. Avoid approaching, feeding or trying to relocate the animal. Do not disturb a burrow in a levee or bank; report the damage separately to whoever manages the structure. Wildlife rules and response programs vary by state, so obtain local direction before any trapping or removal. Repeated sightings at one site can be useful, but do not delay an initial report while seeking perfect photographs.

sources.label: California Department of Fish and Wildlife: nutria

identification: Workers are small and light to reddish brown, with conspicuous upright hairs visible under magnification. Those features can help place an ant in Nylanderia but cannot reliably identify this species. In particular, workers of Nylanderia vividula and N. terricola can be difficult to separate; the North American revision uses male characters to resolve them. Photograph several workers, the trail and the nesting substrate if visible. If winged ants appear, record them too without assuming they are the same species merely because they are nearby.
actions: For ants indoors, note where the trail enters and what attracts it, then remove accessible food residues and moisture while seeking an identification. Do not move soil, potted plants or nesting material to another property in an attempt to relocate a colony. Ask an extension entomologist how to provide specimens if the name matters for a report or management decision. Treat outdoor sightings as observations, not an automatic reason to eliminate native-looking ants. If control is needed inside a building, use a plan based on the confirmed ant and the entry route rather than indiscriminate outdoor spraying.

sources.label: Kallal and LaPolla: Nearctic Nylanderia revision

identification: The winged, live-bearing females described by INRAE are yellow and about 1.6-1.7 millimeters long. Look under magnification for dark markings along the head and thorax, paired marks on the abdomen and the pattern of the short tailpipes. Young aphids have shorter, banded antennae. Photograph the leaf underside, several insects from above and the host leaves, including their arrangement on the twig. Tiny details of the short tailpipes and tail are useful to specialists but are difficult to judge in a phone photograph. Do not use a yellow body alone to distinguish it from related aphids.
actions: Record the host tree as accurately as possible and note whether insects are scattered or clustered on many leaves. If foliage is curling, discoloring or dropping, photograph that separately rather than assuming the aphids caused it. A local extension service can help identify the insects and assess whether any response is needed. Avoid treating an otherwise healthy tree simply because a few aphids are present. When submitting a sample, follow the diagnostic service's instructions and include the affected leaf; do not transfer infested twigs to another living tree.

sources.label: Blackman and Eastop: oak aphid host associations

identification: Watch for unexpected wilting and leaf loss during the growing season, especially when a red oak's upper canopy changes rapidly. Leaves may develop bronzed or brown margins with a distinct boundary against remaining green tissue, and some fall while partly green. Groups of affected neighboring oaks can be an important clue, but are not proof. Photograph the entire crown, several leaves and the positions of nearby oaks. Note the first symptom date, recent pruning or storm damage and which trees changed first. A diagnostic laboratory may need a correctly collected branch sample.
actions: Contact an extension diagnostic service or arborist familiar with oak wilt promptly, and ask before cutting sample branches or removing a tree. Avoid creating fresh wounds during your region's high-risk period; those dates vary with local conditions. Do not move firewood from a suspected infected oak to another area. Confirmed sites may require coordinated work across neighboring properties to interrupt root spread, so removing one tree without a plan may not protect the others. Professional treatment choices should follow the diagnosis, oak group and site conditions, not a generalized home remedy.

sources.label: Michigan State University: forest pest identification

identification: Look for dark workers of two noticeably different sizes traveling from the same nest. Major workers have unusually large, heavily sculptured heads and a thick, curved basal antennal segment. Under magnification, the antennae end in a three-segmented club and the waist has two segments. Small workers can resemble the native Pheidole dentata, so a photograph of one minor worker is not enough. Photograph both worker sizes with a scale reference, the nest entrance and the surrounding ground. A specialist can check head sculpture and antennal shape before confirming the species.
actions: Record the location, habitat and whether you saw an active nest or only wandering workers. If ants arrive with potted plants or soil, hold that material in place while seeking identification instead of moving it to another property. Do not dig through a nest to look for a queen; workers of both sizes are more useful initial evidence and disturbing the site can affect other insects. For a building nuisance, address the entry point and accessible food, then seek advice based on a confirmed identification. Outdoor presence alone is not a reason for broad insecticide treatment.

sources.label: Mississippi Entomological Museum: obscure big-headed ant
Storz and Tschinkel: distribution and ecological associations

identification: Under a microscope, workers have nine antennal segments without a distinct terminal club and a single, small waist node that may be hidden by the abdomen. In this species the first large abdominal segment has dense, close-lying hairs that give it a relatively dull appearance. Eye size and the length of the antenna base are also used in identification. These details separate it from similar rover ants such as Brachymyrmex patagonicus; overall color is not enough. Take close photographs from above and the side and include a size reference if possible.
actions: Note whether the ants are nesting in soil, associated with a potted plant or entering a building, and photograph the trail before cleaning it away. If they are indoors, remove food spills and inspect the entry route while obtaining an identification. Avoid moving occupied pots, soil or decaying wood to another location. An extension entomologist may need collected workers to settle the name, so ask for sampling instructions. Do not assume a management recommendation for another rover ant applies here, and avoid spraying an outdoor area solely because these tiny ants are present.

sources.label: Mississippi Entomological Museum: obscure rover ant
Longino: Brachymyrmex obscurior observations and diagnosis
Ortiz-Sepulveda et al. 2019 original Brachymyrmex revision

identification: Look for hairy, twining stems and broad leaves that may be heart-shaped or deeply divided into three lobes. The underside of the leaf has a soft, silky covering. Large funnel-shaped flowers are blue to violet, with paler bands and a darker throat. Photograph the leaf underside, the flower and its surrounding sepals, and a length of stem showing how the leaves attach. Other morning glories and bindweeds can look similar, so blue flowers or a three-lobed leaf alone are not enough for confirmation.
actions: Keep cut vines and roots out of waterways, woodland edges and informal garden-waste piles. For a small confirmed patch, follow local guidance on removing rooted stems and collecting fragments, then revisit the site for regrowth. Avoid pulling an entire heavy canopy of vines from a tree, which can damage branches or bring material down on you. Large infestations need a plan that protects the plants underneath and allows follow-up. Clean fragments from tools and machinery before moving on, and ask a local weed program about disposal and any treatment appropriate to the site.

identification: Its glossy leaves are divided into several long leaflets radiating from one central point, like the spokes of an umbrella. Mature flowering trees produce long red flower-bearing arms above the foliage, followed by fruits that darken as they ripen. Photograph a complete compound leaf, the trunk base and any flowers or fruit. Do not confuse the species with smaller umbrella-tree ornamentals merely because the leaves share that spoke-like pattern. Young plants may lack flowers, and seedlings growing on another tree can be difficult to see from below.
actions: In regions where the species is invasive, choose a locally appropriate noninvasive replacement rather than planting another fruiting tree. Check nearby ground and accessible tree bases for seedlings, and ask the land manager before removing plants on public land. Do not climb or cut into a host tree to reach an established epiphytic plant. Large octopus trees can be difficult to kill and may need repeated professional treatment, so arrange follow-up rather than assuming one cut has finished the job. Keep removed fruit-bearing material contained during disposal and monitor the surrounding area for new seedlings.

sources.label: UF/IFAS: integrated management of nonnative plants

identification: Males are small, delicate beetles with pale brown wing covers, relatively long legs and unclubbed antennae. Females lack wings and can look more like larvae, but their covering is short and soft rather than arranged in the distinctive bristled rows of the true larva. Photograph adults, larvae or shed skins with a size reference. Check the surrounding object for small chewed areas, loose debris and additional skins. Retain an insect specimen for identification rather than relying on damage alone, which can resemble the work of other collection pests.
actions: If you suspect activity in a specimen drawer, textile or other stored object, isolate the affected item in a suitable sealed enclosure and tell the collection manager or a conservator. Record the exact shelf or drawer and inspect nearby material without carrying it through clean storage areas. Remove unrelated debris and dead insects from the surrounding room, taking care not to vacuum fragile collection material. Treatment should be chosen for the object as well as the insect; household sprays, improvised heat or freezing can damage sensitive artifacts. Continue monitoring after treatment to find any remaining activity.

sources.label: Ransom Center: odd beetle identification cards
Canadian Conservation Institute: materials and damaging insects
University of Illinois: collection pest identification

identification: Adults are elongated, dark brown to blackish beetles with long antennae, patches of grayish hair on the wing covers and shiny raised areas on the section behind the head. Emergence holes are oval rather than the tiny round holes typical of some powderpost beetles. Larvae leave tunnels containing wood fragments and pellet-like waste. Photograph a beetle, the hole with a ruler and the affected timber together. Note the type and approximate age of the wood if known. Old holes can remain long after activity ends, so fresh debris and confirmed larvae matter more than holes alone.
actions: Save an adult specimen in a closed container and contact an extension service or licensed wood-destroying-insect professional for identification and an assessment of activity. If a load-bearing member appears weakened, seek a structural assessment as well. Do not cover holes, replace major timbers or purchase a whole-building treatment before the cause is established. Keep suspect lumber and firewood from being moved to another building. A management plan should account for how deeply larvae are feeding, whether the infestation is active and which wood is affected.

sources.label: Penn State Extension: old house borer
University of Maryland Extension: old house borer

identification: The long, hanging, ribbon-like green fronds are usually undivided but can fork. The blade lacks a strong central midrib and has a network of veins. A narrower fertile spike hangs from the blade near its base or middle and carries the spore-producing structures in two rows. Photograph the whole hanging plant, its attachment to the trunk and any fertile spike. Do not mistake the spike for a flower or seed pod. Other strap-leaved epiphytic ferns may resemble it when no fertile structure is visible.
actions: Photograph a suspected plant where it grows, with the location and host tree if known, and seek confirmation from a regional herbarium or fern specialist. Avoid peeling it from bark or climbing a tree to obtain a specimen. In Hawaii, first establish whether it belongs to the native population before discussing any intervention. For an unexpected Florida occurrence, document whether it appears planted or self-established. Keep cultivated material out of natural areas, but do not infer a need for eradication from the catalog entry alone.

identification: Look for long, narrow, leathery leaves arranged opposite one another or in whorls along woody stems. Clusters of showy flowers appear at the shoot tips and may be pink, white or other cultivated colors. The fruit consists of long narrow pods that split when mature. Photograph the leaf arrangement, a flower cluster and any pods, along with the whole shrub. Flower color alone is unreliable because cultivars differ. Do not taste a leaf or use broken stems for identification, and keep plant material away from children and animals.
actions: If oleander is growing beyond a planting, record how far the plants extend and whether young seedlings are present. Ask a local weed program about its status before deciding on removal. Wear gloves when handling cut material and keep it out of animal feed, cooking fires and places where pets may chew it. Do not burn oleander. For large plants or work near a waterway, arrange a site-appropriate removal and disposal plan. Follow the area afterward for new growth rather than assuming that cutting the top alone resolves an escape.

identification: Look for small yellow bodies with dark legs, antennae and paired black tailpipes projecting from the rear of the abdomen. Young aphids resemble smaller wingless adults; winged forms can appear as colonies spread. Photograph the colony and the plant's growing tip rather than only one insect. Check carefully for butterfly eggs and caterpillars before disturbing milkweed. Also look for predators and swollen, immobile aphid remains left by parasitoids. Those signs can help explain why a colony changes without a treatment, although they do not identify every natural enemy involved.
actions: If the milkweed is growing well, monitor moderate colonies instead of automatically spraying. Where aphids are concentrated on a few shoots, ask local extension guidance about a targeted nonchemical response that protects any butterfly eggs or larvae present. Avoid systemic insecticides on milkweed intended for monarchs or other butterflies. A product described as an aphid treatment is not necessarily safe for those insects. Record yellowing, distorted new growth or a failure to develop normally, and seek advice if damage persists rather than treating the yellow insects as an emergency by themselves.

sources.label: Xerces and partners: milkweed pest care

identification: Adult moths have a dark body with bluish highlights and small pale spots, brown forewings with red along the leading area, and red hindwings. The antennae are comb-like. Caterpillars bear tufts of hairs rather than the dense, continuous hairy covering of a saltmarsh caterpillar. Photograph the larva from above and the side, the plant it is feeding on and, if available, an adult with the wings visible. An orange or hairy caterpillar on oleander is not enough for an identification because several moth species use the plant.
actions: Document the insect and the extent of leaf feeding before deciding whether any response is needed. For a confirmed spotted oleander caterpillar, avoid routine control solely to remove its presence; the Florida account specifically distinguishes it from the pestier look-alike. Do not handle the oleander foliage casually while photographing or collecting insects because the plant itself is poisonous. If the shrub is severely defoliated, ask an extension entomologist to confirm which caterpillar is responsible. Keep the old name with the observation so a reviewer can reconcile historical records without losing their context.

sources.label: Weller and colleagues: Empyreuma species limits
UF/IFAS EENY-017 original PDF: spotted oleander caterpillar moth

identification: Look closely at affected stems for tiny, rounded scale covers associated with shallow or deeper depressions in the plant surface. Colonies can be accompanied by swelling or misshapen twigs. Wax filaments may be visible around the cover under magnification, but a bump or pit alone is not diagnostic. Photograph the whole plant, several affected twigs and the covers with a ruler or other scale reference. Confirming the species requires examination of prepared adult females, so even a clear close-up may only support a preliminary identification.
actions: Keep a suspect nursery or houseplant separate from other plants and avoid distributing cuttings while seeking a diagnosis. Tell the extension service or plant-health inspector which plant is affected and whether it was recently purchased or imported. Ask how to submit a twig sample without losing the attached scales. Do not strip bark from a valuable plant to expose them. If the identification is confirmed, choose a local management plan based on the host and active insect stages, then check new growth and nearby plants for continuing activity rather than judging success from old pits.

sources.label: Cuban original survey: scale insects on medicinal plants

identification: Look for opposite, leathery, narrow to broadly lance-shaped leaves, usually dark green above and pale or silvery beneath in cultivated European olives. Older trunks have gray bark, and small pale flowers develop into fleshy olives with one hard stone. Photograph both leaf surfaces, a twig showing the opposite arrangement and any fruit. A planted tree may have a nursery label that helps clarify its cultivar. Russian olive belongs to a different genus, Elaeagnus, despite its common name, and other shrubs with silvery leaves can also cause confusion.
actions: Check open space near a fruiting tree for self-sown seedlings, especially around places where birds perch. Record whether plants are deliberately maintained or growing independently. Where olive is escaping, remove small confirmed seedlings only with the landowner's permission and revisit the area for further recruitment. Keep fruit and pruning waste out of natural areas. When choosing a replacement near sensitive habitat, consult local planting guidance rather than assuming a cultivar will remain fruitless under all conditions. Established escaped trees may need professional removal and follow-up for regrowth.

sources.label: NSW WeedWise: African and European olive distinctions

identification: Adults are small flies, about 4-5 millimeters long, with mostly clear wings and a small dark mark near the wing tip. Body color varies, so a brown or orange fly alone is not a diagnosis. On fruit, look for small egg-laying punctures, soft damaged areas and pale larvae inside the flesh. Photograph the fruit surface and any fly without releasing insects from a suspect sample. Other damage can scar olives, and specialist examination of the wing pattern helps separate this species from other fruit flies.
actions: Inspect fruit as it develops and follow a local olive-pest monitoring program rather than waiting until harvest to look for damage. Remove leftover or fallen infested fruit using locally recommended disposal, and do not carry suspect olives to another growing area. Ask extension staff how to submit a contained sample if the fly is unexpected in your region. Orchard management may involve coordinated trapping, sanitation and carefully timed treatments; a trap catch by itself does not measure all fruit damage. For home trees, discuss whether maintaining a fruit crop is practical before starting repeated treatments.

identification: Look for fluffy or cotton-like wax around tender olive growth. Beneath it, the young are flattened and greenish to tan; adults are small, pale, strong-jumping insects with a few dark marks on the forewings. Honeydew may support dark sooty mold on nearby surfaces. Mealybugs and other wax-producing insects can look similar from a distance, so photograph the exposed insects as well as the wax. Include the affected buds or flowers, the host leaves and a whole-tree view showing whether damage is localized or widespread.
actions: Check young shoots during active growth and keep notes on flower loss or distorted growth rather than treating wax alone as a measure of severity. Do not distribute infested nursery plants or cuttings. Ask a local extension adviser to confirm the insect and discuss whether management is needed, particularly on young trees or trees grown for fruit. Preserve beneficial insects and avoid unnecessary broad sprays. If pruning is part of a local management plan, keep it proportionate to the tree and its season rather than removing large healthy branches simply to eliminate every waxy patch.

sources.label: Malta: integrated pest management for olives

identification: Female covers are small, oval and grayish, about 2.5 millimeters long. Male covers are more elongated and have a dark spot at one end. The insect beneath a cover is reddish purple. Photograph the covers on a twig and any dark purple marks on otherwise green olives. A scale cover can remain after the insect has died, so a specialist may need to examine several to assess live activity. Other armored scales occur on olives, and fruit spotting alone can have other causes; include both the insect and the damage when seeking identification.
actions: Inspect several parts of the tree and record whether the problem is concentrated on fruit, twigs or foliage. Ask an extension adviser to assess living scales and natural-enemy activity before choosing treatment. Avoid broad insecticides that can disrupt the small parasitoid wasps responsible for much of the existing control. If ants are interfering with beneficial insects, discuss a targeted ant-management approach rather than spraying the canopy indiscriminately. Keep infested nursery stock from being moved to other sites and revisit affected trees to compare new damage with old marks.

sources.label: Moursi and colleagues: olive scale field ecology

identification: The caterpillars are green with a pale yellow head and may reach about two centimeters. Unfortunately, the available Florida account does not provide a dependable larval character separating this species from all similar Palpita. Adults have nearly white wings and resemble the native P. kimballi and P. quadristigmalis. Dark scales on the mouthparts and front legs are clues; definitive confirmation can require examination of adult genitalia. Photograph the caterpillar, webbed leaves and host, and seek advice about obtaining an adult specimen rather than assigning a species name from a green larva alone.
actions: On a nursery plant, keep affected material from being distributed while its identity is checked. Record which shoots are damaged and whether new feeding continues, rather than stripping all webbed leaves immediately. Send photographs and host information to an extension diagnostic service; ask before moving live caterpillars or attempting to rear them. If treatment is needed, it should address active larvae on the confirmed host and protect beneficial insects. Do not apply olive-pest advice for Palpita vitrealis simply because that different species is also called an olive leaf moth in some references.

sources.label: Burla Lemos et al. 2019: first Palpita persimilis record in southeastern Uruguay

identification: Look for spreading stems, leaves divided into rounded leaflets and clusters of small, four-petaled white flowers. Mature narrow pods are particularly important: their seeds lie in one row in each of the pod's two compartments. Ordinary watercress, Nasturtium officinale, usually has two rows in each compartment and different seed-surface markings. The species can hybridize, making some plants difficult to name. Photograph flowers and intact mature pods, then ask a botanist to examine a small permitted sample if necessary. Leaves alone are less dependable, especially on plants growing in deeper water.
actions: Record the waterbody, the extent of the patch and whether it is attached in place or floating downstream. Avoid pulling apart a large patch in moving water, where loose plant material can be carried elsewhere. Clean plant fragments from boots and equipment before leaving the site, and do not transplant wild watercress into another stream or pond. Ask the land manager about identification and any removal plan before disturbing a wetland. Do not use this profile as a foraging guide; correct plant identification does not establish that water or harvested plants are safe to eat.

identification: Look for small, deeply lobed leaves, woody thorns and clusters of usually white flowers followed by red fruits. A typical fruit contains one hard stone, and a flower usually has one style. Those features help distinguish it from several other hawthorns, but hybrids and cultivated forms complicate the picture. Photograph leaves from a flowering or fruiting short shoot, the thorns and a flower or mature fruit. Leaves on vigorous long shoots can look different, so a single large leaf is a poor basis for identification.
actions: Check nearby field margins and woodland edges for seedlings rather than focusing only on the planted parent tree. Wear sturdy gloves around the thorns and obtain permission before working on land you do not manage. Small confirmed plants are easier to address before they become established thickets; large plants may need a coordinated removal and follow-up plan. Keep fruit-bearing debris from being dumped in natural areas. Consult local weed guidance because control requirements vary: a regional recommendation is not a nationwide legal obligation. Revisit cleared sites and encourage appropriate replacement vegetation.

identification: Look for small dark red to nearly black aphids, roughly 1.6-2.3 millimeters long, on leaves or sprouting bulbs. Winged forms are glossy, with long dark antennae, dark wing veins and short, slightly swollen tailpipes. It closely resembles Neotoxoptera oliveri, so color and an onion host do not settle the identification. Photograph a colony, a few individuals under magnification and the affected plant. Note whether they are on newly growing leaves, mature foliage or bulbs in storage, and keep separate records for different crops.
actions: Inspect new transplants and stored planting bulbs before placing them beside healthy stock. Hold suspect material apart and ask an extension diagnostic service for identification if colonies persist or plants decline. Record distorted growth, yellowing or loss of vigor, but do not assume every symptom is caused by aphids; nutrient, root and disease problems can overlap. Avoid sharing infested bulbs or moving discarded plants into another garden. If control is needed, use advice appropriate to the particular edible crop and local conditions rather than copying an ornamental-aphid treatment.

sources.label: Zhang and colleagues: onion aphid host interactions

identification: Look for many hollow, narrow leaves arising from the base and small white to pale pink flowers with a reddish-brown stripe down each of the six flower segments. The plant lacks the characteristic onion smell. Photograph the basal leaf clump, a flower face, the branching flowering stem and any capsules. Other plants are also called onionweed, so that name alone is not a reliable identification. Avoid tasting any part to distinguish it, and use gloves when handling an unfamiliar plant because contact irritation is possible.
actions: Record the patch before mature seed is scattered, noting whether it is in pasture, roadside soil or a natural area. Ask the local weed authority how to handle a confirmed population and whether reporting is required there. Avoid mowing through ripe capsules or carrying contaminated soil and plant debris to clean ground. Clean footwear and machinery after working nearby. Small plants may be easier to address early under local guidance, but follow-up matters because a one-time cut can leave surviving plants or seed. Restore appropriate ground cover where removal exposes bare soil.

identification: Look for bluish or gray-green foliage, broad upper leaves that clasp the stem and a large capsule topped by a flat, radiating disc. Flowers may be white, pink, purple or other cultivated forms, including double flowers. Many ordinary cultivated plants are nearly hairless, but related forms within the broader taxon can have hairs, so use several features together. Photograph the whole plant, an upper leaf where it meets the stem, the flower and an intact capsule. Similar poppies differ in leaf attachment, hairiness and capsule shape; do not identify it only by petal color.
actions: Leave unfamiliar plants intact while obtaining identification from a local botanical or extension service. Record whether they were planted, arose in disturbed soil or recur in the same place over several seasons. Do not collect capsules, distribute seed or move plants to another site as part of an observation. If removal is appropriate, ask the land manager or relevant local authority how to handle the material. This profile is for recognizing and documenting plants, not for cultivation, consumption or processing. Preventing accidental movement and keeping a clear location record are useful first steps.

identification: Mysids have a slender segmented body, prominent eyes and a tail fan, and females carry developing young in a brood pouch. Those features identify the general group, not this species. Specialists examine the rostrum, tail plate, spines and appendages under magnification to distinguish Hyperacanthomysis longirostris from native and other introduced mysids. A photograph of a transparent animal in a jar is rarely enough. Record the collection location, date, waterbody and sampling method, and include salinity if it was actually measured rather than estimated.
actions: Do not release bait, aquarium animals or water from a sample container into another waterbody. Drain and clean nets, boats and sampling equipment according to local aquatic-invasive-species guidance before moving between sites. If you find an unfamiliar mysid outside its documented area, contact the responsible aquatic monitoring program for specimen instructions. Keep the original label and any older scientific name with the record so taxonomic changes can be reconciled. There is no practical basis here for an individual to treat an estuary; useful contributions are careful identification, reporting and prevention of transport.

sources.label: San Francisco Estuary and Watershed Science: mysid monitoring

identification: Look for small oval leaves with a pale, densely hairy underside and impressed veins on the upper surface. Young shoots are downy; older branches arch outward. Small pinkish flowers occur in clusters and are followed by orange-red, egg-shaped fruits, often with three stones. Photograph the leaf underside, a young shoot and a complete flower or fruit cluster. The upper leaf surface can lose hairs as it matures, so compare leaves of different ages. Similar cotoneasters differ in leaf size, hairiness and cluster structure, and some garden labels use older or inconsistent names.
actions: Inspect nearby open ground and woodland edges for seedlings, especially beneath bird perches. Where escape is confirmed, seek a local removal plan and address smaller plants before they become large seed sources. Obtain permission before working beyond your property. Keep fruit-bearing cuttings out of informal compost or garden-waste dumps near natural vegetation. Larger shrubs may regrow after cutting, so plan return visits and replacement ground cover. Work with neighboring landowners when several fruiting hedges are contributing seed, rather than treating one patch and overlooking repeated introduction from nearby plantings.

identification: Look for groups of orange or reddish cups with yellow to orange tentacles when the polyps are open. Colonies may form rounded clumps, but their shape changes with growth conditions and whether the polyps are extended. Other cup corals, including related Tubastraea species, can be difficult to separate by color alone. Photograph the entire colony and a close view of the cups without touching it. Include the type of surface, approximate depth and whether the colony is on a wreck, piling, vessel or natural rock.
actions: Report an unexpected colony to the marine sanctuary, resource agency or invasive-species program responsible for the site. Leave it in place for qualified assessment; scraping or breaking a suspected colony can damage neighboring organisms and is not a suitable casual response. Boat and infrastructure owners should use approved maintenance procedures that contain removed fouling material rather than releasing it elsewhere. Never release aquarium corals or seawater containing living material into coastal waters. Follow-up photographs from the same location can help trained reviewers track changes without disturbing the colony or collecting protected marine life.

sources.label: NOAA: Flower Garden Banks coral guide

identification: Look for fans of long, arching, strap-like leaves arising from the ground and tall, largely leafless flower stalks. The familiar flowers are tawny orange with a yellowish throat; each bloom lasts only a day, although a stalk can carry several buds that open in sequence. True lilies generally have leaves along the flowering stem, which helps distinguish them. Photograph a whole clump and the leaf bases as well as a flower. Many cultivated daylilies are hybrids, so flower color alone should not be used to assign this species.
actions: Record whether a clump is maintained in a garden or spreading into nearby vegetation. Avoid dumping divisions, crowns or soil containing living roots along roadsides or natural-area edges. Where removal is appropriate, work with the landowner to remove the underground growing parts and check for regrowth rather than relying on one cut of the leaves. Protect nearby plants while digging and stabilize disturbed soil afterward. Do not assume that every daylily cultivar behaves like this species. Keep removed material away from cats, for which daylilies are toxic, and use the profile for identification rather than foraging.

identification: Look for arching woody branches, opposite leaves with toothed edges and long clusters of many small tubular flowers. The familiar purple-flowered forms have contrasting orange centers, but cultivated flower colors vary. Photograph the whole shrub, both leaf surfaces, the paired leaf arrangement and a flower cluster. Dry capsules remaining after flowering can help document seed production. Do not confuse the plant with unrelated shrubs sold under similar butterfly-attracting names. Young self-sown plants may lack the characteristic flower spikes, making leaf and stem photographs especially useful.
actions: Check disturbed ground and nearby natural areas for seedlings from a flowering shrub. Where it is invasive, choose a locally suitable replacement and avoid distributing seedlings or seed-bearing cuttings. Obtain permission before removing escaped plants on land you do not manage. Small plants are easier to deal with than established woody shrubs, and any removal should include later checks for regrowth and new seedlings. Consult the current local weed program before buying or replacing a plant because restrictions and approved cultivar exceptions differ by jurisdiction. Keep a record of the cultivar name if one is known.

sources.label: Native Plant Trust: orange-eye butterfly bush

identification: Look for a ground-level rosette of hairy, spoon-shaped leaves and upright, bristly stems carrying clusters of small orange to red-orange, dandelion-like flower heads. Leaves are concentrated near the base rather than distributed evenly up the stem. Runners may connect nearby rosettes, especially at the edge of an expanding patch. Photograph the flowers, the leaf hairs and any visible connecting runners without pulling the patch apart. The native orange mountain dandelion has one flower head per stem rather than a cluster and lacks the black hairs on hawkweed flower heads.
actions: Report a suspected patch to your local weed program, particularly where early detection or control is a priority. Avoid transplanting it as a wildflower or spreading seed-bearing soil and lawn waste. If removal is recommended, plan to address the connected plants and underground growth, then return to check for regrowth. Mowing flowers alone does not remove the spreading network. Clean tools and footwear after working in a patch, and keep disturbed areas covered with appropriate replacement vegetation. Requirements vary by region, so use current local guidance for treatment rather than copying another state's rules.

identification: Look for long, narrow to somewhat broader leaf-like structures called phyllodes, each with a prominent central vein. They are often blue-green and may curve gently, with a small gland near the base. Bright yellow flowers form rounded heads arranged in short clusters. The seed pods are narrow, flattened and hairless. Photograph the phyllode base and vein pattern, flower heads and mature pods. Other wattles can be similar, and young growth may be broader than mature growth, so a single leaf-like structure is not enough for confirmation.
actions: Record whether trees were planted or have produced independent seedlings beyond the planting. Where escape is occurring, stop distributing seed or cuttings and seek a removal plan that accounts for regrowth and the soil seed bank. Small seedlings should be addressed before they become seed-bearing trees, with permission from the landowner. Large trees and work near roads or utilities need qualified help. Keep seed-bearing debris contained, minimize unnecessary soil disturbance and inspect the site after rain or other disturbance. Replant with locally appropriate species rather than leaving open ground for another flush of seedlings.

sources.label: California Invasive Plant Council: orange wattle

identification: Look for light green to blue-green leaves, flattened leaf sheaths and a conspicuous pale membrane where the blade meets the sheath. New leaves are folded in the bud. The flowering head is branched, with crowded groups of small spikelets rather than a single uniform spike. Photograph that head, the plant base and a close view of the leaf collar. Quackgrass can be confused with it, but has clasping auricles and spreading rhizomes; orchardgrass has a fibrous, clumping root system. A mown leaf by itself is much harder to identify.
actions: Decide first whether the grass is part of the intended land use. In an unwanted small patch, removal needs to include the crown and dense root system, followed by checks for surviving shoots. Simply mowing it short may not eliminate it. Avoid moving seed-bearing cuttings or contaminated soil into restoration areas. Larger grassland work needs a plan that protects desirable grasses and keeps soil covered; a treatment that kills orchardgrass can also harm neighboring plants. For pastures, discuss management with a forage adviser rather than removing a useful crop solely because it is introduced.

identification: Wingless adults described in the specialist literature are greenish yellow to pale yellow-green, with an oval dark patch on the upper abdomen. The antennae and paired tailpipes are mostly dark, while the small tail at the rear is pale. They are only about 1.3-2.1 millimeters long, so these details need magnification. Photograph several individuals from above and the side, along with the orchid's affected growth and its label if available. A yellow body alone is not diagnostic. Keep the location and host information with any specimen because both are useful to a specialist.
actions: Separate an affected potted orchid from the rest of a collection while obtaining identification, and inspect new arrivals before placing them among established plants. Note whether the aphids are concentrated on a flower stem, buds or tender leaves and whether that growth is distorted. Ask an orchid-aware extension adviser about a targeted response appropriate to the plant; delicate foliage and flowers may be damaged by improvised sprays. Do not move infested plants into natural areas or share divisions until the problem has been addressed. Continue checking adjacent plants rather than assuming one cleaned shoot ends the infestation.

sources.label: Australian National Insect Collection aphid checklist

identification: Adults are oval and pink beneath a thin white wax coating that still allows the body segments to show. Short wax filaments run around the sides, with the rear pair longer, and a small cottony egg sac may sit beneath the body. These are useful clues but overlap with other Pseudococcus mealybugs. Specialists distinguish it using microscopic pores and other structures on prepared specimens. Photograph visible insects and the affected orchid parts; do not uproot a wild orchid to inspect its roots. A nursery label and recent plant-movement history can help interpret a cultivated infestation.
actions: Isolate an affected potted orchid and pause exchanging divisions or placing nursery-grown orchids into outdoor restoration sites. Ask a plant diagnostic service how to collect a mealybug sample without damaging the orchid. For insects on wild orchids, report the exact location and photographs to the refuge, preserve or land manager rather than collecting the plant or applying a treatment yourself. Inspect neighboring cultivated plants and keep records of follow-up observations. Any treatment needs to account for hidden root colonies and the orchid's sensitivity, not just the visible wax on one leaf.

sources.label: Gutting and colleagues: mealybugs on native Florida orchids

identification: Adults are broad, oval beetles roughly a centimeter long, with colors ranging from almost black to mottled gray or tan with dark patches. They are generally smaller than Japanese beetles and often active around dusk or at night. The larvae curl into a C shape and resemble other white grubs. A specialist distinguishes them by the arrangement of hairs near the rear underside, where this species has parallel rows. Brown turf or a single unidentified grub is not sufficient evidence of Oriental beetle damage.
actions: Inspect roots and soil where plants are declining, and retain photographs of any adults as well as the damaged plants. Ask extension staff to identify grubs before choosing a treatment, because timing depends on the insect and its stage. Check container plants before moving them between gardens or nurseries. Adults can be collected from prized flowers when accessible, but removing adults is not a reliable way to eliminate grubs already in the soil. Monitor the affected area rather than assuming one intervention has resolved the problem.

sources.label: EENY-816/IN1442: The Oriental Beetle, Anomala orientalis (Waterhouse 1875) (Insecta: Coleoptera: Scarabaeidae)

identification: Leaves are alternate and often broadly rounded, but leaf shape alone is unreliable. The most useful distinction is the position of flowers and fruits. Oriental bittersweet bears them in small clusters where leaves join the stem, while American bittersweet normally carries them at the ends of branches. Ripe yellow capsules split to expose reddish seed coverings. Native bittersweet has orange capsules. Hybrids and vines without reproductive structures may need expert examination. Photograph fruit clusters in relation to an entire leafy branch rather than submitting only a handful of berries.
actions: Do not use fruiting branches in outdoor wreaths or dump them with garden debris. Contain mature fruits during cleanup. Small seedlings can be removed with their roots where this will not damage desirable plants. For large vines, plan treatment and follow-up with a qualified land manager; cutting alone can leave a vigorous root system. Avoid pulling heavy cut vines from a tree canopy, where falling branches can injure people or damage the tree. Return to the site to check for sprouts and seedlings.

sources.label: Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station: woody vines

identification: Adults are shiny dark brown to black and approximately an inch long. Males have wings that stop short of the end of the abdomen; females have only small wing pads and can appear wingless. Young stages are also wingless, so a small dark roach should not be identified as an adult female solely by its lack of wings. American and smokybrown cockroaches can occur in similar places but differ in coloration and developed wings. A clear overhead photograph with a size reference helps an identification service.
actions: Repair leaks, reduce standing moisture, and remove refuse or stored clutter that provides shelter. Seal gaps around pipes and doors while preserving necessary ventilation and drainage. Store food securely and use monitoring traps to locate activity and track whether changes are working. Check floor drains and plumbing with a qualified professional if roaches repeatedly emerge there. For a persistent infestation, request an integrated pest-management plan matched to the building. Avoid treating every drain or room indiscriminately when the actual harborages and entry points remain unknown.

sources.label: University of Georgia Extension: Insect and Arthropod Pests of Southeastern Neighborhoods: A Guide to Identification and Management

identification: Look for lobed basal leaves and much smaller, narrow leaves higher on the stem. The foliage can release milky sap when damaged, but there is no need to break a plant for identification. Numerous small yellow heads occur on a branched stem, unlike the single head on each leafless stalk of a typical dandelion. Mature brownish fruits have fine white hairs that aid dispersal. Other hawksbeards and related yellow-flowered weeds can be similar, so include the whole branching stem and the basal leaves in photographs.
actions: Remove small plants before the seed heads mature, gathering the roots and stems rather than leaving living crowns behind. Check nursery pots and the edges of beds for additional rosettes. Mowing alone can leave plants able to grow again, so revisit the patch after cleanup. Remove attached soil and plant debris from equipment and clothing before moving to another site. In a mixed natural-area planting, confirm uncertain yellow-flowered herbs before removal so desirable species are not taken with the weed.

sources.label: UF Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants: Youngia japonica
Indian Institute of Science: Youngia japonica

identification: Adult flies have a contrasting dark and yellowish body and patterned wings, but closely related Bactrocera species can be difficult to separate. The pale, legless larvae live inside fruit, where feeding may produce tunnels and decay. Tiny egg-laying punctures can be hard to notice. A maggot in a mango or other fruit cannot be identified to this species from its general shape. Even laboratory identification requires care because Oriental fruit fly belongs to a complex of similar species, and some commonly used genetic tests cannot separate every member reliably.
actions: Leave suspect fruit at its current location, photograph the insect and damage, and contact the state agriculture department or USDA plant-health office. Record where the fruit came from and whether other fruit from the same source has been moved. Do not mail live larvae or carry infested fruit to another property without instructions. Follow current quarantine and disposal directions rather than composting suspect fruit. Allow survey staff to explain any trapping or inspection work so the response can target the affected area.

identification: Finely divided leaves are a useful starting point: each blade is cut into narrow segments rather than resembling the broad, simply toothed foliage of some other germanders. Blue-violet flowers are carried on slender stalks among branching upper stems, with projecting stamens. Hairiness and size vary among recognized forms. Other members of the mint family can combine divided leaves and blue flowers, so these features do not settle an identification on their own. Photographs should show the whole plant, lower and upper leaves, and the side of an open flower.
actions: Keep a nursery label or the original identification with any observation. If plants are appearing beyond a cultivated bed, record the distance from the parent planting and whether seedlings persist in later seasons. Ask a regional herbarium to confirm the species before removing an unfamiliar mint-family plant from a natural area. Keep seed-bearing garden waste out of open land. There is not yet enough locally applicable evidence here to recommend a particular control program or to assume that every established specimen needs removal.

identification: Leaves alternate in two rows along slender branches. They are narrowly oval with long pointed tips, finely toothed edges, and an uneven or slightly notched base. Three strong veins arise near the leaf base. The upper surface feels rough, while the paler underside is softly hairy. Small greenish flowers occur in clusters at leaf joints, followed by small fruits that turn from pinkish to black. Other trema and hackberry relatives can share rough, toothed leaves, so photographs should include the leaf base, underside and fruiting branch.
actions: In Florida, choose a locally recommended alternative when planning a new planting. Inspect around an existing tree and nearby disturbed ground for young trees beyond the maintained area. Record those observations and have uncertain seedlings identified before removal. Contain fruit-bearing branches during any work so they are not dumped where animals can spread the seeds. Mature trees need a site-specific removal and follow-up plan from a qualified adviser; ordinary pruning should not be assumed to eliminate an established tree or its seedlings.

sources.label: Florida Natural Areas Inventory: Trema orientalis

identification: The body is elongated and cylindrical, usually mottled yellow-brown with dark markings and a pale underside. Several pairs of short barbels surround the small mouth. A single short dorsal fin sits well back along the body. Mature males have a thickened pectoral-fin ray and a more pointed pectoral fin. These details help separate it from an eel, but closely related loaches require more careful examination. Photograph the mouth, side and fins; aquarium color forms may not resemble the mottled wild-looking fish shown in a field guide.
actions: Never release unwanted loaches into outdoor water, even if they are sold as hardy pond fish. Seek a responsible aquarium rehoming option and keep ponds secure against escape. Report an unfamiliar wild catch to the state fisheries agency with the waterbody, date and photographs. Do not carry it alive to another site for identification without instructions. Drain and clean equipment before moving between waters, and leave any population-level response to the responsible aquatic-resource managers.

identification: Adult female covers are flat, roughly circular to oval and yellow to yellowish brown, often with a small darker or translucent spot near the center. The insects are only a few millimeters across. Young mobile stages, called crawlers, are yellow and much smaller. Male covers differ in shape as they develop. Similar Aonidiella species can occur on the same kinds of plants, and color alone is insufficient. A diagnostician may examine the female's body beneath its cover and microscopic ducts and pores to confirm the species.
actions: Inspect newly acquired palms and ornamentals, including leaf undersides and sheltered frond bases, before placing them beside other plants. Keep suspect stock separate and ask a plant clinic how to submit a sample. Reduce avoidable plant stress through appropriate watering and care, and protect beneficial insects that help suppress scale populations. If treatment is needed, have an adviser identify the susceptible life stage and suitable local options. Follow-up matters because several stages can be present together, and old covers may remain after the insects have died.

identification: Orinoco sailfin catfish has a broad, armored body, an underslung suckerlike mouth and a large dorsal fin that spreads like a sail. Pterygoplichthys usually has more dorsal-fin rays than the similar genus Hypostomus. Typical Orinoco sailfin catfish have small, separate dark spots on a lighter background, including along the sides and tail base. Related sailfin catfishes may have merging spots or winding patterns, but color-pattern variation and uncertain identifications limit this shortcut. Photographs should include the spread dorsal fin and the underside when this can be done without unsafe handling.
actions: Retain aquarium purchase information and seek an appropriate rehoming option before the fish becomes too large for its tank. For an unfamiliar wild catch, record the waterbody, size and photographs and consult the state fisheries agency. Do not move the fish alive to another waterbody or assume that any animal called a pleco is this species. Let trained personnel decide whether a specimen is needed. A confirmed local identification is necessary before attaching species-specific impacts or a management program to the observation.

sources.label: USFWS 2026 ecological risk summary: Orinoco sailfin catfish
USFWS 2026 Orinoco sailfin catfish assessment summary

identification: Wingless individuals are pale yellowish, brownish yellow or dull green, with paired darker markings across the abdomen. Winged forms have a more conspicuous dark patch on the back. The two short tubes near the rear, called cornicles, and the shape of the tail-like cauda help specialists distinguish this species from other Myzus aphids. At roughly one or two millimeters long, these details are difficult to resolve in an ordinary photograph. Host identity and photographs of several adults are useful supporting information, but do not replace close examination.
actions: Inspect lower foliage as well as fresh growing tips when a plant has sticky leaves or unexplained decline. Keep newly acquired infested plants separate while seeking identification, particularly in a greenhouse collection. Record the host plant and whether insects are winged or wingless. Ask extension staff about a response suited to the crop and the actual level of damage. Do not infer a virus diagnosis from aphid presence, and avoid moving affected propagation material between growers until the problem has been assessed.

identification: Orosne is an upright plant with narrow leaves and long, delicate flowering clusters. The stems can carry minute glandular hairs. Individual flowers are only a few millimeters long, with pale petals and a small crested part enclosing the reproductive structures. The fruit is a tiny, flattened capsule containing dark, hairy seeds. Seed appendages help separate it from closely similar species such as Polygala fernandesiana. A photograph of the whole plant is useful, but close views of a flower and mature capsule are needed for a stronger identification.
actions: Record whether plants were deliberately grown or appeared independently, and include the surrounding habitat in an observation. Ask a regional botanist to check the identity before removing small milkworts from mixed natural vegetation. In a cultivated bed, contain unwanted fruiting plants rather than shaking their small seeds into adjacent soil. Keep seed-bearing waste out of roadsides and waterways. Do not use an unidentified plant in a home remedy because of medicinal claims associated with its name. Its local ecological significance still needs confirmation.

sources.label: Australian Tropical Rainforest Plants: Polygala paniculata

identification: The body is stout and oval, with a large mouth and a long dorsal fin. Typical adults have dark blotches on an olive or bluish background and a conspicuous reddish eyespot near the upper base of the tail. Young fish can have wavy pale and orange markings on a dark background. Captive color forms may look different. Other introduced cichlids and native sunfishes can be confused with an oscar at a distance, so photograph the full side, head and tail base rather than relying only on body color.
actions: Plan aquarium space and long-term care before obtaining an oscar, and use an appropriate rehoming route if keeping it becomes impractical. Do not transfer a live catch between ponds or canals. Report an unexpected wild observation with the exact waterbody and clear photographs. Anglers should check current fishing rules and fish-consumption guidance for that waterbody before retaining a catch. Local abundance or nonnative status does not remove the need to follow those rules or justify private stocking.

identification: Several branching stems spread outward or rise slightly from the ground. Leaves are small, green and oval to narrowly elliptic, with tiny flowers tucked at their bases. A thin, papery sheath surrounds the stem at each joint. The relatively similar-sized leaves on main and side branches are useful clues, though variation occurs. Specialists also examine the flower covering and the small, dark, three-sided fruits. Closely related prostrate knotweeds overlap in appearance, so a mat's growth habit alone does not establish the subspecies.
actions: Photograph the whole mat and several leafy stem joints, including mature fruits if available. Keep the precise name used by the identifier with the record. Remove unwanted plants from a garden or path before fruits mature only after distinguishing them from desired groundcover. Collect fruiting material and avoid moving contaminated soil into clean beds. In a natural-area survey, ask a botanical specialist which taxonomic treatment applies locally. A subspecies-specific control program should not be borrowed automatically from advice for the broader knotweed group.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Polygonum aviculare subsp. depressum
BSBI: field identification of Polygonum aviculare aggregate

identification: Each flower head has a yellow center surrounded by white rays. Lower leaves are spoon-shaped to oval, with toothed edges and stalks; leaves become smaller and more narrowly shaped up the stem. The upper leaves are alternate and often lack stalks. Plants usually carry individual heads at the ends of slender flowering branches. Shasta daisies and other cultivated Leucanthemum can resemble oxeye daisy, while chamomiles have much more finely divided foliage. Include basal leaves, stem leaves and the underside of a flower head in identification photographs.
actions: Hand-pull or hoe small seedlings and young plants before flowering, taking the crown and roots where practical. Gather flowering material so developing seeds are not scattered during disposal. Larger patches need repeated attention across seasons; mowing can reduce seed production when timed correctly but should not be expected to eradicate the plant. Clean tools and footwear after working in an infestation. For pasture or restoration sites, coordinate control with maintaining desirable cover so the cleared space does not simply fill with new seedlings.

sources.label: University of Nevada Extension: Oxeye daisy

identification: Leaves are distributed along the stem and are usually deeply lobed or divided, with toothed segments. Upper leaves are smaller and generally lack stalks. Several yellow flower heads form a loose cluster near the top of a branching stem. The green bracts beneath each head have dark tips, and mature fruits carry fine hairs. Common groundsel and other Senecio species can share divided leaves and black-tipped bracts; the presence and size of the yellow rays, leaf shape and mature fruits help separate them. Photographs need more than a single flower face.
actions: Record the whole plant, lower and upper leaves, flower-head bracts and any mature fruits. Ask a regional botanist to confirm an unfamiliar ragwort before treating it as a new occurrence. Keep seed-bearing plants out of moved soil or dumped garden waste. If plants are unwanted in a managed bed, remove them before seed dispersal and check the site again for seedlings. For a larger or natural-area population, obtain local advice rather than applying a control program intended for a different ragwort.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Senecio squalidus
Taxonomic revision of Senecio squalidus group

identification: Look for elongated, curved brown or gray covers that resemble miniature oyster shells, often clustered on bark. They are only a few millimeters long and can blend into the branch surface. Eggs remain protected under the female covering, and newly hatched crawlers are tiny and pale. Similar Lepidosaphes species can have comparable covers, so the shape is a useful clue rather than an absolute identification. A diagnostician may need microscopic characters of adult females. Photograph both an infested branch and the plant as a whole.
actions: Inspect declining branches before pruning, and ask extension staff to confirm the scale and the appropriate local crawler period. Remove heavily infested dead or failing branches when this is suitable for the plant, containing the material rather than moving it among other plantings. Check replacement nursery stock carefully. If treatment is warranted, use a locally appropriate plan that accounts for eggs protected under covers and vulnerable moving stages. Reinspect living growth afterward; persistent empty covers should not be mistaken automatically for treatment failure.

sources.label: University of Maryland: Boxwood problems, oystershell scale

identification: Stout, upright canes carry long, coarse leaves, and mature plants can stand well above a person's head. The open flower cluster has many slender branches bearing paired spikelets and conspicuous hairs. The small membrane at the junction of blade and sheath has a finely hairy edge, a feature useful in a grass key. Other large Miscanthus species and cultivated hybrids can look similar. Height and a white leaf midrib are not enough for a confident species identification; include the flowering branches, leaf base and whole clump in photographs.
actions: Keep the original nursery name with a record and ask a grass specialist to check plants that appear beyond cultivation. Inspect the surrounding ground for seedlings and avoid sharing unidentified divisions. Collect unwanted seed-bearing stems rather than dumping them near waterways or open land. Use gloves and protect exposed skin when handling coarse grass foliage. Large clumps require a planned removal approach suited to the site; local impact and reliable species-specific control evidence should be established before recommending broad removal from natural vegetation.

identification: Leaves are glossy, dark green and opposite, often on purplish stalks. Large funnel-shaped flowers are pink to purple or pale, with five spreading lobes. The distinctive fruits are thick pods that usually grow in opposing pairs. When ripe, they release flat brown seeds with long silky hairs that aid movement by wind or water. Broken stems exude milky sap, but do not cut a plant just to test this feature. Photograph the leaves, open flowers and paired pods, and obtain expert help separating the two rubbervine species.
actions: Keep people and livestock away from cut material and avoid contact with the milky sap. Report a suspected escape to the local invasive-plant program before moving or distributing the plant. In Hawaii, ask the relevant island program about its response priorities and assistance. Contain pods and seed-bearing branches during authorized work, and never dump them beside streams. Mature climbing plants need a coordinated plan that protects the supporting vegetation and includes follow-up for seedlings. Do not pull a heavy vine from overhead branches yourself.

identification: Above ground, affected patches may show stunting, yellowing or wilting, with reduced tuber production. These symptoms overlap with drought, nutrient deficiencies and other root problems. Developing females swell on roots and remain pale before becoming brown cysts. The related golden potato cyst nematode passes through a yellow stage, but color differences alone are not sufficient for confirmation. Laboratories examine cysts and juveniles microscopically and use molecular tests. Old records under broad potato-cyst-nematode names may combine species that are now distinguished.
actions: Contact the state agriculture department or USDA plant-health office if this nematode is suspected. Keep soil, rooted plants and equipment from being moved out of the affected area while obtaining instructions. Record crop history, seed-potato sources and recent equipment movements, which can help investigators trace possible pathways. Do not dig and distribute informal samples without asking how they should be collected and packaged. Follow the current official restrictions and cleanup plan; an improvised treatment cannot demonstrate that a field is free of viable cysts.

identification: Pale flax has thin, branching stems with alternate, narrow leaves and no obvious hairiness. Plants may live for a single season or survive as short lived perennials. The pale blue to violet petals have darker veins; occasional flowers are whitish. Small, rounded capsules follow the flowers and contain shiny brown seeds. The leaves are much shorter than the upright stems and have smooth edges. Flowers alone can be confused with other flax species, so photographs should include the stem leaves and mature capsules as well as the blooms. Older references may use Linum angustifolium.
actions: Before removing a wild flax, check the identification with a regional flora or herbarium, especially where native Lewis flax occurs. Photograph an entire flowering stem and a fruiting branch in place. In a garden, keep any unwanted seed-bearing material within the property rather than spreading it along roadsides or in natural areas. A confirmed observation can help document its local distribution; it does not by itself establish a need for landscape-wide control.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Linum bienne
Burke Herbarium: Pacific Northwest Linaceae checklist

identification: Plants are usually about 4 to 12 inches tall, with narrow, alternate leaves and a grayish appearance from closely pressed, star-shaped hairs. The small flowers have four petals and six stamens, features typical of the mustard family. Petals can appear pale yellow or creamy white. Look closely beneath older flowers: the sepals persist as fruits develop, an important feature in separating this plant from similar small alyssums. A photograph of flowers alone may hide that distinction. Include the lowermost leaves, stem hairs and a fruiting branch when seeking an identification.
actions: Check small plants before they disappear into taller vegetation or lose their flowers. If pale alyssum is an unwanted garden volunteer, first confirm the name and ask local extension staff whether it is a concern in your setting. Keep seed-bearing stems out of material being moved to another property. In a natural area, give the land manager a location and clear photographs rather than treating all small yellow-flowered mustards as this species.

identification: Opposite, oval leaves have pointed tips and smooth edges. Small, star-shaped flowers range from dull pink to burgundy; black swallow-wort has darker flowers with shorter, triangular petals. Slender pods eventually split to release flat brown seeds with white silky hairs. The twining habit is useful: native dogbanes stand upright and have clusters of bell-shaped flowers. Check both leaves and flowers before acting. Young plants can be inconspicuous for several years before producing seed, and the established root crown can survive damage to the shoots.
actions: For a small new patch, digging can work if the entire root crown is removed. Recheck the location for regrowth and seedlings. Cutting or collecting pods before seeds mature can reduce spread, but cutting shoots alone does not kill established crowns. Keep pods and living root pieces out of compost and secure them for locally approved disposal. Large patches need a coordinated, multi-year plan with the land manager or extension service, including restoration of vegetation after control.

sources.label: UConn Extension: Black and pale swallow-wort

identification: The long leaves are conspicuously folded lengthwise and arise on stalks from the base. Mature leaves can exceed three feet in length. Small yellow flowers are crowded near ground level on very short stalks, where the foliage can conceal them. Hairy, whitish to greenish fruits follow. Look beneath the leaves without uprooting the plant, and include the flowering base in photographs. Palm seedlings can look similar from a distance, but the basal flower clusters and rhizomatous clump are useful clues. A nursery label may carry either scientific name.
actions: Check the edges of a planted clump for new growth and nearby plants outside cultivation. Because the plant can be propagated by division and runners, keep living rhizomes and discarded divisions out of forest edges and dumped garden waste. If it appears established in a Kauai natural area, share the location and photographs with the local invasive-species program. Seek local advice before disturbing a large patch or moving plants to another island.

sources.label: Kauai Invasive Species Committee: Widespread distribution survey appendix

identification: Cinquefoils in this group require close examination of the leaves, their hairs and the flower structures. A hand-shaped leaf divided into several toothed leaflets can help place a plant among the cinquefoils, but it cannot settle this identification. The amount and arrangement of hair beneath a leaf, the shape of its teeth and the relationship between petals and sepals may all matter. Silver cinquefoil and related plants are part of the identification problem. Take photographs of both leaf surfaces, basal leaves, stem leaves and flowers rather than relying on a single distant image.
actions: Ask a regional herbarium or botanist familiar with Potentilla to evaluate a suspected record. Include the location, habitat and whether the plant was cultivated; collect a specimen only with permission and advice on what parts are needed. Avoid removing a patch solely because an image application suggests this name. Once the identity is resolved, a local specialist can explain whether it represents a native plant, an established introduction or an unusual occurrence worth documenting.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Potentilla sect. Terminales
Kolodziejek: Hair types in selected Potentilla Collinae
Asker and Frost1970 Potentilla collina chemotaxonomy

identification: Flowering stems are generally less than about two feet tall. The narrow to lance-shaped leaf blades can be hairy. Several short flowering branches sit along a central axis, with spikelets arranged on one side. Under magnification, look for the upper glume, a small outer spikelet bract, expanded into a ragged papery wing. This differs from the simple fringe of separate hairs found on some other Paspalum species. A close photograph of mature spikelets is much more informative than a picture of green leaves alone.
actions: For an unfamiliar patch, record whether it is in a lawn, pasture, roadside or natural habitat and photograph a complete seed head. Ask a local grass specialist to confirm the papery-wing character before making a management decision. Keep collected seed heads enclosed and avoid moving loose seed-bearing clippings to another property. On islands where the species is introduced, a confirmed record may be useful to the local herbarium or invasive-species program.

sources.label: Bishop Museum OP55: key to Hawaiian Paspalum, institutional mirror

identification: Plants can reach roughly two feet tall and may have stems that spread along the ground. The leaves are relatively broad for a small annual grass, often hairy, with conspicuously wavy or crinkled margins. Hairs on the leaf sheath arise from small raised bases. At the blade-and-sheath junction, the ligule is a dense rim of hairs. A flowering stem usually carries several short, one-sided branches. The small spikelets are borne singly, a character best checked with magnification. Mature flowering material is essential because a young plant can resemble several other Urochloa species.
actions: If this grass appears unexpectedly in seed, soil or a crop, contact your state plant-health agency or USDA APHIS for identification and movement guidance. Photograph the mature seed head and record the origin of the material and the extent of the patch. Keep suspect seed-bearing plants, seed lots and soil in place while receiving advice. Choose any subsequent control plan for the actual crop and location; recommendations for a perennial wetland grass such as para grass do not automatically fit this annual.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Garden Sydney: Urochloa panicoides
USDA APHIS: Federal Noxious Weed List
USDA APHIS: Corn seeds pest risk assessment, March 2024
USDA AMS: 2026 state noxious-weed seed requirements

identification: Look for loose clumps with spreading or partly reclining stems and bright green, mostly hairless blades. The collar near the base of a blade may be purplish and hairy; the ligule is a thin, ragged membrane rather than simply a row of hairs.
