Contain mature heads before carrying plants away, and inspect newly purchased plants for seedlings before distributing them through a nursery. Keep soil and plant waste out of nearby natural areas. At a restoration site, record the extent and ask the land manager how thickhead fits their weed priorities; check disturbed ground again for new seedlings.

sources.label: UF IFAS: Biology and Management of Thickhead

identification: Adults are shiny blue-green with orange-red legs and reddish antennae ending in a dark club. They are only a few millimeters long and can fly. The thorax is narrower than the wing covers, and the body bears noticeable bristles under magnification. Redshouldered ham beetles differ in having red on the thorax and bases of the wing covers, while the blue bone beetle has dark legs. Larvae look quite different from the metallic adults and may feed within food or occupy nearby protected spaces.
actions: Isolate suspect packages and inspect nearby dried foods, pet food and accumulated residues. Clean shelves, cracks and crevices thoroughly, since beetles and pupal chambers can remain away from the obvious food source. Keep sound products in well-sealed containers and check incoming stock. Save a specimen or clear photograph for extension or a pest professional so similar beetles are not confused. For commercial food handling, follow the facility's food-safety and pest-management procedures. Do not spray food or use improvised fumigation; removing the source and hidden residues is central to lasting control.

identification: Look for four large yellow petals, reddish or red-striped sepals, and a long floral tube. The stigma extends above the anthers. Leaves are elongated and may appear crinkled, while stems bear a mixture of short hairs and longer hairs, often arising from reddish swollen bases. Upright capsules remain after the flowers fade. Native and introduced evening-primroses overlap in appearance, so flower size, bud tips, stem hairs and mature fruit are more useful together than yellow petals alone.
actions: Keep photographs of both the rosette and flowering stage when tracking an uncertain plant. If a garden specimen is producing unwanted offspring, remove developing seed capsules before they open and check nearby bare ground in later seasons. Do not assume all tall yellow evening-primroses nearby are the same taxon. In a meadow or restoration area, confirm identity before removing plants, particularly where native evening-primroses occur. A herbarium or extension botanist can use flowering and fruiting material to help resolve a difficult identification.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Oenothera glazioviana

identification: Adults are mostly metallic blue, with reddish-brown legs, the thorax behind the head and the basal portion of the wing covers. They are typically around six millimeters long. The antennae and abdomen are dark. Redlegged ham beetle has reddish legs but lacks the broad red thorax and wing-base pattern, while blue bone beetle is more uniformly metallic with dark legs. Clear dorsal and side photographs help show these distinctions. Larvae are less easily recognized, so an adult specimen is particularly useful for confirmation.
actions: If beetles are found around stored products, isolate suspect material and seek identification before choosing treatment. Check dried animal products and nearby residues, keeping a record of where adults and larvae occur. Clean accessible storage surfaces and contain infested material so insects are not carried to another room or building. For food businesses, museums or collections, involve the appropriate pest-management or conservation professional. An outdoor observation can simply be documented without removing the surrounding habitat; the species also participates in decomposition and predation rather than only damaging stored goods.

sources.label: Original study: Development of Necrobia ruficollis at constant temperatures

identification: The finely divided, hairy leaves give the rosette a feathery appearance. Small pink to purplish flowers have five petals. Fruits form a long pointed beak, which separates into seed-bearing units with twisting awns as they dry. Related filarees are easy to confuse: redstem filaree has more deeply divided leaves than broadleaf filaree. Stem redness alone is unreliable. Photograph a complete leaf and a mature fruit along with the flowers; seedlings also have characteristic lobed seed leaves that differ from their later foliage.
actions: Work before mature fruits disperse where removal is warranted, and avoid carrying awned seeds on tools, footwear or animals into uninfested areas. Small targeted removals may be practical in a garden or carefully managed restoration plot, but hand removal across extensive infestations is labor-intensive. Ask local weed or restoration staff how to protect native annuals while reducing filaree. Recheck after the next germination period and maintain appropriate ground cover. Do not assume a grass-selective treatment will control this broadleaf plant.

sources.label: US Forest Service FEIS: Erodium cicutarium

identification: Flowering stems carry an open, branching panicle of many tiny spikelets, each containing one floret. Leaves are flat and relatively narrow, with a membranous ligule where blade and sheath meet. Underground rhizomes are important identification clues. Other bentgrasses can look very similar, especially before flowering; a reddish panicle is not sufficient to separate them. A grass specialist may need the ligule, a complete flowering head and the base of the plant. Photograph those structures before mowing or collecting a sample.
actions: Check seed mixtures before using them near wetlands or native-plant restoration sites, since redtop may be deliberately included for rapid cover. If it is spreading beyond a managed area, map the patch and consult the land manager before disturbing a bank or wet soil. Its rhizomes mean that cutting a few stems does not remove the whole plant. USDA guidance notes that repeated close mowing can reduce persistence, but that approach is not appropriate for every wetland or mixed meadow. Plan replacement vegetation and follow-up alongside any removal.

identification: Stems are upright and can grow well above a person's waist. Broad, flat leaves have a prominent midrib and rough edges. The flowering head is a large branching panicle with many several-flowered spikelets and no conspicuous long awns. A membranous ligule sits where each leaf blade joins its sheath. Native American manna grass can look similar, so compare mature spikelets and the roughness and posture of panicle branches rather than relying on height. Photograph a whole flowering stem and close views of these structures.
actions: Report a suspected new patch to the state invasive-plant program and avoid transporting rooted pieces, muddy equipment or ornamental divisions. Wetland work may require authorization, so obtain site-specific advice before digging, covering or treating plants near water. Small patches can sometimes be smothered, while established stands usually need repeated management over several growing seasons. Do not use grazing as an improvised control method. Clean equipment after working in the patch, monitor downstream or adjacent areas, and plan recovery of appropriate native vegetation as the infestation declines.

identification: The upright stem carries many narrow leaves distributed along its length. Large white flowers open into long funnels with yellow toward the throat; cultivated descriptions may also show pink or purple coloring on the outer surfaces. The six tepals surround conspicuous stamens and a long central style. Related trumpet lilies and garden hybrids can be similar, so leaf width, flower orientation and the exterior of the trumpet are useful photographs. A basal clump of leaves without flowers is much harder to identify confidently.
actions: Retain labels for planted bulbs and photograph flowers before cutting stems or moving a clump. If lilies appear outside a known planting, record their distance from it and whether small independent plants recur over several years. Avoid dumping unwanted bulbs, seed capsules or garden soil into natural areas. In an established bed, remove unwanted seed capsules before they mature if you want to limit self-sowing. Ask a local botanist to confirm an unfamiliar wild lily before digging, since native lilies and cultivated hybrids can occur nearby.

identification: Infective young adult females are slender and wormlike. After entering a root with the front of the body, a female remains partly outside and swells as she feeds. Other stages occur in soil close to roots. These organisms are too small for reliable identification with ordinary garden photographs. Poor growth, root injury or uneven crop performance can have many causes, and visible symptoms cannot name the nematode. A laboratory uses extracted specimens, microscopic characters and molecular evidence. Research has found cryptic diversity within material called R. parvus, so a familiar name does not guarantee identical biology in every population.
actions: If a crop is declining, contact an extension or diagnostic laboratory before collecting samples. Follow its instructions for taking representative roots and soil, labeling the host and location, and keeping material in suitable condition. Avoid moving soil from a suspect field on equipment or planting stock. Ask the adviser to interpret nematode numbers alongside crop symptoms and other possible stresses. Do not choose a rotation, resistant variety or nematicide on the basis of a recommendation written for R. reniformis; species-specific host information is essential.

sources.label: Singh et al.: Sugarcane nematodes in Tanzania

identification: Flowering stems carry a loose, branching head with large, flattened spikelets. Each spikelet contains several overlapping florets, giving it a broad, layered appearance. The florets have sharply keeled backs and usually very short awns or nearly none. This contrasts with the long, conspicuous awns of ripgut and some other bromes. Leaves are flat, and the sheaths can be hairy. Photograph a complete head, individual spikelets and the leaf-sheath junction; a green tuft without flowers is difficult to identify accurately.
actions: Check whether a patch is part of an intended forage planting before treating it as a weed. Where plants are unwanted, prevent mature seed heads from being carried in cut vegetation or on equipment to another site. In a crop field, request advice matched to the crop and growth stage rather than borrowing a treatment from a different brome species. Record whether plants return from established bases or as new seedlings after cutting. That distinction helps an adviser plan follow-up and decide whether reducing seed production alone will be sufficient.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Bromus catharticus

identification: The shell is generally conical or somewhat cylindrical, with a toothed opening at the top. Pale shell plates bear dark longitudinal stripes crossed by finer transverse markings, producing the netlike pattern behind the common name. Closely related barnacles can look very similar, and worn or crowded shells may obscure the pattern. Specialists examine the movable plates closing the opening and other internal shell features. Photographs of an intact shell from above and the side help, but a colorful striped barnacle is not automatically this species.
actions: Inspect hulls, submerged equipment and niche areas during routine maintenance, especially before moving between ports. Arrange cleaning through facilities that can contain and dispose of removed fouling material appropriately. Avoid scraping suspect growth into a new harbor or transferring encrusted gear to another coastal site. Report unusual fouling with photographs, the vessel or equipment history and the precise location to the relevant marine biosecurity program. Do not chip barnacles from living shellfish or sensitive habitat merely to obtain a specimen; ask whether photographs or a professionally collected sample are needed.

sources.label: Farrapeira and colleagues: Tugboat fouling transport

identification: Plants have three leaflets, often broadest toward the tip, and small rounded heads of pink to purplish flowers on stalks. Individual flowers are turned into an unusual orientation reflected by the name resupinatum. The calyx enlarges around the developing fruit, producing a swollen, papery-looking structure. Several other clovers have pink flowers or inflated fruiting heads, so inspect mature heads as well as leaves. A photograph taken only during early vegetative growth usually cannot establish the species with confidence.
actions: If growing Persian clover as a cover crop, plan termination before unwanted seed production and select a method appropriate to the field and following crop. California cover-crop guidance includes mowing and other agricultural termination options, but timing and conditions determine success. Watch field margins and subsequent crops for volunteers, and avoid moving mature seed-bearing material into nearby restoration sites. If a clover appears where it was not planted, document flowering and fruiting heads before deciding on removal. Consult local crop advisers when it interferes with production rather than assuming all clovers respond identically.

sources.label: UC ANR: Cover crops for California

identification: The virus cannot be identified by sight. Sudden death may be the first sign, sometimes with a blood-stained nose. Sick rabbits can also become lethargic, stop eating or show breathing or coordination problems. These signs are not unique to rabbit hemorrhagic disease, and absence of visible bleeding does not rule it out. Several dead wild rabbits in one area warrant prompt reporting. Photograph animals only from a distance and record the location; diagnostic testing should be arranged by animal-health or wildlife professionals.
actions: If a domestic rabbit becomes ill or dies suddenly, contact a veterinarian promptly and keep other rabbits separate while following professional instructions. Do not move rabbits, cages or bedding to another property. Ask the veterinarian about vaccination and appropriate cleaning and disinfection for your circumstances. Do not release domestic rabbits or bring wild rabbits into a household group. Leave wild carcasses undisturbed and report unusual mortality to wildlife officials. Obtain disposal instructions before handling a dead rabbit, since moving contaminated material can spread the virus.

sources.label: Torrevillas et al. 2026: Sequenced RHDV2 incursion in Washington

identification: Adults have grizzled brown to gray-brown fur, a paler underside and a largely bare pinkish to red face. The tail is clearly present but shorter than the head-and-body length, unlike the very long tail of some other introduced monkeys. Males are generally larger than females. Young animals may cling to an adult or travel close to the group. Photograph from a distance and include the face, body and tail if reporting an unfamiliar monkey. Location and group size also help wildlife staff distinguish an established group from an escaped animal.
actions: Never offer food, leave food accessible or approach a macaque for a close photograph. Secure food and trash, keep pets away and give a group room to pass. If monkeys repeatedly approach a recreation area or residence, contact park staff or the appropriate wildlife agency rather than trying to catch or relocate them. Do not attempt to retrieve an item by cornering an animal. After a bite, scratch, or contact of macaque fluid with broken skin, eyes, nose or mouth, begin first aid immediately and seek medical care, explaining that a macaque was involved. CDC advises washing exposed skin with soap for 15 minutes or rinsing exposed eyes and other mucous membranes with water or sterile saline for 15 minutes.

sources.label: UF: Introduced rhesus macaques in Silver Springs
UF: Nonnative monkey populations of Florida
University of Michigan Animal Diversity Web: Macaca mulatta

identification: The flowering head has several slender, fingerlike branches arranged near the top of the stem, sometimes in more than one tier. Small spikelets line those branches, which darken as they mature. Leaves are long and narrow, and running stems can root to form additional shoots. Awn length and overall coarseness vary among cultivated types, so one cultivar should not define the whole species. Other Chloris grasses also have fingerlike heads. Photograph the head, individual spikelets and basal runners for a dependable identification.
actions: Inspect boundaries of forage plantings and avoid carrying mature seed heads or rooted runners into nearby natural vegetation. Clean mowing and earthmoving equipment before it leaves an infested area. Where a small unwanted patch is confirmed, seek local advice on removing the rooted plant and checking for regrowth; larger stands need a plan that also restores suitable cover. Repeated mowing can limit standing growth but should not be assumed to eliminate all rooted plants. Match pasture management to the cultivar and location, and avoid copying overseas chemical recommendations.

sources.label: University of Hawaii CTAHR: Rhodes grass
Townsville: Weed and pest management plan2025

identification: Adults are tiny pale, winged insects that rest beneath leaves and may fly briefly when a shrub is disturbed. The oval, flattened immature stages remain attached to leaf undersides after settling. Feeding may produce yellowing, curling and mottling. Sugary honeydew can support black sooty mold, but mold alone does not identify the whitefly because other sap feeders produce it too. Examine the leaf undersides for several life stages and photograph the host. A diagnostic sample should contain the attached immature insects as well as any adults.
actions: Inspect new rhododendrons before adding them to an established collection, and monitor susceptible plants for overwintering immature stages. Keep a suspect potted plant apart while obtaining identification. If the shrub is otherwise healthy, assess whether damage is increasing before choosing treatment. Ask extension for advice appropriate to the plant, season and local whitefly species, since a product aimed at flying adults may miss attached stages beneath leaves. Avoid moving infested nursery plants between properties, and recheck fresh growth and live insects rather than judging success from old sooty deposits alone.

sources.label: Norwegian Biodiversity Information Centre: Massilieurodes chittendeni

identification: On affected rhododendrons, rust infections produce yellow to orange spore pustules, often on leaf undersides. In the spruce phase, infected current-year needles develop yellowed areas and fungal fruiting structures, and needles may be shed prematurely. These are useful signs of a rust disease, not reliable species-level characters. Different hosts, spore stages and seasons can change the appearance. Photograph both sides of leaves or needles, identify the host plant as closely as possible, and note which year's foliage is affected.
actions: Contact a plant-diagnostic service before treating a suspected new occurrence or moving affected nursery stock. Keep samples linked to the exact host and location, and follow the laboratory's instructions for packaging fresh material. Avoid using a management program for a different rhododendron rust without confirmation. Removing nearby spruce or rhododendrons on the basis of orange spots alone can destroy healthy plants without addressing the actual problem. For a cultivated collection, monitor new foliage and document whether symptoms recur while awaiting a species-specific diagnosis.

sources.label: Tree Physiology2025: Norway spruce infection by Chrysomyxa rhododendri
Natural Resources Canada: Small-spored spruce-Labrador tea rusts

identification: Flowering stems carry many short, one-sided branches arranged along a central axis, rather than just the two or three branches seen in some familiar paspalums. Small spikelets occur in pairs along these branches. The leaves are comparatively broad for a grass, and their surfaces may be hairy or nearly smooth. Short, scaly rhizomes occur at the base. Because several Paspalum species share this general form, identification needs a mature flowering head, close views of spikelets and the leaf-sheath junction. Photograph the whole clump as well as those details.
actions: If you encounter an unfamiliar large paspalum outside cultivation, record its location, extent and proximity to planted grass. Keep seed-bearing cuttings and soil from the patch from being moved into another field or natural area. Ask a local grass specialist or herbarium to confirm the name before choosing treatment, especially where native paspalums occur. In Hawaii, include the island and whether the plants are growing independently of a garden or trial plot. Revisit a suspected escape to see whether the patch persists and new plants appear nearby.

identification: Weedy plants can differ from the planted variety in height, flowering time, seed color or the presence of awns, but those characters vary among populations. Easy shattering of mature seed is an especially important clue. Plants may be difficult to distinguish from the crop before flowering, and a single off-type plant is not enough to explain the origin of an infestation. Record the planted variety, the location of suspect patches and photographs through flowering and maturity. An experienced rice adviser can help separate volunteers, mixed seed and established weedy rice.
actions: Use certified planting seed and clean equipment to reduce movement between fields. In California, extension recommends removing identifiable weedy plants before their seed disperses. Handle mature heads carefully so removal does not scatter the seed back into the field. Consult a local rice adviser about follow-up, crop rotation and any herbicide-resistant production system; options differ by region and variety. Continue monitoring over later seasons because dormant seed can survive in the soil. Avoid assuming that a herbicide safe for cultivated rice will selectively remove weedy plants of the same species.

sources.label: UC IPM: Rice special weed problems

identification: The plant forms a persistent tuft of upright stems with relatively stiff, narrow leaves. A large, airy, branching panicle carries numerous small spikelets, each with a single fertile floret. It differs from many bromes whose larger spikelets contain several florets and often long conspicuous awns. The leaf-sheath junction has a membranous ligule. Take photographs of the whole flowering head, individual spikelets and the base of the clump. The several scientific names are synonyms used in different treatments, not evidence that separate weeds are present.
actions: Locate small patches before they produce mature seed and seek local advice on removing the complete rooted clump with minimal disturbance. Avoid tilling through established plants, since fragmented roots and disturbed soil can complicate control. Keep seed-bearing material and contaminated soil from being moved along roads or waterways. After removal, restore appropriate vegetation and check for seedlings or surviving growth. Published control information is limited, so do not assume that grazing or burning will eliminate the grass. Larger infestations need a site-specific plan that protects nearby native plants and erosion-sensitive ground.

identification: Root-feeding members of the revised group are small, pale greenish or brownish-white aphids. In the documented Japanese life cycle, gall-forming stages occur on Ulmus davidiana var. japonica, with stalked, spindle-shaped galls on the upper leaf surface. Other Tetraneura species make similar pouches, and gall shape alone is insufficient. Specialists examine tiny structures such as the claws of first-stage root nymphs and may use genetic evidence. Photograph the host, gall or root colony, but expect a specimen to be necessary for a confident determination.
actions: For a suspected crop problem, consult an extension diagnostic service and provide both affected roots and the host identity using its collection instructions. Do not select a treatment from an old aphid name without checking which species that source meant. Avoid moving infested rooted plants or attached soil to another site while identification is pending. An isolated elm gall does not justify removing the tree. Record whether root colonies, galls or winged aphids were actually observed so a specialist can connect the evidence to the appropriate life stage.

sources.label: Watanabe and colleagues2022: Tetraneura akinire group revision
General and Applied Entomology 51: Australian aphid records

identification: Large, deeply lobed leaves sit on long stalks and are often concentrated toward the ends of upright stems. The leaf undersides and young parts can carry dense pale brown to rusty hairs. Branched clusters of small cream to yellow-white flowers appear above the foliage, followed by small dark fruits. Fatsia and other large-leaved ornamentals can look similar from a distance. Photograph the leaf underside, attachment of the stalk and flowering structure rather than relying only on leaf size. Numerous nearby shoots may be connected underground.
actions: Choose a planting position where expanding shoots can be monitored and removed without damaging neighboring plants or structures. If it spreads beyond the intended bed, follow the underground connection where practical and remove unwanted rooted growth; cutting off the visible shoot alone may leave the source in place. Check again during the growing season. Keep discarded roots and divisions out of unmanaged land, and do not share plants without explaining their spreading habit. If a colony occurs away from gardens, ask a local botanist to confirm it and assess its significance before larger removal work.

identification: Stems are triangular in cross-section, and the narrow leaves are folded into a shallow V. Several long leaflike bracts extend beyond a branching flower head. The flattened spikelets become yellowish to golden brown and contain rows of small scales. Roots are fibrous. Other small flatsedges can look similar, including species with compact heads or different scale patterns, so a photograph of the complete head and close views of spikelets are useful. Do not identify it only from a triangular stem; many sedges share that feature.
actions: Remove small unwanted plants before flowering and seed production where hand weeding is practical, and check again for later seedlings. Keep seed-bearing soil and vegetation from being moved between beds or fields. In crops, coordinate timing with a local adviser because water management and control options depend on the crop and production system. Avoid assuming a treatment for yellow or purple nutsedge fits this annual species. For a wetland occurrence, confirm the identification before disturbing native sedges and follow local guidance on work near water.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Cyperus iria
IRRI: Practical field guide to rice weeds

identification: The leaves and sheaths are generally softly hairy. Mature plants produce an open, loose, often nodding flower head with large several-flowered spikelets. Each floret ends in a long, straight, rough awn. Red brome has a more compact head, while rescuegrass has much shorter awns. The closely related rigid brome can be especially difficult to separate and may have been included under broader names in older accounts. Photograph the head before it breaks apart, along with a complete spikelet and the leaf sheath.
actions: Plan control while plants are young and before mature seed spreads. Small patches may be hand-pulled or cut where that can be done without excessive disturbance, with follow-up for missed plants. Keep dry seed heads away from pets and livestock, and clean attached seeds from clothing and equipment before entering another site. Extensive grassland infestations need a restoration or grazing plan developed with local specialists. A single late mowing may scatter mature seed, so check seed development first and provide suitable replacement cover after reducing the grass.

sources.label: UC WRIC: Ripgut, red and downy brome
Flora of China: Bromus rigidus differential
Oregon Extension: Grass in vineyard sheep will not graze

identification: Plants have hairy leaves and sheaths and a relatively stiff, contracted flowering head. Short branches bear upright, several-flowered spikelets with long, rough awns. Rigid brome has an elliptical attachment scar at the base of the floret. A specialist can compare this with the related ripgut brome, B. diandrus. These are small details requiring magnification and mature material. Head posture alone can change as a plant ages, so photograph complete spikelets as well as the overall flowering head.
actions: Ask a grass specialist to confirm an uncertain identification before applying advice intended for a different brome. Keep mature awned heads from being transported in cut vegetation, soil or equipment to another site. Where a small patch is unwanted, discuss early removal with local weed staff before seed is shed, particularly in a restoration area with native annual grasses. Record the identification used and revisit the patch in later seasons. Do not assume a treatment trial on broadly defined B. diandrus proves the same result for a separately identified B. rigidus population.

identification: The trunk usually has smooth, patchy white, gray or reddish-brown bark that sheds in flakes or short ribbons. Adult leaves are narrow and lance-shaped, while juvenile leaves are broader. Flower buds occur in groups, commonly seven to eleven, followed by woody capsules with valves projecting above the rim. Bud-cap shape varies among subspecies; a pronounced beak is not universal. For identification, photograph mature buds, capsules, adult and juvenile leaves where available, and the trunk. Other smooth-barked gums can look similar from a distance.
actions: Look beyond a planted tree for independently rooted seedlings, particularly along drainage lines or disturbed ground. If regeneration is spreading into natural vegetation, document its extent and consult local land managers about priorities and suitable replacement cover. Have large-tree work assessed by a qualified arborist, especially near buildings, roads or waterways. Avoid moving seed-bearing debris into uninfested areas and monitor the site after any professionally planned removal. Do not assume that concerns reported for blue gum or another eucalyptus establish the same treatment or impact for river red gum.

sources.label: New South Wales Flora: Eucalyptus camaldulensis

identification: River sheoak has gray-brown, finely fissured bark and slender jointed branchlets. Around each joint are usually six to ten small upright leaf teeth. The small woody fruiting structures resemble cones but contain winged fruits rather than pine seeds. Male and female flowers usually occur on separate trees. The relatively small, lightly hairy cones and branchlet details help distinguish it from other Australian pines, but tooth counts overlap and hybrids can be intermediate. Photograph several branchlet joints and mature cones, not just the overall silhouette.
actions: Avoid planting or transporting Australian pines into new natural areas, and check local requirements before acquiring or moving nursery stock. In Florida, obtain species-level advice when a tree is spreading or being considered for removal, since hybrids and similar species complicate identification. Watch nearby open ground for seedlings and record their connection to mature trees. Large trees require professional assessment for safe removal, particularly near structures or water. Follow up with appropriate native vegetation and continued monitoring rather than leaving disturbed bare ground where new seedlings can establish.

sources.label: UF: Field guide to Florida Casuarina
New South Wales Flora: Casuarina cunninghamiana
UF Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants: Casuarina species

identification: Look for deeply divided lower leaves and much narrower, undivided upper leaves that do not clasp the stem. The flowers have two stamens; petals are absent or extremely reduced. Mature fruits are small, elliptical, and slightly notched at the tip. Compared with common pepperweed, Lepidium densiflorum, the fruiting branches are more open and the fruits less distinctly broad toward their tops. Roadside pepperweed also has a characteristic unpleasant odor, although fruit shape and leaf arrangement provide better photographic evidence than smell alone.
actions: Photograph the whole plant, lower leaves, and mature fruiting branches before removing an unfamiliar mustard. Where it is an unwanted garden weed, prevent seed-bearing plants from being carried with soil or garden debris. Keep removed fruiting material contained and check the same disturbed patch for additional plants. For a larger roadside population, send close photographs to a local herbarium or extension office before planning treatment.

identification: Examine the ripe fruits beneath the white parachute of hairs: they are reddish, brick red, or purplish rather than the usual tan or brown of common dandelion. Leaves tend to have narrow, deeply cut segments, but leaf shape changes with growing conditions and is not a reliable identification by itself. Photograph a mature fruit head and a few attached fruits at close range, along with the rosette. Regional treatments have used names including Taraxacum laevigatum and T. scanicum for plants in this group, so an older label may need interpretation.
actions: If the plant is unwanted in a small maintained area, deal with it before mature fruits disperse and avoid carrying seed heads in loose clippings. A photograph taken while fruits are still attached can preserve the distinguishing evidence. Ask a local botanist to verify unusual records, especially when only leaves are available. Choose any lawn management response according to the site's needs and the confirmed plant, rather than its common name alone.

identification: The typical bird is blue-gray with two dark bars across each folded wing, a dark tail tip, and iridescent green or purple neck feathers. Feral flocks also contain white, reddish, spotted, and nearly black birds, so color alone is unreliable. Look at the compact body, small head, ground-feeding behavior, and flocking habit. Nests are rough platforms of twigs or grass on protected, fairly flat surfaces. A mixed-color flock using the same ledge can still consist entirely of rock pigeons.
actions: Remove spilled feed promptly, secure waste containers, and stop deliberate feeding where birds are causing a problem. Inspect sheltered ledges and building openings for recurring use. Properly fitted bird netting or suitable screening can exclude pigeons; installation should avoid trapping birds inside. Sloped ledges and other physical deterrents can make particular roosts less usable. For occupied nests, difficult access, or substantial droppings, arrange advice from a qualified wildlife or building-management professional. Recheck exclusion materials regularly for damage.

identification: Leaves are divided into numerous very narrow segments, giving the plant an airy appearance. The flowers are usually blue or purple, with pink and white forms also occurring. Each has a conspicuous backward-pointing spur, typically 12 to 20 millimeters long. Small bracteoles on the flower stalk sit below the flower rather than touching its sepals. That separation helps distinguish rocket larkspur from Oriental larkspur, whose bracteoles sit much closer to the flower. Lower flower-cluster bracts are divided, and the developing fruits are upright follicles. Include these details when photographing a plant.
actions: To limit unwanted reseeding in a garden, collect flowering or fruiting stems before mature seeds scatter. Keep seed-bearing material together when moving it off the site, and inspect nearby disturbed soil the following growing season. Avoid treating an unfamiliar native larkspur on the strength of flower color alone. A local herbarium or extension office can compare the spur, bracteoles, and fruit with regional species.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Consolida ajacis

identification: The body is translucent with reddish-brown lines, and the head carries a conspicuous toothed rostrum, the pointed extension between the eyes. Specialist descriptions give seven to nine upper teeth and usually three lower teeth. Several upper teeth lie behind the eye socket. These are small structures that require a sharp side view or magnification; a general picture of a transparent shrimp is rarely enough. Native grass shrimps and other introduced Palaemon species can look similar. Color pattern supports examination of the rostrum and other anatomy. Genetic research also reveals cryptic lineages that these visible features cannot resolve.
actions: Photograph a suspected shrimp from the side, record the exact shore or marina, and send the observation to a regional marine monitoring program such as Massachusetts MIMIC. Avoid transferring shrimp, attached growth, or seawater between sites. Keep any requested specimen contained and follow the receiving program's instructions. Do not release aquarium or bait animals into coastal water, and do not attempt broad removal of mixed shrimp communities without expert identification.

sources.label: Gonzalez-Castellano et al.: Palaemon elegans population structure

identification: Look for alternate leaves along the climbing stems and large, branching flower clusters at the ends of shoots or in leaf axils. The genus description gives clusters commonly containing dozens of small flowers. The dry fruit is crowned by enlarged, winglike sepals and contains a single developed seed. These fruits are more informative than a distant photograph of foliage. Florida botanical descriptions also emphasize the large tuber, sometimes visible above the ground. A photograph of the stem base, leaf arrangement, flowers, and mature fruit provides a useful set of features for identification.
actions: Keep a record of plants appearing beyond an intentional planting, particularly seedlings or vines in neighboring unmanaged ground. Photograph the plant before cutting it back, and keep fruiting material from being discarded into natural areas. If an established vine needs removal, seek local horticultural advice about its storage root and the surrounding vegetation. Avoid disturbing an unfamiliar large root structure simply to obtain an identification; flowers and fruits may supply the evidence without excavation.

sources.label: CICY: Agdestis clematidea in the Yucatan (archived PDF)
FNA and Flora de Nicaragua: Agdestis clematidea

identification: The characteristic branch pattern resembles a fish skeleton: short side shoots spread in orderly rows from longer stems. Small, glossy, dark green leaves are roughly a centimeter long and may turn red in autumn. Pink flowers occur singly or in pairs during spring, followed by small red fruits in late summer and fall. Leaf retention varies with climate, so examine branching, leaves, flowers, and fruit together. Many other cotoneasters have red fruit, and larger upright species should not be identified as rockspray solely from berry color.
actions: Inspect nearby beds, walls, and unmanaged edges for seedlings or separate shrubs before deciding how to manage a planting. Photograph any escapes with a close view of the branch pattern and leaves. Keep fruiting cuttings out of natural areas and avoid passing along seedlings whose identity is uncertain. Where removal is needed, obtain local guidance for the confirmed species and revisit the site for new growth. Advice for other invasive cotoneasters may not transfer directly to this one.

identification: Leaves grow in opposite pairs and are broad, thick-looking, gray-green, and often softly pale or hairy. Their stalks are very short and their bases are heart-shaped. Flowers occur in clusters and have five spreading lobes, whitish outside and pinkish within, with purple-brown tips and a raised central crown. The inflated fruits are plump and oval rather than narrow pods. When mature, they contain seeds with long silky hairs. Close photographs of the flower's center and lobes are especially helpful for comparison with giant crownflower; foliage alone can be misleading.
actions: For an unfamiliar crownflower, photograph flowers, fruits, and the whole plant and record whether additional plants occur away from cultivation. In Hawaii, send suspected new or expanding populations to the local invasive species committee. Avoid spreading ripe seed or dumping cut branches into unmanaged ground. Handle the plant cautiously and keep its sap away from eyes and skin. Ask a local land manager for a species-confirmed removal plan before tackling a large shrub.

identification: Affected sticky monkeyflower can have dark, sunken lesions at the stem base and a depleted system of fine feeder roots. Above ground, plants may become stunted, yellow or brown, lose leaves, and develop twig dieback. Severe damage can kill the plant. These symptoms overlap with other Phytophthora species, poor drainage, and irrigation problems. Record the host name, plant supplier, planting date, and whether similar symptoms occur in the same nursery lot. Photographs should include the stem collar and roots, as well as the canopy.
actions: Pause movement or planting of suspect stock and contact a plant diagnostic laboratory for sampling instructions. Use clean propagation material, containers, and growing media. Keep nursery plants off contaminated ground and out of standing water, and manage irrigation to limit splash and drainage between lots. Do not move suspect potting mix or roots to a restoration site. Keep nursery and planting records together so that a confirmed finding can be traced to related plants.

sources.label: US Forest Service / Forest Phytophthoras: Phytophthora tentaculata
Martini et al.: Root and stem rot of oregano in Italy

identification: Adult females are small, creamy-white, elongate insects coated with powdery wax. White deposits may occur around roots, on the potting medium, or against the inside wall of a container. Young insects resemble smaller adults and can be difficult to see. Poor growth, pale leaves, and wilting are possible warning signs, but they also occur with watering or root disease problems. Carefully slip the plant from its pot over a contained surface and photograph the root-ball edge and insects. Microscopic examination by a specialist is needed to distinguish this species reliably.
actions: Separate suspect plants from clean stock and avoid sharing their potting mix, runoff, or used containers. Keep the plant label and source information with the sample. Contact extension or a nursery inspector for confirmation and a suitable response before distributing plants or taking cuttings. Inspect nearby containers as well as the visibly weak plant. Surface sprays directed only at leaves will not reach insects hidden among roots, so management should follow the confirmed diagnosis and growing situation.

identification: Look for a plant that is failing to grow normally, wilting, or developing damaged roots and discolored tissue around the stem base. Those observations describe a root-disease problem, not a species diagnosis. Several water molds, other root pathogens, poor drainage, and damaged roots can produce similar effects. A laboratory may need both isolation and molecular evidence to distinguish members of the cryptogea complex. Record the host, irrigation conditions, supplier, and pattern of affected plants; photographs of roots and the crown are more useful than a picture of wilted leaves alone.
actions: Keep suspect nursery plants and their growing medium from being moved to clean beds or restoration sites while diagnosis is pending. Review irrigation and drainage, including water that passes from one container or bed to another. Use clean stock and clean containers, and retain purchase and planting records. Ask a plant diagnostic laboratory how to collect a representative sample before removing the entire plant. A general Phytophthora result should be interpreted with the laboratory before making species-specific decisions.

identification: The pathogen itself cannot be recognized from a canopy photograph. Investigators examine affected fine roots and soil around an oak and use laboratory isolation, baiting, and diagnostic characters to determine what is present. Reduced vigor or a thinning crown may justify an inspection, but neither symptom is distinctive. Even a general positive result for Phytophthora leaves the species unresolved. Record the oak species when known, changes in soil drainage, recent excavation, and the timing of decline. These details help distinguish a disease investigation from an unsupported visual identification.
actions: Have a declining oak assessed by a qualified arborist or plant diagnostic service before removing it or disturbing its roots. Avoid moving soil and rooted planting material from a suspect site to another oak planting. Check whether irrigation or drainage has recently changed, and seek advice suited to the particular oak and climate. If testing suggests P. quercina, retain the laboratory report and contact the appropriate plant-health authority for confirmation and next steps.

sources.label: Jonsson et al.: Swedish P. quercina pathogenicity

identification: Root-knot nematodes live in plant roots and can produce swellings or galls. The nematodes themselves are too small for reliable unaided identification, and gall shape alone cannot establish M. mali. Several other Meloidogyne species can produce similar root changes. A specialist examines life stages and uses appropriate diagnostic methods to distinguish them. Photograph abnormal roots while keeping their association with the host plant clear. Record where the plant came from, how long it has been growing, and whether neighboring plants show comparable root symptoms or reduced vigor.
actions: Do not move a suspect rooted plant or its soil to another garden, nursery block, or disposal site without advice. Contact a nematology or plant diagnostic laboratory before sampling so the roots and surrounding soil arrive in useful condition. Keep labels and purchase records, and inspect related stock if a nursery shipment is involved. Do not assume that a rotation or resistant variety recommended for a different root-knot nematode will control this species.

sources.label: Ahmed: Meloidogyne mali and ulmi comparison

identification: Leaves are alternate and divided into many paired, small oval or oblong leaflets, with no single terminal leaflet. The plant climbs by twining stems rather than tendrils. Small pale pink, violet, or whitish flowers form clusters in leaf axils. Flattened brown pods open and curl back to expose several hard, shiny seeds, usually scarlet with a sharply contrasting black patch. Photograph leaves, the climbing stem, and pods together: the paired leaflets can resemble other legumes before the distinctive fruit appears. Do not break or taste seeds to investigate them.
actions: Keep children and pets away from pods and fallen seeds. For a small confirmed infestation, obtain local extension advice about removal and collect pods without scattering their contents. Keep seed-bearing material contained during disposal. Larger vines or plants intertwined with desirable vegetation may need professional treatment. Revisit the site repeatedly for seedlings; removing one visible vine does not address seeds already present. Avoid planting or sharing the vine, even where its flowers appear attractive.
After suspected swallowing of a seed or exposure of the eyes or mouth to seed material, seek poison-control or medical advice immediately rather than waiting for symptoms.

sources.label: UF IFAS: Rosary Pea management guide
UF IFAS: Integrated management of invasive plants
USDA Forest Service: Wildland shrubs, Abrus precatorius

identification: The leaves are long and relatively narrow, usually several centimeters long, with conspicuous sunken veins that give the upper surface a wrinkled appearance. Their undersides are pale and hairy. Leaves alternate along the branches. White flowers occur in clusters, and red fruits may remain through winter. Compare these long willowlike leaves with the much smaller leaves and neatly fishbone-patterned branches of rockspray cotoneaster. Cotoneasters lack the prickles and compound leaves familiar on many roses. Photograph both leaf surfaces, the whole shrub, and flowers or fruits rather than relying on red berries alone.
actions: Check for separate plants or seedlings beyond an ornamental planting and record whether they are increasing. Keep fruiting prunings out of natural areas and avoid sharing unidentified seedlings. If removal is needed, ask local extension staff to confirm the species and recommend a response suited to the site. Cultivar names and nursery labels are useful supporting information, but they should accompany photographs rather than substitute for them.

identification: These aphids are pear-shaped, green or pink, with long antennae and a pair of conspicuous tubular cornicles near the rear of the abdomen. Adults can reach about an eighth of an inch long. Look closely at buds and tender shoot tips, where groups feed together. Winged individuals may occur alongside wingless ones. Similar colors occur in potato aphids and other rose-feeding species; a clear close-up and the host plant help, but specialist identification may be necessary. Cast skins and sticky leaves are supporting clues rather than proof of the species.
actions: Check new growth regularly and look for lady beetles, lacewing larvae, and other natural enemies before intervening. Tolerate small colonies when growth remains healthy. A directed water spray can dislodge exposed aphids from sturdy shoots; revisit the plant to see whether numbers recover. Avoid unnecessary broad insecticide use that can disrupt natural enemies. If distortion or heavy colonies persist, ask extension staff for management appropriate to the rose and growing conditions.

sources.label: UC IPM: Roses insects and mites

identification: Wingless adults are usually apple green, sometimes yellowish or pink, and about two to three millimeters long. Their long, straight cornicles are dark and have a netlike surface pattern that requires magnification to examine. Winged adults have darker markings and long antennae. Related Sitobion species can be difficult to distinguish, so a distant photograph of green aphids on grass is insufficient. Record whether the colony is on a bramble, rose, strawberry, or a particular grass, and obtain sharp side and overhead photographs if possible.
actions: In a crop, record the extent of colonization and ask a local crop adviser to confirm the aphid before choosing a response. Keep natural enemies in mind when evaluating small colonies. Do not remove nearby brambles or apply a cereal treatment solely because an aphid resembles this species. If a new regional record is suspected, retain host and location information and follow an entomologist's specimen instructions.

sources.label: Ramirez and Niemeyer: Sitobion fragariae feeding on wheat

identification: The plant may stand upright or lean outward and is densely hairy. Each leaf has three broad, finely toothed leaflets, usually widest toward the tip. The flower heads are nearly spherical, around two centimeters across, and sit at the ends of stems without a conspicuous long stalk. Numerous purple to rosy flowers make up each head. Persistent flower parts remain around the small, single-seeded fruits. Other clovers can have pink heads, so photograph the whole head, its attachment to the stem, a leaf, and the hairy calyx below individual flowers.
actions: First establish whether the clover was intentionally sown and what the site is managed to support. In a natural area, document patch size and ask the land manager whether it is a local priority. Where unwanted plants are being removed, keep maturing heads from scattering and check the same patch in the following growing season. Avoid changing grazing or seeding practices on the basis of a common name alone; consult a local forage or restoration specialist.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney: Trifolium hirtum

identification: Look for large opposite leaves with toothed margins, often oval to heart-shaped. The upper surface is dark green; the underside is paler and fuzzy. Crushed foliage has an unpleasant odor. Fragrant pink to rosy flower clusters sit above the foliage, and dark blue fruits may follow. Shoots appearing some distance from an established shrub can belong to the same spreading root system. Compare both leaf arrangement and flower structure before distinguishing it from unrelated shrubs with pink flower heads. Climate affects whether foliage persists or is shed in winter.
actions: Inspect around an existing planting for new shoots and remove unwanted young plants with their roots, taking care to collect root fragments. Recheck the area because overlooked underground growth can remain. Keep dug roots and fruiting material out of unmanaged land. For a contained ornamental planting, a suitable container can limit root spread. If a large colony is established among desirable plants, seek local extension guidance before extensive digging or treatment.

identification: Leaves occur in opposite pairs and have smooth edges. Three strong veins run from near the leaf base, a particularly useful feature to photograph. Upper surfaces are glossy green, while the undersides are densely covered with soft pale hairs. Young stems are also hairy. Flowers have five pink petals surrounding many conspicuous stamens. Rounded fruits become dark purple. Similar-looking native shrubs should be checked carefully: include the leaf underside and three-veined pattern, not just a photograph of a pink flower or purple berry.
actions: Avoid planting rose myrtle near natural vegetation, and replace an existing landscape plant with a suitable local native alternative where recommended. Report new natural-area patches to the managing agency or local invasive-plant program. For established shrubs, consult extension staff about a removal plan that addresses resprouting and follow-up seedlings. Keep fruiting branches contained during removal. Revisit treated areas rather than treating the loss of aboveground stems as proof that the shrub is gone.

sources.label: Rayamajhi et al.: Rust on Rhodomyrtus in Florida natural areas

identification: Plants form erect clumps with narrow leaves and branching stems that can root at their nodes. Flowering stems are commonly about two to three feet tall. The branched flower heads have reddish hairs around the spikelets, producing their soft pink appearance. Mature heads lose much of that color. Photograph the whole clump, stem nodes, leaf attachment, and a close view of the head. Pink ornamental grasses can look similar from a distance; Melinis nerviglumis is a particular comparison, and foliage details help separate them.
actions: Prevent seed production where a confirmed patch threatens a conservation area. Small plants may be hand-pulled where this can be done without damaging nearby vegetation. Clean clothing, footwear, and equipment before leaving a seeding stand. Do not rely on mowing or fire alone: Florida guidance reports that these do not provide effective control. For extensive infestations, seek a site-specific plan from extension or the land manager and revisit after treatment for new seedlings.

sources.label: USFS FEIS: Fire effects on subtropical invasive plants

identification: Female covers are grayish white, flattened, and roughly circular, reaching about three millimeters across. Male covers are smaller and narrower. Older covers may appear dirty. Eggs and the mobile young stages, called crawlers, are reddish orange. Adult females remain beneath their covers; adult males are tiny winged insects. Examine several canes with a hand lens and photograph the covers close enough to show shape. The contrast between circular female covers and elongated male covers is more useful than the overall whiteness of the stem.
actions: Inspect new rose or caneberry plants before adding them to a planting. Have a suspicious scale identified, especially if it is spreading between plants. Remove heavily affected material when appropriate for the plant's pruning cycle and keep it from contacting clean stock. Monitor for crawler activity with local extension guidance, since this exposed stage differs from protected settled scales. Preserve natural enemies where possible and obtain current, crop-specific advice if an infestation remains damaging after sanitation and routine plant care.

sources.label: UC IPM: Roses insects and mites

identification: The plant has soft, somewhat woody stems that may sprawl outward or grow upright, forming a broad low shrub. Stems and leaves carry long soft hairs, though the density varies. The foliage releases a rose-like scent when bruised. Pink flowers gather in compact, headlike clusters, reflected in the species name capitatum. Pelargoniums produce distinctive long-beaked fruits; mature seeds have an elongated coiling appendage. Compare a flowering specimen with a botanical reference rather than relying on scent or a nursery label, because related scented pelargoniums share several of these features.
actions: Keep garden trimmings and rooted pieces out of coastal vegetation and other unmanaged ground. The species can be propagated from cuttings, so discarded stems should not be treated as harmless litter. Photograph plants found beyond cultivation and record their distance from gardens, whether they flower, and whether younger plants are present. For removal near sensitive coastal plants, ask the land manager or a local botanist to verify the identity and choose an approach that limits soil disturbance.

identification: Adults are narrow, flattened metallic beetles, usually less than a quarter inch long, with coppery or greenish reflections. Larvae are pale and feed beneath the cane bark, producing winding or spiral grooves and gall-like swellings. Later stages occur within the cane. Look for wilted shoots, weakened swollen sections, and tunneling beneath bark on a damaged cane. Adult feeding can leave ragged leaf edges, but that injury alone is not diagnostic. Photograph the swelling and exposed tunnel, and keep a sample for identification if the cause is uncertain.
actions: Inspect brambles and roses for damaged canes during routine pruning. Utah guidance recommends pruning out and destroying infested canes to remove the developing insects. Keep those canes from being stored beside healthy plants. Maintain appropriate irrigation and fertility so berry plantings are not unnecessarily stressed. Before establishing a new bramble bed, inspect nearby roses for infestation. Local adult emergence dates vary, so any additional control should follow regional monitoring advice rather than a calendar copied from another climate.

sources.label: Utah State University: Rose Stem Girdler
Purdue: Emerald ash borer identification guide, similar Agrilus

identification: Wingless adults are relatively large, pale green or yellowish, often with a darker stripe down the back. The cornicles are long and mostly pale, sometimes darker at the tips. Antennal joints are darkened, and the antennae usually extend beyond the bases of the cornicles. Greenbug is a close visual comparison, so use a hand lens and a regional aphid key. Photograph several adults from above and from the side, together with the host plant and the part being colonized. Color alone varies too much for a confident determination.
actions: Check the crop and colony before deciding whether treatment is warranted. Preserve natural enemies and avoid spraying merely because aphids are visible. If the identity is uncertain, contact a farm adviser before applying a control intended for greenbug. For a confirmed cereal infestation, use local scouting and disease guidance rather than transferring garden rose advice. Keep records of colony location, crop stage, and changes in abundance so follow-up decisions reflect what is actually happening.

identification: The insects shelter on stems beneath leaf sheaths, where they can remain hidden during a quick inspection of the leaves. Mature females become brown and hardened, while younger stages are paler. A close examination of a stem with its sheath gently opened can reveal the colony. Other scale insects occur on grasses, including native species, so a photograph of a brown patch is not conclusive. Include the entire cane, the colony's position beneath the sheath, and detailed images of individual insects when reporting a suspected infestation.
actions: Report suspected new infestations to a wetland manager, extension specialist, or state plant-health office. Record the location and condition of the stand, including healthy and declining areas. Avoid transporting cut cane or planting material from an infested stand to another wetland. Do not apply garden insect treatments in marsh habitat or introduce predators on your own. Management is a specialist conservation task, and monitoring the stand over time can be more useful than disturbing it during an attempted removal.

sources.label: LSU AgCenter: Roseau cane die-off FAQ

identification: Wingless adults are rounded and may be dusty pink, wine-colored, or dark olive, with a whitish or grayish waxy coating. Their cornicles are dark, and their antennae are shorter than the body. Winged forms have darker abdominal markings. Look on the undersides of unfolding leaves and within newly curled foliage. Cast skins and sticky honeydew may surround a colony. Other aphids can share the same tree, and color varies, so photograph adults at close range and include the affected leaf cluster and tree growth stage.
actions: Begin checking susceptible trees as buds open, before leaves become tightly curled. Record which shoots contain colonies and whether numbers are increasing. Encourage natural enemies by avoiding unnecessary broad insecticide applications. If colonies are widespread or the tree has a history of damage, consult a local fruit specialist promptly for advice suited to the growth stage. Do not assume that a late spray can reverse injury already produced inside curled leaves.

identification: Look for the boat-shaped leaf tip characteristic of bluegrasses and slender creeping stems that connect shoots at the surface. Flowering plants produce an open branched seed head, but regularly mowed turf may seldom flower. Examine a small connected piece rather than pulling a single detached leaf. Other bluegrasses share the leaf-tip shape, so include stem growth, leaf attachment, and any flowering head in photographs. A regional turf specialist can distinguish rough bluegrass from annual bluegrass, Kentucky bluegrass, and other grasses that occur in mixed lawns.
actions: Map the patch and confirm the species before renovating or treating a lawn. Check whether the grass was part of an intentional seed mixture. Penn State guidance notes that preemergence products do not solve established rough bluegrass in mowed turf, where seed production is uncommon. Ask a turf specialist about a plan suited to the desired lawn species and site conditions. Avoid carrying pieces of creeping stems into clean areas during cultivation or repair, and monitor the edge of a treated patch.

identification: Fronds rise from a scaled underground stem and divide into numerous small segments. Dark brown to purplish-black stalks and branching axes contrast with the green leaflets. Fine hairs occur on the stalks, axes, and leaf surfaces, helping explain the name rough or hairy maidenhair. The spore-bearing structures sit near the leaflet margins beneath folded portions of the leaf edge. Other maidenhair ferns can look similar, including native species, so photograph hairs, the pattern of branching, and the underside of a fertile frond. A whole-frond image is more useful than a single detached leaflet.
actions: In Hawaii, report a suspected expansion into a rare-plant area to the responsible land manager. Avoid moving nursery pots, soil, or fern material from an infested site into clean habitat. Confirm the species before pulling a maidenhair fern, especially where native ferns occur. For established patches, follow a conservation management plan rather than repeatedly disturbing the soil without a clear objective. Recheck nearby shaded ground and record whether the patch is enlarging over time.

sources.label: Ferns of the Hawaiian Islands: Adiantum hispidulum
Oahu Army Natural Resources: Kamaili management appendix

identification: Young fish can be fairly uniform gray, while larger individuals commonly show brown and black mottling. A dark spot on the first dorsal fin is a useful clue, although some fish lack a clear spot. The most helpful comparison is with native sculpins: round gobies have pelvic fins joined into a suction-cup-like disk under the body, while sculpins have separate pelvic fins. Photograph the side of the fish and, if safely possible, the underside showing those fins. Do not rely only on mottled color or a blunt head.
actions: Never move a round goby to another water body or use it as bait. Check bait containers carefully and dispose of unwanted bait according to local instructions. Clean plants, mud, and animals from boats and equipment, drain retained water, and dry equipment before reuse. Report a suspected new occurrence to the state fish or invasive-species program with the exact location and photographs. Ask that program how to handle a specimen rather than transporting a live fish for identification.

identification: The plant has narrow leaves, round or oval stems, and a branched cluster of small flowers at the stem tip. Mature capsules are rounded and project beyond the six small, leaflike flower parts surrounding them. The main leaflike bract often extends above the flower cluster. Saltmarsh rush, Juncus gerardii, is an important lookalike: its anthers are generally longer, and its main bract usually does not conspicuously overtop the cluster. Those differences require close views and sometimes measurement. Photograph a mature capsule, an intact flower, the full cluster, and the leaves attached to the stem.
actions: Document a suspected patch with its habitat and extent before removing plants. For a wetland or a new regional record, ask a local botanist or herbarium to confirm mature material. Avoid moving soil or fruiting rushes between wet places. Where management is warranted, coordinate with the landowner or wetland manager so that native rushes and sensitive soils are protected. Follow-up observations of patch boundaries can establish whether the population is spreading.

identification: The crown is typically spreading and relatively flat-topped, with many branches and finely divided leaves composed of numerous small leaflets. Masses of red-orange flowers can cover the canopy during the flowering season. Long, flattened, dark brown woody pods are especially distinctive; they may remain on the tree through winter and fall later. A tree with fernlike foliage alone could be another tropical legume, so include flowers or mature pods in photographs. Seedlings may not display the broad crown of an established landscape tree, making their connection to a nearby fruiting tree useful context.
actions: Inspect beneath and beyond a fruiting tree for seedlings, especially next to unmanaged habitat. Collect fallen pods where they create a nuisance and keep them from being dumped into natural areas. In southern Florida, follow local guidance intended to prevent escape. If a mature tree needs pruning or removal, use a qualified arborist because of its size and spreading structure. Before planting, consider the available space and consult current regional recommendations for a suitable shade tree.

sources.label: UF IFAS: Delonix regia Royal Poinciana

identification: Plants form low, rounded shrubs, sometimes approaching a meter in height. Leaves are short, fleshy, and roughly cylindrical or rounded on one side, rather than broad and flat. Hairiness varies among plants. The small fruits may be green, yellow, red, or purplish and become dark when dry; color alone does not indicate a different species. Each fruit has a short projecting beak. Compare the leaf shape, fruit attachment, and overall growth form with local saltbushes before identifying it. A close view with a scale is helpful because the fruits are only several millimeters across.
actions: Record whether a suspected plant was intentionally planted and whether younger individuals occur nearby. Keep fruiting cuttings and nursery soil from being discarded into unmanaged ground. For an apparent escape, consult a local herbarium or invasive-plant program before arranging removal. In Hawaii, a verified observation may help clarify the species' local status. Avoid interpreting a database occurrence as proof that every individual requires control; the appropriate response depends on confirmed identity, local spread, and site objectives.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney: Enchylaena tomentosa

identification: The body is olive to golden brown above and pale below, often with dark markings. The mouth points slightly downward. The spiny and soft portions of the dorsal fin are connected, giving the top fin a continuous appearance. Sharp spines also occur around the gill covers. Yellow perch, walleye, and trout-perch are potential sources of confusion, especially when fish are small. Photograph the side with the dorsal fin visible and include the head and gill-cover region. Handle the fish carefully because the spines are sharp; a color match alone is not a reliable identification.
actions: Do not move suspect ruffe between lakes or use them as bait. Inspect bait before fishing and dispose of unwanted bait according to local guidance. Clean boats and equipment, drain retained water, and dry gear before taking it to another water body. Report a suspected new occurrence to the state fish or invasive-species agency with photographs and an exact location. Obtain instructions before retaining or transporting a specimen. Prevention is more practical than attempting to remove an established population yourself.

identification: Look for strongly wrinkled leaflets and stems densely covered with straight prickles. Leaves are divided into several oval, toothed leaflets. The flowers are large and showy, commonly deep pink but sometimes white or pale pink, and rounded red hips follow. Native roses may share flower color or prickly stems, but the combination of heavily textured leaves, dense prickles, and large hips is particularly useful. Photograph a full leaf, a section of stem, and flowers or fruit together. Young shoots emerging around an older plant may be connected below ground.
actions: Wear sturdy gloves when handling the shrub. Small confirmed plants can be pulled with their roots when conditions allow, but avoid destabilizing dune soil or damaging native plants. Cutting larger shrubs once usually leads to regrowth; a removal plan needs repeated follow-up. Remove immature hips from retained garden plants where seed spread is a concern and watch for root sprouts. For coastal infestations, coordinate with the land manager before digging or treating plants, and keep all removed material out of tidal water.

sources.label: Maine Natural Areas Program: Rugosa Rose
University of Maryland extension: Rosa Rugosa

identification: Adults are relatively large for whiteflies, about two and a half millimeters long, with pale wings crossed by irregular light-brown bands. Females place eggs in curved or spiral patterns, usually beneath leaves, and cover them with white wax. Developing colonies add more waxy material. Other whiteflies can also produce wax or patterned egg deposits, so examine adults and immature stages rather than diagnosing from sooty mold alone. Photograph leaf undersides, an adult with its wings visible, and the extent of active colonization on the plant.
actions: Confirm the whitefly and inspect for living immature stages before treating a tree that merely has egg deposits or old wax. Assess plant health as well as the nuisance beneath it. Ask local extension staff about natural enemies and whether intervention is warranted. Avoid indiscriminate broad treatments across every nearby plant. Large palms and trees require professional access and an appropriate management plan. Reinspect new leaves after action, because old wax and mold can remain after the active infestation declines.

sources.label: UF: Rugose spiraling whitefly identification guide
Shanas et al.: Rugose spiraling whitefly in the Old World

identification: Young plants have a rosette of sharply toothed leaves. As flowering stems develop, those basal leaves often wither, leaving small narrow leaves on the branches. Coarse reddish hairs point downward near the base of the stem, a useful close-up feature. Small yellow flower heads are scattered along the branched stems, and mature seeds carry white bristles. Several other plants have dandelionlike rosettes or yellow flower heads; combine the basal hairs, sparse stem leaves, and overall branching pattern before making an identification.
actions: Mark and report a new patch to the local weed program before disturbing its roots. Avoid tilling an infestation, because root fragments can produce new plants. Cutting before seed development may reduce seed output but does not remove the established root system. Clean equipment after work in affected ground and keep seed-bearing stems contained. Established patches generally require an integrated plan and repeated inspections over time. Ask the weed manager which approaches fit the site and protect neighboring desirable vegetation.

sources.label: UC Cooperative Extension: Selected invasive weeds, rush skeletonweed
Pacific Northwest Pest Management: Rush skeletonweed

identification: Leaves alternate along the stems and are narrow, with a silvery or sometimes rusty appearance from tiny surface scales. Branches commonly carry stout thorns. Small fragrant flowers are yellow inside, and the mature olive-shaped fruits are pale cream to brown with a scaly coating. Native silver buffaloberry, Shepherdia argentea, can look similarly gray from a distance, but it has opposite leaves and red fruit. Photograph leaf arrangement, both leaf surfaces, fruit, and thorns before identifying a young tree or planning removal.
actions: Consult the local weed manager for a riparian infestation, particularly near water or unstable banks. Small seedlings or saplings can sometimes be removed with their roots, while cutting a larger tree alone can leave it able to resprout. Plan follow-up for stump growth and new seedlings. Wear protective clothing around the thorns and keep fruiting debris from being spread. For large trees, use trained help and include replacement vegetation and bank protection in the work plan.

sources.label: Colorado Natural Heritage Program: Western Slope wetland plants
Colorado Extension: Noxious Weeds of Clear Creek County
USGS: Restoration following saltcedar and Russian olive control

identification: Wingless adults are pale green, slender, and spindle-shaped, with short antennae and no conspicuous long cornicles. A small projection above the tail gives the rear end a distinctive double-tailed appearance under magnification. Feeding can cause leaves to roll tightly and develop pale, yellowish, or purplish streaks. Gently unroll suspect leaves to look for insects concealed inside; the rolled leaf protects them and is more useful evidence than a general patch of yellow crop. Young or winged forms may be harder to recognize, so keep several clear photographs or obtain a diagnostic sample.
actions: Scout the newest growth and record the proportion of tillers with confirmed aphids and characteristic injury. Do not assume every streaked or rolled leaf contains this species. Use regional crop thresholds and consult a farm adviser before selecting a response. Preserve natural enemies where possible and avoid transferring a recommendation for another grain aphid without checking it. After any management action, revisit affected areas to assess living aphids and new growth rather than expecting damaged leaves to recover their original appearance.

identification: Most foliage is concentrated at the base in a dense tuft of long, narrow leaves. Leaf color ranges from green to blue-green. Flowering stems rise above the leaves and appear relatively bare, ending in short, dense, upright spikes. Small clusters of spikelets occur along the spike axis, and mature seed can shatter readily. The growth form is a bunch rather than a spreading rhizomatous sod. Compare mature spikes and basal foliage with other introduced forage grasses; a blue-green clump alone is not enough to distinguish it from wheatgrasses or other wildryes.
actions: Check pasture or restoration records before removing an unfamiliar clump. Where the grass is intentionally managed, use local forage guidance for grazing and stand condition. Where it is spreading into a native-plant area, map the boundary and seek advice from the land manager about a site-specific response. Prevent unwanted seed movement with equipment and keep seed-bearing material contained. Avoid reseeding a conservation site with this grass without considering the desired plant community and its strong competitive behavior once established.

sources.label: USDA NRCS: Russian Wildrye technical note MT-100

identification: A rust diagnosis begins with affected leaves and the fungal structures on them, but identifying this species requires specialist examination. Researchers used specimen comparisons and DNA sequences to separate it from other mallow rusts. Photograph both sides of affected leaves, the whole plant, and flowers or fruits that help establish the host's identity. Preserve the connection between each leaf sample and its host rather than combining material from several mallow species. A general image of rusty spots is useful for reporting symptoms but cannot confirm Puccinia modiolae.
actions: If an unusual rust appears on bristlemallow or a garden mallow, contact a plant diagnostic laboratory before moving cuttings or seedlings from the affected group. Follow its instructions for collecting and packing leaves. Keep suspect plant material separate from healthy propagation stock, and retain the date and location of the observation. Do not apply a control program for another rust solely on visual resemblance. For an isolated wild plant, documentation and expert identification may be more appropriate than removing surrounding vegetation.

sources.label: Aime and colleagues: Puccinia modiolae in North America
Berndt et al.: First European Puccinia modiolae records

identification: Early symptoms include small yellow spots on either leaf surface. These develop into yellow-orange, powdery pustules that may merge into larger damaged areas.
