Unlike a true thistle, the plant lacks conspicuous sharp leaf spines. Photograph the bracts close up, as several knapweeds have similar flowers and cannot be separated by color alone.
actions: Report unfamiliar patches to a local weed program and protect nearby uninfested ground from seed movement. Wear gloves and long sleeves when handling plants. Small confirmed patches may be removed before seed matures, with flowering or seed-bearing heads contained for disposal. Clean equipment used in the patch and inspect the area repeatedly afterward. Established infestations need a plan that combines suppression, follow-up, and recovery of desirable vegetation rather than leaving bare ground for another flush.

identification: Look for a gray-green basal rosette, later branching stems, and small pink-purple flower heads. The overlapping bracts below each head bear dark fringed tips, giving the spotted appearance. Leaves near the base are more deeply divided than those higher on the stem. These traits support recognition of spotted knapweed, but they do not by themselves resolve every subspecies or taxonomic treatment. Preserve close bract photographs, flowering material, and the name used by the original botanist or source.
actions: For a suspected patch, seek confirmation from the local weed program and explain which scientific name appears in the record. Prevent seed movement on equipment, hay, or soil while identification is being reviewed. Use gloves when handling plants and contain mature heads. A confirmed infestation should follow the local spotted-knapweed management plan, including repeated checks and vegetation recovery. Keep records under the parent species and subspecies linked so the same patch is not mistaken for two separate occurrences.

sources.label: Kew: Centaurea stoebe subsp. micranthos synonymy

identification: Adults hold spotted grayish forewings over the body; opening the wings reveals striking red, black, and white hindwings. Early nymphs are black with white spots, while the final nymphal stage adds red. Fresh egg masses have a gray coating that later resembles a cracked mud smear on a hard surface. Photograph the insect or egg mass and include the surface it was found on. Tan fuzzy spongy-moth egg masses and other insects can be mistaken for lanternfly evidence.
actions: Inspect vehicles, trailers, firewood, garden furniture, and other outdoor items before moving them from an affected area. Follow current state reporting and movement guidance, since the relevant boundaries change. Report a suspected new occurrence with a photograph and precise location. For an established infestation, use extension management advice suited to the plant and life stage. Avoid indiscriminate spraying or exposed sticky traps that can harm other animals; preserving plant health and preventing transport remain useful first steps.

sources.label: Penn State: Spotted lanternfly management guide

identification: The mantle, the saddlelike area behind the head, usually has spots or broken markings rather than continuous dark stripes. Farther back, the tail often carries longer dark bands that may break into spots. The body can become quite large when fully extended, but contracted animals look much shorter. Similar cellar slugs tend toward greener or yellower coloring and different tail patterns. Photograph an active animal from above and the side, including the mantle, tail, and head, without stretching or injuring it.
actions: Look after dark or during damp weather to see which animals are actually feeding on vulnerable plants. Keep newly purchased pots and their undersides free of unwanted hitchhikers before moving them between gardens. Do not relocate slugs to parks or natural areas. If protection is needed, ask local extension staff for a targeted approach that fits the plants and avoids harming other wildlife. Broad treatment based only on a spotted slug photograph can miss the real cause of damage.

identification: Plants have succulent upright stems with narrow, pointed leaves arranged alternately. The leaf margins are clearly toothed. Flowers are clustered in the leaf axils and may be pink, red, purple, or other cultivated colors; a curved spur projects behind the flower. The green capsules are fuzzy and split readily as they mature. Photograph the leaf arrangement, flower position, and capsule surface. Those features help distinguish garden balsam from other touch-me-nots better than flower color or the shared habit of explosive seed release.
actions: In a garden, remove unwanted seed capsules before they ripen if seedlings are spreading beyond the bed. Keep seed-bearing debris out of natural areas and note any plants growing well away from the original planting. For an unexpected wild patch, ask a local botanist to confirm the species before applying guidance written for Himalayan balsam. Record cultivated plants and self-sown escapes separately, and base management on the confirmed plant and local conditions.

identification: Adults have a fairly deep, flattened oval body with several dark blotches along the side. Juveniles look different, often yellow-green with stronger dark vertical bars. A diagonal dark stripe through the eye and a dark mark near the front of the dorsal fin can be particularly noticeable in young fish. Photograph the complete side of the fish and its fins, and record approximate size. Comparing an adult photograph with a barred juvenile alone can create a false impression of two species.
actions: Never release aquarium fish or move a captured tilapia to another waterbody. Keep pond or tank contents from escaping during overflow or disposal, and arrange suitable rehoming for unwanted fish. Report unusual outdoor sightings to the state fisheries agency with photographs and a precise location. Ask that agency about handling a captured fish and current local rules. Preserve both scientific names in the report so older records can be checked without inventing additional populations.

identification: Adults are tiny, with the general appearance of other vinegar flies. Males usually have a dark spot near the leading edge of each wing and dark combs on the forelegs. Females lack those wing spots; their serrated egg-laying structure requires magnification to inspect. Small pale larvae in fruit cannot be identified confidently to this species by eye. Retain adult specimens from monitoring and seek expert confirmation, especially when a first infestation is suspected.
actions: Monitor susceptible fruit from coloring through harvest using local extension guidance, and do not rely on trap numbers alone to judge fruit quality. Harvest frequently, remove infested and overripe fruit from the planting, and cool sound harvested fruit promptly to slow insect development. Keep the canopy reasonably open and correct irrigation leaks where practical. For persistent crop losses, use an integrated plan tailored to the crop and harvest schedule, including exclusion or labeled treatments only when locally appropriate.

sources.label: University of Minnesota: SWD management in the Upper Midwest

identification: Look at the underside of a mature leaf with a hand lens: dark gland dots are an important clue. Leaves are broadly oval to almost round, with a heart-shaped base and a pointed tip. The flowers have the familiar morning-glory funnel, while the rounded fruit remains enclosed by enlarged, leathery sepals. Similar coastal vines have been called Ipomoea campanulata, and historical name confusion makes a flower photograph alone unreliable. Include leaf undersides, sepals, and mature fruit in an identification record.
actions: Photograph the entire vine and its supporting vegetation before cutting anything. A local herbarium or extension botanist can help resolve the name and determine whether the plant is an ornamental escape, an established regional occurrence, or a different vine. Keep garden trimmings and fruit out of natural areas. If removal is advised, plan how to detach the vine without pulling down the vegetation beneath it. For a large vine on a tree, seek advice before cutting; removal can damage the support plant and leave seeds or cut material to manage.

sources.label: NYBG: Stictocardia tiliifolia, Flora of St John

identification: The leaves are short and lance-shaped, often noticeably broader than those of fine lawn grasses. At the junction between blade and sheath, look for a fringe of hairs rather than a long membrane. The seed head carries several short branches along a central stalk; paired, crowded spikelets line these branches. Rooting lower stems can make one plant look like a loose mat. Signalgrasses and crabgrasses overlap in general appearance, so preserve photographs of a mature seed head, the leaf junction, and the rooting nodes.
actions: Record whether the patch is spreading beyond disturbed soil and whether it is displacing planted or native vegetation. Ask a grass specialist to confirm a flowering specimen before choosing treatment. For a small unwanted patch, careful removal before seed shed and containment of rooted stems are sensible precautions, with follow-up for new plants. Avoid moving soil or mower debris from the patch into clean areas. For larger patches, ask local extension staff to fit a plan to the site, its surrounding vegetation, and the amount of seed already present.

sources.label: Flora of North America, Wipff: Urochloa reptans
Kew, Flora of Tropical East Africa: Urochloa reptans

identification: Look for divided, parsley-like leaves, slender branching stems, and small white flowers arranged in compound umbrella-shaped clusters. The developing fruits are oblong and become bristly little burrs. Photograph the bristles closely and include the structures beneath a flower cluster; these help distinguish Torilis species. Japanese hedgeparsley and other members of the carrot family can look similar at a distance. Do not identify a plant from white umbels alone or assume a parsley-like leaf means it is suitable to eat.
actions: Pull small, confirmed patches before flowering while the soil is moist enough to release the roots. Bag plants that already carry developing burrs so seeds do not catch on clothing during removal. Mowing around flowering can reduce seed production, but regrowth may require another visit. Clean footwear, pet fur, and tools before leaving a seeding patch. Work with the land manager on larger sites, and check again in following seasons for seedlings rather than assuming one round of pulling has finished the job.

identification: Look for narrow leaves arranged alternately up a branched stem. Leaf edges may be nearly smooth, wavy, or sparsely toothed. The stems can bend slightly at the nodes, creating a zigzag appearance. Flowers have four pale yellow petals in the mustard-family arrangement, and the developing pods are much longer than they are wide. Fine forked hairs require magnification to see clearly. Other small yellow mustards are easy to confuse with this plant, so photograph mature pods, leaf arrangement, and the complete branching habit.
actions: In a field, record the crop stage and patch size before deciding whether the plants warrant control. Extension staff can identify the mustard and advise whether competition or seed contamination is a practical concern. Small unwanted garden plants can be removed before pods mature, with seed-bearing material contained. Avoid treating every yellow-flowered mustard in nearby native vegetation on the strength of this name alone. For a larger patch, let its effect on the crop and local weed advice guide the response, while keeping nearby native vegetation out of unnecessary treatment.

identification: Several long, narrow branches radiate from the top of a flowering stem like the spokes of an open umbrella. They may spread nearly horizontally as they mature. The leaf blades are narrow, and the leaf junction has a short hairy rim. Examine the small seed-bearing units along each branch, including their projecting awns. Other Chloris species share the windmill arrangement; counting branches alone is not sufficient. Close photographs of spikelets and their awns, together with a ruler, are more useful than a distant picture of the tuft.
actions: Leave a suspected plant in place long enough to obtain clear identification photographs unless its location requires immediate maintenance. Record whether it was deliberately seeded and whether it forms runners into surrounding vegetation. A local herbarium or grass specialist should verify any unusual regional record. Prevent movement of seed-bearing clippings while identification is pending. Where it grows in pasture or seeded ground, bring the planting history and a flowering sample to the land manager before choosing removal or reseeding.

identification: The sprawling stems bear tiny spines and slender green branchlets that do the work of leaves. Small white or pale pink flowers can develop into round red berries. True ferns do not produce flowers or berries, a useful first distinction when checking a hanging basket or escaped groundcover. Names such as Asparagus sprengeri and misapplied Asparagus densiflorus appear in horticultural material. Photograph the overall habit, stem spines, branchlet clusters, and fruit rather than relying on a nursery's common-name label alone.
actions: Where local guidance discourages planting, choose an alternative groundcover and keep fruiting stems from extending into nearby natural areas. Wear gloves when handling the prickly stems, and contain berries before removing a patch. Removal needs to address the crown and its growing points; cutting off the green growth alone allows recovery. The swollen storage tubers are not themselves the parts that produce new shoots. Revisit the site for regrowth and seedlings, and seek local advice for dense patches or sensitive habitat.

identification: Start with the small rosette at ground level. Its leaves are spoon-shaped to narrow and taper toward their bases, often carrying fine hairs. Slender flowering stalks rise above the rosette without stem leaves. Each tiny white flower has four petals that are deeply notched, making it appear to have eight. Later, look for small, flattened oval seedpods. Mouse-ear cress can resemble it before flowering, but its long, slender fruits differ from draba's oval ones. A close photograph with a size reference is particularly helpful.
actions: In a garden or newly seeded lawn, remove unwanted plants while they are small and before their pods open. Where plants are sparse and do not interfere with the site's use, observation may be sufficient. Address the bare ground or poor turf establishment that allows repeated germination instead of assuming a short-lived spring flush needs broad treatment. Record flowering and pod development if identification is uncertain, and ask extension staff for help before applying control intended for a different winter annual.

identification: Greenbugs are small, pale green to yellow-green aphids with a darker green stripe along the back. Look beneath lower leaves as well as on visibly damaged foliage. The paired tubes near the rear of the body, called cornicles, are important identification features. Russian wheat aphids have a different rear-body shape, while rose-grain aphids can be difficult to separate without magnification. Photograph a colony and individual aphids closely. Yellow leaves alone cannot distinguish aphid feeding from drought, nutrient problems, or disease.
actions: Scout several parts of a field, record the crop's growth stage, and look for both aphids and fresh injury. Also note lady beetles, lacewing larvae, and swollen aphid mummies left by parasitoids. Use current local extension thresholds for the crop and season before choosing a treatment; a threshold from another crop or region may be inappropriate. If identification remains uncertain, submit clear images or a safely contained sample to an extension specialist. Preserving beneficial insects can be an important part of keeping greenbug populations below damaging levels.

identification: Possible signs include a swollen abdomen, bulging eyes, darkened skin, pale gills, and small red or purple hemorrhages. Affected fish may gather near incoming water, swim slowly, or lose balance. These signs are not specific: poor water quality and other infections can produce overlapping problems. A photograph cannot diagnose the virus, and fish without visible signs may still be infected. Keep a dated record of deaths, water conditions, recent purchases, and movement between ponds to help a veterinarian investigate.
actions: Contact an aquatic veterinarian promptly if several fish become sick or die unexpectedly. Pause transfers of fish, eggs, pond water, and shared equipment while obtaining advice. Keep equipment dedicated to the affected pond and follow professional instructions for sampling, cleaning, and disposal. Do not release fish or pond contents into natural waters. APHIS advises owners to contact their veterinarian and routes suspected or diagnosed cases through animal-health authorities. There is no simple home treatment; confirmation requires laboratory testing and a coordinated response.

sources.label: USDA APHIS: Spring viremia of carp virus

identification: The aphids are green, pear-shaped, and only about two millimeters long, with long legs and paired cornicles near the rear. Look carefully on the undersides of spruce needles, especially on branches showing early yellowing. Nymphs resemble smaller wingless adults. Record whether the newest needles remain while older ones drop, but treat that pattern as a clue rather than proof. Needle diseases, weather damage, and other pests require different responses. Close photographs of the aphids and the whole affected branch help a specialist separate these possibilities.
actions: Check affected trees early enough to find the insects rather than relying only on needles already shed. Note which spruce species is involved, the extent of crown thinning, and whether the damage is progressing. Consult an arborist or extension specialist for vulnerable garden trees or nursery stock. Broad forest treatment is not equivalent to managing a small ornamental tree, and the reviewed guidance describes limited control options. Avoid spraying on symptoms alone; confirmation and the tree's condition should guide any intervention.

sources.label: European Institute of Planted Forest: Green spruce aphid

identification: A leafy-spurge photograph may show narrow leaves and yellow-green flowering structures, but that general appearance cannot resolve this particular name. Identification needs a specialist's examination of a complete specimen and the taxonomic treatment used by the observer. Include the whole plant, upper and lower leaves, flowering structures, and fruit where available. Retain the original specimen label or report wording. A record identified only as leafy spurge should not automatically be reassigned to this subspecies, especially when the source predates more recent taxonomic work.
actions: Ask a herbarium or regional botanist to establish which taxon the local record represents before planning removal. Keep suspected spurge sap away from skin and eyes, and avoid collecting a specimen without handling guidance. If the site is already managed under a leafy-spurge program, preserve that program's original identification and treatment records while clarification proceeds. Do not transfer biological-control agents, toxicity claims, or management prescriptions from a broadly named spurge account to this unresolved entry. The immediate task is to reconcile the name and evidence, not to assume a new infestation.

sources.label: ITIS: Euphorbia esula subsp. tommasiniana concept
EPPO: Euphorbia esula subsp. saratoi synonym concept
Revision of Berlin Euphorbia herbarium specimens
Conti et al. 2026: Vascular flora of Sirente-Velino Regional Park

identification: Adults in the Florida account are approximately 6.0 to 8.5 millimeters long, with a short snout, mottled wing covers, and a sometimes yellowish head. Their shoulders are distinctly angled and wider than the section just behind the head. Teeth on the leg segments are useful under magnification. The native little leaf notcher, Artipus floridanus, is a particularly important lookalike: it lacks those leg teeth and has less angular shoulders. Photograph the insect from above and from the side, ideally with a size reference.
actions: Check the plant for actual beetles and fresh feeding before choosing any treatment. Record the host plant, the extent of damage, and whether neighboring plants are affected. An extension entomologist can confirm both the weevil and the scientific name used for the local population. Avoid moving infested nursery plants to another property while that check is pending. General insecticide advice for leaf-chewing pests is not a substitute for identification. Confirming the current scientific name helps ensure that subsequent management advice applies to the insect actually present.

sources.label: Sri Lankan Myllocerus taxonomy and examined specimens, 2026

identification: Look for paired, oval leaves with softly hairy surfaces and scalloped edges. The stems are four-angled, and small pale pink to whitish flowers sit in clusters at the upper leaf axils. Lower leaves are stalked, but upper leaves can have very short or absent stalks. Henbit's upper leaves conspicuously clasp the stem; compare that attachment together with the flowers rather than using stalk length alone. Nettles can also cause confusion before flowering, but their sharper leaf teeth and very different flowers provide useful contrasts. Photograph the leaf attachment as carefully as the flower.
actions: Confirm the plant before removing a mixed patch of mint-family herbs. Small unwanted plants can be pulled before they set seed, and disturbed ground should be revisited for another flush. In crop fields, ask extension staff whether the population interferes with establishment or harvest before selecting treatment. If livestock show abnormal behavior near a suspect patch, contact a veterinarian and provide photographs rather than relying on the common name. The response should fit the confirmed plant, the animals present, and the conditions in that particular field.

sources.label: Illustrated Flora of British Columbia: Stachys arvensis

identification: The leaves are simple, opposite, and broadly oval with pointed tips. Young stems, leaves, and flower parts can look velvety or downy. Dense clusters at the ends of branches carry white flowers with a narrow tube and several spreading lobes, often six to nine. Photograph the hairy young growth and leaf arrangement as well as a fully open flower. A garden label saying only star jasmine does not establish Jasminum multiflorum; other jasmine-like plants have different leaf textures, flowers, and growth habits.
actions: Check the scientific name on nursery records and compare it with the plant before deciding what to do. Keep a cultivated shrub within its intended space through ordinary garden maintenance, and dispose of trimmings responsibly. If plants appear beyond the garden, document the location and whether they persist without care rather than assuming invasion from a single shoot. Use current regional assessments to choose landscape plants, particularly near natural areas. The available evidence supports careful identification and observation, not a blanket claim of ecological harm throughout the United States.

sources.label: Indian Institute of Science: Jasminum multiflorum

identification: Look for clumps of narrow, fleshy green leaves and white, star-shaped flowers held above them. The foliage can resemble onion or chive leaves, but appearance is not a safe guide to edibility. Photograph an open flower, the leaves, and the way the clump emerges from the ground. Other spring bulbs can look similar before flowering, so wait for diagnostic features when possible. If lifting a confirmed unwanted clump, note the main bulb and small bulblets that explain why plants return after superficial weeding.
actions: Mark patches while foliage is visible so they can be found again in later seasons. Dig carefully when soil is moist, removing the main bulbs and attached or loose bulblets with as little soil movement as practical. Contain the material for disposal rather than adding it to ordinary compost. Recheck the area each spring for missed bulbs. Larger lawn infestations may require an extension-guided plan compatible with the turf and local pesticide rules; one treatment or one mowing should not be assumed to eliminate a persistent bulb colony.

sources.label: University of Maryland: Star of Bethlehem

identification: The botanical treatments describe stout runners that arch along the surface rather than spreading underground rhizomes. Flowering stems carry about seven to twenty short branches arranged in several whorls, giving the head its layered, star-like shape. Leaf blades are rough to the touch in the flora description. Photograph the runner connections, leaf bases and mature flowering head together. Other stargrasses can look similar, so a seed-head photograph alone is not enough. A grass specialist may need mature specimens and a regional key to confirm the species.
actions: Ask the grower or land manager for the original planting record, but verify the living grass rather than accepting a trade name alone. Keep cut runners and planting material from being moved into nearby natural vegetation. For an unwanted patch, plan follow-up after removal because surviving runners can maintain it. Match grazing, toxicity or control advice to the confirmed species; older stargrass literature often combines different plants. Record the botanist's determination with the photographs so later observations can be compared on the same basis.

sources.label: Tropical Forages: Cynodon species and name misapplication
Flora of Tropical East Africa: Cynodon plectostachyus
Flora of North America: Cynodon plectostachyus, hosted treatment

identification: Look for bright green branchlets arranged in whorls around the main axis. The most useful clue is the small white, star-shaped bulbil, often found on clear anchoring threads near or beneath the sediment. These bulbils can be about the size of a grain of rice. Native Chara and Nitella can resemble the green upper portions and provide valuable aquatic habitat. Photograph any star-shaped structures in place or in material already caught on equipment; do not disturb a large patch simply to find them.
actions: Report a suspected new occurrence to the state aquatic-invasive-species program with photographs and the exact waterbody location. Remove attached plants and debris from boats, trailers, anchors, and gear, drain retained water, and follow local drying or decontamination guidance before another launch. Do not transport a live sample without instructions. Management can require permits and professional planning, and reducing visible growth does not guarantee eradication. Avoid uncoordinated raking or cutting that could spread fragments around the same waterbody.

identification: Look on the undersides of leaves for a rounded central body surrounded by usually seven radiating wax arms. The covering can be translucent, with pale tips, while the female beneath it may appear pink to purplish red. This star-like outline is more informative than color alone. Other wax scales can also form decorative-looking coverings, and definitive identification may require a slide-mounted specimen. Photograph a colony, an individual scale close up, and the leaf surface where it is attached.
actions: Keep a newly purchased infested plant separate from other plants while arranging identification. Record the host, the density of scales, and whether leaves are yellowing or growth is declining. A plant clinic can advise how to collect an affected leaf without spreading insects to other premises. Avoid moving infested cuttings or nursery stock. Bring photographs and host details to an extension entomologist or plant clinic, including any recent purchases and the first date the scales were noticed. Choose any treatment only after a specialist confirms the scale and the site's practical needs.

sources.label: Peronti and colleagues: Brazilian Ceroplastinae revision, 2008

identification: Look for elongated, brick-red pustules breaking through stems and leaf sheaths, sometimes also on leaves or heads. The ruptured surface often has conspicuously ragged edges. Later pustules can become dark and shiny as another spore stage develops. Leaf rust tends to produce a different pattern of smaller pustules, while stripe rust commonly forms lines on leaves. Photograph the affected organ and the distribution of lesions across several plants. A plant-disease laboratory may be needed to confirm the pathogen and any strain-specific concern.
actions: Scout susceptible fields and record the cultivar, growth stage, recent weather, and extent of symptoms. Contact crop extension staff promptly when stem rust is suspected, especially if a cultivar expected to resist it is affected. Use current regional resistance ratings when selecting future seed, and manage volunteer cereal plants according to the crop plan. Fungicide decisions depend on diagnosis, crop stage, disease pressure, and current labels. Do not infer a particular rust race from lesion color or send infected material elsewhere without the receiving laboratory's instructions.

sources.label: UC IPM: Stem rusts of wheat barley and oats

identification: Look for finely divided leaves, hairy branching stems, and small five-petaled flowers that may be pink to purplish. The developing fruit forms a long narrow beak, later separating into individual seed-bearing units. Other Erodium species can look very similar, especially before fruiting. Botanical keys rely on features such as sepal size, fruit-body pits, hairs, and the beak, rather than flower color alone. Photograph mature fruits from several angles with a scale, and retain a clear record of the leaves and branching habit.
actions: If a suspected plant occurs beside grain handling, disturbed soil, or a new planting, note that context without assuming it proves the route of arrival. Ask a herbarium or regional botanist to verify the species before submitting a new distribution record. Small unwanted plants can be contained before seed dispersal once identification is secure. Avoid spreading soil or seed-bearing debris from the spot. Broader treatment is not justified by the available evidence alone; the next useful step is a confirmed identification and an assessment of whether the population persists or expands.

sources.label: Botanical Survey of India: Flora of India volume 4
Native Plant Trust: Erodium identification key

identification: The leaves are large, opposite, and broadly oval to triangular, with coarse, irregular teeth and visible hairs. Stems can be four-angled, and flower clusters sit at their tips. The flower bases may be pink, red, or purple beneath the pale corollas. Double-flowered forms rarely produce fruit, but a lack of berries does not mean a planting cannot spread. Look around the edge of a clump for new shoots connected to the root system. Other ornamental Clerodendrum species have different flower arrangements and should be checked separately.
actions: Inspect beyond the original planting, especially where root suckers approach natural vegetation or a neighboring property. Avoid sharing rooted pieces or dumping garden waste where shoots could establish. Repeated cutting can reduce the visible top growth without stopping underground spread, so a persistent colony needs a longer-term plan. Ask local extension staff or an invasive-plant program whether removal is a regional priority and what methods suit the site. Record regrowth after treatment; the attractive flowers and infrequent fruiting can otherwise hide continued expansion.

identification: Look for opposite leaves covered with hairs and small white flowers gathered in relatively tight clusters. The stems, leaves, and flower parts carry both ordinary and gland-tipped hairs, giving the plant its sticky quality and grayish cast. Flowers have five petals and hairy green sepals. Common chickweed, Stellaria media, is a different plant, and perennial mouse-ear chickweed is another frequent lookalike. Take a close picture of the stem hairs, leaf pair, and flower cluster together. A white flower in a low mat is not enough for identification.
actions: Remove small patches before flowering and seed development, using shallow cultivation or hand weeding where desirable plants can be protected. Mulch suitable garden beds to limit new seedlings, and address thin turf or repeatedly bare soil. Sticky chickweed can tolerate somewhat drier sites than common chickweed, so irrigation changes alone may not solve the problem. Revisit the area during the next cool-season flush. In a mixed patch, identify the plants before broad treatment so native chickweeds or unrelated small wildflowers are not removed by mistake.

sources.label: University of Maryland: Chickweeds identification and management

identification: Prickles cover much of the plant, including stems and parts surrounding the fruit. Leaves are deeply divided into irregular lobes and carry ordinary, star-shaped, and glandular hairs. Flowers are white to pale blue or violet, with prominent yellow anthers. The enlarged prickly calyx partly surrounds the developing berry. Buffalo bur can resemble it in its armature but has yellow flowers and differently shaped leaf lobes. Other prickly nightshades require closer comparison, so photograph flowers, anthers, leaves, and fruit rather than relying on the red berry alone.
actions: Wear protective gloves if handling a confirmed plant, and keep children and pets from treating unfamiliar berries as food. Record whether the plant was deliberately sown, arrived with soil or seed, or occurs along a transport corridor. Ask an extension botanist to verify an unusual record. Contain fruiting material and avoid moving contaminated soil while deciding on removal. For established plants in agricultural ground, ask local crop advisers to assess the patch and the surrounding crop before choosing a response or moving equipment through it.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Solanum sisymbriifolium

identification: The leaves are deeply cut into lobes, with smaller teeth or lobes within those divisions. Branched stems carry yellow flower heads on sticky stalks. Short yellow ray flowers may be visible around the central disk, and the green bracts beneath the head can have faint dark tips. Examine the glandular hairs with a hand lens rather than relying on smell or touching unknown plants. Common groundsel and other Senecio species can look similar; photographs of the flower heads, bracts, leaf divisions, and overall habit are useful together.
actions: Confirm the species before removing a mixed stand of small yellow-flowered plants. In a garden or maintained strip, contain unwanted plants before the fluffy seed heads disperse and avoid moving seed-bearing debris to new ground. Wear gloves during handling and do not use a common name as a guide to edible or medicinal use. For repeated roadside or restoration-site infestations, ask local botanists or extension staff to assess the population. A roadside population and a garden weed may need different responses, especially where removal would disturb wanted vegetation.

sources.label: Illustrated Flora of British Columbia: Senecio viscosus

identification: Look for upright branching stems arising from a woody base. Young stems may be reddish or purplish and sticky with glandular hairs. Opposite bright green leaves are broadly triangular or trowel-shaped, with toothed margins. Dense clusters of small white flower heads form at branch tips, followed by tiny dark seeds with fine pale hairs. Mistflower and other white-flowered relatives can cause confusion. Photograph the leaf shape, opposite arrangement, stem surface, and whole flowering branch rather than identifying it from a cloud of white bloom.
actions: Keep suspected plants away from hay and horse grazing areas while obtaining identification; Australian authorities associate Crofton weed with serious horse poisoning. Contact local extension or weed-control staff before moving plant material, particularly where the species is regulated. Small plants may be removed with their crowns where that can be done without excessive soil disturbance, but established woody patches need follow-up. Prevent seed production and contain cut material. Use a regional management plan for large infestations, and do not import biological-control organisms or copy overseas chemical rates.

identification: Look for opposite, pointed leaves with coarse teeth and small greenish flowers in clusters from the leaf axils. For the European taxon, regional keys emphasize stinging hairs on both leaf surfaces and relatively stiff stem bristles. Native American nettles usually have stinging hairs concentrated on the lower leaf surface, although characters should be assessed together. Do not test the hairs against bare skin. Clear close-ups of both leaf surfaces, the stem, and flowering structures are much more useful than a photograph of the patch from a distance.
actions: Ask a local botanist to confirm the taxon before removing nettles from natural habitat. Wear gloves and protective clothing when working near a suspected patch. Where a confirmed unwanted nettle colony interferes with a path or garden, plan repeated attention to underground regrowth rather than expecting clipping alone to finish the job. Keep location and identification records separate from species-wide nettle reports. Keep close photographs with the identification record so later work follows the confirmed colony, rather than extending removal to native nettles elsewhere along the same stream or path.

sources.label: Native Plant Trust: Urtica dioica subspecies key

identification: Look for a branching, roughly triangular seed head with many flattened, gray to silvery spikelets. Leaf blades are relatively broad for a small lovegrass and may be rough above and smoother beneath. At the blade-sheath junction, the ligule is a very short fringe of hairs; there are no clasping auricles. Other lovegrasses and young summer grasses can be difficult to separate without mature seed heads. Photograph the spikelets and leaf junction with a ruler, and use odor only as a supporting clue rather than the sole test.
actions: Remove small unwanted tufts before seed shed and keep seed-bearing mowing or weeding debris from being spread into clean ground. In beds, reduce repeated bare soil where seedlings establish; in crop fields, use extension guidance that matches the crop and stage of growth. A grass herbicide safe for one planting can damage another. Revisit the site through the warm season for additional seedlings. If the grass is mixed with desirable species, confirm the identification first instead of treating every gray-green seed head as stinkgrass.

identification: The flower heads have a yellow center surrounded by white rays. Leaves become alternate on older growth and are divided into very narrow segments. Compared with corn chamomile, the foliage is generally more finely dissected, and the yellow disk is more strongly domed. Photograph a mature leaf, an open flower head, and the branching stem together. Other chamomiles, small daisies, and plants called dogfennel share parts of this appearance. Wear gloves when handling plants rather than crushing them against the skin to test their smell.
actions: Prevent another seed crop by pulling small patches or cutting plants before seeds mature. Mowing can help when timed early enough, but follow-up is needed if plants regrow or new seedlings appear. In crops, combine prevention and cultural practices with current extension advice; treatment timing and herbicide resistance can affect results. Clean equipment after working in a seeding patch, and avoid moving contaminated hay or soil to clean areas. Confirm uncertain plants before treatment, especially where a field margin contains a mixture of native and introduced flowers.

sources.label: Washington State/OSU: Mayweed chamomile management timing

identification: Look for deeply divided, somewhat ragged leaves and clusters of yellow flower heads with visible petal-like rays around the central disk. The first leaves of seedlings can be much simpler than mature foliage, so a young rosette may not yet show the familiar outline. Common tansy has button-like heads without the same ring of conspicuous rays. Photograph both the leaf divisions and flower heads. A plant's yellow color or unpleasant smell alone is not enough to distinguish tansy ragwort from its lookalikes.
actions: Keep suspected ragwort out of hay and grazing areas while confirming identification, and consult a veterinarian if animals may have eaten contaminated forage. Wear gloves for removal. Small populations can be addressed before flowering, with roots and any developing flower heads contained and the site checked for regrowth. Larger pastures need a coordinated plan with weed-control and livestock advisers. Reestablish suitable pasture or native cover after control to reduce open ground for seedlings. Check current local requirements rather than assuming the same legal rules apply everywhere.

sources.label: Washington Noxious Weed Board: Tansy ragwort

identification: Look for opposite leaves, often oval to lance-shaped, and conspicuous small stipules where the leaf stalks meet the stem. Flowers are small and tubular, usually pale pinkish or lilac with a darker throat. Ground-running stems may root at their joints. Leaf size and hairiness can vary, and closely related Paederia species require attention to fruits and other details. Photograph flowers, leaf pairs, stem joints, and any fruit. Avoid identifying an unfamiliar vine solely by an odor produced when someone crushes a leaf.
actions: Map the rooted portions of a confirmed patch before removing the climbing growth. Take care when freeing vines from desirable vegetation, and contain fragments and fruit rather than dumping them where they can establish. Cutting stems can kill the upper growth while leaving the base able to resprout. Larger natural-area infestations need a planned treatment and repeated checks, often with local invasive-plant staff. Clean tools and avoid moving infested garden material. Follow regional guidance for any herbicide work, particularly where vines are intertwined with plants you want to keep.

sources.label: UF IFAS: Natural area weeds - Skunkvine
Florida Natural Areas Inventory: Paederia foetida

identification: Look for narrow, alternate gray-green leaves and an upright stem that branches repeatedly. Stems and foliage are covered in sticky hairs, and the small yellow heads sit at branch ends or near upper leaves. The overall outline can resemble a little bush even though the plant is annual. Other yellow-flowered roadside herbs may look similar before bloom. Photograph the lower and upper leaves, branching pattern, and flower heads. A camphor-like smell can support identification, but it is not a reason to crush the plant against your skin.
actions: Pull or hoe isolated plants before flowering where removal will not cause excessive disturbance. Once flowers are present, bag the material because seeds may continue to mature after cutting. Mowing can miss low branches, leaving plants able to regrow, so inspect the base afterward. Clean equipment and contain seed-bearing debris. Keep suspect material out of livestock forage and obtain local weed-management advice for larger patches. Follow-up during the growing season is important: removing the visible plants once does not address seedlings that emerge later.

identification: Adults are broad-winged brown moths with uneven pale bands and patches. The dark head and details of the pale cross-lines help separate them from the similar grease moth, Aglossa cuprina, but the distinction can be difficult in worn specimens. Mature larvae are dark brown to black rather than the pale caterpillars familiar from some pantry moths. Photograph the adult from above in good light and record where any larvae were found. A specialist may need additional views or a specimen to make a firm identification.
actions: Inspect nearby hay, spilled feed, stored dry goods, and damp organic debris for larvae, webbing, and moisture problems. Isolate suspect material rather than carrying it through other storage areas, and arrange identification if the source remains unclear. Clean up spills and correct leaks or damp storage conditions as part of an integrated response. Avoid spraying food, feed, or occupied rooms simply because an adult moth appeared. For a commercial storage problem, an extension or stored-product pest specialist can examine the affected material and fit the response to the insects and conditions actually present.

sources.label: UC Riverside, Ebeling: Stored product and household moths
NC Parks moth collection: Aglossa caprealis

identification: Look for trailing, somewhat hairy stems with pairs of small leaves. The leaves are oval to triangular, with toothed margins and several conspicuous veins near the base. Tiny yellow daisy-like heads arise individually from the leaf axils. Its low stature can make it blend into turf until the flowers appear. Photograph a flowering stem close enough to show the opposite leaves and where the flower stalk attaches. Other small lawn daisies may share the yellow color, while chickweeds normally have a different flower structure.
actions: First decide whether the plant is welcome in the landscape. Within its native region, a confirmed horseherb patch may be an intentional or useful groundcover rather than a control target. If it is unwanted in a particular bed, remove it selectively and monitor the boundary instead of treating the whole lawn automatically. Outside the expected range, document the location and ask a regional botanist about its status before moving plants to another property. Preserve the distinction between native habitat, cultivated groundcover, and a newly spreading occurrence when recording observations.

sources.label: Native Plant Society of Texas: Horseherb
Fort Worth Botanic Garden: Asteraceae of East Texas

identification: Look for opposite, glossy, leathery leaves with relatively inconspicuous side veins. The bark is smooth and often reddish or mottled, peeling in patches. White flowers with many conspicuous stamens usually arise in leaf axils, followed by rounded fruits containing numerous small hard seeds. Compare it carefully with common guava and other fruit trees before removal. Photographs of the leaf surfaces, bark, flower, and fruit are more useful than a basket of berries without the branch that produced them.
actions: Where regional guidance discourages planting, replace strawberry guava with a suitable alternative and watch nearby forest edges for seedlings. Young seedlings may be removable by hand, but older plants have strong roots and can produce abundant shoots after cutting. Plan follow-up before felling a mature thicket; a cut stump is not proof of control. Contain fruit and plant debris, and avoid sharing seedlings from a problem population. Large stands or trees near valuable habitat need a locally appropriate professional plan that addresses both regrowth and continuing seed arrival.

identification: The adult moth is highly variable, with a wingspan around one and a half centimeters and often a dark triangular patch along the leading edge of the forewing. Several forms overlap in appearance with Acleris laterana and other relatives. Larval head and neck-shield markings can help, but reliable separation may require a specialist and microscopic examination. Photograph the caterpillar, its shelter, and any adult that is found. Record the host plant and date; these support identification without replacing the anatomical characters.
actions: Inspect a sample of strawberry plants for fresh feeding, occupied leaf shelters, and flower or fruit injury. In a small garden, a few affected leaves can be contained for identification rather than triggering a blanket spray. Avoid moving infested transplants to a new bed. Commercial growers should use local crop scouting advice and consider natural enemies before treatment. Some older North American records may involve a related moth, so local expert confirmation matters before choosing a species-specific response. Keep an uncertain record at the species-complex level until it is confirmed.

sources.label: Sigsgaard et al. 2014: Strawberry cropping practices and Acleris comariana

identification: Leaves alternate along the branches and are oval to lance-shaped, with toothed margins, fine hairs, and an uneven base where the blade joins its stalk. Small white flowers have five petals and many yellow stamens. The smooth rounded fruit is usually red, sometimes orange-yellow, and contains numerous tiny seeds. Photograph the asymmetric leaf base and a flower as well as fruit. A common-name label such as cherry or strawberry tree is insufficient because several unrelated ornamental and fruit trees share those names.
actions: Check whether nearby seedlings are deliberately planted or growing without care, and record their distance from any cultivated tree. Keep fruit waste and discarded seedlings out of natural areas. Before adding this species to a tropical landscape, consult current regional planting guidance and ask whether local escapes are a concern. Small unwanted seedlings can be removed selectively, but larger trees require ordinary arboricultural planning. The appropriate response depends on the tree's local spread and the vegetation around it; an escaped seedling does not by itself demonstrate widespread ecological harm.

sources.label: Kauai Invasive Species Committee: Widespread distribution assessment

identification: The stems are sharply three-angled rather than round and rise from creeping underground rhizomes. Leaves are concentrated at the base, with short blades that can appear V-shaped in cross section. Brownish spikelets form near the top, accompanied by a bract that can make the cluster appear to come from the side of the stem. Other Schoenoplectus and related sedges can share triangular stems. Mature spikelets, scales, and fruits are often needed to separate them, so close photographs and expert examination are important.
actions: Record the exact location, water conditions, and whether the plant occupies a tidal freshwater margin. Ask a wetland botanist or herbarium to verify the identification before disturbing the stand. Avoid digging rhizomes or moving sediment between waterways while the record is unresolved. Any removal in a river margin should be coordinated with the landowner and relevant aquatic or wetland staff. Keep photographs of the flowering stand and its boundaries so later visits can check its extent without repeatedly digging into a sensitive shoreline.

sources.label: Burke Herbarium and FNA: Schoenoplectus triqueter

identification: Portuguese broom has nearly round stems with several narrow ridges, rather than the strongly five-sided stems typical of Scotch broom. Leaves usually have three leaflets, though some new shoots may carry simple leaves, and foliage can be sparse or shed early. Flowers occur singly or in pairs in leaf axils. The pods are slightly inflated and covered all over with long hairs; Scotch broom's flatter pods are hairy mainly along their edges. Photograph a pod and stem close up, not just the yellow flowers.
actions: Remove young plants before they build a seed supply, taking care to limit soil disturbance that can encourage more germination. For established shrubs, choose a method suited to stem size, terrain, and nearby vegetation with local weed-control advice. Do not assume cutting always kills the root system. Revisit cleared ground for seedlings over subsequent seasons, and restore appropriate competing vegetation where practical. Keep mature pods and contaminated soil from moving to new sites. Any biological control or herbicide program should be regionally authorized and matched to the confirmed broom species.

sources.label: US Forest Service: Gorse and Scotch broom guide, comparison chapter

identification: Look for a low conical shell made of six outer plates, often whitish or pinkish with vertical purple or reddish-brown stripes. The opening is broadly diamond-shaped, and the tissue at its margin can show four dark bands. Other six-plated barnacles are easy to confuse, particularly when shells are crowded, worn, or coated with growth. The reticulated striped barnacle has additional horizontal grooves that can create a net-like pattern. Photograph the shell sides and opening while the animal remains attached, with a size reference.
actions: Report an unusual fouling observation to a local marine monitoring or invasive-species program, including the surface, harbor, and vessel movement history if known. Avoid transporting live barnacles on equipment between waterbodies. Arrange hull cleaning through facilities that collect fouling waste and follow local biosecurity requirements rather than scraping organisms into another harbor. Do not remove barnacles from living shellfish or protected shore habitat without guidance. Identification and a regional assessment should determine whether an observation calls for action beyond routine prevention of vessel and equipment fouling.

sources.label: UK marine nonnative species identification guide

identification: Look for a small dark beetle with a pale, interrupted stripe running along each wing cover. Enlarged hind legs let it spring away when disturbed, which can make photographs difficult. Check the undersides of leaves as well as the upper surfaces. Other striped flea beetles can resemble it, and feeding holes alone cannot separate species or exclude other chewing insects. A sharply focused overhead image showing both stripes, accompanied by the crop name and a picture of the damage, is a useful starting point for confirmation.
actions: Inspect newly emerged plants and transplants regularly while they are most vulnerable. Row covers can help protect suitable young plantings when installed before beetles gain access and managed to avoid trapping pests beneath them. Keep nearby weed hosts in mind when planning crop hygiene. Use current local extension guidance if damage is increasing; crop stage and harvest restrictions matter for any pesticide choice. Established plants often tolerate more feeding than seedlings, so avoid treating solely to erase old holes. Recheck after any intervention for new injury rather than judging success from damaged leaves that cannot heal.

sources.label: University of Kentucky: Striped flea beetle
UC IPM: Flea beetles in cole crops

identification: Adult females described in the Florida account are small, oval insects with two dark lengthwise marks showing through the white wax. Long glassy filaments and a pair of trailing wax tails give them a somewhat untidy outline. Inspect stems, leaf junctions, and sheltered plant surfaces with a hand lens. These features suggest the striped-mealybug group; they do not reliably separate Ferrisia virgata from similar Ferrisia species, including F. gilli. A diagnostic laboratory may need prepared adult specimens rather than a distant photograph.
actions: Keep a newly affected potted plant apart from other stock while arranging identification. Record the host, where it was purchased, and which plant parts carry insects. Photograph living females before disturbing their wax. Avoid moving infested cuttings to another property. Ants can protect mealybugs, while lady beetles and parasitoids help suppress them; broad spraying can disrupt those helpers. Ask local extension staff about a response appropriate to the confirmed insect and host. Published control claims for the older species complex need checking before they are used as species-specific instructions.

sources.label: Puig et al. 2021: Cacao mealybugs and virus acquisition
Sangeetha and Drishya 2024: Molecularly identified cassava mealybugs

identification: Affected plants may have poorly developed roots, but nutrient problems, compaction, other nematodes, and root diseases can produce similar symptoms. Individual trichodorid nematodes are too small for ordinary field identification. Specialists extract specimens from soil and examine their feeding and reproductive structures under magnification. A Polish plantation study identified females and males this way. A photograph of a stunted crop cannot confirm T. viruliferus. For useful field documentation, photograph the pattern of affected plants and compare roots from an affected area with nearby apparently healthy plants.
actions: Contact a plant diagnostic laboratory before collecting soil and roots so that sample depth, moisture, packaging, and shipment suit its methods. Tell the laboratory which crop is affected and whether virus testing is also needed. Keep soil from the suspect area off equipment moving to clean fields, and avoid distributing rooted plants from it while the problem is investigated. Do not choose a nematicide from an old species account: registrations and suitability change. A locally supported crop-management plan requires confirmed identification and a current assessment of the field.

sources.label: Journal of Horticultural Research 2022: Paulownia plantation nematodes

identification: Look for low, spreading stems and leaves divided into three rounded or heart-shaped leaflets. Many forms have conspicuous hairs, relatively large stipules where leaves join stems, and dark leaf markings, although markings and hairiness vary. The small flowers are usually white, sometimes pinkish. Follow a fading flower cluster toward the ground to look for the developing burr; this helps distinguish it from clovers that hold their seed heads above the foliage. White clover can look similar before flowering, so retain photographs of stems, stipules, flowers, and fruit.
actions: First establish whether the patch is an intended forage stand. If it is, discuss pasture condition and the appropriate variety with a local forage adviser before changing management. Where a small volunteer patch is unwanted, remove it before burrs mature and return to check for later seedlings. Gather the whole plant and attached burrs rather than simply clipping visible flowers. Avoid moving soil containing seed into a restoration site. Near native vegetation, assess actual spread and local guidance instead of assuming that a useful pasture species is suitable for sowing everywhere.

sources.label: NSW Department of Primary Industries: Subterranean Clover

identification: Look for termite activity such as earthen tubes and insects associated with damaged wood, but recognize that these signs do not identify the species. Soldiers have a pale body and a darker, rounded to teardrop-shaped head. Under magnification, specialists compare hairs around the opening on the front of the head and the profile behind it to separate C. gestroi from C. formosanus. Workers alone are particularly unhelpful for casual identification. Photograph the activity and retain accessible winged insects or soldiers only if this can be done without opening damaged structural material.
actions: Arrange prompt inspection by a licensed termite professional and ask for species confirmation when Asian subterranean termite is suspected. Share photographs and the location of activity. Leave affected structural wood in place for assessment, and avoid spraying a visible tube as though that would eliminate the colony. Do not move suspect timber, stumps, or nursery material elsewhere. Treatment choice and bait placement should follow the building, infestation, and confirmed termite, with subsequent checks to establish whether activity has stopped.

sources.label: University of Hawaii: Expansion of Coptotermes gestroi on Oahu

identification: An armored body and a mouth adapted to attach to surfaces are useful starting points for recognizing this broader group. They are not enough to distinguish H. plecostomus from other Hypostomus or from the sailfin catfishes called Pterygoplichthys. Photograph the whole fish from the side, its fins when naturally visible, and any clear patterning without chasing or injuring it. Include an estimate of size and the waterbody location. Reliable species assignment may require a fish specialist and comparison with museum material or current diagnostic literature.
actions: Never release an aquarium fish into a pond, ditch, spring, or river. If a pet has outgrown its tank, arrange a responsible return or rehoming option through an aquarium retailer or experienced keeper. For a fish seen outdoors, send photographs and location details to the state fisheries agency or its nonnative-species reporting program. Avoid moving a live specimen to another waterbody. Let agency staff decide whether collection or removal is appropriate; the unresolved identity of a pleco is a reason to improve the record before making species-specific management claims.

sources.label: USGS NAS: Hypostomus plecostomus identity caveat
Hemraj-Naraine et al. 2026: Canje River fish surveys, table 3
Weber et al. 2012: Identity of Hypostomus plecostomus

identification: Look for sprawling green or reddish stems, leaves made of three small leaflets, and modest clusters of yellow flowers. The leaflet margins have small teeth. Several yellow-flowered legumes look similar, especially larger hop clover and black medick. Mature fruit can help: black medick develops dark, coiled pods, while the clover does not. Black medick also has a tiny pointed projection at the leaflet tip. Take close photographs of flower heads, leaves, and fruit together; a yellow dot in a lawn is not enough for a reliable identification.
actions: If the plant is simply part of a low-input lawn or pasture, decide whether intervention is needed before treating it. Where a small patch conflicts with a planting or restoration goal, pull plants before seed matures and maintain the desired ground cover afterward. Revisit the area in the next growing season because removing visible plants does not remove seed already present. For pasture changes, seek local forage advice rather than applying a lawn treatment. Confirm the plant first, and avoid broad applications that would also remove wanted clovers and other broadleaf plants.

sources.label: Mississippi State Extension: Small Hop Clover
Royal Botanic Gardens Sydney PlantNET: Trifolium dubium
University of Oxford Plants 400: Trifolium dubium

identification: Typical sudangrass has erect, relatively slender stems, long narrow leaf blades, and an open, branching seed head. The botanical account describes plants reaching several feet tall and paired spikelets along the fine branches. Other sorghums, including forage hybrids and johnsongrass, can look similar from a distance. Photograph the base, leaf attachment, and mature seed head, and keep the seed label if the stand was planted. A farm adviser can use planting history and detailed plant features to distinguish a crop from an unwanted volunteer or another sorghum.
actions: Before grazing or feeding a stressed stand, consult a local forage adviser about appropriate testing and management. Tell them about frost, drought, recent cutting, regrowth, and fertilizer use. Do not rely on a single waiting period or plant height as proof of safety, and do not assume that cutting or drying solves every forage hazard. Where volunteers are unwanted, remove them before seed develops and monitor field margins. Keep crop-management decisions separate from claims about ecological invasion, which require evidence from the location concerned.

sources.label: South Dakota State Extension: Managing Prussic Acid Risk Following Drought

identification: On susceptible oak and tanoak hosts, dark bleeding patches or cankers on the trunk may accompany decline. Other hosts can develop leaf lesions or dying shoots. These signs overlap with injuries and other diseases, and neither a photograph nor a general Phytophthora screening test confirms P. ramorum. A trained sampler and a diagnostic laboratory may be needed. Record the host, location, symptoms, and whether nearby plants are affected. Photograph the trunk and foliage without cutting into bark or removing branches to investigate on your own.
actions: Contact the state plant-health agency, extension service, or an established local sudden-oak-death program before collecting or moving suspect material. Keep plants, soil, cuttings, and woody debris from the affected area in place until you receive instructions. Avoid carrying soil on footwear or tools between sites, and follow the receiving program's cleaning and sampling advice. In nurseries, reducing standing water and unnecessary overhead irrigation can help limit conditions favorable to spread. There is no simple cure for an infected tree; treatment or removal decisions require the host, diagnosis, site, and applicable movement rules.

sources.label: American Phytopathological Society: Sudden Oak Death

identification: Female scale covers are thin, roughly circular, and fairly flat, with a pale to darker brown or purplish-brown appearance. The cast skin is near the center. Male covers are smaller and more elongated. Those features help locate a possible infestation under sheaths, but other armored scales can look much the same. The insect beneath its cover and microscopic characters are important for reliable identification. Photograph the host and the position of the scales, and ask a diagnostic service how to submit a small sample without spreading infested material.
actions: Inspect planting material before it is taken to another field or property, paying particular attention to protected stem bases and leaf sheaths. Keep suspect material separate while identification is pending. Healthy planting cane and natural enemies are useful parts of sugarcane pest management, but the appropriate response depends on infestation level and the host involved. Ask a local crop adviser about monitoring and whether treatment is justified. Do not copy a quarantine rating or pesticide instruction from another jurisdiction, and avoid moving infested cane or ornamental plants while their status is being checked.

sources.label: California Department of Food and Agriculture: Aspidiella sacchari Pest Rating Proposal

identification: The caterpillar is pale cream to yellowish with a brown head and rows of dark spots along the body. Adults are straw-colored moths, but a moth's color alone is not enough to separate related borers. Look for larvae feeding beneath leaf sheaths before they enter stalks, as well as entry holes, internal tunnels, weakened stems, or dead central shoots. Several other borers can produce similar injury. Photograph an exposed larva and its feeding site, record the crop and growth stage, and have uncertain specimens checked by extension staff.
actions: Use local crop scouting guidance, with attention to larvae still feeding outside the stalk. Once larvae are deep inside, a treatment aimed at exposed insects is less likely to reach them. Keep records of infestation levels and the variety grown, since crop susceptibility and tolerance vary. Protect established natural enemies and discuss treatment thresholds with a regional crop adviser rather than spraying after seeing a single moth. Select healthy planting cane and avoid transferring suspect stalks to new plantings. Recheck affected areas to determine whether fresh injury continues after any management decision.

sources.label: LSU AgCenter: Sugarcane Borer Management Guide for Sugarcane Varieties
Texas A&M AgriLife: stalk-boring insect pests

identification: Check sugarcane leaves and sheaths for the insects and for egg clusters inserted into plant tissue, particularly near the midrib. Exposed egg ends may have a small white waxy covering. Several other hoppers live on cane, so color, jumping behavior or a distant photograph will not reliably identify this species. Photograph the insect from above and from the side, include a size reference, and record the host. An entomologist may need magnified structural characters to confirm the identification.
actions: Keep unfamiliar insects and affected planting material at the site while seeking advice from extension or plant-health staff. Record how many plants are affected and whether fresh feeding damage is increasing. Do not assume Fiji disease from the presence of a known vector, or apply a broad insecticide simply because hoppers occur. A crop specialist can distinguish direct insect injury from disease and decide whether monitoring or treatment is warranted. Avoid moving infested cane between growing areas.

sources.label: UF/IFAS: Miscellaneous insect pests of Florida sugarcane

identification: Look for a narrow mine that widens into a blotch within the leaf. The damaged area lies between the leaf surfaces rather than being an open hole chewed through the blade. Photograph the whole leaf and a close view of the mine, including any larva or emergence opening. The moth itself is minute, and similar grass-mining moths can be difficult to separate. Confirmation may require rearing an adult or examination by a specialist; do not rely on the mine shape alone.
actions: Record the crop variety, date, affected leaf position and approximate frequency of mines. Keep a suspect leaf in place until a diagnostic service explains how it should be sampled. Avoid moving live larvae or infested plants between fields. Ask a crop adviser whether damage is continuing on new growth and whether natural enemies are already limiting it. The historical Louisiana findings support careful assessment, not an automatic spray recommendation or a promise that the insect is harmless everywhere.

sources.label: USDA ARS: Louisiana sugarcane leafminer discovery
Kaila 2019: Annotated world catalogue of Elachistinae

identification: Look for smooth, patchy bark in pale gray, cream, yellow or brown tones. Adult leaves are narrow and glossy, with a noticeably darker upper surface and paler underside. Young leaves are broader and often rounded. A useful feature is the placement of flower clusters on leafless portions of branchlets within the crown. The white flowers leave small barrel-shaped or urn-shaped woody capsules with their valves tucked inside. Include bark, leaves, buds and capsules in photographs because foliage alone can be misleading.
actions: Check around established trees for seedlings in places that were not planted, especially along disturbed edges. Record their distance from the likely parent and whether they are surviving among native vegetation. Consult the land manager before removing trees or disturbing habitat. Small seedlings are easier to assess and address than established trees, but mature-tree work needs a qualified arborist. When considering replacement planting, use locally appropriate species and ask about sugar gum spread at comparable nearby sites.

identification: Look for upright, leafy stems and leaves divided like a hand into usually five to seven narrow, toothed leaflets. Flowers have five pale yellow, notched petals around a deeper yellow center. Long stiff hairs stand out from the stems and leaf stalks rather than lying flat. Compared with some native relatives, both leaf surfaces are similarly green and the plant carries many leaves along the stem. These are useful clues together; leaflet number alone is not enough to distinguish every native cinquefoil.
actions: Photograph the flowers, leaf undersides and stem hairs before planning control. For a small confirmed patch, ask the local weed program about digging the root crown and preventing mature seed from scattering. Simply cutting the flowers does not remove the established root system. Clean soil and seeds from equipment before leaving the site, and revisit treated ground for seedlings. Larger infestations need a coordinated plan that also restores desirable vegetation. Follow local requirements and current site-specific guidance if chemical control is considered.

sources.label: US Forest Service: Sulfur cinquefoil review

identification: Look for opposite leaves deeply divided into narrow but visible segments, branching stems and daisy-like flower heads held above the foliage. The central disk is surrounded by yellow, orange or reddish-orange rays. Common garden cosmos has much finer, threadlike leaf divisions and usually different flower colors, although cultivated varieties complicate quick comparisons. Photograph the leaves as well as the flowers and dry fruits. A flower-only picture may not show the features needed to separate similar ornamentals.
actions: Keep intentional plantings distinct from observations of self-sown plants. If it is spreading where unwanted, remove flower heads before mature seed is released and lift young volunteers while the roots are manageable. Avoid tipping garden waste into roadside vegetation or natural areas. Check the same ground in the next growing season for new seedlings. For plants established away from gardens, share photographs and the setting with a local botanical or extension service before assuming they need extensive control.

identification: Look for narrow pale, yellow or pink streaks along green twigs and sunken streaks or blotches on fruit. Affected fruit may be small or misshapen, and older bark can develop a rectangular cracking pattern. Sunburn can resemble some fruit symptoms, while symptom expression varies with cultivar and growing conditions. Photograph fruit, young branches and the whole tree together. A laboratory result is needed to distinguish infection from lookalike damage and to detect trees that carry the viroid without visible signs.
actions: Do not take grafting wood, seeds for nursery production or cuttings from a suspect tree. Contact a plant diagnostic service or avocado extension adviser and follow its sampling instructions. Use tested nursery material for new plantings, and ask about appropriate tool sanitation before pruning other trees. Keep records of where planting material came from and which trees were propagated from it. Finding symptoms does not justify insecticide treatment: the practical concern is infected plant material and mechanical transfer, not a visible insect vector.

sources.label: Plant Health Australia: Tropical horticulture surveillance guide

identification: Look for upright, slightly ridged hairy stems and large, rough leaves arranged alternately. Leaves may be oval, triangular or three-lobed, with toothed edges and hairy undersides. Flower heads commonly have orange-red outer rays around an orange-yellow center and can reach about three inches across. Photograph both the leaf outline and the flower head; a close-up of orange petals alone is not enough to separate all similar ornamentals. Include the whole plant and note whether it was deliberately planted.
actions: If plants appear outside cultivation, record the distance from the nearest garden and whether seedlings return in later years. Remove unwanted young plants on your own property before they set seed, and contain mature seed heads rather than scattering them in yard waste. There is no reason to treat every planted Mexican sunflower as an established invasion. Ask a local herbarium or extension office to confirm the species when a wild population is spreading, especially where the name is being used interchangeably with Tithonia diversifolia.

identification: Plants have upright, branching stems, narrow simple leaves and clusters of bright yellow pea-shaped flowers toward the top. The short pods are inflated and become brown as they mature. Look closely at the leaves: each has a single narrow blade, unlike species with three separate leaflets. Photograph the flowers, pods, leaf attachment and whole plant. Other rattleboxes can look similar and may present different livestock risks, so a common name or a field of yellow flowers is not a reliable identification.
actions: For an unexpected roadside or field-edge population, note whether sunn hemp was recently planted nearby and whether plants are producing mature pods. Ask extension staff to confirm the species before making forage or control decisions. Keep unidentified rattlebox seeds out of animal feed, and do not assume that a cultivar described as suitable for grazing makes every plant safe. Manage an intentional cover crop according to its cultivar and local planting plan. Remove unwanted volunteers before seed develops when that can be done without disturbing protected habitat.

identification: The most distinctive feature is the deeply ribbed fruit, shaped rather like a small flattened pumpkin. Fruits can ripen red, maroon or nearly black. Leaves occur in opposite pairs, have smooth edges and are oval to lance-shaped; new growth is often bronze or reddish. White flowers carry many conspicuous stamens. Photograph a leafy branch and mature fruit together, because other Eugenia species are also sold as hedges. Avoid using taste as an identification test, and do not assume that any red-fruited shrub is Surinam cherry.
actions: Where the plant is invasive, choose a suitable native replacement rather than planting more. Pull small seedlings where permitted, keeping soil disturbance modest, and check nearby shaded areas for additional seedlings. Larger shrubs can resprout after cutting, so repeated clipping alone may not resolve an infestation. A land manager or extension adviser can help plan removal and follow-up for established plants. Keep fruits and seed-bearing debris contained, and record regrowth after treatment so that apparently cleared areas are checked again.

identification: Look for a soft vine at the water edge, with alternate leaves that are often arrow-shaped but can vary considerably. Stems root at their joints, and flowers resemble morning glories: broad funnels in white, pale pink or lilac. Floating stems can hold leaves above the water. Photograph several leaves, the stem joints and any flower, along with the surrounding habitat. Other wetland vines and morning glories can resemble it, so an arrow-shaped leaf by itself is not enough to confirm the identification.
actions: Do not release live plants, roots or cut stems into drains, ponds or natural wetlands. If you find an apparent escape, record its location and extent and contact the state aquatic-plant program before attempting removal. Avoid chopping or dragging plants through water, where rooted pieces may be displaced. Check current cultivation and movement requirements with the relevant agency rather than assuming that supermarket availability authorizes outdoor planting. Keep any removed material contained and follow local disposal instructions; do not move a live sample to another waterbody for comparison.

sources.label: Texas Parks and Wildlife: Regulated aquatic species

identification: Look for thick, fibrous rough bark and broad adult leaves that are darker above than below. Side veins meet the central vein at a wide angle. Large buds and cylindrical woody fruits are particularly useful: the fruit valves can remain joined across the opening. Photograph bark, both leaf surfaces, buds and mature capsules together.
