Many eucalyptus species share rough bark or glossy leaves, so those features alone are insufficient. Juvenile foliage differs from adult foliage and should be labeled as such in a report.
actions: Check around established plantings for seedlings, especially after logging, soil disturbance or canopy opening. Photograph and map new growth before removing it where permitted. Small seedlings are more manageable than mature trees, but cutting established trees may produce coppice shoots that need follow-up. Use a qualified arborist for work involving large stems or nearby structures. Avoid relocating seedlings into natural areas, and ask the local land manager which eucalyptus species are priorities before treating an entire stand based on its common name.

identification: Look for spreading or mounded growth with narrow, alternate leaves and clusters of tiny flowers. Each flower has four separate petals, commonly white but also pink or purple in cultivated forms. Mature plants develop small, short seedpods rather than the long narrow pods seen in many other mustards. Photograph the foliage, flowers and fruit together, including a size reference. Similar Alyssum species may require examination of plant hairs and fruit stalks, so a white-flowered mat should not be identified from color alone.
actions: For plants beyond a garden, note the surrounding habitat and whether new seedlings appear after the original plants die. Remove unwanted volunteers before seed matures on property you manage, taking care not to disturb neighboring native plants. Keep seed-bearing garden waste away from dunes, roadsides and other natural areas. A local flora or herbarium can help confirm an unusual population. The available sources support monitoring and preventing unwanted reseeding; they do not justify a blanket recommendation to eradicate every cultivated alyssum planting.

sources.label: Prigge and Gibson: Santa Monica Mountains Lobularia maritima

identification: Examine mature leaves rather than relying only on the flowers. Sweet autumn clematis usually has opposite, compound leaves with three to five glossy leaflets and mostly smooth edges. Native virgin's bower commonly has clearly toothed leaflet edges. Young growth can be less straightforward, so include several mature leaves, white flowers and the feathery fruit heads in photographs. The vine climbs using its leaf stalks. A dense white-flowered cover over shrubs is a clue, not a complete identification by itself.
actions: Avoid planting the species where it escapes, and use a locally appropriate native vine instead. Pull small seedlings where permitted, or remove established plants with a plan for the roots and subsequent regrowth. Cutting the visible stems alone can leave a living root system. Contain fruiting material and keep cuttings out of unmanaged yard-waste piles. Revisit the site for seedlings and returning shoots, and ask for an identification check before treating a vine that might be native virgin's bower.

identification: Look for opposite leaves on branching, square stems and small, lipped flowers arranged in groups along an upright flowering axis. Leaves are often oval and green, but cultivars can be purple, variegated, small or strongly textured. Scent varies too, so a familiar basil smell does not identify every cultivar or separate all related species. Photograph the whole plant, a leaf pair and flowers. Do not taste an unknown herb to identify it, especially when its growing conditions or treatment history are unknown.
actions: If basil appears beyond cultivation, record its distance from planted beds and check whether it survives or produces new plants in later seasons. Pull unwanted volunteers before seed disperses where you have permission. Keep garden waste within managed disposal routes rather than dumping it in nearby habitat. A suspected persistent wild population deserves a botanical identification, particularly in a warm climate where its behavior may differ from New England. The current evidence supports documenting escapes, not treating ordinary kitchen-garden basil as a nationwide ecological threat.

identification: Leaves are alternate, leathery and narrowly oval, often with wavy edges. The upper surface is glossy dark green. Small yellow-green flowers occur in clusters, and female plants can develop shiny black, oval fruits. Photograph leaf arrangement, the edge of the blade and any fruit. Several unrelated plants are called laurel or bay, including California bay and cherry laurels, so the common name is not a dependable identification. Do not taste a leaf to decide whether a plant is the culinary bay species.
actions: Document seedlings as well as the adult tree, noting whether they occur in irrigated beds, dumped garden material or surrounding natural vegetation. Ask a local herbarium or extension office to confirm an apparent escape before planning removal. Unwanted small plants can be removed from managed ground before they mature, while larger trees require a site-specific assessment. Avoid distributing seedlings into natural areas. For a mature landscape tree, discuss any proposed work with the owner and an arborist, using the observed seedlings and surrounding vegetation to explain the concern.

identification: Look for a tangled, rounded shrub with arching branches and opposite, simple leaves. Small creamy-white tubular flowers have a strong lemon-like scent and can appear in winter or early spring, depending on climate. Orange-red to dark red berries develop later, often partly hidden by foliage. Leaves are broadly oval and relatively dull rather than strongly glossy. Photograph flowers, a leafy branch and the whole shrub. Native honeysuckles deserve protection, and flowering season plus leaf and fruit features is more useful than a red berry alone.
actions: Where winter honeysuckle is spreading, avoid planting additional shrubs and consider a native replacement suited to the site. Document seedlings beyond the garden before removing them where permitted. Young plants are easier to address than an established thicket; larger shrubs need a removal plan and repeated checks for returning growth. Keep fruiting branches contained rather than placing them in woodland brush piles. If identification is uncertain, ask extension staff to review photographs before treating a shrub, and record follow-up observations after any removal.

identification: Look for alternate, oval to oblong leaves with finely toothed edges and conspicuous reddish glands near the top of the leaf stalk. White flowers appear in clusters, followed by fleshy fruits containing a single stone. Fruit color varies among cultivated forms, from yellow or red to very dark. Bark can be reddish brown and peel with age. Photograph the leaf stalk glands, flower arrangement, fruit and bark together; fruit color alone is not enough to distinguish sweet cherry from other Prunus species.
actions: For a tree away from cultivation, record nearby orchards or abandoned gardens and look for smaller trees that may be seedlings. Ask a local botanist or extension office to confirm the identification before removing a tree from natural habitat. Remove unwanted young plants where authorized, and use an arborist for mature trees when removal is appropriate. Do not use unknown leaves, stems or pits as food or animal feed. A useful report explains how the tree is growing and reproducing, not simply that cherries are present.

sources.label: Alaska Natural Heritage Program: Non-native plant identification guide

identification: Look for finely divided, threadlike foliage and broad umbrella-shaped clusters of small yellow flowers. Plants are often much taller than nearby herbs, with several stems arising from a substantial base. The leaves and stems have an anise-like scent, but scent should not replace a careful identification. Photograph the whole plant, leaf divisions and flower clusters. Do not taste an unknown carrot-family plant: other members of the family can be dangerous, and a casual resemblance to a kitchen herb is not a safety check.
actions: Address small patches before mature seed spreads. Where removal is permitted, work carefully around the root crown and minimize soil disturbance. Mowing alone usually leaves the plant able to regrow, and cutting seed-bearing stems can distribute seed. Contain those stems and clean tools before moving to another site. Plan follow-up visits for seedlings and returning shoots, and restore appropriate vegetation rather than leaving bare ground. Large stands need a sustained land-management plan; a single cutting is not evidence that the population has been eliminated.

identification: Look for raised, scabby areas on young citrus fruit that change from pale pink or light brown to darker, cracked or warty patches. The pattern may reflect splashing water, but weather injury, citrus canker and other fungal diseases can look similar. Photograph several fruit at different stages and the host tree as a whole. Note the citrus variety if known and when symptoms first appeared. A photograph can document the problem, but it cannot reliably identify which Elsinoe species caused it.
actions: Keep suspect nursery plants, grafting material and fruit at the site while contacting state plant-health staff or a citrus diagnostic service. Follow their sampling instructions rather than mailing material without notice. Check current movement rules before transferring citrus out of an affected area. Disease management may reduce future infection, but it does not erase existing fruit scars or replace official identification. Record irrigation practices and recent plant purchases to help investigators understand possible spread, and avoid treating an unfamiliar scab as harmless cosmetic damage without checking it.

identification: The green leaves are finely divided two or three times into narrow lobes and are usually nearly hairless. Upper branches carry many tiny, nodding flower heads without conspicuous ray petals. The foliage has a sweet or fruity scent. Biennial wormwood can look similar, but tends to have a tighter, more upright flowering arrangement and much less scent. Photograph the whole flowering branch, a lower leaf and an upper leaf. Those details are more useful than a close view of green foliage alone.
actions: On managed ground, remove unwanted plants before the small seeds mature and scatter. Record whether the same patch produces new plants the following season, especially where garden waste or disturbed soil may be involved. Confirm the identity before removing native Artemisia species nearby. Avoid distributing seed-bearing stems or treating the plant as a home remedy on the basis of its traditional uses. The available evidence supports identification and prevention of unwanted reseeding, while site-specific ecological harm and management priority still need to be established.

identification: Look for upright tufts with narrow, often hairy leaves and compact, spike-like flower heads that turn yellowish brown. At the junction of leaf and stem, a membranous ligule is present and clasping ear-like auricles are absent. Mature spikelets help separate this perennial from the related annual Anthoxanthum ovatum. Native sweetgrass, Anthoxanthum nitens, generally has a more open flower cluster and long spreading rhizomes. Photograph the whole clump, leaf collar and flower head rather than relying on scent or a single grass blade.
actions: In a confirmed small infestation, digging out the complete plant and below-ground growth can be useful where disturbance will not damage sensitive habitat. Mowing before seeds mature may reduce seed production, but grazing alone is not a dependable removal method. Keep seed-bearing material from entering clean meadow areas on equipment or in hay. Ask a local grass specialist to verify uncertain plants before work begins, especially near native sweetgrass. Revisit the site during the next early flowering season and record surviving clumps.

identification: The plant forms a low mat of heart-shaped leaves and usually fragrant violet or white flowers. Leafy runners, called stolons, are especially useful to photograph. A close examination of the hairy ovary or developing capsule can help distinguish it from common blue violet, Viola sororia, which lacks those leafy stolons and has a smooth ovary. Color and fragrance alone are not enough, particularly in garden selections. Include the leaf bases, runners and developing fruits in a report, and avoid pulling apart a patch just to obtain a picture.
actions: If sweet violet is spreading where it is unwanted, first establish which plants belong to it and which are native violets. Remove confirmed small plants and their runners only where you have permission, then watch for new growth around the edge of the patch. Keep garden divisions and soil containing runners out of nearby natural areas. For an observation record, note whether plants are maintained, abandoned or growing beyond a garden. A local flora or botanist can resolve an identification before more extensive work is considered.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Viola odorata

identification: Look for upright, relatively smooth stems carrying opposite, gray-green leaves and clusters of small pink flowers. The upper leaves clasp the stem. Sticky bands below some upper joints are a helpful feature, although they are not always obvious in a distant photograph. Each flower has five shallowly notched petals above a long, narrow calyx tube. Photograph a flower cluster, a stem joint and the leaf attachment. These details distinguish a useful botanical record from a general picture of a pink garden flower.
actions: Record whether the plants were deliberately sown, are persisting in an old bed or are appearing in surrounding unmanaged ground. If confirmed plants are unwanted, remove small patches before seed capsules open and avoid scattering their seed with garden debris. Check the same disturbed ground in later seasons for seedlings. Do not remove a native Silene on the strength of the common name catchfly. Where the identity or ecological significance is uncertain, submit photographs to a local botanical resource before planning wider removal.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria: Garden catchfly

identification: Look for arching woody canes with stout, curved prickles of different sizes. Leaves are divided into usually five to seven leaflets with toothed margins. Small glands, especially on the leaflet undersides, give the foliage a characteristic apple-like scent when handled gently. The flowers typically have five pink petals, followed by orange-red to red hips. Photograph the whole shrub, prickles, leaflet undersides and flowers or hips. Do not rely on a pink flower alone, and use gloves when working around the canes.
actions: Where sweetbriar is confirmed and spreading, avoid adding new plants and plan removal while the patch is still small. Contain fruiting material so hips are not moved to a new site. Larger thickets need a coordinated approach because remaining growth can return after cutting; ask local land managers about methods appropriate for the surrounding vegetation. Check for seedlings and renewed shoots after work. A report should describe the extent of the patch and nearby native plants, not simply label every rose in the area as invasive.

sources.label: Washington Noxious Weed Control Board: Sweet briar rose

identification: The climbing forms use tendrils to hold onto supports and have winged stems with paired leaflets. Showy, fragrant flowers appear in many cultivated colors, so color alone is not a dependable identification feature. Photograph a complete leaf with its tendril, the stem wings and a flower from the side. Native Lathyrus species and perennial ornamental peas can resemble it. A botanical identification should consider the whole plant and its life cycle rather than assigning a name from a seed packet found nearby.
actions: Do not eat ornamental sweet pea seeds or offer them as food; poison-plant references distinguish this species from edible garden peas. If unwanted plants are confirmed, remove them before pods open and keep seed-bearing trimmings out of natural areas. For plants beyond cultivation, note the location of nearby gardens and whether new seedlings appear in later seasons. Ask a local botanist to check uncertain peas before removal, especially in native vegetation. No broad treatment recommendation is warranted without evidence that this particular population needs control.

sources.label: UC Agriculture and Natural Resources: Poisonous plants

identification: Look for trailing stems with alternate, heart-shaped or deeply lobed leaves. Cultivars range from green to lime, purple, or variegated foliage, so color alone is unreliable. Occasional flowers are funnel-shaped, often lavender or pink with a darker center. The swollen underground parts are roots and lack the surface eyes found on ordinary potatoes. Other morning glories can have similar leaves and flowers, making the planting history and several views of the whole plant helpful.
actions: Keep cultivated vines within their intended bed or container and collect trimmings rather than discarding them on a natural-area edge. Photograph unexpected plants where they grow, including the stem, leaves, and any flowers. Note nearby ornamental plantings or vegetable beds before calling a patch an escape. If vigorous regrowth repeatedly appears beyond cultivation, ask local Extension staff to verify it and advise on removal. Use known planting material for gardening; an identification photo is not a food-safety assessment.

identification: Look for blue-green to grayish columns divided into prominent longitudinal ribs, with clusters of spines along their outer edges. University of Arizona's cultivated plants have large white flowers, reddish outer tips, and smooth pink to red fruits. Rib number varies and is not a reliable shortcut to species identification. Photograph a complete branch, its ribs and spine clusters, and any flowers or fruit. The name Cereus peruvianus appears in older horticultural treatments and in Kew's synonym list.
actions: Treat a planted specimen as a garden tree unless there is evidence of separate establishment beyond the planting. Keep fallen pieces and pruning material contained rather than leaving them on open ground. Large, spiny branches are awkward to handle; arrange suitable professional help for substantial pruning or removal. For an unexpected roadside or natural-area cactus, submit clear photographs and the location to a botanical specialist. Do not collect fruit or remove a plant solely because a nursery label matches this catalog entry.

sources.label: University of Arizona Campus Arboretum: Cereus repandus

identification: Adults are tiny, with pale yellow bodies and white wings held at a slight angle over the back. Look underneath leaves for the flattened immature stages, which remain attached while feeding. Late immature Bemisia generally lack the obvious waxy fringe or long filaments of several other whiteflies. These clues help separate groups, but ordinary photographs cannot resolve the cryptic species. A diagnostic laboratory may need molecular evidence; older B- or Q-biotype names should not be treated as photo-identifiable forms.
actions: Inspect new plants, especially leaf undersides, before placing them beside established crops. Monitor affected plants and keep a record of host, location, and symptoms. Preserve natural enemies by avoiding indiscriminate insecticide use, and reduce dusty conditions that disrupt them. Small infestations may be managed with removal of heavily affected leaves or other locally recommended measures. If crop injury or suspected virus symptoms are spreading, ask Extension staff for diagnosis and a current host-specific plan before choosing a product.

sources.label: USDA ARS: Bemisia species delimitation study

identification: Plants typically reach about one to two feet tall, with opposite, narrow leaves and dense rounded flower clusters. Individual flowers commonly have five petals with toothed or fringed edges, although double cultivars obscure that arrangement. Leaves are smooth and may be green or somewhat gray-green. Dry capsules release numerous small, dark seeds. Compare the whole plant with other cultivated pinks rather than relying only on flower color; photographs of leaf arrangement, the flower cluster, and its green base are especially useful.
actions: If you want to limit volunteers, collect spent flowering stems before capsules open and check nearby disturbed soil for seedlings. Keep garden waste out of woodland and meadow margins. Photograph an unexpected patch before disturbing it, and record whether an old house site or garden lies nearby. Ask a local herbarium or Extension office to confirm uncertain plants, particularly when a management decision depends on identity. A planted Sweet William does not warrant removal simply because it appears in a nonnative-species catalog.

identification: An observer cannot reliably identify this parasite from the eel's skin, body color, or swimming behavior. Adult worms live inside the swimbladder, and laboratory examination is needed to distinguish them from other parasites and assess associated damage. Older publications use Anguillicola crassus for the same organism. If an eel is examined through an authorized fisheries survey, retain the host identity, collection location, and sampling details with the parasite record; a worm photograph without that context is much less useful.
actions: Do not move live eels, bait organisms, or water between waterways. Anglers should follow current local bait and fish-movement rules rather than trying to inspect or treat wild eels themselves. Report an unusual finding from a legally caught or professionally examined eel to the state fisheries agency, with photographs and collection information. Ask the agency how it wants a specimen handled before transporting it. Fish-health professionals should direct testing or treatment in aquaculture, where preventing movement of infected stock is especially important.

sources.label: Infection of newly recruited American eels in a US Atlantic tidal creek
Zimmerman and Welsh 2012: Upper Potomac eel parasite study

identification: Plants are usually upright annuals, sometimes with lower stems leaning over and rooting at their joints. Narrow leaves sit in two ranks along the stem. A flowering head commonly has seven to seventeen branches radiating near the tip, with purplish spikelets that give it a soft, brushy appearance. Tiny hairs and the structure of the individual spikelets matter in separating it from other Chloris grasses. A distant picture of a windmill-shaped seed head is useful for finding the group but usually insufficient for a confident species name.
actions: Photograph a whole flowering plant, its stem base, and a close view of the flowering branches. Include a scale and record the habitat rather than collecting loose seed heads. Ask a local grass specialist or Extension office to compare it with other windmill grasses before undertaking control. Where removal is appropriate and authorized, work before seed matures and keep seed-bearing material contained. Brush accumulated seeds and soil from equipment before leaving a patch, especially when moving from disturbed ground into a conservation area.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Chloris barbata via SEINet

identification: Look for broadly triangular to oval fronds divided repeatedly into smaller segments, rather than the simple ladderlike outline associated with many familiar swordferns. Fronds can be pale green to blue-green and feel soft; the stalk base is enlarged and scaly. Fine hairs and the small spore-bearing structures on the underside help specialists distinguish it from related ferns. Photograph both surfaces of a mature frond and the base of the plant. Its old names include Thelypteris torresiana and Dryopteris uliginosa.
actions: Check nursery labels and spontaneous ferns in pots before moving plants between gardens. In Florida, choose a locally suitable alternative rather than planting this high-risk species. Have unfamiliar ferns identified before digging, since native species can share the same general appearance. If removal is warranted, contain mature fronds and follow local disposal advice rather than spreading them with garden waste. Revisit disturbed soil and nearby pots for new plants, and record whether the fern returns after the original clump is removed.

identification: Leaves are opposite, broad, and usually five-lobed, with coarse teeth and a relatively thick texture. The two lower lobes are smaller than the three main ones. Paired winged fruits hang in clusters, while older gray bark can flake to expose orange-colored patches. Winter buds remain green, a useful contrast with the purplish buds described for Norway maple. Cultivars may have purple leaf undersides or variegation, so confirm the structural features rather than expecting every tree to have plain green foliage.
actions: Look around a planted tree for seedlings at increasing distances, especially along shaded margins and lightly managed ground. Photograph leaves, buds, fruit, and bark before assigning the name. Small confirmed seedlings can be addressed with the landowner's permission, but established trees require a site-specific plan and professional attention where branches or roots present hazards. Ask the local conservation or Extension office which replacement trees fit the site. Avoid distributing seedlings from a tree that is escaping into nearby habitat.

identification: On mature growth, the long leaflike structures are flattened stalks called phyllodes. They have several prominent lengthwise veins and are generally narrow, straight or slightly curved. Short cylindrical clusters of yellow flowers arise beside them, followed by elongated pods. Several other wattles also bear yellow spikes, and the broader-leaved coastal form can be difficult to separate from the typical form. Photograph phyllodes, their attachment, flowers, pods, and overall habit rather than relying on a single golden flower cluster.
actions: Where local guidance discourages planting, choose a suitable alternative and avoid sharing seed or seedlings. Check beyond an existing hedge for young plants before they become large enough to flower. Keep pods and disturbed seed-bearing soil from being moved to other sites. Have a land manager or qualified contractor plan removal of substantial shrubs, then monitor the area over multiple seasons for seedlings. Do not use fire or soil disturbance as an improvised seed-bank treatment; management needs to fit the surrounding vegetation and site.

identification: Look for opposite leaves, each divided into two thick, smooth leaflets. The plant branches freely and may form a compact, low shrublike clump. Flowers have five petals and conspicuous orange to reddish stamens extending outward; elongated capsules later hang from the stems. The combination of paired fleshy leaflets and pendant capsules is more useful than flower color alone. Photograph several leaf pairs, the complete flowering or fruiting stem, and the extent of the patch, including any smaller plants around its edges.
actions: Mark the location and contact the local weed authority before transporting a specimen or starting broad excavation. In Washington, ask specifically about current reporting and handling requirements. For a small confirmed infestation, the state guidance emphasizes removing the entire root; fragments left behind can undermine that work. Keep removed material and soil contained, and arrange disposal according to local instructions. Larger or established patches need a coordinated plan and repeat inspections. Avoid spreading gravel or fill from the affected area while identification and treatment are being arranged.

sources.label: Washington Noxious Weed Board: Syrian bean-caper

identification: Adults are small flies, so a clear close photograph with a scale is more useful than a distant view. Size alone is not diagnostic, and this species should not be assigned to every fly seen near a caterpillar. Species-level work normally depends on an entomologist examining suitable material. If a parasitoid emerges during a documented rearing project, the identity of the original caterpillar, dates, location, and preserved associated material are especially valuable alongside photographs of the adult fly.
actions: Do not buy, move, or release this fly as an informal pest-control measure. A suspected observation is most useful when sent to an insect specialist with clear photographs and the circumstances of the find. Avoid spraying ordinary flies simply because caterpillars are declining; many insects nearby may be harmless or beneficial. For organized butterfly or moth monitoring, follow the project's collection and rearing protocol so host-parasitoid records remain reliable. Share repeated, well-documented findings with local conservation researchers rather than inferring an area-wide impact from a single caterpillar.

sources.label: Kellogg et al. 2003: Luna moth parasitism in Virginia
Timms et al. 2012: Parasitoid field study

identification: The original species key describes chestnut-brown wing covers with a pale V-shaped mark before the middle and a pale band near the tip. These are useful clues for photographs, but similar longhorned beetles still require expert comparison. Photograph the adult from above and the side, including its antennae and a size reference, and record the plant or wood product from which it emerged. Exit holes, frass and dying twigs indicate possible wood-borer activity; they cannot identify this species by themselves.
actions: Keep suspect nursery plants, freshly cut branches, or imported wood items at the location where the beetle was found rather than transporting them for informal inspection. Photograph the insect and retain packaging or plant labels if available. Contact your state plant-health agency or Extension diagnostic service for instructions on a specimen and the associated material. Do not cut healthy trees or apply preventive insecticides on the strength of a photograph. Current distribution and regulatory decisions should be checked directly with the agency, since the principal US assessment reviewed here is older.

sources.label: Matsushita 1933: Cerambycidae of the Japanese Empire
Samuelson and Gressitt 1965: Cerambycidae of the Ryukyu Archipelago

identification: Look for narrow, glossy leaves, clusters of small fragrant white flowers, and rounded fruits that become yellow to orange. The fruits open to reveal seeds with a striking red, sticky covering. Bishop Museum specimens document orange, two-valved fruits and glossy foliage in Hawaiian cultivated material. Other Pittosporum species can share several of these features, so photographs of leaves alone are insufficient. Include open fruit, a flower cluster if present, the leaf arrangement on a branch, and the whole tree.
actions: Check the ground and vegetation beyond an ornamental planting for young trees, and note whether they occur under likely bird perches or farther into adjoining habitat. In Hawaii, share unexpected wild populations with the island invasive-species program so they can fit the observation into local survey priorities. Avoid moving seedlings or fruiting branches to other sites while identity is uncertain. Where removal is recommended, arrange a plan appropriate to the tree's size and surroundings, then revisit the area for recruits. In Florida, do not substitute Hawaiian risk findings for the state's current assessment.

sources.label: Kauai Invasive Species Committee: Survey assessment

identification: Leaves are divided twice, with several paired branches bearing paired leaflets. Near the base of the leaf stalk is a conspicuous gland. Flower heads are pale, greenish-yellow to cream, and mature pods are long, flat, and reddish-brown. The relatively large leaflets and pale bark help direct identification, but other related trees need comparison. Photograph an entire compound leaf, the stalk gland, flowers or pods, and bark. A picture of a feathery canopy from a distance is rarely enough.
actions: Record whether the tree was intentionally planted and look for younger trees beyond the maintained area. Keep pods and seedlings from being moved into natural areas while local suitability is being checked. Forestry accounts describe vigorous regrowth after cutting, so do not assume a cut stump represents completed removal. Seek a qualified arborist or land manager for a large tree, and agree on follow-up inspection before work begins. Send a suspected wild population to a local herbarium with detailed photographs rather than labeling it from the common name alone.

sources.label: Indian Tropical Forest Research Institute: White siris

identification: Unmown plants form coarse bunches and may reach two to five feet tall. Leaves are stiff, often held almost at right angles to the stem near the collar. Look closely there for a short membranous ligule and small, blunt clasping projections called auricles. The flowering head opens into a branched panicle, although it can appear narrow and spikelike before full expansion. Several other pasture grasses look similar, so examine the collar and mature flowering head together before assigning a species.
actions: Confirm the grass before undertaking restoration work and map its extent while it is visibly growing. Prevent seed from surrounding stands from continually reaching a treatment area, and keep equipment clean when moving between sites. Mowing alone should not be assumed to remove established fescue. For small isolated clumps, ask whether careful digging is suitable; extensive stands need a coordinated restoration plan. Work with local conservation staff on timing and replacement vegetation so treatment protects desirable plants. Any chemical treatment or prescribed fire belongs within that site-specific professional plan.

identification: Most leaves form a basal rosette, while the upright flowering stem has few leaves and carries several small yellow flower heads. The narrow leaves are not strongly toothed, and long hairs occur particularly along their edges and lower midribs. Flower stalks and the dark bracts beneath the heads have several hair types, features best examined closely. Unlike some other introduced meadow hawkweeds, tall hawkweed does not produce aboveground runners. Photograph the rosette, stem leaves, unopened heads, and the plant's base for comparison.
actions: Ask a knowledgeable local botanist or weed program to confirm a suspected patch. In King County, report the location before beginning a large treatment effort. Small confirmed populations can be dug with the entire root system removed; contain flowering heads so they cannot scatter seed. Mowing alone is a poor solution because plants can regrow and flower again. Follow local disposal instructions rather than putting mature heads into ordinary garden compost. Recheck the site over subsequent seasons and restore suitable vegetation where removal has exposed soil.

sources.label: King County: Tall hawkweed identification and control

identification: Look for alternate, usually heart-shaped leaves on slender twining stems. Fine hairs often lie flat against the leaf surface; related morning glories may have more upright hairs, and leaf shape alone is not decisive. Flowers can be purple, blue, pink, white, or bicolored, followed by rounded seed capsules. A flower's color or a seed packet's cultivar name is not sufficient for species identification. Include the stem hairs, leaf undersides, and green flower bases in photographs when asking for confirmation.
actions: Deal with unwanted seedlings early, before vines become tightly wound through desirable plants. In a garden, remove developing seed capsules if the aim is to prevent volunteers, and revisit the soil in later seasons because buried seed can remain viable. Keep seed-bearing vines out of dumped garden waste. For a crop infestation, obtain current crop-specific advice from Extension rather than pulling mature vines through fragile plants or applying a general garden treatment. In Florida, select an appropriate alternative when planning a new planting near natural habitat.

identification: Plants form loose tufts of upright stems, often three to five feet tall, with flat leaves and a long, relatively narrow branching flower head. Mature spikelets are shiny and contain two florets. One carries a conspicuous bent, twisted awn, a fine bristle that helps distinguish the species when examined closely. The base can be somewhat swollen, but that feature varies. Photograph the whole clump, the collar where blade meets sheath, and several mature spikelets; related pasture grasses are difficult to separate from a distant image.
actions: Have the identification confirmed before treating mixed grassland, especially where desirable native grasses are present. Map patches while the grass is active and note nearby seed sources. In restoration areas, use a plan that couples suppression with recovery of the intended plant community, rather than leaving bare ground. Large established stands warrant advice from the local conservation agency because treatment timing and selectivity matter. Avoid spreading cut material or soil containing mature seed, clean machinery between sites, and revisit treated patches for renewed growth before considering the work complete.

sources.label: Washington Natural Heritage: Tall oatgrass assessment

identification: Young plants form a rosette with coarse, deeply lobed leaves. As the stem rises, upper leaves become smaller and divided into narrow, threadlike segments. Tiny pale-yellow flowers have four petals, and the mature pods are exceptionally slender and several inches long. Look closely at the leaf hairs: tumblemustard has simple hairs, whereas flixweed has branched hairs and more finely divided foliage. London rocket is another lookalike, but differs in upper-leaf shape. A photo of both basal and upper leaves is much more useful than flowers alone.
actions: Check disturbed edges while plants are still small, particularly after soil work or a burn. Confirm the identification, then prevent unwanted plants from reaching the dry, seed-shedding stage using methods suitable for the site. Contain mature plants before moving them so a cleanup does not scatter more seed. Clean equipment that has crossed a seeding patch and monitor the same ground after subsequent rains. Agricultural infestations need advice matched to the crop, while natural-area work should protect recovering native plants and avoid unnecessary soil disturbance.

identification: This is a perennial grass with upright stems and long leaves, forming clumps rather than a low lawnlike mat. Numerous narrow flowering branches spread or droop from near the top of the stalk, producing the windmill outline. Botanical treatments describe crowded, overlapping spikelets and small hairs and awns that must be checked under magnification. Other windmill grasses can look remarkably similar. Photograph the complete flowering head, several individual branches, the leaf collar, and the base; retain the exact location with the images.
actions: Leave a suspected wild plant in place while a regional grass specialist checks it, particularly in southern Florida where native records make indiscriminate removal inappropriate. Send photographs to a local herbarium or conservation botanist and mention both scientific names. Ask whether a voucher is needed before collecting anything from a protected site. Record whether the plant is in a planting, disturbed ground, or a relatively intact habitat. Do not apply a weed-control recommendation borrowed from another Chloris species, and do not use the catalog's inclusion as a reason to eradicate it.

sources.label: South Florida rare plants account: Chloris elata
SEINet Flora of North America: Chloris elata

identification: Leaves are divided into many small paired leaflets, giving branches a feathery appearance. Flowers are pale yellow or cream with reddish veins, followed by oblong pods that turn brown as they ripen. Unlike many legumes, the mature pod remains closed around its seeds and sticky pulp. The bark of older trees is dark and fissured. Other tropical trees have similarly fine foliage, so photographs of flowers and intact mature pods are especially helpful when confirming a tree from a leaf-only observation.
actions: Record whether a tree was planted and whether separate seedlings are appearing beyond its maintained surroundings. Keep fruit waste and unwanted seedlings out of natural-area edges, and choose planting sites with enough space for a mature crown. A large tree's pruning or removal should be planned with a qualified arborist. If a spontaneous population appears to be expanding, send photographs and its location to local botanical or Extension staff. Do not infer that removal is required from this catalog entry, and do not use an uncertain tree identification as food advice.

identification: Look for smooth, broadly winged stems and leaves with just one pair of leaflets, ending in a branched tendril. Flower stalks usually bear one to three purple, pink, or occasionally white flowers. Mature pods are long, flattened, and brown. Other peas can look similar, especially before flowering. The combination of an annual habit, winged stems, paired leaflets, and relatively few flowers helps narrow the identification. Photograph a complete leaf with its tendril, the stem wings, and a flowering stalk rather than only a close-up blossom.
actions: Have unexpected climbing peas identified before pulling a mixed patch, since native and cultivated relatives may be present. Where Tangier pea is unwanted, prevent pods from maturing and keep removed seed-bearing vines contained. Avoid scattering garden seed near unmanaged vegetation, and revisit a cleared area for later seedlings. Ask local Extension or conservation staff whether the species is a management concern at the site. Despite the name pea, it should not be treated as a food plant on the strength of appearance or a casual identification.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Lathyrus tingitanus

identification: Adults are roughly two to four millimeters long, dark brown to black, with contrasting pale markings on the head and upper body. Both fully winged and short-winged adults occur. Young stages begin paler and darken as they mature; they may gather on unfolding leaves and around leaf stalks. Dark sap residues at egg-laying punctures can be another clue, but are not diagnostic. Closely related Tarophagus look similar, and reliable species separation requires specialist examination of adult structures.
actions: Inspect new taro and ornamental elephant-ear plants closely before moving them beside established plants. Photograph insects where they are feeding, including their markings, wing form, the host plant, and any injury. Keep suspect plant material at the site while seeking advice from Extension or the state plant-health service. Preserve natural enemies and avoid broad insecticide use without a confirmed diagnosis and a suitable crop or ornamental recommendation. Do not move or release the planthopper to control unwanted taro; plant damage does not make an unapproved biological-control release appropriate.

sources.label: Gonzalez Vazquez et al. 2020: Tarophagus colocasiae fungal susceptibility

identification: Young and mature foliage can look surprisingly different on the same species. Juvenile leaves are broad, opposite, and often bluish, while adult leaves are longer, curved or lance-shaped, and arranged alternately on stalks. Bark sheds in long strips above a rougher base. Flowers are white, and the woody capsules and warty flower buds provide important identification clues. The wider Eucalyptus globulus group includes forms with different flower-cluster arrangements, so a solitary bud should not be treated as a universal species rule.
actions: Map seedlings and young trees outside the original planting before deciding how much a stand is spreading. Seek an arborist and the relevant land manager for work on large trees, and check site requirements before removal. Cutting alone may be followed by vigorous stump or basal regrowth, so follow-up must be part of the plan. Protect surrounding vegetation and arrange appropriate handling of the substantial branch and bark material. Revisit the grove edge and treated stumps over subsequent seasons, recording both new seedlings and resprouting rather than judging success immediately after felling.

identification: Plants form tufts with slender stems and narrow leaves that often roll inward. The narrow flowering panicle can remain partly enclosed by the upper leaf sheath. Inside its tiny spikelets, the florets carry a row of hairs and a central awn twisted near the base. The position and length of those hairs, side lobes and awn help separate it from other wallaby grasses. Photograph the whole tuft, leaf collar and mature flowering head. Magnification and an expert examination are usually needed to go beyond a tentative identification.
actions: Keep an uncertain record attached to its exact location and photographs rather than assigning it from a common name. Ask a regional herbarium or grass specialist to review suspected plants, especially when working from historical Hawaiian records. Collect material only with permission and according to the specialist's instructions; flowering parts are generally more informative than sterile leaves. Until identity and local status are resolved, avoid mowing, digging, or applying a weed treatment solely because the catalog lists this name. If management is warranted later, use advice specific to the confirmed species and site.

sources.label: Bishop Museum Occasional Papers 100: Rytidosperma biannulare
Bishop Museum: Hawaiian checklist and corrected grass applications

identification: Look for opposite, oval to oblong leaves that are mostly hairless, paired tubular flowers ranging from white to pink, and orange-red berries. The shrub can reach roughly ten feet tall. Morrow's honeysuckle has hairier foliage, while hybrids between it and Tatarian honeysuckle can blur that distinction. Native honeysuckles also occur, so berry color or the familiar flower shape alone is insufficient. Photograph the undersides of leaves, young twigs, flowers, and fruit together.
actions: Check local guidance before purchasing or retaining this shrub near woodland. Where removal is appropriate, start with isolated young plants and fruiting shrubs that supply seed to clean areas. Small plants may be lifted when soil is workable, taking care around neighboring roots. Larger shrubs commonly require repeated attention after cutting; ask extension staff about an appropriate stump or regrowth treatment. Revisit the site for seedlings and replace lost cover with locally suitable shrubs rather than leaving bare ground.

sources.label: University of Alaska: Identification of non-native plants

identification: The branching stems carry alternate leaves that vary considerably in shape: some are triangular or spear-shaped, others narrower, with irregular lobes or teeth. Small green flowers occur in clusters and elongated terminal arrangements. The paired structures enclosing the developing fruit are especially important; they may be three-lobed and become firm toward their joined bases. Other oraches can look very similar before fruiting. Include mature fruit coverings and several leaves from different stem levels in photographs for a botanist.
actions: Map the patch and note whether it occupies recently moved soil, a road shoulder, or cultivated ground. In a garden where it is unwanted, removing annual plants before fruit matures can limit additional seed input. Keep fruiting material out of soil and mulch being moved elsewhere. Avoid clearing a whole salt-tolerant plant community on a tentative identification. A regional herbarium can resolve the name and local status; species-specific United States impact and control evidence remain incomplete in this review.

sources.label: Kew and Flora of Iraq: Atriplex tatarica

identification: Females have two projections on the front of the face and orange-brown pollen-carrying hairs beneath the abdomen. These features help separate them from many native mason bees, but the closely related hornfaced bee, Osmia cornifrons, is a difficult lookalike. A photograph of a bee's back alone often misses the useful characters. Try to record the face, underside, and side without disturbing an occupied nest. Expert examination may be needed, especially for males.
actions: Avoid buying or moving unidentified mason-bee cocoons between regions. If you maintain nesting tubes, ask a local bee specialist how to identify their occupants and manage the tubes responsibly. Do not spray flowering plants or destroy every cavity nest because one unfamiliar bee appears. Record repeated observations, flowering plants visited, and any nest locations for a regional bee survey. Diverse locally native spring flowers and protected natural nesting sites remain useful support for the native bee community.

sources.label: Scientific Reports: Decline of six native mason bee species
Vermont Atlas of Life: Taurus mason bee

identification: Plants form several shoots from the base and carry narrow leaves beneath a slender, cylindrical seed head. The head contains a short series of compact spikelets, and the flower bracts can bear conspicuous awns. The outer glumes have blunt or squared ends and lack awns, a useful detail when separating this species from other goatgrasses. At maturity, the central axis breaks into units carrying spikelets. A complete ripe head is much more informative than an isolated grass blade.
actions: If an unfamiliar goatgrass appears in a grain field, save photographs and contact the crop adviser before seed is harvested or machinery moves to another field. Keep suspected contaminated seed lots separate and document their origin. Small confirmed patches may be removed before seed release when practical. Do not apply recommendations for jointed goatgrass automatically to this species. Local occurrence, crop risk, and an appropriate management program need confirmation; research collections should remain clearly separated from accidental escapes.

sources.label: Flora of North America via NEON: Aegilops tauschii
Wei et al.: Relationships of Aegilops tauschii revealed by DNA fingerprints

identification: Workers are small, fairly uniform in size, and golden to reddish brown, with long legs and antennae and abundant fine hairs. A single waist node and the absence of a stinger help an expert separate them from fire ants. Color and frantic running are not enough for a reliable identification. Nylanderia pubens is especially similar, and male structures may be needed to distinguish the two. Collecting a securely contained sample through an extension office is better than relying on a distant phone photograph.
actions: Inspect potted plants, stored materials, and equipment before moving them from an infested property. Reduce piles of debris that provide shelter and address persistent moisture where feasible. For dense infestations, coordinate with neighbors and a qualified pest professional rather than repeatedly spraying visible trails. Keep ants and liquid products away from energized electrical equipment and have equipment problems assessed safely. Confirm the species first, because an effective plan depends on which ant is present.

identification: Adult females are small, oval, and covered with white mealy wax. Detailed identification accounts describe bare lengthwise areas on the back and wax filaments around the edge, with longer filaments toward the rear. Examine twig junctions rather than only the outer needles. Comstock mealybug can also occur on yew, so white cottony material does not establish this species. A close photograph and a sample of the affected twig can help a diagnostic laboratory make the distinction.
actions: Inspect new yews before planting and keep suspect nursery stock apart until identified. Look for living insects and fresh honeydew before deciding an old sooty coating means an active outbreak. A small, accessible colony can sometimes be addressed by removing a heavily affected twig, but avoid excessive pruning of a stressed shrub. Ask extension staff about monitoring young crawlers and conserving natural enemies. Any treatment should fit the host, season, and confirmed insect rather than a generic mealybug schedule.

identification: Look for leathery, dark green leaves and relatively modest pale flowers with a conspicuous center of stamens. Leaves used for tea are new shoots and buds, but harvest appearance alone is not a safe botanical identification. China-type and Assam-type tea differ in typical leaf size and cold tolerance. Ornamental camellias can look similar, especially without flowers, and a nursery label or expert identification should establish the species before anyone treats an unknown shrub as a food plant.
actions: A healthy, deliberately planted tea shrub does not need removal simply because it appears in this catalog. Maintain it according to local horticultural advice and inspect nearby ground for volunteer seedlings if escape is a concern. Record plants found well away from cultivation rather than assuming a roadside camellia is tea. If a shrub is unwanted, ordinary garden removal and follow-up are appropriate; broad herbicide treatment or an invasive-species report needs a clearer local reason and a confirmed identification.

sources.label: NC State Plant Toolbox: Camellia sinensis

identification: Examine affected leaves and fruit with a hand lens for moving mites, eggs, shed skins, and fine webbing. Color is variable and overlaps with other spider mites. The twospotted spider mite is an important lookalike, and the decisive characters involve microscopic structures such as leg hairs and male reproductive anatomy. Leaf discoloration also has many non-mite causes. Submit affected material to a diagnostic service when the species matters, particularly on nursery stock or an unfamiliar crop.
actions: Inspect incoming plants and keep heavily infested material from brushing against clean stock. Monitor both pest mites and predatory mites before choosing treatment. On citrus, use local crop guidance because damage thresholds and registered options depend on the crop and setting. Avoid repeated, unsystematic pesticide applications that may disrupt predators or select resistance. If plants are moved between regions, ask the receiving nursery or plant-health authority about applicable requirements rather than assuming refrigeration or a visual check eliminates every mite.

sources.label: Spider Mites of Australia: Tetranychus kanzawai

identification: Turn over several leaves. Female coverings are elongated, brown, and boat-shaped; the whitish material associated with immature males can give a colony a fuzzy appearance. Tiny yellow crawlers are the mobile young stage. This mixture differs from a uniform fungal coating, although other scales may share the same plant. A hand lens helps reveal individual covers and whether living insects remain beneath them. Photograph the upper-leaf yellowing and the underside colony together for confirmation.
actions: Inspect new camellias and hollies before adding them to an established planting. Remove severely affected leaves or small branches only where the plant can tolerate that pruning, and keep infested clippings away from clean stock. Monitor fresh growth and crawler activity rather than repeatedly treating old damage. Parasitic wasps can contribute control, so discuss their presence with extension staff before spraying. Established infestations need patient follow-up; choose any treatment for the confirmed scale, host, and current local label.

sources.label: University of Georgia: Tea scale biology and management

identification: Small round entry holes, localized staining, and declining branches can prompt an inspection, but these signs are shared by several wood-boring insects and diseases. The beetles themselves are small enough that a general photograph rarely resolves the species. A trained entomologist may need specimens and, in difficult cases, molecular evidence. Record the tree species, the pattern of affected branches, and whether fresh boring activity is present. Keep healthy and damaged wood in separate photographs so a diagnostician can understand the distribution of symptoms.
actions: Contact an extension plant clinic or qualified arborist before removing a valuable tree. Do not transport suspect branches or firewood to another property. If pruning is advised, ask how the material should be contained and processed locally to prevent beetle movement. Nursery and orchard monitoring should use methods validated for this beetle; ordinary ethanol lures are not reliable substitutes. Research on biological products does not establish a universal cure, and treatment needs to address the particular beetle, host, and fungal association.

sources.label: UF/IFAS EDIS: Invasive Shot Hole Borers Euwallacea fornicatus, E. kuroshio, and E. perbrevis
Avery et al.: Beauveria products and Euwallacea perbrevis

identification: Adults have subdued brownish forewings that conceal more striking orange and dark hindwing markings when folded. Caterpillars can be dark above with paler undersides and contrasting lengthwise lines. Those are clues, not a complete diagnosis: small brown moths and leaf-chewing caterpillars are numerous. Photograph both the insect and the plant it is feeding on, including a whole damaged leaf. A moth specialist can compare wing patterns, and immature stages may need closer examination or molecular confirmation.
actions: On a planted teak tree, check whether feeding is active and how much of the crown is affected before taking action. Young trees and extensive repeated defoliation warrant forestry or extension advice. Avoid moving occupied nursery plants or cut foliage to another growing area. Do not spray an entire garden because a moth comes to a porch light. Regional invasive status and a tested United States response are unresolved here, so observations should go to a knowledgeable local diagnostician first.

sources.label: Nepal FRTC: Field guide to forest insect pests
Mississippi State Moth Photographers Group: Hyblaea puera
North Carolina State Parks: Hyblaea puera

identification: Mature females are flat, brown, and oval to somewhat pear-shaped, sometimes noticeably uneven in outline. Their upper surface has a mosaic of polygonal plates and a raised central ridge, the feature behind the name tessellated. They lack the thick wax covering seen on some other scales. Younger females have not developed the obvious mosaic and may resemble brown soft scale, Coccus hesperidum. Inspect leaf undersides and stems with a hand lens, and have uncertain colonies checked before deciding on treatment.
actions: Examine palms and other incoming ornamentals before placing them beside established plants. Check for live scales, sticky deposits, and fresh growth damage rather than treating sooty mold alone. Where practical, remove a small heavily infested leaf section without damaging the growing point. Ask a nursery or extension specialist about protecting natural enemies and choosing a host-appropriate response. Avoid moving infested pots between properties, and monitor treated plants because surviving young stages can be easy to miss.

sources.label: Gouthami et al. 2026: Coccini of Kerala

identification: Identification requires microscopy of the tiny protective shell, called a test. Published descriptions emphasize an oval or rounded rear region, a collar around the opening, and mineral particles incorporated into the shell. Great Lakes specimens average only a few dozen micrometers long. Closely related testate amoebae share the general construction, and shell dimensions and collar angle matter. A photograph of beach sand cannot establish this species; a documented laboratory examination is needed to separate it from similar organisms.
actions: There is no sensible household removal program for this organism. Do not bleach, excavate, or otherwise treat beach sediment in response to an unconfirmed identification. If it appears in a research sample, retain the sampling date, location, water conditions, preparation method, and microscope images so a specialist can review it. Follow ordinary aquatic biosecurity practices when moving equipment between waters, including removing sediment and draining retained water. There is not enough evidence to say that it causes local harm, and no established species-specific response supports treating the sand.

sources.label: Golemansky and Todorov 2009: Lake Leman testate amoebae

identification: Under a microscope, the shell is narrow and elongated, roughly twice as long as wide, with small angular particles on its surface. The opening sits within a flared collar that may lie near the shell's plane or bend away from it. Reported individuals are only about 22 to 28 micrometers long. Other Psammonobiotus can look similar, so shell proportions and collar structure must be compared carefully. An ordinary water sample or a photograph of an entire sand grain cannot provide a reliable field identification.
actions: Treat a suspected record as a laboratory identification question, not a reason to disturb a shoreline. Preserve images with a scale bar and record the exact sediment sample and preparation method for expert review. Do not release aquarium water or transport wet sediment between water bodies. Clean sampling equipment before reuse elsewhere. No species-specific control method is established in the reviewed account, and broad disinfection of a beach would harm a community without resolving the underlying identification or impact uncertainty.

identification: Look for a rosette of elongated, spoon-shaped or broader leaves followed by smaller leaves along the flowering stem. The flowers have a slender, elongated tube and a small star-like opening, commonly pale or white in the North American treatment. The plant can be hairy or sticky, and the fruit is a small capsule within the persistent calyx. Other Nicotiana species overlap in general appearance. Record the rosette, stem leaves, flower tube, and mature capsule together instead of identifying it from flower color alone.
actions: Ask a regional botanist to confirm plants found outside cultivation, particularly where other native tobaccos occur. If an unwanted garden plant is confirmed, remove it before capsules release seed and revisit the disturbed soil for seedlings. Do not use an uncertain wild tobacco for smoking, food, or home remedies. Keep removed material away from livestock feed and children's play materials. Local impact and tested control remain unresolved in this review, so larger natural-area work should follow a site-specific botanical assessment.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Nicotiana plumbaginifolia
IISc India Flora Online: Nicotiana plumbaginifolia

identification: Plants form tufts rather than spreading by obvious long rhizomes. Narrow leaves have a fringe of hairs at the blade-sheath junction. The branched seed head carries flattened, elongated spikelets containing numerous florets. As the spikelet matures, the arrangement of flower bracts and their shedding pattern helps separate it from other lovegrasses. Several Eragrostis species have similar airy heads, including native species. A botanist will need a mature flowering stem and close views of the leaf junction and individual spikelets.
actions: Before removing a patch, record whether it is an isolated roadside tuft, a persistent population, or part of a mixed native grassland. Have the identification checked if only a leaf or distant photograph is available. In a cultivated bed, a small confirmed unwanted tuft can be removed before seeds mature, with follow-up for new seedlings. Keep seed-bearing cuttings out of soil moved elsewhere. Extensive treatment should wait for local evidence about status, impact, and the vegetation that would replace it.

sources.label: Naturalis: Gramineae of Northern and West Tropical Africa, Eragrostis atrovirens

identification: The plant can reach about five feet, with harsh, narrow gray-green leaves that may turn orange-red in cool conditions. The flowering head is built from paired small branches carrying bristly spikelets rather than one broad, fluffy plume. Short underground growth helps form a compact tussock. Young plants resemble several other bunchgrasses, so flowering material is important. Photograph the paired seed-head branches, leaf junction, and whole tussock; do not rely on reddish winter foliage alone.
actions: Keep vehicles and mowing equipment out of mature seed heads where possible, and clean adhering seed before moving to another site. Prioritize small outlying tussocks rather than beginning in the center of a large stand. Removal must account for the perennial base and later seedlings. Do not use fire or repeated slashing as an assumed cure. Where this grass is newly suspected, ask a local grass specialist or weed authority to confirm identification and develop a site-specific plan that protects neighboring native grasses.

identification: Systemically infected shoots may emerge in spring with orange spore-producing areas, especially beneath leaves, followed by darker powdery stages. Local leaf infections and infections extending into the root system are different conditions. Rust color changes through the life cycle, and other fungi can produce similar spots. Confirm both the host plant and the fungus with a plant diagnostician. Photographs of the whole shoot, leaf undersides, and neighboring healthy thistles provide more useful context than a close-up of orange powder alone.
actions: If rust appears in a Canada thistle patch, record its extent and ask extension staff whether it fits an integrated management program. Do not distribute infected leaves, cultures, or soil to other properties on your own; movement of plant pathogens requires specialist and regulatory guidance. Continue monitoring thistle regeneration instead of assuming the fungus has reached every root. Keep proposed biological control separate from disease on valued plants, and avoid fungicide use simply because a beneficially studied rust looks unattractive.

sources.label: Weed Science: Integrated management of Canada thistle using Puccinia suaveolens

identification: Leaves are alternate, thick, and oval to elongated, with wavy edges. Their upper surfaces are glossy green, while the undersides have a silvery sheen dotted with brownish scales. Branches can bear sharp thorn-like shoots. Small fragrant tubular flowers appear in autumn or early winter, followed by reddish fruit. Autumn olive is deciduous, and cultivated Elaeagnus hybrids can complicate identification. Include a twig, both leaf surfaces, and flowers or fruit when asking for confirmation.
actions: Where the species is invasive, replace it with a locally suitable hedge or screen. Wear sturdy gloves and eye protection when working around the sharp shoots. Young plants are easier to remove before they develop a large root system. Cutting a mature shrub may lead to regrowth, so plan follow-up and seek extension advice about an appropriate stump treatment if needed. Contain fruiting debris and check beneath nearby trees for seedlings. Restore ground cover after removal to reduce opportunities for another weed to establish.

identification: The leaves are round to kidney-shaped with shallow rounded teeth and sparse hairs. Lower leaves are opposite, while flowering stems may have alternate leaves. Individual flowers sit on long, fine stalks arising from leaf axils. Thymeleaf speedwell usually carries its small flowers along a more obvious upright terminal cluster, and ground ivy has a different flower form and larger, strongly scented foliage. Lift the edge of a mat gently to see the intertwining stems and rooted joints without spreading fragments.
actions: Decide first whether the patch is a problem for the site's purpose; a few plants in a diverse lawn do not require blanket treatment. For a small unwanted patch, remove rooted stems carefully and collect fragments before mowing or moving soil. Improve thin turf through locally appropriate mowing, watering, and overseeding practices. Check again after cool weather returns. If treatment is needed, use guidance specific to a perennial creeping speedwell rather than assuming a product for annual lawn weeds will resolve the established mat.

identification: Several slender, rather stiff stems arise from the base, usually reaching only a few inches above the ground. Narrow, sometimes bluish-green leaves cluster in whorls at the nodes. Small greenish-white flowers occur on fine stalks, followed by tiny capsules. Broad-leaved carpetweeds and other Hypertelis can resemble it at a glance. Photograph the basal leaves, stem whorls, open flowers, and fruit with a ruler or another scale. Tiny seed and flower details may require a botanist's lens.
actions: For a suspected new regional record, note the soil type and whether the site was recently cultivated or received imported material. Ask a herbarium to check both the identification and the current scientific name. In a garden, a confirmed unwanted annual can be removed before seed release without disturbing a wide area of soil. Do not assume a local native carpetweed shares this plant's status. United States impact and tested management remain unresolved here, so extensive natural-area treatment should wait for local evidence.

sources.label: Kew and Flora Zambesiaca: Hypertelis cerviana
Flora of North America: Mollugo cerviana

identification: The flowering stalk is distinctly three-sided in cross-section, the feature behind the common name. White, bell-shaped flowers hang in a cluster and have green markings running along the floral segments. Leaves are narrow and arise from the base. Other onions, onion-scented plants, and white-flowered bulbs can be confused with it before flowering. Do not taste a plant to establish its identity. Photograph the stalk, entire flower cluster, and leaf arrangement, and ask a botanist to check an uncertain patch.
actions: Where the plant is unwanted, work before seed matures and remove bulbs as completely as practical. Collect loose bulbs and soil carefully rather than spreading them along a path or into a compost area beside natural vegetation. Recheck the site in the next growing season, because missed bulbs can produce fresh shoots. Avoid moving contaminated soil to another bed. For a dense colony beside a stream or in woodland, seek local weed-management advice before digging extensively or choosing any treatment near water.

identification: Each leaf has three small leaflets, often with a slight notch at the tip, and the lower surfaces can be hairy. Flowers occur in small clusters close to the leaf axils rather than on a long, showy flowering spike. The fruit is divided into separate joints. Desmodium adscendens and D. barbatum can resemble it in general habit, while ordinary clovers also have three leaflets. Flower arrangement, stipules, and the shape of fruit joints help separate these plants; photograph those details together.
actions: Check the identification before removing a mixed patch of low legumes. Record whether the plant stays in a maintained lawn or is expanding into a nearby natural area. Where a small garden colony is unwanted, lift rooted stem sections carefully and collect the fruits before moving clippings or soil. Revisit the edges for surviving rooted nodes. Regional status and tested control remain incomplete in this review, so pasture or conservation-site decisions should be made with local botanical and land-management advice.

sources.label: Flora of Tropical East Africa 1971 via Kew: Grona triflora

identification: Look for toothed leaves that range from broadly oval to narrower shapes, sometimes with shallow lobes. Hair type varies across the plant and among its subspecies; magnification helps reveal simple and star-shaped hairs. Small yellow flowers arise near leaf axils, with three narrow bracts outside the main calyx. Mature fruits break into separate segments, whose structure is useful for identification. Sida species and other false mallows are important lookalikes. Include a ripe fruit and the bracts beneath a flower rather than relying on a single petal photograph.
actions: Have an uncertain plant checked before removing native mallows from a natural area. In a cultivated bed, remove a confirmed unwanted plant before its fruits mature and collect loose fruiting material. Note whether new plants appear repeatedly from disturbed soil or spread beyond the original patch. Avoid carrying fruit-bearing stems on mowing equipment into clean ground. The reviewed sources establish botanical identity and regional records, but United States site-specific impact and an evaluated control program remain unresolved and should guide any larger response.

sources.label: New generic and species records for the flora of Saudi Arabia
IISc India Flora Online: Malvastrum coromandelianum

identification: The plant forms low tufts, with folded leaves and blunt, boat-shaped tips. A few short, stout flowering spikes cluster at the stem tip, each carrying densely arranged spikelets on one side. The common annual goosegrass, Eleusine indica, is usually larger and often has more and longer spikes. Check the perennial base and complete seed head together, because spike number alone varies. Close views of the leaf tip, blade-sheath junction, and spikelet arrangement are particularly helpful for a grass specialist.
actions: In a lawn, identify the grass before treating it as annual goosegrass, since a surviving perennial base changes the follow-up needed. Small unwanted tufts can be lifted before seed matures, taking care to remove the crown. Repair bare areas with suitable cover and avoid transferring seed-bearing soil or clippings. In crops, use local agronomic advice rather than importing a treatment from another country. Regional United States impact and tested control are still gaps in this account, especially for natural-area settings.

sources.label: New Zealand Plant Conservation Network: Eleusine tristachya

identification: Adults are very small and pale, with darker fringed wings and faint abdominal markings. Look at newly expanding leaves, buds, and shoot tips for insects and feeding scars. Broad mites, aphids, herbicide injury, and several other thrips can produce similar symptoms. California guidance specifically warns that field appearance cannot reliably identify chilli thrips to species. A diagnostic laboratory should examine collected insects when the identification matters, especially on nursery plants or in a new production area.
actions: Inspect new plants and isolate suspicious stock before placing it beside susceptible plants. Monitor new growth frequently, using a consistent sample of shoots so changes are visible over time. Contain heavily infested prunings and remove nearby discarded plant material that could shelter pests. Ask extension staff about conserving predators and choosing a crop-appropriate integrated program. Repeated use of one pesticide is not a durable plan. Document the plant host and damage when reporting a suspected new occurrence to a local plant clinic.

identification: Adults are tiny, slender, yellowish insects with narrow fringed wings; young stages lack developed wings. Feeding may leave pale or bronzed surfaces, but damage and body color overlap with other thrips. Examine the affected host and the distribution of insects across leaves and flowers rather than naming the pest from a sticky-trap silhouette. A specialist can inspect microscopic characters. Preserve the crop identity and growing conditions with the sample, because those details help interpret an otherwise ambiguous finding.
actions: Inspect incoming transplants and keep suspect lots separate while seeking identification. Scout regularly instead of waiting for widespread damage, and remove crop residues promptly after harvest. Predators can suppress populations, and research in Guadeloupe found that excessive insecticide use could worsen problems by disrupting that regulation. Work with an adviser on a crop-specific program that includes sanitation and natural enemies. Do not move infested plants or make treatment choices based solely on the general word thrips on a product label.

sources.label: Etienne and Van Waetermeulen: Thrips palmi on eggplant in Guadeloupe
UF/IFAS: Arthropod management for tomato, pepper and eggplant

identification: Females are dark brown, with the head and thorax often paler than the abdomen; males are smaller and lighter. Both can hide in protected plant parts, and feeding may scar or deform new growth. Several other dark thrips can look similar without magnification. Photograph the affected plant and its fresh damage, then arrange for microscopic identification of actual insects. A leaf photograph alone cannot separate this species from mites, other thrips, or some growth disorders.
actions: Hold suspect nursery stock apart and avoid selling, gifting, or moving it until local plant-health staff advise what to do. Keep purchase and shipment information available so a confirmed finding can be traced. Inspect nearby plants, especially fresh growth, and use a consistent monitoring routine after any intervention. Commercial growers should work with extension and regulatory staff on sanitation, biological control, and resistance management. Home gardeners should seek confirmation early rather than repeatedly applying broad insecticides to every damaged plant in the garden.

sources.label: UF/IFAS EDIS: Thrips parvispinus: A New Invasive Pest
Texas A&M: Short-spined thrips pest alert

identification: Look for opposite, toothed leaves and small blue to purple flowers with a two-lipped outline. The floral tube sits within a toothed calyx, and the plant is upright rather than a creeping mat of true thyme. Other small mint-family herbs can look similar, so flower size, calyx structure, and the leaves directly below the flowers deserve close photographs. Record the entire plant and its habitat as well as the flowers. A regional herbarium can compare it with native dragonheads and related mints.
actions: If you find an unfamiliar population, record how many plants occur, whether they are flowering or fruiting, and whether imported soil or transport corridors are nearby. Have the identification checked before removing a rare native lookalike. In a garden, a confirmed unwanted plant can be removed before its fruits mature. Avoid redistributing seed-bearing material. United States impact and control evidence are insufficient here, so conservation-site work should follow a local botanical assessment rather than a generic invasive-mint response.

sources.label: Pliszko 2026: Dracocephalum thymiflorum established in Poland

identification: Leaves are small, opposite, and pointed, with fine rough hairs. Each flower has five white petals that are shorter than the surrounding pointed sepals. The mature capsule is swollen near the base, rather like a tiny flask, and opens with six short teeth.
