Chickweeds can resemble it but commonly have deeply divided petals, while the closely related slender sandwort requires careful fruit and seed comparison. Take close photographs of the sepals and a ripe capsule; flowering stems alone may not resolve the distinction.
actions: In a garden bed or gravel path, small unwanted plants can be pulled before capsules shed seed. Keep disturbance shallow so management does not continually create new bare ground. In a lawn, assess whether thin turf or repeated soil exposure is encouraging annual weeds and address that underlying condition. Avoid broad treatment of a mixed spring flora without confirming the species. Local ecological impact and a species-specific United States control program remain unresolved in this account, so larger interventions need a site-based reason.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Arenaria serpyllifolia

identification: Leaves are opposite, rounded to oval, and nearly smooth, with shallow teeth that can be hard to see. Small pale blue or whitish flowers occur along an upright terminal cluster, often showing darker lines on the petals. The fruit is flattened and notched at the top. Threadstalk speedwell has more conspicuous individual flowers on long fine stalks, while purslane speedwell is annual and has almost unstalked flowers. Close views of flowers, fruit margins, and the rooted stem base help resolve the identification.
actions: In a lawn, consider whether the plant is causing a practical problem before removing it. Where a patch is unwanted, carefully lift rooted stems and improve thin turf using practices suited to the local grass and drainage. In wetlands or mountain vegetation, seek botanical confirmation before disturbance, because local status may differ from that of garden weeds. Record the habitat and flowering date with a sighting. This review leaves regional native status and species-specific ecological impact open rather than prescribing broad removal.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Veronica serpyllifolia

identification: Leaves have three leaflets, usually elongated or oval, with a larger terminal leaflet. Some show a pale mark along the middle, but the mark is not universal. Pink to purple pea-like flowers occur in elongated clusters. Mature fruits divide into several flattened, roughly semicircular joints covered in tiny hooked hairs. Other ticktrefoils share three-part leaves and clinging fruits, so a single leaflet is a weak identification. Include the flower cluster, lower leaf surface, and a complete mature fruit in photographs.
actions: Brush attached fruit segments from clothing, pet fur, and equipment before leaving an infested site, disposing of them where they will not start another patch. In a garden where the plant is unwanted, remove it before fruit matures and revisit for regrowth or seedlings. In pasture or natural vegetation, confirm regional status before choosing control. Do not assume a tropical American native is an invader everywhere. Local impact and management evidence remain incomplete in this account, especially outside the Hawaiian introduction context.

identification: Plants have firm, three-angled stems, long narrow leaves, and a branched cluster of flattened brownish spikelets. Several leaf-like bracts extend beyond the flowering cluster. The underground tubers are useful clues, but digging them from a wetland just to make an identification may be inappropriate. Other flatsedges and nutsedges share much of this appearance. Mature spikelets and fruits, including the number of style branches and fruit shape, are important specialist characters. Photograph the full flowering head and a close view of individual spikelets.
actions: Have a flowering plant identified before treating a wet area for nutsedge. Record water conditions and whether the patch is spreading through soil moved during ditching or cultivation. Where removal is justified, plan for the underground propagules rather than repeatedly clipping the leaves alone. Keep excavated wet soil and plant fragments from being transferred to clean sites. Any work in a marsh or drainage channel should follow local habitat and water-management guidance. United States ecological impact and a tested species-specific response remain unresolved here.

sources.label: Digital Flora of Shanghai: Cyperus serotinus
Flora of North America: Cyperus serotinus

identification: Arching, reed-like stems arise from short underground rhizomes and can reach several meters tall. The broad, smooth, leathery leaf blades alternate along the stems. A small membranous collar occurs where each blade meets its sheath, and the mature flowering branches form a large airy head. It lacks the familiar woody branching structure of many true bamboos. Photograph both the base and a flowering stem, since broad leaves alone can be confused with other large ornamental grasses.
actions: In Florida, choose a locally recommended alternative when a tall screen is needed. For an existing planting, watch the surrounding ground and nearby disturbed areas for young plants, and prevent seed-bearing cuttings from being dumped beyond the garden. A clump that has outgrown its site may require staged removal of the persistent base and follow-up on new shoots. Ask local extension staff about suitable methods before working near drains or natural vegetation. Retain a record of escapes separately from the original cultivated clump.

identification: Look closely at the tight cylindrical head: each small spikelet has two short bristles, giving it a tiny horned appearance. Plants form tufts and often have a swollen stem base rather than a spreading rhizome network. The leaf junction has a pale membranous ligule and no clasping auricles. Meadow foxtail can look similar from a distance, but the placement and form of its awns differ. Native alpine timothy has a shorter, more compact head and should not be removed on a casual comparison.
actions: Keep useful forage management separate from natural-area restoration. Where timothy is unwanted, identify the stand before seed matures and work with the land manager on preventing further seed input while establishing suitable replacement vegetation. Small isolated tufts may be dug out if soil disturbance is acceptable. Avoid introducing hay or seed mixtures containing timothy into projects intended to restore native grassland. Revisit treated areas for seedlings and surviving crowns rather than assuming one cut has removed a perennial.

identification: Each leaf carries several pairs of narrow leaflets and ends in a tendril that may branch. Flowers are small, dull white to pale blue, and grouped on a stalk. Mature pods are short, hairy, and usually contain two seeds, becoming dark as they ripen. Larger purple-flowered vetches are a common source of confusion, while other small-flowered species need closer comparison. Photograph a complete leaf, the flower cluster, and an intact ripe pod; counting leaflets alone is not enough.
actions: Where tiny vetch is unwanted in a garden or young planting, remove it before pods mature, gently freeing the tendrils so neighboring plants are not uprooted. Check whether the vine is actually smothering seedlings or simply occupying an open gap before intervening. Avoid transporting mature pods with cut vegetation or contaminated seed. Crop fields require local advice that considers the crop and season. United States site-specific impact and tested control are not established by the floras reviewed here, so broad natural-area removal needs further justification.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Vicia hirsuta
IISc India Flora Online: Vicia hirsuta

identification: Adults can reach several centimeters in height and width and often have a conspicuous pinkish-red shell. The shell opening and the plates closing it are important identification features. The related California barnacle, Megabalanus californicus, differs in shell pattern, ribbing, and the relative size of the opening. Age and crowding can alter shape, so color alone is insufficient. Photograph the entire attached animal from the side and above, with a scale, and let a marine specialist examine uncertain specimens.
actions: Inspect hulls, trailers, and equipment before moving them between coastal waters. Use an appropriate haul-out or cleaning facility that captures removed organisms rather than scraping living fouling directly into a new harbor. Do not move a colonized buoy or shell as a souvenir. Report unfamiliar large barnacles to the local marine invasive-species program with the exact location and substrate. Broad chemical treatment of docks or natural shores is not justified by a photograph; management should focus on confirmed identification and transport prevention.

sources.label: Shahdadi, Sari and Naderloo 2014: Megabalanus coccopoma
Newman and McConnaughey: Eastern Pacific barnacle in California

identification: Historical accounts describe a very large rounded shell, potentially around nine to twelve centimeters high, and distinctive green egg masses laid above water. Shell shape overlaps strongly with other large Pomacea, including the spotted applesnail, and Florida also has a native applesnail. Egg color and shape can help guide an expert, but neither a large shell nor an unfamiliar clutch settles the name. Photograph the shell from several angles and the egg mass in place, including a size reference and the waterline.
actions: Do not release aquarium snails or move aquatic plants carrying eggs into another water body. Report a suspected unusual applesnail to a local aquatic-species specialist and keep the exact location and photographs. Avoid destroying every snail or egg mass on the assumption that all are nonnative. If removal is recommended, obtain local instructions that protect native species and address the confirmed population. Claims about crop destruction or control methods from other Pomacea species should not be assigned to this unresolved taxon.

sources.label: Cazzaniga 2002: Original review of Pomacea taxonomic characters

identification: A typical tokay has a large head, broad gripping toe pads, and gray to bluish-gray skin marked with orange or reddish spots. Adults are much larger and more robust than the small pale house geckos commonly seen on walls. The loud repeated call can support an identification when heard with a visual sighting, but recordings alone may be misleading. Photograph the animal from a safe distance, including its head, body pattern, and toes; do not grab it to obtain a closer view.
actions: Never release a pet tokay outdoors. If an unwanted captive animal needs a new home, arrange a responsible surrender through a qualified organization. For a free-ranging sighting outside an established area, record the location and contact a local wildlife or invasive-species program. Keep pets away and avoid glue traps or indiscriminate poisons that also harm native animals. Any capture or removal should follow local guidance and be handled by someone prepared to work safely with a large gecko.

sources.label: Center for North American Herpetology: Gekko gecko
University of Florida: Tokay gecko account

identification: Adults are small grayish moths flecked with darker markings. Young caterpillars are pale and relatively smooth, while older larvae may show reddish or purplish bands. Look for blotchy mines and folded leaves as well as fruit injury. Ordinary leafminer tunnels are typically narrow and winding, and leafminers do not fold the leaves. Tomato fruitworms are different caterpillars with more obvious early bristles and bumps. Photograph the larva, its shelter, and damaged fruit before submitting material for confirmation.
actions: Inspect transplants and scout leaves before damage becomes concentrated inside fruit. Remove infested crop residues after harvest and manage volunteer tomatoes or other confirmed host weeds that bridge cropping cycles. In a home garden, promptly containing badly infested leaves and fruit can reduce the amount of occupied material left behind. Commercial growers should use local guidance on monitoring and integrated control, including host-free periods where appropriate. Avoid moving infested transplants between gardens or assuming a spray will reach larvae already protected inside fruit.

sources.label: Texas A&M Vegetable IPM: tomato pinworm
UC IPM: Tomato pinworm crop management

identification: Adults are brown, with paler feet, tibial tips, and parts of the antennae. Both sexes have developed wings. Reliable identification depends on microscopic features, including the eight-segmented antennae and the placement of particular head and body hairs. These characters are beyond a typical garden photograph. C. claratris and other members of the genus are important comparisons. Send actual insects to a diagnostic service and record the host plant, affected tissue, and whether the insects came from imported or locally grown material.
actions: Keep suspect transplants separate and avoid distributing them while identification is pending. Inspect adjacent plants and retain shipment or purchase details so a confirmed detection can be traced. Crop damage should be assessed alongside other possible causes before treatment is chosen. Ask local extension or plant-health staff for a response appropriate to the location; an overseas quarantine instruction is not automatically a United States rule. The Florida flower record supports presence, while local crop impacts and a tested management response still need species-specific evidence.

sources.label: University of Halle ThripsNet: Ceratothripoides brunneus
Skarlinsky et al. 2017: Ceratothripoides brunneus recorded from Florida

identification: The lower leaves are longer than wide and may have a squared or slightly heart-shaped base. Upper leaves become smaller and narrower. Flowering stems carry clusters of small flowers that mature into fruits enclosed by enlarged inner flower segments, often called valves. These valves have conspicuous narrow teeth and may carry raised grain-like swellings. Several other docks have toothed valves too, so their shape, tooth length, and swellings need comparison. Photograph mature fruits with a scale and retain views of the lower leaves.
actions: In a cultivated bed, remove a confirmed unwanted plant before the fruit clusters mature, collecting seed-bearing material rather than scattering it. Note whether repeated seedlings follow irrigation, soil movement, or disturbance. Do not assume treatment for a deep-rooted perennial dock fits this shorter-lived species. A regional herbarium or crop adviser can confirm identity and local relevance. This review does not establish a species-specific United States impact or control program, so extensive work in wet natural habitat should wait for a site-based assessment.

sources.label: IISc India Flora Online: Rumex dentatus

identification: Look for upright green to blue-green grass shoots and an open, branched seed head. At the leaf junction is a very short membrane fringed with hairs. The namesake clue is a stout, sharply pointed, pale rhizome with scale-like leaves. Several grasses share narrow blades and creeping growth, so an aboveground photograph may be insufficient. Where digging is appropriate, photograph a small exposed rhizome in place; do not scatter fragments while trying to identify the plant.
actions: Avoid moving soil, sod, or ditch-cleaning debris from an infested area into clean ground. Small patches require careful removal of underground stems and repeated follow-up; incomplete digging can leave many growing points. Mowing may keep shoots short without eliminating the colony. For shorelines, canals, and wetlands, consult a qualified local manager about site-appropriate treatment and protection of desirable aquatic plants. Work from isolated patches toward larger stands, monitor regrowth, and restore suitable vegetation rather than leaving newly disturbed soil open.

identification: Moso develops tall, stout woody culms, with younger surfaces often powdery and finely hairy. The protective sheaths on emerging shoots have dense brown hairs and spots. Specialist bamboo identification uses these sheaths, branching, and leaf characters together. Ordinary moso culms need not show the distorted pattern associated with tortoise-shell bamboo. Photograph a young shoot with its sheaths, mature culms, branch attachments, and leaves. Height alone cannot distinguish it from other large running bamboos or native cane.
actions: Before planting, consider the Florida risk assessment and obtain locally appropriate alternatives for screening. Existing groves need regular inspection beyond their intended boundary, because underground growth can produce shoots away from the visible clump. If removal is necessary, plan repeated work on new shoots and the rhizome system rather than a single cutting of the tall culms. Do not dump rhizome-bearing soil or divisions into natural areas. A species-level identification does not establish that a plant is the tortoise-shell form.

sources.label: USDA GRIN: Phyllostachys edulis var. heterocycla
Digital Flora of Shanghai: Phyllostachys edulis Heterocycla
University of Florida IFAS: Phyllostachys edulis invasion-risk assessment
Di et al. 2026: Short internodes in the Heterocycla variant of moso bamboo

identification: Leaves are divided into numerous small leaflets, commonly nine to eleven in the reviewed treatment. Pink to brick-red pea flowers form elongated clusters, followed by slender downward-pointing pods. The similar I. spicata typically has fewer, broader leaflets, but dependable separation also uses small flower structures. A sprawling plant with pink flowers cannot be identified securely from growth habit alone. Photograph complete leaves, flowers from the side, mature pods, and the rooting stems, and ask a legume specialist to examine uncertain material.
actions: Keep an unidentified creeping indigo out of hay and grazing areas until it has been assessed. If livestock may have eaten it and seem unwell, contact a veterinarian promptly rather than relying on a plant photograph. For an unwanted patch, prevent movement of rooted stems and seed-bearing soil and plan follow-up after removal. Do not apply toxicity figures or control claims from I. spicata automatically. A regional record needs a verified specimen before its identity can be matched confidently to older accounts of harm.

sources.label: Chiang et al.: Indigofera spicata and hendecaphylla in Taiwan
USDA GRIN: Indigofera hendecaphylla accession corrections

identification: Leaves are opposite, oval, toothed, and rough above, with softer hairs beneath. Slender stems trail along the ground and may root where they touch soil. The flower heads contain many small tubes, usually purple to pinkish with pale centers and yellow throats. Other lantanas and cultivated hybrids can resemble it; a yellow-flowered nursery selection may be a hybrid rather than this species. Photograph leaves, stems, flowers, and fruit together and retain the cultivar label when available.
actions: In Florida, choose a locally recommended alternative instead of planting a species assessed as high risk. Inspect established plants for seedlings and rooted stems beyond the bed, and contain fruiting prunings. Wear gloves when handling the plant and keep it out of grazing material or edible-plant harvests. If removing a mat, check for rooted nodes left behind and revisit after new growth resumes. Do not assume a cultivar is sterile without reliable documentation for that exact selection.

identification: The elongated jaws, narrow waist, and spine-topped waist node identify the general trapjaw form, but species separation needs much closer inspection. In O. ruginodis, the rear face of the waist node has conspicuous transverse wrinkles, and specialists compare head sculpture, body size, and other structures. Color varies and is not sufficient. O. brunneus and O. haematodus are important comparisons. Photograph the ant from the side and above without handling it, and seek identification from an entomologist familiar with regional ants.
actions: Avoid moving colonies, occupied soil, or potted plants between properties. If ants are entering a building, document their route and obtain an identification before selecting a pest-management response. Outdoor ants in a natural area should not be treated simply because their jaws look alarming. Keep children and pets from disturbing a nest and leave any necessary collection to someone equipped to do it safely. Species-specific ecological effects, origin in Florida, and an appropriate local control recommendation remain unresolved in this review.

sources.label: University of Utah ant account: Odontomachus ruginodis
MacGown et al. 2014: Nearctic Odontomachus revision

identification: Plants can grow into a substantial shrub, with pale woody stems and soft hairs on younger parts. Leaves have several broad shallow lobes. The flowers have darker veins near the throat, and three broad outer bracts sit beneath the main calyx. The ripe fruit is a flattened ring of separate segments rather than a fleshy berry. Other tall mallows can resemble it, so photograph the outer bracts, leaf shape, and mature fruit. The old Lavatera name may still appear on nursery or herbarium labels.
actions: Check local status before planting near dunes, seabird habitat, or coastal reserves. Where removal is appropriate, tackle small plants before fruit matures and contain seed-bearing branches. Large stems may require careful cutting and follow-up on the base, especially on unstable coastal soil. Avoid clearing vegetation from nesting areas without land-manager guidance. This review leaves United States site-specific impact and control unresolved, so a botanical confirmation and a local habitat assessment should precede extensive removal.

identification: Look for a substantial branching plant with broad leaves divided into three to five lobes. The conspicuous heads have yellow outer rays surrounding many small disk flowers. Stems are soft-wooded, and mature fruits are flattened, dry, and associated with small persistent awns or scales. Other sunflowers, including the commonly grown annual Tithonia rotundifolia, can cause confusion. Record the overall woody habit, leaf shape, flower head, and fruit rather than identifying it from yellow rays alone.
actions: In Florida, select a locally recommended alternative for new planting. Where an existing shrub is spreading, prevent mature heads and cut branches from being dumped into natural areas. Young escapes are easier to address before they become large and produce more reproductive material. Plan follow-up after cutting because removing the visible canopy is not a complete monitoring program. On slopes or stream edges, coordinate removal and replacement vegetation with the land manager to avoid leaving exposed soil.

identification: The smooth, often waxy-looking leaves give the plant a gray or bluish cast. Flowers are narrow yellow tubes borne near branch tips, and the plant develops a woody framework rather than remaining a small leafy rosette. Other tobaccos and yellow-flowered shrubs can resemble parts of this description, so use the leaves, woody habit, flowers, and fruit together. Never taste a leaf to confirm the name. Photograph the whole plant and the point where a leaf joins the stem.
actions: Keep livestock and children away from an unwanted plant and ensure cut material does not enter feed or garden harvests. Small seedlings are easier to remove before they become woody and set seed; use gloves and avoid scattering mature capsules. Established plants and streamside stands need a local removal plan with follow-up for new seedlings. Do not dump cut branches into a wash where water can move the debris. If ingestion is suspected, seek prompt professional poison or veterinary advice rather than waiting for a botanical identification.

sources.label: UC Irvine: Nicotiana glauca invasive species account

identification: Follow one whole leaf from the twig to its tip. It is a long compound leaf made of many pointed leaflets, rather than a branch of separate leaves. Most leaflet edges are smooth, with a few gland-bearing teeth near the base. Native sumacs usually have toothed leaflets and clusters of red, fuzzy fruits; tree-of-heaven produces loose bunches of twisted, papery wings. Walnuts can look similar, but their twigs have chambered pith rather than the spongy center of tree-of-heaven. Photograph the leaflet bases, twig, and fruits together.
actions: Confirm the tree before cutting, especially where native sumacs and walnuts grow nearby. Small seedlings can be removed with their roots, but established root sprouts require a different plan. Cutting an older tree alone commonly triggers vigorous regrowth. Ask an extension forester or qualified arborist to plan treatment and safe removal, taking nearby structures and desirable trees into account. Mark the treated area and revisit it for root shoots and seedlings over subsequent seasons. Avoid distributing seed-bearing branches in mulch or yard waste.
Wear gloves when handling seedlings or cut material.

sources.label: Virginia Tech: Invasive Plant Species, Ailanthus
Minnesota Department of Agriculture: Tree of heaven, the threat

identification: Look for a low cone with six shell plates, pale vertical ribs, and pinkish or purplish coloration. The opening at the top is roughly triangular. The strongest diagnostic clue is much smaller: the closing plate called the scutum has rows of little pits. Other striped acorn barnacles can resemble it from above, and weathering or attached growth can hide the useful features. A close photograph with a scale helps, but a specialist may need to examine the shell plates to distinguish it reliably from related barnacles.
actions: Record the harbor, substrate, approximate depth, and whether the barnacles are on a boat or a natural surface. For an unexpected record, send photographs to a local marine extension or invasive-species program before collecting material. Boat owners can reduce transport by inspecting submerged fittings and arranging hull cleaning where removed growth and wash water are contained. Do not scrape fouling into another marina or move encrusted equipment between water bodies. Leave barnacles on natural shores undisturbed unless a responsible management program requests removal.

sources.label: Texas A&M Galveston: Purple striped barnacle
Thiyagarajan et al.: Larval development and attachment of Balanus trigonus

identification: Large leathery leaves crowd near the branch tips and broaden toward their rounded ends, giving them a paddle-like outline. Older leaves can turn red or yellow before falling, an unusually autumn-like display in a tropical landscape. The fruits are flattened and almond-shaped, changing from green toward reddish or purplish tones as they mature. Combine these features with the layered branching pattern. The common name does not make this the commercial almond tree, and leaf color alone is too variable to identify a seedling.
actions: Where tropical almond escapes into coastal habitat, check beneath parent trees and along adjacent shorelines for young plants. Record seedlings separately from intentionally planted shade trees so the observation describes actual spread. Remove small unwanted seedlings only with the landowner's permission and arrange professional help for large trees. Keep collected fruit and rooted garden waste out of dunes, mangrove edges, and drainage channels. For a replacement shade tree, use a locally appropriate species and check coastal planting guidance rather than assuming every tropical shoreline needs the same treatment.

identification: Examine both sides of a leaf. The upper surface is green and may become nearly hairless, while the underside carries a pale woolly covering. Leaves narrow toward the base and can be spoon-shaped to slender and tapering. Several long, leaflike bracts extend beyond the rounded terminal flower cluster. Basal leaves may have withered by flowering time. Other cudweeds share the woolly appearance, so include the whole plant, the terminal cluster, and the stem base; a genuine network of runners would be a reason to reconsider this identification.
actions: Photograph a flowering plant before routine mowing or garden cleanup removes the useful features. A herbarium or extension botanist can compare it with regional cudweeds and check whether the name is appropriate for the location. If it is simply an unwanted garden annual, removing it before mature seed is a reasonable containment precaution. Avoid moving seed-bearing soil from the patch into another bed. Broad habitat clearing is not justified by the common name or this catalog entry; local impact and control evidence remain a research gap.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Euchiton sphaericus

identification: The open seed head is narrow in overall outline but loosely branched, with threadlike branches and extremely small spikelets. Leaves are narrow, and the leaf junction has a fringe of hairs. Unlike many weedy dropseeds, the head is not a dense spike. It can resemble Sporobolus pyramidatus, but its branches are not arranged in the same whorled pattern. Another lookalike, Eragrostis amabilis, has several florets in each spikelet; tropical dropseed has one. A hand lens and a mature flowering specimen are more informative than a distant lawn photograph.
actions: Inspect nursery pots, garden edges, and disturbed soil for plants that are setting seed. For a small unwanted patch, remove the annuals before the delicate heads shed their seed and keep the material contained during transport. Clean soil from tools before using them in another bed. Record whether plants persist after the initial disturbance or occur beyond cultivated ground. A local botanist should verify uncertain grass records; neither a new occurrence nor an introduced-range listing alone establishes that an aggressive eradication program is warranted.

sources.label: Bishop Museum Occasional Papers 155: Hawaiian plant records

identification: Look for pointed, heart-based leaves with toothed margins and long, stiff hairs along the stems and flower cups. The flower buds have conspicuously drawn-out tips, and the flowers sit close together rather than on long, widely separated stalks. Mature fruits separate into five small units. Several Sida species have yellow flowers, so flower color is a poor shortcut. Include the leaf base, hairy calyx, clustered flowers, and a mature fruit in photographs. The leaning habit and long-pointed buds are particularly helpful clues in the North American flora.
actions: Note whether the plant is confined to a recently disturbed verge or is expanding into adjacent vegetation. Ask a local herbarium to confirm a flowering and fruiting example before reporting it under this name. Wear gloves when handling the bristly stems. In a small garden patch, removing unwanted plants before fruits mature can limit seed movement; keep fruiting material out of soil or yard waste destined for natural areas. A larger control recommendation should wait for local evidence of establishment and impact, which was not resolved by this research.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Sida urens
Kew-hosted Flora Zambesiaca and East Africa via ColPlanta: Sida urens

identification: Opposite leaves are narrow to oval and sit close to the stem. At their bases, a small sheath with bristlelike tips joins the leaf pair, a useful detail to photograph with a hand lens. Hairy, rounded flower clusters occur at the stem tips and leaf joints. The fruit offers a stronger distinction from similar buttonweeds in Spermacoce: a Mitracarpus capsule opens around its middle like a tiny lid. The seed has a characteristic cross-shaped pattern. Those details are too small for an ordinary landscape photograph and often require specialist examination.
actions: Start with photographs of the branching pattern, opposite leaves, and both flowering and fruiting clusters. Ask a botanist to resolve the species if buttonweeds grow nearby or the record would be new locally. Small unwanted garden plants can be removed before capsules release seed, with flowering material kept contained. Avoid spreading soil from the patch on equipment or transplanted plants. For a roadside, pasture, or natural area, document abundance and surrounding vegetation before choosing treatment; species-specific local management evidence remains incomplete.

sources.label: Flora of Singapore 13: Rubiaceae, Mitracarpus hirtus

identification: Adults have broad white, yellow, and brown wing scales that create a striking mottled pattern. Short, thick antenna segments and tufts of scales near the ends of the middle and hind femora are additional clues. These are small structures best checked under magnification by mosquito-control staff. The familiar description 'tropical mosquito' is not an identification, and a blurred picture of a biting insect cannot separate this species reliably from other mosquitoes. Preserve the location and date even when a usable specimen is unavailable.
actions: Send an unusual patterned-mosquito observation to the local mosquito-control program, including a sharp photograph if one can be taken without attracting insects to bite. Report nearby floating vegetation and persistent water rather than assuming ordinary household containers are the only source. Do not move aquatic plants between ponds or release them into canals. Routine mosquito precautions and maintenance of screens remain sensible, but a sighting is not evidence of a local disease outbreak. Wetland vegetation removal or larval treatment should be planned by the responsible water or mosquito-management agency.

sources.label: Fazekas et al.: First records in Palm Beach County
Journal of the American Mosquito Control Association: Florida Keys record

identification: Species-level identification belongs with a mosquito laboratory. This mosquito is part of the Melanoconion group, where similar-looking species cannot be reliably separated by overall brown color or the fact that they were found near a canal. Useful records include the collection site, date, whether adults or larvae were seen, and the vegetation in the water. A clear specimen allows specialists to examine diagnostic structures. Water lettuce is a habitat clue from the Florida study, but its presence alone does not identify the mosquitoes living around it.
actions: Contact the local mosquito-control district when an unusual concentration occurs near vegetated freshwater. Staff can sample the habitat, identify the mosquitoes, and decide whether surveillance or treatment is justified. Keep ornamental floating plants out of canals and natural wetlands, and coordinate any removal with the water manager so fragments are contained. At home, maintain screens and remove avoidable standing water as routine mosquito prevention. Do not attempt to catch adults by exposing skin, and do not interpret a single adult observation as evidence of disease transmission.

sources.label: Blosser and Burkett-Cadena: Culex panocossa from peninsular Florida
Sloyer et al.: Host associations of Culex panocossa

identification: Look for short flowering stems above the mat and a small seed head with two or three branches. Spikelets sit in orderly rows along one side of those branches. The leaves are narrow to lance-shaped, and the ligule at the leaf junction is a fringe of hairs. Creeping stems and the small head distinguish the general growth form, but several signalgrasses and crabgrasses look alike. Names including Brachiaria distachya and Urochloa subquadripara appear in older or regional treatments, so a specimen should be checked against the taxonomic concept used locally.
actions: For an unwanted lawn patch, first determine which grass is present and whether the problem is spreading stems, seed production, or both. Small plants can be lifted carefully, with creeping stems gathered rather than scattered by raking. Keep rooted fragments and soil out of clean garden beds. In a natural area, record the patch's extent and ask a botanist or land manager whether any intervention is needed. Local turf recommendations should guide larger treatments; this profile does not support labeling all Florida occurrences as damaging invasions.

identification: Look for large, hairy leaves with deep, irregular lobes, straight pale prickles on stems and leaves, and small white flowers with five spreading or reflexed lobes. Young fruits resemble miniature mottled watermelons, but ripe fruits are bright yellow. Other prickly nightshades can share the leaf shape or flower color, so photograph both young and mature fruits together with the leaf surfaces. The combination is much more useful than a thorny stem alone. Do not taste the fruit as an identification test.
actions: Report a suspected new patch to local extension or the state agriculture department, especially on land where livestock or hay move between farms. Keep fruiting plants and contaminated soil off equipment headed to clean fields. Mowing can delay seed production, but it does not kill established plants and can spread material once fruits are present. Work with a pasture specialist on a complete control plan and follow-up for regrowth. Use gloves and protective clothing around the prickles, and keep removed fruit contained rather than leaving it where animals can carry it.

sources.label: Alabama Extension: Tropical Soda Apple Identification and Control

identification: Leaves are generally opposite, broadly oval, softly hairy, and toothed around the edge. Several strong veins spread from near the leaf base. The flower heads lack the broad ray petals of a typical daisy and gather into branched clusters. A hand lens can reveal the small awned scales attached to the fruits. James Cook University's account of the typical subspecies describes flower-head bracts without hairs or glands; variation among treatments means those small characters should be checked carefully. Photograph leaves, bracts, and ripe heads rather than relying on mauve flowers alone.
actions: Remove unwanted garden plants before the heads mature and release seed, taking care not to shake ripe material through the bed. Maintain ground cover where repeated disturbance leaves bare soil available for new seedlings. In a crop, ask extension staff to confirm the species and choose a control suited to the crop and season. Do not move seed-bearing garden waste into natural areas. This research supports identification and seed containment, but a locally tested United States impact and management account is still needed before stronger recommendations.

sources.label: Indian Institute of Science: Ageratum conyzoides
James Cook University: Ageratum conyzoides subsp. conyzoides

identification: Look for five blue flower lobes surrounding a yellow center, carried along a flower cluster that begins curled and gradually straightens. Leaves are simple and narrow to oblong, with short hairs lying close to the surface. The flower cup has straight, appressed hairs rather than strongly hooked ones. Native Myosotis laxa is a particularly useful comparison: true forget-me-not generally has broader flowers and a corolla tube longer than the calyx. Photograph the flower face and side, the leaf hairs, and the stem base to help distinguish the two.
actions: Keep garden plants and divisions away from natural shorelines, and never dispose of pond plants in a stream. If a small confirmed patch needs removal, collect creeping stems and roots rather than leaving fragments in flowing water, and minimize disturbance to the bank. Ask the land manager or local aquatic-plant program before working in a wetland. Revisit the spot for regrowth and seedlings. Larger patches need a site-specific plan; Wisconsin notes limited information on chemical effectiveness, so a generic spray recommendation would be inappropriate.

sources.label: UAA: Identification of Non-Native Plants in Alaska

identification: Each leaf is divided into several pairs of small oval leaflets plus a terminal leaflet. Short clusters of pea-shaped flowers arise beside the leaves. The narrow pods are particularly useful: botanical treatments describe them as straight to gently curved, several centimeters long, and containing multiple seeds. Other indigos, including Indigofera suffruticosa and I. arrecta, can look similar before fruiting. Keep photographs of mature pods, leaflets, and the flower clusters together. A label that says only 'indigo' is not enough to establish the species.
actions: For a cultivated plant, watch for seedlings beyond the intended bed and collect unwanted pods before they open. Do not share seed or rooted material into places where local guidance discourages the species. If an apparent escape occurs near a natural area, document its distance from cultivation and ask a herbarium to confirm fruiting material. Dye history is useful context, not a recommendation to ingest the plant or improvise medicinal preparations. Local ecological effects and suitable treatments remain uncertain. Base any larger response on confirmed spread, the surrounding vegetation and advice for the site.

identification: Florida's account describes dark upper leaf surfaces, whitish or gray hairy undersides, and roughly nine to fifteen deep lobes. Long leaf stalks and cylindrical clusters of small fruits complete the broad picture. An umbrella tree has separate leaflets rather than one deeply cut blade, while castor bean has greener, less woolly leaf undersides. These comparisons can narrow the possibilities, but they do not separate all Cecropia species. Clear photographs of both leaf surfaces, new-growth sheaths, and reproductive structures are needed for expert confirmation.
actions: Treat a suspected escape as a record to verify before planning tree removal. Note whether it is planted, a nearby seedling, or a reproducing stand away from cultivation. Small confirmed seedlings can be removed with permission, while larger trees need a safe arboricultural plan. Keep fruiting branches out of dumped garden waste. Keep the confirmed Florida identity separate from overseas records: a Malesian study found other Cecropia species where old names had been applied inconsistently. Local advice should follow the identified tree and the site.

sources.label: University of South Florida FLIP: Cecropia palmata
Naturalis Blumea: Status of Cecropia introductions in Malesia

identification: The body is slender and flattened, with a particularly large second pair of antennae. Those antennae differ between males and females, and the small teeth and bristles on their segments are important diagnostic features. Corophium heteroceratum is a named lookalike in the Smithsonian account. A tube in mud, or a photograph of a tiny shrimp-shaped animal, cannot distinguish the species. Identification generally requires a preserved specimen and a microscope, so record the exact site, sediment type, salinity if known, and sampling method.
actions: Leave undisturbed mudflat habitat in place unless you are working with an authorized survey. If the animal appears in a sample, retain the original label and contact a marine invertebrate specialist for identification and preservation instructions. Avoid transferring live sediment, bait, or muddy equipment between estuaries. Clean field gear where washings will not enter another water body. There is no reviewed basis here for a homeowner treatment or broad sediment removal. Its detailed species-specific life history, origin, and local impact remain unresolved, and those gaps should accompany any new record.

sources.label: Jones et al. 2009: Hydrodynamic control of phytoplankton loss

identification: The animal extends a delicate feeding crown from its tube and can withdraw behind a modified structure that acts as a plug. A tangle of white tubes is only a starting clue: several tube-building worms create similar growth. Specialists examine the plug and the small bristles of the worm itself. Hydroides norvegica is a particularly important historical confusion, especially in older warm-water records published under that name. Photograph the extended crown if visible, but do not assume that the tube's shape alone provides a species identification.
actions: Boat owners should inspect underwater surfaces and arrange maintenance that captures removed fouling instead of scattering it through a harbor. Aquaculture operators can record where tubes accumulate and seek marine-extension advice before moving fouled gear or shellfish. For an unexpected observation, provide the site, substrate, date, and clear close-ups to a specialist. Do not scrape natural reef or shell habitat simply because a tubeworm is present. Local cleaning and movement practices are the practical focus; the evidence does not justify a universal chemical treatment or a claim that every population is introduced.

sources.label: Lema et al.: Biofilms and Hydroides elegans settlement

identification: Look for opposite, stiff, narrow leaves with coarse teeth and clusters of small purple flowers. The leaves often feel rough, which explains the name sandpaper verbena. Plants can form a low spreading patch rather than the very tall, airy framework of purpletop vervain. Several verbenas share purple flowers, and big-bract verbena is another comparison in Penn State's identification guide. Photograph the leaf arrangement, leaf margins, whole plant, and flower heads; underground connections between shoots can also help explain how a patch is spreading.
actions: If the plant stays within a managed garden and local guidance permits it, monitoring may be sufficient. Where it is unwanted, remove the underground connecting stems as well as the visible shoots and check for regrowth. Cutting flower heads before seed matures can reduce movement beyond the bed. Keep excavated roots out of dumped garden waste, and avoid disturbing neighboring plants while following the rhizomes. A patch outside cultivation should be documented and identified before treatment, particularly where native verbenas occur nearby.

identification: Young spikelets often have a purple tint, later becoming paler as the florets mature. The flowering head is usually fairly compact, though some plants have more open branches. Leaves can be hairy or almost smooth and may lie flat or roll inward. Under magnification, the lemma has two rows of hairs, two pointed side lobes, and a central awn extending beyond them. Other wallaby grasses can be very similar, and the Victorian flora notes intermediate-looking specimens. Identification from a seedless tuft is therefore especially uncertain.
actions: For a suspected new introduced record, photograph the whole clump and collect detailed images of mature spikelets without scattering them. A grass specialist or herbarium can compare the florets with regional species and resolve older names such as Austrodanthonia caespitosa. Do not remove Australian native grassland plants merely because this species appears in an invasive-species catalog. At an unwanted garden escape elsewhere, contain seed heads and seek local advice before disturbing a larger stand. California's watch assessment flags invasion potential, but a tested treatment and the impact of a particular patch still require local advice.

sources.label: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria: Rytidosperma caespitosum

identification: Wingless aphids are small and pale, ranging from yellowish to gray or pinkish brown, with a powdery wax coating. The short dark rear tubes and small tail are useful under magnification. Winged individuals have darker markings, but neither color nor a bulb host proves the species. Other aphids can occupy the same plants. Photograph a colony in place and note exactly where it is feeding, then seek diagnostic help if the identification matters for a nursery shipment or a persistent outbreak.
actions: Inspect bulbs when they arrive, before storage, and again before planting, paying attention to loose outer scales and emerging shoots. Keep a suspect batch separate from healthy stock while an extension or plant-health service checks it. Do not pass infested bulbs to another grower. Remove badly affected material through an appropriate local disposal route and clean storage surfaces before replacing stock. If treatment is needed, choose guidance for the particular bulb crop and storage stage; a foliar aphid treatment may not reach insects concealed beneath scales.

sources.label: TNAU: Tulip bulb aphid on lily
Alford (2012): Pests of Ornamental Trees, Shrubs and Flowers, second edition — publisher citation record

identification: Large, long-stalked leaves are heart-shaped and may be shallowly divided into three lobes. Two conspicuous glands occur near the top of the leaf stalk where it meets the blade. Clusters of white to pale pink flowers, often with red centers, appear before or with the new leaves. Rounded fruits later contain several substantial seeds. A broad leaf alone can suggest other ornamental trees, so photograph the glands, flowers, and fruits together. Do not crack or taste the seeds to compare them with edible nuts.
actions: Check around older planted trees for seedlings and suckering stems, particularly where a garden meets woodland. Keep children and pets away from fallen fruits and wear gloves when gathering material. For small unwanted seedlings, remove the root system where practical; mature trees require a planned treatment and safe felling approach that addresses regrowth. Consult extension or a qualified arborist instead of relying on cutting alone. Contain fruits and roots during disposal, then revisit the site for new shoots and seedlings in following seasons.

identification: The body is oval and flattened, with a thin, translucent outer covering that tears readily. Its soft outline is not a dependable field separation from native Ascidia ceratodes. Photograph the attachment, both siphons, body outline, and any visible internal features without pulling the animal apart. A specialist may need internal anatomy to confirm the name. Its attachment to a natural hard surface does not by itself establish identity or a new introduction. Keep the location and habitat with the observation so the specimen can be interpreted in context.
actions: Report a suspected occurrence outside a known local range to a marine monitoring program, preserving the date and exact location. Ask for collection instructions before taking a specimen, since its delicate covering can be damaged during removal. Boat and equipment owners can reduce transport by inspecting fouling and using cleaning methods that contain removed organisms. Do not scrape similar native sea squirts from rocks on the basis of appearance alone. The sources support surveillance and prevention, but not a species-specific homeowner eradication method or a permanent claim of native-species displacement.

sources.label: Silva and Smith 2008: Population similarity in invasive ascidians

identification: Look for an egg-shaped, grayish to brownish body with a firm, slightly rough outer covering. One siphon opens at the top and the second projects from the side about a third of the way down. Individuals can be fairly large for a sea squirt, but size and color vary. Sea grapes, vase tunicates, and clubbed tunicates can create confusion, and Ascidiella scabra is a close relative requiring detailed examination. Photograph the siphon arrangement and attachment rather than relying on a picture of a contracted blob.
actions: Document the exact location, date, substrate, and approximate extent of a suspected new patch and send the record to the regional aquatic-invasive-species program. Before moving boats, ropes, cages, or shellfish, inspect them for attached animals and follow the receiving area's biosecurity guidance. Arrange cleaning where detached material and washings can be contained. Avoid dropping fouled gear or live scrapings into another harbor. Aquaculture producers should seek a treatment plan that protects the cultured stock as well as workers; a general species profile cannot establish a safe exposure or cleaning schedule.

sources.label: Fisheries and Oceans Canada: European Sea Squirt

identification: The Naturalis account describes a rounded to oval body, up to about four centimeters across, with a thick, leathery, wrinkled covering and fine surface hairs. Both siphons are large and divided into four lobes. Internal features, including folds of the branchial sac and the arrangement of reproductive organs, are used in a full identification. Related sea squirts can look remarkably similar when contracted or covered in debris. A photograph can support an observation, but it cannot reliably resolve this species from every similar animal.
actions: Photograph an unfamiliar specimen in place and record the coast, depth, substrate, date, and scale. Seek identification from a marine invertebrate specialist before describing it as a nonnative occurrence. Do not remove natural shore animals solely because the name appears in a catalog. If it is attached to movable equipment, keep that equipment from entering another water body until the fouling can be assessed and contained. Species-specific reproduction, United States establishment, ecological impact, and tested control were not established by the reviewed sources and need further evidence.

sources.label: Fulgione et al. 2006: Molecular characterization of Microcosmus

identification: Look for small rounded individuals, each with two openings, connected by a visible network of slender stolons. The individuals remain separate rather than merging into a sheet. Bright yellow, angular or star-shaped buds at the ends of stolons are the best field clue; these can detach and begin new colonies. Their absence at one season does not rule the species out. Native Perophora species are important lookalikes, so include photographs of connections, individual bodies, and any terminal buds, not simply the colony's overall color.
actions: Record an unfamiliar colony before it is disturbed and send the images and precise location to a local marine-monitoring program. Do not pull apart or brush a colony into the water, since its detachable buds provide a natural means of spread. Inspect ropes, floats, boats, and aquaculture equipment before transferring them elsewhere, and arrange contained cleaning when necessary. Leave natural attached communities in place unless the responsible manager directs removal. Monitoring should distinguish new colonization from seasonal visibility, and an introduced record should not automatically be described as a documented ecological impact.

sources.label: Marine Biological Association: Non-native species identification guide

identification: Leaves occur in whorls around the stems, giving the foliage a repeated, tiered arrangement. The white to cream flowers have long tubes, and the persistent calyx expands around the shiny blue-black fruit. Photograph leaves, flowers, and fruits together because several Clerodendrum ornamentals share bright calyces. The common name Turk's turban is also used inconsistently in horticulture. Published accounts disagree on some leaf and flower measurements. The combination of whorled leaves, pale tubular flowers and blue fruit with a red calyx is more useful than relying on one disputed dimension.
actions: Watch the perimeter of an established planting for suckers and seedlings, especially where the bed borders a drainage route or natural vegetation. Remove unwanted young growth with its roots and keep rooted cuttings and fruit out of dumped garden waste. Before undertaking a larger removal, confirm the species and ask local extension whether the plant is considered a management priority in that setting. Record actual spread beyond cultivation separately from a maintained ornamental clump. Species-specific local control evidence remains limited, and conflicting descriptive measurements warrant botanical review.

sources.label: Florida Natural Areas Inventory: Clerodendrum indicum

identification: The shrub has branching woody stems, scattered prickles, and broad alternate leaves that may be shallowly lobed. Star-shaped hairs are especially dense on the paler leaf undersides. White flowers occur in branched clusters, followed by many small round berries that turn yellow when mature. Tropical soda apple is a useful comparison, but its fruits are larger and distinctly mottled when young. Include leaf undersides, prickles, flowers, and fruit clusters in a record; young turkey berry leaves may be more deeply lobed than mature ones.
actions: Check roadsides, pasture margins, and recently placed fill for young plants near an established infestation. Small confirmed seedlings can be pulled with gloves and landowner permission, while larger thorny shrubs need a planned removal that addresses roots and later seedlings. Keep fruiting branches and contaminated soil from moving to clean sites. Ask local extension or agriculture staff for management guidance and reporting expectations. Avoid tasting or using wild-collected berries as an identification method, and do not plant or distribute this species where regional guidance treats it as an invasive weed.

identification: Begin with the fruit and stem rather than the yellow flowers. Stems have conspicuous warty bumps and hairs, while the short oval or teardrop-shaped fruits also have a bumpy surface. Lower leaves are strongly lobed and can look somewhat like dandelion leaves; leaves become smaller up the stem. Four-petaled yellow flowers form dense clusters. Yellow rocket, Barbarea vulgaris, is a common lookalike, but it has smoother stems and long, narrow seedpods instead of the distinctive warty fruits of hill mustard.
actions: Map the patch while flowers or fruits make it easy to recognize, then consult local weed staff about priorities and disposal. Preventing seed production matters, but mowing once can leave vigorous regrowth that flowers again. Plan repeat visits through the growing season. Digging established plants can be difficult because of their substantial roots, and soil disturbance may expose more ground for weeds. Keep seed-bearing material and contaminated soil off equipment leaving the site. Where treatment is needed in a meadow or pasture, choose a plan that preserves desirable vegetation and checks for return in later years.

identification: Wingless individuals are small, yellow-green to gray-green or olive, often with a pale wax coating. Winged adults have darker markings on the abdomen and dusky wing veins. These features help locate a suspect colony but do not reliably separate close Lipaphis species or every cabbage-feeding aphid. Cabbage aphid and green peach aphid are other possibilities on the same crop. Photograph adults and the colony, identify the host plant, and retain a specimen for microscopic examination when an exact species record is needed.
actions: Inspect young leaves and flower shoots regularly rather than waiting until a colony has distorted the crop. Keep newly acquired transplants separate if aphids are present, and seek crop-specific extension advice if colonies expand. Preserve predators and parasitoids where possible by avoiding an automatic broad-spectrum spray response. An identification laboratory can resolve the name before a treatment or reporting decision depends on it. Do not transfer virus-vector claims or control thresholds from literature labeled erysimi without checking which species was studied. Locally applicable advice should follow the confirmed aphid and the affected crop.

sources.label: Biological parameters and life table of Lipaphis pseudobrassicae on kale

identification: The flowering head is long and narrow, sometimes contracted and sometimes more open, with the lowest branches conspicuously longer than the gaps between them. Leaves are narrow and may fold as they mature. The tiny spikelets are roughly a millimeter and a half long, and the flowers usually have two anthers, a useful microscopic character reflected in the name. Other dropseeds can appear nearly identical from a distance. Older labels may use Sporobolus diander or S. indicus var. flaccidus, so compare the specimen with a regional key rather than matching the spelling alone.
actions: Record a suspected patch while mature seed heads are available, including the clump base and leaf junction in photographs. A grass specialist can check spikelets and distinguish it from local Sporobolus species. For a small unwanted garden clump, contain mature heads before digging and avoid carrying seed-bearing soil to another site. Monitor the disturbed ground afterward for seedlings. The reviewed sources provide botanical identity and distribution, but not a locally tested United States control program or demonstrated ecological impact; larger interventions need additional site-specific evidence.

sources.label: Flora of North America via NEON: Sporobolus diandrus
Indian Institute of Science: Sporobolus diander

identification: A mature clump may reach about two meters high. Narrow leaves arch from the base, and a pyramidal seed head carries many short branches along a central stem. Leaf blades are mostly hairless away from the junction with the sheath. Vasey grass and other tall Paspalum species can look similar, particularly before flowering. Take close photographs of the seed-head branches, individual spikelets, leaf junction, and clump base, and use a regional grass key rather than size or blue-green color alone.
actions: Locate outlying clumps before working through a large stand so that equipment does not carry seed from the main patch to clean ground. Small confirmed plants can be dug out where soil disturbance is acceptable, including the crown and underground stems. Bag mature heads and remove soil and seed from tools, boots, and machinery before leaving. Large infestations need a site plan and follow-up because mowing leaves the perennial base alive. Seek local guidance for pasture or natural-area treatment; overseas pesticide permissions and seasonal calendars do not establish what is appropriate at a United States site.

identification: Adults are reddish orange with twelve black spots on the wing covers and an elongated oval outline. Common asparagus beetles have a dark bluish-black body with pale cream patches instead. A spotted adult can also be mistaken for a beneficial lady beetle, which generally has a more domed body, shorter antennae, and a less exposed head. Look for the host association and body shape, not spots alone. The orange spotted-beetle larvae feed in berries, unlike the grayish larvae of the common asparagus beetle feeding openly on stems and foliage.
actions: Inspect asparagus during warm afternoons and note whether the damage is to harvestable spears, fern foliage, or berries. In a small planting, hand removal of correctly identified adults may be enough to limit a localized problem. Do not spray simply because berry-feeding larvae are present, and leave predatory beetles undisturbed. Commercial growers should use regional crop guidance and scouting thresholds that distinguish the two asparagus beetles. Record the species and life stage when seeking advice, because a management calendar or damage description for the common beetle may not fit this one.

sources.label: University of Minnesota Extension: Asparagus beetles
AAFC: Crop Profile for Asparagus in Canada, 2021

identification: Workers are roughly a centimeter long and dark reddish brown, with lighter legs and antennae. Long, nearly straight jaws immediately suggest a trap-jaw ant, but they do not establish this species. Specialist characters include paired spines beneath the middle body and crosswise ridges over much of the narrow waist segment. The similar Odontomachus ruginodis averages smaller and lacks those paired underside spines. Other native trap-jaw ants also need consideration, so use clear close photographs and a specialist identification rather than a regional assumption.
actions: Keep bare hands away from suspected nests and do not deliberately provoke workers to demonstrate their jaws or sting. Photograph foraging ants from a safe distance, noting the nest material and exact location. Avoid transferring occupied logs, stumps, or potted material to another property. If a nest creates a problem beside a doorway or work area, ask extension or a pest professional for an identification and a site-specific plan. A single ant sighting does not show the size of a colony or establish a need for treatment. Match any response to the confirmed species and the problem at that site.

sources.label: MacGown et al.: Review of Nearctic Odontomachus
Teixeira et al. 2020: Karyotypic data of five Atlantic rainforest ant taxa

identification: Adults are only about two millimeters long and require magnification for a dependable identification. The rear of the wing covers and their teeth are among the structures used in bark-beetle keys. Beneath the bark, the galleries can form a star-like pattern around a central chamber, with larval tunnels branching away from the larger egg galleries. A gallery pattern is a clue rather than a species diagnosis: several small conifer bark beetles make superficially similar workings. Record the tree species, branch diameter, condition of the wood, and insects present.
actions: Ask a forestry or extension specialist to assess newly declining conifers before assuming that this beetle is the cause. Keep infested branches, logs, and firewood from being moved to another location, and photograph galleries already exposed on fallen or removed material. Do not peel healthy trees merely to search for a specimen. A local management plan should consider drought stress, other bark beetles, and whether breeding material needs removal. United States impact and species-specific treatment evidence remain insufficient here, so European flight dates and forestry prescriptions have not been converted into a national control calendar.

sources.label: Haack 2006: Exotic bark and wood-boring Coleoptera
Bavarian LWF: Bark beetles on conifers

identification: Plants are usually only a few inches tall, with short-stalked toothed leaves and tiny blue flowers in a terminal raceme. The fruit supplies a stronger clue than flower color: the flattened capsule has a deep notch that creates two conspicuous rounded lobes. Glandular hairs may make the upper plant slightly sticky. Other annual speedwells, including plants with similarly notched capsules, need to be compared using a regional key. Photograph mature fruit, its short style, the surrounding calyx, and lower leaves with a scale; flower-only images may not settle the identification.
actions: Before removing a patch in native grassland, confirm the species and ask whether it is a local management priority. In a cultivated bed where it is unwanted, removing small plants before mature capsules open can limit added seed while keeping soil disturbance modest. Clean soil from tools before moving between sites and check the same ground in later growing seasons. Preserve a dated photographic record if the occurrence appears new for the area. Note whether seedlings return and whether the patch is expanding; those observations can help a local adviser decide what follow-up is worthwhile.

identification: Watch the youngest leaves for yellow margins and yellowing between veins, crumpling, and curling. Shortened spaces between leaves can give the plant a compact, bushy appearance, and flowers may fall before fruit develops. Heat-related leaf roll, nutrient deficiencies, aphid injury, and other viruses can resemble parts of this picture. Note which leaves changed first and whether affected plants are scattered or uniform across the planting. Whiteflies strengthen the suspicion but do not confirm the virus; a plant diagnostic laboratory should make the final determination.
actions: Start with clean transplants and varieties carrying appropriate resistance, and inspect leaf undersides for whiteflies during crop scouting. Avoid moving suspect plants into another garden or greenhouse. Ask extension how to submit a sample and whether confirmed infected plants should be removed promptly. Managing whiteflies, volunteer tomatoes, and old crop residues helps reduce opportunities for spread, but spraying an infected plant does not restore it to health. Greenhouse screening and regionally coordinated host-free periods may be useful production tools; their timing should come from local crop guidance.

sources.label: UC IPM: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl
NC State Extension: Tomato Yellow Leaf Curl Virus
Queensland Government: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus

identification: The most memorable larval feature is a crown of spines near the tip of the long breathing siphon. Adults are brown mosquitoes with pale bands on the hind legs. Unlike some similarly banded Culex, the proboscis lacks a complete pale ring, although a pale patch may occur beneath it. These are microscopic identification characters, not something to establish from a distant photograph. Close relatives in the coronator complex share features, so a mosquito-control laboratory may need detailed anatomy or molecular methods for a reliable species assignment.
actions: Remove unnecessary water-holding containers around buildings and keep maintained drainage functioning without disturbing natural wetlands. If larvae persist in a public ditch, stormwater structure, or other water that cannot be emptied safely, contact the local mosquito-control program with the location. Do not move larvae in water to another site or pour household chemicals into breeding habitat. Use ordinary mosquito bite prevention appropriate to local public-health guidance. Finding this species does not by itself establish a disease outbreak, and laboratory vector competence should not be reported as proof that a particular local mosquito carries virus.

sources.label: Alto et al.: Reproductive Biology and Susceptibility of Florida Culex coronator to West Nile Virus

identification: The upright stems are triangular, ending in a conspicuous ring of long, narrow, leaflike bracts. The actual flowers and fruits are much smaller, grouped in branched clusters among those bracts. Most leaves at the stem base are reduced to sheaths. A mature plant can stand well over a meter tall and form a substantial clump. Other ornamental umbrella sedges share this general shape; count and photograph bracts, flowering branches, spikelets, and the stem base. Avoid sliding fingers along the bract margins, which may be finely toothed and sharp.
actions: Keep pond plants and discarded divisions out of streams, drains, and natural wetlands. If an unwanted clump is still small, remove the crown and rhizomes where access and land-management rules permit, and contain any mature seed heads. A clipped top is not proof that the underground plant has died. Revisit the site for new shoots and seedlings, especially after soil disturbance. For plants rooted in a waterway, seek aquatic-weed advice before treatment or excavation so that sediment and fragments are not spread downstream. Confirm the exact species before choosing a replacement under the same umbrella-sedge trade name.

sources.label: CSIRO Australian Tropical Rainforest Plants: Cyperus involucratus
UCLA Santa Monica Mountains flora: Cyperus involucratus

identification: Florida observers described grayish-pink bodies surrounded by wax filaments, with the rear two or three pairs only somewhat longer than the others. White wax may accumulate on nearby roots, and a faint dark stripe can be visible along the back. Live insects closely resemble pineapple mealybugs; several other orchid mealybugs are also possible. Photograph insects and their position on the plant, then seek microscopic identification. Diagnostic pore and hair patterns, or molecular confirmation, are more dependable than counting wax threads from a blurry image.
actions: Separate a suspect orchid from the rest of a collection and avoid sharing divisions, pots, or growing medium until the problem is identified. Inspect roots as well as foliage when repotting, taking care not to scatter contaminated material across the bench. Keep purchase and supplier details with the observation, especially for a recent shipment. Ask an extension diagnostic service or plant-health authority about samples and appropriate treatment for that orchid. The Taiwanese response included official removal and follow-up surveys, but that outcome does not establish a universal home treatment or prove the species absent from other collections.

sources.label: FDACS: An Orchid Mealybug, Pseudococcus dendrobiorum
TARI: New Pseudococcus dendrobiorum in Taiwan

identification: USDA's diagnostic account describes an oval pink to light-orange female whose thin mealy wax still allows the body color to show. Wax filaments line the sides, becoming longer toward the rear; the final pair may approach the body's length. The back lacks a longitudinal dark stripe, and an egg sac is produced beneath the female. These features narrow the possibilities but do not settle the identity. Microscopic patterns of pores and ducts distinguish it from similar Pseudococcus species, including the historically confused Jack Beardsley mealybug.
actions: Isolate a suspect nursery plant and document the host, supplier, purchase date, and precise feeding site before treatment obscures the specimen. Avoid sharing infested cuttings, fruit-bearing plant material, or pots. Ask an identification service to confirm the species, explaining the elisae-jackbeardsleyi confusion when older records are involved. A banana or ornamental crop specialist can then recommend a management approach suitable for the plant and setting. Do not copy a pesticide program or a claim of widespread establishment from an old account until its identification has been checked; the shared common name is not enough.

sources.label: Culik and Gullan 2006: New Brazilian mealybug records
Adventive arthropods in Florida: archived agency specimens

identification: A conspicuous female parasite is pale, broadly oval, segmented, and somewhat asymmetrical. It may occupy enough of the shrimp's gill chamber to create a visible swelling. Males are much smaller, making the pair easy to misunderstand as unrelated organisms. Females can carry a large brood, and photographs of Oregon specimens show egg-filled reproductive structures. Other shrimp parasites occur in the region, including species attached beneath the abdomen rather than inside the gill chamber. Host identity and attachment location are useful clues, but a specialist should confirm the parasite.
actions: Report a suspicious parasitized mud shrimp to an estuary research or marine-invasive-species program with photographs, the collection location, and host details. Follow sampling rules and ask before opening the gill chamber or keeping specimens. Do not move live shrimp or bait between estuaries, and never release unused bait into a different water body. Removing a visible parasite from one shrimp is not an established way to control an estuary population. Management needs coordinated surveillance and research rather than chemical treatment of mudflats or indiscriminate removal of the native host.

sources.label: Oregon State University: Marine Bioinvasion Lab research
Hong et al.: Orthione griffenis from Korean mud shrimp

identification: The flowering head is loose and branched, often with a purplish cast around the developing seeds. Mature seeds have a sharp point and a long, bent awn that can twist with neighboring awns. A small crown of teeth where the awn joins the seed is a particularly useful diagnostic feature. Australian native speargrasses lack that crown, but other needle grasses elsewhere still require a local key. Before flowering, the green clump can resemble many ordinary pasture grasses, so save close photographs of mature seeds and the leaf junction.
actions: Confirm the identity before treating a grassland patch, then mark its edges and keep machinery out until a containment plan is ready. Inspect clothing, animal coats, and equipment for clinging seeds. Small plants may be dug out where appropriate, but include the whole plant because hidden stem and basal seeds can remain after flowering heads are removed. Bag material for locally approved disposal rather than carrying it uncovered. Repeated monitoring and competitive desirable vegetation are important parts of a longer plan. Follow regional weed guidance instead of importing Australian pesticide schedules or disposal requirements into another jurisdiction.

identification: Long arching leaves form a dense mound, with stiff flowering stems rising above it. The plumes may be white, cream, silver, or pinkish, so color alone is unreliable. Leaf edges have sharp teeth that readily cut skin. Jubata grass, Cortaderia jubata, and Ravenna grass are important lookalikes; identification should combine the whole plant, plume structure, leaf base, and flowering details. Pampas grass has female and predominantly pollen-producing plants, with pollination needed for female plants to set seed. Do not infer fertility simply from a cultivar label or attractive plume.
actions: Check nearby open ground, road banks, and drainage margins for young escaped clumps. Wear protective clothing and sturdy gloves when handling the leaves. Contain flower heads before disturbing a seed-bearing plant, and arrange removal of the crown and upper roots rather than merely shortening the foliage. Large clumps may need professional help because of their weight and sharp leaves. After removal, restore suitable vegetation or cover to bare soil and revisit for seedlings. Ask local extension about appropriate replacements and control methods; the urgency and regulatory status vary by region.

sources.label: Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board: Pampas grass
UC ANR: Pampas grass in landscapes

identification: Several sharply triangular stems rise from a fibrous-rooted base, with narrow leaves arranged around the lower plant. At the top, a few leaflike bracts sit beneath rounded masses of very small greenish-brown to purplish spikelets. Some heads are stalked and others nearly stalkless. The whole flowering cluster looks more compact than the broad umbrella of large ornamental sedges. Ricefield bulrush and other Cyperus species can share the same habitat; photograph the stem cross-section, basal leaves, and a close view of the rounded spikelet clusters for confirmation.
actions: In a garden or nursery, correct avoidable irrigation leaks and remove small confirmed plants before they shed seed, keeping muddy tools and pots from carrying seed elsewhere. In rice, use a crop-specific weed plan that combines timely scouting, suitable water management, and control before the sedge replenishes the seed bank. The species grows in shallow water, but a general profile cannot prescribe flood depths for a particular field. If a normal treatment fails, ask a crop adviser about resistance rather than increasing rates. Keep notes on the field, growth stage, and previous control history.

identification: The stems grow in a bunch, often much taller than surrounding lawn or roadside grasses. Each seed head has numerous upward-pointing branches attached along a central axis, with the upper branches generally shorter.
