Small plants can be removed with their roots where permitted; established vines need a plan for both the climbing growth and the root system. Do not pull heavy vines out of a living tree if that could tear its branches. Ask a local weed adviser about larger infestations and return to check for seedlings and regrowth.

identification: Look for curling tendrils, alternate leaves with three to five broad lobes, and small greenish-white flowers where leaves meet the stem. Ripe berries are dark, commonly black. The foliage can resemble native wild cucumber, so include fruit and tendril photographs rather than identifying it from a lobed leaf alone. White bryony has a substantial fleshy root, but you do not need to excavate one just to make an initial report.
actions: Keep children and animals away from the berries and avoid bare-handed handling. Report suspected vines to the land manager or local weed program, especially where they are climbing native shrubs. With permission and an appropriate removal plan, young plants are easier to address before they build a large root or produce fruit. Cutting the vine alone is not a lasting solution because the root can resprout. Contain berries, protect surrounding vegetation during removal, and revisit the site for new shoots and seedlings.

sources.label: Washington Noxious Weed Board: white bryony
USDA NRCS: Inland Northwest forb seedlings
National Park Service: white bryony control protocol

identification: Each true leaf usually has three rounded to egg-shaped leaflets, often with a pale V-shaped mark. The white flower heads, sometimes flushed pink, are made of many small pea-like flowers. Stems creep along the ground and can root where their joints touch soil. Yellow-flowered lookalikes are not white clover, and strawberry clover can resemble it closely. Take photographs of a flower head and a complete leaf rather than assuming that every three-leaflet plant is this species.
actions: First decide whether the patch conflicts with your goals. Tolerating some clover in an existing lawn may be more practical than trying to eradicate it. If you need to limit its spread, address the conditions weakening the desired vegetation and remove small patches with their creeping stems. Avoid unnecessary soil disturbance that creates new openings. In habitat plantings, favor locally appropriate native groundcovers. If chemical control is being considered, use local extension guidance and protect flowering plants and visiting insects from exposure.

identification: Look for hairy stems, paired toothed leaves and clusters of white, hooded flowers around the stem. Lower leaves have longer stalks and a heart-shaped base. The flowers are much larger and more conspicuous than the tiny greenish flowers of a stinging nettle. Field mint and hempnettles can also resemble it before flowering. Use photographs of the flowers and leaf arrangement; touching an unidentified nettle-like plant is not a sensible way to test its name.
actions: Document where the patch ends and whether it is extending into nearby native vegetation. If removal is appropriate on your property, work carefully enough to lift the creeping underground stems, not just the flowering shoots. Keep removed material from being dumped at a woodland edge and revisit the site for regrowth. Ask a regional botanist to confirm plants without flowers before disturbing a large area. A manageable garden escape and an established natural-area population may need different priorities and follow-up.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Lamium album
Alaska invasive plant ranking: Lamium album

identification: Mature leaves are broadly rounded, with a deep notch and distinct teeth along the margin. Their undersides have prominent branching veins. The large white or cream flowers are held above the water and often open from evening into the following morning, although flowering behavior varies. Photograph the leaf edge, the notch, both leaf surfaces where safely visible, and an open flower. American white waterlily has a different leaf margin, while true lotuses belong to the separate genus Nelumbo.
actions: Keep ornamental waterlilies in contained water gardens rather than releasing plants, tubers or pond waste into natural waterways. For an unfamiliar wild patch, report its location, approximate extent and photographs to the water body's manager. Do not wade into unsafe water or uproot native lilies to obtain a sample. Identification should come before any removal plan, and aquatic treatments require advice suited to the actual water body. Record whether the plants are intentionally planted or spreading beyond a maintained pond.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Nymphaea lotus

identification: The shell is usually ivory-colored, sometimes with brown bands, dots or broken lines; other individuals have little pattern. Adults are rounded, roughly half an inch across in many cases, with a relatively low spire. Color alone is unreliable because it varies within the species. Photograph the top, side and opening of the shell with a size reference. Other pale land snails can look similar, so a plant-health specialist should confirm a suspected new occurrence.
actions: Inspect pots, packing corners, fence posts and equipment before moving them out of an affected area. Do not relocate snails outdoors or send live specimens through the mail without instructions. Share photographs and the source of recently received plants with your county agricultural office. For an established garden problem, use a locally appropriate combination of monitoring, habitat management and targeted control. Avoid indiscriminate baiting or releasing predatory snails, which can harm native mollusks and create another problem. Check treated areas again because inactive snails may be missed.

sources.label: UC ANR: white garden snail landscape review
UC IPM: nursery snails and slugs

identification: Look for upright leafy stems with long, broad, bright-green leaves arranged in two ranks. Large white flowers with a butterfly-like outline appear at the tops of the shoots. White garland-lily differs from yellow ginger and kahili ginger, which have yellow flowers; kahili ginger also has conspicuous orange floral parts in an upright flower cluster. Photograph an entire flowering stem, its leaf arrangement and the edge of the clump. Do not assume every tall ginger has the same impact or treatment needs.
actions: Keep garden divisions and discarded underground stems out of streams, forest edges and unmanaged ground. Where it is spreading into natural vegetation, show the land manager photographs of both the clump and surrounding plants. Small patches may be manageable by removing the underground growth, but leftover pieces can require follow-up. Large established patches need a site-specific plan, especially near water. Avoid borrowing herbicide instructions for other Hedychium species; the Hawaii guide discusses several gingers whose treatment responses differ.

identification: The leaves are divided twice, with rows of small leaflets along several side branches, giving them a feathery appearance. Round, pale flower heads occur near branch tips. The flattened pods hang in clusters and turn brown as they mature, holding glossy brown seeds. Several native and introduced legumes have similar foliage and puffball flowers. Include photographs of a whole leaf, flowers and pods so a botanist can distinguish white leadtree from other local species.
actions: Avoid planting it where local invasive-plant guidance recommends alternatives. On your own property, remove confirmed seedlings while their roots are still small and keep pods from being carried into new areas. Established trees can regrow after cutting, so plan follow-up rather than treating one cut as completion. Have an arborist handle plants near buildings or wires, and ask a weed adviser about larger infestations. Restore suitable native vegetation where practical and watch the cleared ground for seedlings after rain and disturbance.

sources.label: UF Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants: leadtree

identification: Female covers are roughly circular and whitish to translucent, with a darker spot formed by older shed skins. Male covers are smaller, narrow and white, often gathered in conspicuous clusters. Yellowed areas on leaves or pinkish blemishes on fruit can accompany feeding. These are screening clues only. Specialists usually identify slide-mounted adult females by microscopic structures. Photograph colonies close up and show the affected fruit, leaf or twig as well as the whole tree.
actions: Keep newly acquired mango plants apart while checking their leaves and stems. If you find suspicious scales, contact an extension diagnostic service or plant-health office and provide the plant's source and movement history. Avoid giving away infested cuttings or moving affected nursery stock before advice. In an established orchard, management should be timed to the insect's vulnerable stages and protect beneficial insects. Do not assume that washing fruit or treating one visible colony eliminates scales hidden elsewhere on the tree.

sources.label: Costa Rican field study of Aulacaspis tubercularis on mango

identification: Unlike a typical three-leaflet clover, each leaf has a single leaflet. Leaf shape varies from oval to elongated, and the plant may spread close to the ground or stand more upright. Small flowers can show pink, purple or orange tones. The narrow pods are divided into a short row of segments rather than forming a broad, flat bean pod. Photograph the leaf attachment and mature fruit; these details help separate it from other small legumes with similar flowers.
actions: If you notice it beyond a maintained planting, record its location, patch size and whether it is increasing over time. A regional botanist can confirm the identification from flowering and fruiting material. Where it interferes with a garden or restoration planting, address small patches before mature pods are moved with soil or mowing equipment. There is no reason to clear an entire area solely because this species appears in the catalog. Let the condition of the surrounding vegetation and local assessment guide the response.

identification: Leaves are alternate, toothed and often glossy. Their outlines can vary considerably on the same tree, from unlobed to deeply divided. The fruits resemble elongated blackberries and may ripen white, pink or dark purple, so the name is not a dependable color guide. Photograph several mature leaves from both surfaces, the twig and any fruit. Red mulberry and hybrids can be difficult to distinguish, and a regional botanist may need more than one leaf to assess them.
actions: Look for seedlings beneath fences, perches and nearby trees, especially around fruiting plantings. Remove confirmed young white mulberries with their roots where you have permission and can avoid disturbing desired plants. Established trees require a safe removal and regrowth plan; use an arborist near structures or utilities. Before replacing a tree, choose a locally appropriate native species from a source that can verify its identity. Continue checking the site for seedlings rather than assuming that removing the parent tree prevents all future arrivals.

identification: The flowers are yellow, despite the name white mustard. Leaves are stalked and divided into irregular lobes, often with noticeable bristles. Mature pods provide a stronger clue than flower color: they are relatively short and stout, usually bristly, and end in a long, flattened beak. Other yellow-flowered mustards, especially wild mustard, can look similar before fruit develops. Photograph lower and upper leaves together with several mature pods and a size reference for a more useful identification.
actions: If mustard appears unexpectedly, check whether it came from a recent cover crop, seed mixture or disturbed agricultural soil. Record that context rather than assuming a new wild introduction. Prevent unwanted plants from producing mature seed when removal is appropriate, and clean equipment before moving it from a seeding patch. Farmers should coordinate control with the crop rotation and any cover-crop plan. In natural areas, confirm the species and local priority before broad treatment; the sources here do not establish identical ecological harm across all places where it grows.

identification: Possible warning signs include white growth on a bat's face or wings, unusual winter daytime flight, damaged wings, or several sick or dead bats near a roost. None of these signs confirms the disease by itself, and infected bats may lack obvious white growth. Wildlife specialists use laboratory examination to establish the diagnosis. Observe from a distance; approaching a hibernating bat for a better picture can disturb it and create unnecessary risk.
actions: Report unusual, sick or dead bats to your state wildlife agency with the location, date and photographs taken without handling them. Do not touch, capture or move bats. Respect cave closures and follow the current decontamination instructions for shoes and gear before visiting another cave or roost. Never apply disinfectants to bats or inside a cave yourself. If there has been direct contact with a bat, contact a health professional or local health department promptly; that exposure question is separate from white-nose syndrome.

sources.label: USGS National Wildlife Health Center: white-nose syndrome
FWS/ODFW: Oregon fungus detection and prevention

identification: Female covers are rounded and whitish or grayish, often with a yellowish spot from earlier shed skins. Male covers are narrow, ridged and bright white; dense groups can make bark look snow-covered. The tiny mobile young are called crawlers. A photograph can show the infestation, but separating white peach scale from white prunicola scale usually requires a specialist to examine prepared specimens. Include the host plant's name and the location, not just a close-up of white spots.
actions: Inspect trunks and substantial branches when assessing a tree that is losing vigor. Ask an extension service to confirm the scale and check whether insects beneath the covers are still alive before planning treatment. On a small ornamental plant, gentle brushing may reduce accessible colonies, but avoid damaging the bark. Larger infestations need monitoring and carefully timed management, often focused on crawlers. Preserve natural enemies where possible and do not use an ornamental-plant treatment on edible fruit unless its label permits that use.

identification: The adult leaves are exceptionally narrow and almost linear, giving the crown a light, fine texture. Much of the trunk has smooth, pale gray to whitish bark, sometimes with rougher bark near the base. Flowers are pale and the fruits are small woody capsules. Several peppermint eucalypts and their hybrids can resemble one another. Photograph mature leaves with a ruler, the trunk from base to branches, and attached buds or capsules rather than identifying it by smell alone.
actions: For a tree beyond a known planting, record whether seedlings of different sizes are appearing nearby. Ask a herbarium or qualified arborist to confirm the species before choosing management. Do not remove a mature tree on the assumption that all eucalyptus species have the same behavior. If seedlings are spreading into a managed habitat, discuss their extent and removal priority with the land manager. Any work near overhead lines or buildings should be handled professionally; documenting the tree does not require climbing it or cutting branches.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Eucalyptus pulchella

identification: The leaves are green above and densely white-haired beneath, often with several rounded lobes. Young branches and buds may also have pale hairs, and younger bark is comparatively smooth and light colored. Leaves vary across shoots, so include both mature branches and vigorous suckers in photographs. Native aspens and cottonwoods lack the same combination of white hair and leaf shape, but hybrids complicate identification. Ask for confirmation when the foliage is intermediate rather than deciding from trunk color alone.
actions: Map the outermost suckers as well as the main trees before planning removal. Small confirmed shoots may be manageable, but repeated cutting alone can stimulate more growth and requires follow-up. Work with a land manager or arborist on established colonies, particularly near wetlands, buildings or utilities. Avoid moving root-bearing soil to another site. After treatment, revisit the entire colony for new shoots and restore suitable plant cover so the cleared space does not become an opening for another unwanted species.

identification: Female covers are small, rounded and white with a yellowish center. Male covers are narrower and elongated, sometimes making crowded branches look dusted with white material. Newly hatched crawlers are much smaller and briefly mobile before settling. White peach scale can look almost identical and was historically confused with this species. Record the host plant and photograph the whole affected branch, then ask an extension specialist whether a sample is needed for microscopic identification.
actions: Start by checking the plant's overall condition and whether live scales are present. Prune badly affected branches only where this will leave a healthy plant, and dispose of infested material without spreading it to other plantings. Monitor for crawlers before choosing a treatment; the protective covers make poorly timed spraying less effective. An extension service can help match monitoring to local conditions and the host plant. Avoid broad spraying simply to remove the appearance of old covers, and preserve beneficial insects that help suppress the population.

sources.label: Virginia Tech: white peach and prunicola scale distinction

identification: Affected plants may yellow, wilt and lose older leaves. Around the bulb base, look for fluffy white growth that later contains very small black, seedlike bodies. Roots can decay so badly that the plant becomes loose in the soil. These signs deserve examination, but other diseases can also produce white fungal growth; southern blight usually develops larger tan to reddish-brown resting bodies. Send photographs and request diagnostic instructions before mailing bulbs or soil.
actions: Keep suspect garlic cloves, onion sets and transplants out of clean growing areas. Mark affected beds, avoid moving their soil, and clean soil from tools and footwear before working elsewhere. Do not put diseased bulbs or contaminated debris into ordinary garden compost. Ask an extension plant clinic to confirm the disease and plan future use of the site. A brief break from onions and garlic does not eliminate the resting bodies, and home remedies should not be treated as a dependable cure for an infested bed.

sources.label: Royal Horticultural Society: onion white rot

identification: In a suspect pine, resin drips, declining needles, round emergence holes and tunnels may prompt a woodwasp investigation. None identifies the fungus on its own. Many organisms decay conifer wood, and native woodwasps can leave similar holes. Reliable fungal identification needs specialist laboratory work, while identifying the insect may require an entomologist. Photographs of the tree, bark damage and any adult insect are useful starting evidence without cutting open the trunk.
actions: Report an unusual cluster of declining pines or a suspected nonnative woodwasp to a state forestry or plant-health service. Leave logs and firewood near their origin while the situation is assessed, rather than moving potentially infested wood to another property. Do not remove every decaying conifer or native woodwasp as a precaution. A forester can evaluate tree condition, identify the organisms involved and decide whether stand management or removal is warranted. Laboratory results should retain the host and locality details needed to interpret them.

sources.label: Nielsen and colleagues: fungal source and native woodwasps
Wilson et al. 2009: first US pine isolation of Amylostereum areolatum

identification: Leaves have three narrow, toothed leaflets. Numerous small white pea-shaped flowers form long, narrow clusters, unlike the rounded flower heads of white clover. Plants are usually biennial, with much taller flowering growth in their second season. Yellow sweetclover is very similar when not flowering; fresh flower color is more useful than dried blooms, which can both look cream colored. Photograph the whole plant and a flowering cluster as well as the leaves.
actions: In a restoration area, identify young plants before they set seed and plan follow-up over several seasons. Cutting flowering stems before seed matures can reduce replenishment, but timing and repeated checks matter. Avoid carrying mature seed on mowing equipment or moving seed-bearing cuttings into clean habitat. Hand removal may suit a small patch where it will not damage neighboring native plants. For larger infestations, a land manager should coordinate control with the desired vegetation and site conditions; a single mowing should not be presented as permanent removal.

sources.label: Maine Natural Areas Program: white sweetclover
Missouri Conservation: white and yellow sweetclovers

identification: Look for upright, ribbed stems and leaves deeply divided into numerous narrow lobes. The flowering stems carry many small white flowers with divided petals, giving the clusters a finely textured appearance. The fruits are elongated capsules rather than the long, narrow pods typical of many mustards. Yellow-flowered mignonettes are different species, and a distant picture of a pale flower spike is not enough to separate them. Photograph leaves, close flower details and mature capsules with a size reference.
actions: If you find it outside a garden, record whether it is a single escape or a patch containing flowering plants and younger individuals. Share those photographs with a regional herbarium or botanical group, especially where records are scarce. If removal is appropriate on land you manage, avoid scattering mature capsules and check the site again after disturbed soil produces new seedlings. Do not infer a need for landscape-wide spraying from the common name alone. The reviewed references support recognition and introduced records but do not establish a species-specific United States control program.

sources.label: Flora of New Zealand: Reseda alba

identification: Leaves are long, narrow and pointed, with fine teeth and silky hairs that can make the foliage look silvery from a distance. Mature bark becomes gray and furrowed. Catkins appear with the developing leaves in spring. Photograph both surfaces of mature leaves, young twigs, buds and the whole tree. Leaf hairiness varies and hybrid trees can combine characters, so reliable identification may require a regional willow specialist and material from more than one season.
actions: Record whether the tree was planted and whether smaller trees are appearing away from it. Do not discard living willow cuttings beside streams or use an unidentified ornamental willow for habitat restoration. If an established tree needs removal, involve an arborist and the relevant land manager, particularly on banks where roots help hold soil. Plan replacement vegetation before disturbing the site. The references here describe identity, habitat and cultivation, but they do not justify treating every United States white willow as an equally harmful invasion.

identification: Watch for a branch whose needles turn yellow and then reddish brown while nearby growth remains green. Infected bark may swell or become sunken and can produce conspicuous resin. Yellow-orange, powdery spore structures around a canker in spring are a stronger clue than needle discoloration alone. Other rusts affect other pine groups, and drought or insects can also kill branches. Photograph the needles, branch attachment and canker, and identify the pine before requesting a diagnosis.
actions: Ask a forestry or extension specialist to assess a suspected infection, particularly on a young tree or a tree near buildings. Removing an infected branch before the fungus reaches the trunk may help, but the position of the infection determines whether pruning is useful. Avoid moving suspect planting stock. Where restoration or replacement is planned, ask about suitable rust-resistant stock rather than assuming every white pine has equal resistance. Do not clear native currants and gooseberries indiscriminately; alternate-host management needs a site-specific plan and is not a simple landscape-wide cure.

sources.label: UC IPM: white pine blister rust in natural areas
PNW handbook: white pine blister rust

identification: The rounded bell has numerous pale spots, with a cluster of branching oral arms beneath it rather than long tentacles around the bell margin. Color and size vary among populations; some are brownish from associated algae, while documented Gulf populations lack those algae. Other spotted jellyfish, especially Mastigias, can look similar. Take photographs from above and, where safely possible, from the side without lifting the animal from the water or handling it.
actions: Report an unfamiliar spotted jellyfish or a large gathering to your state aquatic-resource program or the USGS Nonindigenous Aquatic Species reporting system. Include the waterbody, exact location, date, approximate number and bell size. Note whether the animals were swimming, stranded or caught in fishing gear. Do not move them to another waterbody or release aquarium jellyfish outdoors. Leave collection and any response to specialists; a photograph can start a review, but it cannot establish the identity of a tiny polyp stage or the source of an introduction.

identification: The bird is mostly green, with yellow along part of the wing and a conspicuous white wing patch best seen in flight. Yellow-chevroned parakeets lack that large white flight-feather area, although the birds can resemble one another when perched. Try to photograph both a perched bird and an open wing without disturbing it. Record flock size and repeated observations; mixed flocks mean identifying one bird does not necessarily identify every bird nearby.
actions: Share clear photographs, dates and locations with a local bird-recording group, and note observed nesting activity from a respectful distance. Do not approach nests to obtain evidence or attempt to capture birds simply because they are nonnative. If a bird appears to be a recently lost pet, contact a qualified rescue or animal service rather than releasing another captive bird to join it. The reviewed observations establish identity and introduced history, but they do not support a blanket claim of serious ecological damage in every city where this parakeet has been seen.

sources.label: South American Classification Committee: white-winged name
Falcon and Tremblay 2023: white-winged parakeets in Puerto Rico

identification: The immature stages offer the most useful clue. They can produce two pairs of broad, clear-looking wax tubes rising from the back, a distinctive feature described in Florida's diagnostic account. Adults alone are much harder to identify in a photograph. Turn a leaf gently and photograph the settled immature insects, including their wax structures, with a scale reference. A plant-health specialist may need intact specimens to confirm the species and distinguish old names used in earlier collections.
actions: Inspect newly acquired aroids before placing them beside established plants. Keep a heavily infested potted plant separate while requesting identification, and avoid transporting infested leaves to another property. Include the host name, purchase history and whether neighboring plants are affected in your report. Ask an extension or plant-health service about suitable management for that host rather than applying a generic whitefly spray schedule. Preserve parasitoids where present; the evidence reviewed here does not establish that every visible colony requires chemical treatment.

sources.label: Nagamine and Garcia: new Hawaii whitefly record

identification: Adults are broad-nosed weevils with pale markings along the sides of the body. Naupactus minor is generally smaller than the similar N. leucoloma, but size and the white fringe are not enough for a confident identification. Compared with N. peregrinus, it has flatter eyes and forward-directed hairs on the pronotum, the plate behind the head. Specialists also examine the hind legs. Take sharp photographs from above and the side with a ruler; a preserved specimen may be needed to resolve the name.
actions: When a crop or nursery plant is declining, record both the above-ground insects and any root injury instead of assuming leaf feeding explains everything. Ask an extension diagnostician how to collect a useful sample. Keep soil and suspect nursery material from moving to clean sites while the identification is reviewed. Inspect equipment that has contacted infested ground before moving it. Any control plan should consider the underground stage and the crop involved; an adult-only spray recommendation is not a complete response to root-feeding larvae.

sources.label: Lanteri et al. 2013: five Naupactini damaging soybean in Brazil

identification: Adults have a broad snout and pale markings along the sides. Compared with N. leucoloma, diagnostic descriptions note a somewhat smaller, paler tan beetle with more convex eyes and rearward-directed hairs on the pronotum and more rounded scales. These are close-examination characters, not a dependable phone-photo checklist. Photograph the head, body outline and side markings with a size reference. A specialist may need to examine the beetle before distinguishing it from N. minor or another member of the group.
actions: In nurseries or recently planted fields, note where affected plants occur and whether roots are damaged. Contact an extension service for identification and a sampling plan before treating the site. Avoid moving suspect root balls, soil or debris on equipment to an uninfested area. Check plants arriving from an affected site rather than relying on the absence of flying adults. Management must address the crop and soil-associated stages as well as visible beetles; the available group accounts do not establish a universal treatment for every N. peregrinus occurrence.

sources.label: Hoebeke and colleagues: adventive weevils of North America
Lanteri et al. 2013: five Naupactini damaging soybean in Brazil

identification: The flowers are white and tubular, opening into five spreading lobes, and arise singly or in pairs near the leaf bases. Two leafy bracts sit beneath each flower. Leaves are opposite and generally egg-shaped to pointed, sometimes with lobes or teeth toward the base. The fruit has a rounded base and a pronounced beak. Photograph the vine's attachment, paired leaves, a side view of the flower and any fruit; pale-flowered vines from other families can look similar at a distance.
actions: Avoid planting it where vines or seed can escape into surrounding habitat, and choose a suitable native climber instead. For an escaped patch, trace stems back to their bases before removing them so neighboring plants are not pulled apart. Contain mature fruits and do not discard cuttings in natural areas. Revisit the site for surviving stems or seedlings. Ask the land manager about the appropriate response where a vine is spreading beyond a garden, especially when removal would affect established shrubs or trees.

identification: The slender stems carry opposite, rounded to broadly egg-shaped leaves. Small white flowers occur in loose clusters, and each of the five petals is deeply divided, making the flower appear to have ten petals. Sticky flower parts can cling to clothing or animals. Common chickweed and mouse-ear chickweed are useful comparisons: stem hair patterns and the amount of hair on the leaves help separate them. Photograph a stem segment, both leaves at a node and a close flower rather than only the overall mat.
actions: For an unwanted patch in a garden, confirm the plant before removal and avoid carrying seed-bearing material on footwear into nearby habitat. Record whether the patch is spreading and whether it is in turf, a nursery or natural vegetation. A regional botanist can help interpret the name, since related forms have sometimes been confused in older references. Broad chemical treatment is not justified merely by the label chickweed. Where the plant occurs in a conservation area, let the land manager decide its priority using local evidence and native-status guidance.

identification: The gray-green leaves are alternate, and upper leaves clasp the stem with two small lobes. Numerous tiny, four-petaled white flowers make the top of the plant look broad and flat. Mature fruits are important: this species has heart-shaped pods, while related whitetops have differently shaped fruits. The name whitetop is also used for perennial pepperweed, a different plant. Photograph the leaf attachment, whole flowering stem and several mature pods rather than relying on white flowers alone.
actions: Mark the edge of the patch and avoid moving root-bearing soil to another field or garden. Mowing can reduce seed production, but it does not remove the established root system. Casual cultivation may spread root fragments unless it is part of a sustained management plan. Ask your county weed program or extension service about the best timing and methods for the site, particularly near water or desired crops. Check treated ground repeatedly for returning shoots, and establish suitable vegetation after control so the area is less open to reinvasion.

sources.label: Oregon Department of Agriculture: hoary cress
Lewis and Clark County: whitetop management

identification: The plant has finely divided leaves and small white flowers arranged in branching, umbrella-shaped clusters. The fruits are especially useful: they form a pair of rounded units rather than the elongated, beaked fruits of chervils. Several carrot-family plants have similar foliage, including dangerous species, so a leaf photograph or an odor is not a safe identification test. Photograph the whole plant, stem, flower cluster and mature fruit, with a ruler when possible.
actions: Do not taste an unfamiliar carrot-family plant or collect it as a culinary herb. If wild bishop is suspected, send detailed photographs and the exact location to a regional herbarium or extension service for confirmation. Include whether it appeared in a seeded area, crop field or waste ground, and whether more plants are present nearby. Where confirmed plants are unwanted on managed land, prevent seed from being moved with harvested material or soil. A local assessment is needed before recommending a broad control program; current United States impact and management evidence is limited.

sources.label: Natural History Museum Vienna: Bifora radians

identification: Leaves have three leaflets, generally with smooth edges and some hairs beneath. The plant may stand upright, trail or twine, and older stems can become somewhat woody at the base. Flowers are typically red to reddish purple, followed by long, narrow pods. Mature pods and their seeds help check an identification. Several tropical beans have three leaflets and similar growth, so include flowers and pods in photographs rather than identifying it from foliage alone.
actions: Avoid introducing it into landscapes where it can escape, especially near sensitive coastal habitat. Record the extent of an existing patch and whether it is climbing through other vegetation or producing seed. Contain mature pods during any authorized removal, and watch the site for new plants afterward. Contact a local land manager or extension service before treating a large stand. Florida's species account explicitly identifies gaps in tested control methods, so a confident-looking universal herbicide or mowing prescription would go beyond the available evidence.

sources.label: Proctor 2012 Cayman flora via Kew: Macroptilium lathyroides

identification: The leaves are finely divided and fernlike, and the plant carries clusters of tiny white flowers in branching umbels. Stems are hollow and ribbed, with hairs often easier to see low on the plant. The mature fruits are smooth, elongated and dark, unlike the hooked fruits of some other chervils. Wild carrot, hedge parsleys and poison hemlock can look similar. Do not taste the plant or rely on a single stem-color rule; photograph foliage, stem details, flowers and fruits for confirmation.
actions: Confirm the identification before handling or removing plants, and wear gloves when working with unfamiliar carrot-family vegetation. Small confirmed plants can be dug out with the root crown where ground disturbance is acceptable. Repeated cutting can reduce seed production and weaken plants, but one cut is unlikely to finish the job. Keep seed-bearing cuttings out of hay and clean mowing equipment before moving to another area. Recheck the patch for regrowth and new seedlings, and coordinate larger roadside or conservation-site infestations with the responsible weed program.

sources.label: King County: wild chervil identification and control

identification: Leaves occur in opposite pairs and are divided repeatedly into narrow segments. Flower heads have pink to purple outer rays around a yellowish-green center, followed by slender, dark, single-seeded fruits. The plant can become tall and branching under favorable conditions. Garden cosmos and other daisy-family plants require comparison of leaves, the green structures beneath the flower head and mature fruits. Photograph all of those parts if possible; a close-up of the pink rays alone is not a reliable species determination.
actions: Record whether the plant is intentionally cultivated or reproducing beyond a garden. Keep seed-bearing material from being dumped into natural areas, and check nearby disturbed ground for seedlings if it has escaped. A regional herbarium can help confirm an unusual record. Although this plant has culinary uses in some traditions, do not use an uncertain wild identification as a reason to eat it. The available sources explain recognition and cultivation well, but local habitat impacts and tested United States control recommendations still need more evidence before a stronger management claim is made.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Cosmos caudatus

identification: The leaves are alternate and toothed, often with the lowest tooth on each side extended into a fine bristle. Small yellow flowers give way to slender, upright capsules. The capsule opens into three valves, each ending in a forked tip. A close view is more useful than counting the tips from a distance. Other jutes can have winged, rounded or differently tipped capsules. A mature fruit photographed from the side and directly at its tip is therefore particularly helpful, along with the leaf base and whole plant.
actions: If you think you have found it, document the location, date and setting, including whether it appeared among newly sown plants or disturbed soil. Ask a regional herbarium to confirm the fruit characters before treating the observation as a new established population. Avoid moving seed-bearing plants or contaminated soil elsewhere. A confirmed unwanted annual on managed ground can be removed before seed dispersal, with landowner permission. Evidence for substantial United States impacts or a species-specific control program remains too limited for stronger recommendations.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Corchorus tridens

identification: The flower cluster is open and branching, with drooping spikelets. Mature grains commonly carry long, twisted bristles that bend sharply, and the seed base has a distinctive scar after it separates. At the junction of leaf and stem there is a papery ligule, a small upright membrane. Young plants resemble other grasses and cultivated oats, making close photographs of the leaf collar and mature spikelets more useful than a distant grassy patch. Hairiness varies and should not be the only identifying feature.
actions: Check crop edges and patches that survive the usual weed program before their seeds mature. Keep contaminated grain, seed and machinery from carrying wild oat into clean fields. Ask an extension crop adviser to assess identification, emergence timing and possible herbicide resistance when control fails; simply repeating the same treatment can miss the underlying problem. Combine measures suited to the crop rotation with follow-up scouting. Outside cropland, decide whether removal serves the habitat's needs before disturbing a mixed grassland.

sources.label: NDSU 2025 weed control guide: wild oat

identification: Look for broad, toothed leaflets arranged along a central leaf stalk and flat-topped clusters of small yellow flowers. Flowering stems are stout, hollow and grooved. This is different from the finely divided, white-flowered appearance of wild carrot, although other carrot-family plants still require careful comparison. Photograph the leaves and flower clusters without breaking stems. The flat, brown fruits become more apparent after flowering and can help confirm a record.
actions: Keep people away from damaged stems and do not use a string trimmer through a suspected patch, which could spread sap onto exposed skin. Confirm identification and plan removal with appropriate protective clothing and local guidance. Small plants may be dug below the crown before flowering; larger infestations require careful timing and follow-up to prevent seed production. If sap contacts skin, wash it promptly and protect the area from sunlight; seek medical advice for a significant reaction or eye exposure. Report patches beside public paths to the land manager so they can address both access and control.

sources.label: New York DEC: wild parsnip fact sheet

identification: Lower leaves are rough and lobed, often with a larger end lobe. Flowers have four petals, commonly pale yellow or cream with visible veins. Mature pods are the most helpful feature: they become constricted between seeds and break into separate, closed segments rather than splitting lengthwise like many mustard pods. Photograph both young and mature pods, leaves and flowers. A mixed set of characteristics may need expert review, particularly in California where hybrid populations are well documented.
actions: Remove small unwanted plants before they replenish the seed supply, and keep mature pods out of material moved to another site. In crop fields, consider the weed's emergence timing, crop competition and harvest practices with an extension adviser. Seed capture at harvest can help in suitable systems, but some plants flower below cutting height, so it is not a complete solution by itself. Revisit treated areas for later seedlings and confirm unusual plants before interpreting them as evidence of spread by a single named species.

sources.label: Cornell: wild radish ecology and management

identification: Plants have cane-like stems, long leaves with a prominent pale midrib and large, feathery flower clusters. Size and growth form vary considerably, and some plants resemble cultivated sugarcane or other tall grasses. Narrower stems are a useful clue but not a final identification. Photograph the whole stand, stem joints, leaf collar and flowering head. A botanist may need close examination of the small spikelets to distinguish related grasses or breeding material.
actions: Do not take suspected plants home or move cut stems, rhizomes or soil from the patch. Record its location and contact your state agriculture department or local invasive-plant program for identification and current handling requirements. Avoid burning it as a do-it-yourself control method: survival and regrowth after disturbance are part of its persistence. Cutting the visible stems also leaves underground growth behind. A confirmed infestation needs a coordinated plan that limits movement of viable fragments, checks for regrowth and supports suitable replacement vegetation after control.

sources.label: USDA APHIS: wild sugarcane weed risk assessment
Florida agriculture: noxious weeds field guide
Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute: canal grass

identification: Look closely at the bark for nearly round, gray covers with an orange-yellow center, roughly two millimeters across. Heavy colonies can blend into the trunk until bark develops a bubbled appearance. Oystershell scale, another aspen pest, has elongated, shell-shaped covers instead. Bark texture or tree decline alone cannot identify either insect. Photograph several intact covers beside a scale marker, plus the whole tree and affected branches; a specialist may need actual insects beneath the covers.
actions: Have an extension office or arborist confirm the scale before choosing treatment. Record which trees are affected and whether foliage, branch growth or bark condition is changing. The Chinese life-cycle study found a distinct seasonal crawler period, but its calendar should not be transferred directly to a Colorado garden. Ask for locally appropriate monitoring of that vulnerable stage. Avoid scraping extensive areas of living bark or applying a general insect treatment solely because old covers remain. Where branches over paths are declining, arrange a separate tree-safety assessment.

sources.label: Colorado State University: Oystershell scale, Notes on Poplar Scale
Lellakova-Duskova: Quadraspidiotus gigas morphology and biology
Hu and colleagues: A preliminary study on poplar scale insect

identification: A flowering clump may reach about three feet tall. The branched flower head carries conspicuously flattened, egg-shaped spikelets, each containing several flowers. Their overlapping parts give the edges a toothed or jagged outline; mature spikelets may be green to purple before drying. Check the hairy upper leaf surface and hair tufts around the sheath as supporting clues. The Arizona description notes the absence of rhizomes and stolons. Compare mature spikelets with a regional grass key, since other Eragrostis species can look similar before flowering.
actions: In a pasture, identify the grass and discuss its role with local range staff before removing it or sowing more. At a restoration site, map established clumps and any seedlings spreading beyond the planted area. If removal is appropriate, deal with small clumps before their seed clusters mature and avoid scattering those clusters along access routes. Check nearby disturbed ground during subsequent growing seasons. Do not substitute this introduced forage grass for a locally appropriate native seed mix merely because it is drought tolerant.

identification: Look for a narrow, unbranched seed head with spikelets attached edge-on to the central stalk. The leaves have a shiny underside, and lower stem nodes may be reddish. Mature spikelets usually lack conspicuous long awns. A regional key should check the length of the outer bract and the flower parts, because perennial ryegrass and Italian ryegrass can be confused with this species, and hybrids complicate identification. A photograph of green leaves alone is unlikely to resolve an uncertain plant. Keep the seed head attached to its stem when documenting it.
actions: In an orchard or crop field, mark surviving patches before they shed seed and discuss a seed-prevention plan with an agricultural adviser. Clean equipment before moving from those patches to clean ground. Small escapes can be removed carefully while their seed remains immature. If an appropriately applied treatment repeatedly fails, request identification and resistance advice instead of simply repeating it. Check the scientific name on pasture or cover-crop seed labels: a product called annual ryegrass is not necessarily Lolium rigidum.

sources.label: Simarmata and Penner: Basis for glyphosate resistance in rigid ryegrass from California

identification: The most useful close-up clue is the dense covering of reddish, gland-tipped hairs on the canes, mixed with slender prickles. Leaves commonly have three leaflets, though some have five, and their undersides are conspicuously pale and woolly. The developing fruit is enclosed by the hairy flower cup until near ripeness, when bright red berries become exposed. Ordinary red raspberries and native blackberry relatives can also have prickly canes, but they do not share this whole combination. Photograph the cane hairs, both leaf surfaces and a fruiting cluster rather than relying on berry color.
actions: Check a garden patch against those features before removing nearby native brambles. Wear sturdy gloves and protect your arms from prickles. For a small confirmed escape, remove the rooted base while limiting disturbance to neighboring plants, and contain any ripe fruit so the work does not spread seed. Follow the patch boundary and watch for new seedlings after removal. Larger tangles beside woodland need a staged plan and follow-up; replacing the cleared space with suitable vegetation can help avoid leaving an open seedbed.

sources.label: University of Maryland Extension: Growing raspberries and blackberries
West Chester University: Gordon Natural Area plant inventory

identification: Look for opposite leaves with finely toothed edges and corky ridges running along the twigs. Those ridges give the shrub its winged name, although their prominence varies. Small greenish-yellow flowers have four petals; fall foliage alone is not a reliable identification. Native eastern wahoo, another Euonymus, lacks the characteristic corky wings and has purple flowers. Young sweetgum can also have ridged twigs, but its star-shaped leaves alternate along the stem. Photograph a leafy twig, its ridges and any flowers or fruit before deciding what to remove.
actions: Where the shrub is escaping, begin by locating seedlings under perches and around nearby woods, not just beneath the parent plant. Remove small confirmed seedlings with their roots when soil conditions allow, taking care around desirable understory plants. Plan removal of larger fruiting shrubs with local invasive-plant guidance; cutting a mature shrub once should not be treated as proof of lasting control. Revisit the site for regrowth and new seedlings. Choose a regionally suitable replacement and avoid assuming that compact size means a nursery selection cannot spread.
Keep fruiting cuttings contained and follow local disposal guidance so berries are not scattered into natural areas.

sources.label: Penn State Extension: Burning bush accurate identification

identification: At the species level, wintercreeper is a woody evergreen creeper or climber with opposite, leathery leaves and finely toothed margins. Stems can root where they meet the ground and attach to supports with rootlets. Those characters help recognize wintercreeper, but they do not establish the typical variety. Leaf size, color and a white or yellow border may reflect cultivated selections rather than a dependable variety distinction. Record both creeping and climbing growth when present, along with flowers or fruit, and retain the original label separately.
actions: For an escaped patch, first obtain a species-level identification and follow the local wintercreeper guidance appropriate to that site. Keep this variety name provisional until a botanist has checked the evidence against a stated taxonomic treatment. Do not transport rooted runners or discard fresh cuttings beside woods while identification is pending. In a planting inventory, preserve the old name and document any proposed update rather than silently merging records. Management can address a confirmed wintercreeper escape without pretending that its variety has already been resolved.

sources.label: Nesom: Euonymus fortunei naturalized in Texas
US Forest Service: Wintercreeper review and infraspecific scope
Kew POWO: Euonymus fortunei var. fortunei
USDA GRIN: Euonymus fortunei var. radicans

identification: A plant associated with this name should first be checked as wintercreeper: woody stems, opposite evergreen leaves and a creeping or climbing habit are useful starting points. Rootlets along climbing stems and rooting growth against the soil add supporting evidence. These are species-level clues, not a key to var. radicans. A small-leaved or variegated nursery plant cannot be assigned to this variety from that feature alone. Include close photographs of leaves and stems, the growth form, and any surviving nursery information with an identification request.
actions: Preserve the complete original label when reporting a planting or escape, and ask the reviewer which botanical treatment they are using. Avoid turning a proposed synonym into a new occurrence record without checking whether it duplicates an existing wintercreeper observation. For a confirmed escaping wintercreeper, contain rooted pieces and follow local removal advice while the variety remains unresolved. Do not plant additional material near woodland on the assumption that the radicans name identifies a harmless form. Recheck the site after work for surviving rooted stems.

sources.label: Nesom: Euonymus fortunei naturalized in Texas
USDA GRIN: Euonymus fortunei var. radicans
US Forest Service: Wintercreeper review and infraspecific scope
Kew POWO: Euonymus fortunei var. fortunei

identification: Look for paired, leathery leaves with toothed edges on woody stems. Leaves are commonly oval, and some cultivated plants have pale or yellow markings. Creeping stems root at contact points; climbing stems attach through small rootlets rather than simply lying against the trunk. Inspect the arrangement of several leaves, since a dense evergreen mat can include more than one species. Leaf color alone will not distinguish cultivated forms or settle a variety name. A useful record shows the ground-level network as well as any stems climbing into surrounding vegetation.
actions: Start at the edge of a small escape and trace rooted stems before lifting them, so pieces are not left hidden beneath leaf litter. Contain fresh clippings and rooted fragments instead of dumping them in a brush pile beside woodland. Large mats or vines on mature trees warrant a local management plan; do not pull heavy attached growth from overhead. Check cleared ground repeatedly for surviving stems and seedlings, and protect remaining native plants during the work. Photographs from the same marked boundary can show whether follow-up is actually shrinking the colony.

sources.label: Missouri Department of Conservation: Wintercreeper, climbing euonymus
Missouri Department of Conservation: Wintercreeper control
Nesom: Euonymus fortunei naturalized in Texas

identification: Look for stiff, narrow, leathery leaves with conspicuous spiny teeth and a somewhat wrinkled upper surface. Leaves may appear clustered along the branches, which carry strong, three-part spines. Mature shrubs can become taller than a person and form a tightly branched barrier. Yellow spring flowers and oval dark fruit support the identification. Other evergreen barberries and cultivated hybrids can be confusing, so use a combination of leaf shape, spine arrangement and fruit rather than calling every thorny hedge Japanese barberry. Photograph the branch structure without reaching into the spines.
actions: An established garden shrub does not need removal merely because another barberry is invasive nearby. Inspect the surrounding bed and adjacent natural ground for seedlings, and record any plants appearing beyond cultivation. Have those escapes identified before making a wider control decision. Wear sturdy gloves and eye protection for close pruning work, and keep sharp cut branches out of paths and play areas. If replacement is desired, remove the rooted plant carefully and check for regrowth. Ask local extension staff about suitable alternatives rather than treating a Florida assessment as nationwide planting advice.

identification: You cannot tell whether a mosquito carries West Nile virus by its appearance, and a dead bird does not establish the diagnosis. Fever, headache, body aches or a rash can have many causes. A clinician considers symptoms, exposure and appropriate testing; an online species profile cannot determine an infection. Seek urgent medical care for severe symptoms such as high fever with a stiff neck, confusion or marked muscle weakness. Tell the clinician about recent mosquito exposure, but do not wait for a mosquito or bird identification before seeking help.
actions: Reduce bites with an EPA-registered repellent used according to its label, protective clothing and intact window and door screens. Regularly empty or cover small containers that collect water around the home, and maintain items such as buckets, tires and pool covers so they do not become breeding places. Follow local mosquito-control and public-health advice rather than attempting to drain natural wetlands. There is no licensed human vaccine for West Nile virus; prevention remains valuable even when no local case has been announced. Ask local authorities how they want dead birds reported or handled.

sources.label: New York State Department of Health: Precautions against West Nile virus, August 2026

identification: The large leaves are divided twice: several pairs of side branches each carry paired, oblong leaflets. The leaflet bases are often noticeably uneven. Cream to pale-yellow flowers form fluffy clusters, followed by long, flat pods that turn straw-colored or brown and remain on the tree. The pods are papery rather than strongly constricted between individual seeds. Other trees called mimosa or silk tree also have divided leaves and fluffy flowers, so photograph both a complete leaf and mature pods. The combination of leaflet structure, flower color and persistent rattling pods is more useful than a common name.
actions: Near susceptible natural areas, avoid adding new plantings and inspect beneath mature trees and along nearby boundaries for recruits. Remove small, confirmed seedlings before they become difficult to uproot, and watch for shoots from established roots after work. Contain pods instead of moving them with garden waste into undeveloped land. A large tree needs an arborist's assessment and a site-specific removal plan, especially near buildings or trails. Follow-up should include the surrounding ground, since removing the canopy does not demonstrate that seedlings and root sprouts are gone.

sources.label: World Agroforestry: Albizia lebbeck species account

identification: The botanical description of this variety combines a loose, branching flower head with small, several-flowered spikelets, a short membranous ligule at the leaf base, and fine hairs on particular flower structures. Those details require a flowering specimen and usually magnification. At a glance, the soft, narrow leaves and airy panicle can resemble other woodland bluegrasses. Record the ligule and mature spikelets rather than relying on overall height or leaf color. A grass identified only as Poa nemoralis should not automatically receive this variety name without checking the relevant key.
actions: In a natural woodland, leave an uncertain patch in place while seeking identification from a regional herbarium or grass specialist. Photograph the whole clump, leaf bases and flowering head, and record whether plants are scattered or forming a continuous area. If an unwanted garden volunteer is confirmed, removing it before seed ripens is a modest containment step, not evidence of a proven variety-specific control method. Keep records at the level actually determined. Avoid clearing surrounding native grasses to resolve an uncertain bluegrass name.

sources.label: Flora of China: Poa treatment, Smithsonian repository copy
Plue et al. 2020: Biological Flora of Poa nemoralis
ITIS / New World Grasses: nemoralis subspecies-to-variety crosswalk

identification: The original description concerns a pale, crust-like fruiting body attached broadly to wood, with irregular pores and microscopic structures needed for identification. Florida material called Flavodon subulatus also forms a whitish, irregularly pored crust. Neither that appearance nor softened wood is unique to this fungus. Other crust fungi can look similar, and beetle holes alone cannot identify the fungal partner. A mycologist may need microscopy and sequence evidence, together with a documented specimen, to connect a collection reliably to the changing names.
actions: Photograph the fruiting surface, the surrounding wood and any beetle galleries, and note the tree species and whether the wood is living, dead or fallen. Do not move suspect logs to a new site simply to obtain an identification. Where decay affects limbs over people or structures, have a qualified arborist assess the physical hazard independently of the final fungal name. In natural areas, dead wood has ecological value and should not be removed wholesale on sight of a pale crust. UF guidance does not establish a specific treatment for this beetle-fungus association.

sources.label: Tian and colleagues: Irpex jinshaensis and I. subulatus combination
New Zealand Organisms Register: Oxyporus subulatus
UF/IFAS: Punky wood ambrosia beetle and fungus in Florida
NZOR: Irpex spiculifer and subulatus names
Biota of New Zealand: Irpex spiculifer

identification: An adult is only a few millimeters long and has a segmented crustacean body with conspicuous rear appendages. The last pair is especially enlarged, appearing paddle-like in females and more elongated in males. A backward-pointing spine near the rear is another specialist clue. Gribbles and shipworms may occur in the same timber, but a hole or worn surface does not reveal which animal made it. Some historical tropical records were confused with Tropichelura insulae, so even a wood-dwelling amphipod needs a proper identification rather than a location-based guess.
actions: For a suspected occurrence, document the harbor, date, timber type and visible damage, and obtain clear magnified photographs if specimens are already available safely. Ask a marine-biological or museum specialist how to submit material without spreading live borers. Do not move occupied timber between waterfront sites or release animals collected from it elsewhere. Dock owners should arrange a qualified structural inspection when pilings or load-bearing wood are deteriorating; identifying an amphipod is not a safety assessment. Avoid improvised pesticide applications into the water.

sources.label: Green Etxabe: The wood-boring amphipod Chelura terebrans

identification: This tiny crustacean has a cylindrical, segmented body. Identification requires close examination of antennae and tail structures, including a Y-shaped ridge. Other gribbles, such as Limnoria tripunctata, can occupy similar timber. Burrows and worn surfaces cannot establish the species. Ask a specialist which views or specimen details are needed before assuming that a general photograph will resolve the identification.
actions: Treat a possible new record as a documentation task. Record the precise waterfront location, date and kind of wood, and ask a marine invertebrate specialist about safe specimen submission. Include who found the material and whether it came from a dock, a loose log or an existing survey sample. Do not move occupied wood to another harbor, or cut mangrove roots to search for the animal. Have damaged dock components inspected by a qualified professional regardless of the eventual species identification. The reviewed account documents no species-specific losses, so avoid attributing a local structural failure to this gribble without evidence.

sources.label: Cookson, Cragg and Hendy 2012: Indonesian wood-boring limnoriids

identification: Look for divided leaves, slender seed pods and tiny white flowers with four petals. Typical woodland bittercress has leafy stems that may bend from side to side and bear hairs. Flowers usually have six stamens, whereas hairy bittercress, C. hirsuta, often has four. Those counts are useful clues, not a complete diagnosis: variation occurs, and C. occulta also has six. Examine several flowers and the stem hairs, lower leaves and mature fruits with a current regional key. A single overhead photograph of a nursery pot is unlikely to settle this group.
actions: Keep a doubtful observation at Cardamine species level until a knowledgeable botanist checks it. In cultivated containers or beds, remove unwanted plants before their pods mature and clean loose soil and plant debris from reused equipment. That is practical seed containment, not proof of a species-specific invasion or treatment. Do not clear a damp natural area just because a small bittercress resembles a nursery weed. Preserve photographs and the name used in any older record so a later identification can be traced rather than silently overwritten.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Cardamine flexuosa

identification: The plant has hairy stems and alternate, softly hairy leaves, with broader lower leaves and narrower leaves higher up. Flowers usually show five blue lobes around a yellow center, although cultivated plants may have pink or white flowers. Close examination of the green calyx around a flower or fruit is useful: hooked hairs are part of the botanical description. Other forget-me-nots can look very similar from a distance, so include the calyx, lower leaves and developing fruits in photographs. Flower color and the common name alone are not enough for a reliable determination.
actions: Where it is spreading beyond a bed, remove small confirmed plants before they finish setting seed and contain any fruiting material. Check paths, disturbed soil and the woodland edge as well as the original planting. Repeat visits matter because the disappearance of flowering plants does not prove that future seedlings are gone. Avoid sowing surplus seed or dumping garden waste beside natural areas. If native forget-me-nots occur locally, have an uncertain patch checked before removal. Choose a replacement suited to the site and observe whether it stays within the intended planting.

sources.label: University of Wisconsin-Green Bay: Myosotis sylvatica
Flora Argentina: Boraginaceae treatment including Myosotis sylvatica

identification: Look for an upright, leafy stem, irregularly lobed leaves and small yellow flower heads. The narrow rays can be inconspicuous, so examine a fresh head closely. Woodland ragwort typically has about thirteen main green bracts around the flower head, without the strongly blackened tips characteristic of common groundsel, Senecio vulgaris. Common groundsel usually has more of those bracts and lacks ray flowers. Count several intact heads with a hand lens and compare a regional key; a distant yellow-flower photograph can easily confuse this plant with other ragworts and groundsels.
actions: In a garden or nursery bed, deal with confirmed unwanted plants before seed dispersal and minimize unnecessary soil disturbance during removal. At a logged or otherwise recovering woodland site, document the patch and revisit it across seasons before assuming that a large one-year display requires broad vegetation clearing. Protect desirable seedlings and surviving native cover while working. If persistent recruitment is interfering with a specific restoration objective, ask local land managers for a targeted plan. Where forage is harvested, have uncertain ragworts identified and ask a local forage specialist how their presence affects the management plan.

sources.label: Native Plant Trust: Senecio identification key
Halpern and colleagues: Species replacement during early secondary succession

identification: Look near the ground as well as at the seed heads. The long, stiff leaves fold into a V, and their bases are often strikingly dark purple to nearly black. Smooth, three-sided flowering stems carry several dense, rounded clusters of flattened spikelets, with long leaflike bracts beneath them. A triangular stem alone is not enough: many native sedges share that feature. Photograph the leaf bases, whole flower arrangement and individual clusters before deciding which sedge you have.
actions: Keep machinery out of a suspected patch until identification is confirmed, especially when soil is wet enough to cling to tires. Clean soil and plant pieces from tools before moving to another restoration area. Small confirmed clumps can be dug out, but the dense roots and rhizomes make this laborious; revisit the spot for regrowth. For an established ditch or wetland population, ask the land manager or local extension office to plan treatment that protects nearby native sedges and water.

sources.label: Harris County Flood Control District: Reforestation plant identification guide

identification: The most useful clues are on a flowering plant. Several stalked heads tend to form a fairly flat cluster, and the bracts around each head are usually wrapped in pale, cobwebby hairs. Large lower leaves are heart-shaped at the base and woolly underneath. Common burdock, Arctium minus, usually has shorter-stalked heads in tighter groups; occasional hairy heads can still cause confusion. Check the tiny glandular hairs on the bracts with a hand lens. Hollow versus solid leaf stalks will not reliably settle this species.
actions: Photograph fresh flower heads before their wool thins with age, including a close view of the bracts and a wider view of the branching. Remove any burrs from clothing and equipment before leaving the patch. If plants are unwanted beside a path, preventing mature burrs from being carried elsewhere is a sensible first step while identification is checked. Obtain local advice before undertaking wider removal: the scale of local harm and the suitability of a treatment need to be assessed at the actual site.

sources.label: Flora of North America: Arctium tomentosum

identification: The yellow flower heads sit above conspicuous, stiff, spiny bracts. Grey-green leaves are deeply divided, with strong veins and hard points along their edges; pale, woolly hairs give young growth a somewhat cobwebbed appearance. Despite the prickly leaves, the stem itself lacks the spiny wings seen on many other thistles. This distinction helps separate it from winged thistles, while flower and bract details distinguish it from yellow starthistle. Take clear photographs without grasping a flowering stem barehanded.
actions: Act while a confirmed patch is small and before it produces mature seed. Use gloves and suitable tools to remove isolated plants, and arrange disposal that keeps flower heads from shedding along the route. Its relatively heavy seeds commonly fall near the parent, so check the surrounding ground closely in later seasons. Pasture management also matters: avoid leaving repeatedly disturbed, overgrazed openings for seedlings. Larger infestations need a locally planned program and follow-up; one cutting should not be assumed to finish the job.

sources.label: Oklahoma State University: Thistles in Oklahoma and their identification
Western Australia: Saffron thistle weed guidance

identification: The fine hairs on its dull green pads are a better clue than the presence of obvious spines. Older plants may look nearly spineless, but small patches of barbed bristles remain. Mature plants develop a trunk; orange flowers are followed by reddish, hairy fruits. Indian fig, Opuntia ficus-indica, has hairless pads, while common pricklypear, O. stricta, usually combines hairless pads with yellow flowers. Use a photograph or hand lens to examine the surface rather than rubbing a pad.
actions: Keep children and pets away from loose pads, and avoid moving cuttings between properties. If a confirmed plant needs removal, use protective clothing and tools such as tongs to handle pieces. Small plants may be dug out where disturbance is acceptable; large specimens need an experienced contractor. Collect detached material and ask the local waste service how to dispose of cactus pieces that can root again. Check the removal area for both regrowth and seedlings after suitable rain.

sources.label: Flora of New South Wales: Opuntia tomentosa
Olvera-Carrillo et al.: Germination of Opuntia tomentosa

identification: Look for narrow, simple leaves and a loosely branched flowering structure whose ultimate branch tips become slender, spine-like points. The plant is generally hairless and lacks the conspicuous glandular coating found in several familiar Dysphania species. Tiny flowers occur along the branching structure, followed by small, dark seeds. Michigan Flora separates it from other members of that group using the combination of unglandular surfaces and pointed branchlets. A photograph of leaves alone is unlikely to capture the decisive features.
actions: Record the whole plant and a close view of mature branch tips, with a scale beside them. A herbarium or regional botanist can compare the specimen with both Dysphania and Teloxys treatments. For a plant appearing in a garden or imported soil, avoid spreading the seed-bearing material while that check is made. Do not use the wormseed name as a reason to taste it or prepare a remedy. Wider control recommendations should wait for confirmation of the taxon and evidence that the local population warrants intervention.

sources.label: NEON Biorepository: Dysphania aristata floristic treatment
USDA GRIN: Dysphania aristata and Teloxys aristata

identification: The small yellow flowers have four separate petals, and the narrow seedpods lengthen as flowering progresses. Leaves alternate along the stem and are simple, with edges that may be nearly smooth or lightly toothed. Other wallflowers and small yellow mustards can look similar at a distance. Fine, branched hairs on stems, leaves and fruits help specialists distinguish them, so include close photographs and mature pods. Older attempts to separate northern forms by stem-node counts did not hold consistently in the Alaska survey.
actions: Start with the location and habitat: a cultivated bed, roadside and naturally disturbed riverbank call for different decisions. Photograph a flowering and fruiting plant and ask a regional botanist to confirm the identification and local status. Where it is an unwanted, confirmed garden weed, removing it before the pods ripen can limit seed return. In northern natural areas, leave larger removal decisions to the land manager while nativity is reviewed. The old wormseed name is historical and should not be treated as medical advice.

sources.label: Native Plant Trust Go Botany: Erysimum cheiranthoides
Alaska Center for Conservation Science: nonnative plant list
University of Alaska Anchorage: Delta and Gulkana river plant surveys

identification: A vine can extend several metres, carrying leaves divided into three broad, pointed leaflets. The central leaflet often has an angular outline, quite different from a single heart-shaped yam leaf. Purple and white, pea-shaped flowers grow in clusters along the vine, followed by flattened pods that are hairy when young. The familiar pale-brown storage root is another clue on an already harvested plant. Several climbing legumes share these features, so flowers and mature pods are useful for checking a volunteer vine.
actions: Keep a cultivated vine supported within its growing area and watch nearby disturbed ground for volunteers. If an unwanted escape is confirmed, remove it while accessible and contain mature pods before moving the plant material. Do not assume that its beans or leaves are edible because the root is sold as food: botanical sources identify toxic aboveground parts, including the seeds. Use properly identified cultivated produce rather than tasting a wild vine. A persistent population beyond a garden deserves a local assessment before claims about ecological harm or a wider control program are made.

sources.label: CSIRO Australian Tropical Rainforest Plants: Pachyrhizus erosus

identification: Surface cracking and discolored tissue beneath the skin are reasons to investigate, not a diagnosis. Rot caused by other organisms can accompany nematode injury, and several related Scutellonema species can occur around yam roots. The animals are roughly a millimetre long and require specialist examination. Researchers working with samples from Ghana and Nigeria combined microscopic characters with DNA evidence to distinguish these close relatives. A photograph of a rotten tuber cannot provide that level of certainty.
actions: Do not keep suspect tubers as planting material or pass them to another grower. Separate the affected lot, retain its source information and contact an agricultural diagnostic laboratory for sampling instructions. Starting with healthy planting stock is central to prevention. Ask a crop specialist about the field's other possible hosts before choosing a rotation, since simply changing crops may not break the cycle. Hot-water treatments require a validated procedure for the crop and planting material; do not improvise one. Follow local plant-health guidance for disposing of confirmed infected stock.

sources.label: Kolombia et al. 2017: Morphological and molecular characterisation of Scutellonema

identification: Look for leaves divided into three leaflets and clusters of small yellow pea flowers. Several unrelated yellow-flowered legumes have a similar outline, so examine the pods as well. Typical falcata pods are straight or curved like a sickle, unlike the tightly coiled pods of ordinary purple-flowered alfalfa. Yellow flowers alone are not conclusive: the wider alfalfa complex includes other yellow forms and hybrids. Research documents crosses with cultivated alfalfa, which can blur simple color-based identification.
actions: In a forage field, management should follow the intended crop use and local agronomic advice. If yellow alfalfa appears in a restoration planting, record flowers, mature pods and the position relative to nearby hayfields before deciding whether it is an escape or part of the seed mix. Avoid adding it to a native restoration solely because it attracts insects. Where removal is desired, ask the site manager to account for the perennial crown and surrounding desirable plants. Confirm identity before collecting seed for any future planting.

sources.label: USDA NRCS: Yellow-flowered alfalfa plant guide
American Journal of Botany: Medicago sativa evolutionary study

identification: The leaves occur in opposite pairs on four-sided stems and have toothed edges and fine hairs. Many escaped garden forms have conspicuous silver markings, but leaf pattern alone is not a reliable identification. The yellow flowers are more helpful: each has a hooded upper lip and a smaller lower lip marked with brown or orange. Other deadnettles can have similarly patterned leaves, so photograph flowers as well as foliage. Trace a stem to see whether it has rooted at several points.
actions: For a small confirmed patch, work from the outside inward and lift rooted stems carefully, collecting loose pieces as you go. Check beneath neighboring plants, where runners can be easy to miss. Return to pull regrowth from roots or fragments left behind. Cutting the top alone can leave an active patch, and ordinary garden composting can spread it. Contain removed material and use locally approved disposal.
