For a large woodland infestation, coordinate treatment and replacement planting with the land manager or local weed program.

sources.label: Washington State Noxious Weed Control Board: Yellow archangel
Flora of New South Wales: Lamium galeobdolon

identification: The flowering head has several slender, often reddish-purple branches that spread above the main stem. University of Texas botanists emphasize that these are branches of a small panicle, not truly identical fingers arising from one point. Look closely at hairs near the leaf collar, and photograph the seed head from several angles. The King Ranch form can have hairy stem nodes, but native silver bluestem also has conspicuous node hairs. That character by itself is not a safe reason to remove a grass.
actions: Mark suspected patches while they are flowering, when identification is easier, and have a grass specialist check them before treatment. Avoid carrying ripe seed on mowing or harvesting equipment into intact prairie. Keep a record of patch edges so later visits show whether it is expanding. Established stands require a restoration plan that considers nearby native grasses, since treatments can injure both. Ask local range specialists about timing, follow-up and replacement vegetation; repeated mowing alone should not be assumed to eradicate the perennial plants.

sources.label: University of Texas: Bothriochloa ischaemum morphology
Kansas Department of Agriculture: Noxious and invasive weed update
Texas Parks and Wildlife: Texas-Louisiana coastal prairie

identification: For a plant labeled this way, collect observations that allow a grass specialist to work beyond the label. Photograph the entire plant, its leaf bases and a mature bristly seed head, with a scale. The floristic account associated with yellow foxtail describes an annual with a dense, upright head and conspicuously wrinkled fertile lemmas, the small coverings around individual grass fruits. These are clues for one published interpretation of the name, not a confirmed diagnosis of this catalog entry.
actions: Keep any nursery tag, seed packet or original observation attached to the record. Ask the supplier or identifying botanist which accepted name and botanical authority they intended, and compare that answer with the physical specimen. Until the identity is settled, avoid moving seed-bearing material into another garden or natural area. A suspected volunteer can be documented without broadcasting seed or starting a broad control effort. Specific management should follow the resolved species and local habitat, especially if the plant proves to be a cultivated millet.

sources.label: NEON Biorepository: Setaria helvola and displayed FNA treatment
Original Setaria systematic treatment and helvolum type

identification: The arching, feather-shaped fronds carry many narrow leaflets, while the canelike stems show clear rings where older leaves were attached. Yellow-green stems and leaf midribs help explain its common names. Outdoor plants may produce small yellow flowers and oblong fruits that darken as they mature; houseplants rarely reach that stage. Other palms are sold under the loose name areca palm, so check the botanical label and the clustering stems rather than relying on the shop name alone.
actions: For an indoor plant, provide bright conditions, drainage and enough room for new stems, keeping the potting mix moist without leaving it waterlogged. In an outdoor planting, watch the edge of the clump and any seedlings beyond the maintained bed. Keep unwanted rooted divisions and fruiting material within controlled disposal rather than dumping them in nearby vegetation. If seedlings are appearing in natural habitat, document that local behavior and ask an extension service to assess it. Do not remove a healthy cultivated palm solely because an older label uses Dypsis.

identification: Adults are dark with contrasting pale markings and banded legs. The most helpful feature is a silvery, lyre-shaped pattern on the upper surface of the thorax, just behind the head. Other striped mosquitoes, including the Asian tiger mosquito, can be mistaken for it. A close photograph or a specimen examined by a mosquito-control program is more reliable than leg stripes alone. This species can bite during daylight and around dusk, so an evening-only impression of mosquito activity may miss it.
actions: Once a week, empty and scrub water-holding containers, then turn them over, cover them or remove them. Scrubbing matters because eggs can remain on container surfaces. Cover stored water and repair window and door screens. Wear clothing that covers exposed skin and use an EPA-registered repellent according to its label. If containers cannot be emptied or covered, ask the local mosquito-control service about suitable treatment. Share persistent breeding-site concerns with that service, and use local public-health notices for disease-risk advice rather than trying to diagnose an illness from a bite.

sources.label: European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control: Aedes aegypti factsheet
US EPA: Tips to prevent mosquito bites

identification: Look for stiff, sword-shaped leaves arranged in overlapping fans. When flowering, the large yellow blooms have three broad, downward-facing outer segments and smaller upright inner segments. Outside the flowering season, leaves may be confused with other irises, sweetflag or cattails. Native blueflag irises have blue or violet flowers, but ornamental iris varieties make flower color alone an imperfect shortcut. Photograph the flower structure, leaf fan and seed capsules when present; do not dig up a waterside clump just to inspect it.
actions: Stop sharing divisions and prevent unwanted plants from setting seed where that can be done safely. Wear gloves and avoid sap contact when handling them. Removing flower stalks limits one route of spread but leaves the rhizomes alive. Small confirmed patches may be dug out only where permitted and practical, with all rhizome pieces collected and later regrowth checked. For a large pond-edge stand, involve the land manager or an aquatic-plant specialist. Any treatment near water needs the appropriate local permissions and products specifically suitable for that setting.
Do not put rhizomes or seed capsules in home compost or dump them beside water; contain removed material and follow local disposal instructions.

sources.label: NC State Extension: Yellow flag iris
UF IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants: Iris pseudacorus
Oregon State University: Yellow Flag Iris

identification: Each large leaf divides twice into many small oval leaflets, giving the crown a light, feathery appearance. Upright flower clusters carry yellow blooms with crinkled petals. Flat, thin pods follow, changing from reddish tones to dark brown. Trees sold as yellow poinciana or yellow flamboyant can have confusing common names, so include leaves, flowers and pods in an identification. The short, flattened pods and yellow clusters are useful checks alongside the twice-divided leaves, rather than identifying the tree by canopy shape alone.
actions: Give a planted tree enough space for its eventual crown and have structural pruning assessed by a qualified arborist. Track seedlings outside the maintained planting area, especially beside drainage routes where fallen pods may travel. Unwanted seedlings are easier to address while small, after their identity is confirmed. Do not clear a tree in its native habitat on the strength of an introduced-species label from another country. For a suspected escape elsewhere, record whether young plants are surviving away from cultivation before deciding that broader control is needed.

sources.label: UF IFAS: Peltophorum pterocarpum landscape fact sheet

identification: The rounded to heart-shaped leaves have gently wavy edges and may be purple beneath. Bright yellow flowers rise above the water, each with five fringed petals. That fringe is a particularly useful detail to photograph. Native yellow pond lilies have much larger leaves and rounded, cuplike flowers; white waterlilies have white blooms. A floating leaf alone is not enough to distinguish all these plants. Photograph an open flower and several attached leaves without pulling stems apart.
actions: Do not plant it in a water garden connected to natural water, and never empty unwanted pond plants into a ditch, lake or stream. Clean plant fragments from boats and equipment before moving between waters. Report a suspected new patch to the local aquatic-invasive-species program with photographs and its location. Avoid casual cutting or raking: fragments left behind can spread, and permitted removal requires careful collection and follow-up. Established populations need a site-specific plan that considers native plants, water movement and access. A single cleared surface does not establish that the rooted population is gone.

sources.label: UF IFAS Center for Aquatic and Invasive Plants: Nymphoides peltata
Wang et al. 2005: Clonal growth and sexual reproduction in Nymphoides peltata

identification: Broad, lance-shaped leaves alternate along upright leafy shoots, often forming a dense clump taller than a person. The cream to pale-yellow flowers emerge from a compact head of overlapping green bracts. Kahili ginger, Hedychium gardnerianum, can look similar before flowering but has a more open flower arrangement. Photograph the entire flower head and the leaves together, since a close-up of one pale flower can conceal useful distinctions. Avoid assuming that every ornamental ginger has the same seed or spread behavior.
actions: Keep rhizome pieces out of dumped garden waste, stream margins and fill soil. For a small confirmed escape, consult the local weed program about removing the whole rhizome system and disposing of it so fragments cannot regrow. Cutting stems alone leaves that system in place. Revisit treated ground and the edges of the clump for new shoots, particularly after soil movement or flooding. Large stands on wet slopes or beside streams need a coordinated plan that limits erosion. New Zealand accounts report no observed fruit there; that does not establish that the species is sterile everywhere.

sources.label: New Zealand Plant Conservation Network: Hedychium flavescens
Bishop Museum Plants of Hawaii: Hedychium flavescens
Hawaii DLNR Invasive Species Council: FY09 funded projects

identification: Look for a narrow terminal spike of yellow, two-lipped flowers above toothed, unstalked leaves. Glandular hairs give the stems and leaves a distinctly sticky appearance. The lower flower lip is longer and divided into lobes; the calyx remains around the developing capsule after the corolla falls. Other small yellow-flowered wetland plants can look similar from a distance. Photograph a flower from the side, the leaf attachment, and the hairy stem. Some regional floras use Bellardia viscosa for the same plant, so retain that alternative name when checking older records.
actions: Report a new patch in a sensitive wet meadow to the land manager and avoid walking through mature seed-bearing plants. Small confirmed populations can be removed before seed ripens when the ground can be worked without trampling surrounding wetland vegetation. Contain flowering and fruiting material and clean seeds and mud from footwear before leaving. Do not excavate neighboring native plants in an attempt to trace every parasitic connection. Return in the next growing season to check for seedlings, and base a larger control effort on the local habitat and conservation priorities.

sources.label: California Invasive Plant Council: Parentucellia viscosa assessment

identification: Typical canes are green with a contrasting yellow groove running along one side between the joints. The groove changes position with the branch-bearing side, and some lower cane sections bend into a conspicuous zigzag. Those bends are useful clues but are not present on every cane. Cultivars and other Phyllostachys can complicate color-based identification. Photograph several mature canes, the grooves, lower joints, and branch arrangement. Native American cane and clumping ornamental bamboos should not be assigned this species solely because they form a tall grassy stand.
actions: Avoid planting this species where it can run into natural areas or neighboring land. For an existing escape, map the outermost new shoots and coordinate with adjoining owners before beginning removal. Plan to address rhizomes and repeated regrowth, while checking for buried services before digging. Keep pieces of living rhizome out of shared soil and garden-waste piles. A barrier needs inspection and maintenance and should not be presented as a guarantee. Ask local extension for a management plan appropriate to the stand, access, and nearby plants, and monitor beyond the original planting.

sources.label: USDA Agriculture Handbook 114: Bamboos of the genus Phyllostachys

identification: Look for broad, toothed leaves, often with shallow lobes, and yellow flowers clustered among conspicuous pointed bracts. The current Florida key separates this species from M. urens partly by the mix of star-shaped and simple hairs beneath the leaves; urens has simple hairs there. Mature fruit segments also help: alceifolia has a smooth surface beneath their hairs. These are close-up characters, not a quick flower-color test. Photograph leaf undersides, bracts and ripe fruit together and have uncertain material checked before assigning an old local record.
actions: For a suspected Florida occurrence, ask a herbarium to review the specimen and any historical name before taking control action. In an introduced population elsewhere, record the habitat and whether plants are producing seedlings beyond a disturbed patch. Keep mature fruit and contaminated soil from being moved to clean sites, and obtain local guidance if removal is warranted. Protect native mallows growing nearby. Keep the original specimen name and the botanist's updated determination together. An old label can change how range and harm are interpreted, especially where a native relative is involved.

sources.label: World Flora Online hosting authored Malachra floras
Institute for Regional Conservation: Rare Plants of South Florida

identification: Look for leaves divided into narrow lobes, commonly with three main divisions, and elongated clusters of cream to yellowish flowers. The individual petals are irregularly cut rather than forming a neat four-petaled mustard cross. After flowering, oblong capsules remain along the stalk. Weld, Reseda luteola, generally has undivided narrow leaves, so the foliage is an important comparison point. Photograph a lower leaf, a stem leaf, an open flower, and mature capsules. Common names such as wild mignonette are shared and should not substitute for those details.
actions: Where confirmed plants are unwanted in a garden or crop margin, remove them before capsules release seed and take the crown rather than merely clipping the flower spike. Check the same ground for returning shoots or seedlings, and avoid distributing seed-bearing plants with soil or compost. In a natural area, first establish identity and local priority with a botanist or land manager. Do not apply the legal status or control history of R. luteola to this species. Record patch size and persistence so future management rests on observed behavior at the site.

identification: The upright stems are triangular in cross-section, with glossy, grasslike leaves and straw-colored to golden-brown flower clusters. Yellow nutsedge usually forms a single tuber at the end of a rhizome. Purple nutsedge has darker flowerheads and commonly produces tubers in chains; green kyllinga has a more compact flowerhead and lacks tubers. Examine the underground structures only where digging is appropriate and will not disturb a protected wetland. Neither a yellowish lawn blade nor the common name nutgrass is enough for a reliable identification.
actions: In a managed bed, remove young shoots repeatedly before they replenish the tuber supply, and recover tubers where practical. Correct leaking irrigation and excessive watering, while recognizing that established plants can survive ordinary or dry conditions. Check purchased soil and nursery pots before introducing them. Do not assume one pulling or mowing visit has eliminated the underground population. In natural wet ground, verify local native status before removal. Keep cultivated chufa decisions separate from weed management, and do not treat a wild sedge identification as a food-safety recommendation.

sources.label: CDFA: Cyperus esculentus pest rating proposal
Molecular survey of Cyperus esculentus origin: weed versus crop

identification: Look for a loose clump with narrow leaves, hairy lower leaf sheaths, and a branching flowerhead rather than a dense cylindrical spike. The spikelets contain several florets and shiny outer bracts of unequal size. A magnified floret shows a notched tip and a bent awn arising from the back of the lemma, the small bract around the flower. Related oatgrasses can look very similar when sterile. Photograph the whole clump, leaf junction, and mature spikelets, and use a regional grass key before assigning the species name.
actions: Eating this grass, including hay containing it, has caused harmful calcium deposits in livestock tissues. A documented sheep study found serious heart and vessel damage. Keep suspect forage out of feed pending advice from a veterinarian and forage specialist; do not assume drying makes it safe. Do not add an unidentified oatgrass to a pasture or restoration seed mix. Where a confirmed plant is unwanted in a maintained bed, prevent seed dispersal and remove the perennial crown with minimal disturbance. Inspect nearby ground for seedlings in later seasons and avoid transferring seed-bearing hay or soil. In natural areas, document abundance and surrounding vegetation before choosing an intervention.

sources.label: NEON portal: Northeastern North American flora treatment of Trisetum flavescens
Dirksen et al. 2003: Enzootic calcinosis in sheep after consumption of golden oat grass

identification: Stunting, yellowing, and wilting are warning signs rather than a diagnosis; nutrient problems and other root pests can look similar. Tiny females and cysts associated with roots change from pale to golden and eventually darker colors. Pale cyst nematode, Globodera pallida, is a close lookalike, and field color alone cannot securely separate important findings. A qualified laboratory must examine properly collected soil or root samples. Keep the host crop, field location, planting history, and exact laboratory name together in the record.
actions: Contact the responsible plant-health authority or extension diagnostic service before moving suspect soil, potatoes, or machinery off the field. Follow its sampling and cleaning instructions so wash water and soil do not create another contaminated site. Use certified planting stock from appropriately tested fields and keep potato grading or processing waste out of farmland. Resistant varieties and rotation belong within an official, locally applicable management plan. Check current movement restrictions rather than relying on an old map, and do not infer eradication from one healthy-looking crop or a season without visible symptoms.

sources.label: Canadian Food Inspection Agency: Potato cyst nematodes

identification: Lower leaves have a large rounded terminal lobe and smaller side lobes, with a smooth, shiny surface. Upper leaves become less divided and clasp the flowering stem. Flowers have four yellow petals, followed by slender pods. Wild mustard generally has a different leaf texture and form, while native American yellowrocket, Barbarea orthoceras, may require closer comparison of flowers, hairs, and fruit. Include the rosette and mature pods in photographs. A distant image of a yellow roadside strip loses most of the characters needed for a sound identification.
actions: In a garden or crop margin, remove confirmed unwanted rosettes or young flowering plants before pods mature, taking the crown rather than only the flower stalk. Contain mature seed-bearing material and revisit the disturbed ground for seedlings. Mowing after seed has developed can move the problem along the verge instead of resolving it. For a meadow or streamside patch, obtain a local identification before removing plants that may be native relatives. Keep a record of patch size and flowering stage so any management is timed to the actual population.

sources.label: Penn State Plant Science: Yellow rocket identification

identification: The long narrow leaves clasp the stem, and damaged tissue releases milky sap. A yellow flowerhead is surrounded by long green bracts that project beyond the yellow florets. The hollow stalk swells just below the head, which later becomes a large, loose seed sphere. Meadow salsify has shorter bracts relative to the flowerhead, and purple salsify differs in flower color. Examine the bracts and stalk as well as the leaves. Flowers often close by midday, so a morning photograph may reveal details missing later.
actions: Small unwanted plants are easier to pull or dig when soil is moist, before the seed globe is ready to disperse. Remove the crown and taproot as completely as practical without unnecessarily disturbing surrounding vegetation. Bag mature seedheads before carrying the plants across the site. In a pasture or restoration area, monitor whether scattered plants are becoming dense enough to interfere with desired cover. Montana research found mowing unreliable, so do not assume a single cut solves the problem. Seek local guidance for a larger infestation and check for new seedlings afterward.

identification: Small roundish covers on leaves or fruit are a useful starting point, but yellow and red scale are difficult to distinguish by appearance. Yellow scale is rarely found on mature wood, whereas red scale can occur there as well as on leaves and fruit. This difference in location is a clue, not a definitive test. Specialist identification uses microscopic adult-female structures. Photograph the infested plant part and the covers with a scale for size, and preserve a requested sample according to the diagnostic service's instructions.
actions: Before treating a tree, confirm which scale is present and whether the covers contain living insects. Ask a citrus advisor to assess infestation level, crawler activity, and existing natural enemies. Avoid moving suspect nursery trees or cuttings into another orchard while identification is pending. Keep management specific to the crop and local conditions rather than transferring severe red-scale damage claims or an old spray calendar to yellow scale. Check new stock and follow up after any recommended action; empty scale covers can persist and should not automatically be counted as continuing infestation.

sources.label: UC IPM: California red scale and yellow scale
EPPO PM 3/95: Inspection of citrus production sites

identification: The narrow leaves stand in whorls around the stem, commonly six to eight together and sometimes more. Their margins roll under, making them look even narrower, and their tips are pointed. Numerous small yellow flowers, each with four lobes, form a branching cluster at the top. The fruits are smooth and paired. Many native bedstraws have pale or white flowers, but flower color alone is not enough, especially where hybrids occur. Photograph a complete leaf whorl, the stem, flowers, and fruit rather than relying on a golden patch seen from a distance.
actions: In a garden, watch for shoots moving beyond the intended planting and avoid distributing divisions without checking local suitability. Where a confirmed patch is unwanted, remove the crown and connecting underground stems as thoroughly as practical, then revisit the edges for regrowth. Keep fruiting stems out of material destined for natural areas. For a conservation meadow, first confirm the species and assess its local abundance and effect on desired vegetation. Scattered introduced plants and a spreading dominant patch are different management situations, and the sources do not establish one nationwide level of harm.

sources.label: Native Plant Trust Go Botany: Galium verum

identification: Look for gray-green, slightly woolly foliage and stems edged with narrow wings formed by the leaf bases. Lower leaves are deeply lobed, while upper leaves are smaller and narrower. Yellow flowerheads sit above bracts tipped with long, stiff, spreading spines. Malta starthistle and other related species can resemble it, so photograph the bracts and spines from the side as well as the flower face. A young rosette without flowerheads is less distinctive. Wear suitable gloves when working around confirmed mature plants and avoid pushing through dense stands.
actions: Report a new patch to the county weed program, especially where early control is a priority. Remove small populations before seed develops, contain seed-bearing heads, and revisit the site repeatedly through the growing season. Maintain suitable competing vegetation rather than leaving a large bare patch. Mowing and grazing require careful timing and are not reliable substitutes for a complete plan. Keep horses away from infested pasture and suspect hay, and seek veterinary advice if exposure is suspected. Large infestations need locally coordinated management and follow-up to reduce the remaining seedbank.

sources.label: Washington Noxious Weed Control Board: Yellow starthistle

identification: These are small sap-feeding aphids, but body color and the fact that they occur on sugarcane are not enough for an exact identification. Published descriptions show considerable color variation and contrast between the short darker cornicles and the paler tail-like cauda. Separating M. sacchari from M. sorghi can require measurements of antennae and other structures, and some individuals remain ambiguous without genetic evidence. Photograph the colony, both leaf surfaces, and the host plant, then ask an entomologist how to preserve a sample for confirmation.
actions: In a crop, document which plants are affected, where colonies occur, and whether their numbers and associated damage are increasing. Contact the crop advisor before applying a threshold or treatment schedule from a sorghum outbreak report or a page about Sipha flava. Avoid moving infested planting material while identity is unresolved, and preserve beneficial insects wherever practical. Keep the original laboratory name and any identification method with the field record. Ask which current species name the adviser means and how it was identified before applying a recommendation from an older outbreak account.

sources.label: Nibouche et al. 2021: Melanaphis sacchari and sorghi distinction
UF/IFAS: Yellow sugarcane aphid, Sipha flava
Melanaphis sorghi clonal diversity in the United States and Brazil
North Carolina sorghum pest account: distinct aphid names
Uyi and colleagues (2025), Melanaphis sorghi field study

identification: Each leaf has three toothed leaflets, and the flowers are arranged along elongated stalks rather than packed into the rounded heads of familiar lawn clovers. The flowers have the small, uneven shape typical of the pea family. Yellow flowers separate it from white sweetclover once plants bloom, but leafy plants can be harder to distinguish. Small pods contain one or two seeds. Photograph the leaflets, flower cluster, and growth form together. Do not use a sweet smell or the word clover alone to identify a plant or judge forage quality.
actions: In a prairie or meadow restoration, check for first-year plants as well as conspicuous flowering stems. Remove small patches or cut confirmed plants at an appropriate stage before mature seed is produced, and revisit them for regrowth. Keep seed-bearing hay and roadside cuttings from being spread onto clean restoration ground. Coordinate larger treatments with the site manager so native flowering plants are protected and follow-up is planned. For an agricultural field, use a forage specialist's advice rather than applying a natural-area removal policy to a deliberately managed crop. Regional purpose and site condition determine the response.

identification: This is a relatively large goby for California estuaries, reaching about 30 centimeters. An especially useful comparison is the native longjaw mudsucker: the yellowfin goby's mouth does not extend behind the eye, while the adult mudsucker's large mouth reaches much farther back toward the gills. Other gobies still require a proper identification key. Photograph the whole side and a close view of the head if the fish is already being handled during authorized work. A yellow fin, a bait-shop name, or a distant underwater image is not enough.
actions: Do not release baitfish or transfer fish between waterways, even when they are sold under familiar names such as mudsucker or bullhead. Follow local fishing and bait rules, and ask the fisheries agency how to document a suspected new location. Keep the catch location and date with photographs, and avoid collecting extra fish solely for a casual identification where native species may be present. Drain retained water and clean equipment before moving elsewhere. Management belongs at the waterbody level, with verified identification and an understanding of the other species using the same habitat.

identification: The broad leaves may look heart-shaped or almost bat-shaped, with several strong veins and a long, darker tip. Young leaves can be smaller and more irregular, and leaf arrangement changes along the vine. Smooth twining stems may bear fleshy ear-like lobes at the joints, with bulbils in the leaf axils. Air potato and winged yam are important lookalikes. Photograph the leaf tip, stem, nodes, and bulbils together rather than relying on a single heart-shaped leaf. A yam name does not establish that a wild tuber is edible.
actions: Avoid planting this vine where it may escape, and do not share unidentified bulbils as an ornamental novelty. Keep fallen bulbils and discarded vine material contained and out of drainage routes. For an established escape, seek local invasive-plant advice before tackling the underground tuber or pulling a heavy vine from trees. Check repeatedly for new shoots and small plants beyond the original base. Do not taste the tubers or bulbils; the species is reported toxic on ingestion. Management should protect the supporting vegetation and address both the persistent underground plant and its scattered propagules.

identification: Typical shells are roughly D-shaped, with a relatively flat underside, and often carry dark and light stripes. Some individuals have little obvious striping, so pattern alone is unreliable. Quagga mussels are a close lookalike but usually have a rounder underside; difficult specimens may require expert examination. Attached clusters and their anchoring threads are useful clues. Photograph a shell from several angles with a size reference and record the surface where it was found. Do not pry uncertain mussels from a living native mussel merely to obtain a better picture.
actions: Before leaving a waterbody, inspect boats, trailers, anchors, and gear, remove attached plants and animals, and drain retained water. Use the locally required decontamination and drying procedure before entering another waterbody, including equipment that looks clean. Never transfer live mussels or untreated lake water to a pond or aquarium. Report a suspected new population to the state aquatic-invasive-species program and follow its sampling instructions. Large-scale chemical or mechanical control can harm other organisms and may require permits; household cleaning products should not be applied to a lake. Protect bare feet around shell-covered access points.

identification: The plant has compound leaves with several pairs of glossy leaflets and a terminal leaflet. Pink to pale-purple trumpet flowers have a paler throat marked with darker lines, followed where fruit develops by long narrow capsules containing winged seeds. It rambles over supports rather than attaching with tendrils. Related pink-flowered vines, including Pandorea and the other named Podranea, can be confused in cultivation. Photograph the whole leaf, flower throat, calyx, and any fruit, and keep the nursery label and its botanical name with the record.
actions: Before planting or sharing cuttings, check the current regional assessment and verify the scientific name. In Florida, choose an alternative where the high-risk recommendation applies. Watch existing plantings for growth beyond the maintained area and keep prunings and seed-bearing capsules out of natural vegetation and drainage routes. A large vine may need staged removal to avoid damaging its support or nearby trees. Seek a botanical determination for an apparent escape. Record the botanical treatment used, since some floras include P. brycei here while others distinguish it. A shared common name cannot resolve that difference.
